# Progress Policy Summary

This document is a short summary of Progress' key policies for the 2029 GE and all subsidiary elections prior. It is not a comprehensive policy index but rather collects our most critical priorities for the sake of making it easy to understand the party's identity and fundamental direction.

The summary is up to date as of January 2026. It remains nonetheless an evolving document, and presently incomplete.

Progress' policy can be broken down into three major testaments:

- The Big Four; the Magic Square of Progress; policy areas with the greatest significance to quality of life in Britain. Progress' Big Four are Real Wage Increases (the Economy), Crime & Justice, Nation Rebuilding (with primary focus on the NHS), and Migration.
- Beyond the Big Four, other areas of vital policy that are nonetheless less likely to shape electoral outcomes at scale

#### "The Big Four"

#### The Economy (E)

"Real Wages"

#### E1. The Cheapest Energy on Earth

Governing Principle

Energy is not a sector of the economy. Energy is the economy. Every product manufactured, every home heated, every business operated, every meal cooked, and every job created depends on the availability of affordable, reliable power. When energy is cheap, everything else becomes cheaper: goods cost less to produce, services cost less to deliver, wages stretch further, and businesses can afford to hire, invest, and grow. When energy is expensive, the opposite happens. Costs cascade through every supply chain, every household budget, and every investment decision. Britain’s energy costs are, by a considerable margin, the highest in the industrialised world. This is the single most important fact in British economic life, and the one that current policy is least willing to confront.

The scale of Britain’s energy cost disadvantage is staggering. UK industrial electricity prices reached 26.63 pence per kilowatt-hour in 2024, the highest in the International Energy Agency. This is 125% above the EU-14 median of 11.25p/kWh. French industrial users pay 12–14p/kWh. American manufacturers pay 6–7p/kWh. Canadian industry pays less still. Since 2016/17, British steel producers have paid an estimated £845 million more in electricity costs than their French competitors for equivalent output. Energy-intensive manufacturing output in Britain has fallen by one third since 2021. Factories that could operate profitably anywhere else in the developed world cannot operate profitably here. This is not because Britain lacks resources, engineering capability, or capital. It is because British energy policy has, for more than two decades, treated electricity bills as a vehicle for funding political objectives that have nothing to do with producing cheap power.

Household electricity prices tell the same story. At 30.45p/kWh, UK households pay the second highest electricity prices in the IEA, 45.8% above the median. The energy price cap stands at £1,755 per year for a typical household as of late 2025, some 44% higher than the winter of 2021/22 before the energy crisis. Roughly 9 million households in England, representing 36.3% of the total, spend more than 10% of their income on energy. Five million households spend more than 20%, placing them in deep fuel poverty. The aggregate fuel poverty gap, the amount by which fuel-poor households would need their bills reduced to escape fuel poverty, stands at £1.11 billion. These are not abstract statistics. They represent millions of families choosing between heating and eating, pensioners sitting in cold homes, and working households whose rising wages are consumed entirely by rising energy costs before they reach the supermarket or the petrol station.

The composition of British electricity generation has shifted dramatically in recent years, but the shift has not delivered cheaper power. Renewables now account for approximately 47% of generation, with wind at 30%, solar at 5%, and biomass at 12%. Gas provides 28%. Nuclear has fallen to 11%, its lowest share in half a century, generating just 36 terawatt-hours in 2025 compared with 40.6 TWh the previous year. Coal generation ended entirely in September 2024. Imports via interconnectors account for roughly 10%. The fundamental problem is that Britain has replaced firm, dispatchable baseload generation with intermittent sources that require expensive backup, grid reinforcement, and constraint payments, while simultaneously loading the cost of subsidy schemes, carbon pricing, and environmental levies onto electricity bills. The result is that wholesale electricity prices in Britain remain stubbornly high even when the wind is blowing and the sun is shining, because the system costs of managing intermittency are embedded in every unit of power.

Britain’s nuclear programme, which should be the backbone of a cheap energy strategy, is instead a case study in governance failure. Hinkley Point C, originally projected to cost £16 billion and generate power by 2025, is now estimated at £31–35 billion in 2015 prices, equivalent to approximately £43 billion in 2025 values, with first power not expected until 2029–2031. Its strike price of £92.50/MWh in 2012 prices has inflated to approximately £133/MWh in 2025, making it one of the most expensive sources of electricity ever contracted by a Western government. Sizewell C has reached Final Investment Decision with £14.2 billion in commitments, but construction is only beginning. The Rolls-Royce SMR programme selected Wylfa as its first site in November 2025, with £2.5 billion in government funding, but first power is not expected until the mid-2030s. Meanwhile, the existing Advanced Gas-cooled Reactor fleet is in terminal decline. Heysham 1 and Hartlepool have been extended to March 2028, Heysham 2 and Torness to March 2030. Only Sizewell B, with 1.2 GW of capacity, will remain after 2030 until new build arrives. British nuclear capacity is falling from 5.9 GW today to 1.2 GW by the end of the decade. This is an energy security catastrophe unfolding in plain sight.

The electricity grid is in a state of paralysis. The connection queue reached 739 GW before recent reforms, roughly four times the total capacity needed for the entire 2030 clean power target. Individual projects faced waiting times of up to 15 years for a grid connection. The National Energy System Operator’s reforms in April 2025 cleared the queue to 238 GW by removing more than 300 GW of speculative or non-ready projects, but the underlying problem remains: building transmission infrastructure in Britain takes a decade or more, not because the physical construction is difficult, but because the planning, consultation, and land acquisition process is designed to prevent things from being built. Battery storage was hit hardest by the queue clearance, with 153 GW of projects removed. The grid itself has become the binding constraint on every form of new generation, whether renewable or nuclear.

On top of all of this, British electricity bills carry a weight of environmental and social policy costs that no other major economy imposes at comparable scale. The Climate Change Levy, the Carbon Price Support, Contracts for Difference levy payments, the Renewables Obligation, and various social obligations add approximately £150–200 to every household bill and inflate industrial electricity prices by 20–30%. The Carbon Price Support alone adds approximately £18 per tonne of CO2 on top of the UK Emissions Trading Scheme price of roughly £53 per tonne, giving UK gas generators a total carbon cost of approximately £71 per tonne. This translates to roughly £26 per megawatt-hour added to every unit of gas-fired electricity. No EU member state imposes an equivalent unilateral surcharge. Standing charges add a further £200 or more annually to household bills regardless of consumption. Britain has built a system that punishes both producers and consumers of electricity, and then wonders why energy is expensive.

The binding constraint on British energy has never been physics, engineering, or capital. It has been governance. The sun shines. The wind blows. The nuclear fuel is available. The engineering is understood. The money exists. What has been missing, for decades, is a government willing to treat energy as the national security and economic emergency that it is, and to use the full powers of the state to build at the speed the crisis demands. Progress will be that government. Progress will use emergency planning powers for energy infrastructure. Progress will direct the nuclear regulator to operate on a wartime assessment timeline. Progress will exercise compulsory purchase for grid corridors. Progress will strip every penny of ideological levy from energy bills on day one. And Progress will not rest until Britain has the cheapest energy in the developed world, because cheap energy is not an aspiration. It is the foundation upon which every other economic ambition depends.

###### E1.1: The Nuclear Surge

The Problem

Britain once led the world in civil nuclear power. The Calder Hall reactor in Cumbria, opened in 1956, was the world’s first full-scale commercial nuclear power station. By the mid-1990s, Britain operated 14 nuclear power stations generating roughly a quarter of national electricity. That leadership has been squandered. Today, nuclear provides just 11% of British electricity, the lowest proportion in half a century. The existing fleet of Advanced Gas-cooled Reactors, unique to Britain and designed for a 25-year operating life, has been repeatedly extended but is now reaching the absolute limits of its graphite core integrity. Heysham 1 and Hartlepool will close by March 2028. Heysham 2 and Torness will follow by March 2030. After that, only Sizewell B, a single 1.2 GW pressurised water reactor commissioned in 1995, will remain operational. Britain’s nuclear generating capacity will collapse from 5.9 GW to 1.2 GW within four years. Nothing in the current pipeline will fill the gap in time.

The new build programme has been defined by delay, cost escalation, and institutional paralysis. Hinkley Point C was agreed in 2013 with a projected cost of £16 billion and a completion date of 2025. It is now estimated at £31–35 billion in 2015 prices, equivalent to £43 billion in 2025 values, with first power unlikely before 2029–2031. Its contracted strike price of £92.50/MWh in 2012 prices, inflating to approximately £133/MWh, will be paid by consumers for 35 years. Sizewell C, a replica design that should benefit from every lesson learned at Hinkley, has only just reached Final Investment Decision. The Rolls-Royce SMR programme, announced with significant public funding of £2.5 billion, has selected Wylfa as its first site but does not expect to generate power until the mid-2030s. The Generic Design Assessment by the Office for Nuclear Regulation typically takes four or more years. Planning inquiries add further years. The result is that Britain will not see significant new nuclear capacity for a decade under current timelines.

This is not an engineering failure. It is a governance failure. Serious nuclear nations build at dramatically different speeds. South Korea constructed four 1.4 GW APR-1400 reactors at Barakah in the UAE, delivering first power approximately eight years after first concrete, with subsequent units following at roughly twelve-month intervals. China routinely completes gigawatt-scale reactors in five to six years. France ordered 56 reactors between 1974 and 1985, building at a peak rate of roughly five per year, and transformed its electricity system from 8% nuclear to 75% nuclear in approximately fifteen years. The difference is not technology. The difference is political will, regulatory speed, and the willingness to treat nuclear construction as a national strategic priority rather than a procurement exercise to be managed by committee.

Progress will treat nuclear energy as Britain’s single most important infrastructure programme. The objective is not to add a few gigawatts at the margins. It is to build a fleet that delivers 24 GW of nuclear capacity, making Britain a nuclear-powered economy with baseload electricity costs that undercut every major competitor. This is the foundation upon which every other energy and industrial policy in this framework depends.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The National Energy Security Act will establish the legal framework for Britain’s nuclear surge. Its provisions will include:

- a) Designation of nuclear energy infrastructure as a matter of national security. All nuclear power station construction, including site preparation, grid connection, and associated transport infrastructure, will be classified as Nationally Significant Infrastructure and will proceed under emergency planning consent. Public inquiries will be replaced with a streamlined examination process with a statutory maximum duration of six months. No local authority will have the power to refuse or delay a nuclear project that has received ministerial designation.
- b) Direction to the Office for Nuclear Regulation to conduct an accelerated safety assessment of the Rolls-Royce SMR design, operating in parallel with site preparation and factory construction rather than sequentially. The ONR will be directed to adopt a process equivalent to the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission’s vendor design review, which operates on a 24-month timeline, supplemented by ongoing regulatory engagement during construction. The statutory basis for this direction will be established in the Act. Safety standards will not be reduced. Assessment timelines will be compressed by eliminating sequential gating and enabling concurrent workstreams.
- c) Establishment of a National Nuclear Delivery Authority with powers of compulsory purchase, deemed planning consent for designated nuclear sites, and authority to direct utility companies to provide grid connections within statutory timescales. The Authority will report directly to the Secretary of State for Energy and will operate outside normal departmental procurement rules. Its mandate will be modelled on the wartime powers exercised by the Ministry of Supply: build the fleet, build it fast, remove every obstacle that is not a genuine safety concern.
- d) Extension of the operating licences for all remaining AGR stations to at least March 2032, subject to ongoing safety assessment by the ONR. The Act will establish a presumption in favour of continued operation and will require the ONR to approve life extensions unless it can demonstrate a specific, evidenced, and imminent safety risk. The burden of proof will shift from the operator proving safety to the regulator proving danger. EDF Energy will receive direct financial support for the graphite core monitoring and maintenance programme necessary to sustain operations.
- e) Acceleration of Sizewell C construction to a war-footing timeline. The Act will designate Sizewell C as a national priority project, with construction mobilisation to commence within six months of Royal Assent. The project will target first power within six to seven years, benefiting from every design, supply chain, and construction lesson from Hinkley Point C. The government’s equity stake will be managed through the National Nuclear Delivery Authority with a mandate to maximise construction speed, not to optimise financial returns.

OPERATIONAL

First SMR within 48 months. The Rolls-Royce SMR factory build-out will be treated as a defence procurement priority, with contracts placed through the National Nuclear Delivery Authority rather than through conventional competitive tendering. Site preparation at Wylfa will commence within 90 days of Royal Assent, with civil works proceeding in parallel with the final stages of the regulatory assessment. The target is first power from the first SMR unit within 48 months of a Progress government taking office. This is aggressive but physically achievable: it removes four to six years of governance overhead without asking concrete to cure faster or steel to be fabricated more quickly.

Fleet production at six to nine-month intervals. Once the first SMR unit is generating, subsequent units will be produced on a factory line and deployed to pre-prepared sites at intervals of six to nine months. The target is a fleet of 10 SMR units, providing approximately 4.7 GW of capacity, within seven years of taking office. A fleet of 20 units, providing approximately 9.4 GW, within ten years. Sites will be identified and preparation commenced for all 20 locations within the first 12 months.

24 GW target by 2038. The combined nuclear fleet, comprising Sizewell B (1.2 GW), AGR extensions (approximately 3.5 GW through 2032), Hinkley Point C (3.2 GW), Sizewell C (3.2 GW), and the SMR fleet (9.4 GW by year 10, scaling to 14+ GW thereafter), will deliver a target of 24 GW of nuclear capacity by 2038. At that point, nuclear will provide the majority of British baseload electricity, and wholesale power costs will be structurally lower than any major European competitor.

International partnerships. The Secretary of State for Energy will immediately open negotiations with South Korea (KHNP), France (EDF), and the United States (NuScale, GE Hitachi) for additional reactor designs suitable for rapid deployment at sites beyond the initial Rolls-Royce SMR programme. Britain will not rely on a single reactor design or a single vendor. The objective is maximum speed and maximum capacity, using whatever proven technology can be deployed fastest.

###### E1.2: The Emergency Energy Dividend

The Problem

The nuclear surge described in E1.1 will take years to deliver its full effect on wholesale electricity prices. The first SMR will not generate power for 48 months. Sizewell C will take six to seven years. The full fleet will not be operational until the late 2030s. In the meantime, British households and businesses are paying the highest energy prices in the industrialised world today. A responsible energy strategy must deliver immediate, visible relief while the structural transformation is under construction. Progress will not ask British families to endure a single unnecessary day of inflated bills while the nuclear fleet is being built.

Britain possesses significant fossil fuel generation capacity that is currently underutilised because of a policy framework designed to make it uneconomic. The UK has approximately 30–35 GW of installed gas-fired capacity across its fleet of Combined Cycle Gas Turbine and Open Cycle Gas Turbine plants. Many of these stations are running well below their potential output because Britain’s unilateral Carbon Price Support adds approximately £18 per tonne of CO2 on top of the UK Emissions Trading Scheme price, giving UK gas generators a total carbon cost of approximately £71 per tonne, translating to roughly £26 per megawatt-hour added to every unit of gas-fired electricity. Several CCGT stations have been mothballed entirely, including stations with a combined capacity of approximately 1.5–2 GW that could return to service within months if the economic conditions changed.

The North Sea, meanwhile, still holds 2.9 billion barrels of oil equivalent in proven reserves, with a further 6.2 billion in contingent resources representing discovered but undeveloped petroleum. North Sea gas production has declined 75% from its 1999 peak but continues to meet roughly 40–45% of UK gas demand. The current government has stopped issuing new exploration licences and published a North Sea Future Plan that explicitly commits to no new exploration. At the same time, the Bowland Shale formation in Lancashire and Yorkshire contains significant potential shale gas resources, with initial British Geological Survey estimates suggesting resource volumes comparable to commercially exploited US formations, though with more complex geology. Only two wells were ever subjected to high-volume hydraulic fracturing in the UK, both halted after minor seismic events that exceeded Britain’s extraordinarily restrictive threshold of 0.5 on the Richter scale, a limit set ten thousand times lower than the threshold used safely in the United States.

These are not permanent energy solutions. The nuclear fleet is the permanent solution. But these are immediate energy solutions that can deliver visible price reductions within weeks, not years, while the permanent infrastructure is built. Progress will use every megawatt, every well, and every cubic foot of gas that Britain already possesses to drive down energy costs immediately. The stopgap is not the strategy. The strategy is nuclear dominance. But we will not waste a single day while we build it.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The National Energy Security Act will include emergency provisions for the immediate deployment of existing fossil fuel capacity:

- a) Abolition of the Carbon Price Support with immediate effect from the date of Royal Assent. The CPS is a unilateral UK surcharge on carbon emissions that no EU member state imposes. It adds approximately £18 per tonne on top of the UK ETS price, inflating gas generation costs by roughly £26 per megawatt-hour. Its abolition will reduce the short-run marginal cost of gas-fired electricity immediately, feeding through to wholesale prices within weeks. The estimated revenue impact is approximately £2 billion per year in foregone Treasury receipts, which will be more than offset by the economic stimulus of cheaper electricity across every sector of the economy.
- b) Resumption of North Sea oil and gas exploration licensing. The Act will reverse the current government’s ban on new exploration licences, direct the North Sea Transition Authority to issue licences for all commercially viable prospects within 12 months, and reform the fiscal regime to incentivise maximum extraction from existing and adjacent fields. Near-field tie-backs, connecting undeveloped discoveries to existing pipeline infrastructure, will be designated as priority developments with expedited regulatory approval, targeting additional gas volumes within 18 to 24 months.
- c) Lifting of the fracking moratorium in England. The Act will remove the presumption against issuing Hydraulic Fracturing Consents, raise the seismic threshold from the current 0.5 magnitude to 2.5 magnitude (still far below any level that causes structural damage, and consistent with thresholds used safely in comparable jurisdictions worldwide), and issue new Petroleum Exploration and Development Licences for the Bowland Shale and other prospective formations. Cuadrilla or successor operators will be permitted to resume operations at Preston New Road and other consented sites. Progress frames this as an exploration and insurance programme: we will find out what Britain has, and if it has it, we will use it. The moratorium was a failure of nerve. Progress will not fail.
- d) A statutory power for the Secretary of State to direct owners of mothballed or underutilised gas generation capacity to return to generating status within 90 days, supported by the removal of carbon pricing penalties that rendered their operation uneconomic. Any CCGT or OCGT station with viable physical infrastructure that is not generating due to market conditions rather than safety concerns will be subject to this direction. The estimated recoverable capacity from mothballed plants is 2–4 GW, sufficient to provide meaningful additional supply at peak demand.

OPERATIONAL

Day-one carbon price reduction. The Treasury will be directed to cease collection of the Carbon Price Support from the date of Royal Assent. HMRC guidance will be issued within 48 hours. Gas generators will see an immediate reduction in their carbon cost burden of approximately £18 per tonne, translating to lower wholesale bids within the first settlement period. The wholesale price effect will be visible to the market within days.

North Sea expedited development programme. The Secretary of State will issue a formal direction to the NSTA within 7 days of Royal Assent to begin processing all pending field development plans on an expedited basis, with a target of first approvals within 90 days. Near-field tie-back opportunities adjacent to existing production infrastructure will be prioritised, with a target of additional gas volumes reaching the national transmission system within 18–24 months. The fiscal regime for North Sea production will be reformed within the first Finance Act to ensure that the effective tax rate incentivises maximum extraction rather than accelerated decommissioning.

Shale gas exploration programme. Petroleum Exploration and Development Licences for prospective shale gas formations will be issued within six months of Royal Assent. The Oil and Gas Authority will be directed to engage with operators and publish an exploration roadmap, including drilling targets, environmental monitoring protocols, and community benefit frameworks. First exploratory drilling is targeted within 12 months. First commercial production, if viable, within three to five years. Progress will be transparent with the public: shale gas may or may not prove commercially extractable in British geological conditions, but we will not leave the question unanswered when the answer could be worth billions to the national economy.

Mothballed plant reactivation. Within 30 days of Royal Assent, the Department for Energy Security will compile a register of all mothballed and underutilised gas generation capacity. Operators will be given 60 days to submit reactivation plans. The Secretary of State will exercise the statutory direction power for any plant that fails to comply voluntarily. The target is a minimum of 2 GW of additional gas generation capacity returned to service within 90 days of Royal Assent.

###### E1.3: Grid Liberation

The Problem

The electricity grid has become the single greatest bottleneck in British energy. Every form of new generation, whether nuclear, wind, solar, or gas, depends on a grid connection. Without one, a power station is a stranded asset. The state of Britain’s grid connection system is, by any objective measure, a national disgrace. Before recent reforms, the grid connection queue reached 739 GW, roughly four times the total capacity needed for the entire 2030 clean power target. Individual projects faced waiting times of up to 15 years for a grid connection. The queue was dominated by speculative applications from developers who had secured a place in line with no intention or ability to build in the near term, blocking genuine projects behind them.

The National Energy System Operator’s reforms in April 2025 represented a belated attempt to address the crisis. The queue was cleared from 739 GW to a prioritised pipeline of 238 GW, with more than 300 GW of non-ready projects removed. The system was reformed from a first-come, first-served model to a “first ready, first needed, first connected” model. These reforms were necessary, but they do not solve the fundamental problem: the physical grid itself is inadequate, and building new transmission infrastructure in Britain takes a decade or more because of planning, consultation, and land acquisition barriers.

The construction of a high-voltage transmission line is, physically, a matter of months. The towers are manufactured, the cable is strung, the substations are built. The engineering is not novel. What takes years, and then more years, is the planning application, the environmental impact assessment, the public consultation, the potential judicial review, and the land acquisition process. Britain’s grid is not inadequate because the country lacks steel, cable, or electrical engineers. It is inadequate because the country lacks a government willing to build the infrastructure that the economy needs over the objections of those who would prefer it were built somewhere else, or not at all.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The National Energy Security Act will include the following grid reform provisions:

- a) Establishment of a National Grid Emergency Build Authority with compulsory purchase powers, deemed planning consent for designated transmission corridors, and authority to direct the construction of transmission infrastructure without further approval from any planning authority. The Authority will identify, designate, and build every transmission corridor necessary to connect the new nuclear fleet, onshore and offshore wind farms, and interconnectors to the national grid. Designated corridor routes will be published within six months of Royal Assent.
- b) A statutory maximum connection timeline of 12 months for all Nationally Significant Energy Infrastructure, including nuclear power stations, large-scale wind farms, and major grid reinforcement projects. A statutory maximum of 24 months for all other generation and storage projects. Any connection offer that exceeds these timescales will be automatically escalated to the National Grid Emergency Build Authority for direct delivery.
- c) Reform of the transmission charging regime to eliminate perverse incentives that penalise generation in locations where it is most needed. The current locational charging system, which imposes higher charges on generators in Scotland and northern England where wind resources are strongest, will be replaced with a uniform national transmission charge. The cost of grid reinforcement necessary to accommodate new generation will be socialised across all consumers as a system cost, not loaded onto the generator.
- d) A statutory obligation on the National Grid Electricity System Operator to publish, within 12 months of Royal Assent, a Strategic Grid Plan identifying every transmission upgrade, reinforcement, and new corridor required to accommodate 24 GW of nuclear capacity, the continued growth of offshore wind, and the electrification of heat and transport. The Plan will have statutory force and will constitute deemed planning consent for all identified infrastructure.

OPERATIONAL

£30 billion grid investment programme. The government will commit £30 billion in grid infrastructure investment over the parliament, funded through a combination of direct capital expenditure, regulated asset base models, and the savings delivered by cheaper wholesale electricity as the nuclear programme delivers. This is not a subsidy. It is an investment in the physical infrastructure without which no energy strategy, of any description, can succeed. Every pound spent on grid infrastructure returns multiples in reduced constraint costs, reduced curtailment, and reduced wholesale prices.

Emergency construction mobilisation. Within 60 days of Royal Assent, the National Grid Emergency Build Authority will publish a Priority Construction Schedule identifying the 20 most critical grid upgrades and reinforcements. Construction will commence on the first tranche within six months. The Authority will have the power to requisition land, override local objections, and award contracts on an emergency basis. The model is not peacetime procurement. It is wartime construction.

Connection queue clearance. The NESO will conduct a further review of the 238 GW prioritised pipeline within 90 days of Royal Assent, applying the statutory connection timelines established in the Act. Projects that are ready to connect will receive connection offers within 90 days. Projects that are not ready will be moved to a conditional queue and given 12 months to demonstrate readiness or lose their queue position permanently. The objective is that no viable energy project in Britain waits more than 24 months for a grid connection.

###### E1.4: End of the Green Levy Regime

The Problem

British electricity bills carry a weight of environmental and social policy costs that are unique in the industrialised world. These costs, accumulated over two decades of successive governments using energy bills as a convenient mechanism for funding policy objectives, include the Climate Change Levy, the Carbon Price Support (addressed separately in E1.2), the Contracts for Difference levy, the Renewables Obligation, the Warm Home Discount, the Energy Company Obligation, and various smaller charges. Together, they add approximately £150–200 to every household bill and inflate industrial electricity prices by 20–30%. Standing charges, the fixed daily cost that consumers pay regardless of how much electricity they use, add a further £200 or more per year.

The cumulative effect is that British consumers and businesses are paying a substantial hidden tax on every unit of electricity they consume. This hidden tax funds, among other things, the difference between the market price of electricity and the strike prices agreed under Contracts for Difference with renewable generators, the legacy costs of the Renewables Obligation, energy efficiency programmes delivered through supplier obligations, and social tariff schemes for vulnerable customers. Some of these objectives are legitimate. None of them should be funded through a regressive levy on electricity consumption that falls most heavily on the poorest households and the most energy-intensive businesses.

The principle that Progress will establish is simple: the cost of electricity should reflect the cost of generating and delivering electricity, and nothing else. Policy objectives that the government wishes to fund should be funded through general taxation, where the burden falls according to ability to pay, not through electricity bills, where the burden falls on every household and business regardless of income. A pensioner heating a poorly insulated home should not be subsidising the construction of an offshore wind farm through a hidden levy on every unit of power. A steel manufacturer competing against French and German rivals should not be carrying a 20–30% cost penalty because the British government has chosen to fund its climate policies through industrial electricity prices rather than through the Exchequer.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The National Energy Security Act will include the following provisions on energy levies:

- a) Removal of all environmental and social obligation costs from electricity and gas bills within 21 days of Royal Assent. The Climate Change Levy, the Renewables Obligation levy, the CfD levy, the Warm Home Discount, and the Energy Company Obligation cost recovery mechanism will all be removed from consumer bills. Where these programmes continue to operate, their costs will be met from general taxation through the Consolidated Fund. Where these programmes are no longer justified, they will be abolished.
- b) A cap on the total CfD levy that may be recovered from consumers in any single year. Existing CfD contracts will be honoured, but the annual cost to consumers will be capped at the level prevailing at the date of Royal Assent, with any excess costs absorbed by the Exchequer. Future CfD allocation rounds will be reformed to ensure that strike prices reflect genuine market conditions and that the subsidy cost to consumers is minimised. No new CfD contract will be awarded at a strike price above the projected wholesale price at the time of generation.
- c) Reform of standing charges. The current structure, which imposes a fixed daily charge of approximately 55–65 pence per day regardless of consumption, will be capped at a level that reflects only the genuine fixed costs of maintaining a grid connection. Policy costs, network reinforcement costs, and supplier obligation costs that have been loaded into standing charges will be removed. The target is a standing charge that reflects metering and connection maintenance costs only, reducing the fixed element of bills by £100–150 per year.
- d) Abolition of the Carbon Price Support, as detailed in E1.2. The UK’s unilateral carbon floor price surcharge, which adds approximately £18 per tonne above the ETS price, will be abolished with immediate effect. UK generators will pay the UK ETS price only, aligning their carbon costs with European competitors.

OPERATIONAL

Immediate bill impact. The combined effect of levy removal, standing charge reform, and CPS abolition will deliver an immediate reduction in household energy bills of approximately £300–450 per year. This will be visible in the first quarterly bill after Royal Assent. For a household currently paying £1,755 per year, bills will fall to approximately £1,300–1,400 within the first quarter. This is not a subsidy, a handout, or a temporary measure. It is the permanent removal of costs that should never have been loaded onto electricity bills in the first place.

Industrial electricity price reduction. For industrial consumers, the removal of the Climate Change Levy, CPS, and other policy costs will deliver an immediate price reduction of approximately 20–30%. UK industrial electricity prices will fall from 26–27p/kWh to approximately 18–20p/kWh within the first quarter. This alone will save energy-intensive industries hundreds of millions of pounds annually and begin to close the competitive gap with European and international rivals.

Transparent cost allocation. The Department for Energy Security will publish, within 60 days of Royal Assent, a full accounting of every policy cost previously recovered through electricity bills, the programme it funded, the annual cost, and whether the programme will continue to be funded from general taxation or will be abolished. The public will, for the first time, see exactly how much of their electricity bill was paying for electricity and how much was paying for government policy. Progress believes that transparency is the first step to accountability.

###### E1.5: Industrial Energy Guarantee

The Problem

Britain’s industrial electricity prices are the highest in the International Energy Agency at 26.63p/kWh, 125% above the EU-14 median of 11.25p/kWh. This is not a marginal disadvantage. It is a structural handicap that makes large swathes of British manufacturing unviable. Steel production, chemical processing, glass manufacturing, ceramics, paper production, and aluminium smelting are all energy-intensive activities where electricity cost represents a significant proportion of total production cost. When a British steel producer pays £845 million more in electricity costs than its French competitor over eight years, the consequence is not reduced profit margins. The consequence is closed factories, lost jobs, and the permanent destruction of industrial capacity that took generations to build.

Energy-intensive manufacturing output in Britain has fallen by one third since 2021. This decline is not cyclical. It is structural. Factories are not pausing production until prices fall. They are closing permanently and relocating to jurisdictions where energy is cheaper. The capacity, the skills, the supply chains, and the jobs go with them. Once lost, industrial capacity of this kind takes decades to rebuild, if it can be rebuilt at all. The communities that depended on these industries are left with nothing: no jobs, no tax base, no economic purpose, and no political party willing to tell them the truth about why it happened.

Progress will tell the truth. British industry is being destroyed by British energy policy. Not by Chinese competition, not by automation, not by declining demand, but by a deliberate policy choice to load the cost of climate objectives onto industrial electricity prices while every competitor nation funds equivalent programmes through general taxation or simply does not impose them. Progress will reverse this policy choice and establish, in statute, a guarantee that British industry will never again be priced out of existence by its own government.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The National Energy Security Act will establish:

- a) A Statutory Industrial Energy Price Guarantee. The Secretary of State will be required to set, annually, a maximum industrial electricity price for qualifying energy-intensive industries. The guarantee will be enforceable in law: if the market price of electricity exceeds the guaranteed price, the difference will be met by the Exchequer. Qualifying industries will be defined by energy intensity thresholds consistent with EU definitions, ensuring that the guarantee covers the sectors most at risk of relocation due to energy costs.
- b) A statutory target trajectory for industrial electricity prices. The Act will set binding price targets: the EU-14 median within one parliament, and below 10p/kWh within two parliaments. These targets will be treated as fiscal rules: any policy or regulatory change that would increase industrial electricity prices above the target trajectory will require an explicit impact assessment and parliamentary vote. The objective is to make it legally and politically difficult for any future government to reverse the commitment to competitive industrial energy.
- c) An Industrial Energy Competitiveness Review. The Act will require the Department for Energy Security to publish, annually, a comparative analysis of UK industrial electricity prices against the EU-14 median, US industrial rates, and other major manufacturing competitors. The Review will identify every component of the price differential and the policy changes required to eliminate it. The Secretary of State will be required to respond to the Review within 60 days with a plan to close any identified gap.

OPERATIONAL

Immediate price trajectory. The combined effect of levy removal (E1.4) and Carbon Price Support abolition (E1.2) will deliver Day 90 industrial electricity prices of approximately 18–20p/kWh. Grid efficiency improvements and wholesale price effects will reduce prices further to 15–17p/kWh by Year 2. First SMR power will begin to drive structural wholesale price reductions by Year 4–5, with industrial prices reaching 11–13p/kWh. By Year 7–8, with the SMR fleet generating at scale, prices will target 8–10p/kWh. The long-term objective, achievable within 10–15 years with a 24 GW nuclear fleet, is sub-8p/kWh industrial electricity, competitive with the Nordic countries and within striking distance of North American rates.

Industrial Energy Recovery Fund. A dedicated fund, capitalised at £500 million from general taxation in the first year, will provide bridging support to energy-intensive industries during the transition to structurally lower prices. The fund will offer direct grants to offset the difference between current UK industrial electricity prices and the EU-14 median, targeted at companies that commit to maintaining UK production capacity and employment. The fund is explicitly temporary: it exists to keep British industry alive long enough for the nuclear programme to deliver permanently cheaper power.

Reindustrialisation signal. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Secretary of State will write to the chief executive of every major energy-intensive manufacturer that has closed or relocated UK operations in the past decade, setting out the Industrial Energy Price Guarantee, the price trajectory, and an invitation to discuss the conditions under which they would consider returning production to Britain. Progress understands that industrial capacity, once lost, does not return on its own. It must be actively invited back with credible, legally binding commitments on the cost environment.

###### E1.6: Household Energy Security

The Problem

The energy price cap for a typical household in Britain stands at £1,755 per year as of late 2025, some 44% higher than the winter of 2021/22. For millions of households, particularly those on fixed or low incomes, this represents a crisis of affordability that has no precedent in modern British history. Approximately 9 million households in England, 36.3% of the total, spend more than 10% of their income on energy. Five million households spend more than 20%, meeting any reasonable definition of deep fuel poverty. The aggregate fuel poverty gap stands at £1.11 billion. These households are not making a lifestyle choice. They are being impoverished by the cost of a basic necessity over which they have no control and from which they cannot opt out.

The burden falls disproportionately on those least able to bear it. Pensioners on fixed incomes, families with young children, people with disabilities who need to maintain higher room temperatures or run medical equipment, and households in poorly insulated older housing stock all face energy costs that consume a grossly disproportionate share of their income. The withdrawal of the Winter Fuel Payment from 10 million pensioners in 2024, saving the Exchequer approximately £1.4 billion while energy bills remained at crisis levels, was a policy decision that captured in miniature everything that is wrong with Britain’s approach to energy: the government chose to save money by making the most vulnerable people colder.

Progress does not accept that expensive energy is inevitable. It is not. It is a policy choice, and Progress will make a different choice. The objective is not to manage fuel poverty through targeted subsidies and complex eligibility criteria. The objective is to make energy so cheap that fuel poverty ceases to exist as a meaningful category. When household bills are low enough that no family in Britain has to choose between heating and eating, the problem is solved at source. Every other approach is sticking plaster.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The National Energy Security Act will include:

- a) A statutory commitment that no household in Britain will pay more than a defined proportion of median household income on energy. The Secretary of State will be required to set this threshold annually and to take all necessary steps, including direct financial support where required, to ensure that no household exceeds it. This replaces the current fuel poverty definitions, which measure the problem without requiring the government to solve it, with a binding obligation to act.
- b) Reform of the energy price cap mechanism. The current cap, set quarterly by Ofgem, will be reformed to reflect the actual cost of generating and delivering electricity, net of all policy costs removed under E1.4. The cap methodology will be independently audited annually, and the Secretary of State will have the power to direct Ofgem to adjust the cap if it is found to include costs that do not relate to generation, transmission, or distribution.
- c) Restoration of the Winter Fuel Payment to all pensioners over state pension age, funded from general taxation. The means-testing introduced in 2024 will be reversed. Pensioners should not have to prove they are poor in order to receive help with a bill that their government has made artificially expensive. The permanent solution is cheaper energy for everyone. Until that solution is delivered, the Winter Fuel Payment is a bridge that Progress will restore on day one.

OPERATIONAL

Bill reduction trajectory. Within 21 days of Royal Assent, levy removal and CPS abolition will reduce average household energy bills from £1,755 to approximately £1,300, a saving of over £400 per year. Within 12 months, standing charge reform and efficiency measures will reduce bills further to approximately £1,200. Within 36 months, as grid reform delivers and new capacity approaches, wholesale price effects will reduce bills to approximately £1,000. Within five to seven years, as the nuclear fleet begins generating, bills will fall below £900. Within ten years, with 24 GW of nuclear capacity operational, the target is bills of £700–800 in real terms. The explicit commitment: a Progress government will halve household energy bills within one parliament.

Emergency Winter Support. In the first winter after taking office, before the full effects of levy removal and energy reform have worked through the system, the government will provide an emergency Winter Energy Payment of £300 to all households in receipt of Pension Credit, Universal Credit, or other qualifying benefits. This is a temporary measure that will become unnecessary as bills fall, but Progress will not allow vulnerable households to suffer through a single additional cold winter while the policy changes take effect.

Energy efficiency acceleration. The government will launch, within six months of Royal Assent, a National Home Energy Efficiency Programme targeting the 5 million households in deep fuel poverty. The programme will offer fully funded insulation, boiler upgrades, and draught-proofing to qualifying households, delivered through local authority partnerships with a target of 500,000 homes improved per year. This programme reduces demand, which reduces bills, which reduces the cost of the price guarantee. It is not charity. It is infrastructure investment in the efficiency of the national housing stock.

Summary of Legislative Requirements

The E1 framework is built on the National Energy Security Act, a single piece of primary legislation that establishes the legal basis for Britain’s energy transformation. No additional Acts are required. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, or departmental action.

National Energy Security Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: Designation of nuclear infrastructure as national security priority with emergency planning consent. Accelerated ONR assessment process for SMR designs. National Nuclear Delivery Authority with compulsory purchase and deemed consent powers. AGR life extensions to 2032 with reversed burden of proof. Sizewell C national priority designation. Abolition of the Carbon Price Support. Resumption of North Sea licensing. Lifting of the fracking moratorium with revised seismic threshold of 2.5. Ministerial direction power for mothballed generation. National Grid Emergency Build Authority with compulsory purchase powers. Statutory 12-month and 24-month grid connection maximums. Transmission charging reform. Strategic Grid Plan with deemed consent. Removal of all environmental and social levies from bills within 21 days. CfD levy cap. Standing charge reform. Statutory Industrial Energy Price Guarantee with binding trajectory. Annual competitiveness review. Household energy affordability threshold. Price cap reform. Winter Fuel Payment restoration.

Delivered operationally: First SMR within 48 months. Fleet production at 6–9 month intervals. 24 GW nuclear target by 2038. International reactor partnerships. Day-one CPS abolition. North Sea expedited development programme. Shale gas exploration programme. Mothballed plant reactivation within 90 days. £30 billion grid investment. Emergency construction mobilisation within 60 days. Connection queue clearance within 90 days. Immediate household bill reduction of £300–450. Industrial price reduction of 20–30%. Transparent cost allocation within 60 days. Industrial price trajectory from 18–20p to sub-8p/kWh. £500 million Industrial Energy Recovery Fund. Reindustrialisation outreach within 90 days. Household bill halved within one parliament. Emergency Winter Support. National Home Energy Efficiency Programme targeting 500,000 homes per year.

E1 is the foundation document of the Economic Policy Framework because energy is the foundation of the economy. Every policy that follows, from Prosperity Zones to the Unicorn Farm, from the Tax Reset to the Housing Reset, depends on the availability of cheap, reliable, abundant power. Without it, Britain is swimming against the tide. With it, everything else becomes possible.

Progress will build the nuclear fleet that makes Britain a permanently cheap energy economy. Progress will use every available resource, including existing gas capacity, North Sea production, and shale gas exploration, to deliver immediate relief while the fleet is under construction. Progress will strip every ideological levy from energy bills on day one. And Progress will establish, in statute, legally binding guarantees that British industry and British households will never again be priced out of prosperity by their own government’s energy policy.

This is not a vision document. It is an execution plan. The National Energy Security Act will be introduced within the first King’s Speech. The first bill reductions will be felt within 21 days of Royal Assent. The first SMR will generate power within 48 months. And within a decade, Britain will have the cheapest energy in the developed world. That is the commitment. Progress will deliver it.

#### E2. Prosperity Zones

Governing Principle

Britain is the most regionally unequal industrialised economy in the world. This is not a matter of opinion. It is the conclusion of the OECD, the IMF, Harvard’s Center for Business and Government, and the British government’s own data. In 2023, GDP per capita in London was £63,618. In the North East of England, it was £26,347. London’s GDP per capita stands 76% above the national average, a gap that has doubled since 1921, when it was 37% above. The productivity gap between London and the South East versus the rest of the United Kingdom is now wider than the gap between East and West Germany, wider than the gap between North and South Italy. GVA per worker outside London and the South East is just 71% of the London and South East figure, compared with 80% for East Germany relative to West, and 78% for Southern Italy relative to the North. Britain has achieved, through decades of policy neglect, a degree of internal economic divergence that exceeds the legacy of the Berlin Wall.

This divergence is not an accident of geography or an inevitable consequence of globalisation. It is the product of deliberate policy choices sustained over half a century. The deindustrialisation of the 1980s was faster and more complete in Britain than in any comparable European economy. The service sector growth that replaced manufacturing was overwhelmingly concentrated in London and the South East. Transport infrastructure investment has been systematically skewed towards the capital: per capita transport spending in London has been nearly twice that of other English regions over the past two decades. The UK spends 0.3% of GDP on road infrastructure, compared with 0.5% in Germany and the United States, and 0.65% in France, and the spending that does occur is disproportionately directed at the South East. Research and development expenditure follows the same pattern. Government R&D spending is concentrated in the Golden Triangle of London, Oxford, and Cambridge, while regions with the greatest productivity deficits receive the least. The result is a self-reinforcing cycle: talent and capital flow to where the infrastructure, research, and opportunity already exist, and everywhere else falls further behind.

Every government since the 1960s has claimed to care about this problem. None has solved it. The record of place-based economic policy in Britain is a monument to failure, rebranding, and wasted public money. Enterprise Zones in the 1980s. Enterprise Zones again in the 2010s. Freeports in 2021. Investment Zones in 2023. Industrial Strategy Zones in 2025. Each iteration underperforms against its own targets, gets rebranded by the next government, and is relaunched with fresh promises and the same structural deficiencies. The UK government estimated in 2022 that its freeport programme would create 214,000 jobs. By early 2024, freeports had created approximately 5,600 jobs, just 4% of the target. A House of Commons inquiry found that freeports had missed their job creation goals by 77–96%. The Teesside Freeport, described by the government as a flagship, consumed £560 million of public resources, twenty-two times its original allocation, and was the subject of a damning independent review that identified multiple failures of governance and value for money. The Institute for Fiscal Studies has consistently warned that zone-based policies suffer from two fatal flaws: deadweight, where the economic activity would have occurred anyway, and displacement, where businesses simply relocate from one part of the country to another, creating no net new activity. The Office for Budget Responsibility expects freeports to generate little additional activity, with most of it displaced from other areas.

Progress will not repeat this cycle. The Prosperity Zone programme described in this document is fundamentally different from every previous zone-based initiative in British history, and it is different in the ways that matter. First, the zones are anchored to specific industrial sectors where the UK possesses genuine existing competitive advantage, not generic tax breaks hoping to attract unspecified investment. Second, the zones are capitalised at a scale that makes transformation possible, not £160 million over ten years, which is a rounding error in industrial policy terms, but billions in direct infrastructure investment funded by institutional capital partnerships, land value capture, and the savings generated by radical reform across procurement, defence, welfare, and the civil service. Third, and critically, the zones are not industrial parks with tax incentives. They are new places: designed, built, and governed as self-contained urban environments with world-class housing, public space, and civic infrastructure. The historical model is not the Thatcherite enterprise zone. It is Haussmann’s Paris, Eixample Barcelona, Singapore’s Jurong Industrial Estate, or the garden cities of Letchworth and Welwyn, but reimagined for the twenty-first century with contemporary materials, environmental standards, and the accumulated wisdom of what makes dense human habitation not merely functional but civilised.

The philosophy behind Prosperity Zones is that industrial capability and quality of life are not competing objectives. They are the same objective. A zone that manufactures world-class semiconductors but houses its workers in identikit estates with no public realm, no beauty, and no civic life will not attract or retain the talent it needs. A zone designed as a monument to human capability, verdant, dense, architecturally ambitious, with housing that reflects the richest humanist traditions of European urbanism, will become a magnet for precisely the ambitious, skilled, and productive people upon whom its industrial mission depends. The Prosperity Zones will be hyper-dense wells of fertility, bustling with activity but built according to the most pronounced humanist principles, from which the productive and civic life of the nation will overflow. They will not merely produce goods and services. They will produce a new model for how Britain builds, lives, and works.

The ultimate objective, the measure against which every element of this programme will be judged, is the generation of high-paying jobs at scale in regions that have been starved of them for generations. Every zone designation, every financing mechanism, every planning decision, and every brick laid must serve this objective. If a Prosperity Zone does not produce more jobs, higher wages, and greater career mobility for the people of its region within five years of its establishment, it has failed, and Progress will say so. This is not levelling up. Levelling up was a slogan. This is reindustrialisation, and it will be delivered with the urgency, capital, and political will that the scale of Britain’s regional catastrophe demands. Ground will be broken on the first Prosperity Zone sites on the second day of a Progress government. Not the second month. Not the second year. The second day.

###### E2.1: The Zone Architecture

The Problem

Britain’s previous attempts at zone-based economic policy have failed for identifiable, structural reasons. Enterprise Zones offered generic tax breaks without sectoral focus, attracting warehouses and distribution centres rather than high-value manufacturing or research. Freeports added customs benefits of negligible value in a low-tariff economy; analysis by the UK Trade Policy Observatory found that only 1% of UK import value would benefit from tariff inversion. Investment Zones offered £160 million over ten years per zone, a sum too small to transform a local economy and too diffuse to concentrate the agglomeration effects that make clusters work. None of these programmes addressed the fundamental barriers to regional growth identified in the academic literature: inadequate transport infrastructure connecting cities and their hinterlands, insufficient R&D expenditure outside London, a shortage of STEM-qualified workers in lagging regions, and the absence of a credible, long-term commitment from central government that would justify the private investment decisions necessary to build genuine industrial clusters.

The Prosperity Zone architecture solves each of these failures. Zones are defined by industrial specialism, not geography alone, meaning that the tax, regulatory, and investment environment is tailored to the specific needs of the sectors being developed. Zones are governed by Sandpit Authorities with genuine autonomy to experiment with tax, labour, and regulatory policy within defined parameters, providing the flexibility to respond to local conditions without the paralysis of Whitehall micromanagement. Zones are capitalised at scale through mechanisms, described in E2.4, that mobilise institutional capital, pension fund investment, and land value capture alongside direct government investment funded by reform savings across the public sector. And zones are built, physically built, as complete urban environments with housing, civic infrastructure, and public realm of a quality that has not been attempted in Britain since the original garden city movement, as described in E2.3.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Prosperity Zones Act will be designated as emergency legislation and introduced within the first King’s Speech. Its provisions will include:

- a) A statutory definition of a Prosperity Zone as a designated area within the United Kingdom in which special provisions for planning, taxation, regulation, and governance apply for the purpose of establishing and sustaining a world-class industrial cluster in a defined sector or group of related sectors. The definition will distinguish Prosperity Zones from all previous zone designations and will establish that Prosperity Zone status can only be granted where a credible sectoral anchor exists and where the capital commitment is sufficient to achieve transformation within seven years.
- b) Establishment of Sandpit Authorities as the governing bodies of each Prosperity Zone. Each Sandpit Authority will be a statutory corporation with powers to set local business tax rates within a defined band, to disapply or modify specified regulations within its zone boundary subject to a statutory floor of employment rights and environmental protections, to acquire land by compulsory purchase for zone development, and to issue Prosperity Bonds (described in E2.4) backed by projected land value increases within the zone. Sandpit Authorities will be governed by boards comprising an appointed chair, elected local authority representatives, industry representatives nominated by anchor tenants, a trade union representative, and a representative of the relevant Miniversity. Interim chairs will be appointed from a pre-prepared list within 48 hours of taking office. Full boards will be constituted within 60 days.
- c) Special Planning Exemptions for all development within designated Prosperity Zone boundaries. Zone development will proceed under a Prosperity Zone Development Order, a form of Local Development Order with deemed planning consent for all uses consistent with the zone’s approved masterplan. The masterplan, prepared by the Sandpit Authority and approved by the Secretary of State, will specify land uses, density, building heights, infrastructure requirements, and design codes. Once approved, individual developments that conform to the masterplan will not require further planning permission. This eliminates the single greatest source of delay and cost in British development: the planning application process.
- d) A Tax Neutrality framework. Within Prosperity Zones, corporation tax for qualifying businesses will be set at 10% for the first ten years and 15% for years eleven to twenty, reverting to the prevailing national rate thereafter. Employer National Insurance contributions will be abolished for all zone-based employees earning up to £50,000 per year for the first seven years. Business rates will be replaced by a land value contribution assessed and retained by the Sandpit Authority. The revenue impact of these concessions will be offset by the land value capture mechanisms described in E2.4, which are designed to ensure that the economic gains generated by the zone flow to the public interest rather than being captured entirely by private landowners.
- e) Fast-Track Foreign Startup HQ Relocations. The Act will establish a Prosperity Zone Visa, a new immigration route enabling any company that commits to establishing its headquarters or a substantial operational presence within a designated Prosperity Zone to relocate key personnel to the UK within 30 days, with a simplified sponsorship process and a five-year pathway to settlement. This is designed to make Prosperity Zones globally competitive for the headquartering of high-growth technology and manufacturing companies.

OPERATIONAL

Day 2 ground-breaking. During the transition period between election and taking office, Progress will identify and prepare initial construction sites within each designated zone. On the second day of the government’s administration, the Prime Minister and relevant Cabinet ministers will break ground simultaneously at the first Prosperity Zone sites. This will not be symbolic. Site clearance, access road construction, and enabling works will commence on Day 2 under ministerial direction and emergency planning powers, using powers of prerogative to authorise immediate works in advance of Royal Assent. The Prosperity Zones Act will retrospectively authorise all works commenced in this period. The message is unambiguous: this government builds on day one, talks later.

Zone designation. All eight zones will be pre-designated in the Prosperity Zones Act itself, with geographic boundaries, sectoral focus, and initial governance arrangements specified on the face of the legislation. There will be no expressions of interest, no bidding process, no years of consultation. The zones have been chosen. The sites have been identified. The work begins immediately.

Global Market Bridges. The Department for Business and Trade will negotiate Prosperity Zone access clauses within existing and future bilateral trade agreements. These clauses will provide preferential market access for goods and services produced within designated Prosperity Zones to partner markets, creating a direct link between zone production and international demand. Priority markets will include the United States, ASEAN member states, the European Union, and Commonwealth trading partners. Each zone will have an embedded trade attaché responsible for connecting zone businesses with export opportunities.

Regulatory sandbox framework. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, each Sandpit Authority will publish a Regulatory Experimentation Plan setting out which national regulations it intends to modify or disapply within the zone boundary, the rationale for each modification, and the metrics by which the experiment will be evaluated. Successful regulatory innovations that demonstrably improve productivity or business formation without adverse effects on workers or the environment will be recommended for national adoption. This makes Prosperity Zones not merely beneficiaries of regulatory flexibility but laboratories for national regulatory reform.

###### E2.2: The Designated Zones

The Problem

The choice of which industries to anchor in which geographies is the most consequential decision in any zone-based industrial strategy. Previous programmes failed in part because they were geographically determined without regard to sectoral logic, or sectorally vague without regard to what could realistically be built in each location. Progress has applied two criteria to every designation: the capacity to achieve high output quickly, meaning the zone must build on existing industrial infrastructure, skills, and supply chains rather than starting from nothing, and the capacity to generate high-paying jobs at scale, meaning the zone must be centred on sectors where average salaries significantly exceed the national median and where the job volume is sufficient to transform a regional labour market, not merely add a thin layer of elite roles.

The following eight zones have been selected on this basis. Each is anchored to an existing industrial cluster or capability that gives it a realistic path to world-class output within three to five years. Each is centred on sectors where the average salary is at least 30% above the national median. And each is located in a region where the economic transformation is most urgently needed.

Zone 1: Life Sciences and Drug Development (Golden Triangle: Cambridge–Oxford–London). The UK life sciences sector is already worth £94 billion with over 6,000 companies and 280,000 employees. The Golden Triangle houses AstraZeneca, GSK, and the highest density of biotech startups in Europe. Average salaries in biopharma research and development run £45,000–£75,000, with senior and specialist roles well above £100,000. The Prosperity Zone designation will add to this existing strength a regime of radically accelerated drug approval timelines and clinical trial fast-tracking, modelled on the US FDA’s Breakthrough Therapy Designation and accelerated approval pathways. The Sandpit Authority will have the power to operate a parallel regulatory track for drugs developed and manufactured within the zone, reducing the time from Phase III trial completion to market authorisation to 12 months or less for qualifying therapies. The objective is to make the Golden Triangle the fastest place in the world to develop, approve, and manufacture a new drug.

Zone 2: Precision Manufacturing, Robotics, and Aerospace Components (Midlands: Birmingham–Derby–Coventry). The Midlands manufacturing corridor contains Rolls-Royce (aero-engines), JLR, thousands of precision engineering SMEs, and the densest concentration of advanced manufacturing skills in the UK. Average salaries in aerospace component manufacturing and industrial robotics run £45,000–£65,000, with design and systems engineering roles above £70,000. The zone will build on the Midlands’ genuine world-class capabilities in precision machining, aero-engine components, advanced composites, tooling, and the industrial robotics that will serve every other Prosperity Zone in the programme. The Sandpit Authority will operate an accelerated export certification regime enabling zone-manufactured components to receive dual UK-US and UK-EU type approval, eliminating the regulatory duplication that currently adds cost and delay to every British aerospace and automotive export.

Zone 3: Nuclear and Clean Energy Industrial (Teesside). The nuclear surge described in E1 will generate demand for thousands of pressure vessels, steam generators, turbines, instrumentation packages, control systems, and fuel fabrication assemblies. That supply chain must be domestic. Teesside has the heavy industry skills, the port infrastructure, the industrial land, and the workforce that built the chemical and steel industries of the twentieth century. Average salaries in nuclear supply chain manufacturing run £35,000–£55,000 for skilled trades and £50,000–£80,000 for engineering roles, with significant multiplier effects through the local economy. The zone will also encompass hydrogen production, carbon capture technology, and advanced chemical processing. The existing Teesside Freeport will be absorbed into the Prosperity Zone with enhanced governance and accountability. Demand for this zone’s output is guaranteed by the government’s own procurement through the National Nuclear Delivery Authority established in E1. This is the highest-confidence zone in the programme for speed to output because the customer is the state itself.

Zone 4: Compound Semiconductors and Advanced Electronics (South Wales: Newport–Cardiff). Newport is already the site of the UK’s leading compound semiconductor cluster, centred on IQE and the Compound Semiconductor Applications Catapult. Compound semiconductors (gallium nitride, silicon carbide) are used in defence systems, power electronics, RF communications, 5G and 6G infrastructure, and electric vehicle power management. Average salaries in semiconductor fabrication run £40,000–£60,000, with design engineering roles at £60,000–£100,000 or more. The zone will pursue dominance in the compound semiconductor market, where the UK has genuine existing capability and where demand is growing at 15–20% annually driven by defence, telecommunications, and clean energy applications. The Sandpit Authority will partner directly with TSMC, GlobalFoundries, and US investors to scale fabrication capacity, with the government providing anchor demand through defence procurement commitments.

Zone 5: Defence, Security, and Autonomous Systems (Cheltenham–Bristol–Bath corridor). This corridor already houses GCHQ, MoD Abbey Wood, BAE Systems, Rolls-Royce Defence, and the Bristol and Bath technology cluster. Average salaries in cyber security run £55,000–£85,000, with cleared defence roles significantly higher. The zone will combine cyber security, defence artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, electronic warfare, and space-based intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance into a single integrated cluster. The UK’s Five Eyes intelligence relationships, its existing signals intelligence capability, and its advanced defence research infrastructure through Dstl provide a foundation that no other European country can match. The Sandpit Authority will operate an accelerated security clearance process for zone-based employees and a streamlined export licensing regime for defence technology, addressing the two greatest bureaucratic barriers to scaling Britain’s defence technology sector.

Zone 6: Data, Genomics, and Financial Technology (Edinburgh–Glasgow). Edinburgh is the UK’s second financial centre and houses one of Europe’s strongest AI and data science clusters alongside Edinburgh Genomics and the legacy of the UK’s 100,000 Genomes Project. Glasgow adds the University of Strathclyde’s advanced manufacturing research and a growing technology sector. Average salaries in financial technology run £55,000–£85,000, genomics research £50,000–£80,000, and data science £50,000–£75,000. The zone combines three sectors in which Scotland already competes at or near the global frontier: genomics and precision medicine, financial technology and payments infrastructure, and artificial intelligence and data analytics. The Sandpit Authority will operate a regulatory sandbox for fintech products, enabling zone-based companies to test new financial products and services under real market conditions with streamlined FCA authorisation.

Zone 7: Maritime, Shipbuilding, and Marine Engineering (Clyde–Barrow–Humber). Britain is an island nation that has allowed its shipbuilding capacity to atrophy to a near-monopoly arrangement serving the Royal Navy. The current defence programme requires frigates, destroyers, nuclear submarines, offshore patrol vessels, and fleet replenishment ships over the next three decades. The global market for commercial vessels, offshore wind installation ships, and LNG carriers is booming. A single frigate programme sustains thousands of jobs for a decade. Average salaries in skilled shipbuilding trades run £35,000–£50,000, marine engineering £45,000–£75,000, and naval architecture and systems design above £70,000. The zone will operate across three yards connected by the common governance of a single Sandpit Authority and a shared workforce development programme. Defence demand is guaranteed by the MoD’s shipbuilding pipeline. Commercial demand will be stimulated by a requirement that all UK-flagged offshore wind installation vessels be constructed in British yards.

Zone 8: Space, Satellites, Critical Minerals, and Advanced Materials (Cornwall–Devon, with SaxaVord). This zone is distributed across two geographies with complementary strengths. Cornwall houses the Goonhilly Earth Station, significant lithium and rare earth deposits, and a growing space sector cluster. Devon has 100-year deposits of high-quality tin and copper proximate to existing mining sites. SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland provides satellite launch capability. The zone combines satellite manufacturing, launch operations, and advanced communications with critical mineral extraction and advanced materials research. Average salaries in the space sector run £45,000–£70,000, mining engineering £40,000–£60,000, and materials science research £50,000–£75,000. Britain possesses virtually untapped seams of mineable common and rare earth metals distributed across its islands. These reserves constitute virtually free billion-pound notes lying around in the street. China controls 60% of global rare earth mining and 90% of processing. The Sandpit Authority will have power to grant mining licences and environmental permits within the zone on an expedited basis, with a statutory requirement that all extracted minerals be offered to UK manufacturers before export.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The zone designations described above will be scheduled in the Prosperity Zones Act and will take effect on the date of Royal Assent. The Act will:

- a) Designate the eight zones described above, specifying the geographic boundaries, the sectoral focus, and the initial governance arrangements for each. All designations will be on the face of the Act, not subject to subsequent secondary legislation or consultation.
- b) Require Sandpit Authority interim chairs, appointed within 48 hours, to submit Zone Masterplans for Secretarial approval within six months. Masterplan design commissions will be issued during the transition period so that work is substantially underway before Royal Assent.
- c) Grant each Sandpit Authority the power to exercise compulsory purchase from the date of designation, with land acquisition valuations based on existing use value, not hope value, to prevent speculative inflation of land prices in anticipation of zone development.

OPERATIONAL

Anchor tenant engagement. Within 48 hours of taking office, the Secretary of State will write to every company identified as a potential anchor tenant for each zone, setting out the tax, regulatory, and infrastructure commitments and inviting them to participate in the zone development process. For Zone 3 (Nuclear and Clean Energy), this engagement will be conducted through the National Nuclear Delivery Authority. For Zone 7 (Maritime), through MoD Defence Equipment and Support. The objective is signed anchor tenant commitments for every zone within 90 days.

International recruitment campaign. The Department for Business and Trade will launch a global investment promotion campaign within 30 days of taking office, targeting institutional investors, venture capital firms, and multinational corporations in the sectors relevant to each zone. The campaign will be conducted through British embassies and trade offices in the United States, Norway, Singapore, South Korea, Japan, Taiwan, Canada, and Australia, with dedicated zone prospectuses and investment facilitation services.
