###### E2.3: The New Urbanism

The Problem

Every previous zone-based economic intervention in Britain has produced the same built environment: low-rise sheds on a business park, surrounded by car parks, connected to a dual carriageway, adjacent to an identikit housing estate built to the minimum standards that the developer could negotiate through the planning system. This is not an accident. It is the direct result of a system that separates land use into mutually exclusive categories (residential here, commercial there, industrial over there), that incentivises volume housebuilders to minimise cost per unit rather than maximise quality of place, and that has no mechanism for creating the kind of integrated, dense, beautiful, and productive urban environments that characterise the world’s most successful industrial cities.

The greatest industrial cities in history were also the greatest cities, period. Haussmann’s Paris was built to serve an industrial and commercial empire, but it was also built to be beautiful, with its wide boulevards, uniform cornice lines, verdant squares, and the integration of civic, commercial, and residential uses within the same blocks. Eixample Barcelona achieved extraordinary density while creating a city of light, air, and public space through its chamfered block corners and interior courtyards. The Dutch tradition of urbanism, from the canal houses of Amsterdam to the post-war reconstruction of Rotterdam, has consistently demonstrated that density, beauty, and livability are not in tension. Singapore’s Jurong Industrial Estate proved that heavy industry and high-quality housing could coexist in the same geography when the design intent was present from the outset. The Italian piazza tradition, the Viennese Gemeindebau, the garden cities of Letchworth and Welwyn: all understood that the built environment is not a container for economic activity but a participant in it, and that human beings produce their best work in places that honour their humanity.

Progress rejects the premise that industrial zones must be ugly, that housing must be cheap, and that beauty is a luxury that belongs only to historic city centres and wealthy suburbs. The Prosperity Zones will be the most ambitious new urban development in Britain since the original garden cities. They will give every impression, productively and symbolically, of being hyper-dense wells of fertility, bustling with activity but built according to the most pronounced humanist principles, from which the life of the nation itself will overflow. Profound, green machines for living in, monuments to human agency and opportunity.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Prosperity Zones Act will include:

- a) A statutory design quality requirement for all development within Prosperity Zone boundaries. Every Zone Masterplan must comply with a National Prosperity Zone Design Code, prepared by a newly established Chief Design Officer for Prosperity Zones and approved by the Secretary of State. The Code will specify minimum standards for street widths, building heights, facade materials, green coverage ratios, public realm provision, and the integration of residential and commercial uses. The Code will draw on the European humanist tradition of urban design, the principles of the original garden city movement, and contemporary best practice from cities including Copenhagen, Vienna, Barcelona, and Singapore. It will explicitly prohibit the low-density, single-use, car-dependent development patterns that characterise existing British zone programmes.
- b) A minimum residential density of 100 dwellings per hectare within the core areas of each Prosperity Zone, rising to 200 or more in designated high-density quarters. By comparison, the average density of new-build housing in England is approximately 32 dwellings per hectare, and the densest London boroughs achieve 130–170. The Prosperity Zones will be built to European city-centre densities because the evidence is unambiguous that density, when accompanied by good design, produces more walkable, more sociable, more economically productive, and more environmentally sustainable places than sprawl.
- c) A minimum green coverage ratio of 30% of total zone area, comprising street trees on every residential and commercial street, public parks within 400 metres of every dwelling, green roofs on all buildings above four storeys, and continuous green corridors connecting residential areas to workplaces and civic amenities. The Prosperity Zones will be the greenest new urban developments in British history, not because green infrastructure is decorative but because it is essential to the livability, mental health outcomes, and environmental performance of dense urban environments.
- d) A requirement that all zone housing be designed to Lifetime Homes standards, with a minimum of 20% of dwellings designated as zone-affordable housing. Zone-affordable housing is defined as housing available at rents or purchase prices calibrated so that no zone worker earning the median zone salary or below spends more than 25% of gross income on housing costs. This is not ‘affordable’ in the discredited sense used by the current planning system, where 80% of an unaffordable market rent is called affordable. It is housing that is genuinely affordable relative to the wages earned in the zone, made possible because the Sandpit Authority acquires land at pre-designation existing-use value, builds at cost on its own land, and lets at cost-recovery rents. The model is the Viennese Gemeindebau system, in which the municipality builds, owns, and manages high-quality housing at rents that reflect construction cost rather than speculative land value. Market-rate and zone-affordable units will be integrated within the same buildings and streets. No Prosperity Zone resident should be able to tell, from the quality of their home or the design of their street, whether they are in a market-rate or zone-affordable unit.

OPERATIONAL

Chief Design Officer appointment. Within 48 hours of taking office, the Secretary of State will appoint a Chief Design Officer for Prosperity Zones from a pre-prepared shortlist. The Chief Design Officer will be a practising architect or urban designer of international standing. Their mandate will be to prepare the National Prosperity Zone Design Code within six months and to review and approve every Zone Masterplan for compliance with the Code. The role is modelled on Barcelona’s Chief Architect, who oversees all public realm and building design in the city, ensuring coherence and quality across decades of development.

International design competition. For each zone, the Sandpit Authority will conduct an international design competition for the Zone Masterplan, launched within 30 days of Royal Assent with submissions due within four months. The competition brief will specify the industrial programme, the density and green coverage requirements, the integration of uses, and the aspiration to create a built environment of lasting distinction. This accelerated timeline is achievable because the brief will be prepared during the transition period.

Monumental civic infrastructure. Each Prosperity Zone will include at least one piece of monumental civic architecture: a public building, library, market hall, or civic centre designed to be the symbolic heart of the zone and to demonstrate, in built form, the ambition and seriousness of the enterprise. These buildings will be commissioned through invited design competitions from architects of international reputation. They are not vanity projects. They are the physical expression of the proposition that these are not business parks but new cities, built to endure and to inspire. The Italian tradition of the palazzo pubblico, the Dutch tradition of the stadhuis, and the British tradition of the civic hall all understood that public buildings of quality and permanence are essential to the identity and cohesion of a community. The Prosperity Zones will build in that tradition.

###### E2.4: Financing and Capital Structure

The Problem

The fundamental financing problem with every previous zone programme in Britain is that the capital committed was too small to achieve transformation and too dependent on Treasury allocations that could be cut in any spending review. Investment Zones received £160 million each over ten years. Freeport seed funding was £1 billion nationally. These sums are insufficient to build the transport infrastructure, industrial facilities, housing, and civic amenities necessary to create a genuine agglomeration effect. Shenzhen succeeded not because of its special economic zone designation but because China invested hundreds of billions in infrastructure over decades. Singapore’s Jurong succeeded because the government treated it as a multi-generational national project with funding to match. British zone programmes have expected transformation on a budget that would not build a medium-sized hospital.

Progress will finance the Prosperity Zones through a combination of mechanisms that together provide capital at the scale necessary for transformation, reduce dependence on annual Treasury allocations, and ensure that the economic gains generated by the zones flow to the public interest. Critically, Progress will not seek investment from sovereign wealth funds belonging to regimes whose values and governance standards are incompatible with British democratic principles. The capital pool available from democratic, rule-of-law jurisdictions is more than sufficient.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Prosperity Zones Act will establish:

- a) Institutional co-investment partnerships. The Secretary of State will be empowered to negotiate co-investment agreements with sovereign wealth funds and pension funds from democratic, rule-of-law jurisdictions: Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global ($1.7 trillion), Singapore’s GIC and Temasek ($1.2 trillion combined), Canada’s major pension funds including CPPIB, CDPQ, and OTPP (collectively managing over $1.3 trillion), Australia’s major superannuation funds, and Japan’s Government Pension Investment Fund ($1.6 trillion). These institutions collectively manage over $6 trillion in assets and are actively seeking long-term infrastructure investments in stable jurisdictions. Co-investment agreements will be structured to require technology transfer, local employment commitments, and long-term capital lock-in periods of at least 15 years. Progress will not accept investment from sovereign wealth funds belonging to regimes with which Britain has ethical cross-purposes. Democratic capital for democratic development.
- b) Prosperity Bonds. Each Sandpit Authority will be empowered to issue Prosperity Bonds: long-term (15–30 year) debt instruments backed by projected land value increases within the zone boundary. The mechanism is straightforward: government investment in infrastructure and industrial facilities increases the value of land within and around the zone. The Sandpit Authority captures a portion of that increase through the land value contribution (replacing business rates) and uses the projected future revenue stream to back bond issuance. These bonds will be offered to UK pension funds, insurance companies, and institutional investors seeking long-duration, inflation-linked assets. The estimated issuance capacity across all eight zones, based on conservative land value projections, is £15–25 billion over the first decade.
- c) Reform dividend capitalisation. A defined proportion of the savings generated by Progress’ reform programme across government, including procurement reform (the UK spends £300 billion annually on public procurement, where even marginal efficiency gains yield billions), defence procurement reform (where major programmes have historically overrun by 40–50% in cost), welfare reform (where every person moved from benefits into zone employment reduces the welfare bill directly), and civil service reform (where headcount reduction and operational efficiency release resources for productive investment), will be hypothecated to a Prosperity Zone Capital Fund. The Fund will provide the direct government equity that seeds each zone and leverages the institutional co-investment and bond issuance described above. The principle is that the savings from making government efficient fund the investment in making the economy productive. This is not additional public borrowing. It is the redeployment of money that the state is currently wasting.
- d) Pairing of industrial infrastructure with civil engineering development. Every zone infrastructure contract will be structured as a combined contract requiring the simultaneous delivery of industrial facilities, transport infrastructure, housing, and public realm. This reduces cost through economies of scale and programme management efficiency, and ensures that housing and civic infrastructure is delivered in parallel with the industrial programme rather than as an afterthought.
- e) A land value capture framework. All land within a designated Prosperity Zone boundary will be subject to a Prosperity Zone Land Charge, assessed annually on the unimproved value of the land. The charge will be set by the Sandpit Authority at a rate sufficient to fund the zone’s zone-affordable housing programme, public realm maintenance, and bond debt service. Critically, compulsory purchase within the zone boundary will be at existing-use value, not hope value. This prevents speculative land banking and ensures that the uplift in land value created by public investment is captured for public benefit rather than accruing to private landowners who contributed nothing to the zone’s success.

OPERATIONAL

Investment roadshow. Within 30 days of taking office, the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Secretary of State for Business and Trade will conduct a joint roadshow to Oslo, Singapore, Toronto, Sydney, and Tokyo, presenting the Prosperity Zone investment prospectus to sovereign wealth fund and pension fund principals. The prospectus will include detailed financial models for each zone, projected returns, governance arrangements, and the legal protections provided by the Prosperity Zones Act. The target is signed heads of terms for co-investment in at least four zones within 90 days.

Pension fund engagement. The Prosperity Zone programme board will establish a Pension Fund Advisory Council within 30 days, bringing together the UK’s largest defined benefit pension funds to design Prosperity Bond structures that meet their duration, inflation-linkage, and risk-return requirements. The target is first Prosperity Bond issuance within 12 months of Royal Assent and £5 billion in total issuance within 24 months.

International VC capital mobilisation. Each zone’s Sandpit Authority will establish a Zone Venture Fund, co-invested by government and international venture capital firms, to provide seed and growth capital to startups establishing within the zone. The Prosperity Zone Visa and the tax incentives described in E2.1 will be marketed directly to the global VC community through partnerships with leading firms in Silicon Valley, Tel Aviv, Singapore, and London.

###### E2.5: Miniversities and the Skill Pipeline

The Problem

No industrial cluster can succeed without a workforce that possesses the skills it demands. Britain’s existing skills infrastructure is not designed to serve the Prosperity Zone programme. Universities produce graduates three years after enrolment, with curricula that are often misaligned with employer needs. Further education colleges have been chronically underfunded and carry a stigma that deters able students from vocational pathways. Apprenticeship programmes, while improved in recent years, remain insufficient in scale and too slow to respond to the specific, rapidly evolving skill requirements of cutting-edge industrial sectors. The STEM skills shortage outside London and the South East is identified in the academic literature as one of the binding constraints on regional economic growth.

The Prosperity Zone programme requires a new kind of educational institution: embedded within the zone, designed in partnership with zone employers, delivering training at the speed and specificity that modern industry requires, and carrying none of the institutional baggage of either the traditional university or the traditional further education college. Progress calls these institutions Miniversities. Miniversities are the zone-specific, accelerated application of the national skill capital development principles set out in E5: Skill Capital and Training. Where E5 establishes the national framework for transforming Britain’s approach to skills, vocational training, and career development, the Miniversity programme applies those principles at maximum intensity within the concentrated industrial environment of a Prosperity Zone. They are the tip of the spear.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Prosperity Zones Act will establish:

- a) A statutory requirement for each Prosperity Zone to establish a Miniversity within 12 months of designation. Each Miniversity will be a new educational institution, established as a statutory body governed jointly by the Sandpit Authority and the zone’s anchor employers. Miniversities will offer accelerated technical training programmes of 6–18 months (not three-year degrees), embedded apprenticeships with guaranteed employment outcomes, AI-adaptive learning platforms tailored to individual learner needs, and continuous professional development programmes for existing workers upskilling into zone-relevant roles. These programmes will operate under the same accelerated skill capital development framework established in E5, applied at the compressed timescales and sector-specific intensity that the zone programme demands.
- b) Employer training tax credits. Companies within Prosperity Zones will receive a tax credit proportionate to the number of domestic employees they train to a recognised qualification and retain in permanent employment for at least two years. The credit will be set at £5,000 per qualifying employee for Level 3–4 qualifications and £10,000 for Level 5 and above. This directly incentivises employers to invest in the skills of the zone workforce rather than relying on imported talent, while ensuring that the training leads to genuine, lasting employment rather than churn.
- c) Cross-recognition of Miniversity qualifications. Qualifications awarded by Prosperity Zone Miniversities will be automatically recognised for the purposes of professional registration, further study, and employment throughout the United Kingdom. The quality assurance framework will be designed by the Office for Students in partnership with the relevant industry bodies, ensuring that Miniversity qualifications carry the same weight as equivalent university qualifications while being delivered in a fraction of the time.

OPERATIONAL

Curriculum co-design. Within 30 days of each zone’s designation, the interim Sandpit Authority will convene a Curriculum Design Board comprising anchor tenant employers, the Miniversity principal designate, and representatives of the relevant professional bodies. The Board will specify the skill requirements of the zone’s industrial programme, translate them into modular qualification frameworks aligned with the national skill capital architecture established in E5, and publish a Zone Skills Prospectus within 90 days.

Work-study integration. Every Miniversity programme will include a minimum of 50% workplace-based learning, conducted on-site within zone employers. Students will be paid a training wage during their workplace placements, funded through the employer training tax credit. The model is the German dual education system, adapted for the specific sectoral needs of each Prosperity Zone, delivered at accelerated pace, and embedded within the physical environment of the zone rather than in a campus separated from the world of work.

Career pipeline from school. The Department for Education will designate schools within a 30-mile radius of each Prosperity Zone as Zone Feeder Schools, entitled to additional funding for STEM teaching, zone-specific career guidance, and annual immersion days within the zone itself. The objective is that every young person growing up near a Prosperity Zone understands, from the age of 14, the career opportunities the zone offers and the educational pathway to access them. This is how Singapore, South Korea, and Germany build the skill capital that drives their industrial competitiveness: not by hoping that the right people will appear but by systematically developing them from school age onwards.

###### E2.6: Economic Hybridism and Strategic Trade Protection

The Problem

The reindustrialisation described in this document is not a trivial undertaking. Building world-class industrial clusters takes years. Developing the workforce to staff them takes years. Reaching the production volumes and quality standards necessary to compete on global markets takes years. During this transition, the industries and workers that Progress is seeking to develop will be vulnerable to competition from established producers in countries where labour is cheaper, subsidies are more generous, or the industrial base has been developing for decades without interruption. Free trade, as a general principle, is the most powerful engine of prosperity ever discovered. But free trade applied without qualification to an economy in the process of rebuilding its industrial base is a prescription for the destruction of the very industries being built, before they have the chance to reach competitive scale.

Progress therefore proposes a period of economic hybridism: a commitment to free trade as the long-term organising principle of the British economy, undergirded by a policy of temporary, targeted, and transparently declining trade protection during the transition period. This is not protectionism in the pejorative sense. Protectionism, as a general principle, increases prices, kills innovation, and makes economies inefficient by design. However, cleverly deployed, its bulk can be used to shield the British workforce from excessive turbulence during the transition into its new form. The critical safeguard is that the protection is temporary, declining, and transparent. Every tariff has a published expiry date. Every tariff declines automatically every year. No tariff can be renewed or extended. The public, the trading partners, and the protected industries themselves know from the outset that the protection will end, creating urgency for improvement rather than complacency.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Prosperity Zones Act will include:

- a) Learning tariffs. The Act will establish the power to impose temporary tariffs on imports in sectors directly corresponding to Prosperity Zone industrial programmes, where the Secretary of State is satisfied that the domestic industry is in a developmental phase and that the tariff is necessary to allow it to reach competitive scale. Learning tariffs will be set at a maximum of 20% ad valorem, will decline automatically by a minimum of 3 percentage points per year, and will expire entirely after a maximum of seven years. No tariff may be renewed or extended. The automatic decline creates urgency for domestic producers to improve efficiency, quality, and cost-competitiveness, while the absolute expiry prevents the tariff from becoming a permanent subsidy to inefficiency. This mechanism is modelled on the infant industry protections used successfully by South Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore during their industrialisation phases, all of which combined temporary protection with aggressive investment in capability and an unwavering commitment to eventual full market competition.
- b) Strategic procurement preferences. The Act will require that all government procurement in sectors relevant to Prosperity Zone industrial programmes give preference to domestic suppliers, including smaller operators, where the domestic product meets specified quality and delivery standards and is priced within 15% of the lowest compliant international bid. Procurement contracts will incorporate requirements for training programmes and, where reasonable, technology transfer. The 15% price tolerance will decline by 2 percentage points per year, reaching zero after seven years, at which point all procurement will be conducted on a fully open and competitive basis.
- c) Reciprocal market openings. The Act will empower the Secretary of State to negotiate bilateral agreements with trading partners that phase in UK access to partner markets in tandem with the development of domestic capabilities, creating incentives for continued investment in skills and technology rather than permanent dependence on protection. As learning tariffs decline, partner market access increases proportionally, ensuring that the transition from protection to competition is accompanied by growing export opportunities.

OPERATIONAL

Tariff schedule publication. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Secretary of State will publish a Transition Tariff Schedule specifying the initial tariff rates, the annual decline schedule, and the expiry dates for all learning tariffs. The Schedule will be published in full, debated in Parliament, and subject to annual review by the Trade and Agriculture Commission. Transparency is the safeguard against capture.

Trade negotiation programme. The Department for Business and Trade will open negotiations with the United States, ASEAN, the European Union, and key Commonwealth trading partners within 30 days of taking office to establish reciprocal opening frameworks aligned with the Prosperity Zone programme. The objective is that by the time learning tariffs expire, British producers in each zone sector have negotiated preferential access to at least three major export markets. Protection without export development is a dead end. Progress will ensure that every zone is building for the global market from day one.

Summary of Legislative Requirements

The E2 framework is built on the Prosperity Zones Act, a single piece of emergency primary legislation introduced in the first King’s Speech. No additional Acts are required. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, prerogative power, or departmental action.

Prosperity Zones Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: Statutory definition and designation of eight Prosperity Zones with defined sectoral focus, on the face of the Act. Establishment of Sandpit Authorities with autonomous governance powers including local tax-setting, regulatory modification, compulsory purchase at existing-use value, and Prosperity Bond issuance. Special Planning Exemptions through Zone Development Orders with deemed consent. Tax Neutrality framework with 10% corporation tax for ten years and abolished employer NICs for seven years. Prosperity Zone Visa for fast-track foreign startup relocations. National Prosperity Zone Design Code with statutory design quality requirements. Minimum residential density of 100 dwellings per hectare. Minimum 30% green coverage. Lifetime Homes standards and integrated tenure housing. Zone-affordable housing defined as no more than 25% of median zone salary. Institutional co-investment powers with democratic-jurisdiction sovereign wealth funds and pension funds only. Prosperity Bond issuance authority backed by land value capture. Reform Dividend Capitalisation from procurement, defence, welfare, and civil service savings. Land Value Charge on unimproved value with compulsory purchase at existing-use value. Statutory Miniversities within 12 months per zone operating under E5 skill capital framework. Employer training tax credits. Learning tariffs with mandatory automatic decline and seven-year expiry. Strategic procurement preferences declining to zero over seven years. Reciprocal market opening negotiation powers.

Delivered operationally: Day 2 ground-breaking at first zone sites under prerogative powers. Sandpit Authority interim chairs appointed within 48 hours. Full boards within 60 days. Zone masterplan design commissions during transition period, masterplans submitted within six months. Anchor tenant engagement within 48 hours, signed commitments within 90 days. International investment roadshow within 30 days to Oslo, Singapore, Toronto, Sydney, Tokyo. First Prosperity Bond issuance within 12 months, £5 billion within 24 months. Chief Design Officer appointed within 48 hours. International design competitions launched within 30 days. Monumental civic architecture commissions. Global Market Bridges within trade agreements. Regulatory sandbox frameworks within 90 days. Zone Venture Funds with international VC partnerships. Curriculum co-design within 30 days per zone. Work-study integration at 50% minimum. Zone Feeder Schools with STEM funding. Transition Tariff Schedule within 90 days. Trade negotiations opened within 30 days.

E2 is the spatial expression of Britain’s economic transformation. Where E1 provides the energy that powers the economy, E2 provides the places in which the economy is built. Eight zones, each anchored to an existing industrial strength, each capitalised through democratic institutional investment, reform savings, and land value capture at a scale that makes transformation possible, each built as a new kind of place that integrates world-class industry with world-class urbanism. The Prosperity Zones are not enterprise zones with better marketing. They are new cities, built from scratch on the richest humanist principles, designed to produce high-paying jobs at a scale that transforms the regions that have been abandoned by every government since the 1980s.

The measure of success is simple. Within five years of designation, every Prosperity Zone must demonstrate measurably higher average wages, measurably higher employment, and measurably higher economic output than the surrounding region. If it does not, the programme has failed. Progress believes it will not fail, because for the first time in British history, a government is willing to commit the capital, the political will, the planning authority, and the design ambition necessary to build places that work. Ground will be broken on the second day. The first Miniversity students will enrol within 12 months. The first zone-manufactured products will ship within 24 months. Britain built the industrial cities of the nineteenth century. It built the garden cities of the early twentieth. It is time to build again, and this time to build something worthy of the twenty-first century and the people who will live and work in it.

##### E3+. A Vision of Unicorn Farming

By Damian Horton

If you ran a poll on the UK's ability to create exciting world-leading start-ups, the general view would be that we're punching above our weight globally. More informed people might reel off several great examples, such as DeepMind, ARM and Revolut, as evidence of our reasonable global position.

The reality is much more depressing. DeepMind, whilst British founded, was long-ago acquired by Google/Alphabet. ARM was acquired by Softbank and then re-listed in the United States. Revolut has already indicated that it won't seek a UK Initial Public Offering (IPO), hinting that its future will also be as a foreign company.

These are just the top examples. Lower down, things look worse. Most of the current crop of UK tech unicorns run huge losses on a level of revenue that places them closer to an SME (small or medium sized business) than a potential FTSE 100 constituent or world-beater. The handful of fintech banks, such as Monzo or Starling, are similar to Skipton Building Society (£500m revenue) and far away from JP Morgan. It's worth noting that Revolut, one of the few tech unicorn breakouts, didn't obtain a UK banking license and much of its revenue comes from non-banking products or services.

If we look at our well-established pharmaceutical companies, AstraZeneca and GSK, we can manage global companies within our economy but these are well-established and older businesses. Underneath them there are not the tens of fast-growing pharmaceutical rivals we would hope, which is very different to the US with many competing and up-and-coming companies.

This lack of building new companies leads to several problems. Firstly growth. If we want to get outsized growth it will tend to come from somewhere new. A new technology or product that people are willing to pay extra for at a global scale. Well established companies, whilst well resourced and in many places innovative, cannot be expected to capture all new opportunities. The internet, the cloud and now AI were and are great opportunities, but which established UK companies do we expect to capture those opportunities?

We can't expect Vodafone to pivot or re-allocate large levels of internal resources whilst still providing a core business of communications. We need new companies to do this but we are hopeless at it.

The second big problem from not creating new companies is that it leads to a pretty uncompetitive internal market. Monopolies, Duopolies and markets without ruthless invention can exist when there isn't the pressure from the outside. These can be a secondary spillover benefit of forming many new companies. For example whilst Monzo may not be growing as fast as expected it has forced incumbent banks to up their own offerings, particularly digital banking services.

It is highly likely we'll miss the current artificial intelligence revolution too. The UK isn't setup to capture parts of the market and isn't placed to hold on to any success stories. The purpose of this paper is to discuss where we are going wrong and put forward how the UK can turn the tables to become a unicorn farm much like Silicon Valley.

###### Start-up Ecosystem Diagnosis

I want to share a selection of reasons why UK start-ups are not scaling or succeeding. This isn't a full list but has the major factors at play when considering the proposals in this paper.

The UK is Too Small

The UK is a relatively small economy and due to that it can't support growing technology businesses. This is made more explicit if we narrow down the UK market to being just the private sector, noting that the public sector is a big proportion of the UK economy. With small markets you can't create big companies. Those that want to grow larger then seek to join larger markets and move overseas.

Too Short Term

Many of our start-up investment timelines are too short. Investors and founders look at 5 or 7 years for an eventual company exit, such as acquisition or going public via an IPO. This timeline is far too short and doesn't provide suitable time to build up deep company competitive advantages. We need to have timeframes of 10 to 20+ years as a minimum.

Attempting to Replicate Silicon Valley

We can't think about start-up success without looking at Silicon Valley. Due to the large and influential London financial services sector, desires to replicate venture capital investment then IPOs is an obvious strong influence. However, the UK isn't Silicon Valley. We don't have the hundreds, even thousands, of experienced technology founders who can act as investors and advisors. Looking deeper into the Silicon Valley story, it was heavily supported by NASA and the US Department of Defence acting as a buyer of first resort. The UK isn't copying the Silicon Valley model correctly.

Lack of Public Sector Support

Whilst political parties and Governments might support start-ups, they tend to not be supported at the government departmental level. This is best seen by the lack of procurement and the procurement processes that are in place. For example, looking at many government procurement frameworks, intellectual property (IP) is expected to be handed over to funding departments so that future other suppliers can replicate the technology.

This leads to an avoidance by UK tech of the public sector, a lack of innovation and productivity improvement in the public sector, higher costs for the public sector and, overall, poorer services for the public.

If we want growth, the public sector procurement needs to look at NASA and think of growth start-ups first. One of the major issues is that so many informal barriers have been created. The Subsidy Control Act makes it too difficult to support technology companies, even if it has clauses to allow for it. Fear of vendor lock-in seeks to neutralise IP. Favouritism for consulting and contracting models are always favoured.

Unwilling to Support Private Sector Empires

If we want to create UK technology companies worth above £100 billion we need to recognise that this will create founders with huge levels of paper wealth. To build these companies we will need founders owning more than 10% of the business and ideally towards 30%. £30 billion of individual wealth is seen as unpalatable for many in the UK.

Apple, Facebook, Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, Salesforce and Oracle were all built by founders who stayed with the companies over decades and become empire owners. Dyson (Dyson), Branson (Virgin) and Radcliffe (Ineos) are the small handful of UK empire owners but the majority of their wealth has long moved overseas.

Tax Incentives Support Fast Sales

The tax system really puts you on a path to looking for an exit. Capital gains tax is a more favourable path than dividends. This is particularly acute within smaller businesses. SEIS and EIS tax incentives really target 3-year exits with little or no capital gains tax for investors.

The Ecosystem Views Start-ups as Products

As our financial system is packed with lawyers and bankers, along with company boards who are generally cautious, we end up in situations where UK companies accept acquisition offers far too easily. An acquisition offer which is 30% higher than the last valuation is just too tempting to accept. Short-term wins for bankers (fees), lawyers (fees) and board members (realisation of equity holdings).

###### Taking Action – How to Build a Unicorn Farm

Based on the above information we need to create a system whereby start-ups can more readily form, find it easier to grow, recognise what actual growth is, scale and then stay in the UK. This also needs to lay the foundations for further growth.

One of the big battles is that we need to create a new and better balance between public and private sectors. We need the public sector to change and shift away from internally solving some of the UK's needs or looking for consulting/contracting solutions. This current approach leads to single-use bespoke technologies that create no spillover or wider economic utility.

We need to think that services can be privately delivered yet publicly owned. More interesting would be partial public ownership models which act as UK anchors and seed capital but don't get in the way of international growth or become politicised.

Scaling also needs to be understood. Scaling means increasing company revenue and eventually profit. The UK is lost in the view that investment equals scale. It doesn't. The British approach to building unicorns MUST be revenue driven. This is what Silicon Valley initially did with NASA.

I have broken the process to building a UK unicorn farm into 4 main stages: Seeding, Potting, Planting, and Harvesting.

###### Seeding the Start-ups

We know there are thousands of technology-based public sector challenges. Many of these also overlap with private sector challenges but the UK isn't able to create the new innovative companies to solve those problems.

The high-level seeding process will have 1000 start-ups supplied with capital to build initial solutions for government problems. There needs to be a long list of real problems with some approval to the benefit of that and appropriate sizing and of economic interest.

Each seed should be structured as an investment because this will encourage the public sector to open their problems and this will circumvent numerous challenges within the government procurement system. Seeding should copy a particular Silicon Valley success: Y Combinator's SAFE model. This is a standardised document and investment whereby the same investment amount can be given to all seeded companies, and the valuation is determined at a later investment round. This vastly speeds up the decision process so that the SAFE is initially closer to a loan facility than equity investment. Founders keep full control.

My target initial seed amount is £1m. Enough for a small team to attack a problem for 12 months but not enough to make a profit.

The end result from this process, assuming 1000 start-ups are funded, is that the UK Government will have 1000 companies with basic government procurement experience. This might have 500 failures and 500 successes – which is far better than 1000 successes.

How much will seeding cost?

The aim isn't to use new funding streams for this. Instead, all of Innovate UK's budget should be used for seeding (circa £1 billion). Innovate UK taking equity stakes rather than grants has already been tabled.

If £1 billion is annually invested in 1000 seed companies, we can also limit the company spending to be British-based, such as on local salaries or from buying services from other seeded start-ups. Let's roughly assume £300m is directly recouped by income tax.

The result from this is the annual £1 billion seeding will at a worst-case scenario have a retained value of £800m and only cost £200m (maximum cost). This doesn't yet consider fiscal multipliers, it doesn't yet consider that the government problems may be solved or on the way to be solved and finally we haven't yet considered the longer term upside from creating a UK unicorn farm.

###### Potting the Promising Start-up Buds

Much like growing your own vegetables at home, at some point the seeds start to look like potential plants and need to move from trays into dedicated settings. They need their own pots whilst the failed seeds are discarded so the soil can be re-used (hint: tech talent needs to be re-allocated to the most promising technologies and companies).

Potting starts to include important items such as potentially 3rd party investors that can set the company valuation from the SAFEs. Potting might mean a further seed external capital isn't needed but a real deployable solution is close. Potting might mean the start-up is ready for full procurement. Potting could also mean the start-up is ready to address the same or similar problems outside of the public sector.

One such example of potting might mean scaling into a multi-year multi-million-pound procurement. This might be a £5m project delivered over 2 years and allows the start-up to start filling a wider delivery team.

###### Planting Unicorns

Continuing the horticultural theme, at some point the potted start-ups are ready to flourish and need full planting. This may mean larger investment rounds but it will also mean getting them to win larger government contracts where they are the winning supplier over a much longer period such as 5 years. Contract sizes will range from £20m upwards to £200m with the best current comparable being Anduril Industries in the United States.

One would expect these Potted and Planted start-ups to now be approaching unicorn status with annual revenues direct from government in the £20m to £40m region. Facilitation for wider equity investment could be encouraged but isn't a strict requirement: these companies are not on a treadmill where they raise or go bust as their financial runways dry up.

These companies should also now be serving a wider customer base. They should be redeploying the technology from government contracts into the private sector so that the technology isn't single-use bespoke contracts.

###### Harvesting for Our Future

I'd hope by this point we have many more unicorns forming on the back of a new supportive approach to government procurement and trusting UK tech companies to deliver solutions.

Firstly, the sticky foundations need to continue. Reliable government procurement is one part but also a target 20% government equity ownership might be another part. Having founders looking to continue growth and build empires is also important.

We must not rip up these foundations at the request from a financial sector. Desires for a big IPO will be abound but this isn't needed. The UK public markets have very weak growth capital for companies looking to grow to £20bn plus in size. Why would we rip up the roots keeping these companies in the UK just to please banks with listing fees?

Harvesting also goes further at this stage. Having a number of large technology incumbents means that the planting phase could start to happen away from the public sector. £100m+ contracts could be won from our new domestic technology companies. Spin outs from these new large companies can occur. Research and development, such as closer ties between the private sector and universities, can flourish.

Real differences in how companies are built can be seen in the approach to intellectual property. DoorDash has a patent program that applies across delivery technology today and self-driving delivery technology for the future. Deliveroo has no patents. This difference shows up various aspects that are needed as we get to harvesting. Selling internationally is very competitive and legal disputes will occur. Having a strong and ruthless side to legal and intellectual property is a necessity.

###### Summary

The purpose of this paper was to present a way where the UK can start to build globally successful technology companies. It goes against many of the solutions that are continually churned out: more investment and more skills. These are not the right solutions and may act against what is truly needed: a far better relationship between the private and public sectors. Investment isn't scale and sets us on a path to selling our best companies.

Technology is changing and it will be AI-supported. This means dynamic teams that continually iterate a software service are required. Large-scale waterfall projects will not succeed as technology becomes obsolete before the projects are completed.

Attempting to repeat the past without looking how Silicon Valley was really created – via NASA and procurement – would be foolish at best. We can't afford to miss out on these technology revolutions but time is against us and other countries are becoming dominant.

##### E3+. Funding Technology and Innovation with Property

By Damian Horton

This case-study is based on the following assumptions:

- 1. We are chronically short of equity investment for promising technology start-ups
- 2. The UK is heavily overweight property as an investment
- 3. Capital in investment properties is trapped due to Capital Gains Tax

To highlight the difference between technology investments and property investments, the UK financial sector has only raised £160m so far in 2025. At the same time, the UK has accumulated well past £1 trillion in wealth from investment properties. The Resolution Foundation had this figure at £1 trillion in 2016 with the market increasing a further 50% since then.

However much of the investment property is now trapped. Over the years the investment property prices have doubled or even tripled, and this leads to an unattractive to sell for mostly older Baby Boomer owners. With prices on an investment property doubling and with a higher rate capital gains tax of 24%, the property investor would pay away 12% in capital gains tax if the property were to be sold (after house prices doubling). If house prices had tripled, it would be 16% of total proceeds. This is assuming no borrowing or leverage.

If a property investor had 50% mortgage financing and 50% property equity, the CGT due is an even higher percentage of total proceeds. If property prices doubled in that time, then the same tax is due on the capital gain but on a lower total equity position. CGT due increases to 16%.

For example, if a property investor has £100k and borrows £100k to buy a £200k property. Then that property doubles in value to £400k over (say) 10 years:

- 1. The property increased in value by £200k (the capital gain)
- 2. CGT due to be paid would be £48k (based on 24% × £200k capital gain)
- 3. The investor would have £300k total capital before tax (£400k less £100k borrowing)
- 4. The effective CGT rate is 16% (£48k divided by £300k)
- 5. Property investors are unwilling to “lose” 16% to CGT when selling their property.

Given property investors’ age and desire to pass wealth down to the family, it is often better to hold onto the property and wait until inheritance. This avoids a risk of double taxation, whereby the property investor pays CGT and then Inheritance Tax occurs on the estate and proceeds. Properties and investment capital isn’t being recycled. Waiting until inheritance, where there isn’t CGT, becomes the rational behaviour.

The property investors holding on to their investments leads to other problems. Families looking to buy are met with property owners unwilling to sell. This leads to property shortages and higher home prices. Properties are not getting redeveloped or modernised. Capital in these homes and the homes themselves needs to be reused.

###### Capital Markets Reboot: The Proposition

To encourage property investors to move from investment properties to technology investments. This can be achieved by shielding property investors from capital gains tax if and only if these funds then move into an approved technology investment fund to support UK initial public offerings and technology investments. There will be a minimum holding period of 2 years.

Assessment of Proposition:

- 1. If 5% of investment property wealth is moved across, this is circa £50 billion in technology funding. This far outstrips the £25bn from Megafunds discussed in the Mansion House Accord.
- 2. This approach effectively provides a 12% (16%+ with leverage) subsidy to property investors (CGT shield), which provides some level of downside risk to Technology IPOs.
- 3. This is likely to lead to increased property market liquidity and increased stamp duty receipts.
- 4. We expect minimum losses of CGT collected: many of these investment properties are not sold and remain until inheritance tax to avoid double taxation (CGT is shielded).

In summary, this is simply an acceleration to move capital in property to capital in the technology sector. By forgiving CGT on investment property this allows capital to have greater liquidity only if it flows into a desired area of need (funding innovation).

This Technology Capital Markets Reboot tax incentive to invest in technology isn’t a tax relief on future gains, which has often been the path taken in policy. This policy looks to use tax as downside protection to the riskier Technology investment: one of the reasons people are not investing in technology companies is the fear of losses. This will reduce this risk.

#### E3. Britain, the World’s Largest Unicorn Farm

Governing Principle

If you ran a poll on the United Kingdom’s ability to create world-leading technology companies, the general view would be that Britain is punching above its weight. More informed people might reel off several great examples: DeepMind, ARM, Revolut. The reality is much more depressing. DeepMind, while British-founded, was acquired by Google in 2014. ARM was acquired by SoftBank in 2016 and re-listed on the New York Stock Exchange, not in London. Revolut has indicated it will not seek a UK Initial Public Offering, hinting that its future will be as a foreign company. These are not exceptions. They are the pattern. Britain creates world-class technology, then watches it leave.

The numbers tell the story with brutal clarity. The United Kingdom has 61 unicorns, privately held companies valued at a billion dollars or more, placing it fourth in the world behind the United States (853), China (330), and India (56). London is the fifth-best city in the world for unicorns and comfortably Europe’s leading technology capital, housing more unicorn headquarters than Paris and Berlin combined. The UK creates unicorns at three times the efficiency of the United States: 3.08 unicorns per billion dollars of seed and early-stage venture capital invested, versus 1.22 for the US. Seed-stage investment surged 80% in 2024, with the number of companies securing seed funding rising 30%. Total venture capital investment reached £9 billion, a 12.5% increase year-on-year. By any measure, the UK’s early-stage innovation ecosystem is world-class.

And yet Britain does not capture the value it creates. The London Stock Exchange had just 18 IPOs in 2024, the lowest volume since records began. In 2024, 88 companies left or transferred their listing from the main market, three times the number that arrived. London dropped out of the world’s top 20 IPO markets in the third quarter of 2025, overtaken by Mexico and Singapore. There are 25% fewer companies listed on the UK stock market than a decade ago. ARM, the most important semiconductor architecture company in the world, listed in New York. Flutter Entertainment moved its primary listing to New York. Just Eat abandoned its London listing altogether. Shell’s CEO publicly contemplated leaving for the US. The pattern is unmistakable: Britain incubates companies brilliantly but cannot keep them, cannot scale them, and cannot capture the wealth they generate. The UK is a launchpad, not a home.

The diagnosis is structural, not cultural. First, the capital stack is broken. UK pension funds invest negligibly in venture capital compared to their counterparts in the United States, Canada, and Australia, where pension allocations to VC and private equity are five to ten times higher. The Mansion House Compact’s voluntary 5% allocation to unlisted equities has not materialised in meaningful flows. Meanwhile, over a trillion pounds in wealth sits trapped in investment property, locked in by capital gains tax structures that make selling irrational. The UK’s financial sector has raised only £160 million in 2025 against over £1 trillion in accumulated investment property wealth. The capital is there. It is in the wrong asset class. Second, the ecosystem views startups as products to be sold, not empires to be built. Investment timelines of five to seven years, a financial sector staffed by lawyers and bankers incentivised by acquisition fees, boards that accept offers at 30% premiums over the last valuation, and a tax system that favours capital gains from quick exits over long-term empire building all conspire to ensure that the moment a British company becomes genuinely valuable, it is acquired by an American or Asian buyer and ceases to be British. Third, the public sector is a barrier to startup growth rather than an engine of it. Government procurement frameworks demand IP handover, favour consulting and contracting models, and are too complex for small companies to navigate. The Subsidy Control Act makes it too difficult to support technology companies even where clauses allow for it. Compare this with the United States, where NASA and the Department of Defence created Silicon Valley by acting as the buyer of first resort for emerging technology companies.

Progress will reverse every one of these structural failures. The programme set out in this document will make Britain the easiest place in the developed world to start a company, the best-capitalised place to scale one, the most attractive place to list one, and the hardest place to sell one out from under the country that built it. The objective is not merely more unicorns. The objective is more unicorns that stay British, that scale to ten and then a hundred billion pounds in value, that employ British workers, that list on British exchanges, and that create the kind of enduring industrial empires that define national economic identity for generations. Apple, Google, Nvidia, and Microsoft were all built by founders who stayed with their companies for decades and became empire owners. Britain has Dyson, Branson, and Ratcliffe, and most of their wealth has long moved overseas. Progress will build the conditions in which the next generation of empire builders chooses to stay.

###### E3.1: The Founder’s Republic

The Problem

Starting a company in Britain is not as difficult as starting one in many other countries, but it is far more burdensome than it needs to be, and the regulatory and tax environment that a new company faces in its first three years actively discourages the kind of ambitious, long-term company building that produces globally significant businesses. The R&D tax credit regime was cut for SMEs in 2023, reducing the rate from 33% to 27% effective relief and merging the SME and large company (RDEC) schemes in a way that disproportionately affected smaller companies. National Insurance contributions fall on the employer from the first hire, adding 13.8% to the cost of every employee and making the early scaling of a team punishingly expensive for a company with no revenue. The Enterprise Management Incentives scheme, which allows startups to grant tax-advantaged share options to employees, is capped at companies with gross assets under £30 million, excluding most scale-ups at exactly the point where they need to attract senior talent away from established employers. Disputes over the ‘fair market value’ of options are common, the 92-day reporting window is too short, and the overall complexity of the scheme deters smaller companies from using it at all. GDPR compliance imposes costs on new companies that are disproportionate to their size and resources. FCA approval for fintech startups routinely takes six months or more, during which the company burns cash without generating revenue.

The net effect of these accumulated burdens is that British founders face higher costs, more complexity, and less favourable tax treatment than their counterparts in the United States, Singapore, or Israel. The founders who succeed despite these obstacles are then incentivised by the tax system to sell their companies quickly rather than build them over decades. Capital gains tax is more favourable than dividends, and the EIS and SEIS tax incentive schemes explicitly target three-year exits with minimal capital gains tax for investors. The entire architecture of the British startup ecosystem points toward a fast sale, not long-term empire building.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Enterprise and Innovation Act will establish:

- a) Restoration and expansion of SME R&D tax credits. The Act will re-separate the SME and RDEC (large company) credit schemes, restoring the dedicated SME rate to a minimum of 33% effective relief. The restriction on overseas R&D spend will be relaxed for legitimate outsourcing arrangements where no domestic capability exists, enabling British startups to access the best global talent for specific technical tasks without losing their tax credit eligibility. The merged scheme introduced in 2023 will be reversed because it treated a ten-person startup and a ten-thousand-person multinational as if they faced the same financing constraints, which is absurd.
- b) National Insurance contribution relief for early-stage companies. Employer NICs will be reduced to zero for the first ten employees of any company in its first three years of trading, and to 50% of the standard rate for employees eleven through thirty in the same period. This eliminates the single largest marginal cost of early hiring and directly accelerates the rate at which startups can build their teams. The relief will be automatically applied through HMRC’s PAYE system with no additional application process.
- c) Comprehensive reform of the Enterprise Management Incentives scheme. The gross assets cap will be raised from £30 million to £200 million, ensuring that scale-ups can use EMI options to compete for talent throughout the growth phase. The 92-day reporting window will be extended to 12 months. A statutory safe harbour for fair market value determinations will be introduced, eliminating the disputes that currently deter companies from granting options. The total value of unexercised options that may be held by any individual employee will be raised to £1 million (from £250,000). Additionally, the Act will introduce Non-Qualified Stock Options modelled on the US system, providing a secondary option pathway for employees who exceed EMI limits or whose companies are above the gross assets threshold.
- d) Expansion of EIS and SEIS to benefit non-UK taxpayers. The Enterprise Investment Scheme and Seed Enterprise Investment Scheme will be opened to non-UK-taxpaying investors, enabling international capital to flow into British startups on the same advantageous terms currently available only to domestic investors. This makes the UK the most attractive destination in the world for early-stage technology investment, full stop. The annual investment limits for SEIS will be doubled.
- e) GDPR simplification for small companies. Companies with fewer than 50 employees and annual revenue below £10 million will operate under a simplified data protection compliance regime, reducing the administrative burden while maintaining the substantive protections. The simplified regime will replace the current one-size-fits-all approach with a proportionate framework that recognises that a five-person startup and a global social media platform do not require the same compliance infrastructure.

OPERATIONAL

Expedited FCA approval. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the FCA will implement an accelerated approval pathway for fintech, AI, healthtech, and climate tech startups, reducing the standard approval timeline from six months or more to a maximum of 60 days. The FCA will establish a dedicated Startup Authorisation Unit staffed by officials with commercial technology experience, not career regulators. A regulatory sandbox will be created for each sector, allowing companies to test products under real market conditions with temporary, conditional authorisation while full approval is processed.

24-hour digital incorporation. Companies House will implement full digital incorporation within 90 days, enabling a company to be incorporated, registered for corporation tax, PAYE, and VAT, and issued with all necessary identifiers within 24 hours of application. This already exists in embryonic form. Progress will complete it and eliminate every remaining friction point in the company formation process.

Sponsor licence acceleration. The Home Office will implement an accelerated sponsor licence process for companies within designated growth sectors, reducing the timeline from the current months-long process to 14 days. This enables startups to bring in high-skilled international workers at the speed that their growth demands, not the speed that the Home Office prefers.

###### E3.2: The Unicorn Pipeline

The Problem

The conventional wisdom on why Britain fails to build globally significant technology companies focuses on investment: not enough venture capital, not enough patient capital, not enough pension fund allocation. The conventional wisdom is wrong. Investment is not scale. The UK already creates unicorns at three times the capital efficiency of the United States. The problem is not insufficient investment. The problem is that Britain has no mechanism for converting promising startups into companies with tens or hundreds of millions of pounds in revenue, because the single largest buyer in the economy, the state, does not buy from them.

The United States did not build Silicon Valley through venture capital. It built Silicon Valley through NASA and the Department of Defence acting as buyers of first resort for emerging technology companies. The early contracts that created Fairchild Semiconductor, Intel, and Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works were government procurement contracts. The revenue that sustained these companies through their growth phases came from the federal government. The venture capital ecosystem that grew around them was a consequence of government procurement, not a substitute for it. Britain has attempted to replicate the Silicon Valley model by copying the venture capital layer without replicating the procurement engine that made it work. The result is an ecosystem that can start companies brilliantly but cannot scale them, because there is no domestic buyer large enough to provide the revenue that turns a promising startup into a dominant company.

The British public sector is not merely absent as a customer for technology startups. It is actively hostile. Procurement frameworks demand that intellectual property developed under government contracts be handed over to the funding department so that future suppliers can replicate the technology. This destroys the competitive advantage that makes a startup worth investing in. Favouritism for consulting and contracting models, the complexity of procurement processes that smaller companies cannot navigate, and an institutional culture that equates innovation with risk combine to ensure that government money flows to incumbent suppliers, large consultancies, and legacy contractors. The Subsidy Control Act makes it too difficult to support technology companies even where clauses allow for it. The result is that the public sector gets bespoke, single-use technology that creates no wider economic value, while the startups that could have provided better solutions at lower cost are frozen out.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Enterprise and Innovation Act will establish the Unicorn Pipeline, a four-stage framework for using government procurement as the primary engine of startup growth:

- a) Stage One: Seeding. The Act will restructure Innovate UK as a seeding vehicle. Its entire annual budget, approximately £1 billion, will be redeployed from the current grant and subsidy model to a standardised equity investment model based on Y Combinator’s SAFE (Simple Agreement for Future Equity) structure. One thousand startups per year will receive a standardised £1 million SAFE investment to build initial solutions for identified public sector problems. The SAFE structure means the investment functions initially as a near-loan facility, with valuation determined at a later funding round. Founders keep full control. Spending will be restricted to British-based costs (salaries, services from other seeded companies), ensuring the investment circulates within the domestic economy. At a worst case, with approximately £300 million recouped through income tax on salaries, the net annual cost is £200 million against a retained equity value of £800 million. This does not count the value of the public sector problems solved, the fiscal multiplier effects, or the long-term upside from the companies that succeed.
- b) Stage Two: Potting. Seeded companies that demonstrate viable solutions will progress to potting: multi-year, multi-million-pound procurement contracts with government departments. A £5 million contract delivered over two years allows a startup to build a delivery team and begin generating real revenue, not investment revenue but earned revenue from a paying customer. At this stage, third-party investors may set the company valuation from the original SAFEs. The Act will require every government department to allocate a minimum of 10% of its annual technology procurement budget to companies that have graduated from the seeding stage, ensuring that the pipeline is not dependent on the goodwill of individual departmental heads but is structurally embedded in the procurement system.
- c) Stage Three: Planting. Companies that succeed at the potting stage will be eligible for major government contracts in the range of £20 million to £200 million over five-year terms, comparable to Anduril Industries in the United States. At this stage, companies should be approaching unicorn status with annual revenues from government alone in the £20–£40 million range. These companies are not on a fundraising treadmill where they raise or die. They have revenue, they have customers, and they have a competitive moat built on the technology they developed through the seeding and potting stages. Crucially, the Act will prohibit the mandatory handover of intellectual property developed under government contracts. Startups will retain full ownership of the IP they create, with the government receiving a perpetual, non-exclusive licence to use the technology for its own purposes. This reversal of the current IP regime is the single most important change in this entire document. Without it, government procurement destroys the very asset that makes a startup valuable.
- d) Stage Four: Harvesting. Companies at scale will begin serving wider customer bases, deploying technology developed through government contracts into the private sector, winning £100 million or more contracts from other large UK companies, and generating spin-outs that feed back into the seeding stage. A target government equity stake of up to 20% will serve as a UK anchor, discouraging overseas acquisition while providing the public with a direct return on the investment that created these companies. The Act will establish a British Technology Holding Company to manage the government’s equity stakes in pipeline companies, with a mandate to hold and grow rather than sell. The Holding Company will not interfere in the commercial operations of its portfolio companies but will exercise its shareholder rights to block acquisitions that would move the company’s headquarters, IP, or primary employment base overseas.

OPERATIONAL

Problem identification. Within 60 days of taking office, the Cabinet Office will publish a National Technology Challenge List: a catalogue of the 1,000 most valuable technology problems across all government departments, each specified with sufficient detail for a startup to build a solution. The List will be maintained and updated quarterly. This transforms the diffuse, opaque landscape of government needs into a visible, accessible market that startups can target.

SAFE deployment. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the restructured Innovate UK will begin issuing SAFEs to qualifying startups. The application process will be streamlined to a maximum of 30 days from submission to funding decision. The assessment criteria will prioritise the quality of the team and the specificity of the proposed solution, not the quality of the business plan or the polish of the pitch deck. Companies that fail, and half of them will, contribute their talent pool to the ecosystem. Failure is not waste. It is how capability is distributed.

Procurement integration. Within six months of Royal Assent, the Cabinet Office will issue a Procurement Direction requiring all departments to implement the 10% technology startup allocation. The Direction will specify simplified procurement pathways, maximum contract award timelines of 90 days, and the prohibition on mandatory IP handover. Departmental compliance will be monitored and published quarterly. Non-compliant departments will lose a corresponding proportion of their discretionary procurement budget.

###### E3.3: The Capital Stack

The Problem

The United Kingdom is chronically short of growth-stage equity investment for promising technology companies. Total venture capital investment reached £9 billion in 2024, but later-stage funding relies heavily on international, predominantly American, capital. The lack of large UK-based growth funds means that the moment a company needs £50 million or more to scale, it must turn to Silicon Valley investors who will typically expect the company to relocate its headquarters, or at least its commercial operations, to the United States. The best British companies are bought with American money and become American companies because no domestic capital pool exists at the scale necessary to fund their growth.

The structural cause is the absence of UK pension fund investment in venture capital and growth equity. UK pension funds invest negligibly in VC compared to their counterparts in Canada, Australia, and the United States. The Mansion House Compact of 2023 and the subsequent Mansion House Accord secured voluntary commitments from pension providers to allocate 5–10% of defined contribution default funds to private markets by 2030. These commitments have not materialised in significant flows. Meanwhile, over £1 trillion in accumulated wealth sits in UK investment properties, trapped by capital gains tax structures that make selling irrational for the predominantly older owners. When property prices have doubled, an investor faces an effective CGT rate of 12–16% of total proceeds on sale. With inheritance tax exemptions on death, the rational strategy is to hold until inheritance. Capital in these homes is not being recycled. It is dead money.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Enterprise and Innovation Act will establish:

- a) Mandatory pension fund allocation to UK growth assets. The Act will require all defined contribution pension schemes with assets exceeding £1 billion to allocate a minimum of 5% of their default fund to UK-domiciled venture capital and growth equity funds within three years of Royal Assent, rising to 10% within five years. This is not a voluntary compact. It is a statutory requirement, modelled on the approach that unlocked US pension fund investment in venture capital following the adoption of prudent-man rules in the 1970s and 1980s, which produced a documented 50% increase in local VC commitments in adopting states. UK pension funds collectively manage over £2.5 trillion in assets. A 5% allocation releases £125 billion into UK growth companies. Even a fraction of this sum transforms the capital landscape.
- b) Expansion of British Patient Capital. The British Business Bank’s British Patient Capital vehicle will be expanded to £10 billion and empowered to match private VC investment on a pound-for-pound basis for qualifying growth-stage companies. BPC will operate as a co-investor alongside approved private funds, providing the scale of capital that enables British companies to raise £50–200 million domestically rather than turning to Silicon Valley. The expansion will be funded from the Reform Dividend described in E2.4 and from returns on the government’s equity stakes in Unicorn Pipeline companies.
- c) Government-backed Series A funds. The Act will establish five sector-specific government-backed Series A funds, modelled on Israel’s Bird Foundation and Yozma programme, which transformed Israel from a VC desert into the world’s highest per-capita startup economy. Each fund will be capitalised at £500 million, co-invested with approved private VC firms, and focused on the sectors corresponding to the Prosperity Zones: life sciences, advanced manufacturing, nuclear and clean energy, semiconductors, and defence technology. The funds will operate on commercial terms with the government acting as a patient anchor investor with a 15-year minimum holding period.
- d) The Property-to-Technology Capital Transfer. This is the most novel mechanism in the E3 framework. The Act will provide a full capital gains tax rollover relief for investment property sales where the proceeds are reinvested within 12 months into an approved UK Technology Investment Fund. The investor pays zero CGT on the property sale provided the capital moves into technology equity. There will be a minimum holding period of two years in the technology fund. The mechanism works as follows: property investors currently hold over £1 trillion in investment property wealth that is trapped because CGT makes selling irrational. By forgiving CGT on the condition that the capital flows into technology investment, the government converts dead money in property into productive capital in technology. If 5% of investment property wealth transfers, that is approximately £50 billion in technology funding, dwarfing the £25 billion projected from the Mansion House Accord. The CGT forgone is minimal because these properties were not going to be sold anyway: the revenue the Treasury is forgoing is largely theoretical. The stamp duty receipts from increased property market liquidity will partially offset even the theoretical loss. The CGT rollover also functions as downside protection for investors entering a riskier asset class: one of the primary reasons people do not invest in technology companies is the fear of losses. The 12–16% effective CGT saving provides a cushion against technology investment losses, making the risk-reward calculation significantly more attractive.

OPERATIONAL

Technology Investment Fund accreditation. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the FCA will publish criteria for Technology Investment Fund accreditation. Qualifying funds must invest a minimum of 75% of capital in UK-headquartered or UK-operating technology companies, with no more than 20% in any single company. The accreditation process will be completed within 60 days of application. The objective is to have at least 20 accredited funds operational within 12 months.

Pension fund compliance. Within 30 days of Royal Assent, The Pensions Regulator will issue guidance on the mandatory allocation, including approved fund structures, risk management frameworks, and reporting requirements. Schemes will report their allocation annually, with non-compliance resulting in a financial penalty and regulatory action. The government will lead by example: the National Employment Savings Trust (NEST) will implement the 10% allocation within 12 months.

British Growth Exchange. The London Stock Exchange will be required to establish a dedicated growth market tier, the British Growth Exchange, designed specifically for high-growth technology companies with simplified listing requirements, reduced ongoing compliance costs, and a market-making commitment from designated liquidity providers. The objective is to provide a credible domestic alternative to a Nasdaq listing, eliminating the pull factor that drags British companies to New York. Listing on the British Growth Exchange will be incentivised through a stamp duty exemption on trading in Growth Exchange shares for the first five years.

###### E3.4: Empire Builders

The Problem

The British startup ecosystem is culturally, financially, and legally oriented toward the sale of companies rather than their long-term growth. Founders plan for exits, not empires. The average investment timeline is five to seven years. The tax system rewards capital gains from quick sales over dividends from long-term ownership. EIS and SEIS incentives explicitly target three-year exits. The financial ecosystem, packed with lawyers and bankers who earn fees from acquisitions, actively encourages founders to accept offers rather than build. A board that receives an acquisition offer 30% above the last valuation faces overwhelming pressure to accept. Short-term wins for bankers (fees), lawyers (fees), and board members (realisation of equity holdings) override the long-term interest of the company, its employees, its customers, and the country.

Apple, Facebook, Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, Salesforce, and Oracle were all built by founders who stayed with their companies for decades and became empire owners.
