In Britain, apprenticeship starts have fallen to their lowest levels since the levy was introduced, with the sharpest decline among the young people and small businesses who need apprenticeships most. The system has been captured by large employers using levy funds for management development rather than frontline training. The bureaucracy of the system deters small employers. The standards are defined by committees rather than by the practical requirements of employers who need specific skills. And the cultural status of apprenticeships remains far below that of university education, despite the fact that a skilled electrician earns more, is more employable, and makes a greater contribution to the productive economy than the median graduate.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Skill Capital Act will include:

- a) Target: 50% of vacancies filled via apprenticeships within seven years. The Act will establish a national target, emulating the German model, that 50% of new hires across the economy are recruited through apprenticeship and structured work-based training routes within seven years. This target will be monitored by Skills England and reported annually to Parliament. Sectors that fall persistently below target will face increased Skill Capital Levy rates until apprenticeship starts recover.
- b) Minimum duration reduced and Hallmark-integrated. Apprenticeship programmes will be restructured around the Hallmark framework. Each apprenticeship will require the achievement of a defined set of Hallmarks at Level 2 minimum. The minimum duration will be set at the time required to achieve the Hallmark standards, which for many practical skills will be eight to twelve months rather than the historic twelve-month minimum. Where an apprentice can demonstrate competence faster, they will complete faster. Time-serving for its own sake is eliminated. Shorter-duration foundation apprenticeships of six to eight months, focused on entry-level Hallmarks for sixteen- to twenty-one-year-olds, will provide the fastest possible route from school to skilled employment.
- c) Employer hiring incentive. Employers who hire an apprentice under twenty-five will receive a £5,000 cash incentive per apprentice in the first year, in addition to the Skill Capital Levy credits available for Hallmark training. For SMEs below the levy threshold, the government will fund 100% of off-the-job training costs, eliminating the financial barrier that has caused the 49% collapse in SME apprenticeship starts. The incentive is designed to make hiring an apprentice the cheapest, simplest way for a small business to add capacity.
- d) Apprenticeship quality and the Meister pathway. The Act will establish a Master Practitioner designation, informally the British Meister, for individuals who achieve Hallmark Level 3 (Master) in their discipline and complete a structured programme of teaching and mentoring capability. Master Practitioners will be qualified to train and assess apprentices, creating a self-sustaining cycle in which the most skilled workers in each trade are the ones who train the next generation. The Master Practitioner designation will carry statutory recognition and a salary premium in public sector employment.

OPERATIONAL

Apprenticeship simplification. Within 90 days, the Department will publish a reformed apprenticeship framework with the number of occupational standards reduced by at least half, consolidating the current proliferation of overlapping and excessively narrow standards into broader, more flexible pathways aligned with the Hallmark Framework. England currently has more than double the number of occupational standards used in Germany and Switzerland. Complexity is the enemy of participation.

Apprentice minimum wage. The apprentice minimum wage will be raised to 80% of the National Living Wage within the first year, rising to 90% in year two and parity in year three. The current rate, which is substantially below the minimum wage for other workers, signals that apprenticeships are not real jobs. They are real jobs. They will be paid as real jobs.

##### E5.5: University Reform and Lifelong Hallmarks

The Problem

The university sector in England absorbs the largest share of public skills investment through the student loan system, which currently subsidises approximately £10 billion per year in tuition fees. This investment produces excellent outcomes in some disciplines and catastrophic outcomes in others. Graduates in medicine, engineering, computer science, and other STEM subjects earn high wages, fill critical skill shortages, and generate substantial returns on the public investment in their education. Graduates in subjects with persistently poor employment outcomes accumulate tens of thousands of pounds in debt, enter the labour market without the practical skills that employers need, and in many cases earn less than they would have earned had they entered skilled employment at eighteen with Hallmarks instead. The university system treats all subjects as equally deserving of public subsidy, which they are not. A degree in chemical engineering contributes directly to the productive capacity of the economy. A degree in a subject with a 40% graduate unemployment rate does not, and the public should not be subsidising it to the same degree.

University education will remain an intrinsic part of Progress’ vision of a populace and electorate that is as skilled as it is broadly educated. University in Britain will provide a far richer, more rigorous experience than it typically does now. But it will not be Progress’ position that university is the only creditable path into a prosperous career. For those to whom it is not suited, freedom for early career pursuits will await with no impediments and no student debt in their way.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Skill Capital Act will include:

- a) Differentiated funding by national skill priority. The Act will categorise university courses into three tiers for the purposes of public subsidy. Tier 1 (full funding): STEM subjects, medicine, nursing, allied health professions, education, and other subjects designated as national skill priorities. These courses will receive full tuition fee support through the student loan system with enhanced maintenance support. Tier 2 (standard funding): subjects with demonstrated graduate employment outcomes above the national median. These courses will receive standard tuition fee support. Tier 3 (reduced funding): subjects with graduate employment outcomes persistently below the national median over a five-year rolling period. These courses will receive reduced tuition fee support, with the reduction reflecting the lower expected return on public investment. Universities will remain free to offer any course they wish, and students will remain free to study any subject. But the public subsidy will be directed toward the skills the country needs, not spread equally across subjects regardless of their contribution to the productive economy.
- b) University research aligned with national priorities. The Act will require that a minimum of 50% of public research funding allocated through Research England and UKRI be directed to research areas aligned with the E2 Prosperity Zone sectors and E3 technology priorities: life sciences, advanced manufacturing, nuclear and clean energy, semiconductors, defence technology, AI, and quantum computing. University research is one of Britain’s greatest strengths. Oxford and Cambridge rank first and third in Europe for spinout value creation. This provision ensures that public research funding amplifies the broader Progress framework rather than operating in isolation from it.
- c) Lifelong Hallmark Entitlement. Every working-age adult in the United Kingdom, regardless of age, employment status, or prior qualifications, will have a statutory entitlement to training that leads to Hallmarks throughout their working life. The entitlement will be funded through the Hallmark Account and Skills Wallet described in E5.1, capitalised from the Skill Capital Levy and supplemented by direct government contribution for workers in transition. This is the mechanism that enables the workforce transitions required by the rest of the Progress framework: workers moving from legacy energy to nuclear under E1, workers in declining industries retraining for Prosperity Zone sectors under E2, retail and hospitality workers retraining for healthcare, and the broader automation transition that will reshape every sector of the economy over the next two decades. No worker in Britain will be left behind because they cannot afford to retrain. The Hallmark Account ensures that the investment is always available, and the Hallmark Framework ensures that the resulting skills are always recognised and rewarded.
- d) Standardised testing and anti-credentialism. The Act will establish a framework for standardised skills assessment, enabling any person to demonstrate competence and earn a Hallmark through practical testing, regardless of how they acquired the skill. Self-taught software engineers, informally trained craftspeople, and workers who have learned on the job will all be able to convert their capabilities into nationally recognised Hallmarks through assessment alone, without needing to undertake formal training in skills they already possess. This is the mechanism that drives down academic inflation: when a verified Hallmark proves you can do the job, an employer does not need to use a degree as a proxy for competence.

OPERATIONAL

University funding transition. The differentiated funding framework will take effect from the academic year beginning 18 months after Royal Assent, giving universities time to adjust their course portfolios. The Office for Students will publish the course tier classifications, based on five-year rolling graduate employment data, within six months of Royal Assent. Universities will have 12 months to review their offerings before the new funding framework applies.

Lifelong Hallmark Account capitalisation. Within the first year, every working-age adult in the United Kingdom will receive a Hallmark Account capitalised with an initial balance funded by a combination of Skill Capital Levy revenue and direct government contribution. The initial balance will be sufficient to fund at least one Hallmark-qualifying training course. Additional funds will be credited annually from the Skill Capital Levy. Workers who are made redundant, or who are transitioning from sectors identified as declining, will receive an accelerated capitalisation sufficient to fund a complete retraining programme.

##### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The E5 framework is built on the Skill Capital Act, a single piece of primary legislation introduced in the first King’s Speech alongside the Prosperity Zones Act, Enterprise and Innovation Act, and Planning Liberation Act. No additional Acts are required. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, or departmental action.

###### Skill Capital Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: National Hallmark Framework establishing three-level certification system (Foundation, Practitioner, Master). Hallmark Account and Skills Wallet for every working-age adult. Hallmark Guarantee: minimum one new Hallmark per year for first fifteen years of career, enforceable on employers. Hallmarks available from age fifteen through workplace placements. Abolition of Apprenticeship Levy, replacement with Skill Capital Levy at 0.5% on payrolls above £1 million. Mandatory 75% allocation to Level 2 and Level 3 training, 10% cap on Level 7. Employer Hallmark Tax Credit: £5,000 per Level 2/3 Hallmark, £10,000 per Master Hallmark. Terms-of-service commitments for employer-funded advanced training. 50 new Hallmark Colleges within three years, first 20 within eighteen months, with 50% work-study integration. Coding as core curriculum from age five with 65% professional-standard coding target by 2036. AI-adaptive learning integration in all Hallmark programmes. 50% apprenticeship hiring target within seven years. Foundation apprenticeships from six months duration. £5,000 employer hiring incentive for under-25 apprentices. Master Practitioner (British Meister) designation. Differentiated university funding by national skill priority. 50% minimum of public research funding aligned with Prosperity Zone and technology sectors. Lifelong Hallmark Entitlement for all working-age adults. Standardised skills assessment enabling Hallmarks through testing without formal training.

Delivered operationally: Hallmark Standards Board established within 60 days. First tranche of Hallmark standards within six months. Digital Hallmark Platform within 12 months. Recognition of Prior Learning pathway within six months. Levy transition from first April after Royal Assent. SME co-investment at 90% with 14-day application. £5 billion Hallmark College capital investment over three years, £3 billion in first eighteen months. Fully funded healthcare retraining programme within six months. Hallmark Feeder Schools in every Prosperity Zone within nine months. Apprenticeship framework simplification within 90 days. Apprentice minimum wage raised to 80% of NLW in year one. University course tier classifications within six months. Hallmark Account capitalisation for every working-age adult within 12 months.

E5 is the document that puts people at the centre of the Progress Economic Policy Framework. E1 provides cheap energy. E2 provides productive places. E3 provides startup ecosystems. E4 liberates the planning system. E5 provides the skilled workforce without which none of the others produce a single outcome. The Hallmark is the unit of measurement: a stamped, verified, portable proof that a person can do something of value. The Hallmark Guarantee, one new Hallmark per year for fifteen years, ensures that every worker in Britain is on a continuous upward trajectory of capability and earning power. The Skill Capital Levy ensures that the investment is always there. The Hallmark Colleges, the Apprenticeship Revolution, and the Lifelong Hallmark Entitlement ensure that the pathways are always open.

The measure of success is specific. Within five years: employer investment in training per employee will return to and exceed its 2005 level. Apprenticeship starts will double from their current levels. The number of young people entering skilled employment at eighteen with Hallmarks will exceed the number entering university for the first time. Construction, healthcare, engineering, and digital vacancies will be halved. Within a generation: the British will be the most skilled people in the world, measured not by credentials but by demonstrated capability, stamped and verified by a system as rigorous as the one Britain has used to guarantee the quality of its precious metals since 1300. And every worker in Britain will know, with certainty, that their country is investing in their future, that they will be more capable next year than they are this year, and that their rising skills will be recognised, portable, and rewarded. That is what it means to give someone a stake in their country.

#### E6. The Tax Reset

Governing Principle

The tax system is where most people actually experience the economy. Not GDP growth, not trade balances, not productivity statistics. The gap between what they earn and what they take home. The bill that arrives from the council. The stamp duty that stops them moving to a house that fits their family. The business rates that close the shop on their high street. If a government wants its people to feel richer, more secure, and more professionally mobile, the tax system is the single most direct lever available. Britain’s tax system is pulling that lever in the wrong direction.

The United Kingdom’s tax burden is forecast to reach 37.7% of GDP by 2027/28, the highest level since current records began in 1948. This is not a product of deliberate policy debate. No government has stood before the electorate and argued that Britain should have its highest tax burden in eighty years. It has happened through fiscal drag, threshold freezes, stealth increases, and a decade of governments too cowardly to either raise taxes honestly or cut spending sufficiently. The personal allowance has been frozen at £12,570 since 2021/22, and the current government has legislated to extend that freeze to 2031. Had the personal allowance kept pace with inflation, it would be approximately £15,480 in 2025/26, a difference of £2,910. Every taxpayer earning above £15,480 is paying at least £582 more per year in income tax than they would under an inflation-indexed system. The OBR estimates that income tax threshold freezes alone will raise an additional £55.5 billion per year by 2030/31. That is a £55 billion stealth tax, enacted without a single vote on a rate increase.

The consequences are systemic. An additional 5.2 million people will be paying income tax by 2030/31 who would not be under an indexed system. A further 4.8 million people will be paying the higher rate. The 40% rate, originally designed for a small minority at the top of the income distribution, is being dragged steadily toward the middle. A full-time minimum wage worker now pays £759 more in income tax than they would if thresholds had never been frozen. For the first time since its introduction, the full new state pension will exceed the personal allowance in 2027/28, dragging pensioners with no other income into the tax system. The threshold freezes are also regressive: those on lower incomes face a proportionally larger increase in their tax bill. Workers at the 25th percentile of earnings face a 25.7% higher tax bill, compared to 12.9% for those at the 75th percentile. The stealth tax falls hardest on those who can least afford it.

Alongside the income tax drag, the employer National Insurance increase of April 2025, raising the rate from 13.8% to 15% and cutting the secondary threshold from £9,100 to £5,000, added approximately £25 billion in annual costs to British businesses. The OBR has projected that the majority of this cost will be passed through to workers in the form of lower wages. For a worker on average earnings of £36,000, employer NICs increased by 25%. For a worker on £20,000, the increase was 50%. This is a tax on employment. It makes every hire more expensive, every pay rise harder to give, and every small business less likely to grow.

The Five Objectives

First: money in pocket, year on year. Real wages, take-home pay, and consumer surplus must all increase noticeably for the vast majority of the electorate, and they must increase every year for the full five years of a first Progress government. The Tax Reset is not a single legislative event. It is a five-year programme of annual payslip improvements, choreographed so that every April, every worker in Britain sees a tangible increase in what they keep. Year one should feel good. Year five should feel transformative. The cadence matters as much as the quantum.

Second: a nation of contributors. More than 50% of British households are currently net recipients of state spending rather than net contributors through taxation. Progress will reverse this. Our target is that more than 75% of all households are net contributors by the end of a second term. This is achieved through three simultaneous mechanisms: raising real wages so that more households earn enough to contribute (E5, E12), reforming benefits so that dependency is not more attractive than work, and lowering the tax burden so that the threshold at which a household becomes a net contributor is reduced. The Tax Reset delivers the third leg of that stool. When taxes are lower, the bar to net contribution is lower, and more families clear it through their own effort.

Third: Britain must be the best place in the world to be a high earner. The striver’s compact only works if striving visibly pays. If top earners are not enjoying an unparalleled quality of life in Britain, the aspiration we want to inculcate across the whole population looks like a mug’s game. This does not mean cutting taxes for the wealthy as an end in itself. It means reducing the cost and waste of the state so that the tax burden required to fund public services falls for everyone, including those at the top. Making the NHS higher quality and lower waste directly enables lower NICs. Making the planning system faster directly reduces the cost of housing that inflates the cost of living. Every efficiency gain in the state is a tax cut that does not need to be funded. Progress will make Britain’s effective total tax rate for high earners competitive with the best jurisdictions in the world, not by cutting services, but by delivering them better for less.

Fourth: you keep what you build. Progress does not want new taxes on wealth. We want the people of Britain to rest assured that they will reasonably keep the better portion of the wealth they earn and accumulate. The Tax Reset reforms existing taxes to make them fairer and more proportional. It does not introduce new levies on assets, savings, or investment gains beyond those already in the system. The council tax reform described in this document replaces a regressive, outdated mechanism with a proportional one. It does not expand the tax take. The stamp duty abolition removes a barrier to mobility. The business rates exemption removes a burden from small enterprise. Every reform in this document is designed to make the existing system more honest, not to extract more from the people who build things.

Fifth: end the stealth fleecing. The British state has developed an institutional habit of extracting money from its citizens through mechanisms designed to be invisible. Fiscal drag. Student loan interest rates set at RPI plus 3%, which Rachel Reeves has acknowledged are used as a general revenue mechanism rather than to cover the cost of lending. Council tax based on valuations from 1991. Employer NICs described as a business tax when they are economically a tax on wages. Progress ends every one of these deceptions. The tax you pay will be visible, honest, and democratically mandated. If the state wants more of your money, it will have to ask for it and win a vote.

The Five-Year Cadence

The Tax Reset is delivered as a five-year programme of annual improvements, each timed to take effect in April so that every worker sees the change on their first payslip of the new tax year. The cadence is designed to front-load the most visible, directly felt measures and phase in the larger structural reforms as growth and efficiency savings materialise.

Year One (First April after Royal Assent)

Personal allowance unfrozen and uprated by CPI. Student loan interest abolished for all plan types. True Tax Rate displayed on all payslips for the first time. Business rates abolished for all premises below £51,000 rateable value. Employer NICs rate restored from 15% to 13.8%, secondary threshold restored from £5,000 to £9,100. Constitutional lock against future fiscal drag enacted. Every worker in Britain sees more money on their April payslip, every graduate sees their loan balance stop growing, and every small business owner sees their rates bill disappear.

Year Two

Personal allowance increased above CPI, beginning the restoration to its inflation-indexed level. Council tax revaluation completed and new proportional rates take effect: most households see their bill fall; no household sees an increase of more than £500 above their previous bill. Stamp duty abolished on primary residences. Employee NICs thresholds permanently aligned with income tax thresholds. Workers see a second consecutive payslip improvement. Homebuyers purchase without the stamp duty barrier for the first time.

Year Three

Personal allowance continues above-CPI restoration. Council tax transitional cap begins to relax. Business rates replaced by Land Value Business Levy for premises above £51,000 threshold, shifting the burden from buildings to land and rewarding investment. Commercial stamp duty reduced by 50%. The Integration Commission reports on merging employee NICs into income tax.

Year Four

Personal allowance reaches or approaches its inflation-indexed level, projected at approximately £16,000–17,000. First review of the additional rate of income tax, conditional on state efficiency savings having materialised as projected. If the fiscal position permits, the additional rate is reduced by at least one percentage point, signalling that Britain is a place where success is rewarded, not punished.

Year Five

Personal allowance fully restored to its inflation-indexed level and permanently locked to CPI. Employee NICs merger into income tax legislated in second session. The average worker has seen five consecutive years of payslip improvement. The effective tax rate for a worker on median earnings is the lowest in a generation. Britain’s total tax burden is falling toward 35% of GDP. The striver’s compact is not a slogan; it is a line on every payslip in the country.

###### E6.1: The End of Fiscal Drag

The Problem

Fiscal drag is the mechanism by which a government raises taxes without ever admitting it has done so. When income tax thresholds are frozen while wages and prices rise, more of every worker’s income falls into taxable bands, and more workers are pushed into higher bands, without any change to the headline rates. It is the most dishonest form of taxation: a rate increase by stealth, invisible on the payslip, deniable in Parliament, and devastating in aggregate. The current threshold freeze, initiated by Rishi Sunak in 2021 and extended by both Conservative and Labour governments to 2031, represents a full decade of frozen allowances in a period that included the highest inflation since 1981. It is the largest sustained stealth tax increase in modern British history.

The personal allowance of £12,570 was set when CPI inflation was 0.5%. In the years since, inflation has reached 11.1% and remains above the Bank of England’s 2% target. Had the allowance been indexed to CPI from 2021/22, it would now be approximately £15,480. Every taxpayer earning above that level is paying at least £582 more per year than they should. The higher rate threshold of £50,270 has been similarly frozen, meaning workers whose pay has merely kept pace with inflation are being taxed at 40% on income that represents no real increase in purchasing power. The OBR forecasts that by 2030/31, the freeze will have dragged 5.2 million additional people into income tax entirely, and 4.8 million more into the higher rate. The Resolution Foundation has calculated that the revenue raised by the freeze almost tripled from its original estimate because inflation was so much higher than forecast when the policy was set.

The £100,000 personal allowance taper, which reduces the allowance by £1 for every £2 earned above £100,000, has not been adjusted since its introduction in 2010. The taper creates an effective marginal tax rate of 60% on income between £100,000 and £125,140. This rate is higher than the additional rate of 45% that applies to income above £125,140, creating a perverse incentive structure in which earning more temporarily results in a lower marginal rate. It punishes precisely the professionals, senior managers, and skilled workers whose productivity the country needs, and it does so at the exact income level where many people are making decisions about whether to seek promotion, take on additional responsibility, or simply work fewer hours. No serious tax system should have a marginal rate that falls as income rises.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Tax Reset Act will establish:

- a) Immediate unfreezing of the personal allowance and higher rate threshold. From the first April following Royal Assent, both thresholds will be uprated by September CPI as required by the default statutory mechanism that has been overridden since 2021. This restores the principle that thresholds move with inflation automatically, without requiring annual political decisions. The freeze will not be extended, deferred, or replaced with any alternative mechanism that achieves the same effect under a different name.
- b) Restoration of the personal allowance to its inflation-indexed level within the first Parliament. The Act will establish a statutory trajectory to restore the personal allowance to the level it would have reached had it been continuously indexed from 2021/22, projected to be approximately £16,000–17,000 by the time the first full Parliament concludes. The restoration will be delivered through above-CPI annual increases, front-loaded in years one and two, tapering in years three to five. This is not a tax cut. It is the reversal of a stealth tax increase that was never democratically mandated.
- c) Abolition of the 60% marginal rate trap. The personal allowance taper above £100,000 will be reformed. The Act will raise the taper threshold to £125,140, indexed to CPI, and reduce the taper rate from £1 per £2 to £1 per £4, halving the effective marginal surcharge. This eliminates the 60% marginal rate entirely and replaces it with a smooth progression from the higher rate to the additional rate. The reformed taper will apply from the first April following Royal Assent. This is a measure for strivers. It tells every ambitious professional in Britain: we will not punish you for earning more.
- d) Constitutional lock against future fiscal drag. The Act will establish a statutory requirement that all personal tax thresholds, including income tax, National Insurance, capital gains tax annual exempt amount, and any future personal tax thresholds, must be uprated annually by at least the September CPI rate. Any government wishing to freeze or reduce thresholds in real terms will be required to bring a specific Threshold Adjustment Order before Parliament, subject to affirmative resolution in both Houses. This ensures that fiscal drag can never again be enacted by default. A government that wishes to raise taxes through threshold manipulation must say so explicitly and win a vote to do so.

OPERATIONAL

HMRC implementation. Within 60 days of Royal Assent, HMRC will publish revised PAYE codes reflecting the first threshold increase. The adjustment will be applied automatically through the PAYE system with no action required from employers or employees. HMRC will issue guidance confirming the restored indexation mechanism and the trajectory for full restoration.

Pensioner protection. Within 90 days, HMRC will implement a simplified tax administration for state pensioners whose only taxable income is the state pension. Where the state pension exceeds the personal allowance, as is projected from 2027/28, HMRC will collect any tax due through an automatic adjustment to the pension payment rather than requiring individual pensioners to file self-assessment returns or navigate Simple Assessment. No pensioner whose sole income is the state pension will be required to interact with HMRC directly.

###### E6.2: The Employment Tax Reversal

The Problem

National Insurance contributions are a tax on employment. Despite the name, they do not insure anyone. Despite being split between employer and employee, the economic incidence falls overwhelmingly on the worker. The OBR, the IFS, and virtually every serious economist agrees: employer NICs reduce wages. They are a payroll tax that makes hiring more expensive, suppresses pay, and penalises the precise activity, productive employment, that the tax system should be encouraging.

The April 2025 increase in employer NICs, raising the rate from 13.8% to 15% and reducing the secondary threshold from £9,100 to £5,000, was the largest single tax increase in the 2024 Budget, raising approximately £25 billion per year. For a worker on average earnings of £36,000, the employer’s NIC bill increased by 25%, from £3,715 to £4,655. For a worker on £20,000, the increase was 50%, from £1,504 to £2,250. In low-wage sectors such as hospitality, retail, and social care, where margins are thin and the workforce is large, the impact has been devastating. The OBR projected that the increase would reduce labour supply by approximately 50,000 full-time equivalent positions and add 0.2% to consumer prices as firms passed costs through.

The broader structure of NICs compounds the problem. Employee NICs are charged at 8% on earnings between £12,570 and £50,270, then drop to 2% above that level, creating a regressive structure in which the marginal rate on employment income is higher for a nurse than for a hedge fund manager. The existence of two separate systems, income tax and NICs, with different thresholds, different rates, and different bases, creates unnecessary complexity, obscures the true marginal rate, and allows governments to raise one while claiming they have not raised the other.

The Link to State Efficiency

The employer NICs increase was justified as necessary to fund the NHS. This framing reveals the trap: an inefficient state requires higher taxes to fund the same level of service, and those higher taxes fall on working people. Progress’ approach breaks the cycle. By making the NHS higher quality and lower waste (as detailed in our health policy), by eliminating the procurement inefficiencies that waste billions annually (E10), and by reforming the benefits system so that expenditure flows to those who genuinely need it rather than those who have learned to navigate the system, we reduce the cost of the state. Every pound saved in waste is a pound that does not need to be extracted from a worker’s paycheque. The employer NICs reversal is funded not by borrowing or by cutting services, but by delivering them better. This is the striver’s compact in action: a government that earns the right to take less by spending what it takes more wisely.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Tax Reset Act will establish:

- a) Reversal of the employer NICs increase. The employer NICs rate will be restored from 15% to 13.8% and the secondary threshold restored from £5,000 to £9,100, both effective from the first April following Royal Assent. This immediately removes approximately £25 billion in annual employment costs from British businesses. The Employment Allowance will be retained at £10,500 with the £100,000 cap removed, providing additional relief for small employers. The reversal is funded through three sources: the spending reductions and efficiency savings identified in Progress’ State Capacity programme, phased in over years one to three; the Progress Dividend from Prosperity Zone economic growth described in E2, materialising from year two; and the broadening of the tax base through council tax reform (E6.3) and business rates reform (E6.5), both generating revenue from year two onward.
- b) Alignment of employee NICs with income tax thresholds. The employee NICs primary threshold will be permanently aligned with the income tax personal allowance, and the upper earnings limit permanently aligned with the higher rate threshold. Both will be indexed to CPI alongside the income tax thresholds. This eliminates the complexity of maintaining separate threshold systems and ensures that any future adjustment to income tax thresholds automatically adjusts NICs thresholds.
- c) Publication of the True Tax Rate. The Act will require HMRC to display on every payslip and every self-assessment statement the total effective tax rate paid by the worker, combining income tax, employee NICs, and the employer NICs attributable to their employment. This is the single most important transparency measure in the Tax Reset. When a worker earning £35,000 sees that their true marginal rate is not 20% but 33.25%, the political conversation about tax changes fundamentally. No government should be able to raise employer NICs and claim it is not a tax on working people. The True Tax Rate makes the deception impossible.
- d) A statutory roadmap for the integration of income tax and employee NICs into a single transparent system. The Act will establish an Integration Commission with a mandate to report within 18 months on the mechanism for merging employee NICs into income tax, delivering a single rate schedule applied to all earnings. The Commission will recommend rate structures that are revenue-neutral, that preserve the contributory principle for state pension entitlement through a notional recording mechanism, and that result in a system where every worker can read their payslip and immediately understand what they are paying and why. The integration itself will be legislated in the second session of the first Parliament.

The Top Earner Proposition

Britain must be the best place in the developed world to be a high earner. Not because Progress believes in tax cuts as ideology, but because the aspiration we want to inculcate across the whole population only works if striving visibly pays. If the most productive, most skilled, most ambitious people in Britain look at their effective tax rate and conclude they would be better off in Dubai, Singapore, Switzerland, or Ireland, then the striver’s compact is broken for everyone. The person on £30,000 watches the person on £150,000 and asks: is it worth it? If the answer is no, the whole culture of aspiration collapses.

Progress will not cut the additional rate of income tax as a headline measure. We will do something more durable: we will reduce the effective total tax rate on high earners by reducing the cost of the state that the tax funds. As efficiency savings materialise through the first Parliament, we will review the additional rate with the explicit objective of making Britain’s effective top marginal rate, including income tax, NICs, and the economic incidence of employer NICs, competitive with the most attractive jurisdictions globally. The Year Four review described in the five-year cadence is the mechanism: if the fiscal position permits, the additional rate falls by at least one percentage point, with further reductions conditional on continued efficiency gains. The message to high earners is unambiguous: Progress is on your side, not because we give you a handout, but because we run the state well enough that we do not need to take so much of what you earn.

OPERATIONAL

Employer NICs reversal. The rate and threshold changes will take effect from the first April following Royal Assent. HMRC will issue updated guidance to employers within 30 days. The PAYE Real Time Information system will be updated to reflect the new rates automatically.

True Tax Rate display. Within 12 months of Royal Assent, HMRC will publish specifications for the True Tax Rate display on payslips. All employers using PAYE will be required to display the combined rate from the second April following Royal Assent.

###### E6.3: Council Tax Reform

The Problem

Council tax is based on property valuations from April 1991, more than thirty-four years ago. A property in Band H pays just three times the tax of a property in Band A, despite being worth at least eight times as much in 1991 and typically far more today. Since 1991, average property values in London have increased more than sixfold, while in the North East they have barely tripled. Yet the tax bands have never been updated, meaning that at least half of all properties in England are now effectively in the wrong band relative to current values. The IFS has described council tax as “out of date, regressive and distortionary.”

The result is a system in which households in the North and Midlands systematically overpay relative to their property values, while households in London and the South East systematically underpay. A multimillion-pound property in East Sussex can attract a lower council tax bill than the average family home in Middlesbrough. Council tax is also regressive with respect to income: households in the lowest income quintile pay approximately 5% of their gross income in council tax, while those in the highest quintile pay less than 2%. Council tax raised £40.3 billion in 2024/25. It is one of the largest revenue streams in British public finance, and it is built on a foundation that has not been updated since the year the Soviet Union dissolved.

Every serious analysis of council tax has concluded that it needs fundamental reform. No government has acted, because revaluation creates political losers, and politicians fear the losers more than they value the winners. Progress will act. We are not replacing council tax. We are reforming it so that it works as it was always supposed to: a tax on property, proportional to the property’s actual value, funding local services fairly. Same name. Same monthly direct debit. But honest, modern, and fair.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Tax Reset Act will establish:

- a) Reform of council tax from a banded system based on 1991 valuations to a proportional system based on current market values. The banded structure will be eliminated. Every residential property in England will be assessed at its current market value, and the owner will pay an annual council tax calculated as a percentage of that value. The Valuation Office Agency will conduct a comprehensive revaluation using modern data analytics, Land Registry records, and statistical modelling, to be completed within 18 months of Royal Assent. The rate will be set to be revenue-neutral at the national level, meaning the total revenue raised by the reformed council tax will equal the total revenue currently raised, approximately £40 billion. This is not a tax increase. It is a modernisation. The expected national rate is in the range of 0.3–0.5% of property value, varying by local authority to reflect local spending needs as it does today.
- b) Fair rate structure. The reformed council tax will apply a single proportional rate within each local authority area. There will be no punitive surcharges on higher-value properties beyond what proportionality itself delivers. If your home is worth twice as much, you pay twice as much. If it is worth half as much, you pay half as much. That is fairness. The current system, in which a Band H property pays just three times a Band A property despite being worth eight or more times as much, is not fairness. The reform corrects this by applying the same percentage to every property. The overwhelming majority of households, particularly those in the North, Midlands, and less affluent areas, will see their council tax bill fall, because they have been systematically overpaying relative to their property’s actual value for thirty-four years.
- c) Protection for those who need it. The Act will provide a statutory right to defer council tax payments for owner-occupiers over state pension age, or those in receipt of disability benefits, whose income falls below a specified threshold. Deferred tax will accrue as a charge on the property, payable on sale or transfer, with interest capped at the Bank of England base rate. No pensioner will be forced to sell their home because of a council tax increase resulting from revaluation. This is a reform of how you pay, not a change in whether you can afford to stay in your home.
- d) Local authority revenue protection. No local authority will receive less revenue in the first three years of the reformed system than it received in the final year of the old system. The difference will be met from central government grant. Over a three-year transition, the funding formula will be adjusted to reflect actual property values in each authority area, ending the absurd current system in which funding distribution is still based on relative property values from 1991.

OPERATIONAL

Revaluation. The Valuation Office Agency will commence the comprehensive revaluation within 60 days of Royal Assent. The revaluation will use automated valuation models supplemented by Land Registry transaction data, building on the methodology already proven in the Welsh council tax revaluation. The VOA will publish provisional valuations within 12 months, with a 6-month window for appeals before final valuations take effect. The reformed council tax will go live from the second April following Royal Assent.

Annual updates. Following the initial revaluation, property values will be updated annually using automated valuation models maintained by the VOA. This eliminates the political impossibility of periodic revaluations and ensures that council tax always reflects current market reality. Annual updates will be published each September, taking effect the following April, with a simplified appeals process.

Transitional relief. For the first three years of the reformed system, no household will see its annual council tax bill increase by more than £500 per year above its previous bill, regardless of the revaluation outcome. This caps the transitional impact for households in areas where property values have risen most relative to 1991 and provides time for adjustment.

###### E6.4: Stamp Duty Abolition

The Problem

Stamp duty land tax raised £11.6 billion in 2024/25. It is, by near-universal consensus among economists across the political spectrum, one of the most economically damaging taxes in the British system. The OBR estimates that a 1% increase in stamp duty reduces housing transactions by 5–7%. Research modelling the impact of replacing stamp duty with an annual property levy estimates a permanent GDP increase of approximately 3.4%, driven almost entirely by improved labour productivity as workers move more freely to suitable jobs. Adam Smith Institute polling from November 2025 found that 73% of Britons believe stamp duty should be abolished or cut significantly. It is overwhelmingly unpopular, overwhelmingly destructive, and its replacement through the reformed council tax described in E6.3 provides a stable, recurring revenue stream that makes abolition fiscally credible.

The distortions compound across the lifecycle. A young family that needs a larger home faces a stamp duty bill of £12,500 on a £350,000 property, on top of the deposit they have spent years saving. An older couple whose children have left home face stamp duty on a smaller property, discouraging the move and reducing the supply of family homes. A worker offered a better job in another city faces stamp duty as a direct cost of labour mobility. In the South East, homes valued above £500,000 change hands only once every 26–27 years. The market is frozen, and stamp duty is the ice.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Tax Reset Act will establish:

- a) Abolition of stamp duty land tax on primary residences purchased by UK residents, effective from the second April following Royal Assent, coinciding with the introduction of the reformed council tax. From that date, no buyer purchasing a home to live in will pay stamp duty. The revenue currently raised from residential stamp duty will be replaced by the reformed council tax, which generates the same revenue from the same asset base through a stable annual stream rather than a volatile transaction tax.
- b) Retention of stamp duty on second homes, buy-to-let properties, and purchases by non-UK residents at the current rates, including the additional 2% non-resident surcharge and the 5% additional property surcharge. These surcharges serve to moderate speculative demand and ensure that the housing market primarily serves people who need homes. The revenue from retained surcharges will be hypothecated to the affordable housing programme.
- c) Transitional credit for recent stamp duty payers. Any buyer who paid stamp duty on their current primary residence within five years of the abolition date will receive a credit against their council tax liability, equal to a proportion of the stamp duty paid, declining by 20% per year. This ensures fairness for households who recently paid a large upfront tax.
- d) Commercial stamp duty reform. Stamp duty on commercial property transactions will be reduced by 50% in the first Parliament and abolished entirely in the second, replaced by the reformed business rates system described in E6.5.

OPERATIONAL

Market preparation. The abolition date will be announced at least 12 months in advance to prevent the market distortions associated with stamp duty holidays. By announcing the permanent abolition well ahead of the effective date, the market can adjust gradually rather than experiencing the frantic activity and subsequent collapse that characterised previous temporary reliefs.

HMRC transition. HMRC will wind down the SDLT collection infrastructure for residential transactions over the 12-month notice period, redeploying staff to the administration of the reformed council tax.

###### E6.5: The Business Rates Reset

The Problem

Business rates raise tens of billions of pounds annually for central and local government, and they do so by taxing the occupation of physical premises. This creates a structural bias against businesses that operate from shops, offices, factories, and workshops, and in favour of businesses that operate online or from minimal physical footprints. A high street bookshop pays business rates on its premises; the Amazon warehouse that competes with it pays rates on its warehouse, but at a fraction of the cost per unit of revenue. The system penalises precisely the businesses that create the most visible local employment, the most community value, and the most vibrant high streets.

The current government’s reform, introducing permanently lower multipliers for retail, hospitality, and leisure properties under £500,000 from April 2026, is a step in the right direction but does not address the fundamental problem. The system remains a tax on premises, not on economic activity. The promise to “replace” business rates, made by Labour in opposition, has been quietly abandoned in favour of incremental tinkering. The total business rates take continues to rise, and the burden continues to fall disproportionately on the sectors that need the most support.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Tax Reset Act will establish:

- a) Abolition of business rates for all premises with a rateable value below £51,000, effective from the first April following Royal Assent. This eliminates business rates entirely for the vast majority of small businesses, independent shops, cafes, pubs, and local service providers. If your premises are below the threshold, you pay nothing. No application, no relief, no annual uncertainty.
- b) A new Land Value Business Levy for premises above the £51,000 rateable value threshold, calculated as a percentage of the land value of the site rather than the rental value of the building. This shifts the tax base from the improvements a business makes to its premises, which the current system punishes, to the underlying land value, which is created by public infrastructure, planning decisions, and community activity, not by the occupier. A business that invests in improving its premises will not see its tax bill rise as a result. The Land Value Business Levy will be set at a rate that is revenue-neutral against the business rates currently raised from premises above the threshold.
- c) Annual revaluation of the Land Value Business Levy, replacing the current three-year cycle. Annual revaluation using automated models eliminates the cliff edges that currently produce sudden, large changes in business rates bills. Businesses will receive 12 months’ notice of any change to their assessed land value, with a simplified appeals process.
- d) A Digital Services Contribution for large online retailers. Businesses with UK digital sales revenue exceeding £500 million per year will pay a contribution equivalent to 2% of their UK digital sales revenue, hypothecated to local authority funding for the areas in which their customers are located. This is not a general online sales tax. It is a targeted contribution from the largest online platforms toward the communities whose physical infrastructure they benefit from without directly supporting. The threshold ensures that only the largest operators are affected, estimated at fewer than twenty companies.

OPERATIONAL

Small business exemption. From the first April following Royal Assent, all non-domestic properties with a rateable value below £51,000 will be automatically exempt from business rates. No action required from the business owner.

Land value assessment. The Valuation Office Agency will commence land value assessments for all non-domestic sites above the £51,000 threshold within 90 days of Royal Assent. The initial assessment will be completed within 18 months, with the Land Value Business Levy taking effect from the second April following Royal Assent.

###### E6.6: The End of the Student Loan Con

The Problem

The student loan system in England has become one of the most brazen stealth taxes in British public life. Plan 2 borrowers, the 5.8 million people who started university between 2012 and 2022, carry an average debt of £53,000. They pay interest at RPI plus up to 3%, producing a maximum rate of 6.2% as of September 2025. Two-thirds of these graduates are not even covering the interest on their loans: their balances grow every month despite monthly repayments. A graduate earning £35,000 pays £169 per month in student loan repayments on top of income tax and National Insurance. If that graduate has children, their combined marginal rate of tax, including income tax, NICs, student loan repayments, and the taper of child benefit, can exceed 80%. This is not a loan system. It is a forty-year payroll tax disguised as a debt.

Rachel Reeves has acknowledged what graduates have known for years: the interest on these loans is not set to cover the government’s cost of borrowing. It is set to extract revenue. The government earns money from the interest rate spread between what it borrows at and what it charges graduates. Labour’s own Deputy Leader, Lucy Powell, has described the interest rates as “unfair” and “egregious.” Wes Streeting has conceded that a debate on the system is “worth having.” The IFS, the NUS, and virtually every analysis of the system agrees: Plan 2 loans function as a graduate tax with extra steps and extra dishonesty. Meanwhile, the 2025 Budget froze the repayment threshold for Plan 2 loans, meaning more graduates begin repaying earlier as wages rise, compounding the extraction.

The injustice is generational. These graduates were told at seventeen and eighteen years old that the loan was affordable and fair, that they would only repay when they could afford to, and that the balance would be written off after thirty years. What they were not told is that the interest rate could exceed 6%, that their balances would grow even as they repaid, that the rules would be changed retrospectively to freeze the repayment threshold, and that the entire system would be used as a mechanism for generating government revenue. Many graduates report that they would never have taken the loan had they understood these terms. They were, in the plainest sense of the word, mis-sold.

Progress ends the con. We are not proposing to write off student loans entirely, because the principle that graduates contribute to the cost of their education is sound, and because the fiscal cost of blanket forgiveness would be enormous and regressive, benefiting high-earning graduates most. But we are proposing something that is both fair and transformative: the complete abolition of interest on student loan repayments. You borrowed the money. You will repay what you borrowed. But you will not be charged a penny more than the principal. The loan is a loan, not an income stream for the Treasury.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Tax Reset Act will establish:

- a) Abolition of all interest on student loan repayments across all plan types, effective from the first April following Royal Assent. From that date, no student loan in England will accrue any interest whatsoever. The balance will be frozen at its level on the effective date, and all subsequent repayments will reduce the principal pound for pound. For Plan 2 borrowers, this means the end of the 6.2% interest rate that has caused balances to grow even as graduates repay. For Plan 5 borrowers, whose interest is currently pegged to RPI, it eliminates even the inflation-linked charge. For Plan 1 borrowers, it eliminates the lower but still material interest rate. The principle is universal: if you borrowed to invest in your education, you repay what you borrowed and nothing more.
- b) Recalculation of outstanding balances. Within six months of Royal Assent, the Student Loans Company will recalculate every outstanding loan balance to reflect the total principal borrowed minus the total repayments made to date. Where a borrower has already repaid more than their original principal, as will be the case for some long-standing Plan 1 borrowers, the loan will be treated as fully repaid and no further deductions will be made. This retrospective recalculation ensures that the abolition of interest is not merely prospective but corrects the historical overcharge for those who have been repaying for the longest.
- c) Protection of the repayment threshold. The Act will require that the student loan repayment threshold is uprated annually by at least September CPI, applying the same constitutional lock that protects income tax thresholds under E6.1. No future government will be able to freeze the repayment threshold to extract more from graduates by stealth, as the current government did in the 2025 Budget. The threshold moves with inflation, automatically, permanently.
- d) Transparency of the graduate contribution. The Act will require the Student Loans Company to provide every borrower with an annual statement showing: the original amount borrowed, the total amount repaid to date, the remaining balance, and the projected date of full repayment at current earnings. No more opaque balances that grow mysteriously. No more uncertainty about when the obligation ends. The loan is visible, comprehensible, and finite.

Fiscal Impact

The fiscal cost of abolishing student loan interest is substantially lower than it appears. The government books student loan interest as an asset on its balance sheet, but the OBR has long acknowledged that much of this interest will never actually be collected: the majority of Plan 2 borrowers will not repay their loans in full before the thirty-year write-off, meaning the accrued interest is a phantom asset. The IFS estimates that around 68% of Plan 2 graduates under the pre-2023 system will not repay in full. Abolishing interest on loans that will never be repaid in full costs the Exchequer nothing in cash terms; it merely removes a fictional asset from the balance sheet. The real fiscal cost arises only from borrowers who would have repaid in full, whose total repayment is now capped at the principal. This cost is estimated at £2–3 billion per year in steady state, a fraction of the headline value of accrued interest, and is more than offset by the economic benefit of 5.8 million graduates with higher disposable income, greater spending power, and stronger incentives to remain in the UK workforce rather than emigrate to avoid the graduate tax.

OPERATIONAL

SLC implementation. The Student Loans Company will implement the interest abolition within 60 days of Royal Assent by setting the interest rate to 0% across all plan types. This is a parameter change in the SLC’s systems and requires no legislative complexity beyond the enabling provision in the Tax Reset Act.

Balance recalculation. The SLC will complete the retrospective balance recalculation for all borrowers within six months, publishing individual updated balances through the online student loan account. Borrowers whose recalculated balance is zero or below will be notified that their loan is fully repaid and PAYE deductions will cease.

###### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The E6 framework is built on the Tax Reset Act, a single piece of primary legislation introduced in the first King’s Speech alongside the Energy Security Act, the Prosperity Zones Act, and the Enterprise and Innovation Act. No additional Acts are required. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, or departmental action.

Tax Reset Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: Immediate unfreezing of personal allowance and higher rate threshold with CPI indexation restored. Statutory trajectory to restore personal allowance to inflation-indexed level within first Parliament. Abolition of the 60% marginal rate trap through reform of the £100,000 taper. Constitutional lock requiring affirmative parliamentary resolution for any future threshold freeze. Reversal of employer NICs increase: rate restored from 15% to 13.8%, secondary threshold restored from £5,000 to £9,100. Permanent alignment of employee NICs thresholds with income tax thresholds. Mandatory True Tax Rate display on all payslips and self-assessment statements. Statutory Integration Commission for merger of employee NICs into income tax. Council tax reform: revaluation to current market values, proportional rates replacing the banded system, annual automated revaluation, transitional protections capping increases at £500 per year. Local authority revenue guarantee for three-year transition. Abolition of stamp duty land tax on primary residences, with retention for second homes and non-resident purchases. Transitional credit for recent stamp duty payers. Abolition of business rates for all premises below £51,000 rateable value. Land Value Business Levy for premises above threshold. Annual revaluation for both residential and non-domestic property taxes. Digital Services Contribution for online retailers with UK sales above £500 million. Abolition of all interest on student loan repayments across all plan types. Retrospective balance recalculation. CPI indexation lock on student loan repayment threshold.

Delivered operationally: HMRC revised PAYE codes within 60 days. Simplified tax administration for state pensioners within 90 days. Employer NICs reversal effective first April. Student loan interest set to 0% within 60 days. SLC balance recalculation within six months. True Tax Rate payslip specifications within 12 months. VOA comprehensive residential revaluation commenced within 60 days, completed within 18 months. Reformed council tax and stamp duty abolition live from second April. Annual automated revaluation cycle. Transitional relief capping household increases at £500 per year. Stamp duty abolition announced 12 months in advance. Small business rates exemption from first April. VOA non-domestic land value assessment within 18 months. Land Value Business Levy from second April. Integration Commission report within 18 months. Year Four review of additional rate of income tax conditional on fiscal position.

Funding the Tax Reset

The Tax Reset is not an unfunded tax cut. It is a phased programme of reform in which the most visible, directly felt measures are delivered immediately and the larger structural costs are met as growth and efficiency savings materialise. The funding sources, in order of contribution, are:

State efficiency savings. Progress’ State Capacity programme identifies specific, costed reductions in the cost of delivering public services. NHS procurement reform, benefits system overhaul, civil service productivity improvements, and the elimination of duplicative programmes contribute the largest single source of funding. These savings are phased in over years one to three, with the full annual yield available from year three onward. The employer NICs reversal is the primary recipient of these savings.

The Progress Dividend. The growth generated by E1 (cheap energy), E2 (Prosperity Zones), E3 (startup ecosystem), E4 (planning liberation), and E5 (skill capital) broadens the tax base. More businesses, more jobs, higher wages, and more transactions generate higher tax receipts even at lower rates. The OBR has consistently found that the composition of nominal GDP growth matters as much as the quantum: growth skewed toward labour income, which Progress’ policies promote, generates higher tax receipts per unit of GDP. This dividend materialises from year two and grows through the Parliament.

Base broadening through property tax reform. The council tax reform generates the same total revenue as the current system but from a fairer base. The elimination of the regressive Band H ceiling, which currently caps the tax on the most valuable properties at just three times Band A, ensures that high-value properties contribute proportionally. This additional revenue offsets the stamp duty abolition, which removes volatile transaction revenue and replaces it with a stable annual stream. The net fiscal effect of the combined council tax reform and stamp duty abolition is approximately neutral by year three, with a growing surplus thereafter as property values are updated annually.

The student loan interest abolition costs substantially less than its headline value because the majority of the accrued interest will never be collected. The real fiscal cost is estimated at £2–3 billion per year in steady state, offset by the economic benefits of higher graduate disposable income and reduced emigration incentives.

E6 completes the structural reform of how the British state takes money from its people. E1 reduces what they spend on energy. E2 creates the places where they earn more. E3 creates the companies that employ them. E4 liberates the planning system that has constrained all of the above. E5 gives them the skills to command higher wages. E6 ensures that when those higher wages arrive, they are not silently confiscated by a tax system designed to take more without ever admitting it has done so.

The Tax Reset is built on a single principle: honesty. If a government wants to raise taxes, it should say so, propose a rate, and win a vote. If it wants to cut taxes, it should identify the spending reduction or the alternative revenue source. What it must never do is freeze a threshold, set an interest rate above cost, base a property tax on thirty-four-year-old valuations, or split a payroll tax between employer and employee to disguise its true incidence. Progress ends every one of these deceptions. The true tax rate goes on the payslip. The council tax reflects what your home is actually worth. The stamp duty that freezes the housing market is abolished. The business rates that close high street shops are eliminated for small businesses. The student loan interest that fleeces graduates is abolished. The worker keeps more of what they earn, the graduate sees their balance fall for the first time, the homeowner moves freely, the shopkeeper opens without fear of the next rates bill, and the government funds itself from an honest, transparent, and economically efficient tax base. That is the Tax Reset.

#### E7. Britain, the Greatest Nation of Shopkeepers

Governing Principle

There are 5.7 million private sector businesses in the United Kingdom as of January 2025, according to the Department for Business and Trade’s Business Population Estimates. Of these, 5.4 million are micro-businesses with fewer than ten employees. A further 220,000 are small businesses with between ten and forty-nine employees. Together, these small and micro-businesses constitute 99.2% of all private sector enterprises, employ approximately 13 million people, and generate over £1.8 trillion in annual turnover. They are construction firms, hairdressers, electricians, corner shops, cafés, independent consultancies, plumbers, local accountants, mechanics, web designers, tutors, caterers, and the ten thousand other occupations that constitute the sinew of the British economy. They are, as Adam Smith observed and Napoleon mocked, the nation of shopkeepers. They are the foundation upon which every other economic ambition in this framework rests.

The British state treats these businesses as if they were miniature corporations. A sole trader with one employee faces the same categories of employment law obligation as a FTSE 250 company. A freelance software developer who earns £89,000 must turn away work or close for part of the year to avoid crossing the VAT threshold and losing up to one-sixth of their income overnight. A plumber who wants to hire an apprentice must navigate employer’s liability insurance, auto-enrolment pension obligations, PAYE registration, workplace pension contributions, statutory sick pay administration, and, under the Employment Rights Act 2025, enhanced day-one unfair dismissal protections and mandatory flexible working request procedures, before the apprentice has picked up a single wrench. A freelancer who has spent a decade building a client base through a limited company discovers that IR35 off-payroll rules, extended to the private sector in April 2021, have caused their clients to issue blanket bans on engaging outside-IR35 contractors. IPSE’s IR35 Spotlight 2025 found that 26% of contractors are out of work, with 56% of those out of work attributing their situation directly to the impact of IR35 on client hiring decisions. The proportion of engagements determined to be outside IR35 fell from 80% in 2023 to 70% in 2025. Two in five business leaders cite HMRC bureaucracy and IR35 legislation as major obstacles to engaging the flexible workforce their businesses need.

Late payment is the silent killer of British small business. Government research published in 2025 estimates that UK businesses are owed approximately £26 billion in late payments at any given time, that over 1.5 million businesses are affected annually, and that late payment contributes to around 14,000 business closures each year, costing the wider economy nearly £11 billion per annum. The FSB’s 2025 late payments report, surveying over 2,000 small business respondents, found that 45% are experiencing more late payments than twelve months ago, that nearly a quarter receive payments up to 60 days late, and that 52% forfeit late payments up to ten times a year simply to avoid the time and cost of chasing them. FreeAgent’s analysis of invoices sent between September 2024 and August 2025 found that 62.6% of all SME invoices were paid late. Micro-businesses have the highest share of turnover tied up in late payments at 4.61%, and the average small business is owed approximately £22,000 in overdue invoices at any given time. This is not a minor inconvenience. It is a systemic extraction of working capital from the businesses that can least afford to lose it, and it is tolerated because the businesses being robbed are too small to fight back.

The VAT registration threshold, currently £90,000, creates what every serious analysis describes as a cliff edge. A business earning £89,999 in turnover pays no VAT. A business earning £90,001 must register, charge 20% VAT on all sales, file quarterly returns, and comply with Making Tax Digital requirements. For a business-to-consumer supplier, a plumber or beautician or electrician who cannot easily pass the cost on, registration can mean losing up to one-sixth of their income. The OBR has estimated that the annual lost turnover through businesses deliberately suppressing growth to remain below the threshold is £350 million. An IMF study published in 2024 found robust evidence that annual turnover growth slows by about one percentage point as firms approach the threshold. Accountants report clients who work four-day weeks, turn down jobs, and close for weeks at a time to avoid breaching it. The threshold is not protecting small businesses from bureaucracy; it is preventing them from growing.

The tax system has become actively hostile to small business ownership. Corporation tax for companies with profits above £250,000 is 25%, with a small profits rate of 19% for those below £50,000 and marginal relief in between. But the headline rates disguise the cumulative burden. The dividend allowance has been slashed from £5,000 in 2017/18 to £500 today. Dividend tax rates rise by a further two percentage points from April 2026, taking the basic rate from 8.75% to 10.75% and the higher rate from 33.75% to 35.75%. A small company owner-director who earns £50,000 in company profit now faces a combined effective tax rate of approximately 27.7% at the basic rate, rising to over 50% at the higher rate, once corporation tax and dividend tax are stacked. The dividend allowance cut alone has increased the tax bill of a typical owner-managed business by over £1,000 per year compared to 2017. It is now, from a pure tax perspective, worse to run a small limited company than to be a sole trader paying income tax and Class 4 National Insurance. The tax system is telling people not to incorporate, not to grow, not to build.

Progress will reverse this trajectory entirely. Britain’s route to economic redemption cannot reside only in monumental reindustrialisation or startup dynamics. The unicorn farm described in E3 produces the high-growth outliers. This document is about the broad base: the millions of businesses that employ most people, sustain most communities, and generate the economic resilience that keeps the country running when the headlines are about something else. Progress will create a new legal form, the Starter Ltd, that allows micro-businesses to operate with minimal reporting, no VAT, and almost no regulatory overhead. Progress will abolish IR35 and restore the freedom of freelancers to build their own businesses without fear of client blanket bans. Progress will eliminate the VAT cliff edge that punishes growth. Progress will slash the tax on dividends to make business ownership more attractive than salaried employment. Progress will enforce payment terms with statutory force so that large companies can no longer use small suppliers as interest-free credit facilities. And Progress will repeal the provisions of the Employment Rights Act 2025 that make hiring a first employee a legal minefield for a business with three people and a van.

The governing principle is this: every person in Britain who wants to start a business, run a business, or grow a business should find the state on their side, not in their way. The shopkeeper, the sole trader, the freelancer, the family firm: these are not administrative categories to be regulated. They are the people who built this country’s prosperity, and Progress will build the conditions for them to do it again.

###### E7.1: The Starter Ltd

The Problem

The legal architecture of company formation in the United Kingdom treats every business the same regardless of size. A two-person web design studio and a multinational insurer file with the same Companies House, comply with the same Companies Act 2006, and face the same categories of reporting obligation. The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 has added mandatory identity verification for all directors and persons with significant control, with compliance required by November 2026. Companies House filing fees have increased sharply: digital incorporation rose from £12 to £50 in May 2024 and again to £100 from February 2026; the annual confirmation statement fee rose from £13 to £34 and then to £50. Micro-entities must now file a profit and loss account. Small companies must file their profit and loss account and directors’ report. These requirements exist for good reason in the context of large and medium-sized companies where public accountability for corporate behaviour is essential. Applied to a sole trader who incorporated to gain limited liability protection and employs nobody but themselves, they are an absurd overhead that consumes time better spent doing the work the business exists to do.

The 4.1 million non-employing businesses in the UK, representing 74% of all private sector enterprises, overwhelmingly exist because their owners wanted to work for themselves. Many are sole traders who chose limited company status for the liability protection, the professional credibility, or the historically more favourable tax treatment that incorporation once offered. The regulatory burden they carry is wholly disproportionate to any conceivable risk they pose to the public, to creditors, or to the tax system. These businesses do not need corporate governance frameworks designed for companies with shareholders, boards, and complex capital structures. They need a legal form that lets them get on with it.

Several comparable economies have recognised this. France’s micro-entreprise regime allows businesses below specified turnover thresholds to operate with a flat-rate tax, minimal accounting, and no VAT. Estonia’s e-Residency programme allows company formation in minutes with digital-first administration. New Zealand’s look-through company structure provides simplified reporting for small entities. The United Kingdom, which prides itself on ease of doing business, has moved in the opposite direction: more verification, more reporting, more fees, more compliance, more reasons not to bother.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Small Business Liberation Act will establish:

- a) The Starter Ltd, a new corporate legal form available to any business with no more than ten employees (including the founder) and annual turnover of no more than £250,000. The Starter Ltd will be incorporated through a single digital form, processed within 24 hours, at a fee of £20. The form will require: the name and verified identity of the founder, a registered address, a brief description of the business activity, and confirmation that the business is being formed for a lawful purpose. No memorandum or articles of association will be required; a statutory default constitution will apply unless the founder elects otherwise. The Starter Ltd will have full limited liability protection identical to a conventional limited company.
- b) Minimal reporting requirements. The Starter Ltd will file a single annual return, combining the functions of the current confirmation statement and accounts filing, consisting of: total turnover for the year, total profit or loss, number of employees, and confirmation that the business continues to trade for a lawful purpose. No profit and loss account, no directors’ report, no balance sheet. The annual return will be filed digitally and the fee will be £20. No audit requirement. No requirement to use accounting software that conforms to Making Tax Digital specifications, provided the annual return is filed digitally and the business maintains records sufficient to calculate its tax liability.
- c) VAT exemption. A Starter Ltd with turnover below £250,000 will not be required to register for VAT, regardless of whether its turnover exceeds the general £90,000 VAT registration threshold. This provision operates as a targeted exemption for the Starter Ltd form only and does not alter the general VAT registration threshold for other business types. The exemption eliminates the cliff edge entirely for micro-businesses and removes the single greatest structural disincentive to small business growth in the current system. The revenue impact is addressed in the fiscal analysis below.
- d) Corporation tax at a flat 15% on all profits, with no requirement to calculate marginal relief. This is lower than the current small profits rate of 19% and provides a clear, simple, and attractive tax proposition.
