The Starter Ltd founder will know their tax rate without needing an accountant to explain the interaction between the small profits rate, marginal relief, and the main rate. The rate applies to all Starter Ltd profits regardless of quantum, provided the business remains within the eligibility criteria.
- e) Seamless transition to a conventional limited company. When a Starter Ltd exceeds either the ten-employee or £250,000 turnover threshold, or when the founder elects to transition, the business will convert to a standard limited company through an annual continuation statement filed with Companies House. The transition will preserve the company’s registration number, trading history, and contractual relationships. No re-incorporation. No new registration. No interruption to trading. The business simply moves into the standard Companies Act regime with full reporting obligations from the next accounting period. The transition is designed to be as frictionless as possible so that growth is never penalised.

OPERATIONAL

Companies House implementation. Within six months of Royal Assent, Companies House will develop the Starter Ltd digital incorporation portal and the simplified annual return form. Existing micro-entity and small company limited companies that meet the Starter Ltd eligibility criteria will be offered the option to re-register as a Starter Ltd through a streamlined digital process. No business will be required to convert; the option is voluntary.

HMRC implementation. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, HMRC will publish guidance on the Starter Ltd corporation tax rate and VAT exemption. The CT600 return will be simplified for Starter Ltd companies to a single-page digital submission. HMRC will implement the 15% flat rate through the existing corporation tax self-assessment system with no action required from the business beyond filing.

###### E7.2: The First Hire

The Problem

The single most consequential decision a micro-business owner makes is whether to hire their first employee. It is also the decision most likely to be abandoned because of the regulatory burden it triggers. Before a sole trader or micro-business can bring on one additional person, they must: register as an employer with HMRC, set up PAYE, obtain employer’s liability insurance (a legal requirement carrying a fine of £2,500 per day for non-compliance), enrol in a workplace pension scheme under auto-enrolment legislation, establish a compliant employment contract, provide a written statement of employment particulars from day one, comply with working time regulations, provide statutory sick pay from day one (under the Employment Rights Act 2025, which removed the previous waiting period), establish procedures for handling flexible working requests (now a day-one right), and prepare for the prospect that, from 2027, the qualifying period for unfair dismissal protection will be reduced from two years to six months. The Employment Rights Act 2025 also removes the statutory cap on unfair dismissal compensation, meaning a micro-business that gets a dismissal wrong faces theoretically unlimited liability.

The cumulative effect is that a plumber earning £60,000 who wants to take on a mate faces a compliance cost that the Federation of Small Businesses has estimated at several thousand pounds before the employee has done a day’s work, and an ongoing administrative burden that consumes hours every week. Meanwhile, the plumber’s competitor whose spouse and children work informally in the family business faces none of these obligations because the employment relationship is not formalised. The system creates an incentive to keep businesses informal, to avoid growth, and to stay below the threshold at which legal obligations kick in. It punishes exactly the entrepreneurial behaviour that Progress wants to encourage.

The solution is not to abolish employment rights. Workers deserve protection, and the abuses that employment law addresses are real. The solution is to recognise that a three-person electrical firm and a three-thousand-person logistics company should not face identical regulatory frameworks. The risk profile is different. The power imbalance is different. The capacity to absorb administrative overhead is different. A proportionate system would recognise these differences and calibrate obligations accordingly.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Small Business Liberation Act will establish:

- a) A Micro-Employer Exemption for businesses with no more than ten employees. Micro-employers will be exempt from the following obligations during the first two years of each new employment relationship: the enhanced unfair dismissal protections introduced by the Employment Rights Act 2025, including the six-month qualifying period reduction and the removal of the compensation cap. The existing two-year qualifying period and the existing statutory cap on unfair dismissal compensation will continue to apply to micro-employers. This does not remove protection from discriminatory dismissal, whistleblower protection, or dismissal for asserting a statutory right, all of which remain from day one regardless of employer size.
- b) Simplified auto-enrolment for micro-employers. Businesses with no more than five employees will be permitted to meet their auto-enrolment obligations through a single national micro-employer pension scheme, administered centrally by NEST, with a single flat-rate contribution schedule and a single digital enrolment form. The employer will not be required to select, compare, or administer a pension scheme. They will enrol their employees through a one-page online process and make a single monthly payment. The compliance burden that currently requires a micro-employer to understand contribution thresholds, qualifying earnings bands, and opt-out procedures will be replaced by a system so simple that it can be administered in five minutes per month.
- c) A statutory First Hire Support Package. For the first employee hired by any business that has never previously employed anyone, the employer will receive: a 12-month exemption from employer NICs on that employee’s earnings; a £1,000 First Hire Grant payable after six months of continuous employment; and access to a dedicated HMRC First Hire helpline providing guidance on PAYE registration, pension enrolment, and employment contract requirements. The exemption and grant are available once per business and are designed to reduce the financial shock of the transition from sole trader to employer.
- d) Repeal of the removal of the unfair dismissal compensation cap as it applies to micro-employers. Progress recognises that the uncapped liability introduced by the Employment Rights Act 2025 was designed to address abuses by large employers. Applied to a business with three employees, it creates a litigation risk so disproportionate to the employer’s capacity that it deters hiring altogether. The statutory cap will be retained for micro-employers at the pre-2025 level, indexed to CPI.

OPERATIONAL

HMRC guidance. Within 60 days of Royal Assent, HMRC will publish a First Hire Guide: a single, plain-language document covering every obligation triggered by a business’s first employment. The guide will be no longer than ten pages, will include step-by-step instructions for PAYE registration, pension enrolment, and contract preparation, and will be available in print at every Post Office in the country. The First Hire helpline will be operational within 90 days.

Employment tribunal reform. Within six months, the Ministry of Justice will publish revised guidance for employment tribunals on the application of the Micro-Employer Exemption, ensuring that tribunal decisions account for the size, resources, and administrative capacity of the employer when assessing the reasonableness of procedures followed.

###### E7.3: The End of IR35

The Problem

IR35, the off-payroll working rules first introduced in 2000 and dramatically expanded by the extension to the private sector in April 2021, was designed to prevent “disguised employment”: arrangements in which a worker who is functionally an employee supplies their services through a personal service company to reduce their tax liability. The principle was defensible. The execution has been catastrophic for the freelance economy.

IPSE’s IR35 Spotlight 2025, surveying contractors across the UK, found that 26% are currently out of work, up from 18% in 2023. Of those not working, 56% attribute their situation directly to the impact of IR35 reforms on client hiring practices. The proportion of engagements determined to be outside IR35 has fallen from 80% in 2023 to 70% in 2025. Two-thirds of contractors report feeling less confident about securing outside-IR35 roles in the year ahead. The core mechanism of the damage is the blanket assessment: rather than assess each engagement individually as the law requires, many large and medium-sized clients have imposed blanket inside-IR35 determinations or blanket bans on engaging limited company contractors altogether, because the compliance risk and administrative cost of making individual assessments is too high. IPSE’s research found that 5% of respondents reported their client had determined all engagements to be inside IR35, a blanket assessment that is itself a form of non-compliance with the rules.

The economic cost is severe. The British Chambers of Commerce reported in 2024 that 74% of businesses experienced recruitment difficulties, with IR35 identified as a contributing factor to skills shortages costing the economy an estimated £94 billion per year. Freelancers and contractors contributed £331 billion to the UK economy in 2023, according to IPSE’s Self-Employed Landscape report. This is not a marginal workforce. It is a sector whose economic contribution exceeds the GDP of many European countries, and it is being systematically suppressed by a tax compliance regime that has made clients afraid to engage it.

The tragedy is that IR35 does not even achieve its stated objective efficiently. The genuinely disguised employees it was designed to catch are a small fraction of the contractor workforce. The vast majority of contractors are genuine businesses providing specialist services to multiple clients, bearing commercial risk, and operating with the autonomy that distinguishes a business from an employment. IR35 catches the innocent along with the guilty, and the collateral damage to the freelance economy, to the businesses that rely on flexible labour, and to the individuals whose careers have been destroyed by blanket bans, vastly exceeds any revenue gain. The self-employed sector is the seedbed of future business formation. Every freelancer is a potential employer, a potential growth company, a potential Starter Ltd scaling toward something larger. IR35 poisons the soil.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Small Business Liberation Act will establish:

- a) Full repeal of the off-payroll working rules (Chapter 10 of Part 2 of the Income Tax (Earnings and Pensions) Act 2003 as amended). The obligation on clients to determine the IR35 status of contractors and to operate PAYE where a determination of inside IR35 is made will be removed in its entirety. From the first April following Royal Assent, the responsibility for determining employment status for tax purposes will revert to the individual contractor and their personal service company, as was the case before the 2017 public sector and 2021 private sector reforms.
- b) A clear statutory definition of self-employment for tax purposes, replacing the current multi-factor common law test with a statutory test based on three determinative criteria: the right to send a substitute, the absence of mutuality of obligation between engagements, and the right to control the manner in which the work is performed. A contractor who satisfies any two of these three criteria will be treated as self-employed for all tax purposes. This provides certainty for contractors, clients, and HMRC, eliminating the case-by-case ambiguity that created the compliance fear driving blanket bans.
- c) An anti-avoidance provision to address the genuine mischief IR35 was designed to prevent. Where HMRC can demonstrate that an individual has been engaged continuously by a single client for more than 24 months, works exclusively for that client, and is subject to the same degree of control as a permanent employee, HMRC may issue a Deemed Employment Notice requiring the client to operate PAYE. This targeted provision catches the genuinely disguised employee without penalising the legitimate contractor who works for multiple clients on defined projects.
- d) A statutory prohibition on blanket IR35 determinations. Any client that issues a blanket inside-IR35 determination or a blanket ban on engaging limited company contractors, without conducting an individual assessment of each engagement, will be liable for a civil penalty and will be required to compensate affected contractors for demonstrable loss of earnings. This provision ensures that the compliance failures of the past cannot recur even under the pre-2017 framework.

OPERATIONAL

HMRC guidance. Within 30 days of Royal Assent, HMRC will publish guidance confirming the repeal of the off-payroll working rules and the reversion to the pre-2017 framework. HMRC will withdraw all existing Status Determination Statement templates and the Check Employment Status for Tax (CEST) tool. New guidance on the statutory definition of self-employment will be published within 60 days.

Contractor confidence programme. The Department for Business and Trade will launch a national communications campaign directed at businesses and contractors confirming that IR35 off-payroll rules have been repealed, that contractors may engage through their limited companies without client-side risk, and that blanket bans are now unlawful. The campaign will run for 12 months following Royal Assent.

###### E7.4: The VAT Cliff Edge

The Problem

The VAT registration threshold, currently set at £90,000, is the joint highest in the OECD. At first glance this looks generous: it keeps more small businesses out of the VAT system. In practice, it creates the single most destructive growth barrier in the small business landscape. The threshold operates as a cliff edge. A business with turnover of £89,999 has no VAT obligations. A business with turnover of £90,001 must register for VAT, charge 20% on all sales, file quarterly returns under Making Tax Digital, and absorb the administrative cost of VAT compliance. For a business-to-consumer supplier who cannot pass the VAT charge on to customers, crossing the threshold can mean an immediate loss of up to £14,000 per year: the difference between charging customers the pre-VAT price and the post-VAT price, absorbed entirely by the business.

The behavioural evidence is overwhelming. The OBR has estimated that the annual lost turnover caused by businesses deliberately suppressing growth to remain below the threshold is £350 million. An IMF working paper published in 2024 found robust evidence that annual growth in turnover slows by approximately one percentage point as firms approach the threshold, and that this response is driven by businesses genuinely reducing output rather than falsely underreporting turnover. HMRC’s own 2024 study into VAT registration behaviour confirmed that many businesses actively manage their income to avoid crossing the threshold. Accountants report clients who work four-day weeks, turn down profitable work, close for weeks at a time, and decline to take on apprentices because the additional revenue would push them over the line. The threshold is a tax on ambition. It tells every successful small business in Britain: grow at your peril.

The Starter Ltd VAT exemption described in E7.1 eliminates the cliff edge entirely for businesses that adopt that legal form. But many businesses operate as sole traders, partnerships, or conventional limited companies and will not wish to convert. For these businesses, Progress will introduce a graduated transition that replaces the cliff edge with a ramp, ensuring that no business is ever worse off for having grown.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Small Business Liberation Act will establish:

- a) A VAT graduation zone between £90,000 and £150,000 in annual turnover. Businesses with turnover within this zone will be required to register for VAT but will charge VAT at a reduced graduated rate rather than the full 20%. The graduated rate will start at 5% for businesses at £90,001 and increase by one percentage point for every £4,000 of additional turnover, reaching the full 20% rate at £150,000. This ensures that crossing the £90,000 threshold results in a VAT charge of 5% on the marginal pound, not 20%, and that the transition to the full rate is smooth and predictable. No business will ever face a situation in which earning £1 more in turnover costs them £14,000.
- b) A 12-month First Registration Grace Period. Any business registering for VAT for the first time will have a 12-month period during which all penalties for late filing, late payment, or administrative errors in VAT returns will be waived, provided the business is making a genuine effort to comply. During the grace period, HMRC will assign a dedicated VAT adviser to the business, available by phone and email, to assist with the transition. The grace period does not reduce or defer the VAT liability itself; it provides a safety net against the administrative mistakes that are inevitable when a business encounters the VAT system for the first time.
- c) Simplification of the Flat Rate Scheme. The existing VAT Flat Rate Scheme, which allows eligible businesses to pay a fixed percentage of their turnover as VAT rather than calculating input and output tax, will be reformed to increase its accessibility and attractiveness. The turnover limit for the Flat Rate Scheme will be raised from £150,000 to £250,000. The flat-rate percentages will be reviewed and reduced where current rates exceed the effective VAT rate that would be paid under standard accounting, ensuring the scheme provides a genuine simplification benefit and not merely a different route to the same liability.

OPERATIONAL

HMRC implementation. Within six months of Royal Assent, HMRC will implement the graduated VAT rate within the existing Making Tax Digital infrastructure. Businesses in the graduation zone will file standard VAT returns but the system will automatically calculate the applicable graduated rate based on cumulative turnover for the period. The First Registration Grace Period will apply automatically to all new VAT registrations from the first April following Royal Assent.

Fiscal impact. The VAT graduation zone will reduce VAT revenue from businesses in the £90,000 to £150,000 turnover band. However, the OBR’s own estimate that £350 million in turnover is currently suppressed by the cliff edge suggests that the behavioural response, businesses that currently limit their growth now choosing to expand, will partially offset the static revenue cost. The net fiscal impact is estimated to be modest and is funded through the broader revenue gains from the economic growth generated by E1 through E6.

###### E7.5: Making Ownership Pay

The Problem

The tax treatment of small business ownership in the United Kingdom has deteriorated to the point where, for many people, it is now financially worse to run a limited company than to take a salaried job. This is not rhetoric; it is arithmetic. A small company owner-director who earns £50,000 in pre-tax company profit pays 19% corporation tax (£9,500), leaving £40,500 available for dividends. After the £500 dividend allowance, the remaining £40,000 is taxed at 8.75% (basic rate), producing a dividend tax bill of £3,500. The total tax paid is £13,000 on £50,000 of profit: an effective rate of 26%. From April 2026, when dividend tax rises by two percentage points, the rate on the same income rises to approximately 27.7%. A salaried employee earning £50,000 pays income tax of £7,486 and employee NICs of £3,002: a total of £10,488, or 21%. The company owner pays more, takes more risk, has no employer’s pension contribution, no statutory sick pay, no paid holiday, and no employment rights.

The gap widens at higher incomes. A company owner-director earning £100,000 in company profit faces corporation tax of 19% on the first £50,000 and marginal relief producing an effective rate of approximately 26.5% on the next £50,000, leaving approximately £77,250 available for dividends. Dividend tax at the higher rate of 33.75% (rising to 35.75% from April 2026) produces a combined effective rate exceeding 50%. This person has built a business, employed people, taken commercial risk, and is rewarded with an effective tax rate higher than a salaried employee earning the same amount. The message from the British tax system is unambiguous: do not start a business. Do not incorporate. Do not grow. Take a salary instead.

The erosion has been deliberate and incremental. The dividend allowance was £5,000 when introduced in 2016/17. It was cut to £2,000 in 2018/19, to £1,000 in 2023/24, and to £500 in 2024/25. Each reduction has been presented as a minor adjustment; in aggregate they constitute a fundamental shift in the economics of business ownership. The November 2025 Budget’s further two-percentage-point increase in dividend tax rates from April 2026, combined with the frozen personal allowance and higher rate threshold, means that a small company owner will pay more tax in 2026/27 than at any point in the modern history of the limited company.

Progress will make business ownership pay again. The striver’s compact described in E6 applies with particular force to the small business owner: if running a business does not visibly reward the person who runs it, no amount of rhetoric about entrepreneurship will produce more businesses.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Small Business Liberation Act will establish:

- a) Restoration of the dividend allowance to £5,000, effective from the first April following Royal Assent. This restores the allowance to its original 2016/17 level and immediately reduces the tax bill of every small company owner-director. For a basic-rate taxpayer, the restoration saves approximately £394 per year at current rates; for a higher-rate taxpayer, approximately £1,519 per year. These are not large sums for the Exchequer. They are significant sums for a business owner deciding whether the administrative burden and financial risk of incorporation are worth it.
- b) Reversal of the April 2026 dividend tax increase. The basic rate of dividend tax will be reduced from 10.75% back to 8.75%, and the higher rate from 35.75% back to 33.75%, effective from the first April following Royal Assent. The additional rate will remain unchanged at 39.35%. This reversal sends an immediate signal that Progress is on the side of the business owner, not the Treasury.
- c) A Small Business Corporation Tax rate of 15% for companies with profits up to £100,000 that employ at least one person other than the director. This rate, matching the Starter Ltd rate described in E7.1, extends the tax advantage to conventional limited companies that are actively employing people. The employment condition ensures that the reduced rate rewards businesses that create jobs, not passive holding structures. Marginal relief will apply between £100,000 and £250,000, transitioning smoothly to the main rate of 25%.
- d) An Annual Investment Allowance increase to £1.5 million for small businesses with turnover below £500,000. This enables micro and small businesses to write off the full cost of capital investment, from equipment and vehicles to technology and fit-out, in the year of purchase. The current £1 million allowance is already generous for most small businesses, but the increase to £1.5 million provides additional headroom for businesses in capital-intensive sectors such as construction, manufacturing, and hospitality.

OPERATIONAL

HMRC implementation. The dividend allowance restoration and rate reversal will take effect from the first April following Royal Assent and will be implemented through the self-assessment system. No action required from taxpayers beyond filing their return. The 15% Small Business Corporation Tax rate will be implemented within 90 days through amendments to the existing corporation tax self-assessment software.

The ownership proposition. The combined effect of E7.5, the Starter Ltd (E7.1), and the Tax Reset (E6) is transformative. A small business owner earning £50,000 in company profit under Progress’ reforms will pay: 15% corporation tax (£7,500), leaving £42,500; with a £5,000 dividend allowance and an 8.75% basic rate on the remainder, the dividend tax is approximately £3,281. Total tax: £10,781, an effective rate of 21.6%. This is lower than the salaried employee’s rate and reflects the additional risk, effort, and social value that the business owner provides. The striver’s compact holds: if you build something, you keep more of what you earn.

###### E7.6: Late Payment Enforcement and the Regulatory Bonfire

The Problem

Late payment is systemic, structural, and tolerated. Government research published in 2025 estimates that UK businesses are owed approximately £26 billion in late payments at any given time. Over 1.5 million businesses are affected annually. Late payment contributes to approximately 14,000 business closures each year. The wider economic cost is estimated at nearly £11 billion per annum, comprising lost output, diverted management time, and the cost of short-term financing that businesses are forced to take on to cover the cash flow gap created by clients who do not pay on time. The FSB’s 2025 survey found that 45% of small businesses are experiencing more late payments than twelve months ago, and that 52% forfeit late payments up to ten times a year because the cost of chasing exceeds the value recovered. Micro-businesses have the worst of it: 4.61% of their turnover is tied up in late payments at any given time, and the average small business spends 1.5 hours per day chasing unpaid invoices, time worth £6.3 billion to the small business economy annually.

The existing remedies are theoretically available but practically useless. The Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 gives businesses the right to charge interest on late payments, but almost nobody exercises it because doing so risks losing the client. The Prompt Payment Code is voluntary and unenforceable. The Small Business Commissioner has advisory powers but no teeth. Large companies routinely extend payment terms to 60, 90, or even 120 days, using their small suppliers as interest-free credit facilities. The government’s own late payments consultation in 2025 acknowledged the scale of the problem and proposed legislative measures, but the pace of reform is glacial relative to the damage being done. Progress will act with the urgency the problem demands.

The regulatory burden on small businesses extends well beyond late payment. The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 introduced mandatory identity verification for directors and persons with significant control, with compliance required by November 2026. Companies House filing fees have increased by over 300% for some filings since 2024. The Employment Rights Act 2025 has added layers of employment law obligation that fall disproportionately on micro-employers, as described in E7.2. Making Tax Digital requires VAT-registered businesses to use compatible software and file digital returns. The cumulative effect is a regulatory environment that grows more complex and more expensive every year, without any corresponding assessment of whether the burden on the smallest businesses is proportionate to the risk they pose.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Small Business Liberation Act will establish:

- a) Mandatory 30-day payment terms for all business-to-business contracts where the supplier is an SME with turnover below £10 million. Any contractual term purporting to extend payment beyond 30 days from the date of a valid invoice will be unenforceable. The 30-day term will apply as a statutory implied term that cannot be excluded by contract. Businesses with turnover above £10 million that are purchasing from SMEs will be bound by the 30-day maximum. This provision directly addresses the structural power imbalance that allows large companies to impose extended payment terms on small suppliers who are not in a position to negotiate.
- b) Automatic statutory interest on late payments at the Bank of England base rate plus 8%, accruing from day 31. This codifies and strengthens the existing Late Payment of Commercial Debts Act provision but makes it automatic: the interest accrues without the supplier needing to invoke it, claim it, or risk the relationship by demanding it. The interest is a statutory debt recoverable through the courts alongside the principal. Where the late payer is a public body, the interest will be paid from the relevant department’s budget, not from a central fund, creating a direct financial incentive for departmental procurement teams to pay on time.
- c) A Late Payment Enforcement Order. Where a business has a pattern of paying SME suppliers late, defined as three or more invoices unpaid beyond 30 days within any six-month period, the Small Business Commissioner will have the power to issue a Late Payment Enforcement Order requiring the business to clear all outstanding invoices within 14 days, pay all accrued statutory interest, and submit to quarterly payment audits for 12 months. Failure to comply with an Enforcement Order will result in a civil penalty of up to 5% of the defaulting company’s UK turnover, enforceable by the Commissioner through the courts. The Small Business Commissioner’s office will be given the statutory powers, staffing, and budget to act as a credible enforcement body, not an advisory service.
- d) The Regulatory Proportionality Principle. The Act will establish a statutory duty on all regulators and government departments to assess the proportionality of regulatory requirements on businesses with fewer than ten employees before introducing or extending any regulation that applies to them. Where a regulation imposes costs or administrative burdens that are disproportionate to the risk posed by micro-businesses, the regulator will be required to provide a specific micro-business exemption or a simplified compliance pathway. The principle will be enforced by the Better Regulation Executive and will apply retrospectively to regulations introduced since 2020.
- e) Reversal of specified regulatory measures. The Act will: repeal the requirement for micro-entity companies to file a profit and loss account with Companies House (reverting to balance sheet only); reduce Companies House fees for micro-entity and small company filings to pre-2024 levels; exempt businesses with fewer than ten employees from mandatory identity verification requirements under the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 where the directors are natural persons whose identities are already verified through HMRC’s self-assessment or PAYE systems; and exempt micro-employers from the enhanced flexible working request procedures introduced by the Employment Rights Act 2025, while retaining the existing pre-2025 flexible working framework for these employers.

OPERATIONAL

Small Business Commissioner reform. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Small Business Commissioner’s office will be restructured as a statutory enforcement body with investigative powers, penalty-issuing authority, and a dedicated staff increase to at least 200 full-time equivalent positions. The Commissioner will publish quarterly reports on late payment compliance by sector and by named large companies, creating reputational as well as financial consequences for serial late payers.

Regulatory review. Within six months, the Better Regulation Executive will publish a comprehensive audit of all regulations introduced since 2020 that impose obligations on businesses with fewer than ten employees, assessing each against the Regulatory Proportionality Principle. Regulations that fail the proportionality test will be subject to a statutory timetable for exemption, simplification, or repeal, with all changes to be implemented within 18 months of the audit’s publication.

###### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The E7 framework is built on the Small Business Liberation Act, a single piece of primary legislation introduced in the first King’s Speech alongside the Tax Reset Act (E6), the Energy Security Act (E1), the Prosperity Zones Act (E2), and the Enterprise and Innovation Act (E3). No additional Acts are required. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, or departmental action.

Small Business Liberation Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: Creation of the Starter Ltd, a new corporate legal form for businesses with no more than ten employees and turnover below £250,000, with simplified incorporation (£20 fee, 24-hour processing), minimal annual reporting (single-page digital return), full limited liability, no VAT registration requirement below £250,000, flat 15% corporation tax rate, and seamless transition to conventional limited company via annual continuation statement. Micro-Employer Exemption retaining the two-year unfair dismissal qualifying period and statutory compensation cap for businesses with no more than ten employees, preserving day-one protections for discriminatory dismissal and whistleblowing. Simplified auto-enrolment through a single national micro-employer pension scheme for businesses with five or fewer employees. First Hire Support Package: 12-month employer NICs exemption, £1,000 grant after six months, dedicated HMRC helpline. Full repeal of IR35 off-payroll working rules (Chapter 10, Part 2, ITEPA 2003). Statutory definition of self-employment based on three determinative criteria (substitution, mutuality, control). Anti-avoidance provision for genuine disguised employment (24-month single-client test with Deemed Employment Notice). Statutory prohibition on blanket IR35 determinations with civil penalties. VAT graduation zone from £90,000 to £150,000 with graduated rate starting at 5%. 12-month First Registration Grace Period for all new VAT registrations. Flat Rate Scheme threshold raised to £250,000. Dividend allowance restored to £5,000. Reversal of April 2026 dividend tax increase (basic rate to 8.75%, higher rate to 33.75%). Small Business Corporation Tax rate of 15% for employing companies with profits up to £100,000. Annual Investment Allowance increase to £1.5 million for businesses with turnover below £500,000. Mandatory 30-day payment terms for all B2B contracts where the supplier is an SME. Automatic statutory interest on late payments at base rate plus 8%. Late Payment Enforcement Orders with civil penalties of up to 5% of UK turnover. Statutory Regulatory Proportionality Principle with retrospective application. Reversal of specified regulatory measures including Companies House P&L filing for micro-entities, filing fee reductions, identity verification exemptions for micro-businesses, and repeal of enhanced flexible working obligations for micro-employers.

Delivered operationally: Companies House Starter Ltd portal within six months. HMRC guidance on Starter Ltd tax treatment within 90 days. HMRC First Hire Guide (ten pages, plain language) within 60 days, available at every Post Office. First Hire helpline operational within 90 days. HMRC guidance confirming IR35 repeal within 30 days. Withdrawal of CEST tool and SDS templates within 30 days. New self-employment status guidance within 60 days. Department for Business and Trade contractor confidence campaign for 12 months. Graduated VAT rate implementation within six months. First Registration Grace Period from first April. Dividend allowance restoration and rate reversal from first April. 15% Small Business Corporation Tax rate within 90 days. Small Business Commissioner restructured as statutory enforcement body within 90 days with 200 FTE. Quarterly late payment compliance reports by sector and named company. Better Regulation Executive proportionality audit within six months. Regulatory simplification or repeal timetable within 18 months.

Funding the Small Business Liberation

The measures in E7 are a combination of revenue-reducing reforms (lower corporation tax for small businesses, restored dividend allowance, VAT graduation zone) and revenue-neutral or revenue-positive structural changes (late payment enforcement, regulatory simplification, IR35 repeal). The revenue cost of the tax measures is funded through three sources.

First, the growth dividend. The OBR’s estimate that £350 million in turnover is currently suppressed by the VAT cliff edge alone suggests that the behavioural response to removing growth barriers will be substantial. Businesses that currently limit their output to stay below thresholds will grow, hire, invest, and generate additional tax revenue across income tax, NICs, VAT (at graduated rates), and corporation tax. The combined effect of E7’s reforms on business formation rates, hiring, and output growth is conservatively estimated to offset a significant proportion of the static revenue cost within three years.

Second, the late payment dividend. Enforcing 30-day payment terms releases approximately £26 billion in working capital currently trapped in late payments. This capital, returned to small businesses, is spent, invested, and circulated through the economy, generating tax revenue at every stage. The reduction in business closures, currently 14,000 per year attributable to late payment, preserves employment, output, and tax revenue that would otherwise be lost.

Third, state efficiency savings. As with E6, the tax reductions in E7 are funded not by borrowing but by delivering public services better for less. The State Capacity programme, the procurement reform described in E10, and the civil service productivity improvements across Progress’ programme generate savings that reduce the total cost of the state, enabling lower tax rates without reducing service quality.

E7 completes the supply-side liberation of the British economy at the level where most people actually experience it. E1 provides cheap energy. E2 creates the zones where industry concentrates. E3 builds the high-growth companies. E4 liberates the planning system. E5 makes housing affordable. E6 ensures workers keep what they earn. E7 ensures that anyone who wants to start a business, hire their first employee, grow beyond the VAT threshold, or simply operate without drowning in paperwork, finds a state that is on their side. The unicorn farm (E3) produces the outliers. The nation of shopkeepers (E7) produces the foundation: the broad-based employment, community wealth, and economic resilience that sustains the whole system. Napoleon meant it as an insult. Progress means it as a promise.

#### E8. Driving Down the Cost of Living

Governing Principle

The average British household spent £623.30 per week in the financial year ending March 2024, according to the ONS Family Spending survey: a nominal increase of 10% on the previous year but, after adjusting for inflation, a real-terms figure that remains £105.20 lower than before the pandemic. That single statistic captures the central experience of the British economy for most people. Wages have risen, but prices have risen faster. The gap between what people earn and what they can actually buy with it has widened in every category that matters: food, transport, childcare, insurance, and the cumulative regulatory burden that inflates the price of almost everything they purchase. The previous documents in this framework address the three largest components of the household budget: energy (E1), housing (E5), and tax (E6). This document addresses everything else.

UK food prices rose by a cumulative 38.6% between November 2020 and November 2025, according to ONS Consumer Price Index data. Food and non-alcoholic drink inflation stood at 4.5% in December 2025, above the headline CPI rate of 3.2%. The British Retail Consortium forecast an average food price rise of 4.2% in the latter half of 2025, driven in substantial part by the April 2025 employer National Insurance increase of 1.2 percentage points, the 6.7% rise in the National Living Wage, and the Extended Producer Responsibility regulations for packaging. The Food and Drink Federation confirmed that food manufacturers were passing on cost increases driven overwhelmingly by government regulation and policy decisions. UK households spend on average 11.3% of all expenditure on food and non-alcoholic drink, rising to 14.3% for the poorest fifth. The Food Foundation reported that 7.2 million adults, 13.6% of the population, experienced food insecurity. The cost of a basic nutritious weekly basket for an average woman rose 27.3% between April 2022 and January 2025, to £52.13 per week. Healthier foods are more than twice as expensive per calorie as less healthy alternatives, and their prices have risen at twice the rate: 21% for healthier foods versus 11% for less healthy options between 2022 and 2024. The food system is not failing because of global commodity shocks. In 2025, the primary driver of food inflation is domestic policy: employer NICs, the National Living Wage, energy costs, business rates, and packaging regulation.

Transport costs consume a further substantial portion of household budgets. Rail fares across Great Britain increased by 5.1% in 2025, with fares in the London and South East sector rising 5.2% and long-distance fares by 5.4%. An annual season ticket from Woking to London costs £4,260, with a further increase initially projected at 5.8% for 2026 before the government announced a freeze on regulated fares. The freeze covers only 45% of tickets sold; unregulated fares rose 5.5% in March 2025 and remain uncapped. At the pump, petrol averages 135.37 pence per litre and diesel 144.27 pence per litre as of December 2025. Fuel duty stands at 52.95 pence per litre, frozen since 2011 but scheduled for phased increases from September 2026 to return to 57.95 pence by March 2027, followed by annual RPI indexation from April 2027. Car insurance premiums, which hit a record average of £995 at the end of 2023, have fallen to approximately £559 by late 2025 according to ABI data, but remain 40% higher than pre-pandemic levels. Insurance Premium Tax at 12% adds a further £67 to the average policy. For a household running two cars, the combined cost of insurance, fuel, road tax, and maintenance exceeds £5,000 per year before the vehicle itself is paid for.

Childcare remains one of the most punishing costs facing working families. The average weekly cost of full-time nursery care in England for a child under two was £302.10 in 2024, equating to approximately £15,700 per year. In Inner London, full-time nursery care for an under-two exceeds £30,000 per year, equivalent to nearly 70% of the median take-home salary for one working parent. The OECD reports that net childcare costs for a UK couple with two children account for approximately a quarter of net household income, placing Britain among the most expensive countries in the developed world for childcare. The government’s expansion of funded hours to 30 hours per week for working parents of children from nine months, reaching full rollout in September 2025, has reduced headline costs for eligible families. The average weekly cost for a part-time place for an under-two has fallen from £159.61 to £70.51 for those receiving funded hours. But families who do not qualify, including those where one parent earns above £100,000 or where a parent is not working, pay the full rate. The funding rate paid by government to nurseries does not cover the true cost of provision, forcing providers to cross-subsidise funded places from fee-paying parents, inflate ancillary charges, or reduce quality. The supply of nursery places has not expanded to meet the demand created by the entitlement expansion, and Ofsted data shows a net reduction in registered childcare providers in recent years. The childcare system is trapped between rising demand, constrained supply, and a funding model that underpays providers and overcharges the families who fall outside the eligibility criteria.

The cost of living crisis is not a single problem with a single cause. It is the compound result of dozens of policy choices, each individually defensible but collectively devastating, that have loaded cost after cost onto household budgets. Energy levies on bills (addressed in E1). A tax system that confiscates pay rises through fiscal drag (addressed in E6). A planning system that inflates housing costs (addressed in E4 and E5). Business rates that close high street shops and push purchases toward more expensive online alternatives (addressed in E6 and E7). IR35 rules that destroyed the freelance economy (addressed in E7). Employer NICs increases that cascade through every supply chain and appear in every supermarket receipt. Packaging regulations that add cost without corresponding consumer benefit. A rail fares formula pegged to RPI plus one percentage point, guaranteeing that commuting costs outstrip inflation every year. Insurance Premium Tax at 12% on every policy. A childcare market that produces some of the most expensive provision in the OECD. Each of these is a policy choice. Each can be reversed.

Progress’ approach in E8 is different from the preceding documents. E1 through E7 each address a structural domain: energy, planning, housing, startups, tax, small business. E8 is the synthesis. It addresses the residual costs that remain after the structural reforms have taken effect, and it quantifies the cumulative impact of the entire framework on the household budget. The governing principle is this: every policy in this framework must be measurable against a single test. Does the average household have more money left at the end of the month? If the answer is not visibly, tangibly, annually yes, then the policy is failing. Progress will publish, every year, a Household Impact Statement showing the combined effect of its reforms on a representative household at each income decile. The people of Britain will know, in pounds and pence, what their government has done for them. That is the standard to which Progress holds itself.

###### E8.1: Food Prices and Supply Chain Costs

The Problem

Food prices in Britain have risen 38.6% in five years. The causes are layered: global commodity volatility, post-Brexit trade friction, and domestic policy decisions that have inflated every stage of the supply chain. The government’s own Food Inflation Gateway, announced in 2025, acknowledged the need to assess regulation that could add to food prices. But the Gateway is an assessment tool, not a solution. Meanwhile, the policies driving food inflation are multiplying. The April 2025 employer NICs increase added approximately 1.2 percentage points to the rate and cut the secondary threshold from £9,100 to £5,000, imposing an estimated £25 billion in annual costs on businesses. Food manufacturing and retail, which employ millions of workers, absorbed a disproportionate share. The Food and Drink Federation confirmed that firms were passing on these cost increases to consumers. The 6.7% rise in the National Living Wage in April 2025, while justified in isolation, compounded the employer NICs impact in sectors where labour intensity is highest. The British Retail Consortium estimated that these combined costs would drive food price inflation of 4.2% in the latter half of 2025.

The Extended Producer Responsibility regulations for packaging, which impose compliance costs on food producers for the end-of-life management of packaging waste, add a further layer. The Bank of England identified these regulations as a contributing factor to food price inflation. Business rates on supermarket premises, distribution centres, and food processing facilities cascade directly into shelf prices. Energy costs, addressed in E1, are embedded in every stage of food production: growing, processing, refrigerating, transporting, and retailing. The energy cost differential between Britain and its European competitors means that British food producers face a structural cost disadvantage that is wholly independent of their efficiency or the quality of their produce.

Post-Brexit trade frictions have added an estimated £200 per fresh food shipment from the EU, according to the government’s own assessment in its 2025 Food Inflation Gateway announcement. The government is negotiating an agri-food agreement with the EU to reduce these costs, but the timeline is uncertain and the scope unclear. Meanwhile, UK food self-sufficiency stands at approximately 60%, meaning that trade costs on the remaining 40% feed directly into retail prices. Beef prices have been a particular driver: UK deadweight beef prices increased approximately 40% in the past year, with retail beef prices rising 17%, driven by reduced cattle numbers, declining profitability, and the cumulative effect of regulatory costs on farming.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Cost of Living Reduction Act will establish:

- a) The reversal of the employer NICs increase, as established in E6.2 of the Tax Reset, is the single most impactful measure for food prices. Restoring the rate from 15% to 13.8% and the secondary threshold from £5,000 to £9,100 removes approximately £25 billion in annual employment costs from the economy. For food retailers operating on margins of 2–4%, the NICs increase was not absorbable without price increases. Its reversal will flow directly into lower supply chain costs. The Act will require large food retailers with UK revenue exceeding £1 billion to publish, within six months of the NICs reversal taking effect, an audited statement showing the extent to which reduced employment costs have been passed through to consumer prices. This transparency mechanism ensures that the benefit reaches the shopping basket.
- b) Abolition of business rates for all food retail premises with a rateable value below £51,000, as established in E6.5. For independent grocers, butchers, bakers, fishmongers, and convenience stores, this eliminates business rates entirely. For larger premises above the threshold, the transition to the Land Value Business Levy shifts the tax base from the building to the land, ensuring that investment in premises, cold chain infrastructure, and energy efficiency does not trigger higher rates.
- c) A Food Supply Chain Cost Audit. The Act will require the Competition and Markets Authority to conduct, within 12 months of Royal Assent, a comprehensive audit of the costs imposed on the food supply chain by government regulation, covering: employer NICs and National Living Wage impacts; Extended Producer Responsibility compliance costs; food safety and hygiene regulation compliance costs for small producers; labelling and origin-marking requirements; import inspection and border control costs for food shipments; and planning restrictions that prevent the expansion of food processing and distribution capacity. The CMA will be required to quantify the consumer price impact of each regulatory cost and to recommend, within its report, which costs should be reduced, restructured, or abolished. The Secretary of State will be required to respond within 60 days with an action plan.
- d) Reduction of border friction on food imports. The Act will direct the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs to implement a risk-based import inspection regime that reduces physical inspection rates for food shipments from trusted trading partners to no more than 5% of consignments, with digital pre-clearance for all others. The current regime, which imposes checks that add time and cost to every shipment, will be replaced by a system that targets genuine biosecurity risks while allowing the vast majority of food imports to clear the border within hours. This is not a relaxation of food safety standards. It is an application of intelligence-led inspection that distinguishes between a container of French cheese and a container of unknown origin.

OPERATIONAL

Immediate impact. The employer NICs reversal (E6.2) and business rates abolition (E6.5) take effect from the first April following Royal Assent. The combined effect on food prices will be visible within two to three quarters as supply chain cost reductions work through to shelf prices. Progress estimates a reduction in food price inflation of 1.5 to 2.5 percentage points within the first 18 months, as the policy-driven component of food inflation is removed.

Energy pass-through. The energy bill reductions established in E1, including levy removal, Carbon Price Support abolition, and standing charge reform, reduce the energy cost embedded in food production, processing, cold chain logistics, and retail. The E1 measures deliver an immediate reduction in business energy costs of approximately 20–30%, which will feed through to food prices over the same two-to-three quarter lag. The long-term effect, as the nuclear fleet delivers structurally cheaper electricity, is a permanent reduction in the energy component of food costs.

###### E8.2: Transport Costs

The Problem

Transport is the second largest component of household expenditure after housing. Rail fares have risen relentlessly for three decades. The formula used to set regulated fare increases, pegged to July RPI plus one percentage point in most recent years, guarantees that commuting costs outstrip general inflation every year. Regulated fares increased 4.5% in 2025, with the London and South East sector rising 5.2% and long-distance fares 5.4%. Unregulated fares, which cover advance and first-class tickets and account for 55% of all tickets sold, rose 5.5%. An annual season ticket from Woking to London costs £4,260; from Swansea to Bristol, £6,080. The government announced in the November 2025 Budget that regulated fares would be frozen for 2026, the first time in thirty years. But the freeze is temporary, covers only regulated fares, and does nothing to address the structural cost of commuting that has priced millions of workers out of the rail network entirely.

At the pump, fuel duty stands at 52.95 pence per litre, including a temporary 5 pence cut introduced in March 2022 and extended repeatedly since. The 5p cut is scheduled to expire in stages from September 2026, returning the rate to 57.95 pence by March 2027, with RPI indexation from April 2027. Petrol prices averaged 135.37 pence per litre in December 2025 and diesel 144.27 pence. The total tax content of a litre of petrol, comprising fuel duty and VAT on both the fuel and the duty, amounts to approximately 53% of the pump price. For a household running a single car and covering 8,000 miles per year at an average fuel efficiency of 40 miles per gallon, the annual fuel bill is approximately £1,960 at current prices, of which roughly £1,040 is tax. For a two-car household, the figures double. Fuel duty raises approximately £24.4 billion annually, representing 2% of all government receipts.

Car insurance premiums hit a record average of £995 at the end of 2023 before falling to approximately £559 by late 2025 according to ABI data. The Confused.com price index reports an average comprehensive quote of £726 in the third quarter of 2025. Young drivers aged 17 to 24 pay an average of £1,122 despite recent falls. Inner London drivers pay £1,119 on average. The cost of vehicle repairs totalled £7.5 billion in 2025, accounting for 63% of the £11.9 billion paid out by insurers for vehicle damage. Insurance Premium Tax at 12% adds a further flat surcharge to every policy. The combined annual cost of car ownership, including insurance, fuel, road tax, MOT, and maintenance, exceeds £4,500 for a typical household before any finance or lease payments on the vehicle itself.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Cost of Living Reduction Act will establish:

- a) Permanent reduction of fuel duty to 45 pence per litre, effective from the first April following Royal Assent. This replaces the current temporary 5 pence cut with a permanent 12.95 pence reduction from the pre-2022 rate of 57.95 pence. The planned phased increases from September 2026 will be cancelled. RPI indexation of fuel duty will not be reintroduced. Instead, the fuel duty rate will be reviewed every three years and any increase will require an affirmative vote in both Houses of Parliament, applying the same constitutional lock against stealth taxation established in E6.1. The immediate saving for a household covering 8,000 miles per year at 40 mpg is approximately £200 per year compared to the rates that would have applied under the government’s planned increases. The revenue cost is approximately £4 billion per year compared to planned receipts, offset by the growth dividend from cheaper transport costs across the economy.
- b) Abolition of Insurance Premium Tax on motor insurance. IPT at 12% adds approximately £67 to the average car insurance premium and significantly more for young drivers and those in high-cost areas. It is a tax on a legal obligation: every driver is required by law to hold motor insurance, and the state charges them 12% for complying. The abolition of IPT on motor insurance will reduce the average premium by approximately £67 and the average young driver’s premium by £135. The revenue cost is approximately £2.5 billion per year, funded from the broader efficiency savings and growth dividend described in E6. IPT will remain on other insurance products in the first Parliament, with a review of further abolition conditional on fiscal performance.
- c) Reform of the rail fares formula. The Act will abolish the RPI-plus formula for regulated rail fares and replace it with a statutory cap set at CPI minus one percentage point for the duration of the first Parliament. This ensures that regulated fares fall in real terms every year. The cap will be reviewed at the start of the second Parliament with the objective of transitioning to a distance-based, digitally administered fare structure that rewards off-peak travel and eliminates the absurd pricing anomalies that make it cheaper to fly between British cities than to take the train. The statutory cap will apply to all regulated fares, including season tickets, peak and off-peak returns, and standard singles. Unregulated fares will be subject to a separate statutory cap of CPI plus zero for the first Parliament, preventing operators from shifting fare increases onto the unregulated ticket categories.
- d) A statutory duty on all train operating companies, whether publicly or privately owned, to offer a Universal Off-Peak Fare of no more than 10 pence per mile for all journeys commenced outside peak hours, defined as before 07:00, between 09:30 and 16:00, and after 19:00 on weekdays, and all day on weekends and bank holidays. This provision creates a price anchor that gives every commuter and leisure traveller a guaranteed affordable option. A 50-mile journey off-peak will cost no more than £5.00. A 100-mile journey, no more than £10.00. The revenue impact will be offset by increased ridership as the rail network becomes genuinely affordable for journeys currently made by car.

OPERATIONAL

Fuel duty reduction. The permanent reduction to 45 pence per litre takes effect from the first April following Royal Assent. HMRC will issue guidance within 48 hours. The saving will be visible at the pump within days.

IPT abolition. HMRC will implement the abolition of IPT on motor insurance from the first renewal date following Royal Assent. Insurers will be required to pass through the full saving to policyholders and to display the pre-IPT and post-IPT price on renewal notices for the first 12 months to ensure transparency.

Rail fare reform. The Department for Transport will publish the new fare cap formula within 30 days of Royal Assent, with the first capped fare increase, or decrease, taking effect from the first March following Royal Assent. The Universal Off-Peak Fare will be implemented within six months through a statutory direction to all operators.

###### E8.3: Childcare as Infrastructure

The Problem

Britain has some of the most expensive childcare in the developed world. The OECD reports that net childcare costs for a UK couple with two children account for approximately a quarter of net household income. Full-time nursery care for a child under two costs an average of £239 per week in England as of 2025, or approximately £12,400 per year. In Inner London, the figure exceeds £30,000. For a dual-income household where both parents earn the median wage, childcare for two children consumes a proportion of income that exceeds the mortgage payment in most regions outside London. For a single parent on the minimum wage, the cost of full-time childcare for one child consumes the majority of their net earnings, making paid employment economically irrational.

The government’s expansion of funded hours, reaching 30 hours per week for working parents of children from nine months in September 2025, has reduced costs for eligible families. Average part-time nursery costs for eligible parents of under-twos have fallen from £159.61 to £70.51 per week. But the system has three fundamental flaws. First, the funding rate paid by government to nurseries does not cover the true cost of provision. The gap between the government rate and the actual cost of delivering a nursery place is estimated at 20–40% depending on the provider and region. Nurseries cover this gap by charging higher fees to non-funded parents, adding surcharges for meals, consumables, and activities, or reducing staffing ratios to the legal minimum. The system therefore creates a two-tier market in which funded parents receive subsidised care and non-funded parents cross-subsidise it.

Second, the eligibility criteria exclude significant groups of families. Parents earning above £100,000, parents who are not working, parents in education or training, and parents who are self-employed but have not yet met the minimum earnings threshold are all excluded from funded hours. A mother who has left employment to care for a child and wishes to return to work cannot access funded childcare to enable her return, because she is not currently working. The system is designed to support parents who already have childcare, not to help parents who need childcare in order to obtain employment. This is a design failure that suppresses labour market participation, particularly among women.

Third, the supply of childcare places has not expanded to meet the demand created by the entitlement expansion. Ofsted data shows a net reduction in registered childcare providers in recent years. The staffing crisis in early years is acute: low wages, high qualification requirements, and intense regulatory burden make nursery work unattractive relative to comparable roles in retail or hospitality. The sector cannot recruit and retain staff at the funding rates the government provides, and it cannot raise fees to market-clearing levels because the funded hours framework suppresses the price. The result is a market failure that produces simultaneously high costs for parents, low wages for staff, and inadequate supply of places.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Cost of Living Reduction Act will establish:

- a) Extension of funded childcare hours to all families with children under five, regardless of parental employment status or income, at a rate of 20 hours per week universally and 40 hours per week for families where all parents are in employment, education, or training. The universal 20-hour entitlement removes the eligibility barrier that currently excludes non-working parents and enables mothers to access childcare as a pathway back into the labour market. The 40-hour working entitlement, increased from the current 30 hours, reflects the reality that a full-time working parent requires more than 30 hours of childcare per week once travel time is included. The income cap of £100,000 will be abolished. Childcare is infrastructure, not welfare. A surgeon earning £120,000 who cannot access funded childcare is a surgeon whose productivity the NHS needs, not a beneficiary to be means-tested out of the system.
- b) A reformed funding rate that covers the true cost of provision. The Act will require the Department for Education to calculate, annually, the actual cost of delivering a nursery place at each age band, including staff costs at the median early years practitioner wage, premises costs at the median rent for childcare-appropriate commercial property, regulatory compliance costs, consumables, and a margin sufficient to sustain the provider as a going concern. The funded rate will be set at this level, not at a rate determined by what the Treasury is willing to spend. The difference between the current rate and the true-cost rate will be funded from general taxation as a direct investment in economic infrastructure. The estimated additional cost is £2–3 billion per year, more than offset by the economic return from increased parental labour market participation, which the OBR has estimated at £1.3 billion per year from the current, more limited expansion alone.
- c) Regulatory simplification for childcare providers. The Act will reduce the staff-to-child ratio for children aged two to three from 1:4 to 1:5, aligning with the ratio already used in Scotland and several comparable European countries. For children aged three to four, the ratio will be reduced from 1:8 to 1:10 for settings led by a qualified teacher or early years professional. These changes reduce staffing costs by approximately 15–20%, enabling providers to offer more places at lower cost without reducing the quality of care. The Act will also exempt micro-nurseries with fewer than 20 places from the requirement to have a qualified teacher or early years professional on site at all times, provided all staff hold a Level 3 early years qualification. This removes the single greatest barrier to new nursery formation in areas underserved by the current market.
- d) Tax-Free Childcare reform. The current scheme, which provides £2,000 per child per year (£4,000 for disabled children) through a government top-up of 20% on parental contributions, will be increased to £4,000 per child per year (£8,000 for disabled children), doubling the maximum government contribution. The scheme will be extended to cover childcare for children up to age 12, reflecting the cost of after-school and holiday childcare that currently falls entirely on parents. The income cap will be aligned with the funded hours reform: no cap. The scheme is simple, well-designed, and underused because its generosity is insufficient. Doubling it makes it a meaningful contribution to childcare costs for every working family.

OPERATIONAL

Funding rate review. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Department for Education will commission an independent review of the true cost of childcare provision, to report within six months. The reformed funding rate will take effect from the first September following the review’s publication. In the interim, the existing rate will be increased by 15% as an emergency uplift to prevent further provider closures.

Supply expansion. The regulatory simplification measures will take effect within 60 days of Royal Assent, immediately enabling existing providers to offer more places and new providers to enter the market. The Department for Education will launch a Childcare Provider Formation Fund of £200 million, providing grants of up to £50,000 for new nursery formation in areas identified as having insufficient places. Priority will be given to applications in Prosperity Zones (E2) and areas with the lowest ratio of places to children.

###### E8.4: The Regulatory Cost Cascade

The Problem

Every regulation imposed on a business eventually appears in the price paid by a consumer. This is not a libertarian abstraction. It is arithmetic. When a food manufacturer is required to comply with Extended Producer Responsibility regulations for packaging, the compliance cost is added to the unit cost of production and passed through to the retailer, who passes it to the consumer. When an insurer faces a 23% increase in the value of personal injury claims following updates to the Judicial College Guidelines, and a further 15% increase in whiplash tariffs from May 2025, the insurer raises premiums, and the consumer pays. When a nursery is required to maintain a staff-to-child ratio of 1:3 for children under two, the staffing cost is embedded in the weekly fee. When a housebuilder is required to conduct an environmental impact assessment that takes 18 months, the cost of that delay is added to the price of every home on the development. The cumulative effect of thousands of individual regulations, each individually defensible, each individually small, is a systematic inflation of the price of everything.

The UK’s regulatory burden has grown continuously for decades. The Better Regulation Executive, established to assess and control regulatory costs, has been progressively weakened. The ‘one in, two out’ rule for new regulation, introduced in 2013 and already a dilution of the original ‘one in, one out’ rule, was quietly abandoned by the current government. The Employment Rights Act 2025 alone added significant new obligations on businesses of every size, as described in E7.2. The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 added mandatory identity verification and increased filing fees. Making Tax Digital requires compatible software for VAT returns. Each new obligation is accompanied by an impact assessment that invariably understates the cost to small businesses because it is produced by the department imposing the regulation, not by the businesses bearing it.

The Insurance Premium Tax is a case study in regulatory cost extraction. IPT at 12% is applied to all general insurance products: motor, home, pet, travel, health, and business insurance. It raises approximately £8 billion per year. Unlike VAT, it is not reclaimable by businesses. A small business paying £5,000 per year for commercial insurance pays £600 in IPT, a cost that is embedded in the price of its goods or services and ultimately paid by the consumer. IPT has been increased four times since its introduction in 1994, from 2.5% to 12%, with no corresponding debate about whether insurance, a risk-management product that reduces the burden on the state, should be taxed at all.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Cost of Living Reduction Act will establish:

- a) The Regulatory Cost Transparency Requirement. Every government department and regulatory body that introduces or amends a regulation affecting businesses will be required to publish, alongside the regulation, a Consumer Price Impact Statement estimating the cost that will ultimately be borne by consumers through higher prices. The statement will be independently audited by the Better Regulation Executive. Where the cumulative consumer price impact of a department’s regulations exceeds a threshold set annually by the Secretary of State, the department will be required to identify offsetting regulatory reductions before the new regulation can take effect. This is not a moratorium on regulation. It is a discipline that forces regulators to confront the price consequences of their decisions.
- b) A statutory Regulatory Cost Budget. Each government department will be assigned an annual Regulatory Cost Budget, expressed as the maximum net increase in regulatory compliance costs that may be imposed on businesses in that year. The budget will be set by the Secretary of State for Business, published annually, and enforced by the Better Regulation Executive. Departments that exceed their budget will be required to identify and implement offsetting reductions within six months. The objective is to achieve a net reduction in regulatory costs of 10% within the first Parliament, measured against a 2025 baseline.
- c) Immediate targeted repeals. The Act will repeal or reform the following specific regulatory costs that have the most direct impact on consumer prices: the Extended Producer Responsibility regulations for packaging will be suspended for 24 months pending a cost-benefit review, removing an estimated 1–2 pence per unit from packaged food and drink; Insurance Premium Tax on motor insurance will be abolished as described in E8.2; the identity verification requirements of the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 will be exempted for micro-businesses as established in E7.6; and the enhanced flexible working request procedures of the Employment Rights Act 2025 will be exempted for micro-employers as established in E7.2.
- d) A Consumer Price Commission. The Act will establish a standing commission, housed in the Cabinet Office, with a mandate to identify and recommend the removal of regulations, taxes, and administrative requirements that inflate consumer prices without delivering proportionate public benefit. The Commission will publish an annual report identifying the ten regulatory costs with the greatest consumer price impact, together with recommendations for their reduction or abolition. The Secretary of State will be required to respond to each recommendation within 60 days. The Commission will be staffed with economists, business representatives, and consumer advocates, and will operate with the investigative rigour of the Malebranche (C3) applied to the regulatory state rather than to corruption.

OPERATIONAL

Immediate regulatory relief. The EPR suspension, IPT abolition on motor insurance, and micro-business exemptions take effect within 30 days of Royal Assent. The Regulatory Cost Budget framework will be published within six months, with the first budgets set for the fiscal year beginning in April following Royal Assent.

Consumer Price Commission. The Commission will be established within 90 days of Royal Assent and will publish its first annual report within 12 months. The Commission’s work will be ongoing throughout the Parliament, delivering a cumulative programme of regulatory cost reduction that produces measurable reductions in consumer prices year on year.

###### E8.5: The Household Budget: What Progress Means for Your Monthly Outgoings

The Synthesis

The preceding sections of E8, and the preceding documents in the economic framework, address specific domains of cost. This section does what no government document ever does: it adds them up. It takes a representative household at median income and calculates, in pounds and pence, the combined annual impact of Progress’ reforms on their monthly outgoings. This is the test. If the numbers do not show a household that is visibly, materially better off, then the framework has failed. The numbers show no such failure.

The representative household. Two adults, two children (one aged two, one aged six). One parent earning the median full-time wage of £36,000, the other working part-time earning £18,000. Total gross household income: £54,000. Owner-occupier with a mortgage. One car. The six-year-old attends state school with after-school childcare. The two-year-old attends nursery three days per week. Both adults commute: one by car, one by a combination of rail and bus.

Energy (E1). Current annual energy bill: approximately £1,755. Within 21 days of Royal Assent, levy removal, Carbon Price Support abolition, and standing charge reform reduce this by £300–450. Within one parliament, the bill falls to approximately £900–1,000 as grid reform and early nuclear capacity take effect. Annual saving in year one: £400. Annual saving by year five: £800.

Housing (E5). Stamp duty abolition on primary residences removes the transaction cost barrier for households wishing to move. For this household, already an owner-occupier, the direct benefit is the elimination of stamp duty on any future move, saving approximately £7,500–£15,000 on a typical transaction. Council tax reform (E6.3) is revenue-neutral nationally but redistributive: this household, outside London, is likely to see a modest reduction. The housing supply expansion driven by E4 and E5, combined with cheap energy from E1, will exert downward pressure on mortgage rates and housing costs over the Parliament. Direct annual saving from council tax reform: estimated £100–300.

Tax (E6). Personal allowance unfreezing and above-CPI restoration: the first-year increase of approximately £500 in the personal allowance saves this household approximately £200 in income tax across both earners. By year five, with the allowance restored to approximately £16,000–17,000, the saving rises to approximately £700–900. Employer NICs reversal: the OBR projects that the majority of employer NICs costs are passed through to workers in lower wages; the reversal will therefore support higher wage growth, estimated at 0.5–1% above baseline over the Parliament. Student loan interest abolition: if either parent carries a Plan 2 loan with a balance of £40,000, the abolition of interest prevents the balance growing by approximately £2,000–£2,500 per year, and the retrospective recalculation may reduce the outstanding balance significantly. Direct annual tax saving in year one: £200–400. By year five: £700–900.

Food (E8.1). This household spends approximately £70 per week on food, or £3,640 per year. A reduction in food price inflation of 1.5–2.5 percentage points, driven by the employer NICs reversal, business rates abolition, and energy cost reduction, saves approximately £55–90 per year in year one, rising as structural energy cost reductions feed through the supply chain. Annual saving by year three: £100–180.

Transport (E8.2). Fuel duty reduction to 45 pence per litre saves approximately £200 per year for the car-owning commuter covering 8,000 miles. IPT abolition on motor insurance saves approximately £67. Rail fare cap at CPI minus one percentage point saves the rail commuter approximately £120–200 per year compared to the RPI-plus formula. Annual transport saving: £390–470.

Childcare (E8.3). The two-year-old currently attends nursery three days per week. Under the current system with funded hours, the household pays approximately £210 per week for the unfunded portion, or £10,920 per year. Under Progress’ reforms, the 40-hour working entitlement at the true-cost funding rate eliminates or dramatically reduces the parental contribution. The estimated saving is £4,000–£7,000 per year, depending on the provider and region. After-school childcare for the six-year-old, currently costing approximately £60 per week or £2,340 per year (term-time), is partially offset by the doubled Tax-Free Childcare contribution. Annual childcare saving: £4,500–£7,500.

Regulatory cost reductions (E8.4). The cumulative effect of EPR suspension, IPT abolition, and the broader regulatory cost cascade reductions will flow through to consumer prices across multiple categories. The effect is diffuse and difficult to quantify precisely for a single household, but conservative estimates suggest £100–200 per year in reduced prices across insurance, goods, and services.
