Total annual impact. In year one, the combined savings for this representative household are estimated at £5,600–£9,000, with the range reflecting regional variation and individual circumstances. By year five, with the full effect of tax reform, energy cost reduction, and childcare reform in place, the annual saving rises to £7,000–£10,500. For a household on median income, this represents a 10–15% increase in disposable income in year one, rising to 13–19% by year five. This is not a projection based on GDP growth assumptions or trickle-down theory. It is the direct, calculable result of specific policy changes, each of which has been costed and described in the preceding documents.

The Household Impact Statement. Progress will publish, annually, a Household Impact Statement prepared by the Office for Budget Responsibility or an equivalent independent body, showing the combined effect of all Progress policies on representative households at each income decile. The Statement will use actual price data, actual tax rates, and actual policy implementation timelines to calculate the real impact on real budgets. No government in British history has subjected itself to this level of transparency. Progress will, because the purpose of government is not to produce impressive GDP statistics. It is to ensure that the people who elected it are better off, and can see that they are better off, every year.

Summary of Legislative Requirements

The E8 framework is built on the Cost of Living Reduction Act, a single piece of primary legislation introduced in the first King’s Speech alongside the National Energy Security Act (E1), the Tax Reset Act (E6), the Small Business Liberation Act (E7), and the other foundational Acts of the economic programme. Several E8 measures are delivered through provisions already contained in other Acts, particularly the Tax Reset Act (employer NICs reversal, business rates abolition, IPT reform) and the National Energy Security Act (energy cost reductions). The Cost of Living Reduction Act provides the legislative basis for measures specific to E8 that are not already covered.

Cost of Living Reduction Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: Requirement for large food retailers to publish audited pass-through statements following employer NICs reversal. Food Supply Chain Cost Audit by the CMA within 12 months. Risk-based import inspection regime for food with 5% physical inspection rate for trusted partners. Permanent reduction of fuel duty to 45 pence per litre with constitutional lock against stealth increases. Abolition of Insurance Premium Tax on motor insurance. Reform of rail fares formula to CPI minus one percentage point cap on regulated fares and CPI plus zero on unregulated fares for duration of first Parliament. Universal Off-Peak Fare of no more than 10 pence per mile. Extension of funded childcare to 20 hours universal and 40 hours for working, studying, or training parents, with abolition of the £100,000 income cap. Reformed funding rate covering true cost of provision. Regulatory simplification for childcare providers including revised staff-to-child ratios. Tax-Free Childcare doubled to £4,000 per child per year and extended to age 12. Regulatory Cost Transparency Requirement with Consumer Price Impact Statements. Statutory Regulatory Cost Budget for each government department. Suspension of Extended Producer Responsibility regulations for 24 months. Consumer Price Commission established in the Cabinet Office. Annual Household Impact Statement.

Delivered operationally: Employer NICs reversal and business rates abolition effective first April (delivered via Tax Reset Act). Energy bill reductions within 21 days (delivered via National Energy Security Act). Large retailer pass-through statements within six months. CMA Food Supply Chain Cost Audit within 12 months. Risk-based food import inspection within six months. Fuel duty reduction effective first April. IPT abolition on motor insurance from first renewal following Royal Assent. Rail fare cap published within 30 days, effective first March. Universal Off-Peak Fare within six months. Emergency 15% childcare funding rate uplift within 90 days. Independent childcare cost review within six months. Reformed funding rate from first September following review. Childcare Provider Formation Fund of £200 million. Regulatory simplification for childcare providers within 60 days. Tax-Free Childcare increase from first April. EPR suspension within 30 days. Regulatory Cost Budget framework within six months. Consumer Price Commission established within 90 days, first report within 12 months. Household Impact Statement published annually from year one.

Funding the Cost of Living Reduction

The measures in E8 comprise a combination of revenue-reducing reforms (fuel duty reduction, IPT abolition, childcare funding expansion), revenue-neutral structural changes (regulatory reform, rail fare restructuring, food supply chain transparency), and measures whose costs are borne by other Acts in the framework (employer NICs reversal via E6, energy cost reduction via E1, business rates abolition via E6). The revenue cost of the E8-specific measures is funded through three sources.

First, state efficiency savings. The childcare funding expansion, the single largest cost in E8, is an investment in economic infrastructure that generates a return through increased parental labour market participation, higher household income, higher tax receipts, and reduced benefit expenditure. The OBR estimated that the current, more limited childcare expansion would increase the labour supply by 60,000 full-time equivalents. Progress’ more comprehensive expansion will produce a proportionally greater return.

Second, the growth dividend. Cheaper food, cheaper transport, cheaper childcare, and lower regulatory costs increase consumer spending power, which increases economic activity, which broadens the tax base. The fuel duty reduction is partially self-financing because cheaper fuel reduces business costs across the economy, increases economic activity, and generates additional VAT, corporation tax, and income tax receipts.

Third, the procurement and civil service reforms described in E10 and across Progress’ State Capacity programme. Every pound saved in wasteful procurement, duplicative bureaucracy, and inefficient service delivery is a pound that can be returned to the taxpayer through lower costs rather than higher spending.

E8 completes the household budget story. E1 makes energy cheap. E4 liberates the planning system that inflates the cost of everything built. E5 makes housing affordable. E6 ensures workers keep what they earn. E7 frees the businesses that employ them. E8 addresses everything that remains: the food on the table, the journey to work, the care of the children, and the regulatory burden that inflates the price of every good and service purchased. The combined effect is transformative. A household at median income is £5,600–£9,000 better off in year one and £7,000–£10,500 better off by year five. Not in theory. Not in projections. In pounds, on payslips, in shopping baskets, at the petrol pump, and on the nursery invoice. That is what Progress means by driving down the cost of living.

#### E9. Britain’s Trade Architecture

Governing Principle

Britain is a trading nation that has forgotten how to trade. The United Kingdom’s total trade in goods and services reached £1.9 trillion in the twelve months to November 2025, equivalent to approximately 63% of GDP. Services exports alone were worth £505 billion in 2024, up 9.9% year-on-year, with financial services generating a trade surplus of £94.4 billion, the largest of any nation on Earth. The top three goods exports, pharmaceuticals at £41.2 billion, mechanical power generators at £36.7 billion, and cars at £35.7 billion, demonstrate a productive base of genuine sophistication. The United Kingdom accounts for 38% of global foreign exchange turnover, twice as many US dollars traded in Britain as in the United States, 14.6% of global cross-border banking, and is the world’s second-largest destination for fintech investment. These are not the statistics of a declining economy. They are the statistics of a country that possesses world-class capabilities and does almost nothing to exploit them strategically.

The overall trade deficit was £22 billion in 2024: a goods deficit of £206 billion partially offset by a services surplus of £184 billion. With the European Union, the deficit was £90 billion. With the rest of the world, the United Kingdom ran a surplus of £68 billion. The share of UK exports going to the EU has fallen from 44.5% in 2014 to 41.2% in 2024, and goods exports to the EU have dropped 21% since Brexit, a decline the current government’s SPS alignment deal aims to partially reverse by making Britain a rule-taker in food standards in exchange for reduced border checks. This is the trade strategy of a country that has given up: accepting regulatory submission to the European Union in one domain while failing to exploit the regulatory freedom Brexit was supposed to deliver in every other domain. Five years after leaving the single market, Britain has signed trade agreements covering over 100 countries and territories, yet the combined economic impact of its new deals, the India FTA, the Australia and New Zealand agreements, CPTPP membership, amounts to a projected GDP uplift of less than 0.5% over fifteen years. That is not a trade strategy. It is a public relations exercise.

The world has changed since Britain voted to leave the European Union, and it has changed in ways that make the case for an aggressive, independent British trade policy not weaker but overwhelmingly stronger. The eurozone economy grew by 1.5% in 2025, accelerating from 0.9% in 2024, but Germany, the bloc’s engine, managed just 0.2%, and the European Commission forecasts eurozone growth of only 1.2% in 2026 with debt-to-GDP rising from 88% to 91%. The European Union is ageing, over-regulated, under-invested in defence, and haemorrhaging industrial competitiveness to the United States and China. American adventurism under the second Trump administration, with tariffs now at their highest levels in nearly a century, a headline 15% rate on EU goods, and sector-specific tariffs reaching 50% on steel and aluminium, has shattered the post-war consensus on rules-based trade and created a global environment in which bilateral agility is worth more than multilateral membership. The rise of the Indo-Pacific, the fracturing of global supply chains, the weaponisation of trade by China, the new scramble for critical minerals, and the rearmament of Europe all present opportunities of immense value to a country with Britain’s capabilities, if and only if that country has a government with the wit and the will to seize them.

Brexit was the correct strategic decision executed by the wrong people. The opportunity it created, full regulatory sovereignty, independent trade policy, the ability to move faster and more flexibly than a twenty-seven-member bloc constrained by unanimity and institutional inertia, has been squandered by two successive governments that either did not understand what they had or did not care. The Conservatives signed deals for their symbolic value rather than their economic substance, boasting about CPTPP membership that the OBR projected would add 0.04% to GDP. Labour has begun the process of regulatory re-alignment with the EU through the SPS agreement and emissions trading linkage negotiated at the May 2025 summit, trading regulatory sovereignty for marginal reductions in border friction, while simultaneously failing to negotiate meaningful services access, failing to exploit regulatory divergence in financial services, AI, genomics, and advanced manufacturing, and failing to build the bilateral relationships with the fastest-growing economies on Earth that would actually transform Britain’s trade position. The result is a country with world-class export capabilities, regulatory freedom that no other European nation possesses, and a government that treats trade policy as a branch of diplomacy rather than the engine of national prosperity.

Progress will treat trade as what it is: the mechanism by which the cheap energy of E1, the industrial capacity of E2, the startup ecosystem of E3, the planning liberation of E4, the housing affordability of E5, and the tax competitiveness of E6 are converted into real wages, consumer surplus, and professional mobility for the people of Britain. Every trade agreement, every regulatory decision, every tariff schedule, and every diplomatic engagement will be evaluated against a single question: does this make British workers richer, British companies more competitive, and British consumers better off? If it does, we do it. If it does not, we do not, regardless of the diplomatic courtesies involved.

The Five Objectives

First: regulatory competition as competitive advantage. Britain will diverge from EU regulation wherever divergence creates a genuine competitive advantage for British industry, British exporters, and British consumers, and will do so aggressively, systematically, and without apology. The constraint is not alignment with Brussels. The constraint is the welfare of British citizens. Where EU regulation is good, we will keep it. Where it is not, we will replace it with something better. Where the absence of EU regulation creates an opportunity, we will seize it. This is what sovereign trade policy means.

Second: a deal architecture built for the new world. Progress will negotiate bilateral trade agreements not on the basis of diplomatic friendship or historical sentiment but on the basis of cold economic calculation: which markets are growing fastest, which sectors align with British export strengths, and which partners offer the greatest mutual benefit. The priority is not Europe, though Europe matters. The priority is the world, and particularly the Indo-Pacific, the Gulf, the Commonwealth, and the United States, where the fastest growth, the deepest capital pools, and the most complementary economic structures are found.

Third: services as the spearhead. Britain’s overwhelming comparative advantage is in services: financial services, professional services, digital services, creative industries, education, and the knowledge economy. Services account for 56% of UK exports and generate a trade surplus of £184 billion per year. Every trade negotiation conducted by every previous government has prioritised goods market access over services liberalisation, because goods tariffs are visible and services barriers are complex. Progress will reverse this. Services access will be the primary demand in every bilateral negotiation, and the willingness of a trading partner to open its services markets will be the primary criterion for the depth of the agreement we offer in return.

Fourth: Prosperity Zone export corridors. The eight Prosperity Zones described in E2 are not merely domestic industrial clusters. They are export platforms. Every zone has been designated with a specific set of international markets in mind, and the trade architecture described in this document will provide the market access, the regulatory recognition, and the logistical infrastructure that connects zone production to global demand. The learning tariffs described in E2.6 provide temporary protection during the transition. This document provides the export corridors that make the transition worth making.

Fifth: trade defence and geostrategic autarchy. In a world of American tariffs, Chinese supply chain weaponisation, and European institutional sclerosis, Britain must be capable of feeding, fuelling, arming, and sustaining itself independently of any single trading partner or bloc. This does not mean autarky. It means ensuring that no critical supply chain, no essential commodity, and no strategic capability is dependent on a single source that could be disrupted by geopolitical events beyond Britain’s control. The trade architecture must diversify as aggressively as it liberalises.

###### E9.1: Strategic Divergence

The Problem

The May 2025 UK-EU reset committed Britain to dynamic alignment with EU sanitary and phytosanitary rules and the linking of UK and EU emissions trading schemes, both requiring the UK to follow changes in EU law with no voting rights on their adoption. The government estimates these measures will add £9 billion to the UK economy by 2040. Set against the OBR’s estimate that Brexit has reduced GDP by approximately 4%, this recovers a fraction of a fraction. The SPS agreement trades regulatory sovereignty in food standards for reduced border checks, and the ETS linkage trades carbon market independence for avoidance of the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, which would otherwise have cost UK exporters up to £800 million by 2030. Both are rational responses to problems that a more competent government would never have allowed to develop in the first place.

The deeper failure is that while Labour negotiates alignment in agri-food and carbon, it has made no equivalent effort to exploit divergence in the sectors where Britain’s competitive advantage is greatest: financial services, artificial intelligence, genomics, digital services, advanced manufacturing regulation, clinical trial approval, and data governance. The United Kingdom’s financial and related professional services trade surplus was £119.1 billion in 2024. Financial services alone generated £94.4 billion in exports. The EU’s regulatory framework in these sectors, from MiFID II to the AI Act to GDPR to the Clinical Trials Regulation, is consistently slower, more prescriptive, and more hostile to innovation than the frameworks that could be designed by a sovereign regulator optimising for competitive advantage. And yet Britain has done almost nothing with its regulatory freedom in these domains. Five years of sovereignty, and the most consequential regulatory divergence from the EU has been in gene-edited crops.

Every year that Britain fails to exploit its regulatory freedom is a year in which the value of Brexit diminishes. Regulatory environments are not static. They are competitive landscapes. Singapore, Switzerland, Dubai, and the United States are all competing for the same globally mobile capital, talent, and companies. If Britain does not offer a regulatory environment that is demonstrably better than the EU’s for the sectors where it competes, it will lose those sectors to jurisdictions that do, and no amount of SPS alignment will compensate for the loss.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The British Trade Architecture Act will establish:

- a) A Regulatory Competition Framework. The Act will establish a statutory obligation on every economic regulator in the United Kingdom, including the FCA, the PRA, the CMA, the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, Ofcom, Ofgem, the ICO, and the Health and Safety Executive, to conduct a biennial Competitive Regulatory Assessment comparing their regulatory regime with those of the UK’s five principal competitor jurisdictions in their sector. Where the assessment identifies regulatory requirements that impose costs on British businesses or consumers without a corresponding benefit to safety, stability, or the public interest that is not achieved more efficiently elsewhere, the regulator will be required to propose reforms within six months. This is not deregulation for its own sake. It is the systematic elimination of regulatory costs that serve no purpose other than institutional inertia or inherited EU harmonisation. The Assessment will be published and debated in Parliament.
- b) AI and Data Sovereignty. The Act will establish a British AI Regulatory Framework that explicitly rejects the precautionary, risk-classification approach of the EU AI Act in favour of a principles-based, outcomes-focused regime that permits innovation by default and intervenes only where demonstrable harm has occurred or is imminent. The framework will include a statutory right to deploy AI systems without prior regulatory approval unless the system operates in a defined high-risk context, with high-risk defined narrowly and reviewed annually. The UK’s data protection regime will be reformed to create a British Data Standard that maintains the substantive protections of personal privacy while eliminating the compliance costs that make GDPR a barrier to innovation, particularly for small companies and startups (as initiated in E3.1). The British Data Standard will be designed to achieve adequacy determinations from the EU, the United States, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, and Australia simultaneously, making the UK the only major economy whose data regime is interoperable with every significant digital market. This is the prize: a single regulatory environment from which a company can serve every major market on Earth.
- c) Clinical Trial and Drug Approval Acceleration. The MHRA will be empowered to operate a sovereign accelerated approval pathway for drugs and medical devices, reducing the time from Phase III trial completion to market authorisation to 12 months or less for qualifying therapies, as described in E2 for the Life Sciences Prosperity Zone but applied nationally. The UK will pursue mutual recognition agreements for drug approvals with the US FDA, Japan’s PMDA, Australia’s TGA, and Health Canada, creating a network of fast-track reciprocal approvals that bypasses the EMA entirely. Britain will become the fastest major market in the world to bring a new drug from trial to patient.
- d) Financial Services Divergence Acceleration. The Act will mandate the completion of all outstanding Edinburgh Reforms within six months of Royal Assent and the implementation of a further package of financial services regulatory reforms designed to make London the most competitive major financial centre in the world. The package will include: reform of the Solvency II framework to release capital for productive investment, completing and extending the reforms initiated in 2023; reform of MiFID-inherited trading venue regulation to reduce compliance costs; a new listing regime for the British Growth Exchange described in E3.3; reform of the prospectus regime to reduce the cost and complexity of public offerings; and a statutory innovation mandate for the FCA requiring it to weigh the competitive impact of regulation as a primary consideration alongside consumer protection and market integrity.
- e) Mutual Recognition Agreements. The Act will empower the Secretary of State to negotiate sector-specific mutual recognition agreements with partner countries covering professional qualifications, product standards, conformity assessment, and regulatory approvals. These agreements will be pursued on a bilateral basis, tailored to the specific sectors where mutual recognition delivers the greatest trade benefit, rather than through comprehensive regulatory alignment with any single jurisdiction. Priority sectors for mutual recognition will include financial services, pharmaceuticals, medical devices, engineering services, legal services, architectural services, and digital services. The objective is a web of bilateral mutual recognition agreements that gives British companies and professionals access to multiple markets simultaneously without requiring alignment with any single regulatory framework.

OPERATIONAL

Regulatory Competition Unit. Within 30 days of taking office, the Secretary of State will establish a Regulatory Competition Unit within the Department for Business and Trade, staffed by officials with commercial and regulatory experience drawn from the private sector, with a mandate to identify the twenty highest-value regulatory divergence opportunities within 60 days and to publish a Regulatory Competition Strategy within 90 days. The Unit will maintain a rolling pipeline of divergence opportunities and will serve as the central coordination point for all mutual recognition negotiations.

Adequacy architecture. Within 60 days of Royal Assent, the ICO and the DBT will commence simultaneous adequacy negotiations with the United States, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, and Australia, designed to achieve interoperable data transfer arrangements within 12 months. The objective is that a British company can transfer data to and from every major digital market without additional legal mechanisms, making the UK the data hub of the global economy.

###### E9.2: The Bilateral Deal Architecture

The Problem

Britain’s post-Brexit trade deal programme has been characterised by two failures: the prioritisation of symbolic deals over economically significant ones, and the systematic neglect of services access in favour of goods tariff reductions. The Australia and New Zealand agreements, negotiated from scratch as showcases for post-Brexit trade policy, are projected to increase UK GDP by 0.08% and 0.03% respectively over fifteen years. CPTPP membership adds a further 0.04–0.08%. The India FTA, signed in May 2025, is the most commercially meaningful agreement to date, projected to add £4.8 billion annually, but even this focuses predominantly on goods tariff reductions, with Indian tariffs on whisky falling from 150% to 75% and car tariffs from over 100% to 10%, rather than on the services market access that would deliver the largest gains for the British economy. Meanwhile, the UK’s largest export market, the United States at 22.5% of total exports, has no comprehensive free trade agreement, and the partial deal struck in May 2025 merely reduced some Trump-era tariffs rather than establishing the deep economic partnership that the world’s largest and sixth-largest economies should enjoy.

The fundamental error is that Britain’s trade negotiators have approached every deal as a diplomatic exercise in which the objective is to sign an agreement, any agreement, rather than as an economic exercise in which the objective is to maximise the value of market access obtained. A deal that reduces tariffs on whisky exports to India is good. A deal that opens India’s £400 billion financial services market to British firms would be transformational. A deal with the Gulf states that covers goods is useful. A deal that positions Britain as the financial services, legal services, and technology hub for the entire GCC would be a generational economic event. Progress will negotiate for economic substance, not diplomatic headlines.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The British Trade Architecture Act will establish:

- a) A statutory National Trade Strategy, published within 90 days of Royal Assent and updated annually, setting out the priority markets, the priority sectors, the negotiating objectives, and the metrics by which success will be measured. The Strategy will rank potential trade partners by a composite score incorporating market size, growth rate, sectoral alignment with British export strengths, existing trade volumes, and geostrategic value. The Strategy will be debated in Parliament and will bind the Department for Business and Trade to pursue the priorities it identifies, ending the practice of trade negotiations driven by diplomatic opportunity rather than economic calculation.
- b) Tier One priority partnerships. The Act will designate the following as Tier One trade partners requiring comprehensive, deep economic partnership agreements to be negotiated within the first Parliament: the United States, India, the Gulf Cooperation Council, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Canada, and Singapore. Tier One agreements will go beyond traditional tariff reduction to encompass mutual recognition of professional qualifications, mutual recognition of product standards and conformity assessment, services market access including financial services and digital services, investment protection, government procurement access, and regulatory cooperation in high-technology sectors. The ambition for each Tier One agreement is not a modest percentage point of GDP. It is a step-change in the bilateral economic relationship.
- c) Services-first negotiating mandates. The Act will require that every trade negotiation conducted by the United Kingdom include services market access as a primary objective, and that no agreement be concluded in which the services access obtained is not proportionate to the goods access granted. The Secretary of State will publish, alongside every proposed trade agreement, an assessment of the services value obtained relative to the goods concessions made. This transparency mechanism ensures that the pattern of trading goods access for diplomatic goodwill, while leaving services, where Britain’s advantage is overwhelming, on the table, is permanently ended.
- d) Trade negotiating capacity. The Act will establish a National Trade Negotiation Service as a professional body within the Department for Business and Trade, recruited from the private sector at competitive salaries, with a mandate to build and maintain world-class trade negotiating capability. The current system, in which trade negotiations are conducted by generalist civil servants with limited commercial experience, produces agreements that reflect the priorities of diplomats rather than the interests of businesses. The National Trade Negotiation Service will be staffed by individuals with direct experience in international commerce, financial services, technology, and sector-specific regulation, and will be the sole body authorised to conduct trade negotiations on behalf of the United Kingdom.

OPERATIONAL

US comprehensive partnership. Within 30 days of taking office, the Prime Minister will propose to the US President a comprehensive UK-US Economic Partnership Agreement covering services market access, mutual recognition of financial services regulation, defence technology procurement, digital trade, and investment protection. The partial tariff deal of May 2025 is treated as a floor, not a ceiling. The UK’s offer will include preferential access for US companies to Prosperity Zone investment opportunities and participation in UK defence procurement, in exchange for full UK access to US financial services markets, federal procurement, and the elimination of remaining tariffs on British goods. The objective is the deepest bilateral economic agreement in the world between two allies.

India acceleration. The India FTA signed in May 2025 will be supplemented within six months by a UK-India Services and Technology Partnership, negotiated as a standalone agreement covering financial services access, mutual recognition of professional qualifications (particularly in engineering, medicine, and law), digital trade, and joint investment in AI research. India’s financial services market is projected to reach £400 billion by 2030, and its technology sector is the world’s fastest-growing. A comprehensive services agreement with India is worth multiples of the goods tariff reductions already secured.

GCC economic integration. The GCC trade negotiations, ongoing since June 2022, will be concluded within six months of taking office with a comprehensive agreement that positions Britain as the financial services, legal services, technology, and education hub for the Gulf. The GCC collectively manages sovereign wealth exceeding £4 trillion. A comprehensive agreement that includes financial services passporting, mutual recognition of legal and professional qualifications, and preferential procurement access for British defence and technology companies would be among the most valuable trade agreements in British history.

CPTPP deepening. Britain’s CPTPP membership, operational since December 2024, will be used as a platform for bilateral deepening with individual members rather than as a static multilateral arrangement. Priority bilateral enhancements within the CPTPP framework will target Japan (financial services and advanced manufacturing), Singapore (fintech and digital trade), Vietnam (manufacturing supply chains), and Malaysia (semiconductor materials and halal food exports). The CPTPP’s modern digital trade rules and flexible rules of origin will be leveraged to create supply chain linkages between Prosperity Zone output and Indo-Pacific markets.

###### E9.3: Services Supremacy

The Problem

Services account for 56% of UK exports and generate a trade surplus of £184 billion per year. The United Kingdom is the world’s largest net exporter of financial services, with a combined financial and related professional services trade surplus of £119.1 billion in 2024. British legal services generated net exports of £7.6 billion, accounting services £1.8 billion, and management consultancy services reached £92 billion in turnover. London hosts more than 160 foreign banks, accounts for 38% of global foreign exchange turnover, holds a 43% share of the global specialty insurance market, and is the largest centre for cross-border banking in the world. The UK attracted £2.8 billion in fintech investment across 546 deals in 2024, more than the next five largest European countries combined. This is, by any measure, the most formidable services export machine in Europe and one of the most formidable in the world.

And yet Britain’s trade policy treats services as an afterthought. Every trade agreement negotiated since Brexit has prioritised goods tariff reductions over services market access. The EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement contains minimal provisions on services, and the May 2025 reset focused almost entirely on goods-related issues: SPS alignment, fishing rights, and emissions trading. The India FTA’s most celebrated achievements are tariff reductions on whisky and cars, not the opening of India’s vast financial services or technology markets. The GCC negotiations have stalled in part because the UK has not made a sufficiently ambitious offer on services access. This is strategic malpractice of the highest order. Britain is negotiating from its weakness, goods, rather than its strength, services, and leaving the most valuable opportunities on the table in every deal it strikes.

The barrier to services trade is not tariffs. It is regulation: licensing requirements, local presence mandates, data localisation rules, recognition of professional qualifications, and the thousand administrative obstacles that prevent a British financial adviser, lawyer, engineer, architect, or technology company from serving clients in a foreign market as easily as they serve clients in London. Removing these barriers requires not tariff schedules but mutual recognition agreements, regulatory cooperation frameworks, and the kind of detailed, sector-specific negotiation that generalist trade negotiators are poorly equipped to conduct. This is precisely why Progress has established the National Trade Negotiation Service: to bring the sectoral expertise that services trade negotiations demand.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The British Trade Architecture Act will establish:

- a) A Services Export Strategy, published within 90 days of Royal Assent, identifying the twenty highest-value services export opportunities globally, the regulatory barriers that currently prevent British firms from accessing those markets, and the negotiating strategy for removing each barrier. The Strategy will be prepared by the National Trade Negotiation Service in consultation with the financial services, legal, accounting, technology, creative industries, and education sectors, and will be updated annually.
- b) A statutory Financial Services Equivalence Framework. The Act will empower the Treasury and the FCA to negotiate bilateral financial services equivalence or mutual recognition agreements with any jurisdiction, independent of broader trade negotiations. Financial services access is too valuable and too complex to be bundled into omnibus trade deals where it is traded off against agricultural concessions. The Framework will enable standalone financial services agreements to be negotiated, concluded, and implemented on an accelerated basis, with the objective of securing equivalence or mutual recognition arrangements with the United States, Switzerland, Singapore, Japan, Hong Kong, the UAE, Australia, Canada, and India within the first Parliament.
- c) Digital trade as default. The Act will establish that all UK trade agreements must include a comprehensive digital trade chapter covering the free flow of data across borders, the prohibition of data localisation requirements, the recognition of electronic contracts and digital signatures, the protection of source code and algorithms from mandatory disclosure, and the facilitation of cross-border digital services delivery. The UK’s existing digital trade agreements with Japan, Singapore, and Ukraine will serve as the baseline, with the ambition that the UK’s digital trade provisions become the global standard, adopted by CPTPP partners and incorporated into every future bilateral agreement.
- d) Professional qualifications mutual recognition. The Act will establish a Professional Qualifications Authority with a mandate to negotiate mutual recognition agreements for professional qualifications with priority trading partners. Priority professions will include engineering, medicine, nursing, law, accountancy, architecture, and veterinary science. The Authority will maintain a register of all mutual recognition agreements and will work with professional bodies to ensure that recognition agreements are implemented in practice, not merely signed and forgotten. Every mutual recognition agreement that enables a British professional to practise in a foreign market, and a foreign professional to practise in Britain, increases the human capital available to both economies and deepens the bilateral economic relationship in ways that goods trade cannot match.

OPERATIONAL

Services trade attaché network. Within 60 days of taking office, the Department for Business and Trade will embed dedicated services trade attachés in British embassies in the twenty highest-value services export markets. These attachés will be recruited from the financial services, legal, and technology sectors, not from the diplomatic service, and will have explicit mandates to identify and pursue services market access opportunities, to support British services firms entering the market, and to report regulatory barriers to the National Trade Negotiation Service for inclusion in bilateral negotiations.

London as the world’s financial bridge. The UK will position London explicitly as the financial bridge between the United States, Europe, the Middle East, and Asia. The FCA will establish bilateral regulatory cooperation agreements with every major financial centre, enabling London-regulated firms to serve clients in multiple jurisdictions through a single regulatory relationship. The British Growth Exchange described in E3.3 will be marketed internationally as the listing venue of choice for companies seeking access to European, Middle Eastern, and Asian investors from a single, English-language, common-law platform.

###### E9.4: The Commonwealth Compact

The Problem

The Commonwealth comprises 56 nations with a combined population of 2.7 billion people and a combined GDP exceeding £10 trillion. Intra-Commonwealth trade in goods and services reached a record £680 billion in 2022 and is projected to surpass £800 billion by 2026. Commonwealth partners enjoy 21% lower bilateral trade costs on average, generating 20% more merchandise trade, 22% more food trade, and 400% more modern services trade between member states than between comparable non-Commonwealth country pairs. Intra-Commonwealth FDI stock almost doubled between 2015 and 2022, reaching £1.36 trillion. The Commonwealth includes India, the world’s fastest-growing major economy; Australia, Canada, and Singapore, three of the world’s most sophisticated financial markets; Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa, three of Africa’s largest economies; and Malaysia, a critical node in global semiconductor supply chains. UK exports to the Commonwealth were worth £90 billion in 2023, with a trade surplus of £16 billion, and trade is growing at 9% per year.

Despite these advantages, the Commonwealth has never been used as a serious platform for economic integration. It has no common trade framework, no mutual recognition arrangements, no shared regulatory standards, and no institutional mechanism for converting its cultural and linguistic affinities into economic value. Previous British governments have treated the Commonwealth as a diplomatic forum and a vehicle for development aid rather than as what it could be: the most geographically diverse, culturally connected, and economically complementary trading network on Earth, united by the English language, the common law, and institutional familiarity that reduces transaction costs in ways that no trade agreement can replicate.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The British Trade Architecture Act will establish:

- a) A Commonwealth Economic Partnership Initiative, led by the United Kingdom, proposing a multilateral framework for the progressive reduction of trade barriers, the mutual recognition of professional qualifications, the harmonisation of product standards where appropriate, and the facilitation of investment flows between Commonwealth members. The Initiative will be proposed at the next Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting with the objective of securing agreement from the five largest Commonwealth economies, the United Kingdom, India, Australia, Canada, and Singapore, within the first Parliament. The Initiative is not a customs union. It is a network of bilateral and multilateral arrangements that exploit the Commonwealth advantage to create the deepest possible economic integration between member states.
- b) A Commonwealth Digital Trade Network. The UK will propose the adoption of a common digital trade framework across the Commonwealth, based on the UK’s existing digital trade agreements with Singapore and Ukraine, covering the free flow of data, the recognition of electronic contracts, the prohibition of data localisation, and the facilitation of cross-border digital services. The Commonwealth’s shared use of the English language and common-law legal systems makes it uniquely suited to serve as the backbone of a global digital trade architecture, and the UK’s role as the world’s second-largest fintech destination and the leading centre for cross-border financial services positions it as the natural hub.
- c) Commonwealth Prosperity Fund. The Act will establish a £1 billion fund, capitalised from the reallocation of existing overseas development assistance currently directed at non-Commonwealth recipients, to finance trade facilitation infrastructure, digital connectivity, and regulatory capacity building in Commonwealth developing countries. The Fund will prioritise projects that directly increase bilateral trade with the United Kingdom: port and customs modernisation, digital payment infrastructure, and the training of officials in the regulatory standards necessary for mutual recognition. This is not aid. It is investment in the trade infrastructure that enables Commonwealth countries to buy British goods and services and sell their own into the UK market.

OPERATIONAL

Commonwealth Trade Commissioner. Within 30 days of taking office, the Prime Minister will appoint a Commonwealth Trade Commissioner, a Cabinet-level envoy with a specific mandate to build the Commonwealth Economic Partnership Initiative and to serve as the UK’s senior trade representative to Commonwealth governments. The Commissioner will be drawn from the private sector, not the diplomatic service, and will report directly to the Prime Minister on the progress of Commonwealth economic integration.

Africa and Indo-Pacific trade missions. Within 60 days, the Secretary of State will lead dedicated trade missions to Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, India, Malaysia, and Singapore, focused exclusively on identifying and pursuing the highest-value bilateral trade and investment opportunities. These missions will include representatives from the Prosperity Zone Sandpit Authorities, the National Trade Negotiation Service, and the British Growth Exchange, creating direct connections between Britain’s industrial and financial ecosystems and the fastest-growing Commonwealth markets.

###### E9.5: Export Corridors and Prosperity Zone Trade

The Problem

The eight Prosperity Zones described in E2 are designed to produce world-class goods and services in sectors where the UK has genuine competitive advantage: life sciences, precision manufacturing and aerospace, nuclear supply chain, compound semiconductors, defence technology, data and fintech, maritime engineering, and space and critical minerals. The learning tariffs described in E2.6 provide temporary protection during the developmental phase, declining automatically by a minimum of 3 percentage points per year and expiring entirely after seven years. But protection without export development is a dead end. The tariffs buy time. The trade architecture described in this document provides the markets into which zone production will flow when the tariffs expire.

The link between Prosperity Zone output and international markets must be established from day one, not deferred until zone production reaches maturity. The reason is simple: if zone companies do not build export relationships during the protected period, they will not be competitive when the protection ends. The learning tariffs are designed to create urgency, not complacency. Every zone company should be exporting within 12 months of establishment, using the protected domestic market as a revenue base from which to develop international competitiveness, and every trade agreement negotiated during this period should include specific provisions that open partner markets to zone-produced goods and services.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The British Trade Architecture Act will establish:

- a) Prosperity Zone Trade Chapters in every bilateral trade agreement. The Act will require that every comprehensive trade agreement negotiated by the United Kingdom include a Prosperity Zone chapter providing preferential market access for goods and services produced within designated Prosperity Zones. The chapter will include: expedited customs clearance for zone-certified goods, mutual recognition of zone quality standards, preferential tariff rates phased in alongside the decline of learning tariffs, and facilitated investment flows into and out of the zones. The Prosperity Zone chapter will be a standard component of every UK trade agreement, ensuring that the zone programme and the trade programme reinforce each other.
- b) Dual-certification for zone manufacturing. The Act will empower the Sandpit Authorities, in coordination with the MHRA and other relevant regulators, to issue dual UK-partner country certification for goods manufactured within Prosperity Zones, where mutual recognition agreements exist with the partner country. A component manufactured in the Midlands Precision Manufacturing Zone that receives dual UK-US type approval can be sold into both markets without additional regulatory process. This eliminates the regulatory duplication that currently adds cost and delay to British manufacturing exports and makes Prosperity Zone production uniquely attractive to multinational companies seeking a manufacturing base that serves multiple markets simultaneously.
- c) Zone export targets. The Act will establish statutory export targets for each Prosperity Zone, to be met within three years of designation: a minimum of 30% of zone output by value to be exported, rising to 50% by year five. Export performance will be a criterion in the Sandpit Authority’s annual performance assessment and will determine the allocation of additional government support. The message to zone companies is clear: the domestic market is your launchpad, not your ceiling. The Prosperity Zones will succeed or fail on their ability to compete internationally, and the trade architecture described in this document exists to ensure they can.

OPERATIONAL

Embedded trade attachés in each zone. As established in E2.1, each Prosperity Zone will have an embedded trade attaché responsible for connecting zone businesses with export opportunities. The attachés will work with the National Trade Negotiation Service to identify and pursue market access for zone-specific products, and will maintain direct relationships with trade representatives in priority export markets. The attachés will report monthly to the Sandpit Authority on export pipeline development and barrier identification.

Zone-specific market mapping. Within 60 days of Royal Assent, the Department for Business and Trade will publish a Zone Export Strategy for each of the eight Prosperity Zones, mapping the target export markets, the regulatory requirements in each market, the existing trade agreements that provide access, and the gaps that need to be filled through new negotiations. The Zone Export Strategies will be updated annually and will feed directly into the National Trade Strategy and bilateral negotiating mandates.

###### E9.6: Trade Defence and Economic Security

The Problem

The rules-based international trading system is fracturing. The United States has imposed tariffs at their highest levels in nearly a century, with a 15% headline rate on EU goods and sector-specific tariffs reaching 50% on steel and aluminium. China controls 60% of global rare earth mining and 90% of processing, and has demonstrated its willingness to weaponise supply chains for geopolitical advantage, restricting gallium and germanium exports in 2023 and expanding controls in 2024. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has demonstrated the strategic vulnerability of energy dependence, a lesson E1 addresses through domestic nuclear and energy production. The May 2025 UK-EU reset, whatever its other merits, extends EU fishing access to British waters for twelve years and commits Britain to dynamic regulatory alignment in food standards and carbon markets, constraining sovereign decision-making in exchange for modest economic benefit. In this environment, a trade policy that optimises solely for liberalisation without regard for strategic resilience is a trade policy that leaves Britain exposed.

Progress is a party of free trade. Free trade, as a general principle, is the most powerful engine of prosperity ever discovered. But free trade is a principle, not a suicide pact. The learning tariffs described in E2.6, with their mandatory automatic decline and seven-year expiry, represent the boundary of legitimate trade protection: targeted, temporary, transparent, and declining. Beyond that boundary, Progress will liberalise aggressively. But alongside liberalisation, we will build the strategic resilience that ensures no foreign government, no hostile regime, and no supply chain disruption can hold the British economy hostage.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The British Trade Architecture Act will establish:

- a) A Critical Supply Chain Resilience Framework. The Act will require the Secretary of State to maintain a register of critical supply chains, defined as supply chains in which disruption would materially impair national security, public health, energy supply, food supply, or the operation of essential infrastructure. For each critical supply chain, the Framework will require: identification of single points of failure, a diversification strategy ensuring no critical input is sourced from fewer than three independent suppliers in at least two different geopolitical blocs, and a strategic stockpile requirement for inputs where diversification alone is insufficient. The Framework will cover, at a minimum: semiconductors, rare earth minerals, pharmaceutical active ingredients, energy system components, food staples, and defence technology components.
- b) A British Critical Minerals Strategy. The Act will establish a statutory objective of reducing UK dependence on Chinese-processed rare earth minerals from the current level, approximately 90% of global processing, to below 50% within five years. The strategy will include: accelerated exploitation of domestic rare earth and critical mineral deposits through the Space, Satellites, Critical Minerals and Advanced Materials Prosperity Zone in Cornwall and Devon; bilateral critical minerals partnerships with Australia, Canada, and the United States, all of which possess substantial reserves and share Britain’s interest in diversifying away from Chinese processing; and the establishment of a domestic critical minerals processing capability, co-located with the Compound Semiconductors Prosperity Zone in South Wales, to provide British manufacturers with a domestic source of processed rare earth materials.
- c) Trade defence instruments. The Act will modernise and strengthen the UK’s trade defence regime, ensuring that the Trade Remedies Authority has the resources, the mandate, and the speed to impose anti-dumping duties, countervailing duties, and safeguard measures where British industries are being harmed by unfair trading practices. The current system is too slow, too under-resourced, and too cautious. The TRA will be required to reach preliminary determinations within 60 days of an application, down from the current nine months, and to impose provisional measures immediately where the evidence of dumping or subsidy is clear. Protection of British industries from unfair trade practices is not protectionism. It is the enforcement of the rules that make free trade possible.
- d) Geostrategic trade review. The Act will require that every trade agreement, investment treaty, and regulatory alignment arrangement entered into by the United Kingdom be accompanied by a Geostrategic Impact Assessment, published and debated in Parliament, evaluating the agreement’s effect on Britain’s strategic autonomy, supply chain resilience, and alignment with the values of democratic governance and the rule of law. This assessment will apply retrospectively to the May 2025 UK-EU reset arrangements, and prospectively to all future agreements. No agreement that materially reduces Britain’s strategic autonomy or creates dependence on a regime whose values and governance are incompatible with British democratic principles will be ratified without an explicit parliamentary vote acknowledging the strategic trade-off.

OPERATIONAL

Critical supply chain audit. Within 60 days of taking office, the Cabinet Office will commission a comprehensive audit of the UK’s critical supply chains, identifying all single points of failure and all dependencies on hostile or unreliable supplier states. The audit will be conducted by a team drawn from the National Security Council, the Department for Business and Trade, and the Ministry of Defence, and will report within 90 days. Its recommendations will be implemented through the Critical Supply Chain Resilience Framework.

Allied minerals partnership. Within 30 days of taking office, the Secretary of State will propose to Australia, Canada, the United States, and Japan the formation of a Critical Minerals Alliance: a multilateral partnership for the joint development, processing, and stockpiling of rare earth minerals and other critical materials. The Alliance will coordinate investment in processing capacity, share geological survey data, and establish a common strategic stockpile that any member can draw upon in the event of supply chain disruption. This is the trade defence equivalent of NATO: a collective security arrangement for the supply chains upon which modern industry depends.

Summary of Legislative Requirements

The E9 framework is built on the British Trade Architecture Act, a single piece of primary legislation introduced alongside the Tax Reset Act, the Prosperity Zones Act, and the Enterprise and Innovation Act in the first King’s Speech. No additional Acts are required. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, or departmental action.

British Trade Architecture Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: Regulatory Competition Framework with biennial Competitive Regulatory Assessments for all economic regulators. British AI Regulatory Framework rejecting EU AI Act precautionary approach. British Data Standard achieving simultaneous adequacy with US, EU, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, and Australia. MHRA sovereign accelerated drug approval pathway with 12-month maximum. Financial Services Divergence Acceleration completing and extending Edinburgh Reforms. Mutual recognition agreement negotiating powers for professional qualifications, product standards, and regulatory approvals. National Trade Strategy with statutory priority market rankings. Tier One priority partnerships with the US, India, GCC, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Canada, and Singapore. Services-first negotiating mandates requiring proportionate services access in every agreement. National Trade Negotiation Service as professional negotiating body. Financial Services Equivalence Framework for standalone bilateral agreements. Mandatory digital trade chapters in all trade agreements. Professional Qualifications Authority for mutual recognition negotiations. Commonwealth Economic Partnership Initiative. Commonwealth Digital Trade Network. Commonwealth Prosperity Fund at £1 billion. Prosperity Zone Trade Chapters in all bilateral agreements. Dual-certification powers for zone manufacturing. Statutory zone export targets. Critical Supply Chain Resilience Framework. British Critical Minerals Strategy with 50% Chinese dependency reduction target. Modernised Trade Remedies Authority with 60-day preliminary determinations. Geostrategic Impact Assessment for all trade agreements including retrospective application.

Delivered operationally: Regulatory Competition Unit within 30 days. Twenty highest-value divergence opportunities within 60 days. Regulatory Competition Strategy within 90 days. Simultaneous data adequacy negotiations with five major markets within 60 days. US comprehensive partnership proposed within 30 days. India Services and Technology Partnership within six months. GCC agreement concluded within six months. CPTPP bilateral deepening with four priority members. Services Export Strategy within 90 days. Financial services equivalence negotiations commenced with nine jurisdictions. Services trade attachés in twenty markets within 60 days. Commonwealth Trade Commissioner appointed within 30 days. Africa and Indo-Pacific trade missions within 60 days. Zone Export Strategies for all eight zones within 60 days. Critical supply chain audit commenced within 60 days, reported within 90 days. Critical Minerals Alliance proposed within 30 days. National Trade Strategy published within 90 days.

Funding the Trade Architecture

The British Trade Architecture Act requires minimal direct fiscal expenditure. The Commonwealth Prosperity Fund of £1 billion is funded through reallocation of existing overseas development assistance. The National Trade Negotiation Service, the Regulatory Competition Unit, the services trade attaché network, and the Commonwealth Trade Commissioner are funded through reallocation within the Department for Business and Trade and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, replacing generalist positions with specialist ones at no net additional cost. The critical minerals processing capability is funded through the Prosperity Zone Capital Fund described in E2.4. The trade defence instruments are self-funding through the duties they collect. The revenue generated by the trade agreements themselves, through increased exports, higher tax receipts from a broader economic base, and the attraction of international investment into Prosperity Zones, dwarfs the modest operational costs of the institutions that negotiate and implement them.

E9 completes the outward-facing dimension of Britain’s economic transformation. E1 provides the cheap energy that makes British production competitive. E2 provides the places in which world-class goods and services are produced. E3 provides the companies that produce them. E4 liberates the planning system that enables them to build. E5 ensures the workers can afford to live near where they work. E6 ensures they keep what they earn. E7 frees the small businesses that sustain communities. E8 drives down the cost of everything they buy. E9 connects all of this to the world: the regulatory sovereignty that makes British industry more agile than its European competitors, the bilateral deals that open the fastest-growing markets on Earth, the services supremacy that exploits Britain’s overwhelming comparative advantage, the Commonwealth partnership that leverages the most geographically diverse trading network in existence, the Prosperity Zone export corridors that turn domestic industrial clusters into global champions, and the trade defence that ensures no hostile power can hold Britain’s economy hostage.

The measure of success is specific. Within five years: the UK’s trade deficit with the EU will have narrowed by at least 25% through increased services exports and reduced regulatory friction on zone-produced goods. The UK will have comprehensive Tier One agreements in force with the United States, India, the GCC, and at least two further priority partners. The share of UK exports going to non-EU markets will have increased from 59% to at least 65%. Every Prosperity Zone will be exporting at least 30% of its output by value. The UK’s financial services trade surplus will have grown from £94 billion to over £120 billion. And Britain will have reduced its dependence on Chinese-processed critical minerals by at least 20 percentage points. That is a trade architecture worthy of the name: not a series of diplomatic gestures, but the engine by which a reindustrialised, deregulated, and globally competitive Britain converts its domestic transformation into prosperity for every worker in the country.

#### E10. The Procurement Revolution

Governing Principle

The British state spends £434 billion per year on procurement, according to the Treasury’s Public Expenditure Statistical Analysis for 2024/25, representing roughly a third of all public expenditure. This is the single largest flow of money in the British economy. It buys everything from surgical instruments to submarines, from school dinners to satellite systems, from road resurfacing to the digital infrastructure that runs the welfare state. It is spent, overwhelmingly, with staggering incompetence.

The Infrastructure and Projects Authority, the government’s own watchdog, rated just 11% of all major government projects as likely to succeed in 2024, down from 48% in 2013 and 17% in 2018. Eighty-four per cent of major projects are running with significant issues. The TaxPayers’ Alliance has documented £17.2 billion in cost overruns across just ten major projects, equivalent to £624 per household. The Lower Thames Crossing, the Houses of Parliament renovation, NHS digitalisation, and rail passenger services alone have accumulated 3,372 days of delay and £6.2 billion in overruns. Universal Credit, originally budgeted at £2 billion, consumed over £12 billion before achieving its objectives. The National Programme for IT in the NHS was abandoned in 2011 after £12 billion of expenditure produced almost nothing. HS2, the single largest item on the government’s infrastructure books, was estimated at £37.5 billion in 2009 and is now projected to cost over £81 billion in 2019 prices for Phase 1 alone, which is to say over £100 billion in today’s money, for a railway that is approximately one-third complete despite having been planned to be three-quarters complete, whose CEO wrote to the Transport Secretary in March 2025 that “the organisation has failed in its mission to control costs and deliver to schedule,” and whose northern leg has been cancelled entirely. The Stewart Review of June 2025 found that “the top-down vision of building a railway that would be the best and fastest has been a major factor in undermining attempts to introduce a culture of cost control.” The Transport Secretary called the situation “an appalling mess” and conceded that billions of pounds of taxpayers’ money had been wasted.

The consultancy industry feeds on this failure. Eight firms alone, the Big Four accountancies plus McKinsey, BCG, Bain, and Accenture, have been awarded £8.56 billion in public sector contracts since December 2019 according to data compiled by Tussell. Large consultancies won £1.5 billion in government contracts in 2024, an increase on £1.4 billion in 2023 and £1 billion in 2022. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero is spending £339 million on a single contract with Deloitte. HMRC is spending £286 million on an engagement with PA Consulting. The Home Office has engagements with Accenture worth £240 million. The seven largest consultancy suppliers account for over 40% of total management consultancy procurement spending. Every government in the past two decades has pledged to cut consulting spend. None has succeeded, because the civil service has been hollowed out to the point where it cannot function without external advisers, and the consultancies know this. The government pays to outsource its own competence, and the consultancies, rationally, have no incentive to build the in-house capability that would end their engagement.

Meanwhile, the businesses that should be supplying the state are frozen out. Only 20% of direct public sector procurement spending went to SMEs in 2024, according to the BCC’s SME Procurement Tracker, a proportion that has not meaningfully changed since 2019. Central government spends just 11% of its procurement directly with SMEs; the Ministry of Defence manages 5%. The National Audit Office’s 2025 report on digital procurement found that repeated delays and cost overruns in digital delivery have cost the public sector a minimum of £3 billion across five tracked programmes, with the government’s commercial approach to selecting and working with suppliers identified as a primary cause. The UK public sector spends at least £14 billion annually on digital procurement, and the vast majority flows to incumbent contractors who deliver late, over budget, and below specification. The Procurement Act 2023, which came into force in February 2025, consolidated the legislative framework and introduced some useful transparency measures, but it changed terminology more than it changed incentive structures. The fundamental dynamic remains: a state that cannot build, that cannot buy, and that cannot hold its suppliers to account.

E3 established the principle that government procurement should be an engine of startup growth, creating the Unicorn Pipeline and mandating that every department allocate a minimum of 15% of its technology procurement budget to companies with fewer than 250 employees. E7 established mandatory 30-day payment terms for SME suppliers and gave the Small Business Commissioner enforcement teeth. E10 completes the architecture. It addresses the systemic failures that E3 and E7 cannot fix alone: the consulting cartel that extracts billions while delivering failure, the absence of accountability for officials who commission and manage failed projects, the structural barriers that prevent SMEs from accessing the other 85% of procurement spending, and the failure to use procurement as an instrument of industrial policy by directing state purchasing power toward the Prosperity Zones described in E2. The objective is not to spend less. It is to spend with the same money and get immeasurably more: better outcomes, faster delivery, broader supplier bases, and a procurement system that actively builds British economic capacity rather than passively enriching a closed circle of incumbent contractors.

Progress’ procurement revolution rests on five principles. First, the state will buy outcomes, not time. The consulting and contracting model in which the government pays for hours worked, not results delivered, will be replaced by outcome-based contracts with milestone payments, performance bonds, and clawback provisions. Second, the state will buy from the broad economy, not from a cartel. Mandatory SME allocations, lot-splitting, simplified bidding, and aggressive payment enforcement will ensure that the £434 billion annual spend circulates through the productive economy rather than concentrating in the accounts of a dozen large firms. Third, the state will buy from Prosperity Zone companies as a matter of industrial strategy, using its purchasing power to accelerate zone development and build export-competitive domestic supply chains. Fourth, the state will hold its suppliers and its own officials accountable for failure, through clawback, debarment, personal liability, and the end of the culture in which cost overruns are absorbed, delays are accepted, and nobody is ever fired. Fifth, the state will buy innovation, mandating that a proportion of every department’s budget goes to novel solutions from British companies, modelled on the US Small Business Innovation Research programme that created much of America’s technological superiority by requiring federal agencies to allocate 3.2% of their R&D budgets to small firms.

##### E10.1: Breaking the Consulting Cartel

The Problem

The British civil service has outsourced its own competence. In 2024, the government spent £3.4 billion on management consulting suppliers, according to Tussell, a figure that remains over £1 billion above pre-pandemic levels despite successive pledges by both Conservative and Labour governments to reduce reliance on external advisers. The Chancellor’s pledge to halve consultancy spending by 2026 and save £1.2 billion has not altered the structural dynamic: in the first two quarters of 2024, the eight largest consulting firms secured 348 contracts worth £638 million, and in the second half of the year they secured a further 262 contracts worth £837 million, an increase on the same period in 2023. The Office for Value for Money, established in the 2024 Autumn Budget to eliminate inefficiencies, was found by the Treasury Select Committee to lack resources and have too short a lifespan to be credible.

The pattern is self-reinforcing. Successive governments have imposed headcount constraints on the civil service while increasing the demands on departments, creating a structural dependency on external consultants to perform functions that should be delivered in-house. Consultancies, rationally, design their engagements to perpetuate the dependency: they build bespoke solutions that only they can maintain, they embed their staff in departmental teams for years at a time, and they create knowledge asymmetries that make it impossible for the department to operate without them. Many top-spending departments have a preferred consulting supplier: the Department for International Development’s historic relationship with PwC, the Department for International Trade with EY, the Department for Work and Pensions with Deloitte. These relationships become institutional, and the institutional knowledge that should reside in the civil service migrates to the consultancy instead.

The cost is not merely financial. It is a loss of state capacity. A government that cannot design, commission, or manage its own projects without external advisers is a government that has surrendered its core competence. Every pound spent on a management consultant to tell a department what it should already know is a pound not spent on building the internal capability to know it permanently. Progress’ State Capacity programme, described across this framework, requires a civil service that can think, plan, and execute. The consulting cartel is an obstacle to that objective, and Progress will break it.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Public Procurement Reform Act will establish:

- a) A statutory cap on management consultancy expenditure. No government department, executive agency, or non-departmental public body will spend more than 3% of its annual budget on external management consultancy services, down from the current effective rate that exceeds 5% in several departments. The cap will be enforced by the Treasury and breach will require personal authorisation from the Secretary of State, who must certify in writing that the consultancy engagement is essential, that no internal capability exists or can be developed within the required timeframe, and that the engagement includes a mandatory knowledge transfer plan. The cap will be phased in over 18 months from Royal Assent to allow departments to build the internal capability that replaces external dependency.
- b) Mandatory knowledge transfer in every consultancy engagement. The Act will require that all management consultancy contracts above £500,000 include a binding knowledge transfer obligation requiring the consultant to train designated civil servants to a level at which the function can be performed in-house upon completion of the contract. The knowledge transfer deliverables will be specified in the contract, assessed independently at contract conclusion, and failure to deliver adequate knowledge transfer will constitute a material breach entitling the department to withhold up to 20% of the contract value. No consultancy engagement may be renewed or extended beyond its original term if the knowledge transfer obligation has not been met. This provision ensures that every consultancy engagement has an end date that is real, not theoretical.
- c) Contract duration limits. No management consultancy engagement with a single supplier may exceed three years in total, including extensions and renewals, without a competitive re-tender. Framework agreements that allow repeated call-offs from the same supplier will be subject to a cumulative three-year cap on the total value awarded to any single firm. The current system, in which framework agreements effectively provide open-ended access to favoured suppliers for years at a time, will be replaced by a regime in which incumbency provides no advantage and every significant engagement is genuinely contested.
- d) A State Capability Investment Fund. The Act will require that 50% of the savings generated by the 3% consultancy cap be reinvested in building permanent civil service capability. The fund will finance the recruitment of specialists from the private sector into permanent civil service roles, the establishment of internal centres of expertise in technology, project management, commercial negotiation, and data analysis, and the creation of a Government Consulting Corps: an in-house consultancy function modelled on the Government Digital Service but covering all professional services disciplines. The Corps will be staffed by individuals recruited from the private sector at competitive salaries, employed on renewable five-year terms, and available to departments as a first resort before external consultants are engaged.

OPERATIONAL

Consultancy audit. Within 60 days of taking office, the Cabinet Office will conduct a comprehensive audit of all live management consultancy engagements across central government, publishing the name of each supplier, the contract value, the duration, the department, the original and current cost estimates, and the knowledge transfer provisions in each contract. The audit will be published in full and updated quarterly. Transparency is the precondition for accountability.

Government Consulting Corps. Within six months of Royal Assent, the Cabinet Office will establish the Government Consulting Corps with an initial complement of 500 professionals recruited from the private sector. The Corps will offer salaries competitive with the lower quartile of consulting firm compensation, combined with security of employment and the non-financial advantages of public service. The Corps will be operational within 12 months and will be the default provider of professional services to departments before any external engagement is considered.

##### E10.2: The British Innovation Procurement Mandate

The Problem

The United States did not build its technological superiority through venture capital. It built it through procurement. The Small Business Innovation Research programme, established in 1982, requires eleven federal agencies to allocate 3.2% of their extramural R&D budgets to small firms through a structured three-phase process: feasibility, development, and commercialisation. Since inception, SBIR has funded over 170,000 awards totalling more than $50 billion and has been the seedbed for companies that became global leaders. Studies from the US programme show that companies that won SBIR contracts grew at five times the rate of comparable firms over ten years. NASA, the Department of Defence, and the National Institutes of Health used procurement not merely to acquire goods and services but to create entire industries. The semiconductor industry, the internet, GPS, and the modern pharmaceutical industry all trace their origins to federal procurement contracts that gave small innovative companies their first revenue.

Britain’s equivalent, the Small Business Research Initiative, was established in 2001, explicitly modelled on the American programme. It has been, by any honest assessment, a pale imitation. Since inception, SBRI has awarded just over £500 million in total, less than what the US programme awards in a single year. SBRI has no mandatory departmental allocation, no consistent Phase 3 commercialisation pathway, and no statutory force compelling departments to use it. An independent evaluation described it as a programme that “has not done this as intensively or as extensively as it could” and identified “scope for a significant scaling up.” The UK programme relies on voluntary departmental participation, which means that departments under budget pressure, which is all of them, deprioritise innovation procurement in favour of safe, familiar, and large suppliers. The result is that British government departments buy the same solutions from the same companies, year after year, while the startups and innovative SMEs that could deliver better outcomes at lower cost are locked out.

E3.2 established the Unicorn Pipeline, using Innovate UK as a seeding vehicle deploying £1 billion annually in SAFE investments to 1,000 startups solving identified public sector problems, with subsequent progression to multi-million-pound potting contracts and then to major government contracts. E3.5 mandated a 15% departmental technology procurement allocation for companies with fewer than 250 employees. E10.2 extends this principle from technology procurement to all procurement. Every department buys goods, services, equipment, materials, and solutions that innovative British companies could supply, if the procurement system were designed to let them in rather than keep them out.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Public Procurement Reform Act will establish:

- a) A British Innovation Procurement Mandate.
