The Act will require every government department, executive agency, and non-departmental public body with annual procurement expenditure exceeding £50 million to allocate a minimum of 5% of its total procurement budget, not merely its technology budget, to innovative solutions from companies with fewer than 250 employees and annual revenue below £50 million. “Innovative solutions” will be defined as goods, services, or processes that represent a material improvement over the incumbent solution in cost, quality, speed, or sustainability, as assessed by the department’s Chief Procurement Officer. The 5% mandate operates alongside and in addition to the 15% technology procurement allocation established in E3.5. The distinction is that E3.5 targets technology procurement specifically; E10.2 targets all procurement, including facilities management, logistics, construction, professional services, equipment supply, catering, training, and every other category of government spending.
- b) A three-phase innovation procurement pathway. Modelled on the US SBIR programme but adapted for British conditions and applied beyond R&D to all categories of procurement, the pathway will consist of: Phase 1, Feasibility, in which the department issues a challenge specification and funds up to ten companies at up to £250,000 each to demonstrate a viable solution within six months; Phase 2, Development, in which up to three companies from Phase 1 receive contracts of up to £2 million over 12 months to develop a deployable solution; and Phase 3, Deployment, in which the winning company receives a full procurement contract on standard commercial terms. Phase 3 is the critical difference from the existing SBRI, which has no consistent conversion to live procurement. Without Phase 3, innovation procurement is a research exercise that generates interesting reports but no deployed solutions. With Phase 3, it is a procurement pathway that produces better outcomes at lower cost while building the supply chain that E3 and E7 are designed to cultivate.
- c) A statutory right of first refusal for British innovative companies. Where a department identifies a procurement requirement that could be met by a British company that has previously delivered a successful Phase 2 innovation procurement contract, the department will be required to offer that company a right of first refusal on the full procurement contract before opening it to wider competition. The right of first refusal will be exercised through a simplified sole-source pathway with a maximum decision timeline of 30 days, provided the company’s proposed price is within 10% of the estimated market rate. This provision rewards companies that have invested in solving government problems and ensures that the innovation procurement pathway leads to ongoing commercial relationships, not one-off engagements.

OPERATIONAL

Innovation procurement targets. Within 60 days of Royal Assent, the Cabinet Office will publish departmental innovation procurement targets for the first financial year, breaking down the 5% mandate by department and by procurement category. Departmental compliance will be reported quarterly in the Startup Procurement Scorecard established under E3.5, which will be expanded to cover all innovation procurement, not merely technology. Non-compliant departments will lose a corresponding proportion of their discretionary procurement budget in the following year.

Challenge specifications. Within 90 days, the Cabinet Office will publish the first tranche of innovation procurement challenge specifications, drawn from the National Technology Challenge List established under E3.2 but expanded to include non-technology procurement challenges across all departments. The List will be maintained and updated quarterly, providing a visible, accessible pipeline of opportunities for innovative British companies.

##### E10.3: SME Market Access

The Problem

Small and medium-sized enterprises account for 99.9% of all UK businesses, employ 16.7 million people, and generate over half of private sector turnover. They receive 20% of public procurement spending. This figure has not meaningfully changed in five years. Central government manages just 11% directly with SMEs, down from 12% in 2018. The Ministry of Defence achieves 5%. The NHS is scarcely better. The Procurement Act 2023, which came into force in February 2025, introduced a duty for authorities to consider dividing contracts into smaller lots and shifted evaluation criteria from “Most Economically Advantageous Tender” to “Most Advantageous Tender,” incorporating social value. These are steps in the right direction, but they are permissive, not mandatory. A duty to “consider” lot-splitting is not a duty to lot-split. Departments consider, decline, and award monolithic contracts to the same large suppliers.

The barriers are structural. Procurement processes are designed for companies with bid teams, compliance departments, and the capacity to absorb months of pre-qualification, evaluation, and due diligence. A construction firm with 30 employees and excellent capabilities cannot afford to spend three months preparing a bid with no guarantee of success while simultaneously running its existing projects. The pre-qualification questionnaires alone can run to hundreds of pages. Framework agreements, which now account for over half of strategic supplier contracts, create closed shops: once a framework is populated with its approved suppliers, which are overwhelmingly large firms, new entrants are locked out until the framework expires, typically after four years. The Procurement Act’s “Open Frameworks” concept allows new suppliers to join at set intervals, but the administrative burden of entry remains formidable.

The late payment regime compounds the problem. Government itself is a chronic late payer. The 30-day payment terms mandated by the Public Contract Regulations are routinely breached, and the cascade through the supply chain means that SME subcontractors wait 60, 90, or 120 days for payment even when the prime contractor has been paid on time. E7.6 established mandatory 30-day payment terms for all business-to-business contracts where the supplier is an SME, automatic statutory interest at base rate plus 8%, and Late Payment Enforcement Orders enforceable by a strengthened Small Business Commissioner. E10.3 extends these principles specifically to government procurement, where the state’s own purchasing power makes it both the largest customer in the economy and, for many SMEs, the most important one.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Public Procurement Reform Act will establish:

- a) A mandatory SME procurement target of 33% of direct public sector procurement spending, rising from the current 20%, to be achieved within the first Parliament. The target will be statutory, not aspirational. Every department, executive agency, NHS trust, local authority, and non-departmental public body will publish its SME procurement share annually, and the Cabinet Office will publish a consolidated national scorecard. Departments that fail to meet the target for two consecutive years will be subject to a mandated procurement reform programme overseen by the Cabinet Office, including mandatory lot-splitting for all contracts above £1 million and restrictions on the use of framework agreements that exclude SME participation.
- b) Mandatory lot-splitting. All procurement contracts with a total value above £5 million will be divided into lots of no more than £2 million each, unless the contracting authority certifies in writing that division is technically impossible or would result in a demonstrable reduction in value for money that outweighs the benefits of broader participation. The certification will be reviewed by the Procurement Review Unit established under the Procurement Act 2023 and published on the Central Digital Platform. The current permissive duty to “consider” lot-splitting will be replaced by a mandatory duty to lot-split with a narrow and scrutinised exemption.
- c) Simplified bidding for SMEs. The Act will establish a Simplified Procurement Pathway for all contracts below £2 million. The pathway will consist of a single standardised application form of no more than ten pages, a single pre-qualification questionnaire that, once completed and verified, is valid for all government procurement opportunities for two years, and a maximum decision timeline of 30 days from submission to contract award. The existing system, in which every contracting authority designs its own bespoke procurement process with its own forms, criteria, and timelines, will be replaced by a standardised national process for all contracts below the threshold. This does not reduce the quality of evaluation; it reduces the administrative burden that deters SMEs from bidding.
- d) Cascade payment enforcement. The Act will require that all prime contractors on government contracts above £5 million pay their subcontractors within 30 days of receiving payment from the contracting authority, and that the 30-day cascade obligation extends to every tier of the supply chain. The contracting authority will have the right to pay subcontractors directly if the prime contractor fails to cascade payment within the required period, deducting the amount from sums owed to the prime. This provision complements the late payment enforcement established in E7.6 by ensuring that the government’s own supply chain cannot be used as a mechanism for delayed payment to SMEs. From October 2025, companies bidding for government contracts above £5 million are already required to demonstrate average payment times of 45 days or less; Progress will reduce this to 30 days and extend the requirement to all government contracts regardless of value.
- e) Debarment for persistent late payment. The Act will add persistent late payment to SME subcontractors, defined as three or more invoices unpaid beyond 30 days within any six-month period, as a discretionary exclusion ground under the Procurement Act 2023’s debarment regime. A prime contractor that persistently fails to pay its small suppliers on time will be excluded from bidding for government contracts for a period of 12 months. This provision gives the existing debarment list genuine economic teeth in the area where it matters most to small businesses.

OPERATIONAL

SME Procurement Dashboard. Within 60 days of Royal Assent, the Cabinet Office will publish a national SME Procurement Dashboard on the Central Digital Platform, showing in real time the SME procurement share of every department, agency, and NHS trust. The dashboard will be updated monthly and will track not only direct SME spend but also SME spend through the supply chain, using data from the cascade payment reporting requirements. The dashboard will be public, searchable, and linked to the quarterly Startup Procurement Scorecard.

Simplified Procurement Portal. Within six months, the Crown Commercial Service will launch a Simplified Procurement Portal as a dedicated entry point for SMEs seeking government contracts. The portal will provide a single registration, a reusable pre-qualification profile, automated matching of companies to relevant opportunities, and plain-language guidance on every stage of the procurement process. The portal will integrate with the existing Central Digital Platform but will present a simplified interface designed for companies without dedicated bid teams.

##### E10.4: The Accountability Framework

The Problem

The British government’s procurement failures are not merely expensive. They are consequence-free. The officials who commission projects that overrun by billions are not dismissed, disciplined, or penalised. The contractors who deliver late and over budget are not debarred; they are awarded new contracts. The Senior Responsible Owners who preside over catastrophic failures retire with honours and pensions intact. The Infrastructure and Projects Authority publishes annual reports documenting failure after failure, and nothing changes, because there is no mechanism that connects failure to consequence.

The deeper pathology is the systematic separation of responsibility from authority. In every domain of human endeavour where complex projects are delivered successfully, from military operations to surgical teams to the construction of private-sector megastructures, the pattern is the same: the person who is responsible for the outcome has the authority to make the decisions that determine the outcome. Responsibility without authority produces paralysis: the SRO who is nominally accountable for a £10 billion programme but cannot fire an underperforming contractor without Treasury approval, cannot redirect budget between workstreams without a change-control committee, and cannot make a design decision without convening a stakeholder board, is not accountable in any meaningful sense. They are a name on an organogram. Authority without responsibility produces recklessness: the minister who announces a project, sets a politically convenient timeline, changes scope to accommodate a conference speech, and faces no personal consequence when the project fails is exercising power without accountability. The British procurement system has perfected both failure modes simultaneously. It distributes responsibility so thinly that nobody owns anything, and concentrates authority in committees, boards, and approval chains that ensure no decision is ever made quickly or clearly enough to matter.

HS2 is the paradigm. The project was originally estimated at £37.5 billion. Phase 1 alone is now projected to cost over £81 billion in 2019 prices. Over £40 billion has been spent to date. The northern leg has been cancelled. The CEO appointed in December 2024 described the situation as “unsustainable” and found no reliable earned-value measure. The Stewart Review identified that construction started before designs were mature, that unrealistic schedules drove decisions, and that the supply chain was insufficiently incentivised. It further found that the project had been “subject to evolving political aims” that pushed forward on schedule before there was sufficient design maturity and caused progressive removals of scope. This is the responsibility-authority pathology in its purest form: politicians exercised authority over timelines and scope without bearing responsibility for the consequences, while officials bore nominal responsibility for delivery without possessing authority over the decisions that determined whether delivery was possible. Nobody was accountable because nobody simultaneously held both the power and the obligation. And so nobody has been held accountable. No contractor has been debarred. No official has faced personal consequences. The institutional lesson is clear: failure is free.

The Procurement Act 2023 introduced a debarment list and the Procurement Review Unit. These are useful innovations, but they address future misconduct, not the structural absence of accountability for past and ongoing failure. The debarment list is populated through a process so cumbersome that as of February 2026 it contains negligible entries. The Procurement Review Unit has advisory functions but limited enforcement power. The fundamental problem is cultural and structural: the British government does not treat the waste of public money as a disciplinary offence, does not unite responsibility with authority in identifiable individuals, and does not learn from its own failures. Progress will address all three.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Public Procurement Reform Act will establish:

- a) The principle of unified accountability. The Act will establish, as a statutory principle governing all government procurement above £10 million, that the Senior Responsible Owner of a procurement project must possess both the responsibility for the project’s outcome and the authority to make the decisions that determine that outcome. The SRO will have statutory authority to: select and dismiss contractors within approved procurement parameters; reallocate budget between workstreams up to 10% of total project value without Treasury approval; make design and specification decisions without committee referral provided they remain within the approved project scope; and veto ministerial or departmental requests to change project scope, timeline, or specification without a corresponding adjustment to budget and risk assessment. In return for this authority, the SRO will bear personal accountability for the project’s adherence to its approved budget, timeline, and specification. This is the composite definition of true accountability: responsibility married to authority. One cannot exist without the other. A person who is responsible for an outcome they cannot influence is a scapegoat; a person who influences an outcome they are not responsible for is unaccountable. Progress will tolerate neither.
- b) Personal consequences for project failure. Where a project exceeds its approved budget by more than 20% or its approved timeline by more than 12 months, the SRO will be required to appear before the relevant parliamentary select committee to account for the overrun and will be ineligible for performance-related bonuses for the relevant period. Where the overrun is attributable to management failure rather than genuinely unforeseeable external factors, the SRO will face disciplinary proceedings under the Civil Service Code. Conversely, where the SRO can demonstrate that the overrun resulted from a scope change, timeline acceleration, or budget reduction imposed by a minister or departmental leadership after the project baseline was approved, the accountability will follow the authority: the individual who exercised the authority that caused the failure will be identified in the public record. This provision ends the practice of politicians making impossible promises and officials taking the blame.
- c) Mandatory performance bonds. All government contracts with a total value above £10 million will require the contractor to provide a performance bond of at least 10% of the contract value, to be drawn upon in the event of non-delivery, significant delay, or material failure to meet contractual specifications. The bond will be held by an independent surety and released in stages linked to milestone delivery. For contracts above £100 million, the bond percentage will increase to 15%. Performance bonds are standard in the private sector and in many international procurement regimes; their absence from UK government procurement is an anomaly that Progress will correct.
- d) Clawback provisions. All government contracts with a total value above £5 million will include a statutory clawback provision entitling the government to recover payments made in respect of work that is subsequently found to be defective, incomplete, or materially below specification. The clawback will extend for three years beyond contract completion and will be enforceable without proof of fraud or negligence; it is a strict liability provision reflecting the principle that a contractor who is paid for work that is not delivered to specification should return the money. The clawback will apply to consulting engagements as well as construction and technology contracts, addressing the specific problem of consultancy deliverables that fail to transfer usable knowledge or produce implementable recommendations.
- e) Accelerated debarment. The Act will amend the Procurement Act 2023 to create an accelerated debarment pathway. Where a contractor on a government contract above £10 million fails to deliver on three or more contractual milestones, exceeds the approved budget by more than 25%, or is found to have provided materially misleading information during the procurement process, the Procurement Review Unit will be empowered to place the contractor on the debarment list through an expedited procedure completed within 60 days. The current process, which is too slow to function as a credible deterrent, will be replaced by a procedure fast enough to have real-time consequences.
- f) A Procurement Failures Register. The Act will require the Cabinet Office to maintain and publish a Procurement Failures Register, listing every government contract that has exceeded its approved budget by more than 15%, its approved timeline by more than six months, or has been terminated for non-performance. The Register will identify the contractor, the contracting authority, the SRO, the original and final cost estimates, and the reasons for failure. Where the failure is attributable to a scope change or political intervention after baseline approval, the Register will identify the source of the intervention. Publication is a consequence in itself: contractors named in the Register will face reputational costs that the current system, in which failures are documented in reports that nobody reads, does not impose.
- g) The National Megaproject Office. The Act will establish the National Megaproject Office as a permanent, small, elite body responsible for the governance, assurance, and institutional memory of all government projects with a total value above £1 billion. The Office will not be a department. It will not be a bureaucracy. It will be a unit of no more than 50 people, recruited from the ranks of individuals who have personally delivered complex projects on time and within budget, in both the public and private sectors, domestically and internationally. Its mandate will be threefold. First, knowledge: the Office will maintain a living archive of megaproject management, systematically collecting, synthesising, and codifying lessons from the UK’s own project history and from international experience, including the specific practices that enabled the Olympic Delivery Authority to bring London 2012 in on time and under budget, the management principles that made Lockheed’s Skunk Works the most productive engineering organisation of the twentieth century, the project governance that allows countries with a fraction of Britain’s wealth to build infrastructure at a fraction of Britain’s cost, and the failure modes that have produced the UK’s current 11% project success rate. This archive will not be a library. It will be a set of operational principles, updated continuously, tested against live projects, and made available to every SRO in government. Second, assurance: the Office will conduct independent stage-gate reviews of every megaproject at each critical transition point, from design to procurement, from procurement to construction, from construction to commissioning. The Office will have the statutory authority to recommend that a project be paused if it is not ready to proceed, and the relevant Secretary of State will be required to either accept the recommendation or publish a written explanation for overriding it. Third, continuity: the Office will provide institutional memory that survives changes of government, changes of SRO, and changes of contractor. The single greatest cause of megaproject failure is the loss of knowledge when key personnel leave. The Office will ensure that the accumulated understanding of each project’s risks, decisions, and dependencies is held in an institution that endures, not in the heads of individuals who rotate.
- h) The Procurement Integrity Unit. The Act will establish a Procurement Integrity Unit within the Cabinet Office with statutory investigative powers to examine procurement decisions, contract awards, and contractor performance across all government departments and agencies. The Unit will be empowered to: conduct forensic audits of any government contract above £1 million, including examination of subcontract pricing, cost allocation, and profit margins; compel the production of documents and testimony from both government officials and contractors; refer findings to the Serious Fraud Office or the National Crime Agency where evidence of criminal conduct is identified; and impose administrative penalties for procurement malpractice falling below the criminal threshold, including conflicts of interest, undisclosed relationships between procurement officials and contractors, and the deliberate inflation of cost estimates to secure larger budget allocations. The Unit will operate independently of the departments it investigates and will publish an annual report on procurement integrity across government, identifying systemic vulnerabilities and recommending reforms. The Unit’s existence ensures that the accountability framework is not merely backward-looking, catching failures after they occur, but forward-looking, deterring the practices that produce failures in the first place.

OPERATIONAL

National Megaproject Office establishment. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Cabinet Office will begin recruitment for the National Megaproject Office, drawing candidates from the global pool of individuals with demonstrated megaproject delivery experience. The Office will be led by a Director appointed on a ten-year non-renewable term to provide continuity beyond political cycles. The Director will be selected by an independent panel including individuals with experience of delivering megaprojects internationally. The Office will be operational within six months and will assume assurance responsibility for all live megaprojects within 12 months. The Office will be physically co-located with the Infrastructure and Projects Authority but will be operationally independent, reporting directly to the Chancellor and the Prime Minister.

Procurement Integrity Unit establishment. Within 60 days of Royal Assent, the Cabinet Office will establish the Procurement Integrity Unit with an initial complement of 30 investigators, drawn from backgrounds in forensic accounting, fraud investigation, and procurement law. The Unit will be operational within 90 days and will begin with a systematic review of procurement practices in departments identified by the NAO as having the highest risk profiles. The Unit’s investigative priorities will be determined independently by its Director, who will be appointed on a seven-year term and will be removable only by parliamentary resolution.

Retrospective accountability review. Within 90 days of taking office, the Cabinet Office will commission a review of the ten largest procurement failures of the past decade, identifying the contractors, officials, and decisions responsible for the overruns and assessing whether the failures were attributable to manageable risk or to systemic mismanagement. The review will map the responsibility-authority structure of each failed project, identifying where authority was exercised without accountability and where responsibility was assigned without corresponding authority. The review will report within six months and its findings will inform the first entries on the Procurement Failures Register, the first referrals to the accelerated debarment pathway, and the National Megaproject Office’s initial operational principles.

Project governance reform. Within six months, the Infrastructure and Projects Authority, in consultation with the National Megaproject Office, will publish reformed governance standards for all major government projects, incorporating the principle of unified accountability, mandatory stage-gate reviews with independent cost assurance, a requirement that no project proceed from design to construction until designs are 80% mature, and a prohibition on announcing public delivery dates before a baseline cost estimate has been independently verified. The IPA’s traffic-light rating system, in which the vast majority of projects are rated amber, which communicates nothing useful, will be replaced by a quantified risk assessment published alongside each project’s annual report.

##### E10.5: Prosperity Zone Procurement Preference

The Problem

The eight Prosperity Zones established in E2 are designed to concentrate British industrial capacity in sectors where the UK has genuine competitive advantage: life sciences, precision manufacturing and aerospace, nuclear supply chain, compound semiconductors, defence technology, data and fintech, maritime engineering, and space and critical minerals. The learning tariffs described in E2.6 provide temporary protection during the developmental phase. The export corridors described in E9.5 provide the markets into which zone production will flow. But between protection and export lies a critical gap: the domestic market. And the single largest domestic buyer is the government.

The government currently buys billions of pounds’ worth of goods and services that could be sourced from the Prosperity Zones: pharmaceuticals, medical devices, defence equipment, semiconductor components, nuclear fuel assemblies, marine engineering, satellite systems, fintech infrastructure, and advanced manufacturing. It buys these goods overwhelmingly from foreign suppliers or from large domestic contractors who themselves source from foreign supply chains. The Prosperity Zones will not achieve their potential if the British government continues to buy from abroad what British zone companies can produce at home. Procurement is not merely a mechanism for acquiring goods and services. It is an instrument of industrial policy, and Progress will use it as such.

This is not protectionism. The Prosperity Zones are subject to learning tariffs that decline automatically and expire entirely within seven years. Zone companies are expected to be export-competitive by year three. The procurement preference described in this section operates on the same principle: it provides an additional domestic demand signal during the developmental phase, accelerating the point at which zone companies achieve the scale, efficiency, and track record necessary to compete internationally. It is an investment in British industrial capacity, paid for not through subsidy but through the redirection of money the government was going to spend anyway.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Public Procurement Reform Act will establish:

- a) A Prosperity Zone Procurement Preference. Government departments and agencies will be required to source from Prosperity Zone companies where: the zone company can meet the required specification; the zone company’s price is within 15% of the lowest-cost compliant tender from a non-zone supplier; and the procurement relates to goods or services within the zone’s designated sector as defined in E2.1. The 15% price tolerance reflects the developmental nature of zone production and declines by 3 percentage points per year, reaching zero at year five, at which point zone companies must compete on level terms. The preference does not apply to procurement from allies under reciprocal government procurement access agreements negotiated under E9.2; it applies only to procurement that would otherwise be sourced from companies outside the zone system with no reciprocal benefit to British exporters.
- b) Dual-sourcing requirements. For procurement categories identified as critical to the Prosperity Zone supply chain, including active pharmaceutical ingredients, semiconductor wafers, rare earth components, nuclear fuel assemblies, and defence subsystems, the Act will require contracting authorities to maintain at least two approved suppliers, of which at least one must be a Prosperity Zone company or a company operating within the zone supply chain. This provision reduces single-supplier risk, which E9.6 identifies as a critical vulnerability in British supply chains, while simultaneously creating guaranteed demand for zone production.
- c) Zone procurement targets. Each Prosperity Zone Sandpit Authority, as established in E2.1, will publish annual procurement targets specifying the minimum value of government contracts to be sourced from zone companies. The targets will be set in consultation with the relevant government departments and will be linked to the zone’s developmental stage: higher targets in the early years when domestic demand is critical, declining as zone companies build export revenue. The targets will be incorporated into the Sandpit Authority’s annual performance assessment and into the departmental Startup Procurement Scorecard.

OPERATIONAL

Zone procurement mapping. Within 60 days of Royal Assent, the Department for Business and Trade will publish a Zone Procurement Map for each of the eight Prosperity Zones, identifying every category of government procurement that could be sourced from zone companies, the current value of that procurement, the current suppliers, and the timeline by which zone companies are expected to be capable of supplying. The Zone Procurement Maps will be incorporated into the Zone Export Strategies established under E9.5 and updated annually.

Embedded procurement officers. Within 90 days, the Crown Commercial Service will embed a dedicated procurement officer in each Prosperity Zone Sandpit Authority, responsible for connecting zone companies with government procurement opportunities, assisting with bid preparation, and ensuring that the procurement preference is applied consistently across departments. These officers will work alongside the trade attachés established under E9.5 who focus on export markets, creating a complete domestic-and-international market access service for every zone company.

Summary of Legislative Requirements

The E10 framework is built on the Public Procurement Reform Act, a single piece of primary legislation introduced in the first King’s Speech alongside the Energy Security Act (E1), the Prosperity Zones Act (E2), the Enterprise and Innovation Act (E3), the Planning Liberation Act (E4), the Housing Acceleration Act (E5), the Tax Reset Act (E6), the Small Business Liberation Act (E7), and the British Trade Architecture Act (E9). No additional Acts are required. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, or departmental action.

Public Procurement Reform Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: Statutory 3% cap on departmental management consultancy expenditure with Secretary of State certification for exceptions. Mandatory knowledge transfer obligations in all consultancy contracts above £500,000 with 20% withholding for non-compliance. Three-year maximum duration for consultancy engagements with any single supplier. State Capability Investment Fund reinvesting 50% of consultancy savings in permanent civil service capability. Government Consulting Corps as default provider of professional services. British Innovation Procurement Mandate requiring 5% of total procurement budget directed to innovative solutions from companies with fewer than 250 employees, alongside the 15% technology allocation in E3.5. Three-phase innovation procurement pathway with mandatory Phase 3 deployment. Statutory right of first refusal for companies completing successful Phase 2 contracts. Mandatory 33% SME procurement target across the public sector. Mandatory lot-splitting for contracts above £5 million into lots of no more than £2 million. Simplified Procurement Pathway for contracts below £2 million with 30-day decision timelines. Cascade payment enforcement requiring 30-day payment at every tier of the supply chain. Debarment for persistent late payment to SME subcontractors. Statutory principle of unified accountability requiring SROs to hold both responsibility and authority over project outcomes. SRO statutory authority over contractor management, budget reallocation, design decisions, and scope-change veto. Personal consequences for project failure with accountability following authority where political interventions cause overruns. Mandatory performance bonds for contracts above £10 million. Statutory clawback provisions for defective or incomplete work. Accelerated debarment pathway completed within 60 days. Procurement Failures Register identifying contractors, SROs, and sources of scope changes. National Megaproject Office as a permanent elite body of no more than 50 people providing knowledge, assurance, and continuity for all projects above £1 billion, with stage-gate review authority and a Director appointed on a ten-year term. Procurement Integrity Unit with statutory investigative powers including forensic audit authority, power to compel documents and testimony, referral to SFO and NCA, and administrative penalties for procurement malpractice. Prosperity Zone Procurement Preference with declining 15% price tolerance. Dual-sourcing requirements for critical zone supply chain categories. Zone procurement targets linked to Sandpit Authority performance assessments.

Operational timelines

Consultancy audit across central government within 60 days. Innovation procurement targets published within 60 days. First tranche of innovation challenge specifications within 90 days. SME Procurement Dashboard on Central Digital Platform within 60 days. Zone Procurement Maps within 60 days. Embedded procurement officers in all eight Prosperity Zones within 90 days. Procurement Integrity Unit established with 30 investigators within 60 days, operational within 90 days. National Megaproject Office recruitment begins within 90 days, operational within six months, assuming assurance of all live megaprojects within 12 months. Director appointed on ten-year non-renewable term. Retrospective accountability review of ten largest procurement failures within 90 days, reporting within six months, mapping the responsibility-authority structure of each failure. Reformed IPA governance standards incorporating unified accountability principle within six months. Government Consulting Corps established within six months, operational within 12 months. Simplified Procurement Portal within six months.

Funding the Procurement Revolution

The procurement revolution costs nothing. It redirects existing spending, not new spending. The 3% consultancy cap saves hundreds of millions per year, half of which is reinvested in permanent capability and half of which reduces departmental expenditure. The innovation procurement mandate, the SME targets, and the zone procurement preference do not increase the total procurement budget; they alter where the money goes and what it buys. The accountability framework reduces future cost overruns, which currently waste billions. The performance bonds, clawback provisions, and debarment regime create financial consequences for failure that currently do not exist, recovering public money that is currently written off. The National Megaproject Office and the Procurement Integrity Unit are funded from within existing Cabinet Office and IPA budgets; the Office’s 50-person complement costs less than a single week of HS2 overrun, and the Integrity Unit will recover multiples of its operating cost through the identification of procurement malpractice and the deterrent effect of its existence.

The measure of success is specific. Within five years: the SME share of public procurement will have risen from 20% to at least 33%. Departmental management consultancy expenditure will be below 3% of budget. The Procurement Failures Register will contain every overrun above 15%, and the contractors and officials responsible will be identified by name. The National Megaproject Office will hold a living archive of lessons from every major project in British history and will exercise stage-gate authority over every project above £1 billion. Every SRO on a major project will hold both the responsibility for the outcome and the authority to make the decisions that determine it. Every Prosperity Zone will have a published procurement target and a measurable share of government contracts in its designated sector. The innovation procurement pathway will have funded at least 500 Phase 1 projects, converted at least 100 to Phase 2, and deployed at least 30 into live government procurement. And the default assumption in every government department will have shifted from “buy from the incumbent” to “buy from the best, and build the capability to know the difference.”

E10 completes the demand side of Progress’ economic architecture. E1 provides cheap energy. E2 creates the industrial zones. E3 builds the high-growth companies. E4 liberates the planning system. E5 makes housing affordable. E6 ensures workers keep what they earn. E7 frees the shopkeeper. E8 drives down the cost of living. E9 opens the world’s markets. E10 turns the single largest buyer in the British economy, the state itself, from an obstacle to an engine: buying better, buying British, buying from the broad economy, and holding itself and its suppliers to the standard that £434 billion of public money demands.

#### E11. Return of Paid Overtime and Employee Partnership Schemes

Governing Principle

The British worker is more productive than at any point in the country’s history and is paid, in real terms, approximately what they were paid in 2008. Median weekly pay for full-time employees was £767 at April 2025, according to the ONS Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings. Adjusted for CPI inflation, this is 2% lower than in 2008. For most age groups, real earnings only returned to 2008 levels in April 2025, seventeen years after the financial crisis. The TUC has described this as the worst sustained period of wage stagnation since the Napoleonic Wars, and the data supports the claim. Between 2008 and 2022, UK real wage growth averaged 0.2% per annum, dropping the country from 5th in the OECD growth rankings to 16th. Had UK wages followed the OECD average over this period, the typical worker would be earning approximately £3,600 more per year. They are not. The cumulative loss in real earnings since 2008 exceeds £20,000 per worker.

The causes of this stagnation are structural and well-documented. Productivity growth, which averaged 2.2% per year from 1980 to 2007, collapsed to 0.4% per year from 2008 to 2023. The LSE’s Programme on Innovation and Diffusion found that between 1981 and 2019, productivity rose by 87% but median employee wages rose by only 62%, a 25 percentage point overall decoupling. Three-fifths of this gap is explained by growing inequality, with mean wages pulling away from the median, and a further third by the growth of non-wage labour costs, particularly employer pension contributions driven by auto-enrolment. The result is that even when productivity does grow, the typical worker does not feel it. The gains flow upward to the top of the distribution and sideways into employer costs that never appear in a pay packet. The Oxford Review of Economic Policy, summarising the evidence in 2025, found that real wage growth of 2.5% per year from 1991 to 2007 fell to approximately zero in the subsequent fifteen years, and identified the fall in rent-sharing, where workers receive a declining share of the economic rents generated by their employers, as a contributing factor distinct from the productivity slowdown itself.

Into this landscape of stagnation, the British state has contributed a legal framework that actively facilitates the extraction of free labour from employees. The United Kingdom has no statutory right to paid overtime. There is no legal requirement for employers to compensate workers for hours worked beyond their contracted time. The only constraint is that average hourly pay must not fall below the National Minimum Wage, and that the Working Time Regulations cap the average working week at 48 hours, from which employees can opt out in writing. In practice, the TUC’s analysis of Labour Force Survey data found that 3.8 million people worked unpaid overtime in 2024, putting in an average of 7.2 unpaid hours per week. The total value of this free labour was £31 billion. For those individuals, the average annual cost is £8,000 in wages for work performed and not paid. Teachers lead the prevalence statistics, with 38% working unpaid overtime, followed by health and care managers at 35%. London has the highest regional rate at 17%, against a national average of 13%. The UK is virtually alone among major economies in this position. The United States Fair Labor Standards Act has required employers to pay non-exempt employees at one and a half times their regular rate for all hours above 40 per week since 1938. France mandates overtime premiums above 35 hours. Germany, through sectoral collective agreements, mandates premiums for overtime across most of the economy. The UK offers nothing, by statute, and £31 billion flows from workers to employers every year as a direct result.

Meanwhile, the mechanisms by which workers could build wealth through their employment remain marginal, complicated, and poorly distributed. The UK employee ownership sector has grown substantially since the introduction of Employee Ownership Trusts in 2014, reaching approximately 2,500 companies employing 358,000 people by mid-2025. Employee-owned businesses are demonstrably more productive, with 8–12% higher gross value added per employee, and their workforces report higher engagement, lower absenteeism, and higher retention. But 2,500 companies is a tiny fraction of the 5.5 million businesses in the UK. The 2024 Autumn Budget tightened EOT regulations, and the 2025 Budget cut the CGT relief on sales to EOTs from 100% to 50%, sending precisely the wrong signal at precisely the wrong time. The tax-advantaged employee share schemes, SAYE and SIP, distributed £1.29 billion in income tax and NIC relief in the tax year ending 2024 and have participation rates that start at around 20% in contributory plans. But these schemes are overwhelmingly concentrated in large listed companies; the average SIP award is £220 per employee per year, and the schemes are too complex for most small and medium-sized businesses to establish. Profit-sharing is offered by roughly a third of UK companies, according to IPPR analysis, a proportion that has been stable for over a decade despite evidence that shared capitalism schemes strengthen team-working, reduce absenteeism, and raise productivity. Over 8 million people work in private-sector companies with 500 or more employees, and for the majority of them, the connection between their effort and their reward is a fixed salary that has been stagnant in real terms for a decade and a half.

E1 through E10 built the supply side of Progress’ economic programme. Cheap energy, liberated planning, Prosperity Zones, startup ecosystems, housing reform, tax restructuring, small business liberation, consumer cost reduction, trade architecture, and procurement revolution: collectively, these documents create the conditions for a productive, growing, internationally competitive British economy. But they do not, of themselves, guarantee that the 27 million people who work for someone else will feel the difference. E6 ensures they keep more of what they earn through tax reform. E7 frees the self-employed. E8 reduces the cost of living. These are essential but insufficient. E11 addresses the question that every supply-side programme must eventually answer: what is the mechanism by which the ordinary employee, working for a company they did not found, shares in the wealth they help to create?

Progress’ answer is threefold. First, work performed must be paid for. The era of £31 billion in annual free labour ends with a statutory right to overtime pay, bringing the UK into line with every other major economy. Second, ownership must be broadened. Employee ownership and profit-sharing are not charitable gestures; they are instruments of productivity, retention, and economic resilience, and the state will create powerful incentives to make them the norm rather than the exception. Third, the wealth generated must accumulate in the worker’s hands. A new Worker Capital Account will give every employee a tax-advantaged vehicle in which overtime premiums, profit shares, and share scheme proceeds compound over time, building a stock of personal capital that is distinct from pension savings and accessible for wealth-building purposes such as home deposits, business formation, and education. The objective is specific: within ten years, the majority of British workers will have a direct financial stake in the success of their employer and a measurable stock of personal capital that did not exist before.

##### E11.1: The Paid Overtime Guarantee

The Problem

The absence of a statutory right to paid overtime is an anomaly in British law that has persisted through decades of employment legislation without serious challenge from any party. The Employment Rights Act 1996, the Working Time Regulations 1998, and the National Minimum Wage Act 1998 collectively regulate the employment relationship, but none of them requires an employer to pay a premium, or indeed anything at all, for hours worked beyond an employee’s contracted time. Whether overtime is paid, and at what rate, is left entirely to the contractual agreement between employer and employee. In practice, this means that the employer decides, and the employee accepts or finds another job. Acas, the Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service, states plainly that “there’s no automatic legal right” to overtime pay.

The consequences are enormous and measurable. The TUC’s 2025 analysis of Labour Force Survey data found that 3.8 million people worked unpaid overtime in 2024, contributing £31 billion in free labour, up from £26 billion in 2023. The average worker performing unpaid overtime puts in 7.2 additional hours per week, equivalent to almost a full extra working day, for which they receive nothing. The effective hourly rate for these workers is substantially below their nominal rate, and in some cases, where contracted hours are already close to the National Minimum Wage, the effective rate for total hours worked falls below the legal minimum. The problem is not confined to exploitative employers in low-wage sectors. The worst-affected occupations are teaching, where 38% of the workforce works unpaid overtime, and health and care management, at 35%. These are professionals in public-facing roles whose goodwill and sense of duty are systematically exploited by employers who have structured workloads around the assumption that the work will be done for free.

The international comparison is damning. The United States enacted the Fair Labor Standards Act in 1938, establishing a mandatory overtime premium of one and a half times the regular rate of pay for all hours worked above 40 per week for non-exempt employees. This principle has been in force for 88 years. France’s 35-hour working week triggers overtime premiums for all hours above the threshold, typically at 25% for the first eight overtime hours and 50% thereafter. Germany mandates overtime premiums through sectoral collective agreements covering approximately 80% of the workforce. The European Working Time Directive caps the average working week at 48 hours across the EU, and most member states supplement this with overtime premium requirements. The UK, having retained the 48-hour cap after Brexit but without any overtime premium requirement, occupies a position that combines the limitation on total hours with none of the compensation for additional hours. The result is a system in which an employer can require an employee to work up to 48 hours per week, every week, and pay them no more than they would for 37.5 hours. This is not a labour market; it is a subsidy to employers paid for by their own employees.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Paid Overtime and Worker Participation Act will establish:

- a) A statutory right to overtime pay at a premium rate for all employees. Every employee whose contract specifies normal working hours will be entitled to overtime pay at a rate of not less than one and a quarter times (125%) their normal hourly rate for all hours worked in excess of their contracted weekly hours, and at a rate of not less than one and a half times (150%) their normal hourly rate for all hours worked in excess of 44 hours in any week. These are statutory minimum rates; employers may offer higher rates by contract. For employees on salaried contracts without specified hourly rates, the hourly rate will be calculated by dividing the annual salary by the product of 52 weeks and the contracted weekly hours. Where no weekly hours are specified in the contract, the statutory default of 37.5 hours will apply. The premium applies to all employees regardless of seniority, sector, or salary level, with a limited exemption only for genuine senior executives who hold board-level positions and whose total remuneration exceeds £100,000 per annum.
- b) Mandatory overtime recording and transparency. Every employer with five or more employees will be required to maintain accurate records of all hours worked by each employee, including start times, end times, and any periods of overtime. These records must be retained for a minimum of three years and made available to the employee on request and to HMRC or the Employment Agency Standards Inspectorate on demand. Employers will be required to include on every payslip a clear statement of the total hours worked, the contracted hours, any overtime hours, and the overtime premium paid. Failure to maintain accurate records will create a rebuttable presumption in any tribunal claim that the employee’s account of hours worked is accurate.
- c) Protection against overtime avoidance through contractual manipulation. The Act will prohibit employers from increasing contracted hours in response to the overtime requirement without a genuine change in the role or workload, and will void any contractual variation made for the primary purpose of defeating the overtime entitlement. Zero-hours contract workers will be entitled to overtime pay calculated on the basis of their average weekly hours over the preceding 12 weeks. Employers who restructure contracts, reclassify employees, or adopt any device for the purpose of avoiding overtime obligations will be liable for the overtime that would have been payable plus a penalty equal to 50% of the avoided premium. The Employment Tribunal will have jurisdiction to determine whether a contractual change was made for the primary purpose of avoiding overtime obligations.
- d) An 18-month phased implementation schedule. For employers with 250 or more employees, the overtime entitlement will take effect 6 months from Royal Assent. For employers with 50 to 249 employees, the entitlement will take effect at 12 months. For employers with 10 to 49 employees, the entitlement will take effect at 18 months. Employers with fewer than 10 employees will be subject to the 37.5-hour threshold provision but will have the option of providing time off in lieu at the overtime rate rather than cash payment, provided this is agreed in writing with the employee. The phased schedule gives businesses time to adjust staffing, scheduling, and budgeting while ensuring that the right takes effect as quickly as possible for the workers most affected by unpaid overtime.

OPERATIONAL

HMRC compliance enforcement. HMRC will establish a dedicated Overtime Compliance Unit within six months of Royal Assent, building on the existing National Minimum Wage enforcement infrastructure. The unit will conduct proactive audits of employers identified through payroll data analysis as having high proportions of employees regularly working significantly above contracted hours without corresponding overtime payments. Penalties for non-compliance will mirror NMW enforcement: repayment of all underpaid overtime plus a penalty of up to 200% of the arrears. Repeat offenders will be named publicly.

Sector transition support. The Department for Business will issue sector-specific guidance within 90 days of Royal Assent for the sectors most affected by unpaid overtime: education, health and social care, professional services, and financial services. This guidance will include model contract clauses, hours-recording templates, and worked examples of overtime calculations. For the public sector, where teachers and NHS managers are disproportionately affected, the Department for Education and DHSC will issue workforce planning guidance that adjusts workload assumptions to reflect the statutory cost of overtime, ensuring that the new right drives genuine reductions in excessive hours rather than simply relabelling existing working patterns.

Economic impact monitoring. The Office for Budget Responsibility will be commissioned to produce a full economic impact assessment within 12 months of the first phase taking effect, measuring employment levels, hours worked, overtime payments, and any adjustment in base pay or hiring patterns. Progress expects and intends that the primary effect will be a transfer of income from employers to employees, reversing a portion of the £31 billion annual extraction, and that the secondary effect will be a reduction in excessive working hours as employers internalise the true cost of overtime. Both outcomes are desirable.

##### E11.2: Employee Ownership Acceleration

The Problem

Employee ownership works. The evidence is not ambiguous. Employee-owned businesses in the UK are 8–12% more productive in terms of gross value added per employee than comparable conventionally owned firms. Fifty-seven per cent report that profits have increased since becoming employee-owned, and employee-owned businesses are over 25% more likely to have seen profits increase in the past five years than their non-employee-owned counterparts. Ninety per cent of employee-owned businesses report that employees have some or a lot of say in decisions on working conditions, and 85% report meaningful employee input on new working methods. Research into EOT-owned companies shows higher scores in the values of fairness, trust, excellence, humility, and courage, with no significant differences between seniority levels. Retention is higher, absenteeism is lower, and employee satisfaction is markedly elevated. The HMRC evaluation published in 2025 confirmed that 81% of businesses operating employee share schemes reported positive business impacts, with nearly three-quarters citing improved recruitment and retention.

Despite this evidence, employee ownership in the United Kingdom remains marginal. The sector has grown from approximately 200 employee-owned businesses in 2014, when the Employee Ownership Trust legislation took effect, to approximately 2,500 by mid-2025, employing around 358,000 people. The growth rate is impressive, 1,640% over a decade, and the annual conversion rate has reached 500 companies per year. But 2,500 companies out of 5.5 million registered businesses means that employee ownership accounts for less than 0.05% of British enterprise. The 358,000 employees in the sector represent roughly 1.3% of the private-sector workforce. The model has proven itself. It has not scaled.

The barriers to scaling are identifiable and addressable. First, the tax incentive structure, which was the primary driver of EOT adoption, is being weakened. The 2024 Autumn Budget tightened EOT regulations, and the 2025 Budget reduced the CGT relief on sales to EOTs from 100% to 50%. The signal this sends to business owners contemplating an exit is that the government views EOT relief as a cost to be minimised rather than an investment in a superior ownership model. Second, the £3,600 annual cap on tax-free bonuses paid to employees of EOT-owned companies has not been increased since its introduction in 2014, and in real terms has fallen by approximately 25%. This cap is the most tangible benefit that employees experience from working in an EOT, and its erosion undermines the model’s appeal. Third, the administrative complexity of establishing an EOT, which requires legal advice, valuation, trust documentation, and HMRC advance clearance, makes the model prohibitively expensive for small businesses with fewer than 50 employees, precisely the segment of the economy where succession planning is most urgent and where a sale to employees would most directly preserve local employment and community wealth. Fourth, the EOT model provides indirect ownership through a trust, which is administratively simple but emotionally distant. The employee of an EOT-owned company does not hold shares. They benefit from the trust, but the psychological and financial connection to ownership is weaker than in models where employees hold equity directly.

Progress’ E3 established the principle that British companies should be built to stay: the Unicorn Farm is designed to grow companies that remain headquartered, employing, and paying taxes in Britain rather than being acquired by foreign buyers at the earliest opportunity. Employee ownership is one of the most powerful anchors available. A company whose employees own a meaningful stake is a company that is structurally resistant to extraction. The workforce that owns the business will not vote to sell it to a private equity firm that intends to strip its assets and offshore its operations. Employee ownership, in this framework, is not merely a fairness measure; it is an industrial strategy instrument, and it will be treated as such.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Paid Overtime and Worker Participation Act will establish:

- a) Restoration and expansion of the EOT CGT relief. The Act will restore the full 100% Capital Gains Tax exemption on disposals of controlling interests to qualifying Employee Ownership Trusts, reversing the 2025 Budget reduction. The relief will be available for disposals of 51% or more of the ordinary share capital to an EOT that meets all qualifying conditions. In addition, the Act will extend the relief to partial disposals of 30% or more where the disposal forms part of a planned transition to majority employee ownership to be completed within five years, with the balance of relief released upon completion. The purpose is to encourage gradual transitions and to remove the all-or-nothing character of the current framework that deters business owners who are not ready for a full exit.
- b) An increase in the tax-free bonus cap from £3,600 to £6,000 per employee per year, index-linked to CPI from 2027. The current cap, unchanged since 2014, has eroded in real terms by approximately 25%. The increase to £6,000 restores and exceeds the original value, and the index-linking ensures that the cap does not erode again. The tax-free bonus is the single most visible benefit of employee ownership for the individual worker, and a meaningful annual payment, equivalent to approximately £115 per week, materially improves the attractiveness of the model to both business owners considering transition and employees evaluating the benefits of working in an employee-owned company.
- c) A simplified EOT establishment pathway for businesses with fewer than 100 employees. The Act will create a standardised EOT framework consisting of model trust documents, model articles of association, and a streamlined HMRC advance clearance process with a 30-day statutory decision period. The current process, which typically requires bespoke legal advice costing £20,000 to £50,000 and takes three to six months, will be replaced for qualifying small businesses with a standard-form process costing no more than £5,000 in professional fees and completable within 60 days. HMRC will provide template documentation, a self-assessment tool, and a dedicated helpline. The simplification does not reduce the substantive requirements of the EOT model; it removes the friction that makes the process prohibitive for the businesses that would benefit most from it.
- d) A Direct Ownership Option within the EOT framework. The Act will create a statutory mechanism by which an EOT may, at the discretion of its trustees and with employee consent, allocate individual share entitlements to employees alongside or instead of the collective trust holding. These individual entitlements will carry the same tax advantages as the trust holding, provided they are held for a minimum of three years and the employee remains employed by the company. The purpose is to bridge the gap between indirect trust ownership, which is administratively efficient but psychologically remote, and direct share ownership, which creates a stronger sense of personal stake. Companies will be able to operate either the trust model, the direct model, or a hybrid of both, retaining the flexibility that makes the EOT framework workable across different business types and sizes.

OPERATIONAL

National Employee Ownership Target. Progress will set a target of 10,000 employee-owned businesses employing at least 1 million people by 2030, up from approximately 2,500 employing 358,000 today. This target will be published in the first Budget and progress will be reported annually. The target is ambitious but achievable: at the current conversion rate of 500 businesses per year, and with the enhanced incentives and simplified pathway, reaching 10,000 within five years requires approximately doubling the annual conversion rate, which the restored CGT relief and simplified process are designed to deliver.

Succession Planning Integration. The Department for Business will integrate employee ownership into all government-funded business advisory services within six months. Every business owner who engages with Growth Hubs, the British Business Bank, or HMRC’s business support services and who discusses succession planning or exit strategy will be provided with information on the EOT pathway, its tax advantages, and the simplified establishment process. The current situation, in which business owners learn about EOTs primarily through accountants and corporate finance advisers who may have a commercial interest in recommending a trade sale instead, will be supplemented by a proactive state information campaign.

Prosperity Zone EOT Incentive. Companies established within Prosperity Zones under E2 that transition to employee ownership within their first ten years of operation will receive an additional five-year extension of the enhanced capital allowances and NIC holidays available within the Zone, conditional on the EOT meeting all qualifying conditions and maintaining employee ownership throughout. This connects E11 directly to E2 and E3: companies anchored in Prosperity Zones and owned by their employees are structurally resistant to extraction and structurally committed to their local economy.

##### E11.3: Mandatory Profit-Sharing for Large Enterprises

The Problem

In 2024, over 8 million people in the UK worked in private-sector companies with 500 or more employees, representing 43% of all private-sector employment. These companies generate the majority of private-sector profits, and the gap between their profitability and the wages they pay their median employee has widened over the period of real wage stagnation. The IPPR found that roughly a third of UK companies offer some form of profit-sharing, a proportion that has been stable for a decade. Profit-sharing, where it exists, is overwhelmingly discretionary: it is offered when the company chooses, withdrawn when the company chooses, and structured to benefit senior employees disproportionately. There is no statutory framework requiring any company to share its profits with the people who generate them, and no meaningful tax incentive to encourage it.

The evidence for profit-sharing as a driver of productivity is robust. The IPPR’s 2013 report found that shared capitalism schemes, including profit-sharing, strengthen team-working, create better relationships between staff and management, and are associated with lower absenteeism and higher effort. A Gallup poll found that 40% of employees would leave their current job for an employer that offered profit-sharing, but only 20% of employers currently offer it. This is a market failure: the evidence shows that profit-sharing makes companies more productive and employees more engaged, yet the majority of employers do not adopt it, and the majority of employees do not benefit from it. The coordination problem is classic: individual employers fear that adopting profit-sharing will raise their labour costs without conferring a competitive advantage, because their competitors have not adopted it. The solution is to make the adoption universal for companies above a reasonable size threshold, so that the competitive playing field is level and the productivity benefits are captured across the economy.

The John Lewis Partnership has operated profit-sharing since 1929, distributing a percentage of annual profits to all 80,000 of its employees, known as Partners. The payment has historically ranged from 8% to 24% of salary, with the 2023 payment at 3% following a period of restructuring. John Lewis is consistently ranked among the best employers in the UK, and its model demonstrates that profit-sharing is compatible with commercial success in competitive retail markets. Richer Sounds, which transferred 60% of its shares to an EOT in 2019, has operated a profit-sharing scheme for decades and has the highest sales per square foot of any electronics retailer in the UK. These are not anomalies. They are proof of concept at scale, and the barrier to broader adoption is not feasibility but inertia, complexity, and the absence of a statutory requirement.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Paid Overtime and Worker Participation Act will establish:

- a) A mandatory profit-sharing requirement for all qualifying employers. Every private-sector employer with 250 or more employees will be required to operate a qualifying profit-sharing scheme that distributes to all eligible employees a share of the company’s annual profits above a threshold. The threshold is set at a 5% return on net equity, ensuring that the company retains an adequate return for shareholders before any distribution is triggered. Above the threshold, the company must distribute at least 10% of pre-tax profits to employees through the qualifying scheme. The distribution may be made as cash, as shares through a qualifying share scheme under E11.2 or an existing SAYE/SIP, or as contributions to the Worker Capital Account established under E11.4. The company may choose the method of distribution, but the distribution must be to all eligible employees and must not be weighted more than 3:1 between the highest-paid and lowest-paid participants. Eligible employees are all those with at least 12 months’ continuous service.
- b) Tax incentives for profit-sharing distributions. Profit shares distributed through a qualifying scheme will be exempt from employer National Insurance contributions up to £5,000 per employee per year. Employee National Insurance will be payable at the standard rate, but the employee will have the option of directing the profit share into a Worker Capital Account under E11.4, in which case income tax will be deferred until withdrawal. Corporation tax relief will be available on the full value of distributions made through a qualifying scheme, ensuring that the employer’s effective cost is reduced by the marginal corporate tax rate. The combined effect of the NIC exemption and the corporation tax relief is that profit-sharing is significantly cheaper for the employer than an equivalent increase in base salary, creating a financial incentive to distribute generously above the statutory minimum.
- c) A phased implementation schedule. The requirement will apply to employers with 1,000 or more employees from the first full financial year commencing after Royal Assent. Employers with 500 to 999 employees will be covered from the second full financial year. Employers with 250 to 499 employees will be covered from the third full financial year. This gives smaller qualifying employers three years to establish their schemes and integrate them into their financial planning. Companies already operating a profit-sharing scheme that meets or exceeds the statutory requirements will be deemed to comply. Companies operating employee ownership structures under E11.2 will be deemed to comply if their EOT distributes profits at or above the statutory minimum.
- d) Voluntary adoption incentive for companies below the 250-employee threshold. Companies with fewer than 250 employees that voluntarily establish a qualifying profit-sharing scheme will receive an enhanced NIC exemption of £7,500 per employee per year on profit-sharing distributions, and will qualify for a three-year corporation tax credit equal to 5% of total distributions made. This connects directly to E7’s small business architecture: the incentive is designed to make profit-sharing more attractive for SMEs, so that the benefits of shared capitalism extend beyond the large-employer mandatory requirement to the broad economy. The enhanced incentive will be reviewed after five years to assess adoption rates and economic impact.

OPERATIONAL

HMRC scheme registration. HMRC will create a simplified registration process for qualifying profit-sharing schemes, modelled on the existing SAYE and SIP registration infrastructure. Companies will be able to register their scheme online, using standardised documentation, within 30 days. HMRC will publish model scheme rules, a calculation tool for determining the distributable amount, and sector-specific guidance. The registration process will be operational within six months of Royal Assent, ahead of the first mandatory compliance date.

Annual reporting and transparency. All qualifying employers will be required to publish annually the total value of profit-sharing distributions, the number of employees participating, the average distribution per employee, and the ratio between the highest and lowest individual distributions. This information will be filed with Companies House alongside the annual return and will be publicly accessible. Transparency is a powerful incentive: companies that distribute generously will use it as a recruitment tool, and companies that distribute only the statutory minimum will face scrutiny from their workforce and the public.

##### E11.4: The Worker Capital Account

The Problem

The British worker has two state-supported mechanisms for building financial reserves: the pension and the ISA. The pension is illiquid by design, inaccessible until at least age 55, and oriented toward retirement income. The ISA is flexible but offers no employer contribution mechanism, no linkage to employment income beyond salary, and no integration with the emerging landscape of employee ownership, profit-sharing, and overtime premiums. Neither vehicle is designed to help working people build a stock of accessible capital during their working lives, capital that could fund a house deposit, a business startup, a period of retraining, or a child’s education. The result is that for most workers, the only financial asset they accumulate outside their pension is whatever they manage to save from their net pay, which, given the 15 years of real wage stagnation, is very little. The median household savings balance in the UK is approximately £11,000, and approximately 25% of working-age adults have less than £100 in savings.

E11.1 creates a new stream of income: the overtime premium. E11.2 creates a new source of capital: employee ownership stakes. E11.3 creates a new annual payment: the profit share. Without a vehicle designed to receive and accumulate these new flows, they will be absorbed into current spending, as additional income always is when no structure exists to direct it toward wealth-building. The Worker Capital Account is designed to be that structure: a single, simple, tax-advantaged account into which the new sources of worker income flow and compound, building a stock of personal capital that gives every employee financial resilience, economic mobility, and a genuine sense of stake in the system.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Paid Overtime and Worker Participation Act will establish:

- a) The Worker Capital Account, a new category of individual savings account available to every employee in the United Kingdom. The account will be administered by banks, building societies, and authorised financial institutions under HMRC-approved terms, in the same manner as ISAs. Contributions to the account may be made from three sources: overtime premium payments directed by the employee, profit-sharing distributions directed by the employer or employee, and voluntary employee contributions from net pay. The annual contribution limit will be £12,000, separate from and additional to the ISA allowance and the pension annual allowance. Contributions from overtime premiums and qualifying profit-sharing distributions will be free of income tax at the point of contribution, with tax payable only on withdrawal. Investment growth within the account will be free of capital gains tax. The account may be invested in cash, stocks and shares, or funds, at the employee’s discretion.
- b) Qualifying withdrawal purposes. Withdrawals from the Worker Capital Account will be subject to income tax at the employee’s marginal rate at the time of withdrawal, except for withdrawals made for qualifying purposes, which will be tax-free. Qualifying purposes are: the purchase of a first home (up to £40,000), the formation or capitalisation of a business in which the account holder is a founder or significant shareholder, the payment of tuition fees or training costs for the account holder or their children at a recognised institution, and any withdrawal made after the account has been open for 10 years or more. The 10-year provision ensures that workers who simply hold their account and allow it to compound are rewarded with full tax freedom, creating a powerful incentive for long-term savings behaviour. Withdrawals for non-qualifying purposes before 10 years are subject to income tax but no penalty.
- c) Employer matching incentive. Employers who match employee contributions to Worker Capital Accounts at a rate of at least 50p for every £1 contributed will receive a National Insurance exemption on the matching contribution up to £2,000 per employee per year. This creates a voluntary employer matching mechanism, distinct from the mandatory profit-sharing under E11.3, that allows employers to compete for talent by offering enhanced wealth-building support. The NIC exemption ensures that the effective cost to the employer is significantly below the face value of the contribution, making matching economically attractive. Companies operating in Prosperity Zones under E2 will receive an enhanced exemption covering the full NIC liability on matching contributions up to £3,000 per employee per year.
- d) Portability and continuity. The Worker Capital Account belongs to the individual employee, not the employer, and is fully portable between jobs. When an employee changes employer, the account continues without interruption, and the new employer may make contributions on the same basis as the previous one. Contributions from multiple employers may flow into the same account simultaneously, relevant for workers with multiple jobs. Upon death, the account balance passes to the named beneficiary free of inheritance tax up to £50,000, and above that threshold is treated as part of the estate. The account may be consolidated with a SIPP or ISA at any time, though the tax treatment of the Worker Capital Account will apply to funds that remain within it.

OPERATIONAL

Platform launch. HMRC will publish the Worker Capital Account regulations within six months of Royal Assent and open the scheme to authorised providers within nine months.
