The account will be available to employees from 12 months after Royal Assent, coinciding with the first phase of the overtime guarantee. Major retail banks, building societies, and investment platforms will be invited to offer Worker Capital Accounts as a standard product, and HMRC will maintain a register of approved providers. The government will negotiate with the major banks to ensure that at least one cash-based Worker Capital Account with no minimum balance and no fees is available at launch, ensuring universal accessibility.

Payroll integration. The Department for Business will work with major payroll software providers, including Sage, Xero, and HMRC’s own Basic PAYE Tools, to integrate Worker Capital Account contributions into standard payroll processing within 12 months. Employers will be able to direct overtime premiums, profit-sharing distributions, and matching contributions to the employee’s nominated Worker Capital Account through the same PAYE infrastructure used for pension auto-enrolment. The integration will be mandatory for employers with 50 or more employees and optional for smaller employers, though HMRC will provide guidance and templates to facilitate voluntary adoption.

Financial literacy campaign. The Money and Pensions Service will lead a national campaign to promote the Worker Capital Account, explaining its benefits, its tax advantages, and the qualifying withdrawal purposes. The campaign will target working-age adults with a particular focus on workers in the 25–40 age bracket who are most likely to benefit from the home purchase and business formation withdrawal options. The campaign will launch three months before the account becomes available, ensuring that awareness and demand are established before providers begin accepting applications.

Summary

E11 establishes the legal and institutional architecture through which the 27 million people who work for someone else in the United Kingdom will share directly in the wealth their labour creates. The document rests on a single principle: the supply-side reforms of E1 through E10 build a more productive economy, but productivity gains that do not reach the worker’s bank account are economically incomplete and politically unsustainable. The objective is not redistribution through the tax system, which E6 addresses, but a structural rebalancing of the employment relationship so that effort, loyalty, and skill are rewarded with more than a stagnant salary.

Paid Overtime and Worker Participation Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: Statutory right to overtime pay at 125% of the normal hourly rate for hours above contracted weekly maximum, rising to 150% for hours above 44 per week, with a limited exemption only for senior executives earning above £100,000. Mandatory overtime recording and payslip transparency for all employers with five or more employees, with a rebuttable presumption in favour of the employee where records are absent. Protection against contractual manipulation to avoid overtime obligations, including voiding of arrangements made for the primary purpose of defeating the entitlement. Phased implementation over 18 months by employer size. Restoration of 100% CGT relief on disposals to Employee Ownership Trusts, with extension to partial disposals of 30% or more as part of planned five-year transitions. Increase in the tax-free bonus cap for EOT employees from £3,600 to £6,000 per year, index-linked to CPI. Simplified EOT establishment pathway for businesses with fewer than 100 employees, with standardised documentation, 30-day HMRC clearance, and professional fees capped at £5,000. Direct Ownership Option allowing EOTs to allocate individual share entitlements to employees alongside the collective trust holding. Mandatory profit-sharing for all private-sector employers with 250 or more employees, requiring distribution of at least 10% of pre-tax profits above a 5% return on equity threshold, with a maximum 3:1 weighting ratio between highest and lowest-paid participants. NIC exemption on profit-sharing distributions up to £5,000 per employee per year, with enhanced £7,500 exemption for voluntary adopters below the 250-employee threshold. Phased mandatory implementation over three years by employer size. Worker Capital Account with £12,000 annual contribution limit, tax-free contributions from overtime premiums and qualifying profit shares, tax-free investment growth, and tax-free withdrawals for first homes, business formation, education, or after 10 years. Employer matching incentive with NIC exemption on matching contributions up to £2,000 per year, enhanced to £3,000 in Prosperity Zones.

Operational timelines

HMRC Overtime Compliance Unit established within six months. Sector-specific overtime guidance issued within 90 days. Overtime entitlement takes effect at 6 months for employers with 250+ employees, 12 months for 50–249, and 18 months for 10–49. EOT simplified pathway and model documentation available within six months. Employee ownership integrated into all government business advisory services within six months. National Employee Ownership Target of 10,000 businesses by 2030 published in the first Budget. HMRC profit-sharing scheme registration operational within six months. First mandatory profit-sharing compliance for companies with 1,000+ employees from the first full financial year after Royal Assent. Worker Capital Account regulations published within six months, providers authorised within nine months, accounts available to employees within 12 months. Payroll integration with major providers within 12 months. Financial literacy campaign launched three months before account availability.

Fiscal framework

The overtime guarantee is not funded by the state; it is funded by employers who are currently receiving £31 billion in free labour. The transfer of income from employers to employees is the intended effect, and the macroeconomic consequence is an increase in consumer spending power that drives demand through the economy. The employee ownership provisions have a net Exchequer cost from the restored CGT relief and the enhanced bonus cap, offset by the productivity gains, higher tax receipts, and reduced business failure rates associated with the employee ownership model. The profit-sharing NIC exemptions and corporation tax relief represent a fiscal investment in broadening the ownership of economic output; the exemptions are designed to make profit-sharing cheaper than equivalent wage increases, steering employer behaviour toward a model that evidence shows raises productivity, retention, and engagement. The Worker Capital Account tax deferral will cost the Exchequer in the short term, as income tax on overtime premiums and profit shares is deferred rather than collected at source, but the long-term effect is a population of workers with meaningful personal capital: better able to buy homes, start businesses, fund their own training, and weather economic shocks without recourse to the state.

E11 completes the worker prosperity arm of Progress’ economic framework. E6 ensures workers keep more of what they earn. E7 frees the shopkeeper. E8 reduces the cost of living. E11 ensures that the 27 million employees who are not shopkeepers, not founders, not self-employed, have a direct financial stake in the success of the companies they work for and a mechanism to convert that stake into permanent personal wealth. The supply-side programme of E1 through E10 builds a more productive economy. E11 ensures that the people who make it productive share in what it produces. The next document in the framework, E12, establishes the institutional architecture for the other side of this compact: unions reconceived not as adversaries of enterprise but as partners in it, carrying a dual mandate to protect workers’ rights and contribute to productive outcomes.

#### E12. Dual-Mandate Unions

Governing Principle

Trade unions are the most important institution in the history of British working life that the British state has never known what to do with. They built the Labour Party, won the weekend, established the principle that a worker is a citizen and not a commodity, and provided the collective voice without which the individual employee is a supplicant negotiating the terms of their own dependence. They also, at various points in the twentieth century, held the country to ransom, resisted necessary modernisation, protected restrictive practices that destroyed entire industries, and became so politically powerful that the question of who governs Britain, the elected government or the union leadership, was put to the electorate in a general election and answered decisively. The history of British unions is a history of genuine achievement and genuine failure, and any serious policy must reckon with both.

The current state of British trade unionism is one of managed decline. Total trade union membership in 2024 stood at 6.4 million, representing 22.0% of employees, the lowest density since records in this form began in 1995 and down from 32.4% at that date. The private sector is the site of near-total collapse: just 11.7% of private-sector employees are union members, the lowest figure on record, and only 2.5 million workers out of a private-sector workforce of over 21 million. The public sector retains meaningful density at 49.9%, accounting for 3.9 million of the 6.4 million total, but this concentration means that unions in Britain are increasingly an institution of the state rather than an institution of the economy. The sectoral distribution tells the same story: education at 49% density, health and social work at 39%, public administration at 39%. Finance sits below 10%. Retail, hospitality, and logistics, the sectors that employ millions of the lowest-paid workers, have negligible union presence. The people who need collective representation most have the least of it.

Collective bargaining coverage has followed the same trajectory. The Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings estimates that 39.6% of employees had their pay affected by a collective agreement in 2024. In the public sector, coverage remains at 68%, with 77% of that negotiated at national or industry level. In the private sector, coverage is 15.4%, and under 5% is conducted at anything above enterprise level. Britain once had sectoral bargaining as the norm. Wages Councils set minimum rates and conditions across entire industries from 1909 until their abolition in 1993. Before the Donovan Commission of 1968 recommended the formalisation of workplace bargaining, and before the Thatcher reforms of the 1980s dismantled the institutional architecture, the British worker could expect that the terms of their employment would be set not by individual negotiation with their employer but by collective agreement covering their industry. That system is gone. What replaced it is a labour market in which 84.6% of private-sector workers have no collective agreement of any kind, and the terms of their employment are whatever their employer decides to offer.

The consequences of this collapse were visible in 2022 and 2023, when Britain experienced its worst period of industrial unrest since 1989. Over 5 million working days were lost to strikes between June 2022 and December 2023, the highest total for any comparable period in over 30 years. In the 12 months to May 2023 alone, 3.9 million days were lost, compared to an average of 450,000 per year during the 2010s. Rail workers, nurses, junior doctors, teachers, civil servants, postal workers, and barristers all walked out. Nearly a million NHS appointments were rescheduled. Schools closed. Transport ground to a halt. The immediate cause was the cost-of-living crisis: real wages fell by 2.5% in the year to December 2022, and public-sector workers bore the brunt, with nurses’ real-terms pay down 20% since 2010 and teachers’ starting salaries down 6% in real terms over the same period. But the deeper cause was structural. Unions had no institutional channel through which to address these grievances short of the strike. There was no works council to negotiate scheduling. There was no board-level representation to influence pay policy. There was no sectoral agreement to set minimum terms. The only tool available was the withdrawal of labour, and so labour was withdrawn, at enormous cost to the public and to the workers themselves.

The Nordic countries demonstrate what an alternative looks like. Denmark, Norway, and Sweden maintain union density between 50% and 65%, collective bargaining coverage between 80% and 90%, and strike rates that are, in normal years, a fraction of Britain’s recent experience. They achieve this not through legal compulsion but through institutional architecture: sectoral bargaining sets the floor, pattern bargaining coordinates wage growth with productivity and international competitiveness, and the tradition of cooperation between labour market parties, institutionalised in basic agreements dating to 1899 in Denmark, 1935 in Norway, and 1938 in Sweden, creates a framework in which unions and employers are structural partners rather than occasional adversaries. Germany adds a second dimension: codetermination, the Mitbestimmung that gives workers elected representation on company supervisory boards and mandatory works councils at the shop-floor level. The evidence on codetermination, reviewed comprehensively by Jager, Noy, and Schoefer, points to zero or small positive effects on firm performance, with room for moderate positive effects on productivity, wages, and job stability. A 2025 study of Finnish board-level representation found that worker voice raised labour productivity, consistent with information-sharing theories. Works councils tend to show more positive performance effects than board representation, driven by enhanced trust, reduced turnover, and improved workplace cooperation.

The Labour government’s Employment Rights Act 2025, which received Royal Assent in December 2025, represents the first serious attempt in a generation to address the institutional deficit. It repeals the Strikes (Minimum Service Levels) Act 2023, reverses much of the Trade Union Act 2016, introduces electronic and workplace balloting, strengthens union rights of access, and establishes a Fair Pay Agreement for the adult social care sector through the Adult Social Care Negotiating Body, expected to be operational by autumn 2026 with a first agreement ratified by April 2028. The economic analysis published in January 2026 estimated the total cost to business at approximately one billion pounds per year, excluding the social care agreement. These are welcome steps, and Progress acknowledges them. But they are insufficient. The Fair Pay Agreement covers one sector. The union access provisions facilitate organising but do not create the institutional structures through which worker voice translates into enterprise governance. The Act makes it easier to join a union and easier to strike. It does not make it easier to avoid the need to strike.

The United Kingdom already has, in the Information and Consultation of Employees Regulations 2004, a statutory framework that nominally provides workers in firms with 50 or more employees the right to be informed and consulted on matters affecting their employment. The ICE Regulations were introduced to implement EU Directive 2002/14/EC. They have been, by any honest assessment, a dead letter. The regulations are triggered only when 2% of the workforce formally requests them, a threshold that requires an act of collective organisation that is itself the very thing the regulations were supposed to facilitate. Management has, in virtually all cases, been the instigator of whatever information and consultation arrangements exist, and the research distinguishes between ‘active consulters’ who genuinely engage and ‘communicators’ who use consultation bodies to announce decisions already taken. The penalty for non-compliance, up to 75,000 pounds per violation, has rarely been tested. The ICE Regulations are the ghost of British codetermination: the form of worker voice without the substance.

E11 established the financial mechanisms by which the British worker shares in the wealth they create: paid overtime, employee ownership, mandatory profit-sharing, and the Worker Capital Account. These are instruments of economic participation. They give the worker a financial stake in the enterprise. E12 establishes the institutional architecture for governance participation: the structures through which workers have a voice in how the enterprise is run, how decisions are made, and how the terms and conditions of their employment are determined. Financial participation without governance participation is a cheque without a voice. Governance participation without financial participation is a voice without a stake. Together, E11 and E12 give the British worker both. The dual mandate that gives this document its name is the compact at the heart of Progress’ reconception of unions: institutions that protect workers’ rights and contribute to productive enterprise, that exercise authority in workplace governance and accept responsibility for enterprise outcomes. This is neither the Thatcherite position, which treated unions as enemies to be destroyed, nor the Corbynite position, which treated unions as allies to be empowered without obligation. It is the position that E10 articulated as the principle of unified accountability: responsibility married to authority. A union that sits on the board accepts responsibility for the board’s decisions. A union that negotiates the sectoral agreement accepts responsibility for the sector’s competitiveness. A union that operates the Workplace Partnership Council accepts responsibility for the workplace’s productivity. In return, the union’s authority is real, statutory, and permanent. This is the bargain, and E12 is its architecture.

##### E12.1: The Workplace Partnership Council

The Problem

The German Betriebsrat, the works council, is the most successful institution of shop-floor worker representation in the world. Mandatory in all German establishments with five or more employees where workers request one, the works council has codetermination rights, meaning the employer cannot act without its agreement, over matters including working hours, scheduling, overtime arrangements, monitoring and surveillance, health and safety, and the principles governing performance-related pay. It has consultation rights over planned redundancies, restructuring, and the introduction of new working methods or technologies. It has information rights over the financial position of the enterprise, investment plans, and organisational changes. The works council is elected by all employees, not merely union members, by secret ballot for a four-year term. It operates alongside but separately from collective bargaining, which is conducted by unions at sectoral level. The distinction is critical: the works council deals with the application of general terms to the specific workplace; the union deals with the general terms themselves.

The United Kingdom has nothing comparable. The ICE Regulations 2004 provide a theoretical right to information and consultation in undertakings with 50 or more employees, but the right is dormant unless triggered by a formal employee request, the arrangements are entirely negotiable and may consist of little more than an annual briefing, and the enforcement mechanism has produced negligible case law in over twenty years of operation. The TUC described the regulations as a missed opportunity, and the evidence supports the description. The BIS evaluation of the ICE Regulations found that management was the instigator of all information and consultation arrangements studied, that only a minority of arrangements constituted genuine consultation as opposed to one-way communication, and that the regulations had not created the cultural shift toward routine worker involvement in workplace decisions that the EU Directive intended.

The absence of a functioning works council equivalent means that British workers have no institutional mechanism for influencing the daily decisions that most directly affect their working lives. Shift patterns, overtime allocation, the introduction of monitoring technologies, office reorganisations, changes to working methods, health and safety arrangements: all of these are determined unilaterally by management in the vast majority of British workplaces, with the worker’s only recourse being individual complaint, resignation, or, where a union is recognised, the slow machinery of collective grievance. The result is a workplace culture that is, by European standards, unusually hierarchical, unusually opaque, and unusually reliant on the goodwill of individual managers. When that goodwill fails, the worker has no structural protection. When it succeeds, the worker has no structural guarantee that it will continue.

Progress will establish the Workplace Partnership Council as the British adaptation of the German Betriebsrat, tailored to British conditions and integrated into the broader framework of E11 and E12. The Council is not a union body. It is an all-employee body, elected by the entire workforce, that gives every worker, union member or not, a statutory voice in the governance of their workplace. Its establishment in firms of 50 or more employees is mandatory and does not require a trigger request. Its rights are substantive, not advisory. Its integration with the union framework ensures that workplace-level representation complements rather than undermines sectoral bargaining.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Worker Participation and Dual-Mandate Unions Act will establish:

- a) A mandatory Workplace Partnership Council in every undertaking with 50 or more employees. The Council will be elected by secret ballot of all employees regardless of union membership, for a term of three years, with the number of Council members determined by workforce size: three members for undertakings with 50 to 100 employees, five for 101 to 500, seven for 501 to 2,000, and nine for undertakings with more than 2,000 employees. Elections will be administered by the employer under rules prescribed by the Central Arbitration Committee, with any dispute over the conduct of elections referable to the CAC. The Council will meet at least monthly during working hours, and Council members will have a statutory right to reasonable paid time off for Council duties and training. The employer will provide the Council with appropriate facilities, including a private meeting room and access to independent advice funded by the employer up to a statutory cap determined by workforce size. Establishment is mandatory and does not require a trigger request from employees, replacing the dormant trigger mechanism of the ICE Regulations 2004. The employer must initiate the election process within six months of the relevant commencement date or within six months of reaching the 50-employee threshold, whichever is later.
- b) Codetermination rights over workplace conditions. The Council will have codetermination rights, meaning the employer may not implement changes without the Council’s agreement, over: the start and end of the daily working hours, including breaks and the distribution of working hours across the week; the scheduling and allocation of overtime, including the principles governing which employees are asked to work overtime and the rotation of overtime obligations; the introduction, use, and scope of technical devices designed to monitor employee performance, location, or communications; health and safety arrangements beyond the statutory minimum, including risk assessment procedures and the appointment of safety representatives; the principles and criteria governing performance-related pay, bonus allocation, and any non-contractual benefits; and workplace rules governing conduct, dress codes, and the use of employer facilities. Where the employer and the Council cannot reach agreement on a codetermination matter, either party may refer the dispute to binding arbitration through the Central Arbitration Committee, whose decision will be final and enforceable. This ensures that codetermination is real: the employer cannot proceed without agreement and cannot circumvent the requirement by refusing to negotiate.
- c) Consultation rights over structural changes. The Council will have consultation rights, meaning the employer must consult genuinely with a view to reaching agreement before implementation, over: planned redundancies and the criteria for selection; restructuring, reorganisation, or the merger, sale, or closure of the undertaking or any part of it; the introduction of new working methods, technologies, or significant changes to work organisation; training and skills development plans, with specific reference to the Skill Capital framework established under the E11 suite; and any significant change to the terms and conditions of employment not covered by a collective agreement. Consultation must begin at a sufficiently early stage to allow the Council’s views to influence the decision, and the employer must provide the Council with all relevant information, including the reasons for the proposed change, the likely impact on the workforce, and the alternatives considered. Where the employer proceeds without adequate consultation, the Council may refer the matter to the Employment Tribunal, which may award compensation to affected employees and, in cases of redundancy, extend the protective award to 180 days’ pay as provided under the Employment Rights Act 2025.
- d) Information rights and financial transparency. The Council will have the right to receive, at least quarterly, information on the economic and financial situation of the undertaking, including revenue, operating profit, capital expenditure plans, and workforce planning projections. The Council will also receive annual information on the distribution of remuneration within the undertaking, including the ratio between the highest and lowest paid employees and the median pay by grade. Where the undertaking is subject to the mandatory profit-sharing requirement under E11.3, the Council will receive the calculation of the distributable amount and the proposed distribution method before implementation. Confidential information may be disclosed to the Council subject to a statutory duty of confidence, breach of which by a Council member will be a disciplinary matter but will not entitle the employer to withhold future disclosures. The principle is that the people who generate the wealth are entitled to understand how it is distributed.
- e) A phased implementation schedule. For undertakings with 250 or more employees, the obligation to establish a Workplace Partnership Council will take effect 12 months from Royal Assent. For undertakings with 100 to 249 employees, 18 months. For undertakings with 50 to 99 employees, 24 months. Undertakings that already operate an information and consultation body under the ICE Regulations 2004 or under a voluntary agreement will be deemed to comply provided the existing body meets the statutory requirements for composition, rights, and facilities within 12 months of the relevant commencement date. The ICE Regulations 2004 will be repealed and replaced in their entirety by the Workplace Partnership Council provisions of this Act.

OPERATIONAL

CAC capacity expansion. The Central Arbitration Committee will be expanded within six months of Royal Assent to handle the anticipated volume of election disputes and codetermination arbitrations. The Committee’s complement will be increased by at least 15 additional members with experience in workplace relations, and a dedicated Workplace Partnership Panel will be established to hear codetermination disputes within 30 days of referral. The Ministry of Justice will ensure that the CAC’s budget reflects its expanded mandate.

Model Council constitutions. The Department for Business and Trade will publish, within 90 days of Royal Assent, model constitutions for Workplace Partnership Councils covering different sizes and types of undertaking. The models will include standard election rules, meeting procedures, dispute resolution mechanisms, and templates for information disclosure. Employers may adopt the model constitution directly or negotiate a bespoke constitution with their workforce, provided the bespoke version meets or exceeds the statutory minimum rights.

Council member training. Acas will develop and deliver a national training programme for Workplace Partnership Council members, available within nine months of Royal Assent. The programme will cover financial literacy, employment law, negotiation skills, and health and safety. Council members will have a statutory entitlement to five days of paid training in their first year and three days per year thereafter, funded by the employer.

##### E12.2: Board-Level Worker Representation

The Problem

Worker representation on company boards exists in 18 European member states and Norway. Germany mandates one-third worker representation on supervisory boards of companies with 500 to 2,000 employees and parity representation, half the board, for companies above 2,000, with a shareholder-appointed chairman holding a casting vote. Austria, Denmark, Finland, Norway, and Sweden all mandate some form of board-level worker representation. The institution has been in continuous operation in Germany since 1951, through every economic cycle, every technological revolution, and every competitive challenge of the past 75 years. Germany remains the largest economy in Europe and a manufacturing superpower. The claim that worker directors destroy competitiveness is refuted by seven decades of evidence from the continent’s most successful industrial economy.

The United Kingdom had its own experiment with worker directors. The Port of London Authority, established by Winston Churchill’s Port of London Act 1908, included worker-elected members on its governing board. The Bullock Committee, reporting in 1977, recommended parity representation on the boards of companies with 2,000 or more employees, with worker directors selected through trade union channels. The proposal was never implemented, defeated by a combination of employer opposition, union ambivalence about co-option into management, and the political upheavals of the late 1970s. Theresa May’s 2016 corporate governance green paper floated the idea of worker representatives on boards but retreated to the option of a designated non-executive director for workforce engagement, a provision that imposed no binding obligation and has had no measurable effect on corporate governance in Britain.

The academic evidence on board-level codetermination is more nuanced than either its advocates or its opponents typically acknowledge. The comprehensive review by Jager, Noy, and Schoefer found that the available micro evidence points to zero or small positive effects on worker and firm outcomes, with room for moderate positive effects on productivity, wages, and job stability. A 2020 study published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics found no impact on wages, employment, or profitability, but did find increased capital investment and increased capital intensity. The evidence suggests that board-level representation functions primarily as an information-sharing mechanism rather than a power-shifting one: worker directors gain access to strategic and financial information that informs collective bargaining, and management gains a more intimate understanding of workforce concerns. The limited formal authority of worker directors, who are typically in the minority and lack the ability to outvote shareholders, explains the modest measured effects. But modest measured effects at the firm level are not the same as no effects at the systemic level. A corporate governance regime in which workers are structurally represented creates different incentives, different information flows, and a different relationship between capital and labour than one in which they are not.

E11.2 established the Direct Ownership Option, allowing Employee Ownership Trusts to allocate individual share entitlements to employees. E11.3 mandated profit-sharing for companies with 250 or more employees. These provisions give workers a financial stake. Board-level representation gives them a governance stake. The worker who holds shares through an EOT and receives a profit share and sits on the board through an elected representative is a worker with a complete interest in the enterprise: financial, informational, and decisional. That worker does not need to strike to be heard. They have a seat at the table.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Worker Participation and Dual-Mandate Unions Act will establish:

- a) Mandatory worker directors on the boards of companies with 250 or more employees. Every qualifying company will be required to reserve at least one-third of the seats on its board of directors, or on its supervisory board where the company operates a two-tier structure, for directors elected by the workforce. Worker directors will have the same legal rights, duties, and liabilities as all other directors under the Companies Act 2006, including fiduciary duties to the company. They will be elected by secret ballot of all employees with at least 12 months’ continuous service, for a term of four years, with staggered elections so that not all worker directors are replaced simultaneously. The threshold of 250 employees aligns with the E11.3 profit-sharing threshold, ensuring that the same companies that are required to share profits are required to share governance.
- b) A protected status for worker directors. Worker directors will be protected from dismissal or detriment by reason of the exercise of their board functions. They will have the right to reasonable paid time off for board duties, preparation, and training, and the right of access to all information available to other directors. The employer may not restructure the board, create additional shareholder seats, or alter the articles of association for the primary purpose of diluting worker representation below the one-third threshold. Any such restructuring will require the approval of the Workplace Partnership Council established under E12.1.
- c) Board composition requirements. Worker directors must include at least one representative from the shopfloor or operational workforce and at least one from the administrative or professional workforce, ensuring that board-level representation is not captured by any single occupational group. In companies where a recognised trade union represents a majority of the workforce, the union may nominate candidates for worker director elections, but the election itself will be conducted by secret ballot of all eligible employees. Non-union candidates may also stand. The principle is that worker directors derive their legitimacy from the workforce as a whole, not from any particular union, while recognising the role of unions in identifying and supporting candidates.
- d) A phased implementation aligned with E11. The worker director requirement will take effect for companies with 1,000 or more employees from the first full financial year commencing after Royal Assent, for companies with 500 to 999 employees from the second year, and for companies with 250 to 499 employees from the third year. Companies operating within Prosperity Zones under E2 that establish worker director arrangements within the first year, regardless of size, will receive an additional year of enhanced capital allowances. Companies that have transitioned to employee ownership under E11.2 and whose EOT board already includes employee-elected trustees will be deemed to comply, provided the proportion of employee-elected directors meets the one-third requirement.

OPERATIONAL

Worker director training programme. The Financial Reporting Council, in partnership with Acas and the Institute of Directors, will develop a worker director training programme within six months of Royal Assent. The programme will cover directors’ duties under the Companies Act, financial literacy, corporate governance, strategic planning, and the management of conflicts of interest between the board role and the representative role. Every elected worker director will complete the programme within six months of election, funded by the company.

Corporate governance code integration. The Financial Reporting Council will amend the UK Corporate Governance Code within 12 months of Royal Assent to reflect the statutory worker director requirements, including provisions on the integration of worker directors into board committees, the management of confidential information, and the reporting of worker director attendance and contributions in the annual report. Companies will be required to report annually on how worker directors have influenced board decisions, as part of the stakeholder engagement provisions already required under Section 172 of the Companies Act 2006.

##### E12.3: Sectoral Bargaining Restoration

The Problem

Britain abolished sectoral bargaining in stages. The Wages Councils, which had set minimum pay and conditions across 26 industries since 1909, were progressively weakened through the 1980s and abolished entirely in 1993, with the exception of the Agricultural Wages Board, which survived until 2013. Before the Thatcher reforms, sectoral agreements covered the majority of the British workforce. Employers’ associations negotiated with trade unions at industry level, and the resulting agreements set the floor for pay, hours, overtime rates, holiday entitlements, and training obligations across entire sectors. This system had its flaws, including rigidity, the protection of restrictive practices, and a tendency toward inflationary wage-price spirals. But its abolition was not followed by a superior alternative. It was followed by nothing. The result is a private sector in which collective bargaining coverage is 15.4%, the lowest in the developed world outside the United States, and in which the terms of employment for over 18 million private-sector workers are set by the employer alone.

The EU Adequate Minimum Wage Directive, adopted in 2022, requires member states with collective bargaining coverage below 80% to adopt an action plan to promote collective bargaining. The United Kingdom, no longer bound by EU directives following Brexit, has no such obligation. But the logic of the Directive is sound: a labour market in which fewer than one in five private-sector workers is covered by a collective agreement is a labour market in which employer power is essentially unchecked, in which good employers who invest in wages and conditions are undercut by bad employers who do not, and in which the productivity benefits of collective bargaining, documented across decades of international evidence, are foregone for the overwhelming majority of the workforce.

Labour’s Employment Rights Act 2025 introduces Fair Pay Agreements, but only for the adult social care sector. The consultation on the process was published in September 2025, the negotiating body is expected to be established by autumn 2026, and the first agreement is not anticipated before April 2028. The government’s own economic analysis acknowledges the limitations: increased costs to local authorities and self-funders, limited room for productivity improvements in the sector, and uncertainty about how costs will be distributed. The ambition that Labour originally signalled, broad sectoral bargaining across the economy through Fair Work Agreements, has been reduced to a single pilot in the sector where the case is most obvious and the implementation most complex. Progress acknowledges the difficulty of the adult social care sector and the importance of getting the first agreement right. But one sector is not a framework. It is a pilot.

The Nordic model of pattern bargaining, in which the manufacturing sector concludes the first agreement and sets a wage norm that is then followed by the rest of the economy, demonstrates that sectoral coordination does not require centralised wage-setting or government intervention in every negotiation. It requires institutional infrastructure: employers organised in associations capable of negotiating, unions organised at sectoral level with mandates to agree, and a convention, supported by law where necessary, that agreements reached at sectoral level set the floor below which no employer in the sector may go. The Nordic countries achieve 80% to 90% collective bargaining coverage not because every worker is a union member but because sectoral agreements cover all workers in the sector regardless of union membership. Britain once had this. Progress will rebuild it.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Worker Participation and Dual-Mandate Unions Act will establish:

- a) A Sectoral Fair Pay Agreement framework covering all major sectors of the economy. The Act will establish the legal mechanism by which trade unions and employer bodies may negotiate binding Fair Pay Agreements that set minimum terms and conditions for all workers within a defined sector, regardless of union membership or the size of the employer. A Fair Pay Agreement may cover: minimum pay rates by grade and experience; maximum ordinary working hours and overtime arrangements, supplementing the statutory minimum under E11.1; minimum holiday entitlements above the statutory floor; training and skills development obligations, including minimum training hours per employee per year linked to the Skill Capital framework; and any other terms that the negotiating parties agree to include. The Agreement will be legally binding on all employers within the sector once ratified and cannot be undercut by individual contract.
- b) Tripartite Sectoral Negotiating Bodies. For each sector designated by the Secretary of State, a Sectoral Negotiating Body will be established comprising representatives of trade unions with membership in the sector, employer associations representing firms in the sector, and an independent chair appointed by the Secretary of State. The Body will conduct negotiations toward a Fair Pay Agreement for the sector, with a statutory duty to reach agreement within 18 months of establishment. Where agreement cannot be reached, the independent chair will have the power to refer the dispute to binding arbitration by the Central Arbitration Committee, which will determine the terms of the Agreement. Union representatives on the Body must collectively represent at least 10% of the sector’s workforce; employer representatives must collectively employ at least 25% of the sector’s workforce. Where no employer association exists with sufficient coverage, the Secretary of State may establish a temporary employer panel drawn from major employers in the sector.
- c) A phased sectoral rollout. The Act will designate an initial six sectors for Fair Pay Agreement negotiation within the first Parliament: adult social care (building on the Employment Rights Act 2025 framework and superseding it with a broader agreement), hospitality and accommodation, logistics and warehousing, retail, construction, and facilities management. These sectors are selected because they employ the largest numbers of low-paid workers, have the lowest collective bargaining coverage, and exhibit the most significant gaps between the best and worst employers in terms of pay and conditions. Additional sectors may be designated by the Secretary of State by statutory instrument, subject to consultation with unions and employer bodies, when the following conditions are met: collective bargaining coverage in the sector is below 30%, a trade union or group of unions representing at least 10% of the sector’s workforce requests designation, or the Secretary of State determines that the absence of sectoral bargaining is contributing to significant underpayment, poor working conditions, or competitive distortion.
- d) An extension mechanism. Where a Fair Pay Agreement has been concluded and covers employers responsible for at least 50% of employment in the sector, the Secretary of State will extend the Agreement to cover all employers in the sector by statutory instrument, ensuring universal coverage and eliminating the competitive advantage of non-compliance. This mechanism mirrors the extension provisions that operate in Germany, France, and the Netherlands, and that the EU Adequate Minimum Wage Directive encourages member states to adopt. Extension converts a negotiated agreement into a sectoral standard, preventing the free-rider problem in which non-participating employers undercut the terms agreed by the majority.
- e) Interaction with existing collective agreements. Enterprise-level collective agreements that provide terms more favourable than the relevant Fair Pay Agreement will remain in force. The Fair Pay Agreement sets the floor, not the ceiling. Employers who already exceed the Agreement’s terms will not be required to renegotiate. Employers who fall below the Agreement’s terms will have 12 months from the Agreement’s ratification to bring their terms into compliance. Enforcement will be through the Fair Work Agency established under the Employment Rights Act 2025, with the same powers of inspection, penalty, and prosecution that apply to National Minimum Wage enforcement.

OPERATIONAL

Sector designation and negotiating body establishment. Within 60 days of Royal Assent, the Secretary of State will designate the initial six sectors and publish the criteria for union and employer representation on each Sectoral Negotiating Body. Negotiating Bodies will be operational within six months, with negotiations commencing immediately upon establishment. The 18-month negotiation deadline ensures that the first Fair Pay Agreements are concluded within the first Parliament.

Employer association development. The Department for Business and Trade will fund and support the establishment of employer associations in sectors where no adequate representative body currently exists. Many sectors that once had employer associations have seen them atrophy as sectoral bargaining declined. The Department will provide seed funding, convening support, and administrative infrastructure to help employers organise, recognising that effective sectoral bargaining requires organised employers as well as organised workers. This is not a partisan act; it is an institutional precondition for the framework to function.

Economic monitoring. The Office for Budget Responsibility will be commissioned to produce annual assessments of the economic impact of each Fair Pay Agreement, measuring effects on wages, employment, productivity, business formation, and consumer prices in the relevant sector. The assessments will be published and used to inform the negotiation of subsequent agreements and the designation of additional sectors. Progress expects that the primary effects will be a compression of the wage distribution within each sector, as the worst employers are brought up to the standard set by the best, and a reduction in labour turnover and recruitment costs as workers in covered sectors gain the stability that comes from collectively negotiated terms.

##### E12.4: The Dual Mandate and Union Modernisation

The Problem

The preceding three sections of this document grant unions and workers structural power that they have not held in Britain for over forty years. Workplace Partnership Councils give workers codetermination rights over daily working conditions. Board-level representation gives them a seat at the strategic table. Sectoral bargaining gives their unions the ability to set binding minimum terms across entire industries. These are significant transfers of authority. The question that any serious policy must answer is: what responsibility accompanies this authority?

E10.4 established the principle that governs Progress’ approach to accountability in every domain of public life: responsibility married to authority. A person who is responsible for an outcome they cannot influence is a scapegoat; a person who influences an outcome they are not responsible for is unaccountable. This principle, applied to unions, yields the dual mandate. A union that negotiates a sectoral agreement has the authority to set the terms under which millions of people work. It must therefore accept responsibility for the sector’s competitiveness, for the agreement’s impact on employment, and for the quality of the workforce whose interests it represents. A union whose representative sits on the board of a company has the authority to influence investment decisions, strategic direction, and executive appointments. It must therefore accept responsibility for the company’s performance, not merely for the workers’ share of the company’s output. Authority without responsibility is the Thatcher critique of the 1970s unions made real. Responsibility without authority is the post-Thatcher settlement that left workers voiceless. The dual mandate is the synthesis.

The British trade union movement has historically resisted any formulation that ties union rights to union obligations beyond the obligation to represent their members. This resistance is understandable given the history: every time a government has offered unions a seat at the table, the table has been pulled away. The Social Contract of 1974 to 1979 asked unions to exercise wage restraint in exchange for social policy concessions; the concessions were partially delivered, the restraint collapsed, and the Winter of Discontent destroyed the political settlement that had made it possible. Progress’ proposal is different in a critical respect: the authority being offered is statutory, permanent, and not contingent on the goodwill of the government of the day. Workplace Partnership Councils are mandatory. Board seats are mandatory. Sectoral bargaining is mandatory. The dual mandate is the reciprocal obligation that unions accept in exchange for authority that cannot be taken away by the next government.

Public opinion on unions is characteristically split. YouGov tracking data from 2022 found the public evenly divided on whether unions play a positive or negative role, with 35% positive and 34% negative. Support for workers’ employment rights is significantly stronger than support for union power as such: the TUC’s post-election poll found 77% support for a real living wage, 67% for banning zero-hours contracts, and 48% for making it easier for unions to gain recognition, but only 22% support for removing strike ballot turnout thresholds. The British public wants workers to be treated fairly. It is less sure that it wants unions to be more powerful. The dual mandate is designed to bridge that gap: it offers the public a model of unionism in which greater authority is accompanied by greater accountability, in which the union is not merely an adversary of management but a partner in enterprise, and in which the union’s legitimacy derives not from its ability to disrupt but from its contribution to the productivity and competitiveness of the sector it serves.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Worker Participation and Dual-Mandate Unions Act will establish:

- a) The Dual-Mandate Charter. The Act will create a statutory Dual-Mandate Charter that any trade union may adopt voluntarily. A union that adopts the Charter commits to the following obligations in addition to its existing statutory duties: first, to maintain and publish a Productivity Partnership Strategy, setting out how the union will work with employers to identify and implement productivity improvements, including the adoption of new technologies, the reorganisation of working practices, and the elimination of restrictive practices that reduce output without benefiting workers; second, to act as a delivery partner for skills and training under the Skill Capital framework, investing in the professional development of its members and contributing to sectoral skills planning through the Sectoral Negotiating Bodies established under E12.3; third, to maintain transparent governance and financial reporting, including the annual publication of audited accounts, executive remuneration, and the proportion of subscription income spent on member services versus political activities; and fourth, to conduct all strike ballots through the electronic and workplace balloting mechanisms provided under the Employment Rights Act 2025, ensuring maximum participation and democratic legitimacy.
- b) Incentives for Dual-Mandate Charter adoption. Unions that adopt the Charter will receive: priority standing on Sectoral Negotiating Bodies under E12.3, such that where multiple unions seek representation, Charter-adopting unions will be preferred; eligibility to nominate candidates for worker director positions under E12.2 in workplaces where they hold recognition; access to the Skill Capital fund for the delivery of accredited training programmes to their members and to the broader workforce in their sector; and a tax-advantaged membership subscription for their members, under which union subscriptions up to 500 pounds per year will be deductible from taxable income, providing an effective subsidy of 100 to 225 pounds per year depending on the member’s marginal tax rate. The tax relief recognises that a Dual-Mandate union is not merely a representative body; it is an institution that contributes to the productive capacity of the economy, and its members’ subscriptions are an investment in that capacity.
- c) Union leadership accountability. The Act will require that in any company where a recognised trade union has a representative sitting as a worker director under E12.2, the union’s designated liaison officer for that company will receive a portion of their compensation, no less than 10% and no more than 25%, in a form linked to the company’s performance metrics as agreed between the union and the company. The metrics may include profitability, productivity growth, employee retention, safety record, or any combination agreed in advance. The purpose is structural alignment: the union official who exercises authority over the company’s governance has a personal financial interest in the company’s success, just as the worker director does. This provision does not apply to general union officials who are not designated as liaison officers for specific companies, preserving the independence of the union’s broader negotiating and organising functions.
- d) Strike modernisation. The Act will replace the postal ballot requirement for industrial action with mandatory electronic and workplace balloting, as provided under the Employment Rights Act 2025, and will establish a pre-strike mediation requirement for all disputes in sectors covered by a Fair Pay Agreement under E12.3. Before a union may ballot for industrial action in a covered sector, the dispute must first be referred to the Sectoral Negotiating Body for mediation, with a statutory mediation period of 21 days. If mediation fails, the union may proceed to ballot. The mediation requirement does not apply to disputes over matters not covered by the Fair Pay Agreement, to disputes arising from employer non-compliance with the Agreement, or to situations where the employer has refused to participate in mediation. The purpose is not to restrict the right to strike, which is a fundamental right protected by the European Convention on Human Rights and reaffirmed by the repeal of the Minimum Service Levels Act. The purpose is to ensure that the institutional infrastructure created by E12 is used before the industrial action that E12 is designed to make unnecessary. If the infrastructure works, strikes become rare. If the infrastructure fails, the right to strike remains intact.

OPERATIONAL

Dual-Mandate Charter development. The Department for Business and Trade, in consultation with the TUC and the CBI, will publish the model Dual-Mandate Charter within 90 days of Royal Assent. The Charter will be a living document, reviewed every three years by a tripartite panel. Unions may adopt the Charter at any time; adoption is voluntary but the incentives are designed to make it the rational choice for any union that wishes to participate fully in the institutional architecture of E12.

Skill Capital delivery partnership. The Department for Education, in partnership with the Institute for Apprenticeships and Technical Education, will establish the framework for unions to act as accredited training delivery partners within 12 months of Royal Assent. Dual-Mandate unions will be eligible to receive Skill Capital funding to design and deliver sector-specific training programmes, drawing on their intimate knowledge of the skills gaps and workforce development needs within their industries. The programmes will be subject to Ofsted inspection and quality assurance on the same basis as any other training provider. Unions have historically been among the most effective vehicles for workplace learning, and this provision restores and formalises that role.

National Board of Skills liaison. Each Dual-Mandate union that operates as a Skill Capital delivery partner will designate a National Skills Liaison Officer, responsible for coordinating with the National Board of Skills on sectoral workforce planning, identifying emerging skills gaps, and ensuring that the union’s training programmes align with the national skills strategy. The Liaison Officer will sit on the relevant Sectoral Skills Panel and will report annually to the union’s membership and to the Department for Education on training outcomes, completion rates, and employment impacts.

Summary

E12 completes Progress’ economic policy framework. Across twelve documents, the framework has built an economy designed to produce prosperity and designed to share it. E1 provides cheap energy. E2 creates the industrial zones. E3 builds the high-growth companies. E4 liberates the planning system. E5 makes housing affordable. E6 ensures workers keep what they earn. E7 frees the shopkeeper. E8 drives down the cost of living. E9 opens the world’s markets. E10 turns the state into an engine of competent procurement. E11 gives the 27 million people who work for someone else a direct financial stake in the success of their employer: overtime pay, employee ownership, profit-sharing, and the Worker Capital Account. E12 gives them a voice.

The document establishes four interlocking institutions. The Workplace Partnership Council, mandatory in all undertakings with 50 or more employees, gives every worker codetermination rights over daily working conditions, consultation rights over structural changes, and information rights over the financial health of the enterprise. Board-level worker representation, mandatory in all companies with 250 or more employees, gives workers one-third of the seats on the board, aligning governance participation with the financial participation established by E11. Sectoral bargaining restoration, through binding Fair Pay Agreements negotiated by tripartite Sectoral Negotiating Bodies, rebuilds the institutional infrastructure that once set minimum terms across entire industries, beginning with the six sectors that employ the largest numbers of low-paid workers. And the Dual-Mandate Charter reconceives the role of the union itself: an institution that protects workers’ rights and contributes to productive enterprise, that exercises authority in workplace governance and accepts responsibility for enterprise outcomes.

Worker Participation and Dual-Mandate Unions Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: Mandatory Workplace Partnership Councils in all undertakings with 50 or more employees, with codetermination rights over working hours, overtime allocation, monitoring, health and safety, and performance-related pay; consultation rights over redundancies, restructuring, and new technologies; information rights over financial performance and remuneration distribution. Binding arbitration through the Central Arbitration Committee where codetermination disputes cannot be resolved. Repeal and replacement of the ICE Regulations 2004. Phased implementation over 24 months by employer size. Mandatory worker directors occupying at least one-third of board seats in companies with 250 or more employees, with full directors’ duties and protections, elected by all employees with 12 months’ service for four-year staggered terms. Phased implementation over three years aligned with the E11.3 profit-sharing schedule. Sectoral Fair Pay Agreement framework with legally binding minimum terms, tripartite Sectoral Negotiating Bodies, 18-month negotiation deadline with binding arbitration on failure, and extension mechanism for agreements covering 50% or more of sectoral employment. Six initial sectors designated: adult social care, hospitality, logistics, retail, construction, and facilities management. Dual-Mandate Charter establishing reciprocal union obligations including Productivity Partnership Strategy, skills delivery, transparent governance, and electronic balloting. Tax-advantaged union subscriptions of up to 500 pounds per year deductible from taxable income for members of Charter-adopting unions. Performance-linked compensation for union liaison officers in companies with worker directors. Pre-strike mediation requirement of 21 days for disputes in sectors covered by Fair Pay Agreements, with preserved right to strike where mediation fails.

Operational Timelines

CAC expanded within six months of Royal Assent with dedicated Workplace Partnership Panel. Model Council constitutions published within 90 days. Acas training programme for Council members operational within nine months. Workplace Partnership Councils established in undertakings with 250 or more employees within 12 months, 100 to 249 within 18 months, 50 to 99 within 24 months. Worker director training programme developed within six months. UK Corporate Governance Code amended within 12 months. Worker directors in companies with 1,000 or more employees from the first full financial year after Royal Assent, 500 to 999 from the second year, 250 to 499 from the third year. Six initial sectors designated and Sectoral Negotiating Bodies operational within six months. First Fair Pay Agreements concluded within 24 months of Royal Assent. Extension mechanism applied to agreements covering 50% or more of sectoral employment. Model Dual-Mandate Charter published within 90 days. Skill Capital delivery partnership framework for unions established within 12 months. National Skills Liaison Officers designated within 12 months.

Fiscal Framework

The Workplace Partnership Council and board-level representation provisions impose no cost on the Exchequer. They are funded by employers as a cost of doing business, in the same manner as health and safety compliance, pension auto-enrolment, and the other regulatory obligations that characterise a civilised employment market. The evidence from Germany, where works councils and board-level codetermination have operated for 75 years, demonstrates that these institutions do not reduce firm performance and are associated with moderate positive effects on productivity, investment, and job stability. The sectoral bargaining framework requires the establishment and operation of Sectoral Negotiating Bodies, funded jointly by the Department for Business and Trade and by levies on the participating employer associations and unions, at an estimated cost of 2 to 5 million pounds per sector per year. The Dual-Mandate Charter tax relief on union subscriptions has an estimated Exchequer cost of 100 to 200 million pounds per year at full adoption, a cost that is offset by the productivity partnerships, skills delivery, and reduced industrial disruption that the Charter is designed to produce. The CAC expansion and Acas training programme are funded from existing departmental budgets, supplemented by a modest increase in the employment tribunal levy.

E11 and E12 together complete the worker prosperity arm of Progress’ economic framework. E11 ensures that work performed is paid for, that ownership is broadened, and that the wealth generated accumulates in the worker’s hands. E12 ensures that the worker has a voice in how the enterprise is governed, how the sector is regulated, and how the union itself operates. Financial stake and governance stake. Money and voice. The supply-side programme of E1 through E10 builds a more productive economy. E11 and E12 ensure that the people who make it productive share in what it produces and shape how it operates. The British worker will no longer be a supplicant. They will be a partner, with a stake they can measure and a voice they can exercise, in an economy built for their prosperity.

##### Beyond the Policy Flagship – Economy

The following policies, while not marquee components of Progress' policy platform, are nonetheless important fibres of our vision of A Kingdom United.

##### E9. Space Policy

The space sectors of the US and China are experiencing rapid, transformative growth that is set to take humans to the Moon and Mars within a decade. If we continue as we are, we will be left behind and excluded from the table when it comes to dividing up the resources of the solar system and setting the rules of the interplanetary order. We will enter the 22nd century as a third tier power and lose talent to countries that are expanding into the new frontier. We need a space strategy that builds on our existing strengths, and also prepares for the challenges ahead.

- We should commit to one, long term, unifying project which will provide predictable contracts for British companies of all scales.
- We recommend for this project the construction of a large, rotating habitat in Earth orbit as this project, as it allows cheaper access and thus more people able to travel there. It will be effectively a new overseas territory, and the base for our future space endeavours.
- As part of this we should set up an advanced market commitment to buy resources, such as propellant and construction materials, at the orbit of the proposed habitat.
- These efforts should be organised under a new agency, parallel to the existing UK Space Agency, that is only dedicated to human expansion, leaving UKSA to be science focused.
- We should establish property rights for the products of space mining, and seek reciprocity with other nations who have done the same, through mechanisms such as the Artemis Accords or patent law.
- We should push for a renegotiation of the Outer Space Treaty to be more permissive for commercial action in space, and we should limit our space cooperation with those nations which have ratified the Moon Treaty, as this is not compatible with our goals.
- We should commit to a goal of reaching 1% of government spending directed towards space activities.

##### E10. Student Debt Relief

There is no greater or more direct relief from poverty, nor any more open channel to success, than being able to participate in free, dynamic markets. Debt is a direct impediment to this kind of market participation. To this end, Progress acknowledges the extraordinary depressive weight decades of academic inflation and rampant credentialism has had on not just the employment prospects/professional competitiveness of two generations of Britons, but on the collective debt burden as well.

With this in mind, Progress will absolve those with outstanding student debts of the duty of paying interest on debt repayments.

#### Crime (C)

##### C2. Zero-Crime Britain

###### Governing Principle

Safe streets are a right. In any civilised society, the law-abiding citizen should be able to walk any street, at any hour, without fear. This is not an aspiration. It is a minimum condition of a functioning state. When a government cannot guarantee this, it has failed in its most elementary duty.

Britain’s criminal justice system is failing to meet that duty. The overall charge rate for crime in England and Wales has collapsed from 15.5% in early 2015 to approximately 6.3% for victim-based offences in the year ending March 2025. For sexual offences, the initial charge rate stands at just 4.2%. For rape, it is 2.8%, with a median wait of 434 days from offence to charge. For theft offences, the most common outcome is that no suspect is ever identified: this accounts for over 70% of cases. In plain English, for most categories of crime, the overwhelming likelihood is that nobody will be caught, nobody will be charged, and nobody will be punished. This is not a justice system. It is an invitation to offend.

The consequences ripple outward. The proven reoffending rate for the most recent cohort (October to December 2023) stands at 28.3%, up 2 percentage points year-on-year. For young adults aged 18 to 20, it is 36.2%. For theft offenders, it approaches 50%. Shoplifting has hit its highest level on record, with over half a million offences in 2024/25, a 50% increase on 2019/20. Snatch theft has tripled in the same period. These are not anomalies. They are the predictable output of a system that has abandoned deterrence.

Meanwhile, the prison system that is supposed to house convicted criminals is at breaking point. As of March 2025, prisons in England and Wales held approximately 87,000 inmates against fewer than 80,000 places measured by the Prison Service’s own standard of safe and decent accommodation, a 25% overcrowding rate. The adult male estate operated at up to 99.7% capacity between October 2022 and August 2024. The government’s commitment to deliver 20,000 new prison places by the mid-2020s has produced only 6,518. Completion has been delayed to 2031 at a projected cost 80% over budget. The government’s response has been to release prisoners early, not to build the capacity required to hold them.

Progress rejects every element of this managed decline. Our objective is to reduce crime to zero in Britain. We do not accept that crime is an inevitable feature of modern life. Many developed, democratic nations sustain far lower crime rates than Britain: Japan, Iceland, Singapore, Switzerland, New Zealand. There is nothing unique about Britain’s geography or demography that makes crime an immutable fact of life here. What Britain has is a decades-long failure of political will to build the infrastructure, the deterrence, the institutional machinery, and the culture of enforcement required to make the law-abiding safe and the law-breaking afraid. Progress will supply that will.

The principle that governs everything in this document is simple: society exists to serve the law-abiding, not the law-breaking. Every policy that follows flows from that conviction. The pace at which these policies will be delivered reflects the urgency of the crisis: this programme will be executed at war speed. When it is complete, Britain will be the worst place in the West to be a criminal, and the best place in the West to be a law-abiding citizen.

###### C2.1: Doubling the Police Force

The Problem

As of 31 March 2025, there were 146,442 full-time equivalent police officers in the 43 territorial forces of England and Wales. Despite the previous government’s Police Uplift Programme, which claimed to recruit 20,000 additional officers, the total force strength in 2025 is only 3% higher than in 2010 and 7% lower on a per capita basis once population growth is accounted for. The uplift produced raw headcount but not experienced policing: more than half of all officers now have less than 10 years’ experience, up from a third in 2015/16. Meanwhile, the ratio stands at just 241 officers per 100,000 population, with some forces (Lincolnshire: 150 per 100,000) operating at levels that would be considered critically understaffed in any comparable democracy.

The result is visible in every community. Public confidence in local policing has fallen below 50% and continues to decline. The link between force strength and crime outcomes is elementary: if there are not enough officers to investigate crimes, crimes will not be investigated. If crimes are not investigated, they will not be charged. If they are not charged, deterrence evaporates. The 6.3% charge rate is not a mystery. It is the arithmetic consequence of chronic under-policing.

The Policy

Progress will double the police force of England and Wales within 15 months, with a target of approximately 290,000 officers across the 43 territorial forces. This will be accompanied by a fundamental rearrangement of incentives to attract, retain, and support officers.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Police Expansion and Reform Act will:

- a) Establish a statutory target of no fewer than 290,000 FTE police officers across the 43 territorial forces in England and Wales, to be achieved within 15 months of Royal Assent.
- b) Create a new pay and conditions framework for police officers, including substantial increases to starting salaries, retention bonuses for officers with 5+ years’ service, and enhanced pension terms, designed to make policing competitive with comparable private sector roles.
- c) Establish a statutory duty on the Home Secretary to ensure that no police force area operates below 200 officers per 100,000 population. Where a force falls below this threshold, the Home Secretary must intervene within 21 days.
- d) Create a National Police Reserve, a standing force of trained, deployable officers available for rapid reinforcement of forces experiencing acute demand (major incidents, civil disorder, organised crime operations). This replaces the ad hoc mutual aid arrangements that currently create perverse incentives for forces to hoard capacity.

OPERATIONAL

Recruitment pipeline. A national recruitment drive of unprecedented scale, coordinated by the College of Policing, with fast-track entry for candidates from military, security, and relevant technical backgrounds. The target is to onboard no fewer than 50,000 new officers in the first 9 months, stepping to a maintenance intake thereafter. Given current annual joiner rates of approximately 9,500, this requires a fivefold increase in recruitment throughput. This is achievable only through pay reform, massively expanded training capacity, compressed and parallelised induction programmes, and a fundamental rebranding of policing as a high-status, high-reward career. There is no precedent for this in peacetime. That is the point.

Training reform. The current two-year probationary period will be restructured with mandatory mentorship from officers with 10+ years’ experience. The practice of new officers being mentored by colleagues barely out of probation themselves, a direct consequence of the uplift programme’s speed-over-quality approach, will be prohibited. At least 5 new regional training centres will be operational within 6 months.

Neighbourhood policing restoration. A substantial proportion of new officers will be deployed into neighbourhood policing roles. The visible, consistent presence of known officers in defined local areas is the single most effective tool for deterrence, intelligence-gathering, and community trust. This was hollowed out by austerity. Progress will restore it.

###### C2.2: Prison Expansion and Dual-Class Facility Structure

The Problem

England and Wales’ prison estate is simultaneously overcrowded, decaying, and strategically incoherent. The prison population stands at approximately 87,000 against an operational capacity of roughly 89,000 and a safe, decent capacity of under 80,000. 56% of prisons are classified as overcrowded. 14 prisons have been identified by HMIP as struggling to be fit for purpose. The average cost per prisoner is £53,801 per year, yet much of this expenditure is consumed by the maintenance of Victorian-era facilities rather than by rehabilitative or punitive capacity. The government’s planned 20,000-place expansion is running five years late and 80% over budget. The prison population is projected to reach approximately 100,600 by March 2030 under current sentencing patterns.

The current government’s response to this crisis has been to release prisoners early, including violent offenders, rather than to build the capacity to hold them. The Sentencing Review has proposed releasing prisoners after serving only a third of their sentence. Progress views this as an abdication of the state’s duty to the public. If there are not enough prison places, the answer is to build more prison places, not to release criminals onto the streets.

The Capacity Question

The MoJ’s projection of 100,600 prisoners by 2030 assumes continuation of current sentencing and enforcement patterns. Progress’ policies do not continue current patterns. They transform them. The combined effect of abolishing automatic early release, doubling police strength (and therefore dramatically increasing the charge rate), raising statutory minimum sentences, and introducing compound sentencing for repeat offenders will produce a prison population far in excess of any government projection.

The arithmetic is as follows. First, abolishing automatic early release. Determinate-sentence prisoners currently serve approximately half their sentence before release on licence. The determinate population stands at approximately 50,000. If those prisoners serve their full sentences, the steady-state determinate population roughly doubles to approximately 100,000. Second, doubling the police force and restoring the charge rate to at least its 2015 level of 15.5% (from its current 6.3%) will substantially increase the flow of offenders into courts and prisons. A conservative estimate of the resulting increase in the sentenced inflow is 40 to 60%, though the true figure could be higher given that Progress also intends to prioritise serious and violent crime where custodial sentences are near-certain. Third, increased statutory minimum sentences and compound sentencing for repeat offenders will extend the average time served beyond even the full-term baseline.

Against these demand-side increases, there will be offsetting effects: incapacitation (criminals in prison cannot commit crimes) and deterrence (credible punishment discourages offending). These effects are real but they take time to materialise, and they will not prevent a substantial transitional surge in the prison population.

Progress’ assessment is that Britain will require a minimum of 150,000 and potentially up to 180,000 prison places during the transitional period in which enforcement is being ramped up but the deterrence effect has not yet fully suppressed crime. The target is 100,000 net new places. This is the largest prison construction programme in British history. It is also the only honest response to a policy framework that takes enforcement seriously.

The Policy

Progress will build 100,000 net new prison places through an emergency construction programme commencing within 60 days of Royal Assent, while simultaneously introducing a dual-class prison structure that separates first-time offenders from repeat offenders with fundamentally different regimes.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Criminal Justice Infrastructure Act will:

- a) Establish an emergency prison construction programme with a statutory target of 100,000 net new places. The first 30,000 places are to be delivered within 15 months.
