The Act will grant wartime-style accelerated planning powers for prison construction, including the power to requisition suitable sites and to override the standard planning process entirely. This is emergency national infrastructure and will be treated as such.
- b) Create a dual-class statutory framework for custodial facilities:

Class A: Reform Facilities. For first-time offenders convicted of non-violent, non-sexual, non-trafficking offences. These facilities are predicated on rehabilitation and incentivising against recidivism. Programmes will include mandatory vocational training, education, and structured community work. Offenders who complete their sentence, demonstrate sustained good behaviour, and maintain a clean record for a defined period post-release will be eligible for partial or full expungement of their criminal record for qualifying offences. The principle is: everyone deserves one genuine chance to rebuild.

Class B: Deterrence Facilities. For repeat offenders, violent offenders, sexual offenders, trafficking offenders, and those convicted of serious organised crime. These facilities will be considerably more punitive. Conditions will be austere. Privileges will be minimal. The regime is designed to ensure that the experience of imprisonment is sufficiently unpleasant that no rational person would choose to risk returning. The principle is: if you squander your chance, society will protect itself from you with maximum severity.

- c) Reverse the early release schemes introduced by the current and previous governments. No prisoner will be released before the completion of their full sentence except in cases of terminal illness or exceptional compassion approved by the Lord Chancellor personally.

OPERATIONAL

Construction model. The programme will use modular construction techniques and pre-approved standardised designs to achieve build speeds beyond the current MoJ model. International precedents (particularly from Singapore and the Gulf states) demonstrate that modern prison facilities can be constructed in 12 to 18 months at a fraction of British costs. The current MoJ programme is projected at £210,000 per place, a figure that reflects decades of procurement dysfunction: fragmented contracting, bespoke architectural designs for each facility, interminable planning processes, consultant fees consuming 15 to 20% of project value, and land acquisition at market rates. Progress will eliminate every one of these cost drivers. Standardised modular cell blocks manufactured off-site and assembled on location. MoD and government-owned land deployed at zero acquisition cost. Wartime procurement powers bypassing the consultancy and planning apparatus entirely. A single pre-approved design replicated across every site. At this scale (100,000 places) and with these structural advantages, Progress will target a cost of no more than £80,000 per place, a 62% reduction on the current programme. Total capital cost: approximately £8 billion. For context, the economic and social cost of crime in England and Wales has been estimated by the Home Office at over £60 billion per year. The prison construction programme pays for itself within weeks of the deterrence effect beginning to materialise.

Site selection. The programme will prioritise Ministry of Defence sites (many of which are already secured, serviced, and distant from residential areas), brownfield land, and existing government-owned estate. The use of wartime-style requisition powers will prevent site acquisition from becoming a bottleneck. Temporary modular facilities will be deployed within 90 days to address the immediate overcrowding crisis while permanent construction proceeds.

Closure of unfit facilities. As new capacity comes online, the oldest and most unfit facilities will be decommissioned. This is not a capacity reduction; it is a quality upgrade funded by the expansion. The target is to close all Victorian-era facilities within 30 months.

###### C2.3: Sentencing Reform

The Problem

Britain’s sentencing framework does not reflect the severity with which the public views violent, sexual, and organised crime. Sentences for serious offences are routinely served in fraction. The gap between the sentence announced in court and the time actually served has corroded public trust in the justice system’s willingness to punish. When the public hears that a rapist received “12 years” but was released in 4, the system has lied to them. Progress will not lie to the public.

The Policy

Substantial increases in sentencing for violent crime, sexual crime, drug trafficking, organised crime, human trafficking, and fraud. The introduction of compound sentencing for repeat offenders. The abolition of automatic early release for serious offences. The objective is unambiguous: to make Britain the worst place in the West to be a criminal.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Sentencing (Honesty and Severity) Act will:

- a) Abolish automatic early release for all indictable offences. Sentences imposed by judges will be served in full. If a judge sentences an offender to 10 years, the offender will serve 10 years. No exceptions, no executive discretion, no administrative schemes. The sentence announced in court will be the sentence served. This single reform will do more to restore public trust in criminal justice than any other.
- b) Increase statutory maximum and minimum sentences for the following categories:

Violent crime. GBH with intent (s.18 OAPA 1861): minimum 7 years, up from no current statutory minimum. Manslaughter: minimum 10 years. Murder: mandatory life with a minimum tariff of 25 years, up from the current 15-year starting point for non-aggravated cases.

Sexual crime. Rape: minimum 10 years, with a 15-year minimum for aggravated cases (involving children, multiple victims, or positions of trust). Sexual assault: minimum 3 years. Possession and distribution of child sexual abuse material: minimum 5 years. The charge rate for sexual offences currently stands at 4.2%, with rape at 2.8%. Progress will attack this from both ends: more police to investigate, and sentences severe enough that conviction carries devastating consequences.

Drug trafficking. Supply of Class A drugs: minimum 10 years. Supply where the offender has used children as runners or mules: minimum 15 years. Large-scale importation: minimum 20 years. The county lines model, in which urban gangs exploit children to distribute drugs into rural and coastal towns, is one of the most vicious criminal enterprises in modern Britain. Progress will make the sentences for those who run these operations so severe that the economic calculus of drug trafficking is destroyed.

Organised crime. Participation in organised crime (as defined by the Serious Crime Act 2015): minimum 10 years. Leadership or direction of an organised crime group: minimum 15 years.

Human trafficking. Trafficking for sexual exploitation: minimum 15 years. Trafficking for labour exploitation: minimum 10 years. Facilitation of illegal entry to the UK for profit (the small boats trade and equivalents): minimum 10 years per person trafficked, sentences to run consecutively. This policy intersects with the Progress Population Policy, which addresses illegal migration routes more fully. For the trafficker, the smuggler, and the gangmaster: Britain will be the worst place in the West to do business.

- c) Introduce compound sentencing for repeat offenders. Second conviction for any imprisonable offence: sentence multiplied by 1.5x. Third conviction: sentence multiplied by 2x. Fourth and subsequent convictions: sentence multiplied by 3x. The proven reoffending rate of 28.3%, with nearly 50% for theft offenders, demonstrates that the current system does not deter repeat offending. Compound sentencing will. A first-time shoplifter who receives a community order has been given a chance. A fourth-time shoplifter who receives a sentence three times the standard tariff has been given a clear message.
- d) Create a statutory offence of operating an illegal labour scheme, carrying a minimum sentence of 5 years per worker exploited, sentences to run consecutively. Companies that employ illegal labour will face unlimited fines, mandatory director disqualification, and criminal prosecution of every director and senior manager who knew or ought to have known.

OPERATIONAL

Sentencing Council revision. The Sentencing Council’s guidelines will be revised within 6 weeks of Royal Assent to reflect the new statutory framework. The revision will be led by a panel appointed by the Lord Chancellor, not by the existing Sentencing Council membership, to ensure that the guidelines reflect the intent of the legislation rather than the institutional preferences of the judiciary.

CPS prosecution standards. The Director of Public Prosecutions will be directed to revise CPS charging standards within 6 weeks to reflect the new sentencing regime, with particular emphasis on ensuring that serious offences are charged at the highest applicable level rather than being downgraded for administrative convenience.

###### C2.4: Reform of the Human Rights Act

The Problem

The Human Rights Act 1998 has, in practice, given unelected judges complete power to override punitive and legal codes legislated by elected parliaments. The original intent of the Act, to incorporate the European Convention on Human Rights into domestic law, has been stretched beyond recognition by decades of expansive judicial interpretation. The result is a system in which the rights of convicted criminals are routinely given priority over the rights, safety, and reasonable expectations of law-abiding citizens. Deportation of foreign national offenders is blocked. Sentencing is constrained. Prison conditions are subject to judicial micromanagement. The refrain is now commonplace: “There we go again, a judge giving the rights of criminals priority over the rights of the law-abiding.” Progress intends to ensure this refrain is never heard again.

The Policy

Fundamental reform of the Human Rights Act to restore parliamentary sovereignty over criminal law and sentencing, and to ensure that the rights of the law-abiding take precedence over the judicially interpreted rights of offenders.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A British Bill of Rights Act will:

- a) Repeal the Human Rights Act 1998 in its entirety and replace it with a British Bill of Rights that explicitly affirms the supremacy of Parliament in matters of criminal law, sentencing, and deportation.
- b) Remove the power of domestic courts to issue declarations of incompatibility that effectively compel Parliament to amend primary legislation. The new Bill of Rights will provide that Parliament, not the judiciary, determines the balance between individual rights and public safety.
- c) Restrict judicial interpretation of Convention rights in criminal and immigration cases. Courts will be required to give primary weight to the intent of Parliament as expressed in statute, and secondary weight to Convention jurisprudence. Where the two conflict, statute prevails.
- d) Establish an explicit statutory right to public safety, ranked equally with other fundamental rights, providing courts with a clear basis to prioritise the protection of the law-abiding in all criminal justice decisions.
- e) Remove the right of foreign national offenders to resist deportation on human rights grounds where they have been convicted of any imprisonable offence. This directly addresses the systematic abuse of Article 8 (right to family life) claims by convicted criminals seeking to avoid removal.

OPERATIONAL

ECHR engagement. Progress will engage with the Council of Europe on the basis that the UK’s continued participation in the Convention framework must be compatible with meaningful parliamentary sovereignty over domestic criminal law. If this engagement does not produce acceptable outcomes within 90 days, withdrawal from the ECHR will be initiated. This is a diplomatic and executive matter, not a legislative one, and will be pursued by the Foreign Secretary.

###### C2.5: White Collar Crime and the Malebranche

“If you’re a white-collar criminal, there will be no worse place to be in Europe than Britain.”

The Problem

White-collar crime costs the UK economy tens of billions of pounds annually. Fraud alone accounts for approximately 4.1 million estimated incidents in the year ending June 2025, a 14% increase year-on-year. Yet enforcement is anaemic. The Serious Fraud Office is chronically under-resourced and has a troubled prosecution record. Local authority corruption, procurement fraud, and public spending misuse are investigated sporadically if at all. The revolving door between senior public office and corporate boardrooms creates structural incentives for corruption that no existing body is empowered to address. Institutional corruption is addressed more fully in C3 of this policy framework.

The Policy

Creation of a new Anti-Corruption Unit, the Malebranche, sitting in the Prime Minister’s Office, with sweeping investigatory and prosecutorial powers. The Malebranche will be the most feared anti-corruption body in Europe.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A National Anti-Corruption Act will:

- a) Establish the Malebranche as a statutory body sitting within the Cabinet Office, reporting directly to the Prime Minister, with independent investigatory and prosecutorial powers. Its purview will include: corruption within local authorities, public spending misuse and procurement fraud, honours-buying and cash-for-access, golden passports, collusion with non-aligned foreign interests, and corporate malfeasance where it intersects with public sector activity. The relationship between the Malebranche and Progress’ broader institutional corruption framework (C3) will be defined by memorandum of understanding.
- b) Increase statutory maximum sentences for: perverting the course of justice (minimum 5 years, up from no current minimum), acceptance of bribes by public officials (minimum 7 years), corporate fraud exceeding £1 million (minimum 7 years), and money laundering (minimum 5 years).
- c) Create a statutory offence of documentary destruction by a public authority, carrying a minimum sentence of 3 years for the responsible officer and unlimited fines for the institution. This addresses the widespread practice of government authorities and institutions destroying potentially valuable documentation at their own discretion, eliminating the evidentiary basis for future accountability.
- d) Strengthen whistleblower protections beyond the current Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 framework. Whistleblowers who expose fraud, corruption, or criminal activity within public or private institutions will receive: absolute protection from dismissal or detriment (with criminal sanctions for employers who retaliate), financial rewards of up to 10% of recovered funds or fines, and a dedicated legal support fund.
- e) Create a statutory offence of benefits fraud, distinct from existing fraud provisions, carrying enhanced penalties for systematic or high-value fraud against the welfare system. Repeat offenders will face imprisonment. The current system allows habitual freeloaders to exploit loopholes with near-impunity. They will be rooted out and prosecuted.

OPERATIONAL

Malebranche staffing. The unit will be staffed with seconded investigators from the NCA, HMRC, and SFO, supplemented by forensic accountants, data scientists, and legal specialists recruited from the private sector at competitive salaries. Initial staffing target: 500 personnel. The unit must be operational within 90 days of Royal Assent.

Documentation audit programme. The Malebranche will conduct systematic audits of document retention practices across central and local government within its first 90 days. Institutions found to have destroyed or failed to preserve documents in violation of retention obligations will be referred for prosecution under the new statutory offence.

Retrospective investigation. The Malebranche will have statutory power to investigate historical corruption, procurement fraud, and public spending misuse without time limitation. Where evidence of criminality is found, prosecution will follow regardless of how long ago the conduct occurred.

###### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The C2 Zero-Crime Britain framework requires five pieces of primary legislation. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, departmental procurement, or existing administrative mechanisms. All timelines in this document reflect the urgency of the crisis: this programme will be executed at war speed.

- 1. Police Expansion and Reform Act

On the face of the Act: Statutory target of 290,000 officers within 15 months. New pay and conditions framework. Minimum force strength threshold of 200 per 100,000 with 21-day intervention duty. Creation of National Police Reserve.

Delivered operationally: National recruitment drive (College of Policing, 50,000 in first 9 months). 5 regional training centres within 6 months. Neighbourhood policing restoration programme.

- 2. Criminal Justice Infrastructure Act

On the face of the Act: Emergency prison construction target of 100,000 net new places (first 30,000 within 15 months). Wartime-style accelerated planning and requisition powers. Dual-class statutory framework (Class A reform, Class B deterrence). Reversal of early release schemes.

Delivered operationally: Modular construction programme (£80,000 per place, total £8 billion). Temporary modular facilities within 90 days. MoD/brownfield site deployment. Decommissioning of all Victorian-era facilities within 30 months.

- 3. Sentencing (Honesty and Severity) Act

On the face of the Act: Abolition of automatic early release for indictable offences. Increased statutory minimums for violent, sexual, drug trafficking, organised, and human trafficking offences. Compound sentencing for repeat offenders (1.5x/2x/3x). Illegal labour scheme offence.

Delivered operationally: Sentencing Council guideline revision within 6 weeks. CPS charging standard revision within 6 weeks.

- 4. British Bill of Rights Act

On the face of the Act: Repeal of HRA 1998. Removal of declarations of incompatibility power. Restriction of judicial Convention interpretation in criminal/immigration cases. Statutory right to public safety. Removal of deportation resistance for foreign national offenders.

Delivered operationally: ECHR engagement/withdrawal (Foreign Secretary, 90-day deadline for acceptable outcome).

- 5. National Anti-Corruption Act

On the face of the Act: Establishment of the Malebranche. Increased white-collar sentencing. Documentary destruction offence. Enhanced whistleblower protections with financial rewards. Benefits fraud offence.

Delivered operationally: Malebranche operational within 90 days. Documentation audit within first 90 days. Retrospective investigation programme.

Together, these five Acts constitute the legislative backbone of Zero-Crime Britain. They give the state the officers to investigate, the prisons to hold, the sentences to deter, the legal framework to enforce, and the anti-corruption machinery to ensure that the institutions charged with public safety are themselves held to the highest standard. The objective is not to manage crime. It is to end it. The pace is not negotiable. Britain: the worst place in the West to be a criminal.

##### C1. Championing of Open Justice

###### Governing Principle

The British justice system has drifted into a culture of informational gatekeeping that serves institutional comfort over public safety and democratic accountability. Open justice is not a radical proposition. It is the historic common law default, articulated as far back as Scott v Scott (1913). What has happened over the past several decades is a steady accretion of statutory and administrative exceptions that have functionally inverted the presumption. Progress will restore it, forcefully and comprehensively.

The stakes are not abstract. As of mid-2025, the Crown Court backlog in England and Wales stood at 78,329 outstanding cases, a record high and more than double the 34,184 figure recorded in June 2019. Over 19,000 of those cases had been open for more than a year. In the magistrates’ courts, a further 310,304 cases were outstanding. The median time from charge to completion for a Crown Court defendant was 179 days. Sexual offence cases now account for 18% of the two-year backlog, up from 11% in 2023, with 431 rape cases open for more than two years. This is a system in crisis, and a system in crisis has every incentive to obscure its own dysfunction from public view.

Meanwhile, public trust in the accuracy and honesty of official crime reporting has been corroded by well-documented structural flaws. Police recorded crime statistics lost their National Statistics accreditation in 2014, and while recording accuracy has since improved to approximately 92% from 80%, the data has never regained full accreditation. The Crime Survey for England and Wales was itself temporarily stripped of its National Statistics designation in 2022. When neither of the country’s two primary crime measurement instruments can maintain quality accreditation, the public is right to distrust what it is being told.

Open justice is the antidote. Transparency does not merely allow scrutiny. It compels performance. Progress’ position is simple: every piece of information generated by the criminal justice system belongs, by default, to the public. The burden is always on the institution to justify withholding it, never on the citizen to justify accessing it.

###### C1.1: Abolition of Copyright Restrictions on Court Transcripts

The Problem

Court transcripts in England and Wales are currently subject to Crown copyright and controlled by a small number of commercial transcription providers contracted by HMCTS. Members of the public can request transcripts by completing Form EX107, but face costs that are, in practice, prohibitive. Transcription is charged per folio (72 words), with rates ranging from £0.74 to £2.30 per folio depending on turnaround and court type, and standard turnaround times of 12 working days.

In a November 2023 debate in the House of Commons, it was revealed that a rape victim was quoted £7,500 for a transcript of her own trial, and that other victims had been quoted fees as high as £22,000. The average cost of a transcript order in 2024, according to HMCTS data provided to Parliament, was £117 excluding VAT, but this figure is misleading: it includes short hearings and single-page orders. Multi-day trials, the kind most likely to be of public interest, routinely cost thousands of pounds. This means that a crime victim who cannot remember what was said about her own trauma in court, because of that trauma, must pay a private company thousands of pounds for the privilege of reading the public record of a public proceeding in a public court.

The consequence is that the record of public justice is, in functional terms, privatised. Journalists, researchers, civil society organisations, and ordinary citizens are priced out of systematic scrutiny. Only those with deep pockets or institutional backing can access the raw material of judicial accountability. This is indefensible in a common law system whose entire legitimacy rests on public adjudication.

The Policy

All court transcripts, judgments, sentencing remarks, and judicial directions produced in courts in England and Wales shall be placed into the public domain, free of copyright restriction, and made available through a centralised, searchable, machine-readable digital repository within 48 hours of proceedings concluding.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Court Transparency Act will:

- a) Disapply Crown copyright from all records of court proceedings, including transcripts, judgments, sentencing remarks, and judicial directions.
- b) Establish a statutory duty on HMCTS to publish all such records through a centralised, publicly accessible digital repository within 48 hours of proceedings concluding.
- c) Override the current commercial licensing model for court transcription. The Act will terminate the exclusive contractual arrangements between HMCTS and private transcription providers for the purposes of public access.
- d) Preserve existing statutory anonymisation requirements (for victims of sexual offences under the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 1992, for children under the Children Act 1989, and equivalent provisions) and apply them automatically to all published records.

OPERATIONAL

Centralised digital platform. The Ministry of Justice will commission a publicly accessible digital repository (working title: JusticeOpen), indexed, fully searchable, and accessible via API for researchers, journalists, and civic technology developers. The US PACER system demonstrates the basic feasibility of this architecture, though its execution is poor. Ours will be built to a modern standard with full-text search, structured metadata, and open data export. The infrastructure pattern is well-understood and the technical lift is modest. This is a departmental procurement and delivery exercise requiring no legislation beyond the statutory duty established in the Act.

Transcription reform. HMCTS will transition from outsourced commercial transcription to AI-assisted transcription (speech-to-text models are now extremely capable) with human review, dramatically reducing cost and turnaround. The savings from eliminating the commercial transcription monopoly will substantially offset the cost of the platform. Target: full automated first-pass transcription within 2 hours of proceedings, human-verified publication within 48 hours. This is an operational change to HMCTS procurement and workflow, delivered by ministerial direction.

Retrospective digitisation. A rolling programme to digitise and publish historical transcripts going back a minimum of 30 years, prioritised by public interest (serious criminal cases first, then civil, then ancillary). This can be funded modestly and executed with a combination of OCR, AI tooling, and supervised review. Delivered as a departmental programme with Treasury funding allocated at Spending Review.

###### C1.2: Relaxation of Reporting Restrictions Post-Sentencing

The Problem

Reporting restrictions in England and Wales are governed by a patchwork of statutes: the Contempt of Court Act 1981 (s.4(2) postponement orders), the Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999 (s.45/s.45A), various provisions of the Criminal Justice Act, and judicial discretion under common law. In principle, many of these restrictions exist to protect fair trial rights (Article 6 ECHR) and are lifted or lapse once proceedings conclude. In practice, three things have gone wrong.

First, judges routinely impose restrictions that persist well beyond sentencing, often with no clear statutory basis and no mechanism for review. Second, the sheer complexity of the framework means media organisations self-censor rather than risk contempt proceedings, producing a chilling effect far broader than the actual restrictions warrant. Third, restrictions are sometimes used, whether consciously or not, to shield institutional embarrassment rather than protect justice. The grooming gang cases are the most notorious example, where reporting restrictions contributed to years of public ignorance about the scale and nature of offending in towns like Rotherham, Rochdale, Telford, and Oxford.

The scale of the court backlog makes this worse. With 78,000+ cases outstanding in the Crown Court and a median time to completion approaching six months, reporting restrictions now persist for far longer than they were ever designed to. The system’s dysfunction is compounding the suppression of information.

The Policy

A statutory presumption that all reporting restrictions lapse automatically upon sentencing, with narrowly defined exceptions. Where restrictions are to be maintained post-sentencing, the prosecution or court must apply for continuation and demonstrate, on the balance of probabilities, that a specific and articulable harm to a named individual would result from publication. Institutional embarrassment, public discomfort, and “community tensions” will be explicitly excluded as valid grounds.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

An Open Justice (Reporting) Act will:

- a) Establish a default sunset clause: all reporting restrictions expire at the point of sentencing unless actively renewed by judicial order.
- b) Narrow the permissible grounds for post-sentencing restrictions to: protection of victims of sexual offences who have not waived anonymity; protection of children and vulnerable witnesses where ongoing risk is demonstrated; and genuine national security concerns (subject to review by a designated senior judge, not by the executive).
- c) Create a public right of challenge: any member of the public or any media organisation may apply to lift or vary a restriction, with the court required to hear the application within 14 days.
- d) Explicitly prohibit the use of reporting restrictions to prevent reporting on the demographic characteristics of offenders, patterns of offending by category, or the conduct of public officials in relation to criminal proceedings. This directly addresses the grooming gang precedent and similar cases where restrictions functionally concealed patterns of offending from the communities affected by them.
- e) Amend Section 4(2) of the Contempt of Court Act 1981 to require that all postponement orders include a specific, published expiry date and a written justification that is itself published once the order lapses. No more indefinite, unreviewable suppression orders.

OPERATIONAL

Judicial guidance overhaul. The Lord Chief Justice will be required to issue new Practice Directions within 6 months of Royal Assent, replacing the current Criminal Practice Directions Part I (Open Justice) with guidance reflecting the new statutory presumption. Judicial training on the new framework will be mandatory. This is delivered via the existing Practice Direction mechanism and the Judicial College’s training programme, not by statute.

Media legal defence fund. The government will establish a modest public fund (administered at arm’s length) to support smaller media organisations and independent journalists in challenging reporting restrictions. The current system structurally advantages large outlets with in-house legal teams. This corrects the imbalance and ensures that the right to challenge restrictions is not merely theoretical. Delivered by ministerial direction with funding allocated at Spending Review.

###### C1.3: Public Transparency of Police Body Camera Footage

The Problem

Body-worn video (BWV) was rolled out across almost all police forces in England and Wales between 2014 and 2019. The evidence for its value is strong. A landmark study led by the University of Cambridge’s Institute of Criminology, covering nearly 2,000 officers across UK and US forces over a full year, found that BWV deployment was associated with a 93% reduction in complaints against police. Research published via the College of Policing found that BWV footage was associated with higher rates of conviction in domestic abuse cases and crimes against officers. The Metropolitan Police has reported that suspects have pleaded guilty on seeing recorded evidence rather than contesting officers’ testimony. BWV technology is, in short, one of the most effective tools British policing has adopted in recent decades, and it serves both officers and the public.

The problem is not with the cameras. It is with what happens to the footage afterward. BWV footage is currently controlled entirely by the force that captured it, subject to opaque retention policies that vary from force to force, and released publicly only at the force’s discretion. There is no centralised registry, no standardised retention framework, and no statutory right for members of the public to access footage of their own interactions with police. The public, and indeed officers themselves, cannot benefit fully from BWV’s transparency potential if the footage remains locked inside institutional silos.

This is a missed opportunity. BWV footage is not merely an accountability tool. It is a record of fact. When interactions between citizens and officers are captured on video, both sides benefit from an objective record. Officers are protected from false complaints. Citizens are protected from disputed accounts. Courts receive higher-quality evidence. The system as a whole gains credibility. Progress’ policy is to unlock this potential by making BWV footage systematically accessible, so that the transparency it was designed to provide actually reaches the people it was designed to serve.

The Policy

All police body camera footage from interactions with the public will be logged in a publicly searchable, centrally administered registry. Footage will be accessible to any member of the public who is a party to, or a subject of, the recorded interaction, and to the public at large in cases involving an arrest, use of force, or formal complaint.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Police Transparency Act will:

- a) Establish a statutory duty on all police forces to upload all BWV footage to a centrally administered National BWV Registry within 24 hours of capture.
- b) Create a tiered access model. Tier 1 (Subject access): any person recorded in BWV footage has an automatic right to view and obtain a copy of that footage within 7 days of request, with no exemptions. This protects citizens and officers alike by giving all parties access to the factual record. Tier 2 (Incident access): any footage involving an arrest, use of force (including restraint), stop-and-search, entry to a dwelling, or interaction that results in a formal complaint is publicly accessible via the registry, subject to the anonymisation protocols described below. Tier 3 (General access): all other footage is accessible via FOI request with a statutory presumption of disclosure; the force must demonstrate specific, articulable harm from release, not merely assert it.
- c) Mandate BWV activation for all interactions with members of the public. Failure to activate, or deactivation during an interaction, creates a rebuttable presumption against the officer’s account in any subsequent proceedings. This makes the camera the officer’s best friend when interactions proceed properly, and ensures the factual record is complete when they do not.
- d) Set a minimum retention period of 6 years for all BWV footage (aligned with the limitation period for civil claims against police). Footage relating to serious criminal cases, deaths in custody, or misconduct investigations will be retained indefinitely.
- e) Establish penalties for non-compliance. Officers who fail to activate BWV as required, or who tamper with or delete footage, will face automatic referral to misconduct proceedings. Forces that systematically fail to upload footage to the registry will face financial sanctions via the policing grant.
- f) Disapply the right to erasure for footage captured in the course of policing, as permitted under Schedule 2, Part 1 of the Data Protection Act 2018. Establish the specific legal basis for processing under Article 6(1)(e) (public task) of UK GDPR.

OPERATIONAL

Technical infrastructure. The National BWV Registry will be a cloud-hosted, centrally managed platform built to Government Digital Service standards. It will feature automated facial blurring for bystanders and non-subjects (the technology is mature), searchable metadata (date, time, location, officer ID, incident type, outcome), tamper-evident chain of custody logging where every access, edit, or deletion is permanently recorded, and integration with IOPC case management systems. This is a departmental technology programme delivered by the Home Office, funded through the policing grant and centrally procured.

Data Protection Impact Assessment framework. The Home Office will publish a DPIA template and compliance framework for forces within 3 months of Royal Assent. The anonymisation and tiered access model is specifically designed to be proportionate and defensible, but each force will be required to complete and publish its own DPIA. This is an administrative requirement delivered by Home Office guidance, not statute.

###### C1.4: Additional Open Justice Measures

The following three measures logically extend from the same governing principle and complete the open justice framework.

C1.4a: Open Crime Statistics

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Police Transparency Act (see C1.3 above) will additionally require all police forces to publish granular, disaggregated crime statistics on a monthly basis, in machine-readable format, through a single national portal. Statistics must be disaggregated by offence type, location (to ward level), demographic characteristics of offenders and victims, and outcome.

OPERATIONAL

National crime data portal. The Home Office will commission and maintain a single, publicly accessible portal that aggregates force-level data into a consistent, searchable national dataset. This replaces the current fragmented publication model where the ONS and Home Office publish delayed, heavily aggregated figures on different cycles.

The current system is unfit for purpose. Police recorded crime data lost its National Statistics designation in 2014 after HMICFRS found that only around 80% of crimes that should have been recorded were actually recorded, with even lower accuracy for sexual offences (74%) and violence (67%). While a 2024 review found recording accuracy had improved to approximately 92%, the data has never regained full accreditation. The Crime Survey for England and Wales was itself temporarily stripped of its designation in 2022 due to response rate problems. Meanwhile, police recorded crime figures show 6.6 million crimes in the year ending March 2025, while the CSEW estimates around 9.3 million incidents of headline crime, a persistent and enormous gap between what is recorded and what people actually experience. A resident of a high-crime ward has no timely, granular way to understand what is happening on their streets. Progress will change this by requiring forces to publish raw, disaggregated data monthly, letting citizens, journalists, and researchers see the truth for themselves.

C1.4b: Sentencing Transparency Register

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Court Transparency Act (see C1.1 above) will additionally require the creation of a publicly searchable register of every sentence handed down in every criminal court in England and Wales, linked to the offence, the guideline range, the actual sentence, and the sentencing judge.

OPERATIONAL

Register design and maintenance. HMCTS will build and maintain the register as a component of the JusticeOpen platform. If a judge is consistently sentencing at the bottom of guidelines for violent offences, the public should know. If there are systematic sentencing disparities by geography, demographic, or court, the data should make that visible.

This is not an attack on judicial independence. It is the natural consequence of taking judicial accountability seriously. Judges exercise enormous discretionary power over the liberty and safety of citizens. That power is legitimate only to the extent that it is exercised transparently. The Sentencing Council publishes guidelines; Progress will publish the data that shows whether they are being followed.

C1.4c: Open Complaints and Misconduct Register

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Police Transparency Act (see C1.3 above) will additionally require a publicly accessible register of all complaints against police officers and their outcomes. Complaints will be anonymised by complainant but not by officer for substantiated complaints or repeated patterns.

OPERATIONAL

Register design and maintenance. The IOPC will administer the register, drawing on existing complaints data already collected from forces. Forces currently publish only aggregate statistics. This is insufficient. The public has a right to know whether specific officers have a pattern of complaints, and whether their force is addressing it.

The 93% reduction in complaints associated with BWV deployment in the Cambridge study demonstrates that transparency itself changes behaviour. An open complaints register extends this logic from the individual interaction to the institutional level, giving both the public and the police service itself a clear, honest picture of where problems lie and whether they are being resolved.

###### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The C1 Open Justice framework requires three pieces of primary legislation. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, departmental procurement, or existing administrative mechanisms.

- 1. Court Transparency Act

On the face of the Act: Disapplication of Crown copyright on court records. Statutory duty on HMCTS to publish transcripts within 48 hours. Termination of exclusive commercial transcription licensing. Preservation of existing anonymisation protections. Creation of a publicly searchable sentencing transparency register.

Delivered operationally: JusticeOpen digital platform (departmental procurement). Transition to AI-assisted transcription (HMCTS workflow reform). Retrospective digitisation programme (departmental programme, Treasury-funded). Sentencing register design and integration into JusticeOpen (HMCTS delivery).

- 2. Open Justice (Reporting) Act

On the face of the Act: Default sunset clause on reporting restrictions at sentencing. Narrowed grounds for post-sentencing restrictions. Public right to challenge restrictions within 14 days. Prohibition on demographic suppression in reporting restrictions. Amendment to Contempt of Court Act 1981 s.4(2) requiring expiry dates and published justifications.

Delivered operationally: New Practice Directions from the Lord Chief Justice (judicial mechanism). Mandatory judicial training (Judicial College). Media legal defence fund (ministerial direction, Spending Review funding).

- 3. Police Transparency Act

On the face of the Act: Central BWV upload duty and creation of National BWV Registry. Tiered access model. Mandatory BWV activation with rebuttable presumption. Minimum 6-year retention period. Penalties for non-compliance. Disapplication of right to erasure under DPA 2018 Schedule 2. Statutory duty on forces to publish disaggregated crime statistics monthly. Creation of open complaints and misconduct register.

Delivered operationally: National BWV Registry platform (Home Office technology programme). DPIA framework and compliance guidance (Home Office administrative guidance). National crime data portal (Home Office procurement). Complaints register administration (IOPC).

Together, these three Acts and their accompanying operational programmes constitute a comprehensive framework for open justice in England and Wales. They restore the common law presumption of transparency, close the loopholes that have allowed institutional secrecy to flourish, and give citizens the tools they need to hold the justice system to account. This is not radical. It is overdue.

##### C2+. Unified Judicial Services

Scotland as case-study

Despite Scotland having disproportionately higher spending on its justice system (up to 2x OECD norms by measurements), it is not yielding results. This is due to structural problems which have been a permanent feature of Scotland’s uniquely layered judicial system. Whilst Progress treasure’s Britain’s Common Law tradition, we also must ask reasonably why underperformance is still ongoing.

It is abundantly clear that when state capacity exists, and that all institutions are interlocking with each other in concert, that wonders can truly be achieved. One clear example is Scotland’s often under-appreciated crime reduction strategy of the early devolution era, especially in Greater Glasgow, which was the murder capital of Europe at the time (London now has up to 1.7x the crime rate of Glasgow). This isn’t merely a question of throwing intense resources at a singular problem, but ensuring institutions are fully optimised to work together. We saw the start of this approach, especially when it came to policing and health in Glasgow – but progress has stalled.

At Progress, we must learn from the best, study diligently what works, and adapt it to our local requirements. Throughout the most successful law & order nations, is a functioning judiciary system that the public trusts. This has been undermined in recent years, with constant scandal over delay, inconsistent sentencing, and increasing perceptions of anachronism. Only 15% of Scots believed the judiciary was fair and transparent – in 2015. Collapse has already happened. Once lost, trust is near impossible to regain. Wholesale reform is urgent if we are to rebuild a high-trust society – it is the foundation of all of our objectives. It is non-negotiable. Without trust, everything collapses.

Opaqueness and Abstract Dysfunctionality Breeds Distrust

It is clear that with nearly 2x the spending of comparable nations, more funding will not solve the issue. It is clearly structural. Furthermore, there exists no single functioning digital chain of command for case tracking, sentencing comparison on demand, or for publishing cases in a bid to reclaim transparency.

Compared to other nations, Scotland has a unique opportunity (with expanded scope as a subnational state, but falling short of the complex services of a fully fledged nation state, e.g., pension provision) to create a single digital platform for all government services. For example, if we were to consolidate 32 useless Scottish local authorities into 15 regions, it doesn’t make sense to duplicate website and service procurement between them all. For the most part, local authority websites are all clones of each other – except when they are in direct competition with each other over “who can make the worst council website”?

With Progress’s goals of realising State Capacity, we need to radically rationalise and streamline all institutions so they can integrate and operate together seamlessly, simultaneously easing budget constraints as well as getting closer to closing the fiscal gap. Rationalisation is a goal in itself, but once achieved (which it can be over a Parliamentary term) – it can be fully integrated and transparent.

Scotland is in a unique position. It can integrate all Scottish Government, Police, Health, Transport, Regional/Local, Social Security, Economic, Investment, and Justice services into a single digital platform – mobile first – to allow for a direct, personalised, citizen-to-government interface. Through this single platform (an extension of mygov.scot concept) we can fully publish all judicial decisions, track cases, and enable clear rationale (as well as greater scrutiny) of the judiciary. In the same way you should be able to make a GP appointment or use a smartcard for integrated public transport on this app – you should be able to track cases of you or your family. Combined with rationalisation and digitisation of the judicial structure itself, and education of that new structure, we can bring clarity from opaqueness, restoring understanding and trust.

Efficiency Through Simplicity

Increasing transparency and benchmarking decisions through a real time digital platform will help restore trust in the judicial system. Furthermore, it will make it far faster. How much faster that can be, we simply do not know as there isn’t even a way to track or benchmark these statistics currently. But, once this single digital chain of command is achieved, it will shine light on the darkness and foster greater trust. The publishing of improving statistics, pushed to them daily via a mygov.scot app dashboard, will enable Scots to feel they have greater power over their state, restoring democracy and dignity.

This new digital chain cannot be built into an actually useful state until the structures themselves have been rationalised. In the case of the judicial system in Scotland, it is a mess.

This is an expensive, duplicative, opaque structure which the public does not understand, and does not, on a fundamental level, serve their needs as expected, nor is it suited to face the challenges of the future. The system must – cautiously and reasonably – evolve. We have a unique opportunity to take these challenges and turn them into solutions, enabling Scotland to leapfrog nations at the top of the judicial leaderboard.

Scotland is unique in the sense it has a bifurcated judicial system. This means that criminal courts and civil courts handle cases separately. This used to suit the country’s needs – but not any more. During the postwar era, civil and criminal legislation has become increasingly intertwined, and with a changing criminal landscape, many countries have moved away from this bifurcated system. It’s simply an operating system that is out of date. It must be rationalised, whilst still ensuring it retains the character of a distinctly Common Law system.

New Zealand and Ireland have already accomplished this – a process called “unification” – combining civil and criminal trials into a single court column, allowing cases to rise up or fall down the chain depending on severity or precedent. This fits perfectly in line with our concept of a single digital chain of command. Once accomplished, it will allow the courts to distribute cases in a far more resource effective way, allowing Scotland to clear the covid backlog and return to normalcy.

New Scottish Judicial Service (SJS)

This is the proposed structure for the new, unified, Scottish Judicial Service:

Explanation of SJS Tiers:

Tier 1 – Regional Courts:

- Five Regional Courts, each representing new Strategic Regions of Scotland, replacing 6 Sheriffdoms. Regional Courts serve at least one Regional Authority:

– North East Scotland, based in Aberdeen City: Aberdeen City Region (Aberdeen City, Aberdeenshire), Tay Cities Region (Dundee, Angus, and Perth & Kinross).

– North West Scotland, based in Inverness City: Inverness City Region (Inverness-shire, Moray), Highlands Region (existing Highland Council area minus Inverness-shire), Argyle Region (Argyle & Bute plus Isle of Arran), Western Isles Region, Shetland Region, Orkney Region.

– South East Scotland, based in Edinburgh City: Fife Region, Forth Cities Region (replacing Falkirk, Stirling and Clackmannanshire Council areas), Edinburgh City Region (Edinburgh and Lothian Council areas), and Borders Region.

– South West Scotland, based in Ayr: Ayrshire Region, Dumfries & Galloway Region.

– Glasgow: Glasgow City Region (8 local authorities in Greater Glasgow).

- Divisions within each Regional Court: General Civil & Criminal Division, Special Criminal Division (top 20% of most serious/high frequency offenders), Family & Juvenile Division, Land, Housing & Environment Division, and Tribunals & Administrative Justice Division.
- Each Regional Court will have multiple satellite hubs (approx 30) replacing existing courthouses. They will remain open for rural access, but the fundamental court itself will remain in its capital location for administrative efficiency.
- Replaces: Justice of the Peace Courts, Sheriff Court, Outer House of the Court of Session, Scottish Land Courts, and Tribunals.

Tier 2 – National Court:

- Intermediate appellate court with jurisdiction over all civil, criminal and tribunal appeals, making it Scotland’s Court of Appeal.
- Hears appeals from all divisions of Regional Courts.
- Handles complex or high-stakes constitutional or statutory interpretations not yet escalated to Supreme Court level.
- Composed of panels of 3 to 5 judges, sitting in former High Court of the Justiciary or House of the Court of Session buildings in Glasgow or Edinburgh.
- Divisions: Civil Appeals, Criminal Appeals, Tribunal Appeals, Constitutional Matters (pre-screened before Supreme Court referral).
- Replaces the High Court of the Justiciary, Inner House of the Court of Session, and aspects of the Sheriff Appeals Court.

Tier 3 – Supreme Court:

- Final court of appeal within Scotland (excluding UKSC reserved matters).
- Hears the most significant civil and criminal appeals.
- Constitutional and systemic review jurisdiction.
- 9 to 11 Justices sitting en banc or in panels of 5 to 7, sitting in former High Court of the Justiciary or House of the Court of Session buildings in Glasgow or Edinburgh.
- Separate, but complementary to UK Supreme Court, which handles reserved matters (e.g. Scotland Act), ensuring it remains the highest court of the land.
- Replaces the High Court of the Justiciary and House of the Court of Session functions.
- Apex body of Scottish legal system – protecting the independence of Scotland’s Judiciary from England and Wales, but more importantly, from the Scottish Government and Parliament.

Special Integration & Modernisation Features:

- Mandatory, fully digitised filing and virtual hearings as default.
- Linked to mygov.scot universal app with digital ID.
- Integrated with regional police commands and regional prison estates.
- Special Criminal Division or Panel in each tier, allowing the entire Justice System to prioritise the top 20% of criminals at speed.
- Abolishing wigs and establishing a new three-tiered robe system for simplicity and to enhance public perception of service.
- To cope with new focused caseloads, and to facilitate new digital infrastructure, it will be likely that in the longer term a new court house will be required to be built for each Regional, National, and Supreme Court (7 courts in total). Compare that with the need for new Police commands (5 Regional and 1 National) and new prisons (5 Regional and 1 Special), then all of these institutions could be co-located together, allowing them to work faster in tandem as a single integrated service unit, and along new infrastructure, particularly along the Central Belt with our proposed “Kings Line” project.

This rationalisation is important, not only because it allows us to implement a single digital chain of command, but it is very easy for the public to understand. Approximately 90% of cases will be handled at the Regional level at an accessible location. If it is a particularly complex case, a first case or a case that sets precedent, then it will be escalated up the chain of command accordingly, regardless if it is civil or criminal. The naming conventions, Regional, National or Supreme will match our new proposed local government reforms, making the court naming convention transparently clear of what level it resides and its significance.

Scotland’s unique justice system also comes with a well known caveat: Not Proven. The third verdict in the Scottish Justice system adds extensive time to deliberation of Juries, unnecessarily prolonging the time taken to deliver justice. There have been proposed reforms to abolish this, Progress must see it through. 1/3rd of Scotland’s inmates are awaiting trial – if the court system was operationalised and optimised, it would be far faster, and would free up more prison space than Scotland would ever need.

Furthermore, we should fight against the proposed reforms to increase jury sizes in Scotland. They should be reduced to 9 for all cases. Odd numbers make it easier to acquire consensus, and allows better thresholds (majority/ 2/3rds or half) to be met more clearly. This is not a small jury size, which prevents miscarriages of justice, but shortening the jury count also allows us to expedite the time taking to build juries, which is another blockage in the system. Compare that to the existing system, where cases get bounced around and lost for years without end, these proposed reforms can end a lot of ambiguity.

Service Integration

Why this divisional structure specifically? Along with our new digital platform for the justice system, which will be designed to expedite cases generally, this new chain of command will allow the justice system to ring fence and prioritise the top 20% of criminals with Special Criminal Divisions. This is essential to operationalise. Across the board, in nearly every country, the top 20% of criminals commit 80% of the crime. If resources and efforts were re-prioritised, and that top 20% was arrested and convicted without fail before they can commit their next crime, then Scotland could slash its crime rate by well over half within a decade. It would see Scotland become one of the lowest crime nations on Earth. Combined with Police, Prison, and Data Science integration, it’s not only desirable, but possible.

Police Scotland has 3 Strategic Commands and 14 Regional Commands. These structures should be combined and flattened to 5 Regions. The Scottish Prison Service (SPS) operates 17 prisons – most of them Victorian era. The maintenance is so eye watering that it would be roughly the same amount of money to build 5 new regional super prisons, as well as 1 new high security prison. These boundaries, for the new Regional Courts, Regional Police Commands, and Regional Prisons, would match each other, and allow for far more effective sequencing of services and data science units to effectively target and prioritise the top 20% of criminals. These are all devolved matters for which the Scottish Parliament is responsible.

Judicial independence from England, for centuries, like the public culture in Holyrood, has become an achievement in itself, rather than delivery. In a single sweep, we can put that culture to an end.

##### C3. Institutional Corruption

###### Governing Principle

A state that tolerates corruption in its own institutions has no moral authority to enforce the law against anyone else. The credibility of every policy in this crime framework, from police expansion to sentencing reform to the pursuit of organised crime, rests on the premise that the institutions doing the enforcing are themselves clean. If they are not, the entire edifice is built on sand.

Britain’s institutions are not clean. The United Kingdom’s score on Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index has fallen to 70 in 2025, its lowest ever, down from a top-ten position as recently as 2017. The country now sits 20th in the global ranking for the third consecutive year, behind Estonia, Ireland, and the UAE. The decline is not a statistical artefact. It reflects a systemic pattern of conduct that has been visible to the public for years: pandemic procurement scandals in which billions of pounds of public money were funnelled to politically connected firms with no relevant experience, honours and peerages exchanged for political donations, a revolving door between senior public office and corporate boardrooms that makes a mockery of the public interest, and local authorities in which fraud, embezzlement, and procurement rigging are endemic and almost never prosecuted.

The scale is staggering. The Public Sector Fraud Authority estimated public sector fraud losses at between £39.8 billion and £58.5 billion in the 2024/25 financial year. Local government alone is estimated by CIPFA and the National Audit Office to lose approximately £7.3 billion annually to fraud, error, and corruption, a cumulative total exceeding £100 billion since 2010. The Department for Work and Pensions estimated benefit overpayments at £9.7 billion in 2023/24, with Universal Credit alone accounting for £6.5 billion in overpayments, 12.4% of total UC expenditure. Meanwhile, the government awards approximately £400 billion in contracts per year, yet the UK’s own Anti-Corruption Strategy, published in January 2026, concedes that evidence of corruption in public procurement is “largely anecdotal”. It is anecdotal because nobody is looking. In 2024, defendants were prosecuted for a total of 15 offences under the Bribery Act 2010 in the entire country. Fifteen. This is not enforcement. It is pantomime.

Progress’ position is that institutional corruption is not a secondary concern to be addressed after street crime and violent crime. It is the soil in which all other failures grow. The local authorities that covered up grooming gangs (C4) were institutionally corrupt. The police forces that turned away from community policing (C5) were institutionally captured. The procurement system that wasted billions during Covid was structurally designed to resist scrutiny. Until the institutions themselves are purged, reformed, and subjected to the same severity of enforcement that Progress demands for every other kind of crime, the system will continue to produce the outcomes it was designed to produce: impunity for those with power and accountability only for those without it.

C2 introduced the Malebranche, Progress’ anti-corruption unit, and established its statutory basis. This document provides the full operational framework for the war on institutional corruption. It will be the most comprehensive anti-corruption programme ever attempted in British public life.

###### C3.1: The Malebranche: Full Operational Framework

Statutory Basis

The National Anti-Corruption Act (established in C2.5) creates the Malebranche as a statutory body sitting within the Cabinet Office, reporting directly to the Prime Minister, with independent investigatory and prosecutorial powers. This section elaborates the full scope of those powers and the operational structure of the unit.

Scope and Jurisdiction

The Malebranche will have jurisdiction over all forms of corruption, fraud, and malfeasance involving public money, public office, or public institutions. Specifically:

- a) Local authority corruption. Fraud, embezzlement, procurement rigging, planning corruption, and abuse of office by councillors, officers, and contractors. This is the primary target in the Malebranche’s first year. Local government in Britain is a scandal in slow motion: 103 documented cases of financial misconduct between 2010 and 2025 with confirmed losses exceeding £311 million, and estimated true losses of over £100 billion across the period. Liverpool City Council faced police investigation and government intervention after multiple arrests in its regeneration directorate. Tees Valley Combined Authority was issued a best value notice over opaque land deals in the £450 million Teesworks project. Town clerks in parishes across England have embezzled from precept budgets with near-impunity. The Malebranche will treat local authority corruption as the first front in the war on institutional rot.
- b) Public procurement fraud. £400 billion flows through government contracts annually. The Covid procurement scandal demonstrated that contracts worth hundreds of millions of pounds were awarded through a VIP lane to firms with political connections and no relevant capability. The Malebranche will have statutory power to investigate any government contract, past or present, and to refer findings for criminal prosecution. There will be no time limitation on these powers.
- c) Honours, access, and political corruption. The sale of honours and political access is endemic. The Conservative Party accepted £15 million from a single donor in less than 12 months before the 2024 election. Labour was reported to have granted a donor privileged access to 10 Downing Street. Appointments to donors have been made without following due process. The Malebranche will investigate all such transactions and refer findings for prosecution under enhanced bribery provisions.
- d) Foreign influence and golden passports. Collusion with non-aligned foreign interests, the sale of residency and citizenship rights to individuals whose wealth derives from corruption or criminality abroad, and the use of London as a laundromat for the proceeds of kleptocracy. The Malebranche will work with the NCA’s International Corruption Unit and will have power to refer cases for Unexplained Wealth Orders.
- e) The revolving door. The movement of senior officials, ministers, and regulators into lucrative private sector positions in industries they previously regulated or awarded contracts to. This is structural corruption. The Malebranche will investigate patterns of revolving door movement and, where evidence of corrupt intent is found, refer for prosecution. The broader regulatory framework for the revolving door is addressed in C3.3 below.
- f) Prison and police corruption. In 2024, 45 staff within HM Prison and Probation Service were prosecuted for corruption-related offences. The Malebranche will establish a dedicated unit for corruption within uniformed services, working alongside the IOPC for police cases and HMPPS for prison cases, but with independent prosecutorial authority.

Structure and Staffing

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The National Anti-Corruption Act (C2.5) establishes the Malebranche’s statutory basis, powers, and independence. The following operational elements are on the face of the Act:

- a) The Director of the Malebranche is appointed by the Prime Minister, confirmed by a parliamentary select committee, and removable only by a two-thirds vote of the House of Commons. This ensures independence from the executive while maintaining democratic accountability.
- b) The Malebranche has statutory power to compel the production of documents, compel witnesses to attend for interview, enter and search premises, seize assets, and arrest suspects. These powers are equivalent to those of the NCA and SFO but are exercised independently of both.
- c) The Malebranche has its own prosecutorial authority, independent of the CPS. It can bring criminal charges, apply for confiscation and forfeiture orders, and pursue civil recovery without requiring CPS consent. This eliminates the bottleneck that has crippled the SFO, where complex cases are frequently declined or downgraded by the CPS.
- d) No time limitation applies to Malebranche investigations. Historical corruption, procurement fraud, and public spending misuse can be investigated and prosecuted regardless of when the conduct occurred.

OPERATIONAL

Initial staffing. 500 personnel within 90 days of Royal Assent, drawn from NCA, HMRC, SFO, and private sector recruitment. The unit will be organised into six directorates: Local Government, Procurement, Political Corruption, Foreign Influence, Uniformed Services, and Financial Analysis. Each directorate will be led by a Director-level appointment at Senior Civil Service grade.

Funding. The Malebranche will be funded by a ring-fenced allocation from the Treasury, supplemented by the proceeds of confiscation and civil recovery orders it obtains. The initial annual budget will be £150 million. For context, the Serious Fraud Office’s budget is approximately £75 million; the Malebranche is designed to be twice the SFO’s size and several times its effectiveness.

Relationship with existing bodies. The Malebranche does not replace the NCA, SFO, or HMRC. It sits alongside them with a specific mandate for public sector and political corruption. Where jurisdictions overlap (for example, a fraud case with both private and public sector dimensions), the Malebranche will have primacy for the public sector elements. Memoranda of understanding will be agreed within 60 days of the unit becoming operational.

###### C3.2: Prohibition of Documentary Destruction

The Problem

One of the most effective tools of institutional corruption is the destruction of evidence. Across central and local government, institutions routinely destroy records that might expose malfeasance, mismanagement, or criminality. Retention schedules are treated as maximum holding periods rather than minimum ones. Documents that might embarrass officials or reveal procurement irregularities are shredded, deleted, or “lost” in system migrations. The practice is so widespread and so normalised that it is rarely even recognised as corruption; it is simply how institutions protect themselves from accountability.

The consequence is that by the time an investigation begins, the paper trail has been destroyed. The Malebranche’s retrospective investigation powers are only as effective as the documentary record allows. This policy ensures that the record survives.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The National Anti-Corruption Act (C2.5) creates the statutory offence. This section elaborates the full enforcement framework:

- a) Destruction, concealment, alteration, or failure to preserve any document held by a public authority that is relevant or potentially relevant to any investigation, audit, or accountability proceeding is a criminal offence carrying a minimum sentence of 3 years for the responsible officer and unlimited fines for the institution.
- b) The offence applies retrospectively to any destruction that occurred within the preceding 15 years. Where an officer can be shown to have authorised or directed the destruction of documents that were subsequently sought by an investigation, they are criminally liable regardless of when the destruction occurred.
- c) All public authorities are required to maintain a tamper-evident digital document management system with a complete audit trail of every document created, accessed, modified, or deleted. The system must be operational within 12 months of Royal Assent.
- d) The Data Protection Act 2018’s provisions on erasure and retention are disapplied for documents held by public authorities in connection with their public functions. The default for public records is permanent retention, not scheduled destruction.

OPERATIONAL

Malebranche audit programme. Within 90 days of becoming operational, the Malebranche will conduct systematic audits of document retention practices across central government departments and a sample of 50 local authorities. Where systemic destruction or non-compliance is found, the responsible senior officers will be referred for prosecution. The audits will be published in full.

Technical standard. The Government Digital Service will publish a mandatory technical standard for public authority document management systems within 6 months of Royal Assent. The standard will require immutable audit logging, version control, and automated flagging of bulk deletions. Compliance will be a condition of continued public funding.

###### C3.3: The Revolving Door

The Problem

The movement of ministers, senior civil servants, regulators, and procurement officials into lucrative positions in the industries they previously regulated, funded, or awarded contracts to is one of the most corrosive and least prosecuted forms of institutional corruption. The Advisory Committee on Business Appointments (ACOBA) nominally oversees these transitions but is a toothless body with no enforcement powers. Its recommendations are routinely ignored, and there are no sanctions for non-compliance. The result is a structural incentive for officials to act in the interests of their future employers while still in public office, knowing that no consequence will follow.

The Covid procurement scandal was the most visible manifestation of this dynamic, but it operates constantly at every level of government. Planning officers move to property developers. Defence procurement officials move to defence contractors. Financial regulators move to the banks they were supposed to supervise. Each transition creates a vector for corruption, whether or not any individual transaction involves an explicit quid pro quo.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Public Integrity Act will:

- a) Replace ACOBA with a statutory Public Integrity Commission with binding enforcement powers, including the power to prohibit post-public-service employment for a defined period, to impose financial penalties for non-compliance, and to refer cases to the Malebranche for criminal investigation.
- b) Impose a mandatory 3-year cooling-off period for all ministers, senior civil servants (SCS grade and above), and senior officials of regulatory bodies before they may accept employment, consultancy, or board positions in any sector they had significant dealings with in their last 3 years of public service.
- c) Create a statutory offence of corrupt post-service employment, applicable where a former public official accepts a position that a reasonable person would conclude was offered, in whole or in part, as a reward for decisions made or influence exercised while in office. Minimum sentence: 5 years.
- d) Require all former ministers and SCS officials to make a public declaration of all employment, income, and financial interests for a period of 5 years after leaving public service. Failure to declare is itself an offence carrying a minimum sentence of 12 months.

OPERATIONAL

Public Integrity Commission staffing. The Commission will be operational within 90 days of Royal Assent, initially staffed by secondments from the Cabinet Office propriety and ethics team, supplemented by legal and investigatory staff. Annual budget: £15 million.

Retrospective review. The Commission will conduct a review of all ACOBA cases from the preceding 10 years within its first 6 months. Where cooling-off recommendations were ignored and evidence of corrupt intent exists, cases will be referred to the Malebranche.

###### C3.4: Procurement Transparency and Accountability

The Problem

£400 billion in public money flows through government contracts every year. The system that governs this expenditure is designed to process volume, not to detect corruption. The Procurement Act 2023, which came into force in February 2025, was advertised as a transparency reform but in practice merely consolidated existing opacity into a new statutory framework. There is no systematic audit of contract outcomes. There is no mandatory comparison of contract value to delivered value. There is no consequence for officials who award contracts to firms that fail to deliver. The VIP lane scandal during Covid was not an aberration; it was the system working exactly as it had been built to work, just at a speed that made the corruption visible.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Public Integrity Act will additionally:

- a) Create a statutory duty on all public authorities to publish, in machine-readable format and within 30 days of contract award, the full text of every contract exceeding £25,000, together with the evaluation criteria used, the scores awarded to each bidder, and the identity of every official involved in the decision. No commercial confidentiality exemption will apply to contracts funded by public money.
- b) Establish mandatory post-contract audits for all contracts exceeding £1 million. Within 12 months of contract completion (or termination), an independent audit must compare the contracted deliverables with what was actually delivered and publish the findings. Where the audit identifies a material discrepancy exceeding 20% of contract value, the matter is automatically referred to the Malebranche.
- c) Create a statutory offence of procurement fraud by a public official, carrying a minimum sentence of 5 years. This captures any official who knowingly awards a contract to a bidder who does not meet the published criteria, who fails to declare a conflict of interest, or who receives any benefit (direct or indirect) from a contractor within 5 years of the contract award.
- d) Prohibit the use of emergency procurement powers (which bypass competitive tendering) for any period exceeding 90 days without explicit parliamentary approval. The open-ended emergency powers used during Covid, which remained in effect for over two years, will never be repeated.

OPERATIONAL

National Procurement Transparency Portal. The Cabinet Office will commission a single, publicly searchable portal for all government contracts, replacing the current fragmented publication model. The portal will include full contract texts, evaluation records, audit findings, and contractor performance histories. It will be integrated with the open data infrastructure established under C1. Operational within 9 months of Royal Assent.

Retrospective contract review. The Malebranche will conduct a systematic review of all contracts exceeding £10 million awarded between March 2020 and March 2022 (the Covid emergency procurement period). Where evidence of fraud, favouritism, or VIP lane abuse is found, criminal prosecution will follow. Estimated scope: 1,500 to 2,000 contracts.

###### C3.5: Whistleblower Protection and Incentivisation

The Problem

Corruption is a hidden crime. The people best positioned to expose it are those who work inside the institutions where it occurs. Britain’s existing whistleblower framework, the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 (PIDA), is widely regarded as inadequate. It provides protection against dismissal in theory, but enforcement is slow, costly, and psychologically punishing for the whistleblower. Employment tribunal claims take months or years. Employers find indirect ways to retaliate: reassignment, exclusion, managed performance processes. The financial cost of bringing a claim falls entirely on the whistleblower. The result is a rational calculation for most insiders: keeping quiet is safer than speaking up.

Progress will invert that calculation. Speaking up will be rewarded. Retaliation will be criminal.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Public Integrity Act will additionally:

- a) Replace PIDA with a comprehensive Whistleblower Protection and Reward Act within the Public Integrity Act framework. The new provisions will apply to all public and private sector employees, contractors, and agents.
- b) Provide absolute protection from dismissal, demotion, reassignment, or any other detriment for any person who reports suspected corruption, fraud, or criminal activity to the Malebranche, the Public Integrity Commission, or any law enforcement body. Protection will be immediate and automatic upon registration of the disclosure.
- c) Create a criminal offence of whistleblower retaliation, carrying a minimum sentence of 2 years for any individual who takes or directs retaliatory action against a whistleblower. Corporate liability will attach to any organisation whose employee retaliates, with unlimited fines.
- d) Establish a financial reward scheme. Whistleblowers whose disclosures lead to criminal conviction, civil recovery, or the prevention of fraud will receive a reward of up to 10% of recovered funds or imposed fines, capped at £10 million per disclosure. This is modelled on the US False Claims Act’s qui tam provisions, which have recovered over $75 billion for the US government since 1986. The economics of whistleblowing must change: exposing corruption must be more profitable than participating in it.
- e) Establish a dedicated Whistleblower Legal Support Fund, publicly funded and administered at arm’s length, providing free legal representation to any whistleblower facing proceedings as a result of their disclosure.

OPERATIONAL

Malebranche Whistleblower Directorate. A dedicated directorate within the Malebranche will receive, triage, and investigate all whistleblower disclosures. It will operate a secure, anonymous reporting channel. Every disclosure will receive a formal acknowledgment within 48 hours and a substantive assessment within 30 days.

###### C3.6: Benefits Fraud Enforcement

The Problem

The Department for Work and Pensions estimated benefit overpayments at £9.7 billion in 2023/24, representing 3.7% of all benefit expenditure.
