Universal Credit alone accounted for £6.5 billion in overpayments, 12.4% of total UC expenditure. A significant proportion of this is attributable to fraud rather than administrative error. The current enforcement model is grossly inadequate: the DWP’s fraud investigation capacity has been hollowed out, prosecutions are rare, and the penalties for systematic fraud are laughably low relative to the sums involved.

Too many benefits cheats live well off the taxpayer by exploiting loopholes, fabricating claims, and gaming a system that was designed on the assumption of good faith. That assumption has been exploited beyond breaking point. Progress will enforce the system with the same severity applied to every other form of theft.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The National Anti-Corruption Act (C2.5) creates the statutory offence of benefits fraud. The Public Integrity Act will additionally:

- a) Establish enhanced penalties for systematic or high-value benefits fraud. Fraud exceeding £10,000: minimum 12 months’ imprisonment. Fraud exceeding £50,000: minimum 3 years. Fraud exceeding £100,000: minimum 5 years. Organised benefits fraud (two or more persons acting in concert): minimum 5 years per participant.
- b) Grant the DWP powers to share data directly with HMRC, local authorities, the Land Registry, and Companies House for the purposes of fraud detection, overriding current data protection restrictions that impede cross-referencing.
- c) Require courts to impose mandatory repayment orders equal to the full value of the fraud plus 50% in punitive damages. Where the fraudster cannot pay, the debt will be enforced as a confiscation order under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.

OPERATIONAL

DWP fraud investigation capacity. The DWP’s fraud investigation team will be tripled in size within 6 months of Royal Assent. The target is a tenfold increase in prosecutions for benefits fraud within the first year, rising to twenty-fold within two years.

Data matching. An automated cross-referencing system linking DWP benefits records with HMRC tax records, Land Registry property ownership data, and Companies House directorship records will be operational within 9 months. This will identify claimants who are simultaneously receiving benefits and earning undeclared income, owning property, or directing companies.

###### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The C3 Institutional Corruption framework is built on two pieces of primary legislation: the National Anti-Corruption Act (already established in C2.5) and a new Public Integrity Act. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, departmental procurement, or existing administrative mechanisms.

- 1. National Anti-Corruption Act (established in C2.5)

On the face of the Act: Establishment of the Malebranche with independent investigatory and prosecutorial powers. Documentary destruction offence. Enhanced white-collar sentencing. Benefits fraud offence. Whistleblower financial rewards. No time limitation on investigations.

Delivered operationally: Malebranche staffing (500 personnel within 90 days, £150 million annual budget). Six directorates. Document retention audit programme within 90 days. Retrospective Covid procurement review (1,500+ contracts). Whistleblower Directorate with 48-hour acknowledgment standard.

- 2. Public Integrity Act (new)

On the face of the Act: Replacement of ACOBA with statutory Public Integrity Commission. 3-year cooling-off period for senior officials. Corrupt post-service employment offence (minimum 5 years). Post-service declaration requirement. Full procurement transparency duty. Mandatory post-contract audits. Procurement fraud by public official offence (minimum 5 years). Emergency procurement time limits. Comprehensive whistleblower protection replacing PIDA. Whistleblower retaliation offence (minimum 2 years). Whistleblower reward scheme (up to 10% / £10 million cap). Enhanced benefits fraud penalties with mandatory repayment orders.

Delivered operationally: Public Integrity Commission within 90 days. ACOBA retrospective review within 6 months. National Procurement Transparency Portal within 9 months. GDS technical standard for document management within 6 months. DWP fraud team tripled within 6 months. Automated cross-referencing system within 9 months.

The institutional corruption framework is the moral precondition for everything else in the Progress crime policy. A government that demands severity from its citizens must first demand it from itself. The Malebranche, the Public Integrity Commission, the procurement transparency regime, the whistleblower protections, and the benefits fraud enforcement programme together constitute a comprehensive assault on the culture of impunity that has rotted Britain’s public institutions from the inside out. The public has watched this rot for years. Progress will end it.

##### C4. The Rape Gangs – Reckoning and Remembrance

###### Governing Principle

This is the most important document in the Progress crime policy framework. Every other section, from police expansion to sentencing reform to institutional corruption, exists in part because the events described here were allowed to happen, and because the institutions that should have prevented them failed at every level, often deliberately.

Across dozens of towns and cities in England, over a period spanning at least four decades, thousands of children, overwhelmingly girls, were subjected to systematic sexual exploitation by organised networks of men. They were groomed with alcohol, drugs, and false affection. They were gang-raped in flats, alleyways, warehouses, cars, and hotels. They were beaten, trafficked between towns, held at gunpoint, and sold for sex. Some contracted sexually transmitted infections. Some were forced to have abortions. Some had their children taken from them. Some were murdered. The youngest victims were eleven years old.

The state knew. Social workers knew. Police knew. Teachers knew. Council officials knew. In many cases, they had the names of the perpetrators, the addresses where the abuse was occurring, and direct testimony from the victims. They did nothing. Worse than nothing: in Rotherham, police arrested the fathers of abused girls who attempted to rescue their daughters, while detaining none of the abusers. Police officers referred to child victims as “slags” and described their abuse as a “lifestyle choice.” In Telford, teachers and social workers were actively discouraged from reporting abuse. Across multiple jurisdictions, the exploitation was classified as “child prostitution,” a term that imputes consent to children who cannot give it. In Rotherham, the word “Pakistani” was physically tippexed out of case files. In July 2025, it was reported that five survivors had accused police officers themselves of raping them when they were as young as twelve. Three former officers were arrested; a fourth had died.

The Casey Audit, published in June 2025, confirmed that ethnicity data was not recorded for two-thirds of grooming gang perpetrators. Where data did exist, in Greater Manchester, South Yorkshire, and West Yorkshire, it showed disproportionate numbers of men from Asian ethnic backgrounds among the suspects. In Rotherham’s Operation Stovewood, of 323 suspects and 42 convicted offenders, nearly two-thirds were of Pakistani ethnic background. The Audit found that “flawed data is used repeatedly to dismiss claims about ‘Asian grooming gangs’ as sensationalised, biased or untrue” and that the ethnicity of offenders had been “shied away from” with institutional “obfuscation.”

The scale is documented but not yet fully known. The Jay Report (2014) estimated at least 1,400 victims in Rotherham alone between 1997 and 2013. The Telford Inquiry (2022) found that over 1,000 children were abused across four decades. Rochdale’s inquiry identified 74 probable victims and evidence of a much wider problem. Operation Stovewood, the largest non-familial child sexual exploitation investigation in UK history, identified approximately 1,150 potential victims in Rotherham. The Casey Audit reported that around 500,000 children a year experience some form of child sexual abuse in the UK, with 17,100 contact offences per year flagged as child sexual exploitation. Of group-based CSE cases recorded in 2023, 717 involved organised criminal networks. The true cumulative figure across all affected towns, spanning decades, is unknown because nobody counted.

No public servant has been charged in connection with the institutional cover-up. Not one. Councillors who presided over decades of inaction have retired on full pensions. Police officers who called child rape victims “slags” have faced no criminal sanction. Social workers who were told to stop reporting have not been prosecuted for complicity. The Louise Casey Report on Rotherham Council (2015) found the authority “not fit for purpose,” with a “culture of bullying, sexism, covering up information and silencing whistleblowers.” The elected council was replaced by government commissioners. But nobody went to prison.

The current government’s response has been a statutory inquiry under Baroness Longfield, announced in December 2025, with a three-year timeline and a £65 million budget. Progress considers this entirely inadequate. Three more years of inquiry, after four decades of abuse and a decade of reports, reviews, audits, and recommendations that were ignored. What is needed is not another inquiry. What is needed is a reckoning.

###### C4.1: Unlimited Criminal Liability for Institutional Complicity

The Problem

The institutional failure that allowed the grooming gang scandal to continue for decades was not merely negligent. In many documented cases, it was active: information was suppressed, victims were silenced, whistleblowers were bullied, and ethnicity data was physically deleted from files. Where public officials take active steps to conceal serious criminal offences against children, they are not merely failing in their duty. They are complicit in the offences themselves. The law must reflect this.

At present, there is no specific statutory mechanism for holding public officials criminally liable for the institutional cover-up of child sexual exploitation. The offence of misconduct in public office is common law, vague, and carries no minimum sentence. The offence of perverting the course of justice captures some conduct but was not designed for systemic institutional failure. No offence captures the councillor who knew and said nothing, the senior officer who instructed subordinates to stop investigating, the manager who classified gang rape as “child prostitution” to reduce its statistical visibility. Progress will create one.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Child Protection (Institutional Accountability) Act will:

- a) Create a statutory offence of institutional complicity in child sexual exploitation. Any person holding public office, or exercising a public function, who knew or ought to have known that child sexual exploitation was occurring within their area of responsibility, and who failed to take all reasonable steps to prevent it, report it, or ensure its investigation, commits an offence. Maximum sentence: life imprisonment. This offence is deliberately the most severe available for institutional failure anywhere in British law. It reflects the gravity of what was permitted.
- b) Create a statutory offence of active concealment of child sexual exploitation. Any person who destroys, suppresses, alters, or conceals any information, document, or evidence relating to known or suspected child sexual exploitation commits an offence. Minimum sentence: 7 years. Where the concealment involved suppression of ethnicity data or demographic information about perpetrators, the minimum rises to 10 years. The physical tippexing-out of the word “Pakistani” from case files in Rotherham is the paradigmatic instance. This must never happen again.
- c) Create a statutory offence of obstruction of child protection. Any person who discourages, prevents, or penalises another person from reporting suspected child sexual exploitation, or who retaliates against a person who has made such a report, commits an offence. Minimum sentence: 5 years. This captures the culture documented in Rotherham, Telford, and elsewhere in which social workers and teachers were actively discouraged from reporting what they witnessed.
- d) No time limitation whatsoever. These offences apply retrospectively to all conduct, past and present, without any limitation period. Progress rejects the principle that the passage of time diminishes the gravity of institutional complicity in the mass rape of children. A councillor who knew in 1998 and said nothing is as liable as one who knew in 2018. A police officer who arrested a father for trying to rescue his daughter from a house where she was being raped will face the same law regardless of when the arrest occurred. The limitation on liability is not temporal. It is unlimited.
- e) Liability is personal, not merely institutional. Individuals cannot shelter behind the corporate acts of their council, police force, or social services department. Where a named individual held responsibility and failed to exercise it, that individual is personally liable. Institutional apologies, past or future, do not discharge personal criminal liability.
- f) Senior command responsibility. The Act will incorporate a principle derived from international humanitarian law: a person in a position of authority who knew, or had reason to know, that subordinates were failing to act on reports of child sexual exploitation, and who failed to take all necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish that failure, is criminally liable to the same degree as if they had personally committed the acts of concealment. This captures chief constables, council chief executives, directors of children’s services, and government ministers.

OPERATIONAL

National Criminal Investigation. Within 21 days of Royal Assent, the Malebranche (C3.1) will establish a dedicated Institutional Complicity Unit with a specific mandate to investigate the conduct of public officials in every town and city where grooming gang activity has been documented. The investigation will not be time-limited. It will not be subject to a budget cap. It will not require permission from the local authorities under investigation. Its investigators will have the same powers of compulsion, search, seizure, and arrest as the Malebranche’s other directorates. Every council, every police force, every social services department, every health authority, and every school that received reports and failed to act will be subject to investigation. The Longfield Inquiry, if still operating at the time of Progress taking office, will be subsumed into this investigation or operate alongside it in an advisory capacity.

Immediate review of all closed investigations. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, every police force in England and Wales will be required to submit to the Malebranche a full accounting of every grooming gang investigation that was closed, downgraded, or deprioritised since 1990, with the names of the officers who made those decisions. Where evidence of institutional obstruction is found, those officers will be investigated under the new statutory framework.

###### C4.2: Perpetrator Justice

The Problem

Operation Stovewood, the NCA’s investigation into Rotherham, identified approximately 1,150 potential victims and over 220 suspects. As of late 2025, 47 people have been convicted. Forty-seven, out of more than 220 suspects, in a single town, after a nine-year investigation. The gap between the scale of offending and the scale of justice is an abyss. It is replicated in every other affected area. Many perpetrators have never been charged. Many victims have never been contacted by the police. Many investigations were closed with no further action and were never reopened.

The sentencing reforms in C2.3 apply to future offending. This section addresses the specific and urgent task of pursuing historical perpetrators who have thus far evaded justice.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Child Protection (Institutional Accountability) Act will additionally:

- a) Remove any remaining limitation periods for the prosecution of sexual offences against children. While there is technically no statute of limitations for indictable sexual offences in England and Wales, prosecutorial discretion and CPS charging guidelines have in practice created a de facto limitation by treating historical cases as lower priority. The Act will create a statutory presumption in favour of prosecution for all historical child sexual exploitation cases, regardless of the age of the evidence, and will prohibit the CPS from declining to prosecute on the grounds of delay alone.
- b) Introduce mandatory deportation for any foreign national convicted of child sexual exploitation offences. Where the offender holds dual nationality, British citizenship will be revoked under the powers reformed in C2.4 (HRA reform) prior to deportation. The British Bill of Rights Act’s reforms to judicial override of deportation orders will ensure that no ECHR-based challenge prevents removal.
- c) Apply compound sentencing (C2.3) retrospectively to grooming gang offenders. Where an individual is convicted of multiple offences of child sexual exploitation, sentences will be consecutive, not concurrent, and the compound multiplier will apply. A man convicted of multiple rapes of children across different victims will receive the full aggregated sentence with no concurrency discount.
- d) Create a statutory aggravating factor for child sexual exploitation committed as part of an organised network, adding a minimum uplift of 5 years to any sentence. Where the offending involved trafficking of victims between locations, the uplift rises to 10 years.

OPERATIONAL

National reopening of historical cases. All police forces will be directed to review and reopen every historical grooming gang investigation that was closed without full resolution. The NCA will provide coordination and investigative support. Additional CPS capacity will be funded to handle the resulting caseload. Target: every identifiable perpetrator who has not yet been charged will be charged within 24 months.

Victim contact programme. Every individual identified as a potential victim in any historical grooming gang investigation, including those identified by Operation Stovewood and its equivalents in other forces, will be proactively contacted by specially trained officers and offered the opportunity to provide evidence. No victim will be required to participate, but every victim will be offered the chance. Support services, including legal representation, counselling, and financial assistance, will be provided to every victim who comes forward.

###### C4.3: Remembrance and Public Memorialisation

The Principle

A nation that does not memorialise its worst failures is a nation that will repeat them. The grooming gang scandal is the largest institutional failure of child protection in modern British history. It is comparable in moral weight to the Hillsborough disaster, the infected blood scandal, and the Post Office Horizon scandal, but it exceeds all of them in scale, duration, and the depth of institutional complicity involved. Unlike those scandals, it has no national memorial. There is no public monument to the thousands of children who were raped, trafficked, and destroyed while the state looked the other way. There should be.

Progress will fund and commission a national programme of public works to ensure that these events are permanently inscribed in the national memory. The purpose is threefold: to honour the victims, to record the institutional failure so that it can never be denied or minimised, and to stand as a permanent warning to every public institution in the country of the consequences of moral cowardice.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Child Protection (Institutional Accountability) Act will additionally:

- a) Establish a statutory National Memorial Commission for the Victims of Organised Child Sexual Exploitation. The Commission will be responsible for the design, construction, and maintenance of all memorials and public works described in this section. It will be chaired by a survivor or a representative nominated by survivor groups. Its budget will be ring-fenced and permanent.
- b) Require the construction of a National Memorial in a prominent public location in central London. The memorial will be of a scale and permanence comparable to the national war memorials. It will record the names of every affected town and city, the estimated number of victims, the duration of the abuse, and the institutional failures that permitted it. It will include a space for the names of individual victims who choose to be recorded. It will be a place of national pilgrimage and reflection, not a discreet plaque in a government building.
- c) Require the construction of local memorials in every town and city where grooming gang activity has been documented and confirmed by inquiry, investigation, or criminal conviction. These memorials will be funded by central government and will be sited in prominent public locations chosen in consultation with local survivor groups. They will be permanent and protected by statute from removal or alteration.
- d) Establish a National Day of Remembrance for the Victims of Child Sexual Exploitation, to be observed annually. The date will be chosen in consultation with survivor groups. On this day, flags on all government buildings will be lowered, and a national moment of reflection will be observed. The Prime Minister will make a statement to Parliament.

OPERATIONAL

National Memorial design competition. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the National Memorial Commission will launch an open design competition for the London memorial. The competition will be judged by a panel comprising survivors, architects, and representatives of the arts. The design must convey the scale and severity of what occurred. It must not sanitise, euphemise, or abstract the reality of the abuse. The memorial will be completed within 24 months of design selection.

Local memorial programme. The Commission will work with survivor groups in each affected area to design and construct local memorials. The first memorials will be completed in Rotherham, Telford, Rochdale, and Oxford within 18 months of Royal Assent. Further memorials will follow as investigations confirm additional affected areas. Estimated programme cost: £50 million over 5 years, centrally funded.

Educational programme. The Department for Education will commission a mandatory educational module on the grooming gang scandal for inclusion in the national curriculum at Key Stage 4. The module will cover the events themselves, the institutional failures, the consequences for victims, and the lessons for safeguarding. It will be developed in consultation with survivors and child protection professionals. It will be in place within 2 academic years of Royal Assent.

National archive. All documents, testimony, evidence, and records from every inquiry, investigation, review, and audit into grooming gang activity, including all materials gathered by the Longfield Inquiry, Operation Stovewood, and all local investigations, will be deposited in a permanent, publicly accessible National Archive of Child Sexual Exploitation. The archive will be maintained by the National Archives and will be exempt from any destruction, closure, or restriction on access. The purpose is to ensure that the historical record can never be lost, suppressed, or denied. It will stand in perpetuity.

###### C4.4: Victim Support and Compensation

The Problem

The victims of the grooming gang scandal have received almost nothing from the state that failed to protect them. Many have spent decades struggling with the psychological and physical consequences of their abuse: PTSD, depression, substance dependency, relationship breakdown, loss of employment, and inability to trust institutions. Many became parents at a young age as a result of their abuse and have raised children in the shadow of trauma. The Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority (CICA) has been woefully inadequate: awards are low, the process is adversarial and re-traumatising, and many victims were never informed of their right to claim. Some victims who sought help from local authorities after their abuse were treated with the same contempt they experienced during it.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Child Protection (Institutional Accountability) Act will additionally:

- a) Establish a dedicated Compensation Fund for Victims of Organised Child Sexual Exploitation, separate from the CICA. The Fund will make awards based on an assessment of harm, not a tariff-based calculation. Awards will reflect the severity and duration of the abuse, the age of the victim at the time, the extent of institutional failure that permitted the abuse, and the ongoing impact on the victim’s life. There will be no upper cap on individual awards. The Fund will be financed by a combination of Treasury allocation and the proceeds of confiscation orders obtained from convicted perpetrators.
- b) Provide a statutory right to free, specialist, long-term therapeutic support for every identified victim of grooming gang exploitation, including but not limited to counselling, psychiatric care, substance misuse treatment, and family support. This right will be enforceable and will not be subject to waiting lists, geographical availability, or local authority discretion. It will be funded centrally and delivered through commissioned specialist providers.
- c) Grant victims a statutory right to legal representation, funded by the state, in all proceedings connected with their abuse, including criminal trials, compensation claims, inquiries, and any civil proceedings against public authorities.
- d) Create a statutory right for victims to request a formal review of any decision by a local authority, police force, or other public body that affected them during or after the period of their abuse. Where the review finds that the authority’s conduct contributed to the abuse or its continuation, the authority will be required to issue a formal, public, individual apology and to pay compensation directly from its own budget, in addition to any award from the national Fund.

OPERATIONAL

Immediate interim payments. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, every individual who has been formally identified as a victim in any grooming gang investigation (including but not limited to Operation Stovewood) will be eligible for an interim payment of £25,000 while full compensation assessments are undertaken. The purpose is to provide immediate, tangible recognition that the state owes these individuals a debt.

Dedicated victim liaison. Each affected area will have a dedicated Victim Liaison Office, staffed by specially trained personnel and independent of the local authority and police force. The Liaison Office will serve as a single point of contact for all victims, coordinating access to support services, legal representation, compensation, and updates on criminal investigations.

###### C4.5: Mandatory Ethnicity and Demographic Data Collection

The Problem

The Casey Audit found that ethnicity data was not recorded for two-thirds of grooming gang perpetrators nationally. This is not an accident. It is the institutional expression of the same cowardice that permitted the abuse itself. Where data was available, in Greater Manchester, South Yorkshire, and West Yorkshire, it showed clear patterns of disproportionate offending by men from specific ethnic backgrounds. The failure to collect data nationally made it impossible to understand the scale and nature of the problem, and provided cover for those who wished to deny or minimise it. As Baroness Casey stated, the question of ethnicity had been “shied away from,” and flawed data had been “used repeatedly to dismiss claims.”

Progress will end the data blackout. The collection and publication of complete, accurate demographic data on perpetrators of child sexual exploitation is not a concession to prejudice. It is the essential foundation of any evidence-based response. Patterns that are not measured cannot be addressed. Disproportionalities that are not acknowledged cannot be understood. Communities cannot be held to account for problems they are not permitted to discuss.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Child Protection (Institutional Accountability) Act will additionally:

- a) Make it a statutory duty for all police forces to record the ethnicity, nationality, religion, and immigration status of every individual suspected, charged, or convicted of a child sexual exploitation offence. This data will be collected at the point of first police contact and updated throughout the criminal justice process. It will be published annually in aggregate form by the Home Office.
- b) Make it a statutory duty for the Crown Prosecution Service to record and publish the same demographic data for all CSE cases it handles, together with charging decisions and outcomes.
- c) Make it a criminal offence for any public official to suppress, alter, delete, or fail to record demographic data about suspects or offenders of child sexual exploitation. This directly addresses the Rotherham tippexing incident and any equivalent conduct. Minimum sentence: 3 years, in addition to any sentence for active concealment under C4.1(b).
- d) Require the Home Office to commission and publish, within 12 months of Royal Assent, a comprehensive national retrospective analysis of the ethnicity, nationality, and demographic profile of all identified grooming gang suspects and offenders across all documented cases. The analysis will be conducted by an independent research body and will be published in full, without redaction.

OPERATIONAL

Data system reform. The Home Office will mandate a standardised data collection framework for all 43 police forces in England and Wales within 6 months of Royal Assent. The framework will include mandatory fields for ethnicity, nationality, religion, and immigration status for all sexual offences against children. Forces that fail to comply will face mandatory intervention by HMICFRS.

###### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The C4 framework is built on a single, comprehensive piece of primary legislation: the Child Protection (Institutional Accountability) Act. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, departmental procurement, or existing administrative mechanisms.

Child Protection (Institutional Accountability) Act

On the face of the Act: Offence of institutional complicity in child sexual exploitation (maximum life imprisonment). Offence of active concealment (minimum 7 years; 10 years where ethnicity data suppressed). Offence of obstruction of child protection (minimum 5 years). No limitation period. Personal liability. Senior command responsibility. Statutory presumption in favour of prosecution for historical CSE cases. Mandatory deportation for foreign national CSE offenders. Compound sentencing for grooming gang offenders. Statutory aggravating factor for organised network offending (+5 years; +10 years where trafficking involved). National Memorial Commission. National Memorial in London. Local memorials in all affected areas. National Day of Remembrance. Dedicated Compensation Fund (no cap). Statutory right to therapeutic support. Statutory right to legal representation. Mandatory ethnicity data collection. Criminal offence of suppressing demographic data (minimum 3 years).

Delivered operationally: Malebranche Institutional Complicity Unit within 21 days. Review of all closed investigations within 90 days. National reopening of historical cases. Victim contact programme. Interim payments of £25,000 per identified victim within 90 days. Victim Liaison Offices in all affected areas. National Memorial design competition within 90 days, completion within 24 months. Local memorials in Rotherham, Telford, Rochdale, Oxford within 18 months. Memorial programme: £50 million over 5 years. Educational curriculum module within 2 academic years. National Archive of Child Sexual Exploitation. Standardised data collection framework within 6 months. Comprehensive retrospective national analysis within 12 months.

This is not a policy document in the ordinary sense. It is an act of national repentance. For decades, the British state permitted the organised rape of its children and punished those who tried to stop it. The institutions that were supposed to protect the most vulnerable members of society instead protected themselves, their reputations, and their political comfort. The children were expendable. Progress says they were not expendable. Progress says they will be remembered. Progress says that every person who participated in their abuse, and every person who knew and did nothing, will face justice without limit of time or mercy. And Progress says that the memorials built in their honour will stand as long as the nation endures, so that no future generation can claim ignorance of what was done, what was permitted, and what it cost.

##### C5. Police Reform – Culture, Mission, Accountability

###### Governing Principle

C2 addressed the question of how many police officers Britain needs. This document addresses the question of what kind of police force Britain needs. The two questions are inseparable. Doubling the headcount of a police force that has lost its way would merely produce twice as much of the wrong thing. The expansion programme in C2.1 must be accompanied by a root-and-branch reform of police culture, training, mission, and accountability. Without that reform, the new officers will be absorbed into the same institutional dysfunction that produced the current crisis.

The current crisis is comprehensive. Public confidence in the police has collapsed. In October 2024, 52% of adults surveyed by YouGov said they had no or not very much confidence in the police to tackle crime locally, up from 39% in October 2019. The Baroness Casey Review of the Metropolitan Police (2023) found institutional racism, misogyny, and homophobia, a force that had deprioritised neighbourhood policing to the point where London “no longer has a functioning neighbourhood policing service,” and a culture in which predatory behaviour was allowed to flourish while good officers were too frightened to speak out. The HMICFRS State of Policing Report (2024–25) found that 32% of its graded judgments across all 43 forces were below “adequate.” Only approximately 11,100 officers were assigned to neighbourhood policing roles as of March 2025, just 8% of all officers. More than 50% of serving officers have fewer than 10 years’ experience.

Meanwhile, the police have been expending resources on activity that has nothing to do with crime. Over 133,000 non-crime hate incidents were recorded by 43 police forces since 2014, consuming an estimated 60,000 hours of police time annually. Officers have been sent to investigate social media posts, record the lawful speech of citizens, and enforce ideological orthodoxies that have no basis in criminal law. In 2023, 90% of all crime went unsolved. The British public is entitled to ask why officers are recording non-crimes on a database when nine out of ten actual crimes result in no charge, no prosecution, and no justice.

The root cause is a loss of mission clarity. British policing was founded on the Peelian principles: the police are the public and the public are the police; the test of police efficiency is the absence of crime and disorder, not the visible evidence of police action in dealing with it; the police must secure the willing cooperation of the public in voluntary observance of the law. These principles have been eroded by decades of institutional drift, ideological capture at senior levels, chronic underfunding of frontline functions, and a cultural aversion to confronting difficult truths about crime patterns and institutional failure (as documented in C4). Progress will restore the Peelian mission. The police exist to prevent crime, catch criminals, and keep the public safe. Everything else is a distraction.

###### C5.1: Mission Clarity and the Return to Beat Policing

The Problem

Neighbourhood policing is the foundation of the British policing model. It is the mechanism through which officers know their communities, communities know their officers, intelligence is gathered, trust is built, and crime is prevented before it occurs. The evidence is unambiguous: HMICFRS has stated that neighbourhood policing is “the most effective way to build community confidence.” The College of Policing’s evidence-based guidelines confirm that community engagement, problem identification, and targeted problem-solving are the activities with a causal effect on public confidence.

This foundation has been destroyed. Neighbourhood policing was the area that suffered most from austerity-era cuts. Forces gutted their neighbourhood teams to maintain response and investigation capacity. The Metropolitan Police reorganised 32 borough-based commands into 12 units, severing long-established community connections. Neighbourhood officers who remained were routinely abstracted to cover response shifts, a practice HMICFRS found was happening “without enough oversight or planning.” The result is that communities no longer see their police, police no longer know their communities, and the intelligence that prevents crime has dried up.

The current government’s Neighbourhood Policing Guarantee, announced in April 2025 with £200 million in funding, aims to add 13,000 policing personnel to neighbourhood roles over five years. Progress considers this wholly inadequate in scale and pace. At the current rate, forces agreed to deliver just 2,972 FTE officers and PCSOs in the first year. This is a rounding error against the scale of the problem.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Police Expansion and Reform Act (established in C2.1) will be expanded to include:

- a) A statutory minimum neighbourhood policing ratio. Every police force in England and Wales must maintain a minimum of 1 dedicated neighbourhood officer per 1,000 residents, rising to 1 per 500 in areas designated as high-crime or high-deprivation. These officers must not be abstracted to other duties except in a declared emergency. The abstraction ban will be statutory, not guidance. Forces that breach it will face mandatory HMICFRS intervention.
- b) A statutory duty of mission priority. Every police force must treat the prevention and detection of crime, and the protection of life and property, as its primary statutory duties. No officer time, budget, or resource may be allocated to activity that does not directly contribute to these duties. This provision is designed to provide a clear legal basis for the elimination of non-crime functions that have accumulated within policing over the past two decades.
- c) Abolition of the non-crime hate incident recording regime. The Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022 provisions establishing the NCHI statutory code will be repealed in their entirety. No police force will record, investigate, or retain data on any incident that does not constitute a criminal offence. All existing NCHI records will be deleted within 90 days of Royal Assent. The police will no longer function as monitors of lawful speech. Their job is to catch criminals, not to catalogue opinions.
- d) Abolition of the Macpherson perception test for hate crime recording. The current requirement that a hate crime be recorded as such if “perceived by the victim or any other person” to be motivated by hostility will be replaced with an objective evidential test. An offence will be recorded as a hate crime only where there is objective evidence of hostility as a motivating factor. Perception alone is not evidence.

OPERATIONAL

Neighbourhood policing deployment plan. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, every police force will submit a deployment plan to the Home Office demonstrating how it will meet the statutory neighbourhood policing ratio. The plan must identify the officers by name, their assigned beats, and the communities they serve. The plans will be published and the public will be able to identify their named neighbourhood officer. This is a return to the tradition of the village constable who was known by name to every household on his beat.

Beat policing infrastructure. Within 12 months, every neighbourhood policing team will operate from a physical presence point accessible to the public: a police station, a shop-front office, or a dedicated desk in a community building. The closure of local police stations, which has severed the visible connection between the police and the communities they serve, will be reversed wherever operationally feasible. Where full stations cannot be reopened, satellite offices will be established.

Named officer scheme. Every household in England and Wales will receive notification of the name and contact details of their designated neighbourhood officer within 9 months of Royal Assent. The officer will be required to make proactive contact with community leaders, schools, businesses, and residents’ associations within their beat area within their first 30 days of assignment.

###### C5.2: College of Policing Reform

The Problem

The College of Policing is the professional body for policing in England and Wales. It sets standards, develops training curricula, produces authorised professional practice, and defines the competency frameworks against which officers are assessed and promoted. If there is a single institution responsible for the culture of British policing, it is the College. And the College has failed.

Under successive leadership teams, the College has allowed its training and standards to drift away from operational policing towards an institutional preoccupation with diversity management, identity politics, and ideological compliance. Officers report that promotion boards assess candidates on their ability to articulate the language of equity, diversity, and inclusion rather than their operational competence, crime-fighting record, or leadership under pressure. Training programmes dedicate hours to unconscious bias, micro-aggressions, and intersectionality while the average new recruit receives inadequate preparation for the realities of frontline policing: violent confrontation, evidence-gathering, community engagement, and criminal investigation.

The result is a generation of officers who are fluent in the vocabulary of institutional grievance but who lack the skills, confidence, and institutional support to do the job the public actually needs them to do: prevent crime, catch criminals, and keep people safe. Senior officers who rose through this system carry its assumptions into command positions, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of institutional capture.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Police Expansion and Reform Act will additionally:

- a) Reconstitute the College of Policing under a new governance structure. The current Board will be dissolved and replaced by a Board comprising serving and retired senior officers with distinguished operational records, representatives of the public (including crime victims), and independent members with expertise in professional standards. No member of the Board will hold or have held any position in an advocacy organisation whose primary purpose is the promotion of identity-based politics.
- b) Require the College to conduct a complete curriculum review within 6 months of Royal Assent. Every training module, competency framework, and promotion criterion will be assessed against a single test: does this directly improve the ability of officers to prevent crime, detect crime, protect the public, or maintain public order? Any element that does not meet this test will be removed. The review will be conducted by a panel of operationally experienced officers and published in full.
- c) Require the College to develop and implement a new national training curriculum with a minimum allocation of 70% of training hours to operational skills: criminal law, evidence-gathering, investigative interviewing, physical fitness, self-defence, use of force, community engagement, safeguarding, and emergency response. The remaining 30% may cover professional conduct, ethics, and communications. No training hours will be allocated to ideological content.
- d) Reform the promotion framework. Promotion to sergeant, inspector, and superintendent will be determined primarily by operational competence, crime-fighting effectiveness, and leadership under pressure, assessed through practical examination and peer review. Written examinations will test legal knowledge and operational planning, not ideological fluency. The National Police Promotion Framework will be rewritten within 9 months of Royal Assent.

OPERATIONAL

Ideological audit. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Home Secretary will commission an independent audit of all College of Policing training materials, guidance documents, and authorised professional practice publications. The audit will identify every instance of ideological content, defined as content that promotes a particular political or social worldview rather than operational policing competence, and recommend its removal. The audit report will be published in full.

Training centre overhaul. The 5 regional training centres established under C2.1 for the police expansion programme will operate under the reformed curriculum from day one. Every new officer recruited under the expansion will be trained in operational policing, not institutional ideology. Existing officers will complete a mandatory refresher programme under the new curriculum within 24 months.

###### C5.3: Vetting, Standards, and the Removal of Unfit Officers

The Problem

The Casey Review found that the Metropolitan Police’s vetting system “was set up to root out those involved in organised crime, not racists, misogynists or homophobes.” The headlong rush to recruit under the Police Uplift Programme targets led to vetting shortcuts and the admission of individuals who should never have been given a warrant card. The conviction of serving officers Wayne Couzens (kidnap, rape, and murder) and David Carrick (49 offences including 24 rapes) demonstrated that the system was catastrophically broken. One in ten female officers in the Met reported being sexually harassed or assaulted by colleagues.

Simultaneously, the misconduct system is not fit for purpose. Casey found that investigations were slow, outcomes were inconsistent, and officers who should have been dismissed remained in post. The system protects officers at the expense of the public. Progress will invert that priority.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Police Expansion and Reform Act will additionally:

- a) Mandate face-to-face interviews for all police recruitment, at every stage. No candidate will be admitted to a police force without a structured, in-person interview designed to assess character, integrity, and suitability for public service. The College of Policing will develop a standardised interview framework within 6 months of Royal Assent.
- b) Require enhanced vetting checks to include a full review of social media history (5 years minimum), financial background, and character references from non-family members. Vetting will be conducted by a centralised national vetting unit, not by individual forces, to eliminate inconsistency and local pressure.
- c) Create a statutory power of summary dismissal for chief constables to dismiss any officer where there is clear evidence of criminal conduct, gross misconduct, or conduct that renders them unfit for service, without the requirement to complete a full misconduct hearing prior to removal. The officer will retain a right of appeal to a Police Appeals Tribunal, but will be removed from active duty immediately upon the exercise of the power.
- d) Establish a National Police Barred List, maintained by the College of Policing, recording every individual dismissed from any police force, together with the reason for dismissal. No individual on the barred list may be re-employed by any police force, police staff role, or private security firm providing services to police. The list will be accessible to all forces and relevant employers.
- e) Reform the misconduct system. Misconduct panels will be independently chaired, not chaired by senior officers from the same force. The standard of proof for gross misconduct will remain the balance of probabilities, but panels will be required to apply a rebuttable presumption of dismissal for any officer found to have committed sexual misconduct, domestic abuse, or discriminatory harassment. The presumption may be rebutted only by exceptional circumstances, which must be recorded in writing and published.

OPERATIONAL

Re-vetting programme. Within 12 months of Royal Assent, every serving officer recruited under the Police Uplift Programme (2019–2023) will be subject to enhanced re-vetting under the new national standards. Officers who fail the re-vetting process will be subject to accelerated misconduct proceedings. This is a direct response to the evidence that recruitment targets led to vetting shortcuts.

Integrity testing. All 43 forces will be required to implement proactive integrity testing programmes, including covert testing of officers in positions of trust. Forces that do not maintain an active integrity testing programme will face mandatory HMICFRS intervention.

###### C5.4: Political Neutrality and Operational Independence

The Problem

The British police service is required to be politically neutral. This is not a matter of convention; it is fundamental to the legitimacy of policing by consent. A police force that is perceived to enforce the law selectively, based on the political sympathies of its leadership, forfeits the consent of those it claims to serve.

That perception is now widespread. The summer of 2024 saw sustained public anger over what was perceived as two-tier policing: a perception that protests by certain groups were policed with tolerance while protests by others were met with aggressive enforcement. Whether or not the perception was objectively justified in every instance, the fact that it became a dominant public narrative demonstrates a catastrophic failure of legitimacy. A police force that has lost the trust of a substantial portion of the population it serves is a police force in crisis.

The problem extends beyond protest policing. Senior officers have publicly associated themselves with political causes, made statements on contested social and political questions, and allowed their forces to participate in political campaigns. Police forces have adopted political symbols, marched in ideological parades in uniform, and used official social media accounts to promote political positions. None of this is compatible with the principle of political neutrality. The police are not a campaigning organisation. They are a law enforcement service.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Police Expansion and Reform Act will additionally:

- a) Create a statutory duty of political neutrality for all police officers and police staff. No officer or member of police staff, while on duty or identified as a member of a police force, may express support for or opposition to any political party, campaign, ideology, or contested social or political position. Breach of this duty will be a disciplinary offence carrying a minimum sanction of written warning for a first offence and dismissal for a second.
- b) Prohibit police forces from participating in, endorsing, or displaying symbols associated with any political campaign, ideology, or contested social cause. Police vehicles, uniforms, buildings, and official communications will display only the force crest and operational information. The use of police resources for political messaging is a misuse of public funds and a betrayal of neutrality.
- c) Require that all public order policing be conducted according to a published, standardised national protocol. The protocol will specify the thresholds for intervention, the escalation procedures, and the use-of-force rules that apply to all public assemblies, protests, and demonstrations, regardless of the cause being advanced. The protocol must be applied consistently. Any chief constable who directs differential enforcement based on the political character of a protest will be guilty of misconduct in public office.

OPERATIONAL

Social media audit. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, every police force will conduct an audit of its official social media output over the preceding 3 years. All posts that constitute political commentary, ideological advocacy, or participation in social campaigns unrelated to crime prevention will be removed. The audit results will be submitted to the Home Office.

Public order training. All officers deployed to public order duties will complete mandatory training under the new national protocol within 6 months. The training will emphasise consistent enforcement, proportionality, and the absolute requirement for political neutrality in operational decisions.

###### C5.5: Accountability, Governance, and IOPC Reform

The Problem

The accountability architecture for policing in England and Wales is fragmented, slow, and ineffective. Police and Crime Commissioners (PCCs) were introduced in 2012 to provide democratic oversight but have become, in many areas, an additional layer of bureaucracy with limited practical impact on policing outcomes. The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) investigates complaints and misconduct referrals but is chronically slow: investigations routinely take years, during which officers remain in post and public confidence erodes further. HMICFRS inspects forces and publishes reports, but its intervention powers are limited and its recommendations are advisory. The result is that nobody effectively holds the police to account in real time.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Police Expansion and Reform Act will additionally:

- a) Strengthen HMICFRS intervention powers. Where HMICFRS rates a force as “inadequate” in any graded judgment, or where a force fails to meet the statutory neighbourhood policing ratio, HMICFRS will have a statutory power to direct the force to take specified remedial action within a defined timetable. Failure to comply will trigger the power of the Home Secretary to place the force under special measures, including the appointment of an external management team.
- b) Reform the IOPC. Investigations into serious misconduct must be completed within 12 months. Where an investigation exceeds 12 months, the IOPC Director General must provide a written explanation to the Home Secretary and to the complainant, published in full. The IOPC will be given power to direct the immediate suspension of any officer under investigation for a criminal offence. Current average investigation timelines of multiple years are unacceptable.
- c) Strengthen PCC accountability. PCCs will be required to publish quarterly performance reports against a standardised set of metrics: crime rates by category, charge rates, response times, neighbourhood policing ratios, public confidence scores, and complaint outcomes. These reports will be compiled by HMICFRS from force data, not by the PCC’s office, to ensure independence. Where a PCC fails to hold a force to account for persistent underperformance, the Home Secretary will have power to direct the PCC to take specified action.
- d) Create a statutory right for crime victims to request an independent review of any police decision not to investigate, not to charge, or to close an investigation. The review will be conducted by a body independent of the force and the PCC. Where the review finds the decision was unreasonable, the force will be required to reopen the investigation. This ensures that victims are not left without recourse when the police fail them.

OPERATIONAL

Force performance dashboard. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, HMICFRS will publish a real-time, publicly accessible online dashboard for every police force in England and Wales. The dashboard will display: total recorded crime, charge rate, average response times for emergency and priority calls, neighbourhood policing ratio, public confidence scores, outstanding warrant count, and misconduct case outcomes. The data will be updated monthly. The public has a right to know, in plain terms, whether their police force is doing its job.

Annual Chief Constable accountability hearing. Every chief constable will be required to appear before a public hearing, chaired by the PCC and attended by elected local representatives, at which they will account for their force’s performance against the published metrics. The hearing will be broadcast live. This is not a new concept; it is a restoration of the principle that the police serve the public and must account to the public for how they discharge that duty.

###### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The C5 framework is built on the Police Expansion and Reform Act (already established in C2.1), expanded with additional provisions. No new primary legislation is required beyond the Act already introduced. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, or departmental action.

###### Police Expansion and Reform Act (expanded provisions)

On the face of the Act: Statutory neighbourhood policing ratio (1 per 1,000 residents, 1 per 500 in high-crime areas) with statutory abstraction ban. Statutory duty of mission priority. Abolition of NCHI recording regime and repeal of enabling provisions. Replacement of Macpherson perception test with objective evidential test for hate crime recording. College of Policing reconstituted under new governance. Mandatory curriculum review with 70% operational skills minimum. Promotion framework reform. Mandatory face-to-face recruitment interviews. Centralised national vetting unit. Summary dismissal power for chief constables. National Police Barred List. Reformed misconduct panels with independently chaired hearings and rebuttable presumption of dismissal for sexual misconduct. Statutory duty of political neutrality. Prohibition on political symbols and messaging. Standardised national public order protocol. Strengthened HMICFRS intervention powers. IOPC 12-month investigation deadline. PCC quarterly performance reporting. Statutory right for victims to request independent review of police decisions.

Delivered operationally: Force deployment plans within 6 months. Beat policing infrastructure (physical presence points) within 12 months. Named officer scheme (every household notified) within 9 months. Ideological audit of College of Policing materials within 90 days. Reformed curriculum in all 5 regional training centres from day one. Re-vetting of all Police Uplift Programme recruits within 12 months. Proactive integrity testing in all 43 forces. Social media audit within 90 days. Public order training under new protocol within 6 months. Real-time force performance dashboard within 6 months. Annual chief constable public accountability hearings.

C2 gave Britain the officers. C5 gives Britain the police force those officers must belong to. A police force that knows its communities by name, that prioritises the prevention and detection of crime above all else, that is trained in operational competence rather than ideological compliance, that is held to account transparently and in public, and that maintains absolute political neutrality in all circumstances. This is not a radical proposition. It is a return to the founding principles of British policing. The public has been waiting for it for a very long time. Progress will deliver it.

##### C6. One Law for All

###### Governing Principle

The rule of law means one law, applied equally to all citizens, in all communities, without exception. This is not a cultural preference. It is the foundational principle upon which every other civil liberty depends. The moment a state permits the emergence of parallel legal systems, operating according to different rules, applying different standards, and producing different outcomes for different communities, it has abandoned the principle of legal equality. It has created first-class and second-class citizens, distinguished not by their conduct but by the community into which they were born.

Britain has permitted this to happen. An estimated 85 Sharia councils now operate across England and Wales, issuing religious rulings on marriage, divorce, inheritance, and family disputes. They are not courts of law; they have no formal legal standing; their rulings are technically non-binding. But this technical distinction is meaningless to the women whose lives they govern. An estimated 60–80% of Muslim marriages in the UK are unregistered nikah-only ceremonies, leaving over 100,000 women in marriages that British law does not recognise and cannot protect. These women cannot petition for divorce in English courts, cannot claim financial provision under matrimonial law, have no automatic inheritance rights, no pension entitlements, and no next-of-kin status. When their marriages break down, they must seek a religious divorce from a Sharia council, where proceedings are conducted by panels of almost exclusively male Islamic scholars, where women’s testimony is given lesser weight than men’s, where men can unilaterally divorce by pronouncing talaq while women must petition and justify their case, and where outcomes frequently disadvantage the wife.

The 2018 independent review led by Professor Mona Siddiqui found evidence of discriminatory practice and acknowledged that some councils displayed poor conduct. The government rejected the review’s recommendation for a regulatory framework on the grounds that it might “legitimise an alternative legal system.” It has done nothing since. The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe passed a resolution in 2019 calling on the UK to require civil registration of all Muslim marriages. The government has not acted. Meanwhile, the National Secular Society has warned that these councils “undermine the principle of one law for all,” and Baroness Cox has noted that “the power of Sharia councils lies in how they are perceived by their communities”: whatever the strict legal position, for the women inside these systems, the councils function as courts, their rulings carry the weight of community authority, and refusal to comply carries the threat of social exile.

The same failure of legal universality is visible in the state’s catastrophic failure to enforce laws against harmful cultural practices. Female genital mutilation has been a criminal offence since the Prohibition of Female Circumcision Act 1985. Forty years of criminalisation. An estimated 137,000 women and girls in England and Wales living with the consequences of FGM. An estimated 6,000 new cases annually. The NHS identified over 20,000 affected women between 2015 and 2019 alone. And in four decades, the UK has secured precisely three convictions. Three. France, by comparison, prosecuted over 100 parents and practitioners in more than 40 criminal cases by 2014. Honour-based abuse offences recorded by police totalled 2,949 in the year ending March 2025. Police recorded 109 FGM offences and 125 forced marriage offences in the same period. The Forced Marriage Unit handled 812 contacts in 2024 but, since the enactment of forced marriage legislation, only five convictions have been secured nationally. Over 90% of reported cases fail to proceed to investigation or conviction.

These are not failures of law. The law exists. These are failures of enforcement, driven by institutional cowardice, cultural sensitivity elevated above legal obligation, and a political establishment that would rather tolerate the abuse of women and girls within minority communities than face the accusation of cultural insensitivity. C4 documented this dynamic in the grooming gang scandal. C6 addresses it as a systemic principle. The law of England and Wales applies to every person within its jurisdiction. Where it does not, in practice, apply equally, the state has failed in its most basic duty. Progress will end that failure.

###### C6.1: Abolition of Quasi-Judicial Religious Tribunals

The Problem

Sharia councils are described by their defenders as voluntary mediation services, comparable to Jewish Batei Din or Catholic marriage tribunals. This comparison obscures a critical difference of scale and effect. There are an estimated 85 Sharia councils operating across England and Wales, many attached to mosques, some operating as standalone organisations. They handle principally marriage and divorce cases. The demand for their services is driven by the prevalence of unregistered Islamic marriages: because nikah-only ceremonies are not recognised under English law, civil divorce is unavailable, and women must obtain a religious divorce through a council. This creates a closed system in which women are channelled into a religious adjudication process because the state has failed to ensure that their marriages were legally registered in the first place.

The Arbitration Act 1996 permits parties to agree to resolve certain civil disputes through arbitration, including according to religious principles, provided the outcome does not conflict with English law. The Muslim Arbitration Tribunal operates under this framework. But the Act was designed for commercial disputes between parties of equal bargaining power, not for family law disputes in which one party may be subject to intense community and familial pressure. The 2018 Siddiqui Review acknowledged that some women were pressured into accepting council rulings and that councils operated without adequate oversight. Campaigners have documented cases of women being told to return to abusive husbands, religious texts being used to justify male control, and councils advising anger management rather than criminal prosecution for domestic violence.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Legal Equality Act will:

- a) Prohibit any body, council, tribunal, or organisation from adjudicating on matters of family law, including marriage, divorce, child custody, inheritance, or domestic disputes, unless it is constituted as a court or tribunal under the law of England and Wales, or is operating as a formally regulated mediation service under the oversight of the Family Mediation Council. This prohibition applies regardless of whether the body describes itself as advisory, voluntary, or non-binding. A body that receives applications for divorce, hears evidence from parties, and issues determinations is performing a judicial function. It will be regulated as such or it will cease to operate.
- b) Amend the Arbitration Act 1996 to exclude all matters of family law, child welfare, and matrimonial property from the scope of religious arbitration. No religious arbitration body may issue a determination on any matter that falls within the jurisdiction of the family courts. This removes the legal mechanism by which religious tribunals currently claim binding authority over family disputes.
- c) Create a criminal offence of operating an unregulated quasi-judicial tribunal. Any person who establishes, operates, or participates in the operation of a body that purports to adjudicate on matters of family law outside the regulated framework commits an offence. Maximum sentence: 5 years. Any person who coerces, pressures, or intimidates another person into submitting to the jurisdiction of such a body commits an offence. Maximum sentence: 7 years. This captures both the operators and those who use community pressure to compel compliance.
- d) Permit religious bodies to provide spiritual guidance, pastoral counselling, and voluntary mediation on matters of religious conscience, provided they: (i) do not purport to issue binding or authoritative determinations on legal rights; (ii) display prominently a statutory notice, in English and the relevant community language, stating that the body has no legal authority and that participants have the right to seek legal advice and access the civil courts; (iii) are registered with the Family Mediation Council if they offer mediation services; and (iv) report to the relevant authorities any disclosure of domestic abuse, forced marriage, or child protection concerns, in accordance with the same mandatory reporting duties that apply to all professionals. Freedom of religion is not at issue. The freedom to operate a parallel legal system that disadvantages women is.

OPERATIONAL

Regulatory transition. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, the Ministry of Justice will publish guidance specifying what activities constitute prohibited quasi-judicial functions and what activities are permissible religious guidance. Existing Sharia councils, Batei Din, and any other religious tribunal that handles family matters will have 12 months to either register as regulated mediation services or cease adjudicating on family law. Bodies that fail to comply will be referred to the Crown Prosecution Service.

National awareness campaign. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the government will fund a national awareness campaign, delivered in partnership with women’s organisations including those serving Muslim, Jewish, and other faith communities, informing women of their legal rights under English law, the availability of the civil courts, and the prohibition on unregulated religious adjudication. The campaign will be delivered in community languages and through community organisations.

###### C6.2: Mandatory Civil Registration of All Marriages

The Problem

The Marriage Act 1949 does not require that religious marriage ceremonies be accompanied by civil registration. Anglican and Jewish marriages are automatically registered because their officiants are authorised to register marriages. Marriages in registered buildings or in the presence of a registrar are similarly registered. But Islamic nikah ceremonies conducted in unregistered buildings, without a registrar present, produce no legal marriage. The same applies to certain Hindu, Sikh, and other religious ceremonies. The result is that hundreds of thousands of people, predominantly women, are in relationships they believe to be marriages but which English law treats as cohabitation, providing virtually none of the legal protections of marriage.

The Register Our Marriage campaign, founded by solicitor Aina Khan, has estimated that over 80% of Muslim nikah ceremonies are unregistered. This is not a marginal problem. It is a systemic failure affecting a substantial population, leaving women without property rights, inheritance rights, pension entitlements, or access to matrimonial remedies on relationship breakdown. The Court of Appeal in Akhter v Khan (2020) confirmed that an unregistered nikah ceremony is a “non-marriage,” not even a void marriage, meaning the wife had no access whatsoever to financial remedies. The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe called in 2019 for the UK to require civil registration of Islamic marriages. The government has been “considering” reform since 2018.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Legal Equality Act will additionally:

- a) Require that all marriages conducted in England and Wales, regardless of the faith or tradition under which the ceremony is performed, be accompanied by civil registration to be legally recognised. No religious ceremony of marriage will have legal effect unless and until the marriage is registered under the civil law. This will be achieved by amending the Marriage Act 1949 to extend the registration requirement to all religious ceremonies without exception.
- b) Create a statutory duty on any person who officiates a religious marriage ceremony to inform both parties, in writing and in a language they understand, that the ceremony does not create a legal marriage unless civil registration is completed. Failure to provide this notice will be a criminal offence, carrying a maximum sentence of 2 years. This duty will apply to imams, priests, rabbis, pandits, and all other religious officiants equally.
- c) Create a criminal offence of conducting a religious marriage ceremony for any party who is already legally married to another person, or for any party who is below the legal age of marriage. Maximum sentence: 5 years. This addresses the documented practice of polygamous marriages being facilitated through unregistered religious ceremonies.
- d) Provide that where a couple has undergone a religious ceremony of marriage and has cohabited for a continuous period of 2 or more years, but has not civilly registered the marriage, the court may, on application by either party on the breakdown of the relationship, treat the parties as if they were married for the purposes of financial remedies. This transitional provision protects women who are currently in unregistered marriages from the consequences of non-registration, while the new mandatory registration regime takes effect.

OPERATIONAL

Registration infrastructure. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, the General Register Office will establish a programme to enable civil registration to take place at or immediately following religious ceremonies. This may include: authorising additional religious buildings for marriage registration, training religious officiants as authorised persons where appropriate, and making registrars available to attend religious ceremonies. The purpose is to make compliance as straightforward as possible.

Community engagement. The government will work with faith community leaders to communicate the new requirement and to facilitate compliance. The emphasis will be on protection: the purpose of mandatory registration is to ensure that every person who enters a marriage in good faith receives the legal protections they are entitled to. This is a measure that protects women. Religious leaders who genuinely care for the welfare of their congregants will welcome it.

###### C6.3: Enforcement of Laws Against Harmful Cultural Practices

The Problem

Britain has legislated comprehensively against harmful cultural practices. FGM has been criminal since 1985, with penalties increased to 14 years in 2003, extraterritorial jurisdiction added, a mandatory reporting duty introduced in 2015, and FGM Protection Orders available since the same year. Forced marriage became a criminal offence in 2014, with Forced Marriage Protection Orders available since 2008. Honour-based abuse encompasses multiple existing criminal offences including assault, coercive control, harassment, kidnap, and murder.

The legislation is extensive. The enforcement is a disgrace. FGM: criminalised for 40 years, an estimated 137,000 women affected, 6,000 new cases annually, the NHS identifying over 20,000 affected women between 2015 and 2019, and three criminal convictions in the entire history of the legislation. The first successful prosecution did not occur until 2019, thirty-four years after criminalisation. The first conspiracy conviction came in 2024. France, operating under comparable legislation, has secured over 100 prosecutions. Forced marriage: criminalised since 2014, the Forced Marriage Unit handling over 800 cases annually, and five convictions nationally. The investigator who led the first forced marriage conviction in England reports that over 90% of cases fail to proceed. Honour-based abuse: 2,949 offences recorded in the year ending March 2025, with no reliable data on prosecution or conviction rates, and a recognised pattern of victims waiting an average of five years before reporting.

The gap between legislation and enforcement is not a resource problem. It is a cultural problem within institutions. Police officers lack specialist training. CPS prosecutors lack confidence in pursuing cases. Judges lack familiarity with the dynamics of honour-based offending. And throughout the system, there is an institutional reluctance to pursue cases aggressively within minority communities, born of the same misplaced cultural sensitivity that C4 documented in the grooming gang scandal. The law is clear. The institutions charged with enforcing it have been unwilling to do so. Progress will remove their discretion.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Legal Equality Act will additionally:

- a) Create a statutory duty on all police forces to investigate every reported instance of FGM, forced marriage, and honour-based abuse to the fullest extent. The duty will be enforceable: a force that fails to investigate a reported case, or that closes an investigation without adequate justification, will be liable to mandatory intervention by HMICFRS. The Chief Inspector will publish an annual assessment of each force’s compliance.
- b) Require the CPS to publish annual statistics on charging decisions, prosecution outcomes, and conviction rates for FGM, forced marriage, and honour-based abuse, disaggregated by police force area. The data will be published alongside comparable figures from France, the Netherlands, and other jurisdictions to establish an international benchmark. Three convictions for FGM in 40 years is not enforcement. It is abdication.
- c) Introduce mandatory minimum sentences for FGM: 7 years for performing FGM; 5 years for arranging, aiding, or abetting FGM; 3 years for failing to protect a girl from FGM. Current maxima of 14 years are meaningless when the offence is almost never prosecuted. Mandatory minimums signal that the state treats this as a serious crime and will punish it accordingly.
- d) Make honour-based abuse a standalone criminal offence. At present, honour-based abuse is a label applied to existing offences such as assault, coercive control, and harassment. Creating a distinct offence will: improve recording and data quality; enable targeted prosecution guidance; establish clear sentencing guidelines with a minimum sentence of 3 years; and send an unequivocal signal that the British legal system does not recognise “honour” as a mitigating factor for violence. It is an aggravating factor.
- e) Extend mandatory reporting duties for FGM and forced marriage to all public-facing professionals, including housing officers, benefits advisors, immigration caseworkers, and community interpreters. The current duty covers health professionals, social workers, and teachers. This is insufficient. Extend it to every professional who has contact with at-risk individuals.

OPERATIONAL

Specialist enforcement capacity. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, every police force will be required to maintain a dedicated harmful practices investigation team, or to participate in a regional team shared with neighbouring forces. Team members will receive mandatory specialist training developed by the College of Policing in partnership with survivor organisations and specialist charities including Karma Nirvana, IKWRO, Southall Black Sisters, and FORWARD. The training will cover FGM identification, forced marriage dynamics, honour-based abuse patterns, evidence-gathering in community contexts, and working with vulnerable and isolated victims.

FGM prosecution task force.
