Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the CPS will establish a national FGM prosecution task force, comprising specialist prosecutors with experience in complex safeguarding cases, to review all FGM referrals, reopen cases that were previously declined for prosecution, and develop a national prosecution strategy. The task force will report directly to the Director of Public Prosecutions. Target: a tenfold increase in FGM prosecutions within 3 years.

Border awareness programme. Border Force will implement enhanced monitoring at airports and ports during school holiday periods, the period of peak risk for FGM and forced marriage travel. This will include targeted questioning of families travelling with girls to high-risk countries, distribution of awareness materials in community languages, and mandatory recording of welfare concerns. Where a child is identified as at risk, FGM or Forced Marriage Protection Orders will be sought before the family departs.

###### C6.4: Countering Community Segregation and Institutional Parallelism

The Problem

Parallel legal systems do not emerge in a vacuum. They are the product of communities that have developed, or have been permitted to develop, institutional structures that operate independently of the national framework. Where communities maintain their own dispute resolution mechanisms, their own welfare networks, their own educational institutions, and their own codes of conduct, enforced through social pressure rather than law, the conditions are created in which illegal practices can persist unchallenged and victims have no effective access to the protections of the national legal system.

The Louise Casey Review into integration (2016) warned of communities in which “some women born in the UK are living in regressive, segregated, and isolated circumstances” and where “social and economic isolation of particular groups has contributed to a sense that some communities are operating to a different set of rules.” This is not a commentary on any single community. It is a structural observation: wherever institutions develop that duplicate or supplant the functions of the state, the universality of law is weakened.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Legal Equality Act will additionally:

- a) Create a statutory duty on local authorities to identify and report to the Home Office any institution, organisation, or body operating within their area that performs functions analogous to those of the state’s legal, welfare, or child protection systems, outside the regulated framework. This includes unregistered dispute resolution bodies, informal welfare distribution networks that condition support on compliance with community norms, and educational institutions that teach content incompatible with the values of the national curriculum.
- b) Strengthen the regulation of supplementary schools and out-of-hours education settings. All such settings providing more than 6 hours per week of instruction to children must register with the Department for Education and submit to inspection. Settings that teach content promoting gender inequality, religious supremacism, or hostility towards British law and institutions will be closed.
- c) Create a statutory right for any individual to access the civil courts, legal advice, and state protection services without the consent or knowledge of any community leader, family elder, or religious authority. It will be a criminal offence, carrying a minimum sentence of 2 years, for any person to obstruct, discourage, or prevent another person from accessing the civil legal system, the police, or social services. This provision addresses the documented pattern of community gatekeeping that prevents vulnerable individuals from seeking help outside their community.

OPERATIONAL

Integration audit. Within 12 months of Royal Assent, the Home Office will commission a comprehensive audit of institutional parallelism in England and Wales, identifying areas where parallel governance structures exist, assessing the impact on legal equality and the protection of vulnerable individuals, and making recommendations for further action. The audit will be conducted independently and published in full.

Legal access points. In areas identified as having significant populations of women in unregistered marriages or communities with high rates of honour-based abuse, the government will fund dedicated Legal Access Centres, staffed by qualified lawyers and support workers, providing free, confidential legal advice in community languages. The centres will be located in accessible public buildings, not in community-specific venues, to ensure that access does not require community mediation.

###### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The C6 framework is built on a single piece of primary legislation: the Legal Equality Act. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, or departmental action.

###### Legal Equality Act

On the face of the Act: Prohibition on unregulated quasi-judicial tribunals adjudicating on family law. Amendment to Arbitration Act 1996 excluding family law from religious arbitration. Criminal offence of operating an unregulated tribunal (maximum 5 years) and of coercing submission to one (maximum 7 years). Regulated pathway for religious bodies providing spiritual guidance with mandatory statutory notice, registration, and reporting duties. Mandatory civil registration for all marriages regardless of faith tradition. Criminal offence of failing to inform parties that religious ceremony has no legal effect (maximum 2 years). Criminal offence of conducting religious ceremony for already-married or underage parties (maximum 5 years). Transitional provision treating long-term unregistered cohabitation as marriage for financial remedies. Statutory duty on police to investigate all reported FGM, forced marriage, and honour-based abuse. Mandatory CPS publication of prosecution data with international benchmarks. Mandatory minimum sentences for FGM (7 years performing; 5 years arranging; 3 years failing to protect). Honour-based abuse as standalone criminal offence with minimum 3 years. Extended mandatory reporting duties. Statutory duty on local authorities to report institutional parallelism. Regulation of supplementary schools (6+ hours weekly). Statutory right of access to civil legal system with criminal offence of community gatekeeping (minimum 2 years).

Delivered operationally: Regulatory guidance and 12-month transition period for existing religious tribunals. National awareness campaign within 90 days. Registration infrastructure for civil registration at religious ceremonies within 6 months. Community engagement programme. Specialist harmful practices investigation teams in all 43 forces within 6 months. CPS national FGM prosecution task force within 90 days. Border Force holiday monitoring programme. Integration audit within 12 months. Legal Access Centres in high-need areas.

The principle could not be simpler: one country, one law. Every person in England and Wales is entitled to the same legal protections, the same access to justice, the same rights on the breakdown of a marriage, and the same enforcement of the criminal law, regardless of the community into which they were born, the faith they profess, or the traditions they follow. For decades, Britain has failed this test. Women have been trapped in unrecognised marriages, subjected to unregulated adjudication, mutilated, forced into unions against their will, and controlled through violence justified as honour, while the state has looked away because enforcement was culturally inconvenient. The law was on the statute book. The political will to enforce it was not. Progress will supply the will. The Legal Equality Act will ensure that the law of England and Wales is not merely written. It is enforced. Everywhere. For everyone. Without exception.

##### C7. Judicial Reform

###### Governing Principle

The judiciary is not a policy-making body. It does not have a democratic mandate. It does not answer to the electorate. It cannot be voted out of office. Its legitimacy derives entirely from its role as an impartial interpreter and applier of law made by Parliament. When courts confine themselves to this role, they are the guarantor of the rule of law. When they exceed it, they become a threat to democratic self-governance. Both things can be true simultaneously, and both things are currently true in Britain.

The British court system is in crisis. The Crown Court backlog reached 76,957 cases by the end of March 2025, an 11% increase on the previous year, with over 19,000 cases outstanding for more than a year. The backlog has doubled since 2019, when it stood at approximately 33,000. Median waiting times for defendants entering a not guilty plea reached 44.7 weeks. Some trials are now being listed for 2027. In September 2024, 11,574 open sexual offence cases were waiting in the Crown Court, including 3,291 adult rape cases. Public funding for justice declined by 22.4% in real per-person terms between 2010 and 2023. The government’s response has been to increase sitting days to 110,000 for 2025/26, but the National Audit Office, the Institute for Fiscal Studies, and the Public Accounts Committee have all concluded that the backlog continues to grow because the volume of cases entering the system routinely exceeds disposals. The courts are not keeping pace. Meanwhile, the 2024 UK Judicial Attitude Survey found that 39% of salaried judges intend to leave the judiciary within the next five years, up from 23% in 2014. There are approximately 2,000 salaried judges in England and Wales. Britain is haemorrhaging judicial capacity at the precise moment it needs more of it.

At the same time, serious questions about the constitutional role of the judiciary remain unresolved. The Miller II prorogation judgment (2019), in which the Supreme Court invalidated the Prime Minister’s advice to the Queen to prorogue Parliament, was described by Oxford legal scholar John Finnis as ignoring “most of the immediately relevant statutory and political constraints.” The expansion of judicial review from roughly 500 applications per year in the 1980s to over 15,000 by the 2010s has created what critics describe as a judicialisation of political decision-making. The Human Rights Act 1998 and the European Convention on Human Rights have expanded the interpretive power of courts to the point where Parliament passes legislation and judges, through declarations of incompatibility and creative interpretation, determine its effective scope. The ECHR’s Rule 39 interim measures, most prominently the last-minute injunction that grounded the first Rwanda deportation flight in June 2022, demonstrated the capacity of an international court to override the expressed will of Parliament, government, and the domestic judiciary simultaneously.

C2 addressed the human rights framework through the British Bill of Rights Act, replacing the HRA and recalibrating the relationship between Strasbourg and Westminster. C7 addresses the domestic judicial architecture: the capacity crisis, the appointment system, the constitutional boundaries of judicial power, and the transparency of sentencing. The objective is a judiciary that is adequately resourced, efficiently managed, constitutionally constrained, democratically accountable through Parliament, and trusted by the public it serves. At present, Britain has a judiciary that is none of these things.

###### C7.1: Court Capacity and the Elimination of the Backlog

The Problem

The Crown Court backlog is not merely a logistical inconvenience. It is a systemic failure of justice. Victims of rape are waiting years for their cases to be heard. Witnesses’ memories degrade. Defendants spend extended periods on remand or on bail with their lives suspended. In Essex, 20% of cases are stopped after charge because victims withdraw their support. The Public Accounts Committee found that cases that were ready to be heard were being pushed back to 2026 or 2027 because the Ministry of Justice refused to fund maximum capacity. The Institute for Fiscal Studies found that court productivity has fallen: the number of case disposals per sitting day has declined, meaning the system processes fewer cases per unit of resource than before the pandemic, even as average case complexity has also fallen. The courts are simultaneously less productive and more backlogged than at any point in modern history.

The magistrates’ courts are similarly strained, with a backlog of 310,304 cases as of March 2025. The family courts face delays of months for hearings involving child welfare. The entire justice infrastructure is buckling under the combined weight of chronic underfunding, court closures, insufficient judicial capacity, and a Treasury that treats justice as a discretionary expense rather than a foundational public service. C2 addresses the police and CPS capacity to put criminals before the courts. C7.1 ensures that when they arrive, the courts are capable of hearing their cases.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Courts and Justice Act will:

- a) Establish a statutory minimum court capacity guarantee. The Lord Chancellor will be required by statute to fund sufficient sitting days to ensure that the Crown Court disposes of at least as many cases as it receives in any given financial year. This is the baseline condition for preventing the backlog from growing. It is not ambitious. It is the definition of a functioning court system. The current approach, in which the Treasury allocates an arbitrary number of sitting days unrelated to demand, will be replaced by a statutory demand-led funding model.
- b) Require the construction or recommissioning of additional court capacity sufficient to eliminate the existing backlog within 3 years of Royal Assent. The National Audit Office estimated that even at record sitting-day allocations, the backlog would continue to grow indefinitely. Progress rejects this trajectory. The Act will mandate the Ministry of Justice to produce, within 90 days, a Court Capacity Restoration Plan identifying the number of additional courtrooms, judges, court staff, and sitting days required to clear the backlog to below 40,000 cases within 36 months. Funding will be ring-fenced.
- c) Expand magistrates’ sentencing powers permanently to 12 months for a single either-way offence, reducing the volume of cases sent to the Crown Court for sentencing. This was temporarily implemented but must be made permanent and extended. Cases sent to the Crown Court solely for sentencing now constitute over a third of all Crown Court cases despite accounting for only 10% of court time. Reducing this flow will free significant capacity for trials.
- d) Establish a statutory duty on HMCTS to maintain and publish real-time data on court utilisation, including the number of courtrooms available, the number sitting on any given day, and the reasons for any unused capacity. Reports that the Old Bailey was operating only 8 of 20 courtrooms, and Snaresbrook only 15 of 20, indicate systemic underutilisation. Every closed courtroom in a backlog crisis is an act of institutional negligence. It will be reported, explained, and remedied.

OPERATIONAL

Emergency sitting programme. Within 30 days of Royal Assent, the Lord Chancellor will authorise an emergency sitting programme, deploying all available recorders and deputy judges to maximise courtroom utilisation. Marginal costs are low: a recorder’s daily fee is approximately £800. Ten additional recorders per day, sitting across available courts, would process an estimated 50 additional cases per day for under £10,000. The programme will continue until the backlog falls below the statutory target.

Court recommissioning. HMCTS will conduct a national audit of all court buildings closed since 2010 and identify those that can be recommissioned at lowest cost and shortest lead time. Where buildings have been sold, alternative premises will be identified. Temporary court facilities, including the Nightingale court model used during the pandemic, will be deployed in areas of greatest need. The first additional courts will be operational within 6 months.

Digital case management. HMCTS will implement a national digital case management system standardised across all Crown Court centres within 12 months. The system will automate listing, track case readiness, identify and escalate ineffective trials before they consume court time, and enable pre-trial hearings to be conducted remotely where appropriate. The 2025 data shows 1,441 trials were cancelled in 2023 alone. Every ineffective trial wastes an entire day of court capacity that cannot be recovered.

###### C7.2: Judicial Recruitment, Retention, and Capacity

The Problem

The 2024 UK Judicial Attitude Survey, conducted by Professor Cheryl Thomas KC of UCL, found that 681 salaried judges, representing 39% of the total, intend to leave the judiciary within five years. This is nearly double the 23% recorded in 2014. Judges reported extreme pressure, high workloads, unacceptable building conditions, insufficient administrative support, and growing concerns for their personal safety. Criminal legal aid fees had fallen by one-third in real terms between 2008 and 2021. The Bar Council has documented poor remuneration, lower wellbeing, and lower earnings for criminal barristers compared to other areas of practice. The pipeline into the judiciary passes through the criminal bar, and the criminal bar is haemorrhaging talent.

The Judicial Appointments Commission processes applications for judicial roles but operates within a system that does not recruit at the pace required by the backlog crisis. Court capacity is constrained not only by physical courtrooms and sitting days but by the availability of judges to sit in them. A courtroom without a judge is as useless as a courtroom that has been closed. The recruitment and retention crisis is, therefore, directly connected to the backlog crisis: even if every courtroom in England and Wales were open, there would not be enough judges to sit in them.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Courts and Justice Act will additionally:

- a) Mandate an immediate increase in judicial pay to reflect the responsibilities and pressures of the role and to close the gap with equivalent private-sector legal earnings. The Act will require the Lord Chancellor to implement the Senior Salaries Review Body’s recommendations in full, without delay or modification, and to commission an independent review of judicial remuneration benchmarked against comparable common-law jurisdictions. Judges who feel they are being driven out by inadequate pay are judges the system cannot afford to lose.
- b) Expand the pool of eligible judicial candidates by broadening the routes to judicial appointment. Solicitors, legal academics with substantial practice experience, and CILEX Fellows will be actively recruited alongside barristers. The Judicial Appointments Commission will be required to set annual recruitment targets aligned with the Court Capacity Restoration Plan, and to report publicly on its performance against those targets.
- c) Create a new tier of full-time criminal court judges, sitting below circuit judge level, dedicated exclusively to the hearing of either-way criminal cases. These judges will handle the high-volume, moderate-complexity caseload that currently overwhelms the Crown Court. Recruitment will target experienced criminal practitioners with a minimum of 10 years post-qualification experience. The first cohort of 200 judges will be recruited within 12 months of Royal Assent.
- d) Establish a statutory duty on the Ministry of Justice to maintain court buildings at a standard fit for the administration of justice. The Judicial Attitude Survey documented widespread complaints about building conditions. A court that is physically degraded degrades confidence in the system it houses. Ring-fenced capital funding will be provided for the refurbishment or replacement of the worst-affected court buildings, prioritised by the severity of deficiency and the volume of cases processed.

OPERATIONAL

Criminal legal aid uplift. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Ministry of Justice will implement a further increase in criminal legal aid fees, targeting a total real-terms restoration to 2008 levels. The criminal bar is the nursery of the criminal judiciary. If criminal barristers cannot sustain a career, the judiciary will not be able to recruit from among them. This is not a subsidy. It is infrastructure investment.

Judicial welfare and security. Within 6 months, the Judicial Office will implement enhanced security provisions for judges, including improved court security, guidance on personal safety, and a dedicated judicial welfare service providing confidential support for judges experiencing stress, threats, or the effects of exposure to traumatic case material. Judges who are afraid or exhausted cannot deliver justice.

###### C7.3: Reaffirmation of Parliamentary Sovereignty

The Problem

The doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty is the foundational constitutional principle of the United Kingdom. Parliament can make or unmake any law whatsoever. No court may strike down an Act of Parliament. No body or person has the right to override or set aside the legislation of Parliament. This was the settled understanding for centuries. It has been progressively eroded.

The erosion has occurred through multiple channels. The Human Rights Act 1998, while technically preserving parliamentary sovereignty through the mechanism of declarations of incompatibility rather than strike-down power, created an expectation that Parliament would amend legislation found incompatible with Convention rights, and gave courts the power under Section 3 to interpret legislation “so far as possible” in conformity with the Convention, even where such interpretation departs from the ordinary meaning of the statutory text. The expansion of judicial review from a narrow supervisory jurisdiction into a broad mechanism for challenging the substance, as well as the legality, of government decisions has transferred significant policy-making power from the executive and legislature to the judiciary. The Supreme Court’s judgment in Miller II, in which 11 justices unanimously ruled the prorogation of Parliament unlawful on grounds that had no clear basis in prior authority, represented, in the view of many constitutional scholars and practitioners, a court exercising political judgment under the guise of legal reasoning.

The European Court of Human Rights has added an external dimension. The ECHR’s Rule 39 interim measures, though technically temporary, have in practice been used to override the expressed will of the UK Parliament and government. The June 2022 Rwanda injunction, issued at the last minute by a single Strasbourg judge, grounded a deportation flight that had been authorised by Parliament through primary legislation, approved by the domestic courts, and operationally prepared by the executive. Since 2017, the ECHR has received 660 requests for interim measures in UK cases, of which it granted 15. The power to halt government action at the stroke of a pen, with no democratic mandate, no accountability to the British electorate, and no requirement to explain the legal reasoning in advance, is incompatible with democratic self-governance.

C2’s British Bill of Rights Act addresses the ECHR dimension by replacing the HRA, restoring UK courts as the final authority on Convention rights within British jurisdiction, and empowering ministers to disregard Rule 39 measures. C7.3 addresses the domestic dimension: the constitutional boundaries of judicial review, the interpretive limits of courts, and the primacy of statute.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Courts and Justice Act will additionally:

- a) Enact a statutory restatement of parliamentary sovereignty in the following terms: “Parliament is the supreme legal authority in the United Kingdom. No court, tribunal, or judicial body may set aside, disapply, or refuse to give effect to any provision of an Act of Parliament. The validity of an Act of Parliament may not be questioned in any court.” This does not change the law. It restates it. The purpose of statutory restatement is to remove any ambiguity created by dicta in cases such as Jackson v Attorney General (2005), in which Lord Steyn suggested that courts might refuse to give effect to legislation that attempted to abolish judicial review. Such dicta are constitutionally improper and must not be permitted to calcify into accepted doctrine.
- b) Codify the grounds of judicial review to confine courts to reviewing the legality, procedural propriety, and rationality of government decisions, and to prohibit courts from reviewing the merits or policy wisdom of decisions made by democratically accountable bodies. The line between legality review and merits review has been progressively blurred. Courts have moved from asking “Did the decision-maker have the legal power to do this?” to asking “Was the decision proportionate, appropriate, or the best available option?” The latter question is not a legal question. It is a political question, and political questions belong to Parliament and the electorate.
- c) Restrict the use of Section 3 HRA-style interpretive powers under the new British Bill of Rights Act. Courts will be required to give statutory language its ordinary and natural meaning. Where that meaning produces a result that a court considers incompatible with protected rights, the court may issue a declaration to that effect, but may not reinterpret the statute to produce a meaning Parliament did not intend. The declaration mechanism preserves the dialogue between courts and Parliament. The interpretive override does not: it allows judges to rewrite legislation from the bench.
- d) Designate certain categories of decision as non-justiciable. Matters of high prerogative, including the dissolution and prorogation of Parliament, the conduct of foreign affairs and treaty-making, the deployment of armed forces, and the grant or refusal of honours, will be placed beyond the reach of judicial review by statute. These are political acts, answerable to Parliament and the electorate, not to the courts. The Miller II judgment made judicial intervention in prorogation thinkable. This provision makes it statutorily impossible.
- e) Require that any judicial review application that seeks to challenge a decision of a Secretary of State or a decision taken under primary legislation must be heard by a panel of at least three judges, not a single judge. This reduces the risk of individual judicial overreach and ensures that significant constitutional decisions receive appropriate collegiate deliberation.

OPERATIONAL

Judicial guidance. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, the Lord Chief Justice will issue updated guidance to all judges on the constitutional boundaries of judicial review, the proper scope of statutory interpretation, and the principle of judicial restraint in matters of policy. The guidance will be published and will form part of the mandatory continuing professional development for all serving judges.

Parliamentary scrutiny. The House of Commons will establish a permanent Judicial Review Scrutiny Committee, empowered to examine any judgment of the High Court, Court of Appeal, or Supreme Court that has the effect of constraining, overriding, or reinterpreting primary legislation. The Committee will have the power to summon witnesses and to recommend legislative correction where it considers that a court has exceeded its constitutional role. This is not an attack on judicial independence. It is the exercise of parliamentary sovereignty: the legislature reviewing whether the judiciary has remained within the boundaries the legislature has set.

###### C7.4: Sentencing Transparency and Consistency

The Problem

Public confidence in sentencing is low. Citizens observe cases in the media in which violent offenders receive sentences that appear to bear no relationship to the severity of their crimes. They observe wide disparities between sentences imposed in different courts for apparently similar offences. They observe offenders released on licence at the halfway point of already-inadequate sentences. The combination of opaque sentencing guidelines, broad judicial discretion, automatic early release, and the absence of any mechanism for public accountability produces a system in which the sentence pronounced in court and the sentence actually served are two different things, and the public knows it.

C1.4b established the foundational transparency infrastructure: a Sentencing Transparency Register, created under the Police Transparency Act, providing a publicly searchable record of every sentence handed down in every criminal court in England and Wales, linked to offence, guideline range, actual sentence, and sentencing judge. That register makes judicial patterns visible. C7.4 builds on it. Where C1.4b provides the architecture and the data, C7.4 enriches the register with full sentencing remarks, layers analytical tools on top of it, and delivers the substantive sentencing reforms that give the transparency teeth. The two provisions are designed as a single system: C1 opens the data; C7 ensures the data reveals the truth about what sentences actually mean in practice.

The Sentencing Council for England and Wales sets guidelines, but courts have broad discretion to depart from them. Sentencing remarks are published for some Crown Court cases but not for magistrates’ courts. The unduly lenient sentence referral scheme, operated by the Attorney General, allows victims and members of the public to request a review of sentences that appear too low, but only for a limited range of offences and within 28 days of sentencing. The scheme is underused and poorly publicised. Even with C1.4b’s register in operation, the public will see what sentence was imposed but not why, and will not see the gap between the headline sentence and the time actually served. C7.4 closes both gaps.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Courts and Justice Act will additionally:

- a) Require the publication of full sentencing remarks for all Crown Court cases and all either-way offences in magistrates’ courts, within 7 days of sentencing, as a mandatory data field within the Sentencing Transparency Register established by C1.4b. Sentencing remarks will explain: the offence, the aggravating and mitigating factors, the guideline range, the sentence imposed, and the reasons for any departure from the guideline. C1.4b’s register records the sentence and the judge; C7.4(a) ensures the register also records the reasoning. The register becomes not merely a ledger of outcomes but a complete public record of judicial decision-making.
- b) Expand the unduly lenient sentence referral scheme to cover all criminal offences, not just the current limited range. Remove the 28-day time limit for referrals. Require the Attorney General to publish quarterly statistics on the number of referrals received, the number referred to the Court of Appeal, and the outcomes. Where the Court of Appeal increases a sentence on referral, the reasons will be published alongside the original sentencing remarks.
- c) Require the Sentencing Council to develop and publish a Sentencing Transparency Index, operating as an analytical layer on top of the C1.4b register: a publicly accessible tool that allows any citizen to look up the typical sentence range for any offence, the average sentence actually imposed in the most recent reporting period, and the average time actually served after accounting for early release. The register provides the raw data; the Index interprets it. This will make visible, for the first time, the gap between the headline sentence and the reality of punishment. The public is entitled to know that a “10-year sentence” may mean 5 years in prison. The Transparency Index will make this gap undeniable.
- d) Abolish automatic unconditional release at the halfway point for all offences carrying a maximum sentence of 4 years or more. Offenders serving sentences for violent or sexual offences will serve a minimum of two-thirds of their sentence before becoming eligible for release on licence, subject to assessment by the Parole Board. This is consistent with the sentencing reforms in C2.3 and ensures that the sentence imposed by the court is the sentence the offender actually serves.
- e) Require that every Crown Court judge who imposes a community sentence or suspended sentence for an offence of violence must record, in writing, the specific reasons why immediate custody was not imposed. These reasons will be published as part of the sentencing remarks. The purpose is not to constrain judicial discretion. It is to make judicial discretion visible and accountable. A judge who believes that a violent offender should not go to prison must explain why, in public, in writing.

OPERATIONAL

Sentencing remarks integration. Within 12 months of Royal Assent, HMCTS will complete the integration of full sentencing remarks into the C1.4b Sentencing Transparency Register. The register, already established under the Police Transparency Act, will be extended to include: sentencing remarks in full, reasons for departure from guidelines, and any subsequent variation or appeal outcome. The Sentencing Transparency Index will be built as a public-facing analytical dashboard drawing directly from the register’s data. Historical sentencing remarks will be added retrospectively where they exist in digital form. The result is a single, unified sentencing transparency system: C1.4b provides the platform, C7.4 provides the content and the analytical tools.

Public awareness. The Ministry of Justice will fund a public awareness campaign informing citizens of their right to refer unduly lenient sentences, the expanded scope of the referral scheme, and the existence of the Sentencing Transparency Register and Index. The campaign will target communities with low confidence in the criminal justice system, including those where victims have felt that sentences do not reflect the seriousness of the offences committed against them.

###### C7.5: Countering Lawfare and Vexatious Strategic Litigation

The Problem

The expansion of judicial review and the proliferation of human rights-based legal challenges have created an industry of strategic litigation, sometimes described as “lawfare,” in which well-funded campaign organisations use the courts to achieve policy outcomes they cannot achieve through the democratic process. This is not a conspiracy theory. It is the openly stated strategy of numerous organisations that describe themselves as using litigation to advance social, environmental, or political objectives. The courts are used not to vindicate individual rights but to obstruct government policy, delay the implementation of democratic decisions, and impose costs on the public purse that act as a deterrent against lawful government action.

The Rwanda deportation scheme, whatever its merits, was subjected to sustained legal challenge by multiple organisations whose purpose was not to vindicate the individual rights of named applicants but to prevent the policy from being implemented at all. The total cost of the scheme, including legal costs, reached at least £700 million, with no forced deportations achieved. The cost was the point. Strategic litigants understand that if a government policy can be delayed long enough, and made expensive enough, it will be abandoned. This dynamic gives unelected organisations an effective veto over democratic governance.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Courts and Justice Act will additionally:

- a) Reform the rules on standing in judicial review cases. At present, any person with a “sufficient interest” in a matter may apply for judicial review, a test that has been interpreted broadly enough to allow campaign organisations with no direct personal stake to challenge government decisions. The Act will restrict standing in immigration and national security cases to individuals whose personal rights are directly and individually affected by the decision. Organisations may intervene as interested parties but may not bring proceedings in their own name on behalf of unnamed classes of affected persons.
- b) Introduce a costs-protection cap for judicial review challenges to government policy. Where a judicial review is brought against a decision of a Secretary of State and the challenge fails, the claimant will be liable for the full costs of the government’s defence. The current regime, in which strategic litigants benefit from costs protection that shields them from the consequences of losing, incentivises speculative litigation. Those who bring challenges to government policy must bear the risk of failure in the same way the government bears the risk of losing.
- c) Require courts hearing judicial review applications to consider, at the permission stage, whether the application is brought in good faith to vindicate a genuine individual right or whether it is brought primarily to obstruct or delay the implementation of government policy. Where the court finds that the primary purpose is delay or obstruction, it may refuse permission and award costs against the applicant. This does not prevent legitimate challenges. It prevents the courts from being used as a political tool.
- d) Impose statutory time limits on the determination of judicial review applications. Where a judicial review challenges a decision to remove a person from the United Kingdom, the entire process from application to final determination, including any appeal, must be completed within 90 days. Removal will not be stayed pending judicial review unless the court finds, on an interim basis, a strong prima facie case that the removal would cause irreparable harm to the specific individual applicant. Blanket stays based on the category of case, or on general policy objections, will not be granted.

OPERATIONAL

Judicial review audit. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, the Ministry of Justice will publish a comprehensive audit of all judicial review applications brought against government immigration and deportation decisions in the preceding 5 years, identifying: the success rate, the average cost to the public purse, the average delay caused, the organisations that brought or funded the challenges, and the outcomes. This will establish, for the first time, a transparent public record of the cost and effect of strategic litigation against democratic government.

###### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The C7 framework is built on a single piece of primary legislation: the Courts and Justice Act. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, or departmental action. This Act operates alongside the British Bill of Rights Act (C2.4), which addresses the ECHR and HRA dimensions of judicial reform, and the Police Transparency Act (C1), whose Sentencing Transparency Register (C1.4b) provides the data infrastructure that C7.4 enriches and builds upon.

###### Courts and Justice Act

On the face of the Act: Statutory minimum court capacity guarantee (demand-led funding). Statutory duty to eliminate backlog to below 40,000 within 36 months. Permanent expansion of magistrates’ sentencing powers to 12 months. Statutory duty on HMCTS to publish real-time court utilisation data. Mandatory judicial pay implementation of SSRB recommendations. Broadened routes to judicial appointment. New tier of full-time criminal court judges (200 initial cohort). Statutory duty to maintain court buildings. Statutory restatement of parliamentary sovereignty. Codification of judicial review grounds (legality, procedural propriety, rationality only). Restriction on HRA-style interpretive override. Designation of categories of non-justiciable prerogative acts. Three-judge panels for JR challenges to ministerial decisions. Publication of all sentencing remarks within 7 days as mandatory field in C1.4b Sentencing Transparency Register. Expansion of unduly lenient sentence scheme to all offences with no time limit. Sentencing Transparency Index as analytical layer on C1.4b register. Abolition of automatic halfway release for sentences of 4+ years. Mandatory written reasons for non-custodial sentences for violent offences. Standing reform for JR (immigration/national security). Costs-protection reform. Good-faith test at permission stage. 90-day time limit for immigration JR.

Delivered operationally: Emergency sitting programme within 30 days. Court recommissioning audit and first additional courts within 6 months. National digital case management system within 12 months. Criminal legal aid fee restoration to 2008 real-terms levels within 90 days. Judicial welfare and security enhancements within 6 months. Lord Chief Justice guidance on constitutional boundaries within 6 months. Parliamentary Judicial Review Scrutiny Committee. Sentencing remarks integration into C1.4b register and Transparency Index launch within 12 months. Public awareness campaign on sentencing referrals. Judicial review audit of immigration challenges within 6 months.

The judiciary exists to serve justice. It does not exist to make policy, to express institutional preferences, or to substitute its judgment for that of Parliament. When it confines itself to its proper role, it is the most important institution in a free society: the guarantee that power will be exercised according to law. When it exceeds that role, it becomes what it was designed to prevent: an unaccountable exercise of authority over people who have no means of redress. Progress will resource the courts so that they can deliver justice. Progress will recruit the judges that the system desperately needs. Progress will restore the constitutional boundaries that have been eroded. And Progress will ensure that every sentence imposed in a British court is visible, explicable, and answerable to the public in whose name it is pronounced. The courts belong to the people. It is time they served them.

#### C8. Victims’ Rights and Compensation

##### Governing Principle

A criminal justice system that treats the victim as an afterthought is not a justice system at all. It is a bureaucratic process for managing offenders in which the person who was actually harmed, whether robbed, beaten, raped, or bereaved, is reduced to the status of a witness: useful for securing a conviction, discarded the moment the trial ends or, as is far more common, the moment the case is dropped. Progress’ crime policy framework is built on the premise that safe streets are a right. This document establishes the corollary: that when the state fails to prevent a crime, the victim is owed a debt of recognition, of support, of compensation, and of justice, and that debt will be paid in full.

The scale of victimisation in Britain is staggering. The Crime Survey for England and Wales estimated 9.3 million incidents of headline crime in the year ending September 2025. Police recorded 1.94 million violence against the person offences in 2024/25. An estimated 1.1 million incidents of violence with or without injury were experienced by adults in the year ending December 2024. Behind every one of these numbers is a human being whose life was disrupted, diminished, or destroyed.

The system that is supposed to serve those human beings is failing them comprehensively. The Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority, the state’s primary mechanism for compensating victims of violent crime, paid out just £164 million in 2024/25 and refused 62% of all claims: more than 21,800 applicants turned away. Its tariff, last meaningfully revised in 2012, ranges from £1,000 to £250,000 with a maximum award of £500,000. These sums are not compensation in any meaningful sense of the word; they are tokens. A rape victim may receive £11,000. A bereaved parent may receive £5,500 for the death of a child. The Labour government formally rejected the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse’s recommendations for CICA reform in April 2025, declaring that the scheme’s “universality” was more important than its adequacy. The universality of inadequacy is not a defence.

The Victims’ Code, nominally a charter of rights for victims of crime, has no meaningful enforcement mechanism. The Victims and Prisoners Act 2024 introduced a statutory duty on criminal justice agencies to comply with the Code, but the duty is aspirational rather than actionable: there is no individual right of redress for a victim whose Code rights are breached, no penalty for an agency that fails to comply, and no independent inspectorate with the power to compel compliance. The Victims’ Commissioner’s Annual Survey in 2024, the largest ever undertaken with 6,581 responses, found that while 71% of victims felt the police treated them fairly and with respect, this was “overshadowed by reports of poor communication and inadequate investigations.” Victims reported being left uninformed about the progress of their cases, uninvolved in charging decisions, and unsupported through court proceedings.

Nowhere is the failure more acute than in sexual offences. Only 2.8% of police-recorded rapes in the year ending March 2025 resulted in a charge or summons. The CPS charging rate for rape cases has collapsed from 7.5% in 2016/17 to approximately 3.1% in 2024. Conviction volumes have remained static at 1,400 to 1,600 per year for a decade despite a doubling of reports. The average wait from charge to completion in the Crown Court for adult rape cases is now 417 days. At the end of September 2025, 14,180 sexual offence cases were waiting for a court date, a 77% increase in three years, and 4,455 of those were adult rape cases, representing a 136% increase. Meanwhile, three Rape Crisis centres have closed in the past year, and more than 14,000 survivors sit on waiting lists for specialist support services. The state is failing victims at every stage: failing to prevent the crime, failing to investigate it, failing to prosecute it, failing to support the victim through the process, and failing to compensate them when the process is over.

Victim support services themselves are in crisis. The Ministry of Justice announced £550 million over two years in December 2025 for specialist victim and witness services, but this followed a 4.2% cut in core Police and Crime Commissioner victim funding and a freeze in the Rape and Sexual Abuse Support Fund that amounted to a real-terms cut after inflation and National Insurance increases. The victim surcharge, a levy imposed on convicted offenders to fund victim services, is not paid directly to victims but pooled into a general fund. The entire funding model treats victim support as a discretionary charitable endeavour rather than a core obligation of the state.

Beyond the administrative failures, there exists a deeper and more insidious wrong: the managed humiliation of victims in the service of social cohesion. In the aftermath of terrorist attacks and mass-casualty incidents committed by individuals from specific demographic or ideological backgrounds, the British state has developed a pattern of conduct towards victims that would be extraordinary if it were not so routine. Victims and their families are corralled by government-adjacent agencies, charity bodies, and local authority teams into making public statements of conciliation and forgiveness. The preferred script, perfected after the Manchester Arena bombing and replicated after every subsequent atrocity, is one of resolute non-anger: “don’t look back in anger,” “this will not divide us,” “love wins.” The victims who comply are amplified and celebrated. The victims who do not, who are angry, who demand accountability, who name the ideology or the demographic pattern, are sidelined, pathologised, or worse.

The same dynamic operates in the grooming gang crisis documented in C4. Victims of organised child sexual exploitation, overwhelmingly committed by men from specific ethnic backgrounds, have been subjected by statutory agencies not to support but to management. They have been enrolled in counter-extremism programmes. They have been referred to Prevent-adjacent interventions. They have been treated, in effect, as potential radicalisation risks, as if the natural human response of a rape victim to the identity of her rapist were a security threat to be managed rather than a cry for justice to be answered. Fathers who tried to rescue their daughters were arrested. Mothers who named the perpetrators’ backgrounds were accused of racism. The state apparatus that was supposed to protect these victims instead instrumentalised them, deploying their suffering as raw material for a political narrative in which community cohesion mattered more than justice and the feelings of the perpetrators’ community were given precedence over the rights of the people who were raped.

This is not victim support. It is victim suppression. It is the subordination of individual suffering to collective reputation management, and it constitutes one of the most disgraceful chapters in the modern history of British public administration. Progress will end it. No agency of the state will direct, encourage, pressure, or incentivise any victim of crime to moderate their public response, to suppress their anger, to participate in conciliation programmes they did not request, or to undergo any form of counter-radicalisation or cohesion training as a condition of, or adjunct to, the receipt of victim services. A victim’s anger is not a problem to be managed. It is a legitimate response to a crime, and the only appropriate response from the state is accountability for the perpetrators and justice for the victim. Nothing else. Nothing less.

Progress’ position is unequivocal. The victim comes first. Not as a matter of rhetoric, but as a matter of law, of institutional design, and of financial commitment. This document establishes a comprehensive framework of enforceable victims’ rights, replaces the CICA with a properly funded and properly designed compensation system, guarantees long-term sustainable funding for victim support services, prohibits the managed suppression of victim testimony and anger, and ensures that the criminal justice system, from the moment a crime is reported to the moment the last payment is made, serves the person who was harmed, not the bureaucracies that failed to prevent the harm.

##### C8.1: Criminal Injuries Compensation: Total Reform

The Problem

The Criminal Injuries Compensation Scheme is an insult dressed up as a safety net. A tariff designed in 2012 and barely updated since pays a rape victim as little as £11,000. The CICA received over 42,000 applications in 2024/25, finalised approximately 35,000, and refused 62% of them: more than 21,800 people who were victims of violent crime and were told by the state that their suffering did not qualify, or did not qualify sufficiently, for financial recognition. The scheme excludes victims of online sexual abuse, coercive control, and stalking unless a “crime of violence” can be demonstrated. It imposes a two-year application deadline that fails to account for the reality that many victims of child sexual abuse, domestic violence, and trafficking do not come forward for years or decades. It reduces or withholds awards from applicants with unspent criminal convictions, regardless of the nature of those convictions or their relevance to the crime suffered. Between 82% and 100% of trafficking victims who applied to CICA were refused compensation in 2023/24. The Labour government rejected the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse’s recommendations to reform the scheme. This is not a system that works. It is a system that exists so that the government can say a system exists.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Victims’ Rights and Compensation Act will:

- a) Abolish the Criminal Injuries Compensation Scheme 2012 and replace it with a new Criminal Injuries Compensation Scheme designed from first principles. The new scheme will be harm-based, not tariff-based. Compensation will be assessed by reference to the actual harm suffered by the victim, encompassing physical, psychological, financial, and consequential damage, not by reference to a fixed tariff that assigns an arbitrary monetary value to a category of injury. Independent medical and psychological assessments will determine the quantum of compensation. The maximum award will be uncapped for the most serious cases; no victim of violent crime will be told that their suffering exceeds the scheme’s budget.
- b) Expand the scope of the scheme to include victims of all criminal conduct that causes physical or psychological harm, including coercive control, stalking, online sexual abuse, and exploitation. The current restriction to “crimes of violence” is an anachronism that excludes entire categories of serious harm. The new scheme will be defined by the harm suffered, not the technical classification of the offence.
- c) Abolish the two-year application deadline. Victims will be entitled to apply at any time. For victims of child sexual abuse and trafficking, the practical consequence of a time limit is the exclusion of the most vulnerable applicants. This is indefensible and it ends.
- d) Abolish the unspent convictions rule. A victim’s criminal record is irrelevant to the harm they suffered. A woman who was raped does not become less raped because she has a shoplifting conviction. This rule exists to exclude the marginalised and the vulnerable, precisely the people most likely to be victimised, and Progress will repeal it entirely.
- e) Establish a system of interim payments. Within 30 days of a valid application, the scheme will make an interim payment of no less than £5,000 to any applicant whose claim involves a serious violent or sexual offence. This mirrors the approach taken in C4 (The Rape Gangs: Reckoning and Remembrance), where interim payments of £25,000 were mandated within 90 days. Victims should not have to wait months or years for financial recognition while the bureaucracy processes their claim.
- f) Require the scheme to be administered by a fully independent body, the Victims’ Compensation Board, separate from the Ministry of Justice, with its own budget, its own staff, and its own accountability to Parliament. The current arrangement, in which the CICA is an executive agency of the MoJ, creates an inherent conflict of interest: the department responsible for funding the scheme is also the department with an institutional incentive to minimise payouts.

OPERATIONAL

Transition plan. The Victims’ Compensation Board will be operational within 6 months of Royal Assent. All pending CICA applications will be transferred to the new body and reassessed under the new harm-based methodology. No applicant will receive less under the new scheme than they would have received under the old one.

Funding. The Victims’ Compensation Board will be funded from general taxation, supplemented by a reformed Offender Compensation Levy (see C8.5 below). The initial annual budget will be £500 million, reflecting the true scale of violent crime in England and Wales. For context, CICA paid out £164 million in 2024/25; the new scheme will more than triple this baseline. The cost is a fraction of the estimated £50 billion annual social and economic cost of crime against individuals in England and Wales, as calculated by the Home Office’s own methodology.

##### C8.2: Enforceable Victims’ Rights

The Problem

The Victims’ Code of Practice, first introduced in 2006 and most recently revised in 2024, sets out twelve rights for victims of crime: the right to be treated with respect, to be kept informed, to be referred to support services, to make a Victim Personal Statement, to be told about the outcome of the case, and so on. These rights exist on paper. They do not exist in practice, because there is no consequence for breaching them.

The Victims and Prisoners Act 2024 imposed a statutory duty on criminal justice agencies to comply with the Code, but the duty is a dead letter. There is no individual right of action for a victim whose Code rights are breached. There is no financial penalty for an agency that fails to comply. The Victims’ Commissioner can publish reports and make recommendations; agencies are required to respond to those recommendations within 56 days, but they are not required to act on them. The entire framework is built on the assumption that agencies will comply because they ought to, not because they must. The evidence demonstrates that they do not.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Victims’ Rights and Compensation Act will additionally:

- a) Create an enforceable statutory right for every victim of crime to receive the services and protections set out in the Victims’ Code. Breach of any Code right by any criminal justice agency will give rise to a right of complaint to the Victims’ Commissioner, who will have the power to investigate, to issue binding directions, and to award compensation of up to £10,000 per breach to the victim. This transforms the Code from an aspiration into an entitlement.
- b) Establish a Victims’ Ombudsman within the office of the Victims’ Commissioner, with statutory investigatory powers equivalent to those of the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman. The Ombudsman will investigate systemic failures in Code compliance, publish findings, and have the power to require remedial action within specified timeframes. Non-compliance with a direction of the Ombudsman will be treated as contempt.
- c) Require every police force, CPS area, and court service to appoint a Victims’ Liaison Director at senior level, personally accountable for Code compliance within their area. Annual compliance reports will be published and performance against Code standards will form part of the HMICFRS inspection framework for police forces and the CPS inspectorate’s assessment of prosecution areas.
- d) Mandate automatic notification to victims at every stage of the criminal justice process: at the point of charge, at every adjournment, at trial listing, at verdict, at sentencing, and at any point where the offender applies for parole, early release, or licence variation. Failure to notify will be a breach of the Code giving rise to the right of complaint and compensation described in (a) above. No victim will ever again discover that their attacker has been released by reading it in a newspaper.

OPERATIONAL

Digital Victims’ Portal. Within 9 months of Royal Assent, the Ministry of Justice will commission a single digital portal, integrated with the JusticeOpen platform established under C1, through which every victim can track the status of their case in real time, access support services, submit Victim Personal Statements, and communicate with their Victims’ Liaison Director. The portal will be built to GOV.UK service standards and will be accessible via web and mobile application. No victim will have to telephone a police switchboard to find out what is happening with their case.

Victims’ Commissioner powers. The Victims’ Commissioner’s office will be expanded to a staffing complement of no fewer than 80 within 6 months, with an annual budget of £15 million. The Commissioner will be empowered to conduct own-initiative investigations without waiting for a complaint, to require agencies to produce documents and data within 14 days, and to publish thematic reports with binding recommendations. The Commissioner’s annual compliance report will be laid before Parliament and debated.

##### C8.3: Guaranteed Victim Support Services

The Problem

Victim support in Britain is funded as if it were a charitable afterthought rather than a core function of the state. The Ministry of Justice’s Rape and Sexual Abuse Support Fund, the only ring-fenced government funding stream specifically for specialist sexual violence services, totalled £21.3 million for 2026/27. Three Rape Crisis centres closed in the past year. More than 14,000 survivors of sexual violence are on waiting lists for specialist support, with over 80% of those waiting specifically for counselling services. Two-thirds of Rape Crisis centres reported in summer 2025 that they could be forced to cut vital services, and 27% were at risk of imminent closure. Rape Crisis centres collectively supported over 80,000 victims and survivors in the past year, including a quarter who were children, yet the sector is being dismantled by funding attrition.

The broader victim support landscape is no better. The government froze MoJ funding for victim and witness services at 2024/25 levels in the 2025/26 settlement, amounting to a real-terms cut after inflation and the National Insurance employer contribution increase. Police and Crime Commissioners’ core victim funding was cut by 4.2%. Victim Support itself warned that the funding deficit equated to approximately 85 staff delivering frontline support for victims of violent assault, sexual violence, domestic abuse, hate crime, and fraud. The entire model is precarious, fragmented, and dependent on short-term funding cycles that make long-term planning impossible.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Victims’ Rights and Compensation Act will additionally:

- a) Create a statutory duty on the Secretary of State to fund victim support services at a level sufficient to ensure that no victim of a serious violent or sexual offence waits more than 30 days for access to specialist support from the date of referral. This duty will be enforceable by the Victims’ Commissioner through judicial review. The era of waiting lists measured in months and years for trauma support ends.
- b) Establish the Victims’ Services Guarantee Fund, ring-fenced from general MoJ expenditure, funded at an initial level of £300 million per year. The Fund will provide multi-year (minimum five-year) core funding to specialist victim support organisations, including Rape Crisis centres, domestic abuse services, Independent Sexual Violence Advisers, Independent Domestic Violence Advisers, bereavement support services, and specialist services for child victims, trafficking victims, and victims with complex needs. No more annual cliff-edges. No more centres closing because a funding cycle expired.
- c) Guarantee that every victim of rape or serious sexual assault has access to a free, independent legal adviser from the point of report to the police through to the conclusion of any court proceedings. The adviser will not represent the Crown; they will represent the victim. Their role will include advising on disclosure of personal records, challenging improper cross-examination, and ensuring the victim’s rights under the Code are enforced in real time. Progress will legislate for this, not merely pledge it.

OPERATIONAL

National Victims’ Services Map. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, the Victims’ Commissioner will publish a comprehensive national map of all victim support services, identifying coverage gaps by geography, crime type, and demographic group. The map will be updated quarterly and will inform funding allocation decisions by the Victims’ Services Guarantee Fund.

Workforce strategy. The government will commission a national workforce strategy for victim support within 90 days, addressing recruitment, retention, training, supervision, and pay. Independent Sexual Violence Advisers and Independent Domestic Violence Advisers will be brought onto nationally agreed pay scales reflecting the specialist nature of their work and the severity of the secondary trauma they absorb. The current model, in which ISVAs and IDVAs are paid at or near minimum wage while performing some of the most demanding work in the criminal justice system, is unsustainable and it is wrong.

##### C8.4: The Right to Justice: Tackling Victim Attrition

The Problem

The single greatest failing of the criminal justice system from the victim’s perspective is not inadequate compensation or insufficient support services. It is the near-certainty that nothing will happen. Of the 71,227 police-recorded rapes in England and Wales in the year ending December 2024, fewer than 3 in 100 resulted in a charge. The CPS conviction rate for adult rape cases was approximately 51% of those that reached court, but so few cases reach court that the conviction rate is meaningless as a measure of justice. Annually, between 1,400 and 1,600 rape convictions are secured in a country that records over 70,000 rape offences and in which the Crime Survey estimates that around one million adults experienced sexual assault in the year ending December 2024. The justice gap is not a gap. It is a chasm.

Victim withdrawal is the proximate cause of much of this attrition, but victim withdrawal is itself a consequence of system failure. Victims withdraw because investigations take too long, because they are not kept informed, because the process of disclosure, the handing over of medical records, therapy notes, school records, and phone data, is experienced as a second violation, and because the prospect of cross-examination in a court system that treats them as an inconvenience rather than the person the process exists to serve is more than they can bear. For those whose cases do proceed, the average wait from charge to completion in the Crown Court for adult rape is 417 days. One in three rape trials is postponed at least once. Some survivors have endured more than six postponements. At the end of September 2025, there were 14,180 sexual offence cases waiting for a Crown Court date, of which 4,455 were adult rape, a 136% increase in three years.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Victims’ Rights and Compensation Act will additionally:

- a) Create a statutory right for victims of rape and serious sexual offences to have their case heard in a specialist Sexual Offences Court, listed as a priority and subject to a statutory time limit of 6 months from charge to trial commencement. Where the time limit is exceeded, the trial judge must record the reasons for the delay and the Victims’ Commissioner must be notified. This is not a target. It is a statutory obligation. The necessary increase in Crown Court sitting days is addressed in C7 (Judicial Reform); the necessary increase in police and CPS capacity is addressed in C2 (Zero-Crime Britain) and C5 (Police Reform).
- b) Prohibit the disclosure of a victim’s counselling and therapy records in any criminal proceeding except where a judge is satisfied, on application made on notice to the victim, that the records contain material that is directly relevant to a specific issue in the case and that the public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to the victim. The current practice, in which defence teams routinely request wholesale disclosure of therapy records on speculative grounds, deters victims from seeking therapeutic support and deters survivors from reporting. The Victims and Prisoners Act 2024 introduced limited protections; Progress will make them absolute.
- c) Guarantee every victim of a serious indictable offence the right to a pre-trial conference with the prosecuting advocate, at which the victim will be briefed on the trial process, the evidence to be called, and the likely lines of cross-examination. This is standard practice in several Commonwealth jurisdictions and in parts of the United States. In England and Wales, victims routinely arrive at court having never met the barrister who will present their case and with no understanding of what they will face. This is unconscionable.
- d) Require the CPS to provide a written explanation to the victim within 14 days of any decision not to charge or to discontinue a prosecution. The explanation must set out the evidence considered, the reasons for the decision, and the victim’s right to seek a review under the Victims’ Right to Review scheme. Where the review overturns the original decision, the reviewing officer’s assessment must be published to inform future charging practice.

OPERATIONAL

Specialist Sexual Offences Courts. Within 12 months of Royal Assent, the Lord Chancellor will designate no fewer than 15 Crown Court centres as Specialist Sexual Offences Courts, with dedicated courtrooms, trained judiciary, specialist RASSO prosecutors, and victim waiting areas that are physically separated from areas accessible to the defendant or the defendant’s family. These courts will pilot the 6-month charge-to-trial standard. The court expansion programme under C7 will increase this to full national coverage within 24 months.

Victim attrition monitoring. Every police force will be required to publish quarterly data on victim attrition rates by offence type, broken down by the stage at which the victim withdrew and the reason recorded. The data will be published on the open crime statistics portal established under C1 and will form a key performance indicator in HMICFRS inspections. Forces with persistently high victim withdrawal rates will be subject to enhanced scrutiny and, where necessary, intervention under the policing reform powers established in C5.

##### C8.5: Offender-Funded Compensation and the Restorative Levy

The Problem

The victim surcharge, introduced in 2007 and increased by 25% between 2020 and 2022, is a levy imposed on all convicted offenders to fund victim and witness services. It is not paid to the victim of the crime for which the offender was convicted. It is pooled into a general Victim and Witness Fund and distributed through opaque bureaucratic channels. The amounts are derisory: a fine-only sentence attracts a surcharge calculated as a percentage of the fine; a custodial sentence of up to 6 months attracts a surcharge of £154; a sentence of life imprisonment attracts a surcharge of £228. The surcharge raises an estimated additional £20 million per year, a trivial sum relative to the scale of the problem. Meanwhile, courts have the power to order compensation directly to a victim, but in practice this power is used inconsistently and the amounts awarded are modest. The entire model is inverted: victims fund their own recovery through taxes, while offenders’ financial contribution to the harm they caused is negligible.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Victims’ Rights and Compensation Act will additionally:

- a) Replace the victim surcharge with a Restorative Levy, calculated as a meaningful proportion of the offender’s assessed financial means, with a statutory minimum that reflects the seriousness of the offence. For indictable-only offences: minimum £1,000 or 25% of the offender’s realisable assets, whichever is greater. For either-way offences: minimum £500 or 15% of realisable assets. For summary-only offences: minimum £200 or 10% of realisable assets. Where the offender has no realisable assets, the minimum will be enforced as a debt upon release, recoverable by attachment of earnings. The levy will be ring-fenced for the Victims’ Services Guarantee Fund.
- b) Make compensation orders mandatory in all cases involving an identifiable victim, unless the court is satisfied that the offender has no means and no prospect of means. The current discretionary model, in which judges may or may not order compensation depending on their assessment of the offender’s ability to pay, produces grotesque inconsistencies. Compensation orders will be enforceable as civil debts and will survive bankruptcy.
- c) Introduce a Proceeds of Crime (Victim Priority) provision. Where confiscation orders are made under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002, the first call on recovered funds will be compensation to identified victims, not the Consolidated Fund. Currently, proceeds of crime go to the Treasury. Progress will ensure they go first to the people who were harmed.

OPERATIONAL

Asset recovery capacity. The Malebranche (C3) and NCA will be tasked with a dedicated asset recovery programme targeting convicted offenders who have not paid court-ordered compensation. Within 12 months of Royal Assent, a specialist Asset Recovery and Victim Compensation Unit will be established within the Malebranche, with powers to trace, freeze, and confiscate offender assets for the purpose of satisfying outstanding compensation orders. The unit will operate on a self-funding model: its costs will be met from the assets it recovers.

Compensation enforcement. Outstanding compensation orders will accrue interest at 8% per annum. Where an offender fails to make payments, enforcement will be escalated automatically through the same mechanisms used for council tax and HMRC debt: attachment of earnings, deduction from benefits, seizure of goods, and ultimately committal. Victims will not be required to take enforcement action themselves; the state will collect what is owed.

##### C8.6: Prohibition of Managed Victim Suppression

The Problem

A pattern of conduct has developed across local authorities, police forces, counter-terrorism agencies, and government-funded third-sector organisations in which victims of crime, particularly victims of terrorism and of sexual offences committed by perpetrators from specific ethnic or ideological backgrounds, are subjected to a form of institutional management that has nothing to do with their welfare and everything to do with the state’s desire to control the public narrative.

The mechanics are consistent. In the immediate aftermath of an atrocity or a high-profile prosecution, victims and their families are approached by government-linked “support” workers, local authority liaison officers, and charity organisations whose funding depends on their alignment with government priorities. They are encouraged, and in some cases pressured, to make public statements emphasising forgiveness, unity, and the irrelevance of the perpetrators’ background. Those who comply are given platforms and praised. Those who do not are quietly marginalised, denied access to media opportunities, or characterised as vulnerable to radicalisation.

The most grotesque manifestation of this pattern is the referral of victims themselves to counter-extremism and anti-radicalisation programmes. Victims of grooming gangs, whose abusers were overwhelmingly from particular ethnic communities, have been subjected to interventions designed not to help them recover from sexual exploitation but to ensure that their natural anger does not produce “community tension.” The victims of the Manchester Arena bombing were managed through a public grief apparatus that prioritised social cohesion messaging over individual accountability. The consistent message from the state to victims of ideologically or demographically patterned crime is this: your suffering is acknowledged, but only insofar as it can be made useful to the government’s cohesion objectives. If your suffering produces anger that is inconvenient, you will be treated not as a victim but as a risk.

This amounts to the systematic gaslighting of crime victims by their own government. A thirteen-year-old girl who was raped by a group of men and who is then told by a social worker that her anger at those men’s shared background constitutes a safeguarding concern is not being supported. She is being abused a second time, this time by the state. A mother whose daughter was murdered in a terrorist attack and who is then steered by a Home Office-funded “resilience” programme into public expressions of forgiveness she does not feel is not being helped to grieve. She is being recruited as a propaganda asset. The fact that these practices are carried out by well-meaning professionals does not diminish their obscenity; it compounds it, because it means the institutions responsible are incapable of recognising the harm they are doing.

This is a profound moral wrong, and it will be prohibited by law under a Progress government.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Victims’ Rights and Compensation Act will additionally:

- a) Create a statutory offence of coerced victim suppression. It will be a criminal offence for any public official, public authority employee, or publicly funded organisation to direct, pressure, incentivise, or condition the provision of victim services upon any victim of crime making, or refraining from making, any public statement about the crime, the perpetrators, or the circumstances of the offence. Minimum sentence: 12 months. This applies whether the coercion is explicit or implicit, and it applies regardless of the claimed purpose, including community cohesion, counter-extremism, or social harmony. The victim’s right to speak, or to remain silent, about what was done to them is absolute and unconditional.
- b) Prohibit the referral or enrolment of any crime victim in any counter-radicalisation, counter-extremism, de-radicalisation, or community cohesion programme as a consequence of, or in connection with, their status as a victim. A crime victim is not a security risk. A crime victim’s anger is not radicalisation. The conflation of victimhood with extremism risk, which has been a recurring feature of the state’s response to grooming gang survivors and terrorism survivors alike, is an institutional pathology that Progress will excise from the system root and branch.
- c) Require all victim support organisations in receipt of public funding to certify annually that they have not, directly or indirectly, sought to influence, manage, or moderate any victim’s public statements, emotional responses, or engagement with media. False certification will be treated as fraud and will result in immediate termination of funding, recovery of sums paid, and referral to the Malebranche for investigation.
- d) Grant the Victims’ Commissioner a specific statutory duty to monitor and investigate any allegation of managed victim suppression, with the power to compel testimony from officials, access internal communications, and publish findings. The Commissioner’s investigation powers in respect of this provision will be equivalent to those of a statutory inquiry under the Inquiries Act 2005, and recommendations arising from such investigations will be binding on the agencies concerned.

OPERATIONAL

Immediate review. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Victims’ Commissioner will conduct a comprehensive review of all victim liaison, victim support, and community cohesion programmes operated by or funded by central government, local authorities, police forces, and the Home Office, to identify any programme or practice in which victim management has been conflated with counter-extremism objectives or narrative control. Findings will be published in full. Where evidence of systematic victim suppression is found, the responsible officials will be referred for prosecution under the new offence created by this section.

Training prohibition. No victim of crime will be required, requested, or encouraged to participate in any training programme, workshop, or intervention whose purpose or effect is to moderate their response to the crime they suffered. This includes, without limitation, “community cohesion” workshops, “building resilience” programmes administered by counter-terrorism bodies, and any programme that treats the victim’s anger, grief, or public expression of either as a problem to be solved rather than a response to be respected. The only appropriate state response to a victim’s anger is justice for the victim and accountability for the perpetrator.
