###### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The C8 Victims’ Rights and Compensation framework is built on one piece of primary legislation: the Victims’ Rights and Compensation Act. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, departmental procurement, or existing administrative mechanisms.

###### Victims’ Rights and Compensation Act (new)

On the face of the Act: Abolition of the Criminal Injuries Compensation Scheme 2012 and replacement with a harm-based compensation scheme administered by the Victims’ Compensation Board. Uncapped maximum awards. Expanded scope to include coercive control, stalking, and online sexual abuse. Abolition of the two-year application deadline and the unspent convictions rule. Interim payments of £5,000 within 30 days for serious offences. Enforceable statutory victims’ rights with individual right of complaint and compensation for breach. Victims’ Ombudsman with investigatory and binding direction powers. Mandatory notification at every stage of proceedings. Statutory duty to fund victim support services with 30-day access guarantee. Victims’ Services Guarantee Fund at £300 million per year with five-year minimum funding cycles. Free independent legal advisers for victims of rape and serious sexual assault. Specialist Sexual Offences Courts with 6-month charge-to-trial statutory standard. Prohibition on speculative disclosure of therapy records. Pre-trial conference right for victims of serious indictable offences. Mandatory CPS written explanation for non-charge decisions. Restorative Levy replacing the victim surcharge. Mandatory compensation orders. Proceeds of Crime victim priority provision. Criminal offence of coerced victim suppression (minimum 12 months). Prohibition on referral of victims to counter-radicalisation or cohesion programmes. Annual certification requirement for publicly funded victim support organisations. Victims’ Commissioner statutory duty to investigate managed victim suppression.

Delivered operationally: Victims’ Compensation Board operational within 6 months (£500 million annual budget). Digital Victims’ Portal within 9 months, integrated with JusticeOpen (C1). Victims’ Commissioner expanded to 80 staff, £15 million annual budget. National Victims’ Services Map within 6 months. National workforce strategy for ISVAs and IDVAs within 90 days. 15 Specialist Sexual Offences Courts within 12 months, full national coverage within 24 months. Quarterly victim attrition data publication. Asset Recovery and Victim Compensation Unit within the Malebranche (C3) within 12 months. Compensation enforcement via attachment of earnings and automated escalation. Comprehensive review of all victim support and cohesion programmes within 90 days.

The criminal justice system exists to serve the victim. Not to manage offenders, not to process paperwork, not to provide employment for lawyers and civil servants, and emphatically not to launder the reputations of communities, institutions, or ideologies at the victim’s expense. Every reform in this framework, from the police expansion in C2 to the court reform in C7, from the grooming gang reckoning in C4 to the anti-corruption regime in C3, is ultimately justified by one question: does it deliver justice for the person who was harmed? This document ensures that the answer is not left to chance, to goodwill, or to the discretion of officials who have demonstrated, conclusively and over decades, that they will not deliver it unless compelled. Progress will compel them. The victim comes first. This is not radical. It is overdue.

#### C9. Cybercrime and Online Harms

##### Governing Principle

Britain is being robbed, surveilled, exploited, and attacked through its own digital infrastructure, and the state’s response to this reality is a patchwork of underfunded agencies, obsolete legislation, and toothless regulators that collectively amount to a policy of managed decline. Cybercrime is not a niche concern. It is, by volume, the dominant form of crime in England and Wales. Fraud alone accounts for 41% of all crime recorded by the Crime Survey, with an estimated 3.44 million adult victims in the year ending March 2025, a 25% increase on the previous year. The financial losses are staggering: over £1.17 billion stolen through payment fraud in 2024, with a further 3.31 million confirmed cases of unauthorised fraud reported to UK Finance. The broader economic cost of fraud to the United Kingdom is estimated by Cifas at £219 billion per year. Cybercrime against businesses runs to an estimated 8.58 million incidents annually. The National Cyber Security Centre handled 204 nationally significant cyber incidents between September 2024 and August 2025, a 130% increase on the previous year. A single ransomware attack on Marks & Spencer in April 2025 cost the company an estimated £300 million.

The law that governs how Britain responds to this threat was written in 1990, five months after Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web and at a time when fewer than one in ten British households had a personal computer. The Computer Misuse Act is 35 years old. It criminalises legitimate cybersecurity research. It fails to account for the existence of ransomware, crypto-laundering, AI-enabled fraud, botnets, or state-sponsored cyber espionage. The CyberUp Campaign, backed by the CBI, BT, techUK, NCC Group, and the former Chief Executive of the National Cyber Security Centre, has spent half a decade asking successive governments to reform it. Every attempt has been blocked, deferred, or quietly shelved. The most recent attempt, amendments to the Data (Use and Access) Bill in January 2025, was rejected by the government on the grounds that reform might “create a loophole.” The loophole already exists: it is the one through which £219 billion per year disappears.

The policing response to fraud and cybercrime is a national embarrassment. Fraud constitutes over 40% of all crime but receives less than 1% of police resources. Of the more than 300,000 reports made to Action Fraud each year, fewer than 1% result in a criminal justice outcome where an offender is charged or prosecuted. Of the approximately 27,000 cases passed from Action Fraud to local police forces for investigation, fewer than 5% result in a charge. In the year ending December 2024 there were just 4,176 fraud prosecutions in England and Wales, against 3.44 million estimated victims. Only an estimated 14% of frauds against individuals are even reported. The overwhelming majority of fraud victims in Britain will never see a police officer, will never receive a phone call, and will never see anyone held accountable for the crime committed against them. The Parliamentary Public Accounts Committee described Action Fraud as having earned the nickname “Inaction Fraud.” The name is deserved.

The Online Safety Act 2023 was presented to the British public as a measure to protect children online. In practice, it is a censorship framework designed to give the state, through its appointed regulator, the power to determine what lawful speech British citizens may encounter on the internet. The Act’s genesis is instructive. Among those who gave oral evidence to the Commons Public Bill Committee in May 2022, shaping the legislation’s scope and priorities, was Liron Velleman, described in Hansard as a “political organiser” for Hope Not Hate. In January 2026, Velleman pleaded guilty at Highbury Corner Magistrates’ Court to attempting to engage in sexual communication with a child and attempting to cause a child aged 13 to 15 to look at an image of sexual activity, having been caught in a Metropolitan Police sting operation. A man who helped design legislation ostensibly intended to protect children online was himself targeting children for sexual exploitation online. The Centre for Countering Digital Hate, whose CEO Imran Ahmed was the first witness to the Bill’s pre-legislative committee in 2021 and who boasts that “Our campaigning resulted in the Online Safety Act,” has since had its director’s US green card revoked and faces sanctions from the US State Department as a member of what the Trump Administration has designated the “censorship industrial complex.” These are the organisations that built the Online Safety Act. Their interest was never child protection. It was the suppression of political speech that threatened their institutional influence.

The Act’s record confirms this analysis. In its first year of substantive enforcement from March 2025, Ofcom launched five enforcement programmes and opened 21 investigations into 69 sites. Its largest fine was just over £1 million, against 4chan. Meanwhile, the Internet Watch Foundation acted on 312,030 reports of child sexual abuse material in 2025, the worst year in its 30-year history. AI-generated child sexual abuse videos increased by 26,362% in a single year, from 13 in 2024 to 3,440 in 2025, with 65% classified as the most extreme Category A material depicting rape, sexual torture, and bestiality. The National Crime Agency estimates that between 710,000 and 840,000 adults in the United Kingdom pose varying degrees of sexual risk to children. The Online Safety Act did not prevent any of this. What it did was create the regulatory architecture for a government agency to police lawful speech, to categorise political opinions as “harmful content,” and to compel platforms to suppress material that is entirely legal but inconvenient to the political establishment. Hope Not Hate’s own written evidence to the Bill committee complained that protections for “democratically important” content could “open up the opportunity for abuse by far-right activists and organisations.” The quiet part was always loud.

The state-sponsored cyber threat to Britain’s critical national infrastructure is escalating. The NCSC has publicly attributed sustained cyber campaigns to China (the Flax Typhoon and Salt Typhoon operations targeting government and critical networks), Russia (the Authentic Antics malware targeting email accounts and ongoing operations linked to the war in Ukraine), Iran (attacks on UK and US critical infrastructure), and North Korea (fake IT worker scams funnelling money to the DPRK regime). The NCSC has warned that the gap between the threat posed to critical national infrastructure and the ability of its owners and operators to defend against it is widening. The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, introduced in the King’s Speech, is an acknowledgement of the problem. It is not a solution. A solution would require treating cyber defence as what it is: a core national security function equivalent in urgency to conventional military preparedness.

Progress’ position is that the digital domain is sovereign territory. Crimes committed through digital infrastructure are crimes, not regrettable externalities of technological progress. Fraud committed online is theft. Child sexual abuse material distributed via file-sharing services is child sexual abuse. Ransomware attacks on hospitals are attacks on public safety. State-sponsored penetration of critical infrastructure is an act of hostile intelligence. The appropriate response is not a phased regulatory roadmap or an interdepartmental working group. It is the full application of criminal law, properly resourced law enforcement, and the subordination of platform commercial interests to the safety of the public. This document sets out how Progress will deliver that response.

##### C9.1: The Cyber Crime Act: Replacing the Computer Misuse Act 1990

The Problem

The Computer Misuse Act 1990 is the foundational law governing cybercrime in Britain. It was enacted before the existence of the World Wide Web, before broadband, before smartphones, before social media, before ransomware, before cryptocurrency, before artificial intelligence, and before the digital economy that now constitutes a significant proportion of national GDP. It contains three substantive offences relating to unauthorised access to computer material, unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences, and unauthorised modification of computer material. These provisions were designed for a world of standalone desktop computers accessed by telephone modems. They are manifestly unfit for a world in which a single ransomware group can paralyse a national health service blood-testing provider, in which state-sponsored actors operate botnets of 260,000 compromised devices, and in which AI-generated deepfakes are used to execute £20 million CEO fraud attacks via video conference.

The Act’s most destructive failure is not its inadequacy as a tool against criminals but its inadvertent criminalisation of the people trying to stop them. The CyberUp Campaign has documented, through extensive industry consultation, that 80% of cybersecurity professionals in the UK are concerned that they may be prosecuted for doing their jobs. Vulnerability research, threat intelligence activities, and academic security research all potentially fall within the scope of the Act’s prohibition on “unauthorised access.” Countries including the Netherlands, France, the United States, Germany, Belgium, and Malta have updated their legal frameworks to protect legitimate security research. Britain has not. The economic cost is real: the CyberUp Campaign estimates that nearly 600 of the UK’s approximately 2,000 active cybersecurity firms have experienced economic losses due to the CMA’s restrictions, and that reform could unlock an estimated £1.8 billion in additional annual sector revenue and 7,000 new jobs.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Cyber Crime Act will:

- a) Repeal the Computer Misuse Act 1990 in its entirety and replace it with a modern, comprehensive statute that reflects the realities of twenty-first century cybercrime. The new Act will create specific offences for ransomware (including the development, distribution, and deployment of ransomware, and the laundering of ransom payments through cryptocurrency or other channels), for the operation of botnets, for the development and sale of malware-as-a-service, for the use of AI to generate fraudulent content including deepfakes used to facilitate financial crime, and for the unauthorised harvesting and sale of personal data.
- b) Introduce a statutory public interest defence for cybersecurity professionals and researchers. Any person who accesses a computer system without authorisation for the purpose of identifying, analysing, or reporting a vulnerability, threat, or security weakness, acting in good faith and in accordance with professional standards, will have a complete defence to prosecution. The defence will be defined by reference to the CyberUp Campaign’s established framework: the harm-benefit principle (benefits must outweigh potential harms), the proportionality principle (reasonable steps to minimise harm), the intent principle (good faith, honesty, and sincerity), and the competence principle (relevant qualifications, accreditation, or professional standing). This defence is long overdue. It has been recommended by Sir Patrick Vallance in his Pro-Innovation Regulation of Technologies Review, supported by the former CEO of the NCSC, and endorsed by the CBI, BT, and the overwhelming majority of the cybersecurity industry.
- c) Create specific aggravated offences for cyberattacks on critical national infrastructure, including but not limited to energy, water, transport, health, financial services, telecommunications, and government systems. Attacks on CNI will carry maximum sentences equivalent to those available for terrorism offences, reflecting the reality that a successful cyberattack on a hospital or power grid can cause harm indistinguishable from a physical attack.
- d) Introduce a strict liability offence for the knowing payment of ransomware demands by any public body, critical national infrastructure operator, or organisation above a specified size, except where the Secretary of State has granted a written exemption on grounds of immediate risk to life. The current position, in which ransom payments are tacitly tolerated and frequently concealed, funds the criminal ecosystem and incentivises further attacks. Progress will make the payment of ransom a matter of last resort, subject to disclosure, regulatory scrutiny, and ministerial accountability.
- e) Extend the territorial reach of cybercrime offences to cover any offence where the victim, the computer system, or the effect of the conduct is located within the United Kingdom, regardless of the physical location of the offender. The Act will include provision for mutual legal assistance treaties and extradition requests to be expedited for cybercrime offences, and for the recognition and enforcement of foreign cyber crime judgments.

OPERATIONAL

Legislative timetable. The Cyber Crime Act will be introduced within the first session of Parliament. The statutory defence for cybersecurity professionals will take effect on Royal Assent; the repeal of the CMA 1990 and the commencement of the new offence framework will take effect 6 months from Royal Assent to allow for operational preparation by law enforcement and the CPS.

Guidance. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the CPS and NCSC will jointly publish prosecution guidance setting out the application of the new statutory defence, the evidential thresholds for the new offences, and the interaction between the Cyber Crime Act and the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, the National Security Act 2023, and the Children’s Online Protection Act established under C9.4.

##### C9.2: The National Cyber Crime Force

The Problem

Britain does not have a dedicated national cyber crime law enforcement capability commensurate with the scale of the threat. Responsibility is fragmented across the National Crime Agency’s National Cyber Crime Unit, the City of London Police (as national lead for fraud), 43 territorial police forces (most with minimal specialist cyber capacity), the National Fraud Intelligence Bureau, Action Fraud (the reporting centre), and a constellation of regulators and intelligence agencies including the NCSC, GCHQ, the SFO, and the FCA. The result is a system in which no single body has ownership of the problem, no single budget is allocated to solving it, and no single authority can be held accountable when it is not solved.

The numbers expose the dysfunction. Fraud constitutes 41% of all crime but receives less than 1% of police resources. Of the 20,000 officers recruited under the Police Uplift Programme, only 380 were allocated to fraud. Action Fraud receives more than 300,000 direct reports per year and a further 900,000 from industry, but fewer than 1% of reported cases produce a criminal justice outcome. The City of London Police received £38.7 million in 2023/24 as the national lead force for fraud; this is less than what a single ransomware attack cost Marks & Spencer. The NCSC, which is part of GCHQ and not a law enforcement body, is carrying an increasingly unsustainable burden of incident response, handling 1,727 incident tips in 2024/25, of which 429 required direct support and 204 were classified as nationally significant.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Cyber Crime Act will additionally:

- a) Establish a National Cyber Crime Force as a standalone law enforcement agency, separate from the NCA, the City of London Police, and territorial forces, with sole national responsibility for the investigation and prosecution of serious and organised cybercrime, online fraud, and cyber-enabled economic crime. The Force will absorb the NCA’s National Cyber Crime Unit, the City of London Police’s fraud investigation capability, the National Fraud Intelligence Bureau, and the operational elements of Action Fraud. It will be led by a Director General appointed by the Home Secretary, accountable to Parliament through the Home Affairs Select Committee.
- b) Require the National Cyber Crime Force to achieve, within 24 months, a response standard under which every reported cyber crime and fraud involving a loss of £5,000 or more, or involving a vulnerable victim regardless of loss, receives an active investigation with a named investigating officer. The current model, in which over 99% of reports are logged and filed without investigation, is not policing. It is record-keeping. Progress will end it.
- c) Grant the National Cyber Crime Force extraterritorial investigative powers, including the authority to execute cross-border digital evidence requests, to conduct undercover operations on foreign-hosted platforms, and to work jointly with international partners through Europol, INTERPOL, and bilateral arrangements. The Force will maintain permanent liaison officers in key jurisdictions including the United States, the EU, Singapore, and Australia.

OPERATIONAL

Establishment. The National Cyber Crime Force will be established within 12 months of Royal Assent, with an initial staffing complement of 5,000 officers and specialists. Recruitment will draw on police officers with existing cyber and fraud expertise, civilian analysts, and direct entry from the cybersecurity industry. The Force will be headquartered in London with regional offices in Manchester, Birmingham, Edinburgh, Cardiff, and Belfast.

Funding. The initial annual budget will be £750 million, funded from a combination of the Home Office police grant, a new Digital Crime Levy on technology companies operating in the UK (proportionate to UK user base and revenue), and the proceeds of confiscation orders under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 and the new Cyber Crime Act. For context, the current national expenditure on fraud and cybercrime investigation across all agencies is estimated at well below £200 million. The new budget reflects the true scale of the problem.

Action Fraud replacement. The current Action Fraud reporting system will be replaced within 9 months by a new National Cyber Crime Reporting Service, integrated into the National Cyber Crime Force. Every report will receive an automated risk assessment within 24 hours. Every victim will receive a case update within 14 days. The new service will be designed to GOV.UK standards and will provide victims with a dashboard showing the status of their report, any actions taken, and any intelligence generated. No victim will ever again submit a report and hear nothing.

##### C9.3: Fraud: From Tolerance to Prosecution

The Problem

Fraud is the most common crime in England and Wales, affecting an estimated 3.44 million adults in the year ending March 2025. It costs the country an estimated £219 billion per year. Over £1.17 billion was stolen through payment fraud alone in 2024, with 3.31 million confirmed cases of unauthorised fraud. Authorised push payment fraud, where victims are manipulated into transferring money to criminals, accounted for £450.7 million. Investment scams, though fewer in number, saw losses increase 34% to £144.4 million. Romance scams increased 35% in the first half of 2025. Seventy per cent of all fraud cases are enabled by online platforms, and 16% originate through telecommunications networks.

The state’s response to this epidemic is negligible. There were 4,176 fraud prosecutions in the year ending December 2024. Set against 3.44 million victims, this represents a prosecution rate so low that it functions as an implicit guarantee of impunity for perpetrators. The technology and telecommunications sectors, through whose platforms the vast majority of fraud is enabled and executed, bear minimal accountability. Social media companies, search engines, online marketplaces, and telecommunications providers profit from the infrastructure that makes fraud possible while externalising the cost to victims and the financial services sector. The financial services industry prevented £1.45 billion of unauthorised fraud in 2024, a 16% increase, effectively subsidising the failure of every other sector to act.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Cyber Crime Act will additionally:

- a) Introduce a mandatory fraud prevention duty on technology companies, social media platforms, online marketplaces, telecommunications providers, and any digital intermediary through which fraud is enabled. Platforms will be required to verify the identity of advertisers, to remove fraudulent content within 24 hours of notification, and to cooperate with the National Cyber Crime Force by providing relevant data within 48 hours of a lawful request. Failure to comply will attract penalties of up to 4% of global turnover per incident, enforced by Ofcom with the National Cyber Crime Force as co-regulator.
- b) Create a strict liability offence for technology and telecommunications companies that repeatedly fail to prevent the use of their platforms to commit fraud, where the company has been notified of specific fraud typologies and has failed to implement reasonable and effective preventive measures. The offence will carry unlimited fines and, in cases of persistent and egregious failure, the power to restrict the company’s operations in the United Kingdom.
- c) Mandate real-time fraud data sharing between financial institutions, technology companies, and law enforcement. The current system, in which suspicious activity reports are filed, processed over months, and rarely result in action, will be replaced with a live intelligence-sharing platform operated by the National Cyber Crime Force. Financial institutions and platforms will be required to share transactional fraud indicators in real time, within the limits of data protection law, to enable immediate intervention.
- d) Establish a National Fraud Compensation Fund, funded by the Digital Crime Levy and by proceeds recovered from convicted fraudsters, to compensate victims of fraud who are not otherwise reimbursed by their financial institution. No victim of fraud, whether their loss is £500 or £500,000, should be left without recourse because the perpetrator is overseas, unidentified, or insolvent.

OPERATIONAL

Prosecution targets. The National Cyber Crime Force will be tasked with increasing fraud prosecutions from the current 4,176 per year to a minimum of 20,000 within 36 months. This remains a fraction of the total number of offences committed, but it represents a fivefold increase from the current baseline and will, for the first time, create a credible deterrent effect. The Force will prioritise high-harm cases (vulnerable victims, life savings lost, organised fraud networks) and high-volume cases (platform-enabled mass fraud where a single prosecution can disrupt thousands of offences).

SIM farm ban enforcement. The government’s ban on SIM farms, introduced in April 2025, will be enforced aggressively by the National Cyber Crime Force in coordination with Ofcom and the Malebranche (C3). The possession, manufacture, or distribution of SIM farm equipment for the purpose of facilitating fraud or enabling unlawful bulk communications will carry a maximum sentence of 5 years under the Cyber Crime Act.

##### C9.4: Abolition of the Online Safety Act and the Children’s Online Protection Act

The Problem

The Online Safety Act 2023 is a censorship statute disguised as a child protection measure. Its legislative history, its operational record, and its structural design all point to the same conclusion: it was built not to protect children, but to give the state discretionary power over lawful speech on the internet. Progress will repeal it in its entirety and replace it with legislation that does what the Online Safety Act claimed to do but never did: protect children online, while guaranteeing the freedom of expression that is the birthright of every British citizen.

The Act’s provenance is disqualifying. Its passage through Parliament was shaped by organisations whose primary function is the suppression of political dissent. Hope Not Hate, which describes itself as an anti-extremism charity, gave both written and oral evidence to the Public Bill Committee in May 2022. Its written submission to Parliament explicitly complained that protections for “democratically important” content could be exploited by “far-right activists and organisations”; in other words, that the Act’s free speech provisions were too generous. Hope Not Hate’s oral evidence was delivered by its political organiser, Liron Velleman. In January 2026, Velleman pleaded guilty at Highbury Corner Magistrates’ Court to attempting to engage in sexual communication with a child and attempting to cause a child aged 13 to 15 to look at an image of sexual activity. He had sent naked photographs of himself to a person he believed to be a 13-year-old girl, asked whether she was a virgin, demanded to see her in her school uniform, and requested explicit images in return. He was caught by a Metropolitan Police decoy operation. The man who sat before a House of Commons committee and helped shape Britain’s online child protection law was himself, at the time or shortly thereafter, a predator targeting children online. This is not an unfortunate coincidence. It is an indictment of the entire ecosystem of self-appointed “online safety” organisations whose access to Parliament and whose influence over legislation has never been subjected to the scrutiny it demands.

The Centre for Countering Digital Hate, whose CEO Imran Ahmed was the first witness to the Bill’s pre-legislative Joint Committee in September 2021 and whose website boasts that “Our campaigning resulted in the Online Safety Act in the UK,” is an organisation that exists to pressure platforms into removing lawful political speech. Ahmed’s US green card has been revoked by the Trump Administration. The US State Department has designated members of the broader “censorship industrial complex,” of which the CCDH is a conspicuous component, for sanctions. These are the architects of British internet regulation. Their interests were ideological, not protective.

The Act’s operational record confirms the structural critique. After receiving Royal Assent in October 2023, the Act did not begin substantive enforcement until March 2025, an implementation lag of seventeen months during which children were no safer than before. In its first year, Ofcom opened 21 investigations and issued its largest fine at just over £1 million. In the same period, the Internet Watch Foundation identified 312,030 confirmed instances of child sexual abuse material, a record; AI-generated CSAM videos increased from 13 to 3,440 (a 26,362% increase); and the NCA estimated that up to 840,000 adults in the United Kingdom pose varying degrees of sexual risk to children. The Online Safety Act contributed nothing measurable to the prevention of these harms. What it did produce was an architecture of regulatory power under which a government-appointed regulator can compel platforms to remove or restrict access to content that is entirely lawful but that the regulator, guided by codes of practice developed in consultation with organisations like Hope Not Hate and the CCDH, deems “harmful.” The removal of the “legal but harmful” provisions for adults in November 2022, presented as a concession to free speech, was replaced by user empowerment duties and terms-of-service enforcement mechanisms that achieve the same censorship outcome through a different procedural route.

The Act’s categorisation system, under which platforms designated as Category 1 services face the most onerous duties, was delayed by the need for secondary legislation to set threshold conditions. Category 1 duties include obligations around user identity verification, transparency reporting, and content moderation standards that collectively give the regulator influence over the editorial policies of private platforms. The Act grants the Secretary of State powers to amend codes of practice to reflect government policy, a provision described by multiple witnesses during the Bill’s passage as a “chilling potential infringement on the independence of the regulator.” In effect, the government can direct the regulator, and the regulator can direct the platforms, and the platforms can suppress the speech. The chain of censorship is complete, and at no point does it require a court order, a criminal conviction, or any finding that the suppressed speech was unlawful.

Progress’ position is unequivocal. Freedom of expression online is an absolute right for any content that does not constitute a direct incitement to violence or a criminal offence under existing law. The protection of children online is a legitimate and urgent objective, but it does not require, and must never be used as a pretext for, the regulation of lawful adult speech. These two objectives, freedom and protection, are not in tension. They require different instruments. The Online Safety Act conflated them deliberately, using the urgency of child protection to smuggle in a general-purpose censorship regime. Progress will separate them.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Children’s Online Protection Act will:

- a) Repeal the Online Safety Act 2023 in its entirety. All codes of practice, guidance, enforcement programmes, investigations, and regulatory apparatus established under the Act will be wound down within 6 months of Royal Assent. Ofcom’s online safety regulatory functions under the Act will cease. The categorisation of services, the illegal content duties as they apply to lawful speech, the user empowerment duties, the terms-of-service enforcement mechanisms, and the Secretary of State’s powers to direct codes of practice will all be abolished. Any content that is lawful under existing criminal law will be lawful to publish, share, and access online, without qualification, without regulatory interference, and without the mediation of a government-appointed censor.
- b) Enact a statutory guarantee of freedom of expression online. No public authority, regulator, or government-funded organisation may direct, pressure, incentivise, or request any platform, internet service provider, or communications provider to remove, restrict, demote, or de-amplify any content that is lawful under existing criminal law. This guarantee will be enforceable by any person whose lawful content has been removed or restricted as a consequence of government or regulatory pressure, through an action for judicial review or a claim for damages. The only lawful basis for the removal of content will be: (i) it constitutes a criminal offence under existing law, including but not limited to direct incitement to violence, terrorism offences under the Terrorism Act 2000, child sexual abuse material under the Protection of Children Act 1978, and offences under the Malicious Communications Act 1988; or (ii) it is removed by the platform pursuant to its own terms of service, applied consistently and without government direction.
- c) Establish a Children’s Internet Safety Commission as a standalone statutory body, separate from Ofcom, with the sole mandate of protecting children under 18 from exposure to criminal content online and from being contacted, groomed, or exploited by adults through online platforms. The Commission will have no jurisdiction over lawful adult speech. Its powers will be limited to: requiring platforms to implement robust age verification for services that host pornographic or graphically violent content; requiring platforms to implement effective systems to prevent adults from contacting children they do not know through direct messaging or private channels; requiring platforms to deploy certified hash-matching and AI detection tools for child sexual abuse material; and enforcing mandatory reporting of CSAM to the NCA within 4 hours of discovery.
- d) Require all platforms likely to be accessed by children under 16 to offer a verified “child account” mode, in which direct messaging from unknown accounts is disabled by default, algorithmic recommendation of content is restricted to age-appropriate categories, and in-app purchasing is disabled without parental authorisation. Platforms will be required to make the child account mode the default for any account identified as belonging to a user under 16, with parental override available through a verified parental account. These are practical, technical measures that protect children from specific, identifiable risks. They do not require the regulation of what adults may say, read, or share.
- e) Prohibit any public body, regulator, or publicly funded organisation from maintaining, funding, or participating in any programme, partnership, or initiative whose purpose or effect is the identification, flagging, reporting, or suppression of lawful speech online. This includes but is not limited to counter-disinformation units, trusted flagger programmes, and any arrangement under which government or government-funded bodies communicate removal requests to platforms outside the framework of a court order or criminal investigation. The Southport riots of 2024 were invoked to justify expanded online censorship. The correct response to disinformation is more speech, better information, and the prosecution of those who commit criminal offences. It is not the empowerment of a regulator to decide which truths the public may hear.

OPERATIONAL

Transition. The repeal of the Online Safety Act and the establishment of the Children’s Internet Safety Commission will be completed within 6 months of Royal Assent. During the transition period, Ofcom’s existing child protection enforcement actions (specifically those relating to age verification for pornography providers, CSAM detection, and child safety on services accessed by children) will be transferred to the new Commission. All other enforcement actions, investigations, and regulatory programmes under the Online Safety Act will be discontinued.

Children’s Internet Safety Commission. The Commission will be established as a standalone body with an initial staffing complement of 300, led by a Commissioner appointed by the Lord Chancellor (not the Secretary of State for DSIT) and accountable to Parliament through the Education Select Committee. Annual budget of £50 million, funded by the Digital Crime Levy. The Commission will have no role in regulating adult speech, no power to designate lawful content as “harmful,” and no authority to direct platforms on matters unrelated to child protection.

Review of OSA-era enforcement. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Children’s Internet Safety Commission will publish a review of all enforcement actions taken by Ofcom under the Online Safety Act, identifying which actions related to the protection of children from criminal content and which related to the suppression of lawful speech. Any organisation that provided evidence or advice to Ofcom, to the Public Bill Committee, or to the Joint Committee on the draft Online Safety Bill and whose representatives have subsequently been convicted of criminal offences, sanctioned by foreign governments, or found to have made materially misleading representations to Parliament will be identified by name. The review will be laid before Parliament.

##### C9.5: Child Sexual Abuse Material: Zero Tolerance Online

The Problem

The Internet Watch Foundation acted on 312,030 reports confirmed as containing child sexual abuse material in 2025, the worst year in its 30-year history. This represents an 830% increase since the IWF was empowered to proactively seek out such material in 2014. In 2024, 21% of the material reviewed by the IWF was classified as Category A, depicting the most extreme forms of abuse including penetrative sexual activity, bestiality, and sadism. The National Crime Agency estimates that between 710,000 and 840,000 adults in the United Kingdom pose varying degrees of sexual risk to children, and that offending by 10 to 17-year-olds accounts for approximately half of all police-recorded child sexual abuse crimes.

The proliferation of AI-generated child sexual abuse material constitutes an emergent crisis of extraordinary severity. In 2025, the IWF discovered 3,440 AI-generated videos of child sexual abuse, an increase of 26,362% from the 13 videos found in 2024. Of those videos, 65% were classified as Category A. AI-generated content now accounts for 56% of all illegal content identified by the IWF, up from 41% the previous year. The technology to generate photorealistic child sexual abuse material is now available to anyone with minimal technical knowledge. Fine-tuned AI models specifically optimised to produce such material are being shared on dark web forums. The Crime and Policing Bill has introduced a new offence covering AI models optimised to create child sexual abuse material, but the broader problem, the capacity of mainstream generative AI tools to be manipulated for this purpose, requires a systemic response that goes beyond criminal sanctions for model developers.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Cyber Crime Act will additionally:

- a) Create a statutory obligation on all providers of generative AI systems available in the United Kingdom to implement and maintain effective safeguards against the generation of child sexual abuse material. The obligation will require testing, red-teaming, and independent audit of these safeguards before any generative AI system is made available to the public. Failure to implement effective safeguards will be a criminal offence carrying a maximum sentence of 10 years and an unlimited fine. This is not a regulatory duty to be managed through codes of practice. It is a criminal prohibition, because the generation of child sexual abuse material, whether by a human or by a machine, is the generation of child sexual abuse material.
- b) Mandate that all online platforms operating in the UK deploy certified hash-matching technology (such as PhotoDNA and the IWF’s hash list) and AI-based detection tools for the proactive identification and removal of child sexual abuse material. Platforms that fail to deploy such tools within 6 months of the Act coming into force will be subject to enforcement action by the Children’s Internet Safety Commission, including fines and, for repeat non-compliance, ISP-level blocking.
- c) Introduce mandatory reporting obligations for all technology companies, internet service providers, cloud storage providers, and communications platforms. Any such company that becomes aware of child sexual abuse material on its platform or infrastructure must report the material to the National Crime Agency within 4 hours of discovery and preserve all associated metadata, account information, and communications for a minimum of 12 months. Failure to report within the specified period will be a criminal offence. The United States has operated mandatory reporting through NCMEC since 2008; there is no justification for Britain’s continued failure to legislate equivalent requirements.
- d) Increase maximum sentences for the production, distribution, and possession of child sexual abuse material to 14 years for production and distribution and 7 years for possession, with mandatory minimum sentences of 5 years for production and distribution and 2 years for possession. Current sentencing practice fails to reflect the severity of these offences and the lifelong harm they inflict on victims.

OPERATIONAL

IWF funding and powers. The Internet Watch Foundation’s annual budget will be supplemented by a statutory grant of no less than £30 million per year, funded by the Digital Crime Levy, tripling its current capacity. The IWF will be designated as a statutory body with enhanced legal powers to issue takedown notices directly to hosting providers, domain registrars, and content delivery networks, with non-compliance treated as a criminal offence.

Specialist NCA unit. Within 6 months, the NCA will establish a dedicated AI-CSAM Unit, staffed by no fewer than 200 specialist officers and AI technical experts, tasked exclusively with the identification, investigation, and prosecution of offenders who use artificial intelligence tools to generate, distribute, or possess child sexual abuse material. The unit will work in partnership with the IWF, GCHQ, and international partners including the FBI, Europol, and the Five Eyes alliance.

##### C9.6: Critical National Infrastructure Cyber Defence

The Problem

The NCSC has stated, in successive annual reviews, that the gap between the cyber threat to Britain’s critical national infrastructure and the ability of CNI owners and operators to defend against it is widening. The majority of the UK’s critical national infrastructure is privately owned. The operators of energy grids, water systems, transport networks, telecommunications infrastructure, and financial market platforms have commercial incentives that do not always align with the level of cyber resilience required to protect the public from the consequences of a successful attack. The Synnovis ransomware attack in August 2024, which disrupted NHS blood-testing services across London for weeks, demonstrated what happens when a single point of failure in a critical supply chain is exploited. The retail sector attacks by the DragonForce ransomware group on Marks & Spencer, Co-op, and Harrods in 2025 demonstrated the pace at which sophisticated criminal groups can strike multiple targets. The NCSC identified state-sponsored campaigns from China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea targeting UK critical infrastructure throughout 2024 and 2025.

The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, introduced in the King’s Speech, proposes to strengthen the regulatory framework for CNI cyber resilience by expanding the scope of the existing Network and Information Systems Regulations. This is a necessary but insufficient step. The bill addresses regulatory compliance. It does not address the fundamental question of who defends Britain’s critical infrastructure against state-sponsored attacks that exceed the defensive capabilities of private sector operators, however well-regulated they may be.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Critical National Infrastructure (Cyber Defence) Act will:

- a) Designate cyber defence of critical national infrastructure as a core national security function, to be coordinated by a new National Cyber Defence Command operating under the authority of the National Security Council. The Command will integrate the defensive capabilities of the NCSC, the offensive capabilities of the National Cyber Force (the joint GCHQ/Ministry of Defence cyber operations unit), and the law enforcement capabilities of the National Cyber Crime Force established under C9.2. Its mandate will be the active defence of UK critical infrastructure against state-sponsored and sophisticated criminal threats.
- b) Impose mandatory cyber resilience standards on all designated critical national infrastructure operators, to be set by the NCSC and enforced by sector-specific regulators. Standards will include mandatory penetration testing at specified intervals, mandatory incident reporting within 2 hours of detection, mandatory deployment of specified defensive technologies, and mandatory participation in NCSC threat-sharing programmes. Non-compliant operators will be subject to financial penalties and, in cases of persistent non-compliance, to the appointment of a government-nominated cyber resilience director with executive authority over the operator’s digital security.
- c) Create a statutory duty on all CNI operators to maintain tested and validated cyber incident response and recovery plans, subject to annual audit by the NCSC. The plans must demonstrate the capacity to restore essential services within defined recovery time objectives: 4 hours for the most critical services (emergency services, energy supply, water treatment) and 24 hours for all other designated services. The Synnovis attack demonstrated that the absence of tested recovery plans can prolong the impact of an attack from days to weeks.
- d) Establish a National Cyber Reserve, a pool of vetted and trained civilian cybersecurity professionals who can be mobilised to support the response to a significant cyber incident affecting critical national infrastructure. Reserve members will be drawn from the private sector cybersecurity industry, will receive ongoing training and security clearance, and will be callable on terms similar to those governing military reservists. The reserve will provide the surge capacity that the NCSC currently lacks when multiple significant incidents occur simultaneously.

OPERATIONAL

National Cyber Defence Command. The Command will be established within 12 months, co-located with the NCSC in London with a secondary operations centre in a geographically separate location for resilience. Initial staffing complement of 1,500, rising to 3,000 within 36 months. Annual budget of £500 million, drawn from the defence and security budget, reflecting the reality that cyber defence is now as operationally critical as conventional military capability.

CNI resilience audit. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, the NCSC will complete a comprehensive cyber resilience assessment of all designated critical national infrastructure operators. The results will be classified but a summary, identifying systemic weaknesses without compromising operational security, will be reported to the Intelligence and Security Committee and the relevant sector-specific regulator. Operators identified as presenting unacceptable risk will be given 90 days to remediate or face regulatory intervention.

Cyber Reserve. The National Cyber Reserve will be established within 18 months, with an initial target of 2,000 vetted members. The Reserve will be managed by the National Cyber Defence Command and will conduct regular exercises simulating simultaneous attacks on multiple CNI sectors.

###### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The C9 Cybercrime and Online Harms framework is built on three pieces of primary legislation: the Cyber Crime Act, the Children’s Online Protection Act (which repeals and replaces the Online Safety Act 2023), and the Critical National Infrastructure (Cyber Defence) Act. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, departmental procurement, or existing administrative mechanisms.

###### Cyber Crime Act (new)

On the face of the Act: Repeal of the Computer Misuse Act 1990. New offences for ransomware, botnet operation, malware-as-a-service, AI-enabled fraud, and unauthorised data harvesting. Statutory public interest defence for cybersecurity professionals. Aggravated offences for attacks on critical national infrastructure. Strict liability offence for ransom payments by public bodies and CNI operators without ministerial exemption. Extended territorial jurisdiction. Establishment of the National Cyber Crime Force with sole national responsibility for serious cybercrime and fraud investigation. Response standard: active investigation for all reported cybercrimes involving losses of £5,000 or more. Mandatory fraud prevention duty on technology and telecommunications companies. Strict liability offence for repeated platform failure to prevent fraud. Real-time fraud data sharing mandate. National Fraud Compensation Fund. Statutory obligation on generative AI providers to prevent generation of child sexual abuse material (criminal offence, maximum 10 years). Mandatory hash-matching and AI detection for all platforms. Mandatory CSAM reporting within 4 hours. Increased sentences for CSAM offences (14 years production/distribution, 7 years possession, mandatory minimums).

###### Children’s Online Protection Act (new; repeals Online Safety Act 2023)

On the face of the Act: Repeal of the Online Safety Act 2023 in its entirety. Statutory guarantee of freedom of expression online: no public authority may direct platforms to remove lawful content. Establishment of the Children’s Internet Safety Commission (standalone body, sole mandate of child protection, no jurisdiction over lawful adult speech). Mandatory age verification for pornographic and graphically violent services. Mandatory child account modes for platforms accessed by under-16s. Mandatory prevention of unsolicited adult-to-child direct messaging. Prohibition on public bodies maintaining or funding programmes for the suppression of lawful online speech, including counter-disinformation units and trusted flagger programmes. Review of all OSA-era enforcement actions. Named identification of organisations whose representatives have been convicted of criminal offences or sanctioned by foreign governments.

###### Critical National Infrastructure (Cyber Defence) Act (new)

On the face of the Act: Designation of CNI cyber defence as a core national security function. Establishment of the National Cyber Defence Command under the National Security Council. Mandatory cyber resilience standards for all designated CNI operators, enforced by sector regulators. Mandatory penetration testing, 2-hour incident reporting, and deployment of specified defensive technologies. Recovery time objectives: 4 hours for most critical services, 24 hours for all others. Annual audit of incident response and recovery plans. Establishment of the National Cyber Reserve.

Delivered operationally: Statutory defence for cybersecurity professionals on Royal Assent. CPS/NCSC joint prosecution guidance within 90 days. National Cyber Crime Force established within 12 months (5,000 staff, £750 million annual budget, headquartered London with regional offices). Action Fraud replaced by National Cyber Crime Reporting Service within 9 months. Fraud prosecution target: 20,000 per year within 36 months (up from 4,176). Online Safety Act repealed and Children’s Internet Safety Commission established within 6 months (300 staff, £50 million annual budget, Commissioner appointed by Lord Chancellor). Review of all OSA-era enforcement actions within 90 days. IWF statutory grant £30 million per year. NCA AI-CSAM Unit (200 specialists) within 6 months. National Cyber Defence Command within 12 months (1,500 staff rising to 3,000, £500 million annual budget). CNI resilience audit within 6 months. National Cyber Reserve (2,000 members) within 18 months.

The digital world is not a separate jurisdiction. It is not a space in which the normal obligations of the state to protect its citizens are suspended in deference to corporate innovation or technological complexity. Equally, it is not a space in which the normal rights of citizens to speak freely are suspended in deference to the sensitivities of politicians, regulators, or the constellation of publicly funded organisations that have built careers on the suppression of inconvenient speech. The internet is the space in which the majority of theft now occurs, in which children are sexually exploited at an industrial scale, in which hostile states conduct espionage and sabotage, and in which the critical infrastructure on which every citizen depends is under persistent attack. These are law enforcement and national security challenges. They require law enforcement and national security responses. They do not require, and they will never justify, a government censor sitting between British citizens and the lawful expression of their opinions. Progress will protect children, prosecute criminals, defend critical infrastructure, and guarantee the absolute right of every British adult to speak, publish, and share any content that does not constitute a criminal offence under existing law. The Online Safety Act failed on every count: it did not protect children, it did not prosecute criminals, it did not defend infrastructure, and it threatened the liberty of every citizen. It will be repealed, and it will not be mourned.

C10. Knife Crime and Street Violence

Governing Principle

In the year ending March 2025, police in England and Wales recorded approximately 53,000 offences involving a knife or sharp instrument. In 2023/24, 262 people were killed with knives, accounting for 46% of all homicides. Knives were involved in 49% of attempted homicides, 40% of completed homicides, and 28% of robberies. In London alone, knife-enabled robbery accounted for 59% of all knife crime, with 10,017 knife-point robberies recorded in 2024/25, more than double the 4,494 recorded in the final year of the previous mayoralty. The Metropolitan Police recorded the highest rate of knife offences in England and Wales at 182 per 100,000 population. NHS hospitals recorded 3,500 admissions for assault by sharp object in 2024/25. Forty-eight per cent of knife crime victims in London were aged 25 or under. In the year ending March 2024, 57 people under the age of 25 were killed in knife attacks nationally, 17 of them under 16.

Simultaneously, Britain’s streets have become an open market for organised theft. Snatch theft more than doubled in the year ending June 2024, reaching an estimated 78,000 incidents, the equivalent of more than 200 per day. Mobile phone theft in London increased by 40% in 2024 to over 70,000 incidents, with 61,233 phones snatched on the streets of central London in 2025 alone. The annual financial cost to London residents and visitors is estimated at £70 million. Street thefts nationally rose by 50% in 2024, reaching 483,000 incidents. Robbery increased by 6% to over 81,000 offences. Shoplifting hit a record 529,994 offences in the year ending June 2025, a 13% increase on the previous year and 50% higher than pre-pandemic levels. Organised criminal gangs, many operating on mopeds and e-bikes capable of speeds exceeding 60 mph, execute serial thefts with near-impunity, knowing that the probability of being caught, charged, and imprisoned is negligible.

The criminal justice response to these crimes is contemptible. Of the approximately 20,754 knife and offensive weapon offences formally dealt with by the courts in the year ending March 2025, only 30.9% resulted in an immediate custodial sentence. The average sentence for knife possession was 7.9 months. For a crime that carries the potential to end a life, the typical consequence is a sentence shorter than a university term. The mandatory minimum for a second knife possession offence is six months, a sentence that, even if served in full, returns the offender to the streets within half a year. For children, the picture is worse: only 7% of juvenile knife offenders received immediate custody, with 61% receiving community sentences. Threatening with a knife or offensive weapon, an offence that causes severe psychological trauma and often precedes lethal violence, carries a maximum of four years. The charge rate for robbery offences, the category that captures most knife-enabled street crime, took an average of 67 days to process in the year ending March 2025. For theft from the person, the charge rate is derisory: over 70% of cases are closed with no suspect identified.

The government’s response has been the Crime and Policing Bill, introduced in February 2025, which it has branded “Ronan’s Law” after Ronan Kanda, murdered in 2022 by two teenagers using ninja swords purchased online. The Bill creates a new offence of possessing a knife with intent to cause harm (maximum four years), increases penalties for selling weapons to under-18s, gives police powers to seize knives from private property, and introduces online sales regulations. These are incremental measures applied to an emergency. A new possession-with-intent offence carrying a four-year maximum, in a system where the average custodial sentence for knife possession is under eight months, is not a deterrent. It is a gesture. The government’s own target of halving knife crime within a decade requires sustained annual reductions of 7 to 8%, a pace that has never been achieved outside pandemic-induced lockdowns. Progress does not intend to manage knife crime over a decade. Progress intends to end it.

The root causes of knife crime and street violence are not mysterious. They are the intersection of three failures that this policy framework addresses comprehensively: a failure of deterrence (C2), a failure of policing (C2, C5), and a failure of intervention in the lives of young people before they reach the point of carrying a weapon. C2 established the police numbers, the prison capacity, and the sentencing framework required to make the threat of punishment credible. C5 established the neighbourhood policing model, the mission clarity, and the accountability structures required to make the police presence visible and effective. This document, C10, addresses the specific operational challenge of knife crime and street violence: the weapons supply chain, the enforcement architecture, the technological tools for detection and disruption, the street robbery epidemic, and the targeted intervention programmes that will prevent the next generation of young people from picking up a knife in the first place.

The principle is the same as it is throughout Progress’ crime framework: society exists to serve the law-abiding, not the law-breaking. A teenager who walks to school in fear of being stabbed is not being served. A woman whose phone is snatched from her hand by a moped-mounted thief is not being served. A shopkeeper who watches organised gangs strip his shelves while the police decline to attend is not being served. Progress will make Britain’s streets safe. Not in a decade. Now.

C10.1: Knife Possession, Supply, and Sentencing

The Problem

The current legislative framework for knife crime is a patchwork of statutes accumulated over decades, none of which were designed for the scale and character of the present crisis. Section 139 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 makes it an offence to possess a knife or bladed article in a public place, carrying a maximum of four years’ imprisonment. Section 1 of the Prevention of Crime Act 1953 criminalises possession of an offensive weapon in a public place, also with a four-year maximum. Section 315 of the Sentencing Act 2020 provides for a mandatory minimum sentence of six months for a second or subsequent possession offence, but courts routinely decline to impose even this modest minimum. In the year ending June 2025, 20,734 knife and offensive weapon offences were formally dealt with by the courts. Only 31.1% resulted in immediate custody. The average custodial sentence for offensive weapon possession has actually decreased by 16% over the past decade, from 8.6 months to 7.2 months. The system is becoming more lenient, not less, in the face of a crisis that has claimed thousands of lives.

The supply side is equally dysfunctional. Despite successive bans on zombie knives, machetes, and ninja swords, and despite the government’s new online sales restrictions, the weapons that kill people on British streets are overwhelmingly ordinary kitchen knives and everyday bladed tools. The Home Office’s own data confirms that knives or daggers accounted for 44% of sharp instrument homicides, with kitchen knives at 19%. Banning exotic weapon types, while politically visible, does not address the fundamental reality that the weapon of choice in most knife crime is already in every household in Britain. The supply-side interventions that matter are not bans on specific blade types. They are the detection, seizure, and punishment of individuals who carry any blade with criminal intent.

Sixty-eight per cent of knife offenders dealt with by the courts are first-time offenders, a figure that has remained broadly stable for a decade. This means the current deterrence framework is failing to prevent people from carrying knives in the first instance. The 32% who are repeat offenders demonstrate that the sentences imposed on first conviction are insufficient to deter reoffending. Both populations require different but equally serious responses. For first-time carriers, the sentence must be severe enough to function as genuine deterrence. For repeat carriers, the sentence must be long enough to incapacitate and to communicate unambiguously that carrying a weapon on a British street will result in the forfeiture of years of liberty.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Street Safety Act will:

- a) Increase the maximum sentence for possession of a knife or bladed article in a public place (s.139 CJA 1988) from four years to ten years’ imprisonment. Increase the maximum sentence for possession of an offensive weapon in a public place (s.1 PCA 1953) from four years to ten years. Increase the maximum sentence for the new offence of possession with intent to cause harm (Crime and Policing Bill) from four years to fourteen years. These increases bring knife possession sentencing into alignment with the severity of the harm that knife carrying enables. A four-year maximum for carrying a weapon that can end a life in seconds is an absurdity. Progress will end it.
- b) Introduce a statutory minimum sentence of two years’ immediate custody for any adult convicted of a first offence of knife or offensive weapon possession in a public place. This replaces the current regime in which first-time possession routinely results in a community sentence or a suspended sentence. The minimum will be disapplied only where the court is satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that exceptional circumstances exist that would make the minimum sentence unjust, and those circumstances must be recorded in writing and published. For juveniles aged 16 and 17, the minimum will be twelve months in a Young Offender Institution. For children aged 10 to 15, the court must impose a mandatory referral to the Youth Violence Intervention Programme (established below) with a Serious Violence Reduction Order as a condition of the referral.
- c) Apply Progress’ compound sentencing framework (C2.3) to knife and offensive weapon offences. A second conviction for knife possession will carry a minimum of three years (the two-year minimum multiplied by 1.5x). A third conviction will carry a minimum of four years (2x). A fourth and subsequent conviction will carry a minimum of six years (3x). These sentences will be served in full under C2.3’s abolition of automatic early release for indictable offences. A person convicted of knife possession for the fourth time will serve six years, in full, in a Class B Deterrence Facility (C2.2). The current system, in which repeat knife carriers cycle through community sentences and short custodial terms before eventually killing or being killed, is a moral obscenity. Progress will replace it with certainty.
- d) Create a statutory offence of knife-enabled robbery, distinct from the general offence of robbery under the Theft Act 1968, carrying a minimum sentence of five years’ immediate custody. Where the victim is a child, an elderly person, or a person with a disability, the minimum will be seven years. Where the offence is committed as part of an organised pattern of robbery (three or more offences within a 12-month period), the minimum will be ten years. This addresses the epidemic of knife-point phone snatching, watch theft, and street robbery that has made British streets feel unsafe for millions of citizens. The current robbery charge rate of approximately 10%, combined with sentences that rarely exceed three years, has created a business model for organised street crime. Progress will destroy that business model.
- e) Create a statutory offence of manufacturing, importing, or distributing weapons for criminal use, carrying a minimum sentence of seven years. This targets the commercial supply chain that profits from the sale of weapons designed or marketed for violence. Any person who manufactures, imports, or sells a prohibited weapon, or who sells any bladed article in circumstances where they know or ought to know that it will be used for criminal purposes, will face a sentence designed to make the trade economically and personally ruinous.
- f) Legalise the possession and use of defensive sprays (pepper spray, PAVA spray, and equivalent incapacitant devices) by women for the purpose of personal self-defence. Under current law, these devices are classified as firearms under section 5(1)(b) of the Firearms Act 1968, making their possession a criminal offence carrying a maximum sentence of ten years’ imprisonment. This is an absurdity. A woman walking home at night who carries a £10 canister of pepper spray faces a longer maximum sentence than a man convicted of carrying a knife. The law as it stands prioritises the safety of the attacker over the safety of the victim. Progress will reverse that priority. Women aged 18 and over will be permitted to purchase, possess, and use approved defensive spray devices, subject to a registration scheme administered by local police forces. Approved devices will be limited to those meeting specifications set by the Home Office (maximum capacity, concentration, and range), sold only by licensed retailers, and registered to a named individual at the point of sale. Use of a defensive spray in circumstances that do not constitute lawful self-defence will remain a criminal offence. The right to self-defence is fundamental. For too long, the law has demanded that women rely entirely on a police force that cannot be everywhere at once and a criminal justice system that prosecutes fewer than 3% of reported rapes. Progress will give women a legal means to protect themselves.

OPERATIONAL

CPS prosecution directive. Within 6 weeks of Royal Assent, the Director of Public Prosecutions will issue a directive requiring that all knife possession offences be charged at the highest applicable level. No knife offence will be downgraded for administrative convenience. Where a knife is used in the commission of another offence (robbery, assault, threatening behaviour), the knife element must be charged as a separate and additional count. Plea bargains that involve dropping knife counts in exchange for guilty pleas on lesser offences will be prohibited except with the personal authorisation of a senior CPS district manager, whose decision must be recorded and auditable.

Sentencing Council revision. The Sentencing Council’s guidelines for knife and offensive weapon offences will be revised within 6 weeks of Royal Assent by a panel appointed by the Lord Chancellor to reflect the new statutory framework. The revised guidelines will establish the two-year minimum as the starting point for first-time adult possession, with upward departure for aggravating factors including location (near schools, hospitals, or transport hubs), time (night-time offences), and context (gang association, concurrent drug offences).

C10.2: Detection, Enforcement, and the Knife Crime Strike Force

The Problem

The police’s primary tool for detecting knife carrying is stop and search, exercised under section 1 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (where reasonable suspicion exists) and section 60 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 (where a senior officer authorises suspicionless search in a defined area). Stop and search is politically contentious, operationally imprecise, and disproportionately applied to young Black men. The result is that it has been progressively constrained by political pressure, judicial scrutiny, and institutional caution. Officers are reluctant to use it. Supervisors are reluctant to authorise it. The communities in which knife crime is most concentrated are simultaneously the communities in which stop and search is most resented and most needed.

The consequence of this paralysis is that knife carriers operate with a high degree of confidence that they will not be detected. The probability of being stopped, searched, found in possession, charged, convicted, and sentenced to immediate custody is vanishingly small. For every 53,000 recorded knife offences, there were approximately 20,000 convictions and 6,400 immediate custodial sentences. The gap between the number of people carrying knives on British streets and the number who face any meaningful consequence is enormous.

Technology offers a partial solution that has been almost entirely ignored. Knife detection technology, using millimetre-wave scanning, AI-powered video analytics, and metal detection archways, has been trialled in transport hubs and public spaces internationally with promising results. Britain has been slow to deploy these technologies at scale, in part because of civil liberties concerns and in part because of the absence of any strategic coordination between forces, transport authorities, and local government.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Street Safety Act will additionally:

- a) Establish a National Knife Crime Strike Force as a specialist unit within the National Crime Agency, with a staffing complement of 500 officers seconded from territorial forces and directly recruited specialists. The Strike Force will have a single mission: the identification, disruption, and prosecution of individuals and networks responsible for serious knife crime, knife-enabled robbery, and the supply of weapons for criminal use. It will operate across force boundaries, coordinate intelligence from all 43 territorial forces, and maintain a national knife crime intelligence database linking offenders, incidents, weapons, and geographic patterns. Local forces investigate local knife crime. The Strike Force targets the organised networks: the county lines operations that arm teenagers, the moped robbery gangs that terrorise city centres, the online marketplaces that sell prohibited weapons, and the cross-border supply chains that bring machetes and zombie-style knives into Britain.
- b) Create a statutory framework for Knife Detection Zones. The Home Secretary will have power, on the recommendation of a chief constable and with the approval of the local Police and Crime Commissioner, to designate any public area as a Knife Detection Zone for a renewable period of up to 12 months. Within a designated Zone, police will have authority to deploy: walk-through metal detection archways at entry points to transport hubs, shopping centres, entertainment venues, and public events; AI-powered CCTV analytics trained to identify concealed weapons by gait, posture, and behavioural indicators; and mobile scanning units deployed to street-level hotspots. Persons entering a Knife Detection Zone will be deemed to have consented to electronic screening. Alerts generated by screening technology will constitute reasonable grounds for stop and search under PACE section 1. This converts stop and search from a discretionary, subjective, and politically fraught decision into an objective, technology-led, and evidence-based process.
- c) Reform the legal framework for section 60 authorisations. The current requirement for a senior officer to authorise suspicionless stop and search within a defined area will be retained, but the threshold for authorisation will be lowered from “reasonable belief” that serious violence “may” occur to a test of “reasonable grounds to suspect” that serious violence is occurring or is likely to occur. The maximum duration of an initial section 60 authorisation will be extended from 24 hours to 72 hours, renewable. Forces that deploy section 60 in Knife Detection Zones will benefit from the technological evidence base generated by the Zone’s detection infrastructure, substantially reducing the risk of disproportionate or arbitrary application.

OPERATIONAL

Knife Detection Zone deployment. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, the Home Office will fund and coordinate the deployment of Knife Detection Zones in the 50 highest knife-crime areas in England and Wales, as identified by the ONS police force area data. Priority areas will include major transport hubs (rail stations, bus stations, Underground stations), town centres and high streets with the highest robbery and knife offence rates, and areas surrounding schools in high-crime postcodes. The deployment will be funded by a £100 million capital allocation from the Street Safety Fund (established below), with ongoing operational costs met by local forces supplemented by Home Office grant.

Strike Force operational launch. The National Knife Crime Strike Force will be operational within 6 months of Royal Assent. Its first operational priorities will be: dismantling the moped and e-bike robbery networks operating in London, Manchester, and Birmingham; disrupting the online marketplace for prohibited weapons; and targeting the county lines networks that supply knives to juveniles alongside drugs. The Strike Force will publish quarterly performance reports: arrests, charges, convictions, weapons seized, networks disrupted.

Stop and search transparency. Every stop and search conducted in a Knife Detection Zone will be automatically logged with the technology-generated alert that triggered it, the outcome of the search, and the demographic data of the person searched. This data will be published monthly by force area. The objective is to demonstrate that technology-led stop and search is more effective, more targeted, and less discriminatory than the discretionary model it supplements. Where the data shows disproportionality that cannot be explained by the geographic distribution of knife crime, forces will be required to adjust their deployment.

C10.3: Street Robbery and the Moped Crime Epidemic

The Problem

Britain has become the phone theft capital of Europe. An estimated 230 phones are stolen from people’s hands every day, nearly double the rate five years ago. London accounts for 42% of all phone thefts in the country and 16% of all phone thefts recorded across Europe. In 2024, over 70,000 mobile phones were stolen in London, a 40% increase on the previous year. The financial cost is estimated at £70 million per year in London alone, with the average stolen device valued at approximately £1,200 and 80% of stolen phones being iPhones. Phone theft has increased by 425% since 2021.

The operational model is brazen and industrialised. Thieves on mopeds and high-powered e-bikes, often capable of speeds exceeding 60 mph, snatch phones from victims’ hands in broad daylight. They operate in pairs: one rides, one grabs. Phones are immediately placed in Faraday bags or switched to aeroplane mode to prevent tracking. They are then passed through a laundering chain: wiped, shipped overseas (frequently to markets in Africa and Asia), and resold. The Metropolitan Police dismantled a single network suspected of smuggling up to 40,000 stolen phones from Britain. This is not petty theft. It is organised crime operating at an industrial scale.

The police response has been operationally limited. HMICFRS described the charge rates for serious acquisitive crime as “unacceptable and unsustainable,” finding that “too many offenders remain at liberty and most victims aren’t getting the justice they deserve.” Operation Opal, the national intelligence unit for serious organised acquisitive crime, launched an intelligence probe into the stolen phone market in September 2024. The Metropolitan Police’s Operation Viper and Operation Swipe have produced localised reductions, but the national picture remains one of escalation. The charge rate for theft from the person remains below 3%. Victims know, and criminals know, that the likelihood of facing any consequence is negligible.

Knife-enabled robbery represents the most dangerous intersection of these trends. In 2024/25, there were 10,017 robberies involving knives in London, compared to 4,494 under the previous mayoralty. The Metropolitan Police’s own data shows that 60% of knife-enabled crime in London is knife-enabled robbery. Victims are threatened with blades for their phones, watches, jewellery, and bags.
