The trauma is lasting. The criminals are, in many cases, the same organised networks running the moped theft operations, now escalating from snatch theft to armed robbery as the impunity deepens.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Street Safety Act will additionally:

- a) Create a statutory offence of organised street robbery, defined as three or more robbery or theft-from-person offences committed by the same individual or identifiable network within a 12-month period. The offence will carry a minimum sentence of ten years. Where the offences are committed using a motor vehicle (including mopeds, motorcycles, and e-bikes), an additional mandatory disqualification from driving for life will apply, and the vehicle will be subject to mandatory forfeiture and destruction. The current practice of treating each snatch theft as an isolated incident, to be dealt with individually and usually not at all, ignores the organised and serial nature of the crime. Progress will treat it as what it is: organised crime.
- b) Create a statutory offence of operating or participating in a stolen goods laundering network, carrying a minimum sentence of seven years. This targets the infrastructure that makes phone theft profitable: the middlemen who collect stolen devices, the workshops that wipe and refurbish them, the exporters who ship them overseas, and the online platforms that facilitate resale. The offence will apply to any person who, in the course of a commercial enterprise, handles, processes, transports, exports, or facilitates the sale of goods that they know or ought to know are stolen. Where the network handles more than 100 stolen items within a 12-month period, the minimum sentence will be ten years.
- c) Require all mobile phone manufacturers and network operators selling devices in the United Kingdom to implement a mandatory remote kill-switch capability, activated within 4 hours of a theft report being registered with the police or the network operator. A killed device must be permanently and irreversibly disabled: incapable of being reactivated, re-registered on any network, or operated in any capacity. The device’s unique identifiers (IMEI, serial number) will be added to a national stolen device register, maintained by the NCA, which will be shared in real time with international law enforcement databases and with all UK network operators. The objective is simple: make stolen phones worthless. If a stolen phone cannot be reactivated, it cannot be resold. If it cannot be resold, there is no incentive to steal it. This is the single most effective intervention available to disrupt the stolen phone market, and it has been delayed for years by the unwillingness of successive governments to impose binding obligations on manufacturers.
- d) Grant police forces an explicit statutory power to pursue and intercept suspects on mopeds, motorcycles, and e-bikes who are fleeing after committing or attempting to commit a theft or robbery. The current operational constraints, under which officers are reluctant to pursue moped-mounted criminals for fear of causing injury and facing disciplinary or criminal proceedings, will be replaced by a statutory safe harbour. Officers acting in good faith in the pursuit of a suspect who has committed or is reasonably suspected of committing a robbery or theft offence will be immune from civil liability and from disciplinary proceedings arising from injury to the suspect during the pursuit, provided the pursuit is conducted in accordance with published pursuit protocols. The message to moped criminals is clear: you will be chased, you will be caught, and you will not hide behind the health and safety of the officer who catches you.

OPERATIONAL

Street robbery task force. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Metropolitan Police, West Midlands Police, Greater Manchester Police, and the six next highest-robbery forces will each establish dedicated street robbery task forces, funded by the Street Safety Fund. These units will focus exclusively on the identification, surveillance, and arrest of organised street robbery networks, with particular emphasis on moped and e-bike theft gangs. The task forces will be coordinated nationally by the Knife Crime Strike Force and will share intelligence with the NCA’s organised crime mapping capability.

Stolen device register. The national stolen device register will be operational within 6 months of Royal Assent, maintained by the NCA and integrated with INTERPOL’s stolen property database. Network operators will be required to check all device activations against the register in real time. Any attempt to activate a device on the register will generate an automatic alert to the NCA and to the local police force in whose area the activation was attempted.

Moped pursuit capability. Within 6 months, every metropolitan and urban force will maintain a dedicated moped pursuit capability: trained officers on high-performance motorcycles, equipped with tactical pursuit and containment training, and supported by helicopter and drone assets. The current situation, in which criminals on mopeds can escape simply by removing their helmets (in the expectation that police will break off pursuit), is a public humiliation for law enforcement. It will end.

C10.4: Youth Violence Prevention and Intervention

The Problem

Eighteen per cent of all knife and offensive weapon offences resulting in a caution or conviction involve juveniles aged 10 to 17. In the year ending March 2024, over 3,200 knife offences were committed by children. This figure is 20% higher than a decade ago. Black children are disproportionately represented, making up 14% of juvenile knife offences while comprising 6% of the youth population. The reasons are structural: poverty, exclusion from school, family breakdown, county lines exploitation, peer pressure, and the entirely rational calculation by some young people that in communities where the police are absent and the gangs are present, carrying a knife is the only form of protection available.

The evidence on what works to prevent youth knife crime is clear. Early intervention, targeted at children identified as at risk before they offend, is significantly more effective than criminal justice processing after the fact. The Youth Endowment Fund’s systematic reviews have found that mentoring programmes, cognitive behavioural therapy, and pre-court diversion have moderate to strong impacts on reducing violent reoffending. Hot-spot policing, when implemented with a problem-oriented approach, reduces both crime and calls for service. By contrast, knife crime education programmes have weak or no evidence of effectiveness and may, paradoxically, increase fear and knife carrying among children who were not previously at risk. Mandatory minimum sentencing for children is associated with increased reoffending through the criminogenic effects of early system contact.

Progress does not accept the false choice between enforcement and intervention. Both are required. C2 and C5 provide the enforcement architecture: the police numbers, the sentencing framework, the neighbourhood presence. C10.4 provides the intervention architecture: the targeted programmes, the institutional support, and the pathway out of violence for young people who have not yet passed the point of no return. The distinction is critical. For adults who carry knives, the response is enforcement: detection, prosecution, and imprisonment at a severity that destroys the incentive to carry. For children and young people who are at risk of carrying, the response is intervention: identification, engagement, and the provision of credible alternatives to the street. For children who have already offended, the response is a combination: meaningful consequences that communicate the seriousness of the offence, combined with structured programmes that address the underlying causes.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Street Safety Act will additionally:

- a) Establish a statutory Youth Violence Intervention Programme, managed by the Children’s Internet Safety Commission’s counterpart in the physical world: a new Youth Safety Commission, established as a standalone body with a sole mandate of preventing youth involvement in serious violence. The Commission will be independent of the Home Office and the Ministry of Justice, accountable to Parliament through the Education Select Committee, and led by a Commissioner appointed by the Lord Chancellor. Its functions will include: maintaining a national register of children and young people assessed as at high risk of involvement in serious violence; commissioning and quality-assuring local intervention programmes; setting national standards for youth violence prevention; and publishing annual data on youth violence outcomes.
- b) Create a statutory duty on local authorities, schools, NHS trusts, and police forces to participate in a multi-agency Youth Violence Reduction Partnership in every local authority area with a knife crime rate above the national average. The Partnership will be required to identify children at risk of involvement in serious violence, using a standardised risk assessment framework developed by the Youth Safety Commission, and to ensure that every identified child is offered an individually tailored intervention programme within 30 days of identification. Interventions must include, at a minimum: assignment of a dedicated mentor; access to cognitive behavioural therapy; a structured education or vocational training pathway; and, where the child has been excluded from school, immediate provision of alternative full-time education. No identified child will be left without an active intervention. The current system, in which children fall through gaps between agencies, are excluded from school, and drift into gang association because nobody provides a credible alternative, is a production line for knife crime. Progress will dismantle it.
- c) Create a statutory offence of criminal exploitation of a child, carrying a minimum sentence of ten years, where an adult causes, incites, controls, or coerces a child under 18 to carry a weapon, distribute drugs, or participate in robbery or other serious criminal activity. This directly targets the county lines model and the gang structures that recruit, arm, and exploit children. The Crime and Policing Bill proposes a similar offence but without the sentencing severity that Progress considers necessary. The adults who put knives in children’s hands, who use children as drug runners and weapons carriers to insulate themselves from prosecution, are among the most culpable offenders in the criminal justice system. Their sentences must reflect that culpability.
- d) Require every secondary school in England and Wales to provide a minimum of two hours per week of structured physical activity, team sport, or martial arts training, funded by the Street Safety Fund and delivered in partnership with local sports clubs and community organisations. This is not a knife crime education programme. The evidence shows that knife awareness campaigns do not work and may increase fear. This is the provision of structured, supervised, physically demanding activity that builds discipline, confidence, social connection, and an identity that is not defined by the street. The evidence base for sport-based intervention in reducing youth violence is strong. The funding will prioritise schools in the 20% most deprived areas, where 70% of knife crime occurs.

OPERATIONAL

Youth Safety Commission. The Commission will be established within 6 months of Royal Assent with an initial staffing complement of 200 and an annual budget of £150 million, funded by the Street Safety Fund. The Commission will immediately begin the process of establishing Youth Violence Reduction Partnerships in every qualifying local authority area, with a target of full coverage within 12 months.

Mentor recruitment. The Youth Safety Commission will recruit and train 5,000 youth mentors within its first 12 months, drawn from communities with the highest knife crime rates. Mentors will be paid professionals, not volunteers, recruited at salaries competitive with teaching assistants and required to hold or obtain a recognised qualification in youth work. The mentor-to-child ratio will be no greater than 1:8. The programme will prioritise the recruitment of mentors who themselves have lived experience of the criminal justice system and who have demonstrably turned their lives around. Credibility with the young people they serve is not optional. It is the programme’s most valuable asset.

School exclusion intervention. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Department for Education will issue guidance requiring that no child may be permanently excluded from school without a mandatory referral to the Youth Violence Reduction Partnership for risk assessment. Where a child is assessed as at risk of involvement in serious violence, the local authority must provide full-time alternative education within 5 working days. The current average gap between exclusion and alternative provision, during which excluded children are effectively abandoned to the street, will be eliminated.

C10.5: The Street Safety Fund

The Problem

Knife crime and street violence impose costs that dwarf the investment required to prevent them. The economic and social cost of violent crime in England and Wales is estimated at over £16 billion per year. The NHS cost of treating knife injuries alone runs to hundreds of millions annually. The cost to communities in fear, reduced economic activity, business closures, depressed property values, and the destruction of young lives is incalculable. Every intervention described in this document requires funding. The question is not whether Britain can afford to invest in street safety. It is whether Britain can afford not to.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Street Safety Act will additionally:

- a) Establish a Street Safety Fund with an annual budget of £500 million for the first five years, funded from general taxation and supplemented by the proceeds of criminal asset recovery under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002. The Fund will be ring-fenced and administered by the Home Office, with allocations determined by a formula weighting: knife crime rate (40%), deprivation index (30%), youth population (20%), and recent crime trajectory (10%). No local authority or police force area with a knife crime rate above the national average will receive less than a minimum floor allocation.
- b) Mandate that the Fund’s allocations be distributed as follows: 40% to policing (Knife Detection Zones, street robbery task forces, moped pursuit capability, Strike Force operations); 30% to youth intervention (Youth Safety Commission, Youth Violence Reduction Partnerships, mentor recruitment, school sport programmes); 20% to technology (knife detection infrastructure, stolen device register, CCTV and analytics deployment, pursuit assets); and 10% to community safety infrastructure (street lighting, CCTV in high-crime areas, physical security improvements to retail premises in high-theft areas).
- c) Require the Home Secretary to publish an annual Street Safety Report, laid before Parliament, detailing: the total funds allocated and spent; the knife crime rate, street robbery rate, and phone theft rate for every police force area; the number of Knife Detection Zones in operation; the number of children engaged in Youth Violence Reduction Partnerships; the number of weapons seized, offenders convicted, and networks disrupted by the Strike Force; and the demographic data for stop and search conducted in Knife Detection Zones. The Report will be debated annually in the House of Commons. Accountability is not optional. The public will know exactly what their money has achieved.

OPERATIONAL

Fund establishment. The Street Safety Fund will be operational within 90 days of Royal Assent, with initial allocations to the 50 highest-priority areas released within 30 days thereafter. The Fund’s first-year allocation of £500 million will be front-loaded, with 60% released in the first six months to enable rapid deployment of Knife Detection Zones, Strike Force operations, and Youth Violence Reduction Partnerships.

Criminal asset recovery. The NCA will be directed to prioritise criminal asset recovery from organised street crime networks, moped robbery gangs, and stolen goods laundering operations. Recovered assets will be hypothecated to the Street Safety Fund, creating a direct financial link between the disruption of criminal enterprises and the funding of the communities those enterprises have terrorised.

Summary of Legislative Requirements

The C10 framework requires one new piece of primary legislation: the Street Safety Act. This Act builds on the enforcement architecture established in C2 (police expansion, prison capacity, sentencing reform, compound sentencing) and the policing model established in C5 (neighbourhood policing, mission clarity, political neutrality, accountability). It does not duplicate those frameworks. It extends them with targeted provisions for knife crime, street robbery, and youth violence. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, or departmental action.

Street Safety Act

On the face of the Act: Maximum sentences for knife and offensive weapon possession increased to ten years. Statutory minimum of two years’ immediate custody for first adult possession offence. Compound sentencing applied to knife offences (3/4/6-year minimums for second, third, and fourth offences). New statutory offence of knife-enabled robbery (minimum five years, seven for vulnerable victims, ten for organised patterns). New offence of manufacturing, importing, or distributing weapons for criminal use (minimum seven years). Legalisation of defensive sprays (pepper spray, PAVA) for women aged 18 and over, with registration scheme and approved device specifications. New offence of organised street robbery (minimum ten years, lifetime driving ban for vehicle-enabled offences). New offence of operating a stolen goods laundering network (minimum seven years). Mandatory remote kill-switch for mobile devices sold in the UK. Statutory safe harbour for police pursuit of moped and e-bike suspects. National Knife Crime Strike Force (500 officers, NCA-based). Knife Detection Zone framework. Reformed section 60 authorisation threshold. Youth Safety Commission (standalone statutory body, sole mandate of preventing youth involvement in serious violence). Statutory Youth Violence Intervention Programme. Multi-agency Youth Violence Reduction Partnerships. Criminal exploitation of a child offence (minimum ten years). Mandatory school sport provision. Street Safety Fund (£500 million annual budget, five-year ring-fence).

Delivered operationally: CPS knife crime prosecution directive within 6 weeks. Sentencing Council guideline revision within 6 weeks. Knife Detection Zones deployed in 50 highest-crime areas within 6 months. National Knife Crime Strike Force operational within 6 months. Street robbery task forces in the ten highest-robbery forces within 90 days. National stolen device register within 6 months. Moped pursuit capability in all metropolitan and urban forces within 6 months. Youth Safety Commission established within 6 months (200 staff, £150 million annual budget). 5,000 youth mentors recruited within 12 months. Youth Violence Reduction Partnerships in all qualifying local authority areas within 12 months. School exclusion intervention guidance within 90 days. Street Safety Fund operational within 90 days with front-loaded first-year allocation. Annual Street Safety Report laid before Parliament. Quarterly Strike Force performance reports.

C2 gave Britain the officers and the prisons. C5 gave Britain the police culture and the accountability. C10 gives Britain the specific, targeted, operational machinery to end the two crises that most visibly define the failure of public safety on British streets: the knife that kills teenagers, and the organised thief who snatches phones from the hands of citizens in broad daylight. The knife carrier will face years in prison, served in full. The moped thief will be chased, caught, and imprisoned. The gang leader who puts a knife in a child’s hand will serve a decade. The phone that is stolen will be rendered worthless within hours. The child who is at risk will be identified, engaged, and offered a way out before the street claims another life. These are not aspirations. They are operational commitments, funded, staffed, and enforceable. Britain’s streets belong to the law-abiding. Progress will ensure they know it.

C11. Drugs

Governing Principle

In 2024, 5,565 people in England and Wales died from drug poisoning. This is the highest number since records began in 1993. It is the eleventh consecutive year that the figure has risen. Drug-related deaths have doubled since 2012. Opiates and opioids were involved in almost half of those deaths. Cocaine-related deaths rose for the thirteenth consecutive year, reaching 1,279. Deaths involving nitazenes, a class of synthetic opioids approximately 50 times more potent than heroin, nearly quadrupled in a single year, from 52 in 2023 to 195 in 2024, with over 750 deaths linked to nitazenes between June 2023 and August 2025. An average of 40 people die from opioid-related causes in the United Kingdom every week. In the treatment system, 4,273 people died while in contact with drug and alcohol treatment services in 2024/25. These are not statistics. They are a body count, and it is rising.

The illicit drugs market in the United Kingdom is estimated to be worth £9.4 billion per year. It is the commercial engine of organised crime. Fifty-two per cent of homicides are now drug-related, up from 43% in 2012. Sixty-two per cent of those convicted of theft and 47% of those convicted of robbery have a history of drug offences. The county lines model, in which urban gangs exploit children to distribute crack cocaine and heroin into rural and coastal towns, has put an estimated 15,500 children at risk of criminal exploitation in the year ending March 2025, a figure the Home Office acknowledges is likely to be a significant underestimate. Three quarters of offenders charged under the County Lines Programme have a history of violent crime or weapons offences. Since July 2024, the Programme has closed 3,042 deal lines, made 8,226 arrests, and generated 4,323 safeguarding referrals. Yet new lines emerge as fast as old ones are shut down. The drug market is a hydra: every head severed grows back, because the demand that feeds it is constant and the profits that drive it are enormous.

The synthetic opioid threat is the most dangerous drug development in a generation. The National Crime Agency has warned that there has never been a more dangerous time to take drugs in the United Kingdom. Nitazenes are cheap to produce, simple to synthesise from precursor chemicals sourced primarily from China and India, and are being found mixed into heroin, counterfeit benzodiazepines, and fake painkillers, often without the knowledge of the user. The NCA’s Project Housebuilder and the government’s Synthetic Opioids Taskforce represent a recognition of the threat. They do not represent a solution. Britain is one supply chain disruption, one change in Afghan poppy production, or one entrepreneurial cartel away from a fentanyl-scale crisis that would make the current death toll look modest. The collapse in Afghan poppy cultivation since the Taliban ban has already begun to reduce heroin purity and push dealers towards synthetic alternatives. The window to prevent Britain from following the American trajectory is narrow, and it is closing.

Approximately 2.9 million adults aged 16 to 59 in England and Wales reported using drugs in the year ending March 2024, representing 8.8% of the age group. Among young adults aged 16 to 24, the figure is 16.5%. Cannabis remains the most widely used drug, with 6.8% of adults reporting use. Cocaine use in London is higher than any other English region, at 3.5%. Ketamine consumption increased by 85% in a single year based on wastewater analysis. Meanwhile, the drug treatment system, despite a £533 million investment over three years under the government’s 10-year strategy, is struggling to keep pace. There were 310,863 adults in contact with treatment services in 2023/24, and 16,212 children. The treatment completion rate stands at 47%. In the prison system, 52,401 adults received treatment for drug and alcohol problems in secure settings in 2024/25, with 46% being treated for opiate use. Drug arrests have fallen from 73,492 in 2015/16 to 60,705 in 2022/23. The enforcement system is shrinking while the market it is supposed to suppress is expanding.

Progress rejects the two dominant orthodoxies that have paralysed British drugs policy for decades. The first is the libertarian position that drug use is a private matter and that decriminalisation or legalisation is the answer. It is not. Recreational drug use is not victimless. It funds the county lines gangs that enslave children. It funds the organised crime networks that commit murder, trafficking, and extortion. It generates the addiction that drives 62% of theft convictions. Every gram of cocaine consumed at a dinner party in Clapham is connected, by an unbroken chain of commerce, to the exploitation of a child in a cuckooed flat in Blackpool. Progress will not pretend otherwise, and it will not legalise the supply chain that produces this misery.

The second orthodoxy is that enforcement alone can suppress a market worth £9.4 billion. It cannot. Britain has been enforcing drug laws with declining resources and declining conviction rates for two decades, and the market has grown. Enforcement is necessary but not sufficient. It must be combined with a treatment and recovery system of a scale and quality that this country has never attempted, and it must be prosecuted with an intensity and a ferocity that the drug trade has never faced. Progress does not intend to manage the drug market. Progress intends to wage war on it. The people who operate this trade, from the international trafficker to the county lines line holder, have chosen to enter a profession that enslaves children, poisons communities, and kills thousands of British citizens every year. They have chosen to go to war with the British state. Progress will ensure they understand what that means. The war will be relentless. The consequences will be financial, personal, social, and permanent. There will be no quiet reintegration, no fresh start, no second act. The drug trade will be made the most dangerous, the most financially ruinous, and the most socially annihilating career choice available in Britain. That is the objective. That is the promise.

C11.1: The Synthetic Opioid Emergency

The Problem

Britain stands at the threshold of a synthetic opioid crisis. The conditions that produced the American catastrophe, which has killed over 500,000 people since 1999, are beginning to materialise. Afghan poppy cultivation has collapsed following the Taliban’s ban, reducing global heroin supply and purity. Dealers are compensating by cutting heroin with nitazenes and other synthetic opioids to maintain potency. Nitazene-related deaths in the UK increased by 60% between the second half of 2023 and the first half of 2024, with a further 133 deaths recorded in the second half of 2024. Over 750 deaths have been linked to nitazenes since June 2023. The NCA assesses that nitazenes and fentanyl are broadly equivalent in potency, approximately 50 times stronger than heroin. A dose measured in micrograms can be fatal. Users frequently do not know they are consuming synthetic opioids: the substances are mixed into heroin, pressed into counterfeit pills disguised as benzodiazepines and painkillers, and sold through the same county lines networks that distribute crack and heroin.

Xylazine, a veterinary tranquilliser not approved for human use, is also increasing in prevalence in the UK drug supply. When combined with opioids, it dangerously lowers consciousness and heart rate, and it is not reversed by naloxone. In the United States, the combination of fentanyl and xylazine has caused devastating tissue necrosis and wound complications in addition to overdose. The NCA has confirmed xylazine involvement in drug-related deaths in the UK. The precursor chemicals for nitazene production are sourced primarily from China, where a ban on nitazene compounds was introduced in 2025 but is expected to displace rather than eliminate production, as China’s 2019 fentanyl ban demonstrated.

The government’s response has been to expand access to naloxone, the opioid overdose reversal medication, and to invest £3.4 billion over three years in drug and alcohol treatment services. These are necessary measures. They are not a strategy for preventing a synthetic opioid epidemic. Naloxone reverses overdoses after they occur. It does not prevent them. And naloxone is less effective against the highest-potency nitazenes, which may require multiple doses. The strategic imperative is to prevent synthetic opioids from establishing themselves as a mass-market product in the UK drug supply. This requires interdiction at the border, disruption of precursor supply chains, intelligence-led targeting of the networks introducing synthetics into the domestic market, and an emergency response infrastructure that can contain outbreaks before they become epidemics.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Drug Enforcement and Recovery Act will:

- a) Declare a Synthetic Opioid National Emergency, granting the Home Secretary emergency powers for a period of 24 months (renewable by statutory instrument) to: direct Border Force to implement enhanced screening of all parcels, packages, and freight consignments from identified source countries for synthetic opioid precursors and finished products; authorise the NCA to conduct warrantless interception of communications and financial transactions where there is intelligence linking a network to synthetic opioid supply; and direct the deployment of military chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) detection assets to support Border Force at ports of entry. Synthetic opioids can kill in quantities invisible to the naked eye. The detection challenge is not analogous to intercepting bales of cannabis or kilogrammes of cocaine. It requires specialist equipment and expertise that currently resides in the military, not in civilian border agencies.
- b) Create a statutory offence of importing, manufacturing, or distributing synthetic opioids, carrying a minimum sentence of fifteen years. Where the offence results in death, the minimum sentence will be twenty years. Where the offence involves the adulteration of other drugs with synthetic opioids without the knowledge of the end user, the minimum will be twenty years regardless of whether a death results, on the basis that the offence constitutes the reckless endangerment of life on a potentially mass scale. These sentences reflect the catastrophic harm potential of synthetic opioids. A single kilogramme of fentanyl can produce approximately 500,000 fatal doses. The sentencing framework must communicate that synthetic opioid trafficking is treated by the British state with a severity equivalent to the most serious categories of violent crime.
- c) Establish a statutory Synthetic Opioid Early Warning System, operated by the UK Health Security Agency in coordination with the NCA, NHS England, and all 43 territorial police forces. The System will maintain real-time surveillance of: drug-related deaths and non-fatal overdoses reported by hospitals and ambulance services; forensic toxicology results from post-mortem examinations; drug checking results from seized samples; and intelligence from treatment services, homelessness services, and prison healthcare. When the System detects a cluster of synthetic opioid-related incidents in any area, an automatic alert protocol will trigger: immediate notification of local health services, police, and treatment providers; deployment of emergency naloxone supplies; targeted outreach to the local drug-using population; and intelligence-led enforcement action against the supply source.

OPERATIONAL

Border interdiction surge. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, Border Force will implement enhanced screening at all major postal hubs, parcel distribution centres, and freight entry points for synthetic opioid precursors and finished products. The screening will deploy spectroscopic and mass spectrometry equipment capable of detecting fentanyl and nitazene compounds in quantities below one gramme. Screening capacity will be funded by a £50 million emergency allocation from the Drug Enforcement Fund (established below). Postal and courier operators will be placed under a statutory duty to cooperate with Border Force screening, including the provision of manifest data and access to sorting facilities.

Precursor diplomacy. The Foreign Secretary will be directed to engage with China and India, the primary source countries for synthetic opioid precursors, within 60 days of Royal Assent. The engagement will pursue binding agreements on the scheduling of precursor chemicals, the sharing of production and export intelligence, and the mutual recognition of enforcement actions. Where diplomatic engagement does not produce acceptable outcomes within 6 months, the government will impose targeted sanctions on identified chemical manufacturers and export brokers, using the Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018.

Naloxone universal access. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, naloxone will be reclassified from a prescription-only medication to a pharmacy-available medication, obtainable without prescription from any pharmacy in England and Wales. All police officers, paramedics, firefighters, prison staff, probation officers, and homelessness outreach workers will be required to carry naloxone and to be trained in its administration. Naloxone vending machines will be deployed in the 100 highest-risk locations, as identified by the Early Warning System, within 12 months.

C11.2: Drug Supply, Trafficking, and Counter-Narcotics Warfare

The Problem

The UK drug supply chain operates at every level of scale and sophistication. At the top, international trafficking networks import cocaine, heroin, and synthetic drugs through maritime routes, air freight, postal services, and the Channel Tunnel. Criminals from the Balkans dominate the cocaine market, but British traffickers remain significant. The NCA was aware of 4,772 organised crime groups operating in the UK at the end of 2019, a quarter of which were estimated to be involved in drug trafficking and supply. At the middle market level, regional organised crime groups distribute wholesale quantities to urban dealing networks. At the street level, the county lines model has industrialised the retail distribution of crack cocaine and heroin, using dedicated mobile phone deal lines to take orders and exploited children and vulnerable adults to deliver the product.

The county lines model is the most violent and exploitative form of drug supply in modern Britain. It is strongly linked to knife crime, child criminal exploitation, cuckooing (the takeover of a vulnerable person’s home as a dealing base), and modern slavery. The Home Office estimates that approximately 15,500 children were identified as at risk or involved in child criminal exploitation in the year ending March 2025. The County Lines Programme has closed over 5,000 deal lines and charged over 11,000 individuals since its inception in 2019. The programme has produced measurable results: a 29% reduction in drug-misuse hospitalisations in the exporting force areas, and significant safeguarding outcomes. But the programme operates within funding cycles, its capacity is limited, and the county lines model adapts. New lines replace closed ones. New children replace safeguarded ones.

The fundamental failure of British drug enforcement is that it has been conducted as a policing operation against a military-scale adversary. The drug trade in Britain is a £9.4 billion enterprise that commands armies of foot soldiers, controls territory, uses extreme violence to enforce discipline, corrupts public officials, and deploys counter-surveillance and counter-intelligence techniques that rival those of state actors. The state’s response has been to fight this war with declining police numbers, a fragmented intelligence architecture, and an operational posture calibrated to manage the problem rather than destroy it. Drug arrests have fallen by 17% in a decade. Convictions have fallen by 14%. The market has grown. Progress will not manage this problem. Progress will prosecute a war of annihilation against the drug economy, using every instrument of state power, on terms that make participation in the trade an existential risk to the liberty, wealth, social standing, and future prospects of every person involved.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Drug Enforcement and Recovery Act will additionally:

- a) Increase statutory minimum sentences for drug supply offences as follows. Supply of Class A drugs: minimum ten years (as established in C2.3). Supply where the offender has used children as runners or mules: minimum fifteen years (as established in C2.3). Large-scale importation of Class A drugs: minimum twenty years (as established in C2.3). These sentences, combined with C2.3’s abolition of automatic early release, mean that a convicted Class A supplier will serve a minimum of ten years in full in a Class B Deterrence Facility. The current average sentence for Class A supply, served in half, does not destroy the economic calculus of the trade. These sentences will.
- b) Grant the National Crime Agency counter-terrorism parity for drug enforcement operations. The NCA’s drug enforcement directorate will be authorised to exercise the same surveillance, interception, covert entry, and tactical capabilities currently available to MI5 and counter-terrorism policing under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 and the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000, subject to the same judicial oversight via Investigatory Powers Commissioners. Drug enforcement officers conducting operations against trafficking networks will be afforded the same legal protections as officers conducting counter-terrorism operations, including statutory safe harbour for the use of reasonable force during interdiction and arrest. The operational posture of British drug enforcement will communicate unambiguously that the state treats drug trafficking as a threat to national security equivalent in kind, if not in form, to terrorism.
- c) Create a statutory framework for Drug Supply Disruption Orders, a new civil-criminal hybrid power enabling the NCA or a chief constable to apply to the Crown Court for an order targeting a suspected drug supply network. The Order may include: asset freezing of identified individuals and associated entities; telecommunications disruption (requiring network operators to disconnect specified phone numbers used as deal lines); travel restrictions; and enhanced surveillance authorisations. The standard of proof for a Disruption Order will be the civil standard (balance of probabilities), but the order will be subject to judicial oversight and a right of appeal. This provides a tool to disrupt networks that are known to law enforcement but against which the criminal standard of proof has not yet been met, closing the operational gap between intelligence and prosecution.
- d) Establish a statutory duty on all Regional Organised Crime Units to maintain a dedicated middle-market drug intelligence capability. The current gap between the NCA’s focus on international traffickers and local forces’ focus on street dealers will be closed by requiring each ROCU to identify, map, and target the wholesale distributors operating within its region. Each ROCU will publish an annual threat assessment of middle-market drug activity, and the NCA will coordinate a national picture from these assessments. ROCUs will be funded for this expanded capability through the Drug Enforcement Fund.
- e) Expand the County Lines Programme from a funded programme to a permanent statutory enforcement function, embedded within the NCA, with a dedicated annual budget and staffing complement. The Programme will be required to maintain operational tempo sufficient to close a minimum of 5,000 deal lines per year and to ensure that every child identified as at risk of county lines exploitation receives a safeguarding referral within 48 hours. The Programme’s performance will be reported to Parliament annually as part of the Drug Enforcement Report (established below).

OPERATIONAL

Middle-market enforcement surge. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, each ROCU will receive a ring-fenced allocation from the Drug Enforcement Fund to establish or expand its middle-market drug intelligence capability. The initial allocation will fund a minimum of 20 additional intelligence analysts and investigators per ROCU, targeted exclusively at the wholesale distribution networks that connect international supply to street-level dealing.

Deal line disruption. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Home Secretary will issue a direction to all telecommunications operators requiring them to disconnect any phone number identified by the NCA or a territorial police force as a county lines deal line within 24 hours of notification. Operators that fail to comply will face enforcement action under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016.

Intelligence reward scheme. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, the NCA will establish a statutory intelligence reward programme, funded from recovered criminal assets, offering payments of up to £100,000 for information leading directly to the conviction of a major drug supplier or the dismantling of a trafficking network. The scheme will be complemented by enhanced witness protection provisions for informants who provide evidence against trafficking networks. The objective is to turn the drug economy’s own participants into its destroyers, incentivising betrayal and magnifying the paranoia that is the natural condition of criminal enterprise.

C11.3: Financial and Economic Warfare Against the Drug Trade

The Problem

Imprisonment alone does not destroy a drug trafficking operation. It removes individuals. It does not remove the wealth that those individuals have accumulated, the infrastructure they have built, or the professional networks that have enabled them. A trafficker who serves ten years and emerges to find his assets intact, his properties still standing, and his associates still operational, is not defeated. He is inconvenienced. The financial architecture of the drug trade is as important as its physical logistics, and it is far less frequently targeted. The Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 provides for confiscation of criminal assets, but the process is reactive, slow, and chronically underused. In 2022/23, POCA confiscation orders totalled approximately £148 million against a drug market estimated at £9.4 billion. The state recovers pennies for every pound the trade generates. Meanwhile, the professional enablers, the solicitors, accountants, estate agents, and financial intermediaries who wash drug money through property, businesses, and offshore structures, operate with near-total impunity because the burden of proving their knowledge is prohibitively high.

Progress will wage economic war on the drug trade with the same intensity it brings to operational enforcement. The objective is not merely to imprison drug traffickers but to annihilate them financially, socially, and professionally. Every asset seized. Every property forfeited. Every bank account emptied. Every business dissolved. Every professional enabler prosecuted and struck off. Every convicted trafficker placed on a public register and subject to lifetime financial restrictions that make re-entry into commercial life contingent on the approval of the state. The drug trade must be made not merely illegal but economically suicidal. The message to anyone contemplating entry into the profession is this: if you are caught, you will lose everything, you will never get it back, and everyone will know.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Drug Enforcement and Recovery Act will additionally:

- a) Introduce a statutory rebuttable presumption of criminal origin for all assets held by any person convicted of a drug supply or trafficking offence, and for all assets held by their spouse, civil partner, cohabitant, or any person identified by the court as an associate of the convicted person. Upon conviction, the burden of proof will shift: every asset is presumed to be the product of drug trafficking unless the holder can demonstrate, on the balance of probabilities, that it was acquired through legitimate, documented income. Assets that cannot be so justified will be subject to automatic confiscation. This reversal of the burden of proof transforms asset recovery from a laborious post-conviction exercise into an automatic and comprehensive consequence of conviction. Houses will be seized. Vehicles will be forfeited. Bank accounts will be frozen and emptied. Jewellery, watches, designer goods, and cash holdings will be confiscated. The financial destruction will be total and it will be public.
- b) Create a Serious Crime Financial Restriction Order, imposed automatically on any person convicted of a drug supply or trafficking offence and lasting for a minimum of 15 years (lifetime for Class A supply convictions). The Order will prohibit the subject from: holding a directorship or position of significant control in any company; opening or operating a business bank account; holding a premises licence, personal licence, or any other licence required to operate a commercial enterprise; obtaining credit, a mortgage, or any form of secured lending above £1,000 without prior written approval from the NCA; and holding or acquiring any real property without NCA approval. The Order will be registered on a public database maintained by the NCA and accessible to banks, lenders, landlords, employers, and licensing authorities. The objective is to make the drug trade a one-way door into permanent economic marginalisation. The trafficker who has enriched himself at the expense of communities destroyed by addiction will discover that the wealth is gone, the commercial life is closed, and the restrictions are permanent.
- c) Establish a Drug Trafficker Register, analogous in structure to the Sex Offenders Register under Part 2 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003. Any person convicted of a drug supply, trafficking, or importation offence will be required to register with the police within 72 hours of conviction (or release from custody) and to notify the police of their name, address, date of birth, national insurance number, employment status, bank accounts, and any change in these particulars, for a minimum period of 15 years (lifetime for Class A supply). Failure to comply with registration requirements will be a criminal offence carrying a maximum of five years’ imprisonment. The Register itself will be maintained by the NCA. Conviction details, including the offender’s name, photograph, offence, sentence, and the nature and scale of the operation, will be published on a government-maintained public database for the duration of the registration period. There will be no anonymity. There will be no quiet return to respectability. The social stigma is not a side effect of the policy. It is the policy.
- d) Create a statutory offence of professional facilitation of drug trafficking, carrying a minimum sentence of five years’ imprisonment, automatic striking off from the relevant professional register, and personal civil liability for the full value of the transactions facilitated. The offence will apply to any solicitor, accountant, estate agent, financial adviser, or other regulated professional who, in the course of their professional duties, processes, facilitates, or fails to report a transaction that they know or ought to know is connected to drug trafficking. A rebuttable presumption of knowledge will apply where the professional has handled transactions for a person subsequently convicted of drug supply or trafficking: the professional will be presumed to have known the criminal origin of the funds unless they can demonstrate that they conducted adequate due diligence and that the criminal connection could not reasonably have been identified. This provision targets the enabler class that makes the drug economy function: the solicitors who conveyance drug-purchased properties, the accountants who file drug-funded tax returns, and the estate agents who take commissions on drug-financed lettings. Their professional immunity is over.
- e) Mandate the physical destruction of properties used as drug factories, cannabis cultivation sites, or distribution hubs, and the public destruction of vehicles used in drug supply operations. Properties will be subject to mandatory forfeiture under POCA and, where the local authority certifies that the property has been structurally compromised by its criminal use (as is frequently the case with cannabis farms), to mandatory demolition at the cost of the convicted occupant. Vehicles used in drug supply will be seized, crushed, and the destruction filmed and published on the NCA’s public-facing channels. The visual spectacle of destruction communicates something that a prison sentence behind closed doors does not. It communicates that the state does not merely punish the drug trade. It erases the physical infrastructure of the trade from the built environment.

OPERATIONAL

Asset recovery surge. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, the NCA will establish a dedicated Drug Asset Recovery Unit with a staffing complement of 200 financial investigators, forensic accountants, and lawyers. The Unit’s sole function will be the identification, freezing, confiscation, and realisation of drug trafficking assets under the reversed burden of proof framework. The Unit will be tasked with quadrupling annual POCA recoveries from drug crime within 36 months, from approximately £148 million to £600 million. Recovered assets will be hypothecated to the Drug Enforcement Fund.

Professional enabler enforcement. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Solicitors Regulation Authority, the Financial Conduct Authority, HMRC (in respect of accountants), and the relevant estate agent regulators will be directed to establish joint investigation teams with the NCA, focused on identifying and prosecuting professionals who have facilitated drug money laundering. Each regulator will be required to report annually on the number of professionals investigated, prosecuted, and struck off for drug-related facilitation.

Public destruction programme. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, the NCA will coordinate a national programme of vehicle destruction and property demolition, conducted in public, filmed, and published online. The programme will commence with the vehicles and properties seized in the first wave of operations under the enhanced enforcement provisions. The visual record of state destruction of criminal assets will be maintained as a permanent public resource on the NCA’s website.

C11.4: Treatment, Recovery, and Compulsory Rehabilitation

The Problem

The drug treatment system in England serves over 310,000 adults per year across approximately 600 sites. It is, by any honest assessment, underperforming. The treatment completion rate stands at 47%: fewer than half of those who enter treatment leave it free from dependence. Over a quarter of people currently in treatment have been in treatment continuously since they started, and 71% of those have been in treatment for five years or more. The system is maintaining people in a state of managed dependency rather than moving them towards recovery. In the prison system, 52,401 adults received treatment in secure settings in 2024/25, with 46% being treated for opiate use. Yet the link between prison treatment and community aftercare is fragile: too many prisoners are released without a seamless handover to community treatment, and the reoffending rate for drug-dependent offenders reflects this failure.

Dame Carol Black’s independent review of drugs found that the treatment system had been hollowed out by a decade of disinvestment. Between 2013 and 2020, local authority spending on drug treatment fell by 17% in real terms. The government’s 10-year drugs strategy committed £533 million over three years to rebuild treatment capacity. This investment has begun to produce results: the number of adults in treatment has risen to its highest level since 2009/10, and over 3,900 additional staff have been recruited. But the structural problems, fragmented commissioning, a workforce that is undertrained and undervalued, a lack of residential rehabilitation capacity, and a failure to integrate treatment with housing, employment, and mental health services, persist.

The most severe Class A addictions, particularly heroin and crack cocaine dependency, present a distinct challenge that the voluntary treatment model is structurally incapable of addressing. Opioid dependency physically rewires the brain’s reward pathways. The withdrawal and post-acute withdrawal syndrome can last 12 to 24 months. Short interventions do not work because they do not outlast the physiological dependency cycle. The average heroin user cycles through four to six treatment episodes before achieving sustained recovery, if they achieve it at all. Each cycle involves continued criminal activity, continued health deterioration, and continued public cost. The voluntary model asks the most severely addicted individuals, people whose neurochemistry has been fundamentally altered by years of substance abuse, to exercise the very faculty that their addiction has destroyed: the capacity for sustained, autonomous decision-making. This is not compassion. It is negligence dressed as respect for autonomy.

Progress will create what no British government has yet been willing to create: a system of compulsory rehabilitation for the most severely Class A dependent individuals, designed to outlast the full metabolic cycle of addiction, to rebuild the habits and personality structures that addiction has dismantled, and to prepare the individual for re-entry into society. This is the most operationally ambitious and legally complex proposal in the framework. It requires a bespoke statutory power, robust judicial oversight, a phased therapeutic model, and compatibility with the United Kingdom’s domestic legal architecture. The compatibility question is addressed directly. Provisions of this Act that engage rights under the European Convention on Human Rights will be legislated with the same crystal-clear parliamentary intent that Progress employs across its wider reform programme. As Lord Wolfson’s advice to the then Leader of the Opposition confirmed, Parliament retains the power to pass whatever legislation it wishes, and courts are obliged to give effect to that legislation. The Drug Enforcement and Recovery Act will, where necessary, include express provisions disapplying section 3 and section 4 of the Human Rights Act 1998 in respect of specified clauses, requiring courts to give effect to the Act’s provisions without reference to Convention rights, and treating any tension with Strasbourg as a matter of international diplomacy rather than domestic legal constraint. This is consistent with Progress’ broader programme of Human Rights Act reform, under which the HRA will be amended to restore the supremacy of Parliament over the judiciary in matters of public policy.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Drug Enforcement and Recovery Act will additionally:

- a) Create a statutory power of Compulsory Recovery Detention, distinct from both criminal sentencing and mental health detention under the Mental Health Act 1983. The power will authorise the Crown Court to order the compulsory detention of an individual in a Drug Recovery Facility for a period of up to 24 months, on the application of a local authority, the NHS, or a chief constable, where the following conditions are met: a clinical assessment by two independent medical practitioners confirms Class A drug dependency; the individual has failed to engage with or complete voluntary treatment on at least two occasions within the preceding five years, or their dependency poses an immediate and serious risk to their own life; and no less restrictive intervention is reasonably available to achieve the objective of sustained recovery. The Order will be made by a judge of the Crown Court following an adversarial hearing at which the individual is entitled to legal representation, funded by legal aid. The Order is not a punishment. It is a compulsory therapeutic intervention, justified by the same principle that justifies compulsory detention under the Mental Health Act: that where an individual’s condition renders them incapable of making decisions that protect their own life, the state has both the right and the duty to intervene.
- b) Structure the 24-month Compulsory Recovery Detention in four phases, each with defined objectives and milestones. Phase 1 (months 1 to 3): medically supervised detoxification, physical and mental health stabilisation, comprehensive clinical assessment, and the commencement of psychological therapy. Phase 2 (months 4 to 12): intensive cognitive behavioural therapy, trauma processing, physical fitness and structured routine, vocational training, and the systematic rebuilding of daily discipline. This is the phase in which the metabolic link to the addiction is broken and new habits and identity structures are established. Phase 3 (months 13 to 18): graduated responsibility, supervised community access, employment placement, and family reconnection. The individual begins to operate semi-independently while remaining resident in the Facility. Phase 4 (months 19 to 24): semi-independent living within the Facility campus or approved community housing, full-time work or education, establishment of community support networks, and preparation for independent living. The key distinction from imprisonment is that every hour of every day is structured around recovery, not punishment. But the confinement is non-negotiable. The point at which an addict most wants to leave is precisely the point at which leaving would guarantee relapse.
- c) Establish safeguards for Compulsory Recovery Detention that ensure the process is clinically governed, judicially supervised, and subject to independent oversight. Mandatory judicial review of the Detention Order at 6-month intervals, at which the court must be satisfied that the individual continues to meet the criteria for detention and that the therapeutic programme is being delivered to the required standard. Right of appeal to a specialist tribunal, sitting with both a judge and a clinical assessor, at any point during the detention. Independent inspection of all Drug Recovery Facilities by the Care Quality Commission, with the power to require immediate changes to practice or, in extremis, to recommend the release of individuals where the therapeutic environment is inadequate. A statutory advocate appointed for every person subject to Compulsory Recovery Detention, with the right of access to the individual, their clinical records, and the Facility at all times. Clinical review panels with the power to recommend early release where recovery milestones are met ahead of schedule.
- d) Create a Mandatory Drug Recovery Order, available to the Crown Court and magistrates’ courts as a sentencing option for any offender convicted of an acquisitive crime (theft, robbery, burglary, fraud, handling stolen goods) who is assessed as drug-dependent. The Order will require the offender to complete a minimum 12-month residential rehabilitation programme in a Drug Recovery Facility, followed by a minimum 12-month structured community aftercare programme comprising continued treatment, regular drug testing, housing support, employment or vocational training, and supervision by a dedicated recovery officer. Breach of the Order will result in immediate recall and the imposition of the custodial sentence that the Order replaced. This is distinct from the Compulsory Recovery Detention power: the Recovery Order is a sentencing option for offenders; the Compulsory Detention power is a civil order for non-offenders whose addiction poses a risk to their own life.
- e) Establish a national network of Drug Recovery Facilities, operated under contract to the Ministry of Justice and inspected by both HMIP and the CQC. The target is 10,000 residential rehabilitation places, delivered through a combination of new-build facilities and the repurposing of existing institutional estate (decommissioned military sites, former care homes, and surplus public buildings). Each Facility will provide: medically supervised detoxification; cognitive behavioural therapy and trauma-informed care; vocational training and employment preparation; physical fitness programmes; family reconnection support; and structured reintroduction to community living. The Facilities will be staffed by a combination of clinical professionals (doctors, nurses, psychologists) and recovery workers, including those with lived experience of addiction and recovery. The target cost per place per year is £30,000, representing a saving against the £53,801 annual cost of imprisonment and a fraction of the estimated £58,000 annual cost to the public of an untreated drug-dependent offender in terms of crime, health, and welfare.
- f) Require every prison in England and Wales to establish a Drug-Free Wing, available to prisoners who commit to abstinence-based recovery. Prisoners in Drug-Free Wings will receive enhanced privileges, access to education and vocational training, and priority consideration for early progression to open conditions. Entry to a Drug-Free Wing will require a commitment to random drug testing, participation in a structured recovery programme, and peer support.
- g) Create a statutory duty on local authorities to commission a minimum level of residential rehabilitation capacity, defined as one residential rehabilitation place per 1,000 population in areas where drug-related death rates exceed the national average.

OPERATIONAL

Drug Recovery Facility construction. The first 3,000 residential rehabilitation places will be operational within 12 months of Royal Assent, using the same modular construction and site requisition approach established for prison construction in C2.2. The full 10,000-place network will be complete within 36 months. Sites will be selected to ensure geographic coverage across all regions, with priority given to areas with the highest drug-related death rates.

Treatment workforce expansion. The government will fund a further 5,000 drug and alcohol treatment workers over 24 months, building on the 3,900 recruited under the current strategy. Recruitment will prioritise: clinical staff for medically supervised detoxification; psychologists and counsellors for trauma-informed care; and recovery workers with lived experience.

Prison-to-community continuity. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, every prison will be required to establish a formal handover protocol ensuring that every drug-dependent prisoner is connected to a community treatment provider, a named GP, and a housing provider before release. No drug-dependent prisoner will be released without a confirmed treatment appointment within 48 hours of release and a confirmed address. The current practice of releasing drug-dependent prisoners onto the street with a list of phone numbers is a death sentence for some and a reoffending guarantee for most.

C11.5: Demand Reduction, Enforcement, and the Drug Enforcement Fund

The Problem

The demand side of the drug market is the engine that sustains the supply side. The £9.4 billion UK drug market exists because millions of people buy its products. The enforcement of drug possession laws has been progressively deprioritised. Drug arrests have fallen by 17% over a decade. In many urban areas, cannabis use is de facto decriminalised. The message communicated to the public is that personal drug use is a low-priority, low-consequence activity. This message is false. Every purchase of cocaine, heroin, cannabis, or any other controlled substance funds organised crime, violence, exploitation, and death. The casual user who insists that their recreational habit is a private matter is either ignorant of or indifferent to the chain of harm that connects their consumption to the county lines child soldier, the cuckooed pensioner, and the stabbed teenager.

Progress does not propose to imprison every recreational cannabis user. That would be neither practical nor proportionate. But Progress does insist that the possession of controlled substances remains a criminal offence, that the offence is enforced, and that the consequence is sufficiently serious to communicate that drug use is not tolerated. The current reality, in which possession offences are routinely dealt with by a caution or a warning, or are simply ignored, does not achieve this.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Drug Enforcement and Recovery Act will additionally:

- a) Introduce a structured escalation framework for personal possession offences. First offence: a mandatory Drug Awareness Course (48 hours of structured education on the harms of drug use, funded by the offender at a cost of £500, with fee waiver for those on means-tested benefits) and a criminal record entry. Second offence: a mandatory community service order of 200 hours, combined with a Drug Testing Requirement for 12 months. Third offence: a mandatory custodial sentence of 6 months. This framework replaces the current de facto decriminalisation of possession with a system of escalating consequence that provides education and opportunity for behaviour change before imposing imprisonment, but that makes unambiguously clear that persistence will be met with imprisonment.
- b) Create a statutory Drug Demand Reduction Programme, requiring the Home Office to fund and coordinate a national public education campaign on the link between drug consumption and organised crime harm. The campaign will not rely on abstract slogans or celebrity endorsements. It will present, in graphic and specific detail, the documented consequences of the drug trade: the children exploited by county lines, the families destroyed by addiction, the victims of drug-related violence, and the communities blighted by open drug markets.
- c) Establish a Drug Enforcement Fund with an annual budget of £500 million for the first five years, funded from general taxation and supplemented by the proceeds of criminal asset recovery from drug trafficking. The Fund will be ring-fenced and administered by the Home Office, with allocations as follows: 35% to enforcement (border interdiction, NCA operations, ROCU middle-market capability, County Lines Programme, local force drug enforcement, counter-narcotics warfare capabilities, intelligence reward scheme); 30% to treatment and recovery (Drug Recovery Facilities, Compulsory Recovery Detention, treatment workforce, prison-to-community continuity, naloxone deployment); 15% to financial and economic warfare (Drug Asset Recovery Unit, professional enabler enforcement, destruction programme); 10% to the Synthetic Opioid Emergency Response (Early Warning System, border screening, precursor diplomacy); and 10% to demand reduction (Drug Awareness Courses, national education campaign, drug testing infrastructure).
- d) Require the Home Secretary to lay before Parliament an annual Drug Enforcement Report, detailing: drug-related deaths by substance, region, and demographic; the number of drug supply prosecutions, convictions, and sentences; the number of deal lines closed and county lines networks disrupted; the total criminal assets confiscated and the number of Serious Crime Financial Restriction Orders in force; the number of Drug Trafficker Register entries; the number of professional enablers prosecuted; the number of properties demolished and vehicles destroyed; the number of Compulsory Recovery Detention Orders issued, in force, and completed; the number of Mandatory Drug Recovery Orders issued and completed; the number of children safeguarded from county lines exploitation; the synthetic opioid early warning alert count; and the treatment completion rate across all settings. The Report will be debated annually in the House of Commons.

OPERATIONAL

Drug Enforcement Fund. The Fund will be operational within 90 days of Royal Assent, with initial allocations released within 30 days thereafter. The first-year allocation of £500 million will be front-loaded, with 60% released in the first six months to fund the synthetic opioid border surge, the ROCU middle-market expansion, the Drug Asset Recovery Unit, the intelligence reward scheme, and the first tranche of Drug Recovery Facilities.

Drug testing expansion. Within 12 months, drug testing capacity will be expanded to support the structured escalation framework for possession offences and the Drug Testing Requirement for second offenders.

Schools education. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, the Department for Education will update the PSHE curriculum to include mandatory, evidence-based education on drug harms, with specific modules on synthetic opioids and the connection between drug consumption and organised crime.

###### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The C11 framework requires one new piece of primary legislation: the Drug Enforcement and Recovery Act. This Act builds on the sentencing framework established in C2.3 and the policing and neighbourhood structures established in C5. It does not duplicate those frameworks. It extends them with targeted provisions for synthetic opioids, counter-narcotics warfare, financial annihilation of the drug economy, compulsory rehabilitation, and demand reduction. Provisions engaging Convention rights will be legislated with express disapplication of sections 3 and 4 of the Human Rights Act 1998, consistent with Progress’ broader programme of HRA reform and the principle of parliamentary sovereignty as confirmed by Lord Wolfson. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, or departmental action.

###### Drug Enforcement and Recovery Act

On the face of the Act: Synthetic Opioid National Emergency declaration with enhanced border screening, NCA warrantless interception powers, and military CBRN asset deployment. New offence of synthetic opioid importation, manufacture, or distribution (minimum fifteen years, twenty where death results or adulteration without user knowledge). Statutory Synthetic Opioid Early Warning System. Counter-terrorism parity for NCA drug enforcement operations. Drug Supply Disruption Orders (civil-criminal hybrid). Statutory duty on ROCUs to maintain middle-market drug intelligence capability. County Lines Programme established as permanent statutory enforcement function within NCA. Intelligence reward scheme (up to £100,000). Rebuttable presumption of criminal origin for all assets of convicted drug traffickers and associates. Serious Crime Financial Restriction Orders (lifetime for Class A supply: directorship ban, business account ban, credit restrictions, property restrictions). Drug Trafficker Register (public database, 15-year minimum registration, lifetime for Class A). Offence of professional facilitation of drug trafficking (minimum five years, automatic striking off, personal liability). Mandatory destruction of drug premises and vehicles. Compulsory Recovery Detention (up to 24 months, Crown Court order, four-phase therapeutic model, judicial review at 6-month intervals, statutory advocate, CQC inspection). Mandatory Drug Recovery Orders (12-month residential plus 12-month aftercare for drug-dependent offenders). National network of 10,000 Drug Recovery Facility places. Drug-Free Wings in every prison. Statutory local authority rehabilitation commissioning duty. Structured escalation framework for personal possession. Drug Demand Reduction Programme. Drug Enforcement Fund (£500 million annual budget, five-year ring-fence). Annual Drug Enforcement Report to Parliament. Express disapplication of HRA sections 3 and 4 for specified provisions.

Delivered operationally: Border interdiction surge within 90 days (£50 million emergency allocation). Precursor diplomacy with China and India within 60 days (sanctions if no agreement within 6 months). Naloxone reclassified to pharmacy-available within 6 months, universal carry requirement, vending machines in 100 locations within 12 months. ROCU middle-market intelligence capability funded within 6 months (20 additional analysts per ROCU). Deal line disconnection within 24 hours (Home Secretary direction within 90 days). Intelligence reward scheme operational within 6 months. Drug Asset Recovery Unit (200 staff) within 6 months, target quadrupling of POCA recoveries within 36 months. Professional enabler joint investigation teams within 90 days. Public destruction programme within 6 months. First 3,000 Drug Recovery Facility places within 12 months, full 10,000 within 36 months. 5,000 additional treatment workers within 24 months. Prison-to-community handover protocols within 6 months. Drug testing expansion within 12 months. PSHE curriculum update within 6 months. Drug Enforcement Fund operational within 90 days.

C2 established the principle that Britain will be the worst place in the West to be a criminal. C11 makes it the worst place in the world to be a drug trafficker. The dealer will face sentences measured in decades, served in full. Every asset will be confiscated. Every property will be demolished. Every vehicle will be crushed. Every bank account will be emptied. Every professional who enabled the laundering will be prosecuted, struck off, and personally liable. The convicted trafficker’s name, photograph, and crimes will be published on a public register for the rest of their natural life. They will be barred from holding a directorship, opening a business, obtaining credit, or buying property without the permission of the state. The intelligence services and tactical capabilities deployed against terrorist networks will be deployed against them. Their associates will be offered six-figure rewards to betray them. Their county lines will be disconnected within 24 hours. Their middle-market wholesalers will be mapped and targeted by dedicated intelligence teams. And the addicted population that constitutes their customer base will, for the first time, be offered a genuine pathway out of dependency: 10,000 residential rehabilitation places, compulsory where voluntary engagement has failed, structured over 24 months to outlast the metabolic cycle of addiction, and designed to return functioning citizens to society rather than recycling dependent offenders through a revolving door of short sentences and ineffective community orders. The drug economy in Britain will be dismantled. The war will be relentless, the consequences permanent, and the outcome non-negotiable.

#### C12. Terrorism and Counter-Extremism

Governing Principle

Since March 2017, MI5 and Counter Terrorism Policing have together disrupted 43 late-stage attack plots in the United Kingdom. Some of those plotters were in the final days of planning mass murder, attempting to acquire firearms and explosives. In 2024, there were 248 terrorism-related arrests. As of March 2024, 246 individuals were in custody for terrorism-connected offences. Since the beginning of 2020, 19 late-stage attacks have been disrupted and hundreds of other developing threats intervened in across the country. The UK terror threat level stands at SUBSTANTIAL, meaning an attack is likely. One in five of the 232 terrorism arrests in 2024 involved children under the age of 17. The most complex and interconnected threat environment that MI5 has ever seen is not a projection. It is the present.

Islamist terrorism is, has been, and remains the dominant threat to the United Kingdom by every operational metric that exists. It accounts for 75% of MI5’s caseload and 80% of Counter Terrorism Policing’s live investigations. Since the 2017 Westminster Bridge attack, the vast majority of both realised and foiled plots have been Islamist in nature. The attacks at Westminster Bridge (2017), Manchester Arena (2017), London Bridge (2017), Parsons Green (2017), Fishmongers’ Hall (2019), HMP Whitemoor (2020), Streatham (2020), Reading (2020), Southend (2021), Liverpool (2021), and Hartlepool (2023) were all Islamist in motivation. Of the 43,000 extremists on MI5’s watchlist, approximately nine tenths are Islamist extremists. Instability across the Middle East, Africa, and Central Asia has allowed both Al-Qaeda and Islamic State to encourage and indirectly incite would-be attackers in the West. Islamic State is attempting to rebuild its forces in Syria following the collapse of the Assad regime. The individual and small-group attack model, using knives, vehicles, and improvised explosives, makes detection harder and the attack surface wider. This is the threat. It is overwhelmingly Islamist. Any counter-terrorism policy that does not begin and end with that fact is not a counter-terrorism policy. It is a political exercise.

The ideological infrastructure of Islamist terrorism in Britain does not begin with the individual who picks up a knife. It begins with the network of organisations, institutions, and ideologies that construct the intellectual and theological framework within which violence becomes a rational, righteous, and divinely mandated act. The Muslim Brotherhood and its affiliated organisations represent the most significant element of this infrastructure. The Brotherhood’s explicit objective, the establishment of an Islamist polity governed by its interpretation of Sharia, is in direct and irreconcilable conflict with British constitutional democracy, the rule of law, and the principle of equal citizenship. The Brotherhood operates through a web of affiliates, front organisations, charitable foundations, and community bodies that penetrate civic life, educational institutions, and political discourse. The 2015 government review of the Muslim Brotherhood, commissioned by David Cameron and conducted by Sir John Jenkins, found that aspects of the Brotherhood’s ideology and activities were contrary to British values and national interests, that the organisation had a highly ambiguous relationship with violent extremism, and that parts of it had significant involvement in funding, supporting, and promoting violence. The review recommended enhanced scrutiny but no proscription. That decision was a failure of political nerve. It will be corrected.

Beyond the Brotherhood, the broader ecosystem of mosques, Islamic centres, madrassas, and community organisations in the United Kingdom has never been subjected to a systematic, intelligence-led audit of its relationship to extremist ideology and terrorist risk.
