Individual investigations following specific attacks have revealed troubling connections: the Manchester Arena bomber Salman Abedi attended the Didsbury Mosque, whose former imam was later found to have links to extremist networks. The 7/7 bombers were linked to extremist preachers operating from mosques in Leeds and Dewsbury. The Finsbury Park Mosque under Abu Hamza al-Masri was a notorious hub for jihadist recruitment before his eventual prosecution. These are not isolated cases. They are visible manifestations of a network that has never been comprehensively mapped because the political will to do so has never existed. The fear of being accused of targeting a religion has paralysed the state’s willingness to investigate the institutions through which extremist ideology is propagated. Progress does not share that fear. A mosque is entitled to exactly the same protections as any other institution in Britain: no more, and no less. An institution that operates lawfully has nothing to fear from an audit. An institution that is propagating extremist ideology, hosting extremist preachers, distributing extremist literature, or providing cover for terrorist recruitment is not a place of worship. It is a threat to national security, and it will be treated as such.

The non-governmental organisation ecosystem presents a parallel vulnerability. Organisations that present themselves as human rights bodies, community advocacy groups, or civil liberties campaigners have, in documented cases, functioned as apologists for Islamist extremism, campaigned to delegitimise counter-terrorism programmes, and provided platforms for individuals and ideologies directly connected to terrorist movements. CAGE, an organisation that described the Islamic State executioner Mohammed Emwazi as a “beautiful young man” and has systematically campaigned to undermine every aspect of British counter-terrorism policy, is the most prominent but far from the only example. The Independent Reviewer of Terrorism Legislation, Sir William Shawcross, identified a concerted campaign by Islamist groups to delegitimise Prevent through disinformation and to smear those who cooperate with it as disloyal or sinful. This is not civil society. It is the soft-power arm of an extremist movement, and it has been allowed to operate without scrutiny for too long.

Extreme right-wing terrorism is a secondary threat that warrants monitoring and operational attention where it manifests. Far-right convictions have increased since 2016, and a number of plots have been disrupted. The Counter-Extremism Directorate will address this threat within its overall mandate, proportionate to the scale it represents.

The state threat landscape is simultaneously escalating. MI5 has reported a 35% increase in the number of individuals investigated for state threat activity in the UK in the past year. Russia continues to deploy proxies to spread chaos and incite violence. Iran has been linked to over twenty potentially lethal plots against UK targets. China conducts espionage against Parliament, universities, and critical infrastructure. These state-backed operations increasingly overlap with the terrorism threat in their methods and their impact on domestic security.

The Prevent programme, the apparatus that was supposed to prevent radicalisation before it reaches the point at which MI5 becomes involved, has failed. It has not merely underperformed. It has been institutionally captured by the very forces it was supposed to counter. Sir William Shawcross found that Prevent had shown “cultural timidity and an institutional hesitancy to tackle Islamism for fear of charges of Islamophobia.” He found that despite Islamist terrorism accounting for 75% of MI5’s caseload, only 16% of Prevent referrals in 2021/22 were categorised as Islamist. He identified organisations such as CAGE and the Muslim Engagement and Development network as having conducted sustained campaigns to delegitimise Prevent and to intimidate those who cooperated with it. The programme’s own practitioners operated in an environment where honest identification of the predominant threat risked professional and personal consequences. This is not a programme that requires reform. It is a programme that has been compromised from within, and it requires investigation, closure, and replacement with an institution that is not contaminated by the failures of its predecessor.

Progress’ position is that the United Kingdom faces a terrorism threat that is overwhelmingly Islamist in character, growing in volume, and sustained by an ideological and institutional infrastructure that has been allowed to operate with near-total impunity. The response must begin with honesty: Islamist terrorism is the threat. The Muslim Brotherhood and its affiliates must be proscribed. Every mosque, Islamic centre, and religious institution in Britain must be subject to the same scrutiny that any institution would face where there are reasonable grounds to suspect a connection to extremist ideology or terrorist activity. The NGO ecosystem must be audited for organisations that function as apologists for, or enablers of, Islamist extremism. Prevent must be investigated for institutional capture, shut down, and replaced with an intelligence-led counter-extremism directorate that takes its priorities from MI5, not from political anxiety. State-backed threats must be treated as acts of hostile intelligence. And the most dangerous offenders must face sentences that reflect the permanent nature of the threat they pose. That is the programme. It is not negotiable.

###### C12.1: Counter-Terrorism Enforcement and Sentencing

The Problem

The Terrorism Act 2000, the Terrorism Act 2006, and the Counter-Terrorism and Sentencing Act 2021 provide the core legislative framework for terrorism offences. The maximum sentence for preparing an act of terrorism (section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006) is life imprisonment. The Counter-Terrorism and Sentencing Act 2021 introduced a minimum 14-year sentence for the most serious terrorism offences, with a minimum two-thirds to be served before parole eligibility. These are serious sentences. But the broader framework contains weaknesses. Offences of possessing terrorist material (section 58), disseminating terrorist publications (section 2 of the 2006 Act), and supporting proscribed organisations (section 12 of the 2000 Act) carry maximum sentences of between 10 and 15 years but no statutory minimums. The result is significant variation in sentencing for offences that, while not involving the physical execution of an attack, constitute essential elements of the terrorist ecosystem: the propaganda, the recruitment, the radicalisation, and the material support that make attacks possible.

The management of convicted terrorists after release presents a persistent risk. The attacks at Fishmongers’ Hall (Usman Khan, released on licence from a terrorism sentence) and Streatham (Sudesh Amman, under active surveillance by armed officers following release from a terrorism sentence) demonstrated that the prison and probation system is unable to guarantee that released terrorists will not attempt further attacks. The fundamental problem is that radicalisation is an ideological commitment that is not reliably extinguished by imprisonment, and the tools available to manage released terrorists are designed for conventional offenders, not for individuals motivated by a desire for martyrdom.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Counter-Terrorism (Strengthening) Act will:

- a) Introduce statutory minimum sentences for the following terrorism-related offences: possession of material useful for terrorism (section 58, Terrorism Act 2000): minimum five years. Dissemination of terrorist publications (section 2, Terrorism Act 2006): minimum seven years. Inviting support for a proscribed organisation (section 12(1), Terrorism Act 2000): minimum seven years. Expressing support for a proscribed organisation in a manner reckless as to encouragement (section 12(1A)): minimum five years. Failure to disclose information about acts of terrorism (section 38B, Terrorism Act 2000): minimum three years. These minimums ensure that the enabling infrastructure of terrorism, the propaganda, the recruitment, and the material support, is punished with a severity that reflects its role in making attacks possible. A person who disseminates an Islamic State propaganda video that inspires a knife attack is not a peripheral figure. They are a combatant.
- b) Create a Terrorism Indefinite Detention Order, available to the Crown Court at sentencing for any offence carrying a maximum of life imprisonment under terrorism legislation. Where the court is satisfied, on the basis of expert evidence, that the offender continues to pose a serious risk of committing or facilitating a terrorist act and that no licence conditions or supervision arrangements can adequately manage that risk, the court may order that the offender be detained indefinitely beyond the minimum term, with annual review by the Parole Board sitting with a specialist national security assessor. The Order recognises a truth that the current system denies: some terrorists cannot be safely released. The ideology that motivated them is not a behavioural disorder that can be treated. It is a commitment that may persist for the rest of their lives. The state’s obligation to protect the public from mass-casualty attack must take precedence over the offender’s expectation of release.
- c) Extend the Serious Crime Prevention Order framework (Serious Crime Act 2007) to create a Terrorism Prevention and Restriction Order (TPRO), replacing the existing Terrorism Prevention and Investigation Measures (TPIMs). TPROs will be available on the application of the Home Secretary, authorised by a High Court judge, and will include all existing TPIM conditions (residence, travel, communication, association restrictions) plus: mandatory electronic monitoring by GPS ankle tag; curfew of up to 16 hours; prohibition on the use of encrypted communications or any internet-connected device not approved and monitored by the security services; mandatory attendance at a deradicalisation programme; and a prohibition on contact with any individual assessed by MI5 as an extremist associate. The duration of a TPRO will be renewable annually with no maximum limit, for as long as the security services assess that the individual continues to pose a threat. The current two-year maximum for TPIMs, after which the most dangerous individuals who cannot be prosecuted walk free of all restrictions, is a structural vulnerability that Progress will close.

OPERATIONAL

Post-release monitoring. Within 6 months of Royal Assent, every individual released from a terrorism sentence will be subject to a mandatory minimum 15-year licence period, during which they will be managed under MAPPA Category 3 arrangements with a dedicated counter-terrorism probation officer, mandatory GPS tagging, and monthly reporting.

Prison radicalisation response. Within 6 months, every prison holding terrorism-convicted or terrorism-risk inmates will establish a dedicated Separation Centre, physically and operationally distinct from the general population, staffed by officers with specialist counter-terrorism training. No convicted terrorist will be housed in general population.

###### C12.2: The Muslim Brotherhood, Institutional Audit, and NGO Accountability

The Problem

The Muslim Brotherhood is an international Islamist political movement founded in Egypt in 1928 with the stated objective of establishing a global Islamic polity governed by Sharia. Its ideology holds that Islam is a total system encompassing all aspects of life, politics, law, and society, and that the achievement of this system justifies gradualist infiltration of civic institutions as well as, in some of its iterations, the use of violence. The Brotherhood and its affiliates operate in the United Kingdom through a network of organisations, charities, educational bodies, and community groups. The 2015 government review conducted by Sir John Jenkins found that aspects of the Brotherhood’s ideology and activities were contrary to British values and national interests, that the organisation had a “highly ambiguous” relationship with violent extremism, that parts of it had significant involvement in funding and promoting violence, and that its ideology created an environment conducive to radicalisation even where the Brotherhood itself did not directly commission attacks.

Despite these findings, the Brotherhood was not proscribed. The Jenkins review recommended enhanced scrutiny but stopped short of recommending proscription, citing the complexity of the Brotherhood’s organisational structure and the difficulty of defining its boundaries. This was a failure of political nerve dressed as pragmatic nuance. The Brotherhood’s European affiliates, including organisations operating in the United Kingdom, have been identified by intelligence services across the continent as promoting an ideology that is fundamentally incompatible with democratic governance, individual liberty, and the separation of religion and state. Several European countries have taken steps to restrict Brotherhood-affiliated activity. Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Bahrain have designated the Brotherhood as a terrorist organisation. The United Kingdom’s refusal to proscribe the Brotherhood has made Britain a permissive operating environment for an organisation that, even on the most charitable reading of its activities, functions as a conveyor belt towards the ideological space in which Islamist terrorism becomes conceivable.

The broader institutional landscape has never been comprehensively audited. There are approximately 1,750 mosques in England and Wales, along with hundreds of Islamic centres, madrassas, and community organisations. The overwhelming majority operate lawfully and serve their communities. But the absence of systematic, intelligence-led scrutiny means that the minority of institutions that propagate extremist ideology, host extremist preachers, distribute extremist literature, or provide material or logistical support to terrorist networks have been able to operate in an environment where investigation is inhibited by political sensitivity. Every major Islamist terrorism investigation in the United Kingdom has revealed institutional connections: the Manchester Arena bomber’s links to the Didsbury Mosque, the 7/7 bombers’ connections to extremist preachers in Leeds and Dewsbury, the Finsbury Park Mosque’s role as a recruitment hub under Abu Hamza. These are not anomalies. They are visible manifestations of a network that has never been comprehensively mapped.

The NGO ecosystem presents a distinct but related vulnerability. Organisations that present themselves as civil liberties bodies, community advocacy groups, or human rights campaigners have, in documented and well-evidenced cases, functioned as apologists for Islamist extremism and as active opponents of British counter-terrorism policy. CAGE, which described the Islamic State executioner Mohammed Emwazi as a “beautiful young man” and has systematically campaigned against every element of the CONTEST strategy, is the most visible example. But the ecosystem extends well beyond CAGE. Organisations that receive public funding, charitable status, or government engagement while simultaneously campaigning to undermine counter-terrorism, platforming extremist speakers, or promoting ideological positions that are the direct precursors to terrorist violence, represent a structural vulnerability in Britain’s national security architecture.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Counter-Terrorism (Strengthening) Act will additionally:

- a) Proscribe the Muslim Brotherhood and all organisations identified by MI5, the NCA, and the Counter-Extremism Directorate as Brotherhood affiliates operating in the United Kingdom, under Schedule 2 of the Terrorism Act 2000. Proscription will make it a criminal offence to belong to, invite support for, arrange meetings for, or wear clothing or display articles associated with the Brotherhood or its affiliates. The Home Secretary will direct MI5 and the CED to compile a comprehensive list of Brotherhood-affiliated organisations, charities, educational bodies, and community groups operating in the UK within 6 months of Royal Assent, with proscription orders laid before Parliament as identification is completed. Assets of proscribed organisations will be subject to seizure under the Terrorist Asset-Freezing etc. Act 2010.
- b) Establish a statutory National Institutional Audit of all mosques, Islamic centres, madrassas, and religious educational establishments in England and Wales. The Audit will be conducted by the Counter-Extremism Directorate in coordination with MI5, CT Policing, the Charity Commission, and Ofsted (in respect of educational institutions). The Audit will assess each institution against a defined set of criteria: the content of sermons and religious instruction (whether extremist ideology is promoted); the presence of literature, media, or online materials that glorify, justify, or encourage violence or the overthrow of democratic governance; links between institutional leadership and proscribed organisations, designated individuals, or organisations of extremist concern; the receipt of foreign funding from states or entities associated with the promotion of extremist ideology; and safeguarding practices, particularly in respect of children attending madrassas and supplementary schools. The Audit is not an investigation of Islam. It is an investigation of institutions, which are subject to the law of the land regardless of their religious character. Any institution found to be propagating extremist ideology, hosting extremist preachers, or providing material support to terrorist networks will be referred to CT Policing for investigation and, where the evidence supports it, prosecution. Where an institution is a registered charity, the Charity Commission will exercise its powers to open a statutory inquiry and, where necessary, to remove trustees and wind up the charity.
- c) Establish a statutory NGO Counter-Extremism Audit, conducted by the Counter-Extremism Directorate in coordination with the Charity Commission, HMRC, and the National Crime Agency. The Audit will cover every non-governmental organisation, charity, community interest company, or unincorporated association that: has received public funding from any government department, local authority, or public body within the preceding ten years; holds charitable status and operates in a field connected to community relations, human rights, civil liberties, counter-extremism, or interfaith dialogue; or has been identified by MI5 or CT Policing as having links to individuals or organisations of extremist concern. The Audit will assess: whether the organisation has platformed, funded, employed, or promoted individuals connected to proscribed organisations or terrorist activity; whether the organisation has received funding from foreign states or entities associated with the promotion of extremist ideology; whether the organisation has conducted campaigns designed to delegitimise or undermine British counter-terrorism policy; and whether the organisation’s activities, taken as a whole, create a material risk that individuals will be drawn into terrorism. Organisations found to meet the threshold for the extremism facilitation offence (established in C12.3) will be referred for prosecution. Organisations found to have misused charitable status will be referred to the Charity Commission for statutory inquiry. Organisations that have received public funding while engaging in activities contrary to counter-terrorism objectives will be required to repay that funding and will be permanently barred from future public contracts and grants.

OPERATIONAL

Brotherhood identification programme. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, MI5 and the CED will commence the compilation of a comprehensive register of Muslim Brotherhood-affiliated organisations, charities, and community bodies operating in the United Kingdom. The register will draw on existing intelligence holdings, the Jenkins review evidence base, European partner agency assessments, and open-source research. Proscription orders will be laid before Parliament on a rolling basis as identification is completed, with the objective of completing the programme within 18 months.

Institutional Audit commencement. The National Institutional Audit will commence within 6 months of Royal Assent, prioritising the 500 institutions identified by MI5 and CT Policing as presenting the highest risk. The Audit will be completed for all institutions within 36 months. Institutions that cooperate fully and are found to present no risk will receive a published certificate of compliance. Institutions that refuse to cooperate will be referred to CT Policing.

NGO Audit commencement. The NGO Counter-Extremism Audit will commence within 6 months of Royal Assent. The CED will publish the criteria and methodology within 90 days. Organisations that are found to present no risk will be removed from the register. Organisations that present material risk will be subject to enhanced monitoring, and those that meet the prosecution threshold will be referred immediately.

###### C12.3: Prevent Investigation, Closure, and the Counter-Extremism Directorate

The Problem

The Prevent programme was not merely ineffective. It was institutionally captured. Sir William Shawcross’s independent review, published in February 2023, documented a programme that had been systematically compromised from within. Prevent had shown, in Shawcross’s words, “cultural timidity and an institutional hesitancy to tackle Islamism for fear of charges of Islamophobia.” Despite Islamist terrorism accounting for 75% of MI5’s caseload and 80% of CT Policing’s live investigations, only 16% of Prevent referrals in 2021/22 were categorised as Islamist. The programme had allocated its resources in a manner that bore no relationship to the actual threat picture. It had allowed organisations hostile to its mission, organisations that Shawcross identified as having “excused and legitimised violence by Islamist terrorists,” to shape its direction, delegitimise its practitioners, and narrow its operational focus.

This did not happen by accident. It happened because Prevent was designed as a community engagement programme rather than an intelligence-led counter-extremism operation. Its statutory duty was placed on schools, universities, NHS trusts, and local authorities, organisations whose culture, training, and institutional incentives are oriented towards inclusivity, safeguarding, and community relations, not towards the identification and disruption of ideological threats to national security. Frontline Prevent practitioners operated in an environment where honest identification of the Islamist threat risked accusations of racism, professional consequences, and community backlash orchestrated by the very groups that the programme was supposed to counter. The institutional capture was not a side effect of poor management. It was the predictable consequence of embedding a counter-terrorism function in institutions that are structurally incapable of resisting ideological pressure.

Progress does not propose to reform Prevent. Prevent cannot be reformed because the institution itself has been contaminated. The programme’s brand is toxic in the communities where it needs to operate. Its practitioners have been demoralised and intimidated. Its leadership has demonstrated, over two decades, an inability to align the programme’s operational focus with the actual threat. And the organisations that captured it remain in place, ready to capture any successor programme that operates on the same assumptions. What is required is threefold: first, a formal investigation into how institutional capture occurred, who was responsible, and what the consequences of that capture were for national security; second, the closure of Prevent as a programme and the dissolution of its organisational infrastructure; and third, the creation of an entirely new institution, designed from the ground up with an architecture that is immune to the failures that destroyed its predecessor.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Counter-Terrorism (Strengthening) Act will additionally:

- a) Establish a statutory Prevent Investigation Commission, appointed by the Home Secretary within 60 days of Royal Assent, with the following terms of reference: to investigate the extent and nature of institutional capture of the Prevent programme by organisations and individuals hostile to its counter-terrorism mission; to identify the organisations, individuals, and decision-making processes responsible for the misallocation of Prevent resources away from the Islamist threat; to assess the national security consequences of the programme’s failure to maintain operational focus on the predominant threat over the period 2011 to 2025; to determine whether any organisation or individual that influenced Prevent’s direction or resource allocation had links to proscribed organisations, organisations of extremist concern, or foreign state actors; and to make recommendations for criminal referrals, disciplinary action, and the recovery of public funds where appropriate. The Commission will have statutory powers to compel the production of documents and the attendance of witnesses, equivalent to those of a public inquiry under the Inquiries Act 2005. Its report will be published in full within 12 months.
- b) Dissolve the Prevent programme, the Channel programme, the Commission for Countering Extremism, and the Research, Information and Communications Unit (RICU) within 6 months of Royal Assent, upon the establishment of their statutory successor. All staff currently employed in these programmes will be assessed for transfer to the new directorate on the basis of competence and commitment to the counter-extremism mission. Staff found by the Prevent Investigation Commission to have been complicit in the institutional capture of Prevent, or to have failed to discharge their duties due to ideological bias or political timidity, will not be transferred.
- c) Establish a Counter-Extremism Directorate (CED) as a statutory body within the Home Office, operationally independent, led by a Director appointed by the Home Secretary and accountable to the Intelligence and Security Committee of Parliament. The CED will have a single mission: preventing individuals from becoming terrorists or supporting terrorism. It will not be a community cohesion programme, a safeguarding programme, or a social services referral pathway. It is an intelligence-led counter-extremism operation. The Director will be drawn from the senior ranks of MI5, CT Policing, or the intelligence community. No individual who has held a leadership position in Prevent or the Commission for Countering Extremism will be eligible for appointment. The CED will absorb the counter-extremism functions of its dissolved predecessors, but its organisational culture, leadership, priorities, and operating model will be entirely new.
- d) Require the CED to maintain a threat-proportionate allocation of resources, defined as follows: the proportion of CED resources allocated to each ideological category must not deviate by more than 15 percentage points from the proportion of MI5’s operational caseload attributable to that category. If MI5 assesses that 75% of its caseload is Islamist, the CED’s resource allocation must reflect that reality within the permitted band. This statutory requirement eliminates the possibility of a repeat of Prevent’s most damaging failure: the allocation of resources in a manner driven by political anxiety rather than by the threat.
- e) Create a statutory offence of extremism facilitation, carrying a maximum of ten years’ imprisonment, defined as: the systematic promotion of an ideology that advocates, justifies, or glorifies the use of violence to achieve political, religious, or ideological objectives, where the promotion is conducted through an organised platform (a registered organisation, an educational institution, a place of worship, or a media outlet) and is assessed by the CED to create a material risk that one or more individuals will be drawn into terrorism. This offence closes the gap between lawful expression and proscription.
- f) Reform the proscription framework (Terrorism Act 2000, Schedule 2) to enable the proscription of organisations that promote non-violent extremism where the Home Secretary is satisfied, on the basis of intelligence assessed by MI5 and the CED, that the organisation’s ideology, activities, or associations create a material risk that individuals will be drawn into terrorism. The current proscription threshold, limited to organisations “concerned in terrorism,” is too high for organisations that operate in the pre-criminal space.

OPERATIONAL

CED establishment. The Counter-Extremism Directorate will be operational within 6 months of Royal Assent with an initial staffing complement of 500, including intelligence analysts, intervention specialists, and regional coordinators deployed in every police force area. The Director will be appointed within 90 days of Royal Assent.

Frontline training. Within 12 months, every professional subject to the counter-extremism statutory duty will complete a mandatory, standardised training programme developed by the CED. The training will replace the inconsistent and often ineffective training currently delivered under Prevent and will be specifically designed to address Islamist radicalisation indicators as the primary focus, with secondary modules on other ideological pathways.

Online extremism unit. Within 6 months, the CED will establish a dedicated Online Extremism Unit tasked with identifying and disrupting extremist content, recruitment activity, and radicalisation networks operating on social media platforms, encrypted messaging services, and the dark web.

###### C12.4: State Threats and Hostile Foreign Intelligence

The Problem

The National Security Act 2023 introduced new offences for espionage, foreign interference, sabotage, and obtaining or disclosing trade secrets. It created a Foreign Influence Registration Scheme and gave MI5 and law enforcement new tools to investigate and disrupt state threat activity. These were necessary reforms. They are not sufficient for the threat that has materialised since. MI5 has reported a 35% increase in individuals investigated for state threat activity in the past year. Russia deploys proxies to conduct surveillance, sabotage, arson, and physical violence on British soil. Iran has been linked to over twenty potentially lethal plots against UK targets. China conducts espionage targeting Parliament, universities, and critical national infrastructure.

The operational challenge is that state-backed threats increasingly use the same methods as terrorism but are conducted by or on behalf of foreign intelligence services. The legal and institutional frameworks for dealing with terrorism and state threats have historically been separate. A Russian proxy who commits arson on a military recruitment centre is engaged in an act of hostile intelligence that is functionally indistinguishable from terrorism. It should be treated as such.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Counter-Terrorism (Strengthening) Act will additionally:

- a) Create a statutory offence of hostile state-directed violence, carrying a minimum sentence of twenty years, defined as: any act of violence, sabotage, arson, or physical intimidation committed in the United Kingdom at the direction of, on behalf of, or for the benefit of a foreign intelligence service, foreign government, or foreign political organisation. Where the act results in death, the minimum sentence will be life imprisonment with a whole-life order. This offence addresses the specific phenomenon of state-backed violence on British soil: the poisoning of Sergei and Yulia Skripal, the assassination of Alexander Litvinenko, the Iranian plots against dissidents, and the Russian proxy operations that MI5 has disrupted.
- b) Extend the Counter-Extremism Directorate’s mandate to include state-directed radicalisation and proxy recruitment. Where a foreign state is assessed by MI5 to be using social media, diaspora community networks, or other channels to recruit proxies for sabotage, violence, or intimidation in the United Kingdom, the CED will be authorised to conduct counter-influence operations, to refer identified proxies to CT Policing for investigation, and to publish declassified intelligence identifying the state-backed networks.
- c) Establish a statutory Hostile State Activity Fund, capitalised from the seizure of assets belonging to individuals and entities sanctioned under the Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018, the National Security Act 2023, and the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002. The Fund will finance counter-intelligence operations, protective security for targeted individuals, and the hardening of critical national infrastructure against state-directed sabotage.

OPERATIONAL

Diplomatic response framework. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Foreign Secretary will publish a Hostile State Activity Response Framework, setting out the escalatory measures available in response to state-backed threats: diplomatic expulsions, targeted sanctions, asset seizures, cyber countermeasures, and the declassification and publication of intelligence identifying state-backed operations.

Critical infrastructure protection. Within 12 months, the National Protective Security Authority will complete a vulnerability assessment of all Category 1 and Category 2 critical national infrastructure sites against state-directed sabotage, and will publish binding minimum security standards for each category.

###### C12.5: Deradicalisation, Rehabilitation, and Community Resilience

The Problem

The Channel programme supported approximately 1,400 individuals in 2024/25. The evidence base for deradicalisation programmes globally is weak: there are few rigorous evaluations, long-term outcomes are difficult to measure, and the recidivism evidence is mixed. The Fishmongers’ Hall attack was carried out by Usman Khan while attending a prisoner rehabilitation event, having supposedly been deradicalised. The Streatham attack was carried out by Sudesh Amman days after release from prison. Both had been through deradicalisation programming. Neither was deradicalised.

The structural problem is that deradicalisation is treated as a therapeutic intervention analogous to treating a mental health condition. It is not. Ideological commitment is a belief system, not a pathology. The tools for challenging it are intellectual and ideological, not clinical. They require credible counter-narratives delivered by credible voices, sustained engagement over years, and an honest reckoning with the specific ideology that motivates the individual. In the case of Islamist radicalisation, this means theological counter-argument delivered by scholars with the authority to challenge extremist interpretations of scripture. Generic programmes that treat all extremism as interchangeable, that avoid naming the specific ideology for fear of causing offence, and that rely on cognitive behavioural techniques designed for anger management rather than ideological conversion, do not work.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Counter-Terrorism (Strengthening) Act will additionally:

- a) Replace the Channel programme with a Deradicalisation and Disengagement Programme (DDP), administered by the Counter-Extremism Directorate, and structured as follows. Tier 1 (Early Intervention): for individuals referred to the CED who are assessed as at low to moderate risk. Intervention will involve mentoring by a trained practitioner with specific expertise in the relevant ideology, cognitive reframing sessions, and practical support. Duration: 6 to 12 months. Tier 2 (Intensive Engagement): for individuals assessed as at high risk or who have failed to disengage under Tier 1. Intervention will involve daily structured engagement, mandatory attendance at an ideology-specific counter-narrative programme, and enhanced monitoring. Duration: 12 to 24 months. Tier 3 (Post-Conviction Deradicalisation): for convicted terrorists serving sentences in Separation Centres. A dedicated deradicalisation team, including theologians, psychologists, and former extremists, will deliver an intensive programme throughout the sentence. No convicted terrorist will be recommended for release by the Parole Board without a positive assessment from the Tier 3 team and the concurrence of MI5.
- b) Establish an Islamist Counter-Narrative Capability as the primary function of the CED’s counter-narrative division. The capability will be staffed by theologians, scholars of Islamic jurisprudence, and former Islamists who can challenge extremist interpretations of scripture with theological authority. Islamist radicalisation is driven by a theological argument. It must be countered by a theological argument, delivered by voices that carry authority within the tradition. The CED will also maintain a secondary capability for other ideological pathways as required.
- c) Create a statutory Community Resilience Duty, requiring every local authority in England and Wales to maintain a Community Resilience Plan, developed in partnership with the CED, CT Policing, local faith communities, and educational institutions. The Plan will identify local radicalisation risks, set out the intervention resources available, and establish clear escalation pathways from community concern to CED referral. Communities that are most affected by Islamist radicalisation will have a statutory guarantee that the resources to counter it are present in their area.

OPERATIONAL

DDP implementation. The Deradicalisation and Disengagement Programme will be operational within 6 months of Royal Assent. All individuals currently supported by Channel will be transitioned to the DDP with continuity of care. The Tier 3 post-conviction programme will be deployed in every Separation Centre within 12 months.

Counter-narrative materials. Within 12 months, the CED will publish a comprehensive suite of Islamist counter-narrative materials developed in partnership with Islamic scholars, academic institutions, and former extremists.

Former extremist recruitment. The CED will recruit and employ former extremists who have demonstrably disengaged from extremism, as practitioners, mentors, and public communicators. A former jihadist who has turned his back on violence carries an authority that no civil servant or academic can replicate.

###### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The C12 framework requires one new piece of primary legislation: the Counter-Terrorism (Strengthening) Act. This Act builds on the existing Terrorism Act 2000, Terrorism Act 2006, Counter-Terrorism and Sentencing Act 2021, and National Security Act 2023. It does not replace those statutes. It strengthens them with statutory minimum sentences for enabling offences, indefinite detention for the most dangerous offenders, reformed restriction orders, the proscription of the Muslim Brotherhood, a statutory institutional and NGO audit, the investigation and closure of Prevent, a new counter-extremism directorate, state threat provisions, and a deradicalisation framework aligned to the actual threat picture.

###### Counter-Terrorism (Strengthening) Act

On the face of the Act: Statutory minimum sentences for terrorist material possession (5 years), terrorist publication dissemination (7 years), inviting support for proscribed organisations (7 years), expressing support recklessly (5 years), failure to disclose (3 years). Terrorism Indefinite Detention Order (Crown Court, annual Parole Board review with national security assessor). Terrorism Prevention and Restriction Orders replacing TPIMs (no maximum duration, GPS tagging, encrypted communication ban, mandatory deradicalisation, approved internet devices only). Proscription of the Muslim Brotherhood and all identified affiliates, with asset seizure under the Terrorist Asset-Freezing etc. Act 2010. National Institutional Audit of all mosques, Islamic centres, madrassas, and religious educational establishments (CED-led, MI5/CT Policing/Charity Commission/Ofsted coordination, defined criteria, criminal referral for non-compliance). NGO Counter-Extremism Audit (CED-led, covering all publicly funded or charitable organisations in the community relations, human rights, and counter-extremism space, with prosecution referral, public funding recovery, and permanent funding bar). Prevent Investigation Commission (statutory inquiry powers, 12-month report, criminal referral and disciplinary recommendations). Dissolution of Prevent, Channel, Commission for Countering Extremism, and RICU. Counter-Extremism Directorate (statutory body, 500 staff, ISC accountability, threat-proportionate resource allocation within 15 percentage points of MI5 caseload). Extremism facilitation offence (max 10 years). Reformed proscription framework (non-violent extremism where material risk). Hostile state-directed violence offence (min 20 years, whole-life for death). CED mandate extended to state-directed radicalisation and proxy recruitment. Hostile State Activity Fund. Deradicalisation and Disengagement Programme (three-tier). Islamist counter-narrative capability as primary CED function. Community Resilience Duty on local authorities.

Delivered operationally: CED Director appointed within 90 days, Directorate operational within 6 months (500 staff, regional coordinators in every force area). Prevent Investigation Commission appointed within 60 days, report within 12 months. Brotherhood identification programme commenced within 90 days, proscription orders on rolling basis, programme completed within 18 months. National Institutional Audit commenced within 6 months (500 highest-risk institutions first), completed within 36 months. NGO Counter-Extremism Audit commenced within 6 months (criteria published within 90 days). Mandatory counter-extremism training for all frontline professionals within 12 months (Islamist radicalisation as primary focus). Online Extremism Unit within 6 months. 15-year mandatory licence period for all released terrorism offenders. Separation Centres in every prison holding terrorism offenders within 6 months. DDP operational within 6 months, Tier 3 in all Separation Centres within 12 months. Islamist counter-narrative materials published within 12 months. Former extremist recruitment programme. Hostile State Activity Response Framework published within 90 days. Critical infrastructure vulnerability assessment within 12 months. Community Resilience Plans in all local authority areas within 12 months.

The terrorist threat to Britain is Islamist. It has been Islamist for a generation. Every major realised attack, the overwhelming majority of foiled plots, three quarters of MI5’s caseload, and four fifths of CT Policing’s live investigations confirm it. The ideological infrastructure that sustains this threat, the Brotherhood, the extremist mosques, the NGOs that function as apologists, the captured prevention programme that refused to name it, has been allowed to operate in Britain without comprehensive scrutiny because the political class was afraid of what scrutiny would reveal and what honesty would cost. Progress is not afraid. The Brotherhood will be proscribed. The institutions will be audited. The NGOs will be held accountable. Prevent will be investigated for the institutional capture that rendered it useless, and it will be replaced by a directorate that takes its priorities from the intelligence services, not from the organisations it was supposed to counter. The most dangerous offenders will face sentences without a guaranteed end date. State-backed threats will be treated as acts of hostile intelligence. Britain does not negotiate with terrorists. Under Progress, it will not negotiate with the ideologies, the institutions, or the enablers that produce them.

#### C13. Technology-Driven Policing

Governing Principle

Britain is one of the most surveilled countries in the democratic world and one of the worst at converting surveillance into criminal justice outcomes. The United Kingdom has approximately 13,000 ANPR cameras generating 55 million number plate reads per day. Local authorities, transport operators, and private businesses operate millions of CCTV cameras. The Metropolitan Police deployed live facial recognition 117 times between January and August 2024, producing 360 arrests. Body-worn video is issued across all 43 Home Office forces. The national ANPR network, the CCTV estate, the custody image databases, the DNA database with its 5.8 million profiles, and the IDENT1 fingerprint database with 7.5 million sets of prints constitute an infrastructure of extraordinary breadth. Yet digital forensics backlogs mean that seized devices wait months for examination. Intelligence systems cannot communicate across force boundaries without manual intervention. The Police National Computer, built in the 1970s, coexists with dozens of incompatible force-level systems. And the charge rate for recorded crime stands at 5.5%, meaning that 94.5% of crimes reported to the police result in no charge at all.

The instinct of government, when confronted with this failure, is to build more: more cameras, more databases, more surveillance infrastructure, more coverage. This instinct is wrong. Britain does not have a surveillance deficit. It has a capability deficit. The problem is not that the state collects too little data. It is that the state cannot process, integrate, analyse, or act on the data it already collects. Adding 12,000 more ANPR cameras to a system that already generates 55 million daily reads without the analytical infrastructure to exploit them is not a policing strategy. It is a storage problem. Mandating CCTV minimums for every local authority, including those with low crime rates and no operational need, is not enhancing public safety. It is normalising mass surveillance for its own sake. Rolling out facial recognition vans to every force area, regardless of whether the local crime picture justifies the deployment, is not concentrating capability. It is dispersing it.

Progress’ position is the opposite of the surveillance-maximalist orthodoxy. The objective is not to blanket Britain in cameras and sensors. The objective is to ensure that the technology the police already possess, and the cutting-edge capabilities that are now available, are concentrated where they will produce arrests, charges, and convictions for serious crime, and that the analytical, forensic, and intelligence infrastructure exists to convert raw data into criminal justice outcomes. This means fewer cameras where cameras serve no operational purpose, and dramatically better technology where it does. It means a national digital forensics capability that can process a seized phone in days, not months. It means a biometric integration platform that connects DNA, fingerprints, facial recognition, and custody images into a single investigative tool, so that no identification is missed because evidence sits in one database unlinked to another. It means AI-powered analytics that direct resources to where crime is occurring and identify connections between cases that human analysis would take weeks to find. And it means a national agency with the authority to set standards, procure systems, and eliminate the fragmentation that turns 43 police forces into 43 separate technology ecosystems.

The civil liberties argument, properly understood, supports this approach. The legitimate concern about police technology is not that it exists but that it is deployed indiscriminately, without clear rules, without independent oversight, and without evidence that it produces results proportionate to the intrusion. A national surveillance infrastructure that watches everyone and catches almost nobody is the worst of both worlds: maximum intrusion for minimum effect. A concentrated, intelligence-led technology capability that is deployed where the evidence justifies it, governed by clear statutory rules, subject to independent audit, and measured by criminal justice outcomes is both more effective and more proportionate than the status quo. Progress will reduce the overall footprint of state surveillance while dramatically increasing the quality, speed, and effectiveness of technology-enabled police work. The measure of success is not how many cameras are deployed. It is how many offenders are convicted.

###### C13.1: Surveillance Rationalisation and the National Audit

The Problem

The existing surveillance infrastructure in England and Wales has grown organically over four decades without strategic direction. Local authorities installed CCTV in response to specific incidents or funding opportunities. ANPR cameras were deployed on major road networks by individual forces. Private sector CCTV proliferated without coordination. The result is a patchwork: dense coverage in some areas, none in others, with no systematic relationship between where cameras are positioned and where they are operationally needed. Many local authority CCTV systems are outdated, poorly maintained, and produce footage of such low quality that it is of limited evidential value. Cameras that were installed in response to a crime problem that has since moved or dissipated continue to operate because no mechanism exists to assess whether they remain justified.

The cost of maintaining this infrastructure falls on local authorities whose budgets are already under severe pressure. The result is not just waste but a perverse outcome: councils spend money maintaining cameras that serve no operational purpose while lacking the funds to invest in the cameras, or the analytical capability, that would actually reduce crime in their area. Meanwhile, the sheer volume of footage generated by the existing estate overwhelms the capacity of police to review it. Body-worn video, CCTV, ANPR, and dashcam footage from a single incident can run to hundreds of hours. Without the technology to triage and analyse this footage automatically, it sits in storage until an officer has time to watch it, which in many cases means it is never watched at all.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

A Police Technology and Digital Enforcement Act will:

- a) Require the National Police Technology Agency (established below) to conduct a comprehensive National Surveillance Audit within 12 months of Royal Assent. The Audit will assess every publicly operated CCTV system, every ANPR installation, and every police-operated surveillance capability in England and Wales against a defined set of criteria: evidential utility (has the system contributed to arrests, charges, or convictions in the preceding 24 months?); image quality (does the system produce footage of sufficient quality to be used in criminal proceedings?); operational justification (is the system positioned in a location where the current crime picture, based on recorded crime data and intelligence assessments, justifies its continued operation?); and cost-effectiveness (does the system produce outcomes proportionate to the cost of its operation and maintenance?). Systems that fail to meet the operational justification threshold will be recommended for decommissioning. Systems that meet the threshold but fail on image quality will be recommended for upgrade or replacement. The Audit will be published in full, and its recommendations will be binding on local authorities and police forces, subject to a right of appeal to the Home Secretary.
- b) Establish a statutory principle of operational justification for all new surveillance deployments. No new publicly operated CCTV system, ANPR installation, or biometric surveillance capability may be deployed unless the deploying authority can demonstrate, in a published assessment, that the deployment is justified by the current crime picture in the deployment area, is proportionate to the policing objective, and is subject to a defined review period after which the deployment will be reassessed against the same criteria. This principle does not apply to temporary deployments for specific operations (major events, ongoing investigations) or to the targeted deployments established in other parts of the framework (Knife Detection Zones under C10, for example). It applies to permanent infrastructure. The effect is to reverse the current default: instead of surveillance being deployed unless someone objects, it is deployed only where it is justified and removed when it is not.

OPERATIONAL

National Surveillance Audit. The Audit will commence within 6 months of Royal Assent and will be completed within 12 months. The NPTA will deploy audit teams to every local authority area and every police force. Decommissioning recommendations will be implemented within 6 months of publication. The estimated saving from decommissioning unjustified systems will be hypothecated to the Police Technology Fund to fund the capability investments established in this framework.

Decommissioning programme. Systems recommended for decommissioning will be removed at the cost of the NPTA, not the local authority. Equipment that is still functional and meets quality standards will be redeployed to locations where the Audit has identified an operational need, rather than being scrapped.

###### C13.2: Facial Recognition, Biometrics, and Concentrated Deployment

The Problem

Live facial recognition has demonstrated its value in producing arrests for serious crime. Between September 2024 and September 2025, the Metropolitan Police recorded 962 arrests directly attributable to LFR, including for rape, domestic abuse, knife crime, GBH, and robbery. Over a quarter of those arrests related to violence against women and girls. The Croydon permanent installation produced 103 arrests in its pilot period. Retrospective facial recognition, which matches still images from CCTV against the custody image database, led to 127 arrests following the 2024 summer disorder. The technology works. But it works best when it is deployed in the right place, at the right time, against the right watchlist. A facial recognition van deployed in a rural market town with a low crime rate and no individuals on the watchlist known to frequent the area is not an effective use of the technology. It is a political gesture.

There is no dedicated legislation governing police use of facial recognition in England and Wales. The government acknowledged in December 2025 that the existing patchwork of the Data Protection Act 2018, the Human Rights Act 1998, the Equality Act 2010, and PACE 1984 does not give police the confidence to deploy at scale, nor the public the confidence that deployment is governed by clear rules. The government launched a consultation in December 2025 and expects new legislation in approximately two years. Progress will not wait. The biometric landscape beyond facial recognition is equally fragmented. The National DNA Database holds approximately 5.8 million profiles. The IDENT1 fingerprint database holds approximately 7.5 million sets. Custody image databases hold millions of photographs. These systems are powerful individually but unconnected operationally. A DNA match in one force area is not automatically cross-referenced with facial recognition data or fingerprint evidence in another.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Police Technology and Digital Enforcement Act will additionally:

- a) Establish a comprehensive statutory framework for the use of live facial recognition by police forces in England and Wales. The framework will define: the categories of offence for which an individual may be placed on a watchlist (any offence carrying a maximum sentence of 12 months or more, any individual wanted on warrant, any individual subject to a court order prohibiting them from a specific area, and any individual assessed as posing an immediate risk to public safety); the authorisation required for deployment (superintendent or above, with a published deployment assessment demonstrating that the deployment location is justified by the crime picture and the presence of watchlist subjects in the area); the retention period for biometric data (data of non-matched individuals deleted automatically within 24 hours; match data retained for the duration of any resulting investigation and 12 months thereafter); and the oversight arrangements (deployment records submitted to the Biometrics and Surveillance Commissioner within 7 days, annual report to Parliament on use, accuracy, and outcomes).
- b) Create a National Facial Recognition Capability (NFRC), centrally operated by the National Police Technology Agency and available to all police forces on a deployment-request basis. The NFRC will not distribute LFR units to every force. It will maintain a fleet of mobile LFR units operated by specialist NPTA teams, deployable to any force area within 24 hours on the request of a chief constable or the NCA, where the requesting force demonstrates that the deployment meets the statutory criteria. The NFRC will also operate fixed installations in the locations identified by the National Surveillance Audit as having the highest concentration of wanted individuals and the highest rates of violent crime: city centre transport hubs, major retail areas in the highest-crime force areas, and locations identified by the NCA as county lines distribution points. Fixed installations will be subject to 12-month review against the operational justification standard. This model concentrates capability where it produces results, rather than distributing it across 43 forces regardless of need.
- c) Establish a National Biometric Integration Platform (NBIP), merging the operational outputs of the National DNA Database, the IDENT1 fingerprint system, the national custody image database, and the NFRC into a single investigative interface. An officer conducting an investigation will be able to search across all biometric databases simultaneously from a single terminal. A DNA sample recovered from a crime scene will be automatically cross-referenced with fingerprint, facial recognition, and custody image data. The platform will be subject to the same access controls, audit trails, and oversight arrangements as the individual databases it integrates. This is not a surveillance expansion. It is the elimination of waste: ensuring that identification opportunities are not missed because evidence exists in one system but has never been checked against another.

OPERATIONAL

NFRC fleet. Within 12 months of Royal Assent, the NPTA will operate a national fleet of 30 mobile LFR units and will have installed fixed LFR at a maximum of 20 locations nationally, selected by crime data and intelligence assessment. Deployment will be reviewed at 12-month intervals and installations that fail the operational justification test will be removed.

Biometric Integration Platform. The NBIP will be operational within 24 months of Royal Assent. The platform will be developed by the NPTA in partnership with the Home Office, the Forensic Science Regulator, and the NCA. Procurement will prioritise UK-developed technology and will exclude suppliers from states assessed by the NCSC as presenting a risk to UK data security.

###### C13.3: Digital Forensics and the National Police Technology Agency

The Problem

Digital evidence is now involved in the majority of criminal investigations. Mobile phones, computers, cloud storage, social media accounts, encrypted messaging applications, and connected devices generate evidence essential to the prosecution of offences from fraud and child sexual exploitation to murder and terrorism. The volume of digital evidence has grown exponentially while the capacity to process it has not kept pace. Digital forensics backlogs across police forces mean that seized devices routinely wait months for examination. Victims of sexual offences are asked to surrender their phones for extended periods while investigations crawl through extraction queues. Evidence on devices with limited battery life or volatile memory degrades or is lost entirely. The Forensic Science Regulator has repeatedly raised concerns about quality and consistency.

The problem is structural. Each of the 43 Home Office forces maintains its own digital forensic capability, with its own equipment, staff, processes, and backlog. There is no national standard for turnaround times, no national procurement, and no surge capacity. A force dealing with a complex child exploitation network may have the same digital forensic capacity as a force dealing with routine volume crime. Beyond forensics, each force maintains its own IT systems, data platforms, and supplier contracts. The Police National Computer coexists with the Police National Database, HOLMES, and dozens of force-level systems that cannot communicate without manual intervention. The absence of a single national technology body with the authority to set standards, procure systems, and mandate interoperability is the root cause of a problem that has persisted for decades.

This is the capability deficit that matters more than any camera. A police force that can seize a phone but cannot examine it for four months is not conducting an investigation. It is conducting an exercise in delay. A force that identifies a DNA match but cannot cross-reference it with facial recognition data held by another force is not exploiting its intelligence. It is wasting it. The investments that will produce the largest improvement in criminal justice outcomes are not in surveillance hardware. They are in the forensic, analytical, and data infrastructure that converts evidence into convictions.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Police Technology and Digital Enforcement Act will additionally:

- a) Establish the National Police Technology Agency (NPTA) as a statutory non-departmental public body, accountable to the Home Secretary, with the following functions: setting mandatory national standards for all police technology systems (IT infrastructure, data platforms, biometric systems, digital forensic equipment, communications); procuring technology at national scale on behalf of all police forces, eliminating the duplication and waste of 43 separate procurement processes; operating the National Facial Recognition Capability, the National Biometric Integration Platform, and any future national-scale technology infrastructure; maintaining a national digital forensics surge capability deployable to any force within 48 hours; conducting research and development into emerging policing technologies in partnership with UK universities and the private sector; and conducting the National Surveillance Audit and enforcing the operational justification standard. The NPTA will be led by a Chief Executive appointed by the Home Secretary, with a board comprising representatives of policing, the intelligence community, the technology sector, and the Biometrics and Surveillance Commissioner. The NPTA will absorb the technology functions currently dispersed across the Home Office, the College of Policing, and the NPCC.
- b) Create a National Digital Forensics Service (NDFS), operated by the NPTA, providing digital forensic examination capability to all police forces on a centralised basis. The NDFS will maintain regional forensic hubs, each equipped to the same standard and staffed by accredited digital forensic practitioners, in each of the nine English regions and in Wales. The Service will set mandatory maximum turnaround times: 48 hours for priority cases (terrorism, child sexual exploitation, murder, kidnap); 14 days for serious crime (rape, serious violence, Class A drug supply); and 30 days for all other cases. Forces will retain the ability to conduct initial device triage at force level, but full forensic examination will be conducted by the NDFS. The Service will be funded centrally and will eliminate the current postcode lottery in which the speed of a criminal investigation depends on the digital forensic capacity of the investigating force.
- c) Mandate the adoption of a single national police data platform, replacing the current fragmented landscape of force-level systems. The platform will integrate crime recording, intelligence management, case management, custody records, and biometric data into a single system accessible to all forces, subject to appropriate access controls and audit trails. All forces will be required to migrate to the national platform within 36 months of Royal Assent. The current situation, in which an officer investigating a crime that crosses force boundaries must make manual requests for information from neighbouring forces, is a structural impediment to effective policing that technology resolved in the private sector decades ago.
- d) Create a statutory duty on technology companies to provide lawful access to encrypted communications data where a warrant has been issued by a judge under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016. Providers must acknowledge a warrant within 2 hours and provide the requested data within 24 hours, or within 4 hours in cases designated as urgent (terrorism, imminent threat to life, child sexual exploitation). Providers that fail to comply will be subject to escalating financial penalties, starting at £10 million per incident and increasing to 4% of global annual turnover for persistent non-compliance. This provision does not require the creation of backdoors or the weakening of encryption for all users. It requires companies to comply with lawful judicial orders within timelines that reflect the operational urgency of criminal investigations.

OPERATIONAL

NPTA establishment. The National Police Technology Agency will be established within 6 months of Royal Assent, with an initial staffing complement of 500. The Chief Executive will be appointed within 90 days. The first national technology standards will be published within 12 months.

Digital forensics surge. Within 6 months, the NPTA will establish a national digital forensics surge capability of 50 accredited examiners, deployable to any force within 48 hours. The full National Digital Forensics Service with 10 regional hubs will be operational within 24 months.

Data platform migration. The national police data platform will be procured within 12 months. Pilot migration will commence with 5 forces within 18 months. Full national migration will be complete within 36 months.

Body-worn video standardisation. Within 12 months, the NPTA will issue a mandatory national standard for body-worn video, including minimum recording quality, mandatory activation protocols, data retention periods, and integration with the NBIP. All forces will comply within 24 months.

###### C13.4: Predictive Analytics, AI, and Investigative Intelligence

The Problem

Predictive policing uses data analysis to identify patterns in criminal behaviour, forecast where and when crimes are likely to occur, and direct resources accordingly. The concept is not new: police have always used intelligence to anticipate crime. What is new is the volume of data available and the computational power to analyse it. The use of predictive analytics in UK policing is inconsistent. Some forces use sophisticated tools; others use basic data visualisation or nothing at all.

The objection to predictive policing, that it entrenches existing discrimination by directing resources to already over-policed areas, is a criticism of bad implementation, not of the technology. A model trained on biased arrest data will produce biased predictions. A model trained on crime outcome data, victim reports, and multi-source intelligence will produce predictions that reflect where crime is actually occurring and where victims are actually being harmed. The solution is not to abandon the technology but to build it properly: with transparent models, independent audit, and a statutory framework that ensures accountability.

Artificial intelligence has applications across the policing mission that do not involve surveillance at all. AI can automate the review of digital evidence, directly addressing the forensic backlog that is the single greatest bottleneck in the criminal justice system. AI can analyse financial transactions for money laundering patterns, supporting the asset recovery functions established in C2 and C11. AI can process open-source intelligence at a scale that human analysts cannot achieve. And AI can identify connections between apparently unrelated cases, suspects, and locations, generating investigative leads that would otherwise take weeks of manual work. These are analytical and investigative tools. They process data that has already been lawfully collected. They do not expand the surveillance footprint. They make the existing footprint produce results.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Police Technology and Digital Enforcement Act will additionally:

- a) Require the NPTA to develop and deploy a national predictive analytics capability, available to all police forces, that integrates crime data, intelligence data, and other relevant sources to generate daily risk assessments and resource allocation recommendations. The capability will be developed in partnership with UK universities and the Alan Turing Institute. The models will be published (subject to redaction of operationally sensitive parameters) and independently audited annually by the Biometrics and Surveillance Commissioner for accuracy, fairness, and the absence of discriminatory bias. Forces will not be required to follow the recommendations, but they will be required to record their resource allocation decisions and to explain any significant deviation.
- b) Establish a Police AI Development Programme within the NPTA, tasked with developing, testing, and deploying AI-powered tools for: automated digital evidence review (triaging seized devices for priority content, reducing forensic backlog); financial transaction analysis (supporting anti-money laundering and asset recovery under C2, C9, and C11); open-source intelligence processing (monitoring publicly available online content for indicators of criminal activity, including terrorist content, child sexual exploitation material, and organised crime communications); and investigative link analysis (identifying connections between cases, suspects, locations, and criminal networks across force boundaries). All AI tools will be subject to oversight by the Biometrics and Surveillance Commissioner and to national standards set by the NPTA. The Programme will not develop tools for general population surveillance, behavioural prediction of non-suspects, or social media monitoring of lawful activity.
- c) Create a statutory framework for the use of AI-generated evidence in criminal proceedings. Evidence derived from AI analysis will be admissible in court provided that: the AI system is certified by the NPTA as meeting national standards for accuracy and reliability; the methodology of the analysis is disclosed to the defence; and the AI-generated evidence is corroborated by at least one independent source (human analysis, physical evidence, or testimony). This framework provides legal certainty for prosecutors and defence alike.

OPERATIONAL

Predictive analytics pilot. Within 12 months, the NPTA will deploy a pilot predictive analytics capability in 10 force areas, selected to represent a range of policing environments. National deployment will follow within 24 months.

AI development. The Police AI Development Programme will be established within 6 months, with an initial budget of £50 million. The Programme will be co-located with the Alan Turing Institute. The first operational tools (automated evidence triage and investigative link analysis) will be deployed within 18 months.

###### C13.5: The Police Technology Fund

The Problem

Police technology is currently funded through a combination of the Home Office police grant, local precept funding, specific transformation grants, and individual force capital budgets. The result is radical inequality. The Metropolitan Police can invest in facial recognition, advanced ANPR, and digital forensic laboratories. A smaller force, dealing with the same categories of crime but with a fraction of the budget, may operate CCTV systems that are a decade out of date and a digital forensic capability that consists of a single examiner with a backlog measured in months. This is not local priority-setting. It is a structural failure that means the technological capability available to protect the public depends on which side of a force boundary a crime occurs.

The solution is not to give every force the same hardware. It is to centralise the capabilities that must be national (digital forensics, biometric integration, the data platform, AI tools, the facial recognition fleet) so that every force has access to the same standard of service regardless of its individual budget. The NPTA exists to provide this. The Police Technology Fund exists to pay for it.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Police Technology and Digital Enforcement Act will additionally:

- a) Establish a Police Technology Fund with an annual budget of £350 million for the first five years, ring-fenced within the Home Office police settlement and administered by the NPTA. The Fund will be allocated as follows: 35% to the National Digital Forensics Service and regional forensic hubs; 25% to the national police data platform and force migration; 20% to the Police AI Development Programme, predictive analytics, and the National Biometric Integration Platform; 10% to the National Facial Recognition Capability (fleet operation, fixed installations, specialist teams); and 10% to the Biometrics and Surveillance Commissioner’s office, the National Surveillance Audit, independent oversight, and research and development. The allocation reflects the principle of this framework: the largest investment goes to the capability that will produce the largest improvement in criminal justice outcomes, which is the forensic and data infrastructure, not the surveillance hardware.
- b) Require the Home Secretary to lay before Parliament an annual Police Technology Report, detailing: the number and outcomes of LFR deployments nationally; the results of the National Surveillance Audit (systems decommissioned, systems upgraded, net change in surveillance footprint); the turnaround times for digital forensic examination across all forces; the accuracy rates and bias audit results for facial recognition, predictive analytics, and AI systems; the progress of the national data platform migration; the Police Technology Fund expenditure and outcomes; and the number of arrests, charges, and convictions attributable to technology-enabled identification and investigation. The Report will be debated annually in the House of Commons.

OPERATIONAL

Police Technology Fund. The Fund will be operational within 90 days of Royal Assent, with initial allocations released within 30 days thereafter. The first-year allocation will be front-loaded, with 60% released in the first six months to fund the NPTA establishment, digital forensics surge capability, and the national data platform procurement.

Technology equalisation. Within 6 months, the NPTA will identify the 15 forces with the lowest technological baseline and provide targeted investment to bring them to national standards within 24 months. This investment will focus on forensic and data capability, not on surveillance hardware.

###### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The C13 framework requires one new piece of primary legislation: the Police Technology and Digital Enforcement Act. This Act builds on the policing architecture established in C5 and the enforcement capabilities established across the framework. It does not duplicate existing provisions. It creates the national technology infrastructure, the unified legal framework, and the central agency that British policing has lacked for decades, while establishing for the first time the principle that surveillance infrastructure must be justified by operational results, not expanded as a default.

###### Police Technology and Digital Enforcement Act

On the face of the Act: National Surveillance Audit (mandatory assessment of all publicly operated CCTV, ANPR, and biometric systems against evidential utility, image quality, operational justification, and cost-effectiveness; binding decommissioning recommendations; published results). Statutory principle of operational justification for all new surveillance deployments (crime-picture assessment, proportionality, defined review period). Statutory framework for live facial recognition (watchlist criteria, deployment authorisation with crime-picture justification, data retention, Biometrics Commissioner oversight). National Facial Recognition Capability (NPTA-operated fleet of 30 mobile units, maximum 20 fixed installations, deployment-request model, 12-month review against operational justification). National Biometric Integration Platform (DNA, fingerprints, facial recognition, custody images in single investigative interface). National Police Technology Agency (statutory NDPB: national standards, procurement, operations, audit, R&D, surge capability). National Digital Forensics Service (10 regional hubs, mandatory turnaround: 48 hours priority, 14 days serious, 30 days other). Mandatory national police data platform (36-month migration). Encrypted communications compliance duty (2-hour acknowledgement, 24-hour data provision, penalties to 4% global turnover). National predictive analytics capability (published models, annual bias audit). Police AI Development Programme (evidence triage, financial analysis, OSINT, link analysis; no general population surveillance). AI evidence admissibility framework (NPTA certification, methodology disclosure, corroboration). Police Technology Fund (£350 million annual, five-year ring-fence, 35% forensics, 25% data, 20% AI/biometrics, 10% facial recognition, 10% oversight). Annual Police Technology Report to Parliament.

Delivered operationally: NPTA established within 6 months (500 staff, Chief Executive within 90 days). National Surveillance Audit commenced within 6 months, completed within 12 months, decommissioning within 6 months of publication. NFRC fleet of 30 mobile LFR units and maximum 20 fixed installations within 12 months. NBIP operational within 24 months. National technology standards published within 12 months. Digital forensics surge (50 examiners) within 6 months. Full NDFS with 10 regional hubs within 24 months. National data platform procured within 12 months, pilot (5 forces) within 18 months, full migration within 36 months. BWV national standard within 12 months, compliance within 24 months. Predictive analytics pilot (10 forces) within 12 months, national within 24 months. AI Development Programme established within 6 months (£50 million), first tools within 18 months. AI evidence certification within 12 months. Police Technology Fund operational within 90 days. Technology equalisation for 15 lowest-baseline forces within 6 months.
