C1 opened the courts. C2 built the prisons. C3 created the anti-corruption architecture. C4 addressed the most shameful institutional failure in modern British policing. C5 rebuilt the force. C6 established equal application of the law. C7 reformed the judiciary. C8 guaranteed the rights of victims. C9 confronted cybercrime and reformed online safety. C10 armed the state against knife crime and street violence. C11 declared war on the drug economy. C12 named the terrorist threat and dismantled the captured prevention apparatus. C13 closes the framework by doing something that no British government has attempted: making the police technology estate smaller and better at the same time. The surveillance footprint will be reduced where it serves no operational purpose. The capability footprint will be expanded where it converts evidence into convictions. Every officer in every force will have access to a national forensic service that processes evidence in days, not months. A biometric platform that links DNA, fingerprints, and facial recognition into a single search. An AI capability that identifies investigative leads in hours, not weeks. And a data platform that eliminates the force boundaries that criminals exploit and that fragmented IT systems enforce. The measure of this framework is not how many cameras Britain operates. It is how many criminals Britain convicts. Under Progress, the answer to both questions will change: fewer of the first, and dramatically more of the second.

#### Civil Service Reform & the NHS (CR)

“Nation Rebuilding”

###### Get Our NHS Back

We believe that the NHS, where care is free-at-point-of-need, remains one of our crown jewels. We also believe that it has fallen into an appalling state in which it cannot provide the standard of care that Britons deserve. We will help decentralise its operations, cut unnecessary administrative layers and budgetary expenses that reduce service quality while costing the taxpayer money, so that it can provide the standard of care it once did, the standard of care all Britons so sorely need.

###### “The Most High-Performance Civil Service in the World”

We believe Britons are owed a high-performing state capacity. To achieve this, we will commence a civil service pare back, eliminating unnecessary jobs that are a drain on the taxpayer, while opening up competing public sector agencies that can progressively take over from, and do a better job than, existing underperforming institutions.

###### The Cheapest Energy in Europe, Through Planning & Procurement Reform

We will eliminate a number of planning and procurement laws which simultaneously make it impossible to build anything, while wasting eye-watering sums of taxpayer money that go directly into the pockets of lawyers and consultants. We will then build national infrastructure (Rolls Royce SNRs in every polity and Oklo/Enron egg fusion reactors thereafter) and housing stock at a pace never seen before, so that within 10 years, Britain will have the world's cheapest energy per-capita and that every Briton will have the chance to comfortably own a home.

###### Immigration Reform

Things being as they are, with no new infrastructure being built, continuing to permit unchecked immigration is no good for either our existing citizenry, nor for migrants themselves. We will impose a 10-year to-nil reduction on low-skilled migrant labour. We will heavily incentivise high-skilled migration, according to strict number limits, to help our new PZs and startup economy flourish.

###### Support for the Disabled

The Tories spent years ineptly trying to reduce benefits crime, and instead shafted the disabled. Labour are about to do the same to pay for the public sector pay increases they've promised their henchmen and cronies. Our targeted elimination of benefits cheating will allow us to address the standard of care to Britain's disabled citizens that those citizens deserve.

###### Support for Veterans

We in Britain do not have much of a military culture. This means that the sacrifice that tens of thousands of British servicemen and -women make for our wellbeing every day frequently goes overlooked. We will honour the service done on our behalf by the Armed Forces by providing special tracks-to-prosperity, tailored medical care, and more, for our veterans, so that the homecoming will be worth it.

###### Support for New Mums, Improved Early-Years Care

Our lives are formed by our earliest years. We believe that new mums should be given every support possible to ensure that their babies' early days go by joyously and safely. We will make access to GP call-outs and other early years support an NHS priority.

#### Civil Service Reform

###### Overview

Core Mission: Restore democratic control of the government machine by giving elected ministers the authority to appoint, direct, and dismiss the officials who execute policy.

Key Challenge: The Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010 created a statutory framework in which the permanent bureaucracy selects its own leaders, defines its own standards of merit, and operates without meaningful accountability to elected representatives. The result is a system of 550,000 officials that no politician controls.

Strategic Approach:

- Amend CRAG 2010 to restore ministerial appointment authority
- Reconstitute the Civil Service Commission as an advisory body
- Introduce the Directly Responsible Individual model for personal accountability
- Open the Senior Civil Service to external talent
- Establish the Office of the Prime Minister as the centre of government delivery

#### The NHS

###### Overview

Core Mission: Refocus the NHS on its fundamental purpose while addressing systemic inefficiencies and preparing for demographic challenges.

Key Challenge: The NHS faces a perfect storm of financial constraints, an ageing population driving increased demand, and eventual population collapse creating future oversupply – all while maintaining care quality and public trust.

Strategic Approach:

- Reject privatisation as a false solution
- Return to core competencies in acute care
- Implement radical workforce and procurement reforms
- Build sustainable public health infrastructure

#### NHS1. Back to Basics

Governing Principle

The National Health Service was founded in 1948 to do something that no institution in British history had done before: guarantee that every person in the country, regardless of income, could receive medical treatment when they were sick. A crown jewel of British humanism, the genius of the NHS was its simplicity: you fall ill, you are treated, you do not receive a bill. Seventy-seven years later, that simplicity has been buried under decades of mission creep, institutional sprawl, and a political culture that treats the NHS as the answer to every social problem the state has failed to solve elsewhere. The result is an institution that spends over £200 billion per year and cannot get a patient through its emergency department in under four hours.

Public satisfaction with the NHS has collapsed to the lowest level in the forty-one-year history of the British Social Attitudes survey. In 2024, just 21% of the public said they were satisfied with the way the NHS runs, a catastrophic fall of 39 percentage points since the months before the pandemic. Six in ten people, 59%, said they were dissatisfied, the highest level of dissatisfaction ever recorded. Satisfaction with accident and emergency waiting times stands at 12%. Satisfaction with GP waiting times stands at 23%. Satisfaction with NHS dentistry has fallen to 20%. Only 14% of the public believe the NHS spends its money efficiently. These are not the numbers of a health service under temporary strain. They are the numbers of an institution that has lost the confidence of the people it exists to serve.

The scale of operational failure is commensurate with the collapse in trust. As of late 2025, 7.4 million patient pathways are on the elective care waiting list in England. Only 62% of patients are being treated within the 18-week constitutional standard, against a target of 92% that was last achieved in September 2015. In January 2026, more than 71,500 patients waited over twelve hours for an emergency admission, a figure approximately 25 times higher than in January 2020. Cancer targets are consistently missed: only 71.9% of patients received their first cancer treatment within 62 days of an urgent referral in December 2025, against an operational standard of 85%. General and acute bed occupancy has not fallen below 91% in any month since September 2021, consistently exceeding the 85% threshold above which safety and efficiency are compromised. An average of 12,663 patients remained in hospital each day throughout 2024/25 despite being medically fit for discharge, costing the NHS an estimated £2.6 billion per year in delayed bed days. The system is not merely underperforming. It is structurally incapable of meeting the demands placed upon it.

The instinct of every government since 1948 has been to respond to NHS failure with more money. Between 2013/14 and 2023/24, NHS spending per capita rose by 23%, with spending in the acute sector increasing by 32%. The Department of Health and Social Care budget for 2024/25 was £204.7 billion, of which approximately £187 billion was allocated to NHS England for the delivery of health services. Staff costs consume 50% of day-to-day expenditure. The NHS is one of the largest employers on earth, with approximately 1.37 million full-time equivalent staff in England. Despite all of this, NHS productivity remains between 5% and 11% below pre-pandemic levels, depending on the measure used. The 10 Year Health Plan published in July 2025 described the need to “urgently resolve the NHS productivity crisis.” The relationship between inputs and outputs has broken. More money is not producing more care.

Progress’ diagnosis is different from every other party’s. Labour says the NHS is “broken” and proposes more funding, more staff, more reorganisation. The Conservatives managed a decade of declining performance while increasing the budget. Reform UK gestures toward insurance models that terrify the median voter and would destroy the founding covenant of universal care. None of them asks the prior question: what should the NHS actually do? What is it for? What are the boundaries of its mission? Until that question is answered honestly, every reform will fail, because every reform will be attempting to make an institution do more of everything when the evidence screams that it should do fewer things, better.

The NHS was built for acute medicine. Trauma. Emergency care. Cancer treatment. Life-and-limb surgery. The management of severe acute illness: chest infections, sepsis, stroke, cardiac events, hip fractures. These are the functions at which a large, publicly funded, universally accessible health service excels, because they are the functions that require immediate access to expensive equipment, specialist expertise, and round-the-clock capacity that no individual could afford to maintain and no market could efficiently allocate. When a person collapses with a stroke, the NHS is magnificent. When a person needs a hip replacement, the NHS has the infrastructure to deliver it. When a child develops sepsis, the NHS saves their life. These are the functions the British public values most, the functions that justify the institution’s existence, and the functions that are now being starved of resource and attention because the NHS has been asked to be everything to everyone.

The mission creep is not hypothetical. It is quantifiable. Over the past three decades, the NHS has progressively absorbed responsibilities for community mental health services, social prescribing, lifestyle interventions, long-term condition management that could be delivered in primary or community settings, and a vast apparatus of administrative, managerial, and regulatory functions that did not exist when the service was founded. Each individual expansion was justified. Each was well-intentioned. But in aggregate, they have diluted the acute care mission to the point where the NHS cannot perform its core functions. The beds are full of patients who should not be there, either because they are medically fit for discharge but have nowhere to go, because they have mental health needs that an acute ward cannot meet, or because they have chronic conditions that should be managed in the community. Every bed occupied by a patient who does not need acute care is a bed unavailable for a patient who does.

Progress will restore the NHS to its core mission. This is not an austerity measure. It is not a reduction in the services available to the British public. It is a recognition that an institution which tries to do everything will do nothing well, and that the British people deserve a health service that is world-class at the things that matter most: keeping them alive when they are critically ill, treating them promptly when they need surgery, diagnosing and treating cancer at the earliest possible stage, and providing acute psychiatric care for those in severe mental health crisis. Every other service currently housed within the NHS will continue to be provided. It will simply be provided by institutions better structured to deliver it, freeing the NHS to concentrate its vast resources on the functions it was designed to perform and the functions the public needs it to perform.

Back to Basics is not a slogan. It is an operational programme. It begins with the creation of a Treatment Coverage Commission to define, transparently and on the basis of clinical evidence, exactly which conditions and treatments the NHS will and will not provide. It continues with a comprehensive acute capacity programme that expands bed numbers, reduces occupancy rates to safe levels, and eliminates the delayed discharge crisis that costs the NHS billions of pounds and thousands of lives every year. It reorients the workforce toward the acute core, ending the dependence on agency staff and international recruitment. And it culminates in the most significant expansion of inpatient psychiatric bed capacity in a generation, reversing the catastrophic 90% reduction in mental illness beds since 1960 and ensuring that patients in severe mental health crisis receive specialist care rather than being warehoused in general acute wards or sent hundreds of miles from home. The NHS will do less. But what it does, it will do superbly.

##### NHS1.1: Defining the Core Mission

The Problem

The NHS has no statutory definition of what it does and does not treat. The National Health Service Act 2006 imposes a duty on the Secretary of State to “continue the promotion in England of a comprehensive health service designed to secure improvement in the physical and mental health of the people of England, and in the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of physical and mental illness.” The word “comprehensive” has been interpreted, over seventy-seven years, as meaning “everything.” There is no mechanism, short of a politically toxic public argument, by which the NHS can decline to provide a treatment, withdraw a service, or state that a particular condition falls outside its remit. The result is an institution with infinite demand and finite resources, in which clinical priorities are determined not by strategic design but by the path of least political resistance.

NICE, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, performs a narrow version of this function: it assesses whether specific drugs and treatments are cost-effective and recommends whether the NHS should fund them. But NICE operates only at the level of individual technologies and treatments. It does not address the structural question of which categories of care the NHS should provide, which should be provided by other public bodies, and which should be the responsibility of the individual. There is no body that asks: should the NHS run weight management clinics, or should local authority public health services do so? Should the NHS provide community mental health follow-up for stable patients, or should specialist mental health trusts outside the acute hospital system deliver that care? Should the NHS fund cosmetic procedures, fertility treatments beyond a defined number of cycles, or treatments for conditions that are primarily lifestyle-related? These are political questions disguised as clinical ones, and no institution currently exists to answer them transparently.

The absence of a defined core mission means that when budgets are constrained, as they always are, the cuts fall on whatever is politically easiest rather than whatever is clinically least important. Elective surgery waiting lists grow because elective patients do not die in the waiting room. Community mental health services are hollowed out because their users are dispersed and politically weak. Capital investment is raided to cover revenue overruns because buildings do not complain. The acute core, the function the public depends on most, is progressively starved because it is surrounded by a penumbra of services that absorb resource without scrutiny. The NHS does not need more money. It needs a mission.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Core Mission Act will establish:

- a) A statutory definition of the NHS Core Mission. The Act will define the primary purpose of the NHS as the provision of acute medical and surgical care, emergency and trauma services, cancer diagnosis and treatment, critical care, maternity services, and acute psychiatric care. These are the functions that the NHS is obligated to provide universally, free at the point of use, to the highest achievable standard, and with the shortest achievable waiting times. The Core Mission functions will be listed in a schedule to the Act and may be amended only by affirmative resolution of both Houses of Parliament. This is the irreducible core: the functions that justify the NHS’s existence and command its first claim on every pound of resource.
- b) Establishment of the Treatment Coverage Commission (TCC). The Act will create an independent statutory body, the Treatment Coverage Commission, with a mandate to review, on a rolling five-year cycle, every category of treatment and service currently provided by the NHS and to recommend whether each should remain within the NHS Core Mission, be transferred to another public body, be subject to a defined contribution from the patient, or be withdrawn from public provision entirely. The TCC will be chaired by a clinician of national standing and will include practising doctors, nurses, health economists, patient representatives, and ethicists. Its recommendations will be published and will be binding unless overridden by a vote of the House of Commons within 90 days of publication. This mechanism ensures that the scope of the NHS is determined by clinical evidence and transparent democratic debate, not by institutional inertia or political cowardice.
- c) A statutory right to Core Mission treatment within defined maximum waiting times. The Act will establish, for the first time, a legally enforceable maximum waiting time for each Core Mission function. For emergency and trauma care, the existing four-hour A&E standard will be placed on a statutory footing with a compliance target of 95%. For cancer, a maximum of 31 days from decision to treat to first treatment and 62 days from urgent referral to first treatment. For elective surgery within the Core Mission, a maximum of 18 weeks from referral to treatment. For acute psychiatric admission, a maximum of four hours from presentation to assessment and 24 hours from decision to admit to placement in a specialist psychiatric bed. Breach of these statutory waiting times will trigger automatic escalation procedures, including mandatory reporting to Parliament through the TCC’s annual report.
- d) Protected funding for Core Mission functions. The Act will require that no less than 70% of the NHS revenue budget is allocated directly to Core Mission functions, ring-fenced and reported separately in the NHS annual accounts. This prevents the slow diversion of acute care funding to peripheral services that has characterised the last three decades. Non-Core Mission services that remain within the NHS during the transition period will be funded from the remaining allocation, with a clear trajectory toward transfer to appropriate alternative providers.

OPERATIONAL

Core Mission audit. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, NHS England will commence a comprehensive audit of every service and treatment currently provided across the NHS, categorised by Core Mission status. The audit will identify the total expenditure, workforce allocation, and bed-day consumption attributable to non-Core Mission services. The results will be published within 12 months and will form the evidence base for the TCC’s first cycle of recommendations. This audit has never been conducted. The NHS does not know, with precision, how much of its budget is spent on functions outside the acute care mission. That ignorance ends.

Transition planning for non-Core Mission services. Within 18 months of Royal Assent, the TCC will publish its first set of binding recommendations on services to be transferred out of the NHS. Transfers will be phased over a three-year period to ensure continuity of care. No patient currently receiving treatment will lose access to that treatment during the transition. The receiving bodies, whether local authority public health services, specialist mental health organisations, community interest companies, or reformed social care providers, will be established, funded, and operationally ready before any transfer takes effect. Progress does not abandon patients. It ensures they receive care from the institution best equipped to provide it.

##### NHS1.2: Acute Capacity Expansion

The Problem

The United Kingdom has 2.35 hospital beds per 1,000 population. Portugal has 3.51. Belgium has 5.41. Germany has 7.82. Over the past thirty years, the number of overnight hospital beds in England has halved. General and acute overnight beds fell from 108,958 in 2010/11 to 101,432 in 2019/20, a 6.9% reduction in a decade of rising demand and an ageing population. Since the pandemic, bed numbers have partially recovered: there were an average of 105,694 general and acute overnight beds in 2024/25, 4.2% above the pre-pandemic low but still below the levels of a decade earlier. This modest recovery has been insufficient to relieve the pressure. In no month of 2024/25 did general and acute bed occupancy fall below 91.4%, consistently exceeding the Royal College of Emergency Medicine’s recommended ceiling of 85%. In the first quarter of 2025/26, occupancy dropped slightly as available beds dipped to 104,198, but the underlying dynamic is unchanged: demand far exceeds supply.

The consequences of chronic bed shortages cascade through every part of the system. Emergency departments cannot admit patients because there are no beds to admit them to, producing the twelve-hour trolley waits that have become a defining feature of the modern NHS. Elective operations are cancelled because beds are occupied by patients who cannot be discharged. The average number of patients in hospital each day despite being fit for discharge reached 12,663 in 2024/25, occupying 12% of all general and acute beds. The Institute for Government estimates that the NHS spends £220 million per month, approximately £2.6 billion per year, on delayed discharge. That is more than the entire annual budget of the courts and tribunals system. These patients are not receiving active treatment. They are waiting for social care placements, community support packages, or simply for someone to organise their safe return home. Every day they occupy an acute bed is a day that bed is unavailable for a patient who needs acute care.

The bed shortage also compromises safety. When occupancy exceeds 85%, the risk of hospital-acquired infection rises, patients are placed in clinically inappropriate wards, and staff are stretched beyond safe limits. Corridor care, the practice of treating patients on trolleys in hospital corridors because no bed is available, has become normalised. In January 2026, more than 71,500 patients waited over twelve hours for an emergency admission. This is not an aberration. It is the steady state of a system that does not have enough beds for the population it serves.

Progress will expand acute bed capacity to a level that allows the NHS to function safely and efficiently, while simultaneously attacking the delayed discharge crisis that wastes billions of pounds and thousands of beds every year. The two problems are inseparable: expanding beds without fixing discharge is building a larger car park at the entrance to a blocked motorway. Both must be addressed together.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Core Mission Act will establish:

- a) A statutory minimum of 120,000 general and acute overnight beds across NHS England, to be achieved within the first Parliament. This represents an increase of approximately 15,000 beds from the current level of approximately 105,000, restoring capacity to the levels of the early 2010s while accounting for population growth since that period. The bed expansion will be funded through the NHS capital budget, with additional investment from the capital freed by estate rationalisation as non-Core Mission services are transferred out of NHS premises. New beds will be concentrated in the regions with the highest occupancy rates and the most severe delayed discharge problems, using a needs-based allocation formula that weights population, age profile, deprivation, and current performance against the four-hour A&E standard.
- b) A statutory maximum bed occupancy target of 90%, enforced through mandatory reporting and escalation. The Act will require every NHS trust to maintain average overnight bed occupancy below 90% across each rolling quarter. Trusts that exceed 92% in any month will be required to activate surge capacity protocols. Trusts that exceed 92% for two consecutive quarters will be placed in mandatory improvement, with direct intervention from NHS England and the redeployment of resource from non-Core Mission services. The 85% threshold recommended by the Royal College of Emergency Medicine remains the long-term aspiration; the 90% statutory ceiling is the enforceable minimum that prevents the worst consequences of overcrowding.
- c) A statutory Discharge Guarantee. Every patient who is medically fit for discharge will be discharged from hospital within 48 hours. The Act will impose a joint duty on the NHS, local authorities, and social care providers to ensure that discharge arrangements are in place within this timeframe. Where the delay is attributable to the absence of a social care placement, the local authority will be required to fund an interim placement from its own resources until a permanent arrangement is made. Where the delay is attributable to NHS administrative failure, the trust will bear the cost of the additional bed days. The financial incentive is unambiguous: delayed discharge is expensive for whoever causes it. The current system, in which no one is financially responsible for delay, produces the inevitable result that delays are tolerated.
- d) A Bed Capacity Review, conducted every five years by the Treatment Coverage Commission, assessing whether the statutory bed minimum remains sufficient for projected demand. The review will consider population projections, changes in the disease burden, the impact of preventive health measures (NHS5), and technological changes that affect the need for inpatient care. The bed minimum may be adjusted upward by ministerial direction but may be reduced only by affirmative resolution of both Houses of Parliament. This ensures that the political temptation to close beds for short-term savings, which has driven three decades of decline, is constrained by democratic accountability.

OPERATIONAL

Rapid bed expansion. Within 30 days of Royal Assent, NHS England will identify all mothballed wards, decommissioned bed capacity, and underutilised estate across the acute trust portfolio. Wards that can be brought back into service with refurbishment rather than new construction will be prioritised for immediate reopening, with a target of 3,000 additional beds within the first 12 months. Simultaneously, NHS England will commission a programme of modular ward construction for sites where existing estate cannot be expanded, using the same rapid-build methodology deployed for Nightingale hospitals during the pandemic but to a permanent standard of care.

Discharge transformation. Within 60 days, NHS England will publish a National Discharge Protocol, standardising the discharge process across all acute trusts and eliminating the variation that currently produces wildly different discharge performance between otherwise comparable hospitals. The Protocol will require that discharge planning begins on the day of admission, not on the day the patient is declared fit for discharge. It will mandate the use of integrated discharge teams, jointly staffed by NHS and local authority personnel, in every acute trust. It will establish a national digital discharge platform (linked to the systems architecture described in NHS3) that provides real-time visibility of available social care placements, community nursing capacity, and step-down bed availability. The platform will replace the current system of phone calls, faxes, and personal relationships that characterises discharge planning in most hospitals.

Corridor care elimination. Within 90 days of Royal Assent, NHS England will issue binding operational guidance that corridor care is not an acceptable standard of care under any circumstances. Trusts that resort to corridor care will be required to file an immediate report to the Chief Medical Officer and the CQC, with a root-cause analysis and remediation plan within seven days. The normalisation of corridor care is a symptom of system failure, not a coping strategy. Progress will not tolerate it.

##### NHS1.3: Workforce Reorientation

The Problem

The NHS workforce has expanded significantly since 2015, yet much of that expansion has been in roles that do not directly deliver Core Mission care. The number of managers across the NHS decreased between 2010 and 2019, but the overall workforce grew substantially through the addition of clinical and non-clinical roles in community services, administrative functions, and support services. Simultaneously, the workforce that has grown is younger, less experienced, and more reliant on international recruitment than at any point in the NHS’s history. In 2018, one in 28 nurses or midwives were new registrants on the professional register; by 2024, this had doubled to one in 14. In 2023, 42% of nurses and midwives who joined the NHS were non-UK nationals, compared to 21% in 2018. This is not, in itself, a problem; internationally recruited staff are valued colleagues. But it is a symptom of a system that has failed to train sufficient domestic professionals and that relies on recruitment from countries that can ill afford to lose their own healthcare workers.

The mismatch between workforce growth and productivity improvement is the central puzzle of NHS performance. Staff numbers have risen faster than activity, producing the paradox of more employees delivering less care per pound spent. Part of the explanation is the inexperience of the expanded workforce. Part is the pandemic’s lingering effect on staff health and morale, with sickness absence rates remaining above pre-pandemic levels and mental health conditions accounting for nearly a quarter of all absence. But the largest part is structural: too many staff are deployed in services that are not part of the Core Mission, while the acute functions that define the NHS’s purpose are understaffed, overstretched, and burning through agency spend to fill gaps that permanent recruitment cannot close.

Progress’ workforce strategy for the NHS is inseparable from the Core Mission reform. As non-Core Mission services are transferred to specialist providers, the workforce associated with those services will transfer with them, under TUPE protections, to the receiving organisations. The NHS workforce that remains will be concentrated on Core Mission delivery: acute medicine, surgery, emergency care, cancer treatment, critical care, maternity, and acute psychiatry. This concentration of expertise will be accompanied by a domestic training expansion that eliminates the dependence on international recruitment within a decade, producing a workforce that is British-trained, permanently employed, and deployed where the need is greatest.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Core Mission Act will establish:

- a) A statutory Workforce Reorientation Plan, to be published within 12 months of Royal Assent, identifying every NHS role that is associated with a non-Core Mission service and establishing the timeline, terms, and receiving organisations for TUPE transfer. No worker will lose their job. No worker will see their terms and conditions reduced. But every worker will be employed by the organisation best placed to support the work they do. A psychiatric community nurse following up stable patients in the community will be employed by the specialist community mental health provider, not by an acute NHS trust whose primary business is emergency surgery and cancer treatment.
- b) A Domestic Training Guarantee. Within five years, the number of medical school places in England will increase by 50%, and the number of nursing training places by 30%, fully funded by the state. The Act will establish a statutory duty on the Secretary of State to ensure that domestic training places are sufficient to meet projected NHS workforce needs without reliance on international recruitment as the primary source of staff. International recruitment will continue as a supplement, not a substitute. The long-term workforce plan published in 2023 identified the need for these expansions but provided no statutory mechanism to ensure they are delivered. Progress will legislate the commitment.
- c) A statutory cap on agency spend, declining to zero for Core Mission clinical roles within the first Parliament. The NHS spent approximately £3 billion on agency staff in 2022/23, a figure that has been reduced through recent controls but that remains a significant drain on resources. For every pound spent on an agency nurse, less than 60 pence reaches the patient; the remainder is margin, administrative cost, and the inefficiency of deploying temporary staff who do not know the ward, the systems, or the patients. The Act will require that all Core Mission clinical roles are filled by permanent or bank staff within the first Parliament, with agency use permitted only in declared emergencies. The funding currently consumed by agency margins will be redirected to the permanent workforce, improving both the quality and the cost-effectiveness of care.

OPERATIONAL

TUPE transfer programme. Within 18 months of Royal Assent, the first wave of TUPE transfers for non-Core Mission workforce will be completed, coinciding with the transfer of community mental health services (NHS1.4d). NHS England will work with receiving organisations to ensure that pension arrangements, pay scales, and career progression pathways are at least equivalent to those available within the NHS. Staff consultation will begin within 60 days of Royal Assent.

Training place expansion. Within the first year, the Department for Education and DHSC will jointly publish the Medical and Nursing Training Expansion Plan, identifying the university capacity, clinical placement infrastructure, and funding required to deliver the 50% increase in medical school places and 30% increase in nursing places. New medical schools will be established in underserved regions, linked to the Prosperity Zones described in E2, ensuring that training capacity is built where the workforce is needed, not only where it has historically been concentrated.

Retention and return-to-practice. NHS England will launch a Core Mission Retention Programme offering enhanced terms for staff in shortage specialties within the acute core: emergency medicine, anaesthetics, general surgery, oncology, acute psychiatry, and critical care nursing. The programme will include salary supplements, protected continuing professional development time, and a commitment that no clinician in a Core Mission role will be required to work more than 48 hours per week averaged over a reference period, in compliance with the Working Time Directive and in recognition that exhausted clinicians make mistakes. A parallel Return-to-Practice programme will target qualified professionals who have left the NHS, offering funded retraining, flexible working arrangements, and a guaranteed Core Mission role on completion.

##### NHS1.4: Psychiatric Care Restoration

The Problem

The reduction in NHS mental health inpatient beds is one of the most consequential policy failures in the history of the British state. Between 1960 and 2020, the number of mental illness beds in NHS hospitals in England fell by 90.6%. Between 2010/11 and 2023/24, mental health beds decreased by a further 24%, from 23,515 to 17,789. In the final quarter of 2024/25, NHS trusts reported a total of just 17,999 available mental health beds, of which 89.5% were occupied, exceeding the recommended maximum of 85%. The deinstitutionalisation programme that began in the 1960s was founded on the promise that community care would replace institutional care. That promise was never honoured. The beds were closed. The community services were never adequately built. The result is a system in which people in severe mental health crisis are routinely denied the specialist inpatient care they need.

The consequences are visible in every emergency department in the country. A&E attendances for psychiatric conditions more than doubled between 2009/10 and 2019/20. Patients in mental health crisis occupy general acute beds because no psychiatric bed is available, depriving both the mental health patient of specialist care and the acute system of capacity. In December 2023, almost three in five mental health inpatients were treated in facilities more than 60 miles from where they lived, sent out of area because no local bed was available, a practice that delays recovery, increases cost, and severs patients from the support networks essential to their treatment. In March 2024, NHS mental health units recorded 49,677 days of delayed discharge, the highest figure since at least January 2016. The King’s Fund has found that between 17% and 20% of available acute mental health and psychiatric intensive care bed capacity is now provided by the independent sector, filling gaps the NHS has created by closing its own beds.

The human cost is incalculable. Patients in psychotic crisis wait in A&E corridors for days. Suicidal patients are assessed by non-specialist staff because no psychiatric professional is available. Families drive hundreds of miles to visit relatives admitted to beds far from home. Coroners issue Prevention of Future Deaths reports citing inadequate bed capacity, and the reports are filed and ignored. The Royal College of Psychiatrists’ 2025 survey of its members across England found that the challenging conditions under which psychiatrists work to provide safe care for acutely unwell patients are becoming untenable. Crisis resolution and home treatment teams, designed to provide an alternative to admission, are operating well below the standards required, with non-clinical staff sometimes making clinical decisions and crisis line calls going unanswered. The system is not managing demand in the community. It is failing to manage demand anywhere.

Progress will reverse the catastrophic decline in psychiatric bed capacity. This is not a return to the institutional model of the mid-twentieth century. It is a recognition that for patients who are acutely unwell, at risk to themselves or others, and in need of specialist psychiatric intervention, inpatient care is the safest, most effective, and most humane form of treatment. The community mental health model will continue to serve the majority of mental health patients, but it will be transferred out of the NHS and into specialist organisations better structured to deliver it (NHS1.1). Acute psychiatric care, the treatment of severe mental illness in crisis, will remain within the NHS Core Mission and will receive the bed capacity, specialist staffing, and capital investment it has been denied for decades.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Core Mission Act will establish:

- a) A statutory minimum of 25,000 specialist psychiatric inpatient beds across NHS England, to be achieved within the first Parliament. This represents an increase of approximately 7,000 beds from the current level of approximately 18,000, restoring capacity to the levels of the early 2010s before the most recent phase of closures. The beds will be distributed according to population need, using the same weighted capitation methodology that allocates general NHS funding, with additional weighting for deprivation, prevalence of severe mental illness, and current out-of-area placement rates. Priority investment will be directed to the areas with the highest rates of inappropriate out-of-area placements and the most persistent bed occupancy above 85%.
- b) Elimination of inappropriate out-of-area placements within 24 months of Royal Assent. The Act will impose a statutory duty on integrated care boards to ensure that no patient requiring acute psychiatric admission is placed in a facility more than 30 miles from their home, except where the patient requires specialist care not available locally. The target of eliminating inappropriate out-of-area placements was first set by NHS England for 2020/21. It has been missed every year since. Progress will place it on a statutory footing with enforceable consequences: any ICB that fails to meet the standard for two consecutive quarters will be placed in mandatory improvement measures, with direct intervention from the TCC.
- c) Statutory maximum waiting times for acute psychiatric care. No patient presenting in mental health crisis will wait more than four hours for assessment by a qualified psychiatrist or psychiatric registrar. No patient for whom a decision to admit has been made will wait more than 24 hours for placement in a specialist psychiatric bed. These standards will apply to all NHS facilities, including emergency departments, and will be monitored with the same rigour as the four-hour A&E target for physical presentations.
- d) Transfer of community and social mental health services to specialist providers. Stable, community-based mental health follow-up, social prescribing for mental health, talking therapies (IAPT/NHS Talking Therapies), and long-term condition monitoring for patients with managed mental health conditions will be transferred from NHS acute trusts to specialist mental health community organisations, commissioned and funded through local authority public health budgets with ring-fenced central government grant. The transfer will be phased over three years, with no disruption to patient care. The NHS will retain responsibility only for acute psychiatric care: crisis intervention, inpatient treatment for severe mental illness, psychiatric intensive care, and forensic psychiatry. This concentrates NHS psychiatric resources on the patients who need them most.

OPERATIONAL

Bed capacity programme. Within 60 days of Royal Assent, NHS England will publish a Psychiatric Bed Restoration Plan identifying the specific sites, capital investment, and workforce requirements to deliver 25,000 specialist beds within the Parliament. The plan will prioritise the refurbishment and reopening of recently closed psychiatric wards where the physical infrastructure remains viable, before proceeding to new-build capacity. Capital funding will be drawn from the NHS capital budget, supplemented by the proceeds of estate rationalisation as non-Core Mission services are transferred out of the NHS and surplus estate is released.

Workforce pipeline. The psychiatric bed expansion cannot succeed without a commensurate expansion in the specialist workforce. Within 90 days, Health Education England’s successor functions within DHSC will publish a Psychiatric Workforce Acceleration Plan, increasing training places for psychiatrists, psychiatric nurses, and mental health support workers. The plan will include a Psychiatric Return-to-Practice programme offering financial incentives for qualified psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses who have left the profession to return, and a Psychiatric Visa pathway within the existing Health and Care Worker visa route, providing expedited entry for internationally qualified psychiatrists who meet UK standards. Domestic training is the long-term solution. International recruitment is the bridge.

Quality standards. Every specialist psychiatric inpatient facility will meet CQC standards for safe and effective care, with a maximum bed occupancy of 85%, adequate staffing ratios published and enforced, and mandatory implementation of the NHS England Patient Safety Incident Response Framework. The era of warehousing mental health patients in overcrowded, understaffed facilities is over. Progress will build a psychiatric inpatient estate that the country can be proud of.

Summary of Legislative Requirements

The NHS1 framework is built on the NHS Core Mission Act, a single piece of primary legislation introduced in the first King’s Speech alongside the Tax Reset Act, the Energy Security and Affordability Act, and the other centrepiece legislation of a first Progress government. No additional Acts are required. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, NHS England operational guidance, or departmental action.

NHS Core Mission Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: Statutory definition of the NHS Core Mission encompassing acute medical and surgical care, emergency and trauma services, cancer diagnosis and treatment, critical care, maternity services, and acute psychiatric care. Establishment of the Treatment Coverage Commission with a rolling five-year review mandate and binding recommendations. Statutory right to Core Mission treatment within defined maximum waiting times: four hours for A&E, 18 weeks for elective surgery, 31/62 days for cancer, four hours for psychiatric assessment, 24 hours for psychiatric admission. Protected funding: minimum 70% of NHS revenue budget ring-fenced for Core Mission functions. Statutory minimum of 120,000 general and acute overnight beds. Maximum bed occupancy target of 90%. Discharge Guarantee: 48-hour maximum from fit-for-discharge to discharge. Five-yearly Bed Capacity Review. Workforce Reorientation Plan with TUPE protections. Domestic Training Guarantee: 50% increase in medical school places, 30% increase in nursing places. Agency spend cap declining to zero for Core Mission clinical roles. Statutory minimum of 25,000 specialist psychiatric inpatient beds. Elimination of inappropriate out-of-area placements within 24 months. Transfer of community and social mental health services to specialist providers.

Delivered operationally: Core Mission audit commenced within 90 days. TCC first recommendations within 18 months. Non-Core Mission service transfers phased over three years. Rapid bed expansion: 3,000 additional beds within 12 months. National Discharge Protocol within 60 days. Corridor care elimination guidance within 90 days. TUPE transfer first wave within 18 months. Medical and Nursing Training Expansion Plan within 12 months. Core Mission Retention Programme and Return-to-Practice Programme launched within six months. Psychiatric Bed Restoration Plan within 60 days. Psychiatric Workforce Acceleration Plan within 90 days.

Funding the Back to Basics Programme

The Back to Basics programme is not an unfunded expansion of NHS spending. It is a reallocation of existing spending toward the functions that matter most, combined with targeted capital investment in bed capacity and workforce training. The funding sources, in order of contribution, are as follows.

Reallocation from non-Core Mission services. As services are transferred out of the NHS and into specialist providers, the revenue currently funding those services within the NHS is reallocated. Community mental health services, talking therapies, social prescribing, and other non-Core Mission functions currently consume a significant share of NHS revenue. That share will be redirected to fund the bed expansion, the psychiatric restoration, and the workforce reorientation described in this document. The receiving organisations will be funded through local authority public health budgets, supplemented by ring-fenced central government grant. The total quantum of public spending on these services does not decrease. Its allocation changes.

Efficiency savings from reduced delayed discharge. The Discharge Guarantee and associated operational reforms will progressively reduce the £2.6 billion per year currently spent on patients who are medically fit for discharge but remain in hospital. Every bed freed by timely discharge is a bed available for acute care, reducing the capital cost of the bed expansion programme. The target is a 50% reduction in delayed discharge costs within the first Parliament, yielding approximately £1.3 billion per year in freed capacity.

Capital investment. The bed expansion programme will require capital investment of approximately £2–3 billion over the Parliament, funded through the NHS capital budget as supplemented by the capital released through estate rationalisation. The NHS estate currently includes facilities that serve non-Core Mission functions. As those functions are transferred, surplus estate will be sold or repurposed, with the proceeds reinvested in acute and psychiatric bed capacity.

Agency spend reduction. The elimination of agency dependence for Core Mission clinical roles will free approximately £1–2 billion per year in margin and administrative costs currently extracted by staffing agencies. This funding is redirected to the permanent workforce through the Domestic Training Guarantee and the Core Mission Retention Programme.

NHS1 establishes the foundation upon which every subsequent document in the NHS Policy Framework is built. Without a defined core mission, workforce reform (NHS2) optimises for the wrong objectives. Without adequate bed capacity, information systems (NHS3) track patients through a system that cannot treat them. Without the separation of acute and non-acute functions, procurement reform (NHS4) purchases supplies for an institution that does not know what it is. Without clarity about what the NHS does and does not do, public health policy (NHS5) has no boundary against which to operate. Without beds and workforce, infrastructure investment (NHS6) builds facilities with nothing to put in them. Without the Discharge Guarantee, social care integration (NHS7) remains an aspiration rather than an operational reality.

Back to Basics is the beginning. It answers the question that seventy-seven years of British politics has refused to ask: what is the NHS for? The answer is simple. The NHS exists to keep the people of Britain alive when they are critically ill, to treat them promptly when they need surgery, to diagnose and treat cancer at the earliest possible stage, to deliver their children safely, and to provide specialist psychiatric care for those in severe mental health crisis. Everything else is important. Everything else will continue to be provided, by the public sector, to a high standard. But it will not be provided by the NHS, because the NHS has a more important job to do, and it has been failing at that job because we have asked it to do too much. That failure ends. The NHS goes back to basics, and the basics are done superbly.

#### NHS2. Workforce Crisis Management

Governing Principle

The NHS employs approximately 1.5 million people on a headcount basis in England, making it the largest employer in the country and one of the largest on earth. The hospital and community health service workforce reached 1.38 million full-time equivalents in October 2025, an increase of more than 20% since 2019. There are 153,570 FTE doctors, 371,490 FTE nurses and health visitors, and nearly 150,000 FTE staff in general practice. Staff costs consume approximately half of all day-to-day NHS expenditure. By any measure, this is a workforce of extraordinary scale. It is also a workforce in crisis.

The crisis is not one of headcount. The NHS has more staff than at any point in its history. The crisis is one of deployment, morale, capability, and structural design. Despite the record numbers, only 34% of staff agree that there are enough people at their organisation to do their jobs properly. Forty-one per cent report feeling unwell as a result of work-related stress. Thirty per cent report feeling burnt out at work often or all the time. Among ambulance staff, the burnout figure approaches 40%. Over 460,000 NHS staff go to work each day feeling the impact of burnout. In 2022, a record 170,000 staff, including 41,000 nurses, left NHS hospital and community health services. The 2024 NHS Staff Survey, the largest workforce study in the world with 747,288 respondents, found that fewer than two-thirds of staff would be happy with the standard of care provided by their organisation if a friend or relative needed treatment. The NHS is not short of people. It is haemorrhaging the people it has.

The workforce is also younger, less experienced, and more reliant on international recruitment than at any point in the institution’s history. In 2018, one in 28 nurses or midwives were new registrants on the professional register; by 2024, this had doubled to one in 14. In 2023, 42% of nurses and midwives who joined the NHS were non-UK nationals, compared to 21% in 2018. The number of international staff from outside the European Economic Area has doubled from approximately 105,000 in 2020 to approximately 240,000 in 2025. This influx was necessary to fill gaps created by decades of under-investment in domestic training, and internationally recruited colleagues are valued members of every clinical team. But a workforce strategy that depends on recruiting from countries that cannot afford to lose their own healthcare workers, and that produces a staff cohort with lower average experience levels in the UK system, is not a strategy. It is a sticking plaster.

Meanwhile, the staff who remain are not spending their time doing what they were trained to do. Healthcare professionals across all roles report spending an average of 13.5 hours per week generating clinical documentation, a 25% increase in just seven years. Consultant doctors spend 15.1 hours per week on documentation, with an average of 4.7 hours completed outside working hours. The Royal College of Nursing has estimated that nursing staff spend 2.5 million working hours per week on non-essential paperwork and clerical tasks. More than three quarters of nurses say that non-essential paperwork prevents them from providing direct patient care. The NHS Confederation’s own review found that clinical staff spend up to 10 hours per week collecting or checking data, and that more than one third of this work is neither useful nor relevant to patient care. The system does not trust its clinicians to practise medicine. It trusts them to fill in forms.

The regulatory apparatus that was supposed to ensure quality has instead become part of the problem. In July 2024, the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care described the Care Quality Commission as a “failing organisation” following the Dash review. CQC inspections fell from approximately 15,800 in 2019/20 to just 6,700 in 2023/24. The NHS Providers’ 2024 survey found that providers consider the regulatory system to be “burdensome, duplicative and detached from the considerable pressures providers face.” Six overlapping regulators in the health and social care sector hamper effective oversight. The CQC’s Single Assessment Framework, introduced in early 2024, was so widely criticised that the regulator launched a consultation on replacing it less than eighteen months after its rollout, and its Chief Executive resigned in October 2025. The compliance industry has grown around the regulatory apparatus like ivy around a building, extracting resource and attention while contributing nothing to patient care.

The result of all of this is the central paradox of the modern NHS: more staff, less productivity. NHS productivity remains between 5% and 11% below pre-pandemic levels, depending on the measure used. Staff numbers have risen faster than activity. The NHS Confederation has noted that managers make up approximately 2% of the NHS workforce, compared to 9.5% of the overall UK workforce, and that the NHS spends approximately 2 pence in the pound on administration compared to 5 pence in Germany and 6 pence in France. The institution is simultaneously over-staffed in aggregate and desperately short of the right staff in the right roles doing the right work. It employs more people every year and delivers less care per pound spent.

Progress’ diagnosis is structural. The NHS has been subject to three decades of taskification: the progressive fragmentation of holistic clinical roles into narrow, process-driven tasks that can be performed by less qualified, less experienced, and less expensive staff. A ward sister who once commanded a ward, knew every patient by name, and exercised independent clinical judgement has been replaced by a rotating cast of agency nurses, healthcare assistants, and administrative requirements that leave no one person responsible for the overall care of the patient. A consultant who trained for fifteen years to exercise expert clinical decision-making spends a third of the working week generating documentation. A GP who should be diagnosing and treating patients runs a triage system designed by managers who have never examined a patient. The taskification was done in the name of efficiency. It has produced the opposite.

Back to Basics (NHS1) established the core mission and the structural architecture of a reformed NHS. Workforce Crisis Management is the companion reform that makes that architecture operational. It addresses three inseparable failures: the degradation of clinical professionalism that has turned expert practitioners into process workers; the regulatory and bureaucratic burden that consumes clinical time without improving patient outcomes; and the absence of strategic redundancy that leaves the system permanently operating at maximum capacity with no resilience against surges in demand. These three failures feed each other. Overworked, demoralised clinicians in an over-regulated system running at full capacity cannot deliver safe care, cannot innovate, and cannot stay. Progress will break the cycle. The NHS will become a service worth working for, and its workforce will be freed to do what it was trained to do: care for the sick.

##### NHS2.1: Re-Professionalise Healthcare Staff

The Problem

The defining workforce failure of the modern NHS is taskification: the systematic replacement of broad, expert clinical roles with narrow, fragmented task-based functions. A generation ago, a senior ward nurse managed the ward. She knew her patients, exercised clinical judgement, directed the team, and was accountable for outcomes. Today, the ward nurse’s role has been sliced into discrete tasks distributed across a hierarchy of bands, with healthcare assistants performing observations, specialist nurses performing procedures, and the ward nurse herself spending the plurality of her time on documentation, handovers, and compliance. No one person holds the clinical picture. The patient experiences a parade of faces, none of whom knows the full story of their care.

The economics of taskification appeared attractive. Healthcare assistants cost less than registered nurses. Band 2 and 3 staff cost less than Band 5 and 6. If a task can be safely delegated to a less qualified worker, the logic goes, it should be. But the logic is false, because it treats clinical care as a collection of independent tasks rather than an integrated judgement. The healthcare assistant who records a patient’s observations may record them accurately but will not recognise the subtle pattern that tells an experienced nurse the patient is deteriorating. The junior doctor who follows the protocol will follow it correctly but will not recognise the case where the protocol is wrong. Clinical expertise is not the ability to perform a task. It is the ability to synthesise information, recognise patterns, and exercise judgement under uncertainty. Every layer of taskification removes a layer of judgement, and every layer of judgement removed is a failure of care waiting to happen.

The evidence from the Francis Inquiry into Mid Staffordshire was unambiguous: the decision to reduce the number of nursing posts, driven by cost savings, directly contributed to patient safety failures and avoidable deaths. NICE subsequently found evidence of “increased risk of harm associated with a registered nurse caring for more than 8 patients.” The Royal College of Nursing has found that the risk of death increases by 3% each day a patient experiences a registered nurse staffing shortage. Yet as of 2024, the registered nurse vacancy rate remained at approximately 7.5%, equivalent to 31,000 vacant posts. On many NHS wards, much of the direct nursing care is provided by healthcare assistants who have had an average of two weeks’ training. The research evidence consistently demonstrates that the number of registered nurses, and their qualification levels, makes a measurable difference to patient outcomes including mortality.

The pay structure reinforces the problem. A newly qualified Band 5 nurse starts on approximately 31,000 pounds per year, taking home approximately 1,984 pounds per month after deductions. A Band 6 specialist nurse earns between 38,682 and 46,580 pounds. These are the salaries of professionals who hold degrees, bear legal responsibility for patient safety, work unsocial hours, and are routinely subjected to physical violence and verbal abuse. The 2024 Staff Survey found that one in seven NHS staff experienced at least one act of physical violence from patients or the public in the past year. Among ambulance staff, more than a third experienced physical violence. Only 32% of staff are satisfied with their pay. Almost a quarter of doctors and half of nurses surveyed by Bain in 2024 were considering switching careers entirely, citing burnout, excessive workloads, and lack of recognition as the primary drivers.

Progress will reverse taskification, restore clinical professionalism, and make the NHS a service that attracts and retains the best clinical talent in the country. This is not achieved by adding more staff to a broken model. It is achieved by restructuring roles, restoring professional autonomy, improving pay to competitive levels, and ensuring that the people the nation trusts with its health are treated with the respect their expertise demands.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Workforce Act will establish:

- a) Statutory safe staffing ratios for all acute inpatient settings. The Act will mandate a maximum ratio of one registered nurse to six patients on general adult acute wards during the day and one to eight at night, with more intensive ratios for specialist settings: one to one in critical care, one to four in acute psychiatric wards, one to four in paediatric wards. These ratios will be set in a schedule to the Act and may be adjusted only by affirmative resolution of both Houses of Parliament. England will join Wales, Scotland, Victoria (Australia), California, and Queensland in legislating safe staffing floors rather than leaving them to the discretion of cost-constrained local management. Every NHS trust will be required to publish actual staffing levels against the statutory ratios on a shift-by-shift basis, with automatic escalation to the CQC and NHS England when ratios are breached for more than 48 consecutive hours. The era of staffing decisions driven by budget rather than safety ends.
- b) A statutory Clinical Professionalism Framework replacing the taskified model. The Act will establish a legal obligation on NHS trusts to design clinical roles around integrated patient responsibility rather than fragmented task performance. Every inpatient ward will have a named senior nurse, of Band 6 or above, who holds clinical accountability for the care of every patient on the ward throughout their shift. Every patient pathway within the Core Mission will have a named consultant who retains clinical oversight from referral to discharge. The Framework will be developed jointly by the Royal Colleges, the Nursing and Midwifery Council, and the General Medical Council, published within 12 months of Royal Assent, and enforced through the CQC inspection regime. This is not a return to hierarchy for its own sake. It is a return to accountability: someone is responsible, someone is visible, and someone is answerable.
- c) A Pay Competitiveness Guarantee. The Act will establish a statutory duty on the Secretary of State to ensure that NHS pay for Core Mission clinical roles is competitive with equivalent roles in the wider economy and in comparable international health systems. Within 12 months of Royal Assent, the NHS Pay Review Body will conduct a comprehensive pay benchmarking exercise comparing NHS clinical salaries, adjusted for total compensation including pension, to equivalent roles in the private healthcare sector, comparable public sector professions, and OECD health systems. Where the benchmarking reveals a shortfall of more than 10% against the comparator median, the Secretary of State will be required to present a remediation plan to Parliament within six months. The commitment is specific: a Band 5 nurse, a registrar, an emergency medicine consultant should be able to live comfortably in the community they serve without needing a second job, agency shifts, or a working partner to meet the mortgage. If the pay does not achieve that, it is wrong, and it will be corrected.
- d) A statutory Senior Clinical Retention Premium for experienced clinicians in acute Core Mission roles. Clinicians with more than ten years’ post-qualification experience working in emergency medicine, anaesthetics, general surgery, oncology, acute psychiatry, critical care nursing, or midwifery will receive a retention supplement of 15% above their standard pay point, funded from the savings generated by the elimination of agency dependence (NHS1.3). The NHS loses its most experienced clinicians because their expertise is not financially recognised. A consultant who has practised for twenty years earns only marginally more than one who qualified five years ago, while carrying vastly greater clinical responsibility and institutional knowledge. The retention premium corrects this. Experience is the most valuable asset in acute care. Progress will pay for it.

OPERATIONAL

Ward leadership restoration.

Within 90 days of Royal Assent, NHS England will issue operational guidance requiring every acute inpatient ward to have a supernumerary ward manager (Band 7) or senior nurse (Band 6) who is not counted within the staffing ratios and whose role is ward-level clinical leadership, patient safety oversight, and staff supervision. This role existed across the NHS before the austerity-era cuts removed it. The Francis Inquiry identified the loss of senior ward leadership as a direct contributor to care failures. Progress restores it.

Pay benchmarking.

Within six months, the NHS Pay Review Body will publish the initial findings of the comprehensive benchmarking exercise. Within 12 months, the Secretary of State will present the first Pay Competitiveness report to Parliament.

Role redesign programme.

Within 12 months, NHS England will publish the Clinical Professionalism Framework implementation plan, developed with the Royal Colleges, specifying how each acute trust will transition from taskified role structures to integrated clinical accountability models. Trusts will have 24 months to achieve full compliance. The transition will be supported by a national change management programme, funded from the Core Mission revenue allocation.

##### NHS2.2: Reduce Regulatory Burden

The Problem

The NHS operates under the oversight of six overlapping regulators in health and social care. The Care Quality Commission inspects and rates providers. NHS England sets standards, allocates resources, and monitors performance. The General Medical Council regulates doctors. The Nursing and Midwifery Council regulates nurses and midwives. The Health and Care Professions Council regulates allied health professionals. Monitor, now part of NHS England, oversees foundation trust finances. Each regulator requires data. Each requires reports. Each requires evidence of compliance. Each has its own framework, its own terminology, its own inspection methodology, and its own definition of what constitutes acceptable practice. The combined effect is a compliance apparatus that consumes vast quantities of clinical time, produces vast quantities of documentation, and has signally failed to prevent the care failures it was designed to detect.

The numbers are damning. Healthcare professionals spend an average of 13.5 hours per week on clinical documentation, up 25% in seven years. Consultant doctors spend 15.1 hours per week, with 4.7 hours completed in their own time. Clinicians spend 62 minutes per day searching for information within clinical records. The RCN has estimated that nursing staff collectively spend 2.5 million working hours per week on non-essential paperwork. The NHS Confederation found that clinical staff report more than one third of the data they collect is neither useful nor relevant to patient care, and that the NHS spends more than one billion pounds per year collecting and checking data. More than four out of ten clinicians, managers, and board members spend between one and three hours of every working day personally collecting and recording information. Three-quarters told the Confederation that certain information collected for regulators or national requirements is irrelevant. The system collects data for the sake of collecting data.

The CQC, the institution at the apex of the regulatory structure, is itself in crisis. The Dash review of 2024 found that inspections had collapsed from approximately 15,800 in 2019/20 to just 6,700 in 2023/24, partly due to the failed rollout of the Single Assessment Framework. The review found a “stark reduction in activity,” considerable delays in re-inspecting providers with poor ratings, and providers “stuck in ‘requires improvement’ despite improving services.” The CQC had experienced a loss of sector expertise and “considerable loss of credibility.” Providers found the regulatory system “burdensome, duplicative and detached” from operational realities. Eighteen months after launching the Single Assessment Framework, the CQC launched a consultation on replacing it, essentially admitting the framework had failed. The Chief Executive resigned. This is not an institution that is protecting patients. It is an institution that is consuming resources while failing at its primary function.

The deeper problem is cultural. The NHS regulatory model is punitive rather than developmental. It is designed to detect failure after it has happened, not to support improvement before failure occurs. Clinicians operate under the constant threat of regulatory action, complaint investigation, and professional sanction for outcomes that are inherent to the uncertainty of medicine. Healthcare is probabilistic. Patients die despite correct treatment. Complications occur despite competent surgery. Diagnoses are missed despite thorough assessment, because medicine is practised under uncertainty with incomplete information and finite time. A regulatory model that treats every adverse outcome as a potential failure of care, rather than distinguishing between negligence and the irreducible uncertainty of clinical practice, creates a culture of defensive medicine: more tests ordered, more documentation produced, more referrals made, not because they improve patient care but because they protect the clinician from regulatory consequences. Defensive medicine is expensive, wasteful, and paradoxically dangerous, because it clogs the system with unnecessary activity while diverting attention from the patients who genuinely need it.

Progress will dismantle the compliance industry, consolidate the regulatory architecture, and replace a punitive model with one that distinguishes between genuine negligence and the inherent uncertainty of clinical practice. The objective is not less accountability. It is better accountability: fewer forms, fewer reports, fewer overlapping inspections, and more time spent at the bedside.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Workforce Act will establish:

- a) Consolidation of health and social care regulation into a single body: the Health Standards Authority (HSA). The Act will abolish the CQC and transfer its functions, together with the relevant inspection and quality assurance functions currently performed by NHS England, into a new statutory body with a single mandate: to ensure that NHS providers deliver safe, effective care. The HSA will be smaller, more focused, and staffed by practising clinicians and experienced healthcare managers rather than professional inspectors with no clinical background. It will inspect less frequently but more thoroughly, using unannounced visits rather than pre-arranged inspections, and will assess clinical outcomes rather than process compliance. The HSA will be required to publish a Clinical Burden Assessment for every new data collection, reporting requirement, or inspection criterion it introduces, demonstrating that the expected improvement in patient outcomes justifies the clinical time consumed. If the burden cannot be justified, it cannot be imposed.
- b) A statutory Documentation Reduction Target. The Act will require that total clinician time spent on documentation is reduced by 40% within the first Parliament, measured against the 2022 baseline of 13.5 hours per week. The target will be achieved through three mechanisms: the elimination of duplicative reporting requirements through the HSA consolidation; the deployment of automated clinical documentation systems including ambient AI transcription, speech-to-text clinical noting, and structured data extraction from existing clinical systems (linked to the digital architecture described in NHS3); and the statutory prohibition of any data collection requirement that cannot be demonstrated to improve patient care or safety. The NHS Confederation found that more than one billion pounds per year is spent on data collection. Every pound of that spending that does not improve patient outcomes is a pound diverted from care.
- c) A statutory Safe Harbour for clinical decision-making. The Act will establish a legal framework under which clinicians who make decisions in good faith, in accordance with their training and the standards of their profession, within the constraints of the resources available, are protected from regulatory sanction for adverse outcomes that fall within the accepted range of clinical uncertainty. This is not immunity from accountability. Negligence, recklessness, and dishonesty will remain fully subject to professional regulation and, where appropriate, criminal sanction. But the framework will require that any regulatory investigation of a clinical decision must first establish whether the decision fell outside the range of reasonable clinical practice before proceeding. The current system, in which any complaint or adverse outcome can trigger a prolonged investigation regardless of whether the clinician did anything wrong, is destroying morale and driving clinicians out of the profession. The Safe Harbour tells every doctor and nurse in the country: if you act in good faith and within your competence, we will defend you, not persecute you.
- d) A statutory cap on the proportion of NHS revenue that may be spent on regulatory compliance, set at no more than 1.5% of total NHS revenue. The current cost of regulatory compliance across the NHS is not precisely known, because it is dispersed across every trust and embedded in the time of every clinician. The HSA will be required to measure and publish total compliance costs within 18 months of Royal Assent. Any increase in compliance spending above the cap will require explicit approval from the Secretary of State, with a published justification demonstrating the patient safety benefit. The regulatory apparatus grows because no one measures its cost. Progress will measure it, cap it, and hold it accountable.

OPERATIONAL

Documentation audit.

Within 60 days of Royal Assent, NHS England will commission a comprehensive audit of every documentation requirement imposed on clinical staff, from every source: national bodies, regional bodies, trusts, and external regulators. The audit will classify each requirement as clinically essential, operationally useful, or eliminable. Requirements classified as eliminable will be withdrawn within 90 days of the audit’s publication. Requirements classified as operationally useful will be reviewed for automation potential under the NHS3 digital architecture. Only clinically essential documentation will remain as a manual requirement for clinical staff. This audit has never been conducted comprehensively. The documentation burden has grown organically for decades, with each new requirement added and none ever removed. That accretion ends.

HSA transition.

Within 12 months of Royal Assent, the Secretary of State will publish the Health Standards Authority Establishment Plan, setting out the organisational structure, staffing model, inspection methodology, and transition timeline for the new body. The CQC’s existing workforce will be offered roles in the HSA under TUPE protections. The transition will be completed within 24 months, with no gap in regulatory oversight during the changeover.

Safe Harbour implementation.

Within six months, the General Medical Council and Nursing and Midwifery Council will publish joint guidance on the operation of the Safe Harbour framework, including worked examples of decisions that fall within and outside the protected range. Training on the Safe Harbour will be incorporated into mandatory professional development for all NHS clinical staff within 12 months.

##### NHS2.3: Build Strategic Redundancy

The Problem

The NHS operates, by design and by financial pressure, at the edge of its capacity at all times. General and acute bed occupancy has not fallen below 91% in any month since September 2021, consistently exceeding the 85% threshold above which safety and efficiency are compromised.
