The workforce is deployed with minimal surplus: the 2024 Staff Survey found that only 34% of staff agree there are enough people to do their jobs properly. The vacancy rate, while falling, remained at 6.7% in the second quarter of 2025/26, representing 100,020 vacant posts. The system is designed to be full. It has no slack, no reserves, and no margin for error.

This is a catastrophic design choice. Every complex system requires redundancy to function safely. Aviation builds redundancy into every aircraft: multiple engines, multiple navigation systems, multiple communication channels. Military planning operates on the principle that reserves must be maintained even at the cost of immediate combat power. Manufacturing holds buffer stock to absorb supply chain disruptions. Only the NHS, responsible for the health of 57 million people, operates on the assumption that demand will always exactly match supply and that nothing will ever go wrong simultaneously across the system.

The consequences are visible every winter and after every surge event. When demand rises, as it inevitably does during respiratory virus seasons, heatwaves, or pandemic waves, the system has no capacity to absorb the increase. Elective operations are cancelled. Emergency departments overflow. Corridor care becomes the norm. Staff are redeployed from one overstretched service to another, degrading both. Agency spending spikes as trusts scramble to fill gaps that permanent staffing levels were never designed to cover. The NHS spent approximately 3 billion pounds on agency staff in 2022/23. This is not spending on patient care. It is spending on the failure to plan for predictable variation in demand.

The absence of strategic redundancy also destroys the workforce. Staff who operate at maximum capacity continuously, with no recovery time, no margin for error, and no prospect of a quieter shift, burn out. The 2024 Staff Survey records that 41% of staff feel unwell due to work-related stress. Sickness absence in the NHS was 5.3% in September 2025, with anxiety, stress, depression, and other psychiatric conditions accounting for more than 30% of all days lost. Staff who are absent increase the pressure on those who remain, who in turn become more likely to become absent themselves. The system consumes its own workforce.

The financial argument against redundancy is superficially compelling and fundamentally wrong. Maintaining a workforce that is 10% larger than the minimum required to meet average demand costs more in wages during normal periods. But the cost of not having that surplus is far higher: agency spending of billions of pounds per year, cancelled operations that must be rescheduled at additional cost, patients whose conditions deteriorate while waiting and who then require more expensive treatment, and staff turnover driven by burnout that requires expensive recruitment and training to replace. Strategic redundancy is not waste. It is insurance, and the premium is far cheaper than the claims.

Progress will build strategic redundancy into every level of the NHS workforce, creating a system that can absorb predictable surges in demand without cancelling operations, without burning out its staff, and without spending billions on agency workers who do not know the ward, the systems, or the patients.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Workforce Act will establish:

- a) A statutory Workforce Surge Capacity of 10% above the baseline staffing required to meet the statutory safe staffing ratios defined in NHS2.1. The Act will require every NHS trust to maintain a permanently employed workforce that is at least 10% larger than the minimum required to staff all Core Mission services at the statutory ratios during normal demand periods. This surplus provides immediate capacity to absorb demand surges, cover sickness absence, and allow staff to take leave without degrading patient care. The 10% surplus is funded through the reallocation of agency spending: the NHS currently spends billions per year on temporary staff at premium rates to cover gaps that a properly resourced permanent workforce would not have. Replacing agency dependency with permanent surplus is both safer and cheaper.
- b) A statutory requirement for Demand Forecasting and Capacity Planning. The Act will require NHS England, working with integrated care boards, to publish an annual Demand Forecast for the following three years, covering anticipated admissions, emergency presentations, and elective demand by region, season, and specialty. Trusts will be required to demonstrate that their workforce plans, including the 10% surplus, are aligned with the demand forecast. The forecast will be updated quarterly and will trigger automatic escalation when projected demand exceeds planned capacity by more than 5%. The current system does not forecast. It reacts. Every winter crisis is treated as an unforeseen event, despite being entirely predictable. Progress will plan for what every historical dataset shows will happen.
- c) A National Clinical Reserve. The Act will establish a voluntary register of qualified clinicians, including retired professionals, part-time workers, and clinicians who have left the NHS but retain their registration, who are willing to be called upon during declared surge periods. Members of the National Clinical Reserve will receive an annual retainer, funded revalidation, and guaranteed pay at substantive NHS rates, not agency rates, when deployed. The Reserve replaces the current system in which trusts compete against each other to hire the same pool of agency staff at escalating prices. It creates a national resource that can be directed where it is needed most, at a cost that is transparent and controlled.
- d) A statutory prohibition on the use of agency staff for Core Mission clinical roles except during declared surge periods or emergencies. This provision, complementing the agency spend cap established in NHS1.3, will take full effect within the first Parliament once the Workforce Surge Capacity and National Clinical Reserve are operational. The prohibition eliminates the perverse incentive structure in which trusts offer agency rates that undercut their own permanent recruitment: why would a nurse accept a permanent Band 5 position at 31,000 pounds per year when she can earn more through an agency, working the same ward, with no long-term commitment? The prohibition removes the option. If you want to work in the NHS, you work for the NHS. The pay, conditions, and respect will be worth it.

OPERATIONAL

Demand forecasting.

Within 90 days of Royal Assent, NHS England will publish the first annual Demand Forecast, using historical admission data, population projections, seasonal patterns, and epidemiological intelligence. The forecast methodology will be developed in partnership with the UK Health Security Agency and academic epidemiology centres. Trusts will receive regional and specialty-level demand projections within 120 days, enabling immediate workforce planning adjustments for the following financial year.

National Clinical Reserve.

Within six months, NHS England will open the National Clinical Reserve register. All clinicians who have left the NHS within the past ten years and retain their professional registration will be contacted directly and offered enrolment. Retired clinicians whose registration has lapsed within five years will be offered funded revalidation programmes through the Return-to-Practice initiative established under NHS1.3. The Reserve will be operational within 12 months of Royal Assent.

Workforce surge planning.

Within 12 months, every NHS trust will have published a Surge Staffing Plan demonstrating how it will achieve and maintain the 10% workforce surplus. Plans will be assessed by the Treatment Coverage Commission as part of its five-yearly Bed Capacity Review (NHS1.2d), ensuring that workforce capacity is aligned with bed capacity and demand projections. Trusts that fail to maintain the required surplus will be placed in mandatory improvement, with direct intervention from NHS England.

##### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The NHS2 framework is built on the NHS Workforce Act, a single piece of primary legislation introduced alongside the NHS Core Mission Act (NHS1), the Tax Reset Act (E6), and the other centrepiece legislation of a first Progress government. No additional Acts are required. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, NHS England operational guidance, or departmental action.

NHS Workforce Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: Statutory safe staffing ratios for all acute inpatient settings, with maximum ratios of 1:6 on general adult acute wards during the day, 1:8 at night, and more intensive ratios for specialist settings. Clinical Professionalism Framework establishing integrated patient responsibility over taskified role structures. Pay Competitiveness Guarantee with mandatory benchmarking and remediation. Senior Clinical Retention Premium of 15% for experienced clinicians in acute Core Mission roles. Consolidation of health and social care regulation into the Health Standards Authority, replacing the CQC. Statutory Documentation Reduction Target of 40% within the first Parliament. Safe Harbour for good-faith clinical decision-making. Regulatory compliance spending cap of 1.5% of NHS revenue. Workforce Surge Capacity of 10% above baseline staffing. Statutory Demand Forecasting and Capacity Planning. National Clinical Reserve of qualified clinicians for surge deployment. Prohibition of agency staff for Core Mission clinical roles outside declared emergencies.

Delivered operationally: Supernumerary ward leadership guidance within 90 days. Pay benchmarking initial findings within six months, full report within 12 months. Clinical Professionalism Framework implementation plan within 12 months, full compliance within 36 months. Documentation audit commenced within 60 days. HSA Establishment Plan within 12 months, full transition within 24 months. Safe Harbour joint guidance within six months. Demand Forecast published within 90 days. National Clinical Reserve register opened within six months, operational within 12 months. Trust Surge Staffing Plans published within 12 months.

##### Funding the Workforce Crisis Management Programme

The Workforce Crisis Management programme is funded through the reallocation of existing spending that is currently wasted, not through additional expenditure. The funding sources, in order of contribution, are as follows.

Agency spend elimination.

The NHS spent approximately 3 billion pounds on agency staff in 2022/23. For every pound spent on an agency worker, a significant portion is absorbed by agency margins, administrative costs, and the inefficiency of deploying temporary staff who do not know the ward or the patients. The Workforce Surge Capacity and agency prohibition will progressively eliminate agency dependency for Core Mission roles, redirecting the full quantum of current agency spending to fund the 10% permanent workforce surplus, the Senior Clinical Retention Premium, and the National Clinical Reserve retainer payments. The permanent surplus is cheaper than the agency spend it replaces.

Regulatory compliance savings.

The consolidation of six regulators into the Health Standards Authority, the elimination of duplicative reporting requirements, and the Documentation Reduction Target will free more than one billion pounds per year in clinical time currently spent on non-essential data collection and compliance activity. This time is not a cash saving; it is a productivity saving, translating directly into increased clinical capacity: more patients seen, more operations performed, more appointments delivered, using the same workforce doing more of what it was trained to do.

Retention savings.

Staff turnover in the NHS costs billions per year in recruitment, training, and the lost productivity of vacant posts. The annual cost of replacing a single registered nurse is estimated at 10,000 to 15,000 pounds, accounting for recruitment, temporary cover, induction, and the reduced productivity of new starters. With more than 40,000 nurses leaving the NHS in peak years, turnover costs exceed 400 million pounds per year for nursing staff alone. The Pay Competitiveness Guarantee, the Senior Clinical Retention Premium, the restoration of clinical professionalism, and the reduction in regulatory burden are all designed to reduce turnover. Every percentage point reduction in turnover saves tens of millions of pounds that can be reinvested in patient care.

Defensive medicine reduction.

The Safe Harbour provision will, over time, reduce the volume of defensive medicine practised across the NHS: unnecessary tests, unnecessary referrals, and unnecessary admissions ordered not because they benefit the patient but because they protect the clinician. While the financial benefit is difficult to quantify precisely, international evidence suggests that defensive medicine adds between 5% and 10% to healthcare costs in systems with punitive regulatory cultures. Even a modest reduction in defensive medicine across the NHS would free significant resources for direct patient care.

NHS2 does not operate in isolation. It is the human counterpart to the structural reforms of NHS1. Without a defined core mission (NHS1.1), workforce reform optimises for the wrong objectives. Without adequate bed capacity (NHS1.2), even the best-staffed workforce cannot treat patients who have nowhere to be treated. Without the Discharge Guarantee (NHS1.2c), beds remain occupied by patients who do not need them, and staff spend time managing administrative delays rather than delivering care. Without the psychiatric bed expansion (NHS1.4), acute wards remain occupied by mental health patients who need specialist care, degrading the experience for both patients and staff. And without the workforce reforms in this document, the beds built by NHS1 will be staffed by agency workers who do not know the patients, regulated by an apparatus that consumes more time than it saves, and operated at a capacity that guarantees burnout and failure.

The NHS workforce is not the problem. It is the solution, if the system lets it be. Progress will let it be. The forms will be fewer. The regulators will be competent. The pay will be fair. The shifts will be staffed. The wards will have leaders. The clinicians will practise medicine. And the patients of the National Health Service will receive the care they deserve from professionals who have the time, the authority, and the support to deliver it.

#### NHS3. Information Systems and Data Capitalisation

Governing Principle

The NHS produces more data than almost any other institution on Earth. Every GP appointment, every blood test, every prescription, every hospital admission, every scan, every discharge note, every death certificate feeds into a body of clinical information covering more than sixty million people over more than seventy-five years. This data is, by any honest accounting, one of the most valuable assets the British state possesses. It is also one of the worst managed.

NHS IT spending reached approximately 4.1 billion pounds in 2024/25, averaging 2.3% of trust budgets, and the government earmarked a further 3.4 billion in the 2024 Spring Budget for digital transformation. Despite this, the system remains fragmented to a degree that would be considered scandalous in any private enterprise of comparable scale. As of May 2025, 91% of secondary care trusts had electronic patient records, with the government targeting universal coverage by March 2026. Seven trusts still had none. The NHS was still spending 230.5 million pounds per year on paper records despite nominally near-universal EPR coverage. There was no statistical correlation between a trust’s digital maturity score and its spending on paper, which tells you everything about the quality of the digital systems. Digitally mature trusts were found to operate approximately 13% more efficiently than their less mature peers, a gap that represents billions in lost productivity across the system.

The catastrophe of the National Programme for IT haunts every discussion of NHS digital infrastructure. NPfIT launched in 2002 with a budget of 6.2 billion pounds. It was dismantled in September 2011 having cost over 10 billion and generated only approximately 2.6 billion in actual benefits. The Public Accounts Committee called it one of the worst and most expensive contracting fiascos in history. It failed because it imposed a single top-down solution on a system of enormous local variation, with no clinician engagement, rushed procurement, unclear scope, and a centralised approach that treated the NHS as a monolith rather than a federation. The lesson is definitive: top-down mandates destroy value; bottom-up competition and incremental deployment create it.

The cyber security position is equally alarming. The 2017 WannaCry attack cost the NHS an estimated 92 million pounds, affected 80 of 236 trusts and 603 primary care organisations, cancelled at least 19,000 appointments, and diverted ambulances from five hospitals. In June 2024, the ransomware attack on Synnovis, a pathology services provider for London hospitals, led to the cancellation of over 10,000 outpatient appointments and 1,710 elective procedures. It took sixteen weeks for services to return to near-normal levels. One patient death has been confirmed as a direct consequence. Patient names and NHS numbers were published online. These are not isolated incidents. Between mid-2015 and the end of 2016, 88 of the NHS’s 260 trusts were hit by ransomware. The systems that store and move patient data are, in many trusts, built on infrastructure that an undergraduate computer science student would recognise as indefensible.

Meanwhile, the data itself sits in silos that pharmaceutical companies, medical researchers, and health technology developers would pay enormous sums to access. EY has valued the curated NHS dataset at several billion pounds, with potential benefits of up to 9.6 billion per annum if properly exploited. A 2025 report by SCI and LEK Consulting estimated that consolidating NHS data into a single accessible infrastructure for commercial research could add more than 10 billion pounds in gross value added per year to the UK economy. The NHS 10-Year Health Plan, published in July 2025, explicitly supports data commercialisation, stating that the government will explore ways to derive commercial value from access to anonymous health data, including access charges and equity stakes. The UK Health Minister proposed monetising NHS data in December 2025. The government and Wellcome Trust are investing 600 million pounds to create the Health Data Research Service. And yet the NHS has not, to date, generated any meaningful commercial revenue from its data. The asset exists. The demand exists. The institutional capacity to connect them does not.

Finally, the NHS has no integrated system for mapping disease prevalence to workforce needs. Trauma and orthopaedics has the largest waiting list at approximately 860,000 patients. Oral surgery has the worst 18-week breach rate at 49%. The waiting list stood at 7.29 million cases in December 2025, consisting of approximately 6.17 million individual patients. The median wait was 13.4 weeks, up from 8.3 weeks pre-pandemic. These numbers are not mysteries. They are the predictable consequences of a system that does not systematically measure what diseases its population has, does not use that data to determine what workforce it needs, and therefore cannot set realistic targets for how long patients should wait. The Disease Monitoring Service described in this document connects disease prevalence data directly to workforce planning and waiting time targeting for the first time in NHS history.

NHS3 addresses three failures: the failure to build information systems that work, the failure to capitalise on the data those systems produce, and the failure to use that data to plan the workforce the country needs. The primary legislation vehicle is the NHS Information Systems Act. It is the digital backbone that makes every other NHS reform deliverable.

##### NHS3.1: Modernise Data Infrastructure

The Problem

The NHS does not have a data infrastructure problem. It has dozens of them, overlapping, contradicting each other, and each defended by its own institutional constituency. The Spine processes 1.4 billion transactions per month and functions as the national messaging backbone, but it is a transport layer, not an intelligence layer. The Federated Data Platform, built on Palantir’s Foundry technology and awarded in November 2023, is rolling out across integrated care systems with a target of universal adoption by 2028/29, but it is a data integration tool grafted onto a landscape of fundamentally incompatible source systems. The government announced a single patient record accessible via the NHS App from 2028, but every previous attempt to build a unified patient record has failed, and nothing in the current approach addresses the reasons why.

The variation in trust-level IT capability is staggering. Guy’s and St Thomas’ spent 109 million pounds on IT in 2024/25. George Eliot Hospital spent 600,000. The gap is not proportional to the difference in patient volumes or complexity. It reflects a system in which IT investment decisions are made locally, with no national minimum standard for infrastructure quality, no competitive pressure to adopt best-in-class systems, and no consequence for running clinical operations on technology that would be unacceptable in a medium-sized logistics company.

Interoperability remains the foundational failure. The NHS uses a mixture of HL7 Version 2 messaging, which dates from the late 1980s, alongside partial adoption of HL7 FHIR, the modern API-driven standard built on RESTful web services that the rest of the developed world is converging on. FHIR enables granular, modular data access using discrete resources such as Patient, Observation, Medication, and Encounter. It supports JSON and XML, integrates natively with modern web applications, and has the richest open-source ecosystem of any health data standard. The NHS has not mandated FHIR adoption. It should. Every new system procured or developed for the NHS should be required to expose FHIR-compliant APIs, and every existing system should be required to implement FHIR interfaces within a defined transition period. This is not optional. Without a mandatory interoperability standard, every other digital initiative is building on quicksand.

Cyber resilience is not a secondary concern. It is an operational prerequisite. The WannaCry attack succeeded because trusts were running unpatched operating systems that Microsoft had ceased to support. The Synnovis attack succeeded through inadequate access controls at a third-party supplier. In May 2025, NHS England and the Department of Health issued an open letter to supplier CEOs asking them to sign a charter of cyber security best practice, emphasising multi-factor authentication, 24/7 monitoring, and strong backup systems. Asking is not sufficient. Requiring is. The NHS Information Systems Act will make compliance with defined cyber security standards a condition of NHS contracts, enforceable by financial penalty and, for repeated non-compliance, contract termination.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Information Systems Act will establish:

- a) Tournament-style funding for next-generation NHS backend systems. The Act will create the NHS Digital Innovation Fund, capitalized at no less than 500 million pounds over the first Parliament, to fund competitive parallel development of replacement systems for the NHS’s core digital infrastructure. The Fund will operate on a staged elimination model: multiple vendors, including NHS internal teams, university consortia, and private sector providers, will receive seed funding to develop minimum viable products against defined functional specifications. After twelve months, an independent technical panel including practising clinicians, software engineers, and data scientists will evaluate submissions against performance benchmarks covering interoperability, clinical usability, data integrity, security, and total cost of ownership. The top three to five performers will receive second-stage funding for pilot deployment in volunteer trusts. After a further twelve months of live operation, the best-performing system or systems will receive full deployment funding. This is the anti-NPfIT. Instead of one contractor, one specification, and one chance to get it right, we create competitive pressure, clinician-led evaluation, and staged de-risking. The tournament model has been validated in defence procurement, technology accelerators, and infrastructure investment. It has never been applied to NHS IT. It will be.
- b) Mandatory FHIR compliance. From the first April following Royal Assent, all new digital systems procured by or for the NHS must expose HL7 FHIR R4-compliant APIs for all patient-facing data. Existing systems that hold or process patient data must implement FHIR interfaces within 36 months. The Act will empower the Health Standards Authority, established under NHS2, to certify FHIR compliance and to withdraw certification from systems that fail to meet the standard. Non-compliant systems will be ineligible for NHS funding after the transition period. This creates a hard deadline that vendors cannot lobby their way around. The NHS will speak one digital language.
- c) National minimum cyber security standards for all NHS-connected systems. The Act will define mandatory requirements including multi-factor authentication on all clinical and administrative systems, 24/7 security monitoring with automated incident response, encrypted data at rest and in transit, maximum patch deployment timelines of 14 days for critical vulnerabilities and 30 days for all others, mandatory penetration testing at least annually, and air-gapped backup systems tested quarterly. Compliance will be a condition of all NHS contracts, including those with third-party suppliers and subcontractors. The Health Standards Authority will conduct or commission annual cyber resilience assessments of all trusts and major suppliers. Results will be published. Trusts rated inadequate will be placed in mandatory remediation with dedicated technical support. Supplier contracts will contain liquidated damages clauses for cyber security breaches attributable to non-compliance with the mandatory standards.
- d) The NHS Data Architecture Standard. The Act will mandate a national data architecture specifying how patient data flows between primary care, secondary care, social care, community services, mental health, and public health bodies. The architecture will be designed around the principle that data follows the patient, not the institution. A patient’s complete clinical record, inclusive of GP consultations, hospital admissions, prescriptions, diagnostic results, and social care assessments, will be accessible to any authorised clinician treating that patient, in real time, through a single authenticated interface. The architecture will use the Federated Data Platform as the integration layer, with FHIR as the interchange standard, and will be designed to support the Disease Monitoring Service described in NHS3.3 and the Statutory Demand Forecasting system established under NHS2. The single patient record announced by the current government will be delivered within this architecture, not as a parallel initiative.

OPERATIONAL

NHS Digital Innovation Fund.

Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Department of Health will publish the first tournament specification, covering electronic patient records for secondary care. The specification will be developed in consultation with the Royal Colleges, NHS trust CIOs, and practising clinicians. First-stage funding awards will be made within six months. The second tournament specification, covering primary care systems integration, will be published within twelve months.

FHIR transition programme.

Within 60 days of Royal Assent, the Health Standards Authority will publish a FHIR compliance roadmap, including detailed technical specifications, a vendor support programme, and a trust-by-trust transition schedule prioritised by patient volume and digital maturity. Trusts with the lowest digital maturity scores will receive dedicated technical teams to support the transition.

Cyber resilience.

Within 120 days of Royal Assent, the Health Standards Authority will publish the mandatory cyber security standards and begin the first cycle of trust assessments. All NHS contracts executed after Royal Assent will contain the mandatory cyber security clauses.

##### NHS3.2: National Health Asset Monetisation

The Problem

The NHS holds patient-level data covering more than sixty million registered individuals, spanning decades of clinical history. This is, by any reasonable measure, the most comprehensive longitudinal health dataset in the world. The UK Biobank, which contains deep phenotypic and genomic data on 500,000 participants, is already considered the single most valuable research dataset globally. The NHS dataset is orders of magnitude larger, and when curated and linked, orders of magnitude more valuable.

The demand is real and quantifiable. EY’s analysis found that electronic health record data alone has an estimated value of less than 100 pounds per patient record, but that value rises to between 1,000 and 5,000 pounds per record when combined with genomic and phenotypic data. At those unit values, the full NHS dataset is worth tens of billions of pounds. More practically, SCI and LEK Consulting estimated in 2025 that consolidating NHS data for commercial research access could generate more than 10 billion pounds in gross value added per year. Internal NHS estimates from 2019 meetings with Microsoft, Amazon, and pharmaceutical companies valued the data at up to 10 billion per year in direct revenue potential. McKinsey’s analysis of the Federated Data Platform estimated that digital and data use-cases deployed at scale could unlock value equivalent to 15 to 25 billion pounds per year.

The government knows this. The NHS 10-Year Health Plan published in July 2025 explicitly stated that the government will explore ways to derive commercial value from access to anonymous health data, including access charges and equity stakes. The Health Minister proposed monetising NHS data in December 2025. The government and Wellcome Trust announced 600 million pounds for the Health Data Research Service in April 2025, to be located at the Wellcome Genome Campus in Cambridgeshire, providing a single access point for anonymised national-scale datasets. Clinical trial setup targets have been cut from over 250 days in 2022 to 150 days by March 2026.

And yet the NHS generates essentially no commercial revenue from this asset. The data sits fragmented across CPRD, NHS Digital (now part of NHS England), individual trusts, and research databases, each with different access procedures, different governance frameworks, different pricing models, and different technical formats. Researchers spend months navigating bureaucratic access procedures. Pharmaceutical companies that could accelerate drug development using NHS real-world evidence take their investment to jurisdictions with simpler data access frameworks. Public support for responsible data use is strong: surveys consistently show 60 to 70% public approval for pharmaceutical use of NHS data. But 50% of the public are worried about data being sold without proper consent, and privacy experts have legitimate concerns about the robustness of anonymisation techniques. The challenge is not whether to monetise. It is how to do it in a way that generates substantial revenue, maintains public trust, and positions Britain as the global centre of health data research.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Information Systems Act will establish:

- a) The National Health Data Asset. The Act will formally designate the totality of NHS patient data as a national asset held in trust for the British public. This designation creates a legal framework for its stewardship and commercial exploitation. The Act will establish the NHS Data Authority, a statutory body responsible for curating, governing, and commercially licensing access to anonymised NHS data. The Authority will absorb the data governance functions currently scattered across NHS England, CPRD, and individual trusts, creating a single point of access for all external parties. It will work in close coordination with the Health Data Research Service to avoid duplication and ensure that the HDRS serves as the primary technical access point while the NHS Data Authority retains commercial and governance control.
- b) A tiered access and pricing model. The Act will establish three tiers of data access. The first tier, Open Research, will provide free access to aggregated, fully anonymised population-level datasets for academic researchers at accredited UK institutions and for public health purposes. The second tier, Commercial Research, will provide paid access to anonymised patient-level datasets for pharmaceutical companies, health technology firms, and other commercial entities. The third tier, Premium Partnership, will provide access to curated, linked datasets including genomic, phenotypic, and longitudinal clinical data, under bespoke commercial agreements that may include equity stakes, milestone payments, and revenue sharing in addition to access fees. Preferential pricing will be offered to UK-headquartered companies, creating a competitive advantage for Britain’s life sciences and health technology sectors and incentivising firms to domicile research operations in the UK.
- c) The Patient Data Compact. The Act will enshrine in law a set of non-negotiable principles governing the use of NHS data. First, no individual patient data will ever be shared in identifiable form without explicit, informed consent. Second, all commercial access will use anonymised or pseudonymised datasets subject to the highest technical standards of de-identification, independently audited annually. Third, patients will have an absolute right to opt out of their data being included in commercially licensed datasets, exercisable through the NHS App with immediate effect. Fourth, a minimum of 25% of all commercial data revenue will be hypothecated directly to NHS front-line services, ring-fenced from departmental budgets. Fifth, a public register of all data access agreements, including the identity of the licensee, the scope of data accessed, the purpose, and the fees paid, will be maintained and published quarterly by the NHS Data Authority. This is the compact that earns public trust: full transparency, full opt-out, and visible reinvestment of the proceeds.
- d) Revenue targets and accountability. The Act will require the NHS Data Authority to generate no less than 500 million pounds in commercial data licensing revenue within three years of its establishment, rising to no less than 1.5 billion pounds per year within five years. These targets are conservative relative to the valuations described above. They are achievable because the demand already exists, the data already exists, and the only missing element is an institutional vehicle capable of connecting the two at commercial scale. The Authority will report annually to Parliament on revenue generated, data access agreements executed, patient opt-out rates, and the allocation of hypothecated revenue to front-line services.

OPERATIONAL

NHS Data Authority establishment.

Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Secretary of State will appoint the founding board of the NHS Data Authority, comprising data scientists, commercial licensing specialists, clinical informaticists, patient representatives, and privacy experts. The Authority will be operational within six months, inheriting existing data governance functions and beginning the first round of commercial licensing negotiations.

Data curation programme.

Within 12 months, the Authority will complete the first phase of data curation, linking primary care, secondary care, and prescribing data into a single anonymised national dataset covering at least 40 million patient records. The curation process will implement standardised FHIR-based data structures as mandated by NHS3.1, ensuring that the commercial dataset is technically accessible to modern analytical tools without bespoke data engineering.

First commercial licences.

Within 18 months, the Authority will execute its first commercial data access agreements under the tiered pricing model. A dedicated business development team will target the top fifty pharmaceutical companies and the top twenty health technology firms globally, offering early-mover advantages including preferential pricing and priority access to premium datasets.

Patient communication.

Within 60 days of Royal Assent, NHS England will launch a national public information campaign explaining the data monetisation programme, the Patient Data Compact, and the opt-out mechanism. The campaign will be developed with input from patient advocacy groups and will be designed to build trust through radical transparency rather than institutional reassurance.

##### NHS3.3: Disease Monitoring Service

The Problem

The NHS does not systematically know what diseases its population has. It knows what patients present with when they arrive at a hospital or GP surgery. It knows what was coded on a discharge summary. It has surveillance systems run by the UK Health Security Agency that track notifiable infectious diseases and antimicrobial resistance. But it has no integrated, real-time system that maps the prevalence and incidence of the full spectrum of diseases across the population, stratified by geography, age, ethnicity, and deprivation, and uses that data to determine what clinical workforce the country needs and how long patients should expect to wait.

The consequences are visible in the waiting list. Trauma and orthopaedics has the largest list at approximately 860,000 patients. Oral surgery has the worst 18-week breach rate at 49%. The elective waiting list stands at 7.29 million cases. Research published in 2025 found that the list must halve to approximately 3.4 million to meet the constitutional 92% target of patients treated within 18 weeks. The largest absolute reduction needed is in trauma and orthopaedics, requiring a cut of 519,000. Meanwhile, cardiothoracic surgery patients are the most severely affected by long waits. Workforce planning for medical specialties continues to be driven by historic training post allocations rather than prospective disease burden modelling. The Royal College of Physicians noted in late 2024 that high-demand specialties such as dermatology, radiology, cardiology, gastroenterology, and ophthalmology have seen limited post expansion due to supervision limits and budget constraints, not because the demand has plateaued.

UKHSA’s surveillance systems are focused on infectious diseases and operate largely independently of the NHS’s operational planning. UKHSA’s first annual report, published in March 2025, found that infectious diseases were the primary reason for over 20% of hospital bed usage, at an annual cost of almost 6 billion pounds in 2023/24. TB cases increased 11% in 2023 and a further 13% in 2024. Measles outbreaks are recurring due to vaccination rates falling below the 95% target. The new electronic notifications of infectious diseases system went live on 1 April 2025, but NOIDs data publishing was simultaneously paused for development work. The system is improving, but it covers only notifiable infectious diseases. Non-communicable diseases, which account for the overwhelming majority of NHS demand, including cardiovascular disease, musculoskeletal conditions, cancer, diabetes, respiratory disease, and mental illness, are not subject to any comparable national prevalence monitoring system.

The NHS Statutory Demand Forecasting system established under NHS2 requires a data feed that does not yet exist. The Disease Monitoring Service creates it.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Information Systems Act will establish:

- a) The Disease Monitoring Service. The Act will create a statutory national service responsible for the continuous measurement and publication of disease prevalence and incidence across England, covering both communicable and non-communicable conditions. The Service will operate as a division of the NHS Data Authority established under NHS3.2, using the same curated national dataset but with an explicit mandate to produce operational intelligence rather than research access. The Service will publish quarterly National Disease Maps showing the prevalence and incidence of no fewer than fifty priority conditions, stratified by Integrated Care System geography, age band, sex, ethnicity, and deprivation quintile. These maps will be publicly available and machine-readable.
- b) Statutory linkage to workforce planning. The Act will require Health Education England and its successors to use Disease Monitoring Service data as the primary input for medical training post allocations. The current system, in which specialty training numbers are determined by a combination of historic precedent, supervision capacity, and budget availability, will be supplemented by a statutory requirement that training post numbers must be demonstrably responsive to projected disease burden. Where the Disease Monitoring Service identifies a sustained increase in prevalence of a condition in a given region, the workforce planning system must respond with increased training posts in the relevant specialty within two planning cycles. The Service will produce annual Workforce Alignment Reports showing the gap between current specialty workforce capacity and projected disease-driven demand, by specialty and by region. These reports will be laid before Parliament.
- c) Realistic waiting time targets by specialty. The Act will require the Secretary of State to set specialty-specific waiting time targets that reflect actual disease burden, workforce capacity, and treatment complexity, rather than applying a single uniform target across all specialties. The current approach, in which 92% within 18 weeks applies identically to a routine dermatology referral and a complex cardiothoracic procedure, produces targets that are simultaneously too ambitious for some specialties and insufficiently ambitious for others. The Disease Monitoring Service will provide the evidence base for differentiated targets, which will be reviewed and updated annually. The principle is simple: targets should be achievable with the workforce available, and the workforce should be planned to make targets progressively more ambitious over time. This creates a virtuous cycle in which data drives workforce planning, workforce planning drives capacity, and capacity drives target achievement.
- d) Integration with UKHSA surveillance. The Disease Monitoring Service will incorporate UKHSA’s existing infectious disease surveillance systems, including the electronic notifications system, the antimicrobial resistance monitoring programme, and the pathogen genomics capability, into a single unified national health surveillance architecture. UKHSA will retain operational responsibility for outbreak response, but the epidemiological data it generates will flow into the Disease Monitoring Service’s National Disease Maps. This ensures that the NHS’s operational planning reflects the full spectrum of disease, not just the non-communicable conditions that dominate elective waiting lists but also the infectious diseases that UKHSA’s 2025 report found were responsible for over 20% of hospital bed usage.

OPERATIONAL

Service establishment.

Within 120 days of Royal Assent, the NHS Data Authority will establish the Disease Monitoring Service as an operational division, appointing a Chief Epidemiologist and recruiting an initial team of no fewer than fifty data scientists, epidemiologists, and health informaticists. The Service will be operational within nine months, producing its first interim National Disease Map within twelve months.

Data pipeline.

The Service will draw on three primary data sources: the curated national dataset held by the NHS Data Authority (NHS3.2), UKHSA surveillance feeds, and ONS mortality and demographic data. The FHIR-compliant data architecture mandated by NHS3.1 will enable automated ingestion from primary and secondary care systems. The Disease Monitoring Service will not require clinicians to submit additional data returns. It will extract the intelligence from data that is already being captured.

First Workforce Alignment Report.

Within 18 months of Royal Assent, the Disease Monitoring Service will publish its first Workforce Alignment Report, identifying the top ten specialty-region combinations where the gap between disease burden and workforce capacity is widest. This report will directly inform the next round of training post allocations and will be used by the Treatment Coverage Commission established under NHS1 to refine the scope of NHS core services.

Waiting time target review.

Within 24 months, the Secretary of State will publish the first set of specialty-specific waiting time targets informed by Disease Monitoring Service data. The targets will be accompanied by a public methodology document showing exactly how disease prevalence, workforce capacity, and treatment complexity were used to derive each target. No target will be set without a credible workforce plan to achieve it.

##### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The NHS3 framework is built on the NHS Information Systems Act, a single piece of primary legislation introduced alongside the NHS Core Mission Act (NHS1), the NHS Workforce Act (NHS2), and the Tax Reset Act (E6) in the first King’s Speech. No additional Acts are required. All other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, or departmental action.

NHS Information Systems Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: NHS Digital Innovation Fund for tournament-style competitive procurement of next-generation backend systems, capitalized at no less than 500 million pounds. Mandatory HL7 FHIR R4 compliance for all new NHS digital systems from first April following Royal Assent, with 36-month transition for existing systems. National minimum cyber security standards as a condition of all NHS contracts, enforceable by the Health Standards Authority. NHS Data Architecture Standard mandating federated, FHIR-based data flows with the principle that data follows the patient. Formal designation of NHS patient data as a national asset. Establishment of the NHS Data Authority as statutory body for data curation, governance, and commercial licensing. Tiered access and pricing model with preferential rates for UK-headquartered companies. Patient Data Compact enshrining anonymisation, opt-out rights, transparency, and 25% revenue hypothecation. Revenue targets of 500 million pounds within three years, 1.5 billion within five years. Disease Monitoring Service for continuous national disease prevalence and incidence monitoring. Statutory linkage of Disease Monitoring Service data to medical training post allocations. Specialty-specific waiting time targets informed by disease burden, workforce capacity, and treatment complexity. Integration of UKHSA surveillance systems into unified national health surveillance architecture.

Delivered operationally: First tournament specification published within 90 days. FHIR compliance roadmap published within 60 days. Mandatory cyber security standards published within 120 days. NHS Data Authority board appointed within 90 days, operational within six months. First phase of data curation covering 40 million records completed within 12 months. First commercial data licences executed within 18 months. National public information campaign on data monetisation within 60 days. Disease Monitoring Service team recruited within 120 days, operational within nine months. First interim National Disease Map within 12 months. First Workforce Alignment Report within 18 months. First specialty-specific waiting time targets within 24 months.

##### Funding NHS3

The NHS3 programme is funded through four sources.

NHS Digital Innovation Fund.

The 500 million pound capitalisation is drawn from the existing NHS IT budget of 4.1 billion per year and the 3.4 billion earmarked for digital transformation. This is not additional spending. It is a redirection of existing spending away from fragmented local procurement and toward competitive national development. The tournament model is designed to produce better systems at lower total cost than the current approach, in which each trust procures independently and the NHS pays for hundreds of incompatible implementations of essentially the same functionality.

Efficiency savings from digital modernisation.

Digitally mature trusts operate approximately 13% more efficiently than their less mature peers. Applying even half of that efficiency gain across the entire trust estate, as the FHIR mandate and tournament-funded systems take effect, generates annual savings in the low billions. McKinsey’s analysis of the Federated Data Platform estimated system-wide value of 15 to 25 billion pounds per year from digital and data use-cases deployed at scale. Even a fraction of that figure more than pays for the investment.

Data monetisation revenue.

The NHS Data Authority’s commercial licensing programme is projected to generate 500 million pounds within three years and 1.5 billion within five. The first revenues will materialise within 18 months as commercial data access agreements are executed. This is a genuinely new revenue stream that does not exist today, generated from an asset the NHS already possesses.

Avoided costs from cyber resilience.

The WannaCry attack alone cost 92 million pounds. The Synnovis attack caused 16 weeks of disruption to London pathology services. Each major cyber incident imposes costs in cancelled procedures, diverted patients, staff overtime, system restoration, and reputational damage. The mandatory cyber security standards described in NHS3.1 are an investment that pays for itself by preventing incidents that currently impose costs of tens of millions per event.

NHS3 is the enabler. Without modern data infrastructure, the NHS Data Authority cannot curate the national dataset. Without the curated dataset, the Disease Monitoring Service cannot map prevalence. Without prevalence data, workforce planning remains guesswork. Without workforce planning, waiting times remain a political target rather than an operational output. NHS3 turns information from an administrative byproduct into the strategic asset that makes every other NHS reform measurable, accountable, and achievable.

#### NHS4. Procurement and Anti-Corruption Measures

Governing Principle

The NHS spends over 30 billion pounds a year through procurement, on clinical services, medicines, equipment, IT, building maintenance, catering, and cleaning. Of that, approximately 8 billion pounds is spent annually on medical equipment and consumables alone, from surgical gloves to prosthetic hips. A further 20 billion is spent on medicines and medical devices. The remainder covers facilities management, technology, consultancy, and everything else a system of 1.37 million employees needs to function. This is the largest single pool of public purchasing power in Europe. It should be a weapon. It is a wound.

The fundamental problem is that the NHS does not procure like a system. It procures like 200 separate organisations that happen to share a name. Lord Carter’s review in 2016 found staggering variation in the prices trusts paid for identical products: one hospital paying 5.44 pounds for a box of latex gloves while another paid 2.39 for the same product. A single pack of twelve bandages cost anywhere from 35 pence to 16.47 pounds depending on which trust was buying. A pack of 100 adhesive plasters ranged from 1.68 to 21.76 pounds. A sample of just 22 trusts revealed they used 30,000 suppliers, 20,000 different product brands, and more than 400,000 manufacturer product codes, with over 7,000 people authorised to place orders. The National Audit Office estimated in 2011 that at least 500 million pounds per year could be saved if trusts collaborated on purchasing. That was fourteen years ago. The waste continues.

NHS Supply Chain was created in 2019 to fix this. It was given a target of capturing 80% of the medical equipment and consumables market and delivering 2.4 billion pounds in savings by 2023/24. It has achieved neither. As of 2023/24, NHS Supply Chain’s market share was approximately 57% against a revised target of 62%. Trusts continue to spend approximately 3.4 billion pounds outside NHS Supply Chain. Customer satisfaction is in long-term decline, falling from 67% in 2021/22 to 54% in 2023/24. Over 70% of trusts reported using other supply routes because the products they needed were not available through Supply Chain. Orders through its eDirect system were delivered an average of 22 days late between June 2022 and March 2023. NHS Supply Chain claimed to have exceeded its 2.4 billion savings target, but neither NHS England nor the Department of Health validated these claims, and trusts themselves said they did not recognise the reported savings. The Public Accounts Committee described the situation bluntly: billions of pounds of spending power is not being harnessed.

The Private Finance Initiative offers the starkest illustration of procurement failure in NHS history. Over 700 PFI contracts were signed from the late 1990s, nominally delivering 13 billion pounds in capital investment. The total bill to the taxpayer will exceed 80 billion pounds. NHS trusts were paying 2.1 billion per year on PFI repayments in 2024, rising to over 2.5 billion by 2030. One hospital was charged 333 pounds to change a lightbulb. Another was charged over 5,000 pounds for a new sink. PFI hospitals were built on average with a quarter fewer beds than the facilities they replaced. Seven NHS trusts were spending more than 5% of their total revenue on PFI repayments. The scheme was scrapped in 2018, but the contracts remain, draining resources from patient care for decades to come. South Tees Hospitals Trust’s PFI contract for James Cook University Hospital will cost approximately 1.8 billion pounds over its lifetime for a hospital that cost 151 million to build, roughly twelve times the initial investment. The trust’s annual report identifies the PFI as the largest single contributor to its structural deficit.

The COVID-19 PPE procurement scandal demonstrated what happens when weak procurement governance meets political pressure. The Department of Health spent 13.1 billion pounds on almost 38 billion items of PPE. Some 394 contracts worth 7.9 billion were awarded through emergency procurement routes, largely to new or unknown suppliers. The VIP lane, through which suppliers were referred by government officials, ministers, and MPs, accounted for 115 contracts worth 3.8 billion. The High Court ruled the VIP lane unlawful. Contracts awarded through it were on average 80% more expensive than those procured through standard routes, with some agreed at more than four times the average unit price. An estimated 8.7 billion in PPE was written off. A quarter of the money spent through the VIP lane went on equipment that was not fit for purpose. The Good Law Project calculated that VIP lane contracts were inflated by 925 million pounds. As of mid-2025, only 70 million of an estimated 324 million lost to fraud had been recovered.

The individual cases are instructive. PPE Medpro, a company owned by the husband of Conservative Baroness Michelle Mone, was awarded over 200 million pounds in contracts through the VIP lane when the company was just weeks old. Meller Designs, a fashion company owned by a Conservative donor, supplied medical gowns at 12.64 pounds each against an average price of 5.87, and 8.46 million pounds of its equipment was unusable. Its profits rose from 143,000 to over 13.2 million in a single year, an increase of approximately 9,000%. The logistics firm Uniserve saw its profits increase by over 500% in the year to June 2020. A Transparency International UK study found that over 135 contracts worth more than 15 billion pounds raised red flags for possible corruption, accounting for nearly a third of pandemic-related spending. The National Crime Agency is separately investigating possible criminal offences. In September 2025, the government won its legal claim against PPE Medpro for the return of millions paid for pandemic PPE. This was not an aberration. It was the predictable consequence of a system with no mandatory central purchasing, no price benchmarking, no transparency requirements, and no meaningful anti-corruption enforcement in procurement.

Medicines procurement operates through a parallel system that is equally opaque. Total NHS spending on medicines, appliances, and medical devices was 20.9 billion pounds in 2024/25. Under the Voluntary Scheme for Branded Medicines Pricing, Access and Growth, pharmaceutical companies repay revenue above a capped spending limit. The 2025 repayment rate for newer medicines reached 22.9%, the highest in the scheme’s history, with industry paying approximately 3.5 billion back to the government. Following the December 2025 UK-US pharmaceuticals trade deal, the 2026 rate was reduced to 14.5%, and the NICE cost-effectiveness threshold was raised for the first time since 1999, from a range of 20,000 to 30,000 pounds per QALY to 25,000 to 35,000 pounds per QALY. But the rebate mechanism is structurally opaque: repayments flow to the Department of Health and Social Care’s central budget, not to individual trust budgets where the medicines are actually consumed. Trusts see costs rising by 44.3% over four years while the offsetting rebates remain invisible in their accounts. Meanwhile, generic medicine pricing remains vulnerable to exploitation, as the Competition and Markets Authority’s May 2025 fine against Advanz for excessive pricing of liothyronine demonstrates. Medicine supply disruption notifications increased approximately 20% in 2024, to over 1,900 in a single year. The system manages aggregate pharmaceutical spending at the national level but provides no trust-level transparency, no real-time price benchmarking, and no mechanism for clinicians to understand the true net cost of what they prescribe.

The supply chain itself is structurally vulnerable. The Centre for Long-Term Resilience reported in March 2025 that the UK is perilously vulnerable to disruptions in the supply of critical medical countermeasures, including antimicrobials, vaccines, and diagnostic tools, and is less prepared than it was at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. UK life sciences manufacturing volumes declined between 2009 and 2021. The country is heavily reliant on China for active pharmaceutical ingredients, including the API for gentamicin, a vital antibiotic. During the pandemic, NHS nurses were famously forced to use bin bags as improvised PPE because international suppliers prioritised their own domestic markets. The lesson is not subtle: in a crisis, countries that do not manufacture critical supplies domestically do not have critical supplies. The NHS’s procurement system must be restructured to ensure that this dependency is reduced rather than entrenched.

The Procurement Act 2023, which came into force on 24 February 2025, represents the first post-Brexit overhaul of UK public procurement law. It consolidates previous regulations into a single framework and introduces greater flexibility through its competitive flexible procedure. But flexibility without accountability is an invitation to abuse. The Act does not mandate central purchasing for the NHS. It does not cap prices. It does not create a transparent price index that the public can scrutinise. It does not address the 30-year legacy of PFI. And it explicitly excludes healthcare service procurements, which operate under a separate Provider Selection Regime. NHS4 fills these gaps. It creates the institutional architecture to make the NHS’s 30 billion pound annual procurement spend work for patients rather than for intermediaries, consultants, and politically connected suppliers.

##### NHS4.1: End Procurement Abuse

The Problem

The NHS procurement system fails in three distinct ways. First, it is fragmented: 200 trusts procuring independently, using 30,000 suppliers and 400,000 product codes, with no national price discipline and no consequence for overpaying. Second, it is rigid where it should be flexible and flexible where it should be rigid: the rules make it difficult to move quickly on technology procurement where speed matters, while making it trivially easy to waste money on commodities where prices should be nationally fixed. Third, it has no effective anti-corruption mechanism: the PPE scandal proved that billions can flow to politically connected suppliers with no prior experience, at inflated prices, for products that do not work, with no one held accountable until years after the damage is done.

The fragmentation is structural. Each NHS trust is a legally independent body with its own board, its own procurement team, its own supplier relationships, and its own budget. Foundation trusts have even greater autonomy. The result is that the world’s fifth-largest employer purchases basic consumables in the same way a collection of independent corner shops would: each negotiating separately, each paying a different price, each maintaining separate supply relationships with overlapping suppliers. A sample of 22 trusts revealed 652 different types of surgical and examination gloves, 1,751 different cannulas, and 260 different types of administration sets. This is not clinical choice. This is procurement chaos masquerading as local autonomy. No clinician needs 652 types of gloves. The variation exists because no one has ever been required to rationalise it, and no one has ever been penalised for the cost of failing to do so.

Lord Carter’s review identified 700 million pounds in potential procurement savings from eliminating price variation alone, on top of 1 billion from estates and facilities management. The National Audit Office has consistently found that the NHS is not making the most of its spending power. NHS Supply Chain’s transformation programme, estimated to cost 144 million pounds, is pursuing a new savings target of just 1 billion from January 2022 to 2030. As of October 2023, it had achieved only 230 million against a target of 280.1 million. This is inadequate. The system does not need marginal improvement. It needs structural replacement of the incentives, institutions, and rules that govern how the NHS spends public money.

The current system actively punishes cooperation. NHS Supply Chain’s operating costs are funded through a top-slice of trust allocations, meaning every trust pays for the system whether it uses it or not. But trusts can and do use NHS Supply Chain’s negotiated prices as leverage to secure discounts from alternative suppliers, free-riding on the national bargaining power while undermining it. When trusts bypass Supply Chain, they reduce its market share, which reduces its bargaining power, which makes its prices less competitive, which encourages more trusts to bypass it. This is a classic collective action problem. The solution is not better persuasion. It is mandatory participation.

Technology procurement presents a specific failure. The NHS’s catastrophic experience with NPfIT, described in NHS3, was partly a procurement failure: a single contract worth over 10 billion pounds awarded through a centralised process that produced the wrong systems for the wrong users at the wrong price. The current procurement framework, despite the Procurement Act 2023’s flexibility provisions, still channels technology acquisitions through processes designed for commodity purchasing. Buying an MRI scanner and buying a next-generation AI-assisted diagnostic platform are fundamentally different activities. The first is a commodity with known specifications. The second is an innovation bet that requires iterative evaluation, clinical testing, and staged deployment. The procurement rules should reflect this distinction. Currently, they do not. The Procurement Act’s competitive flexible procedure offers some latitude, but it does not create the staged evaluation, parallel development, and clinical pilot model that technology procurement requires. The Technology Procurement Protocol established under this Act fills that gap.

The absence of anti-corruption enforcement is the most damaging failure of all. The COVID-19 PPE experience demonstrated that when an emergency arises, the NHS procurement system has no institutional immune response to political interference. The VIP lane was not created by rogue officials. It was created by the system’s design: a procurement architecture in which informal referrals, ministerial involvement, and political connections could bypass due diligence because there was no statutory prohibition on such interference, no criminal sanction for self-dealing, and no independent enforcement body with the power to investigate and void contracts in real time. The Procurement Act 2023 introduces exclusion and debarment provisions for suppliers who have committed offences, but it does not address the demand side: the officials, ministers, and political operatives who steered contracts to favoured suppliers. NHS4 addresses both sides of the corruption equation.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Procurement and Anti-Corruption Act will establish:

- a) The NHS National Procurement Authority. The Act will create a statutory body responsible for all procurement of common items across the NHS. The Authority will replace NHS Supply Chain’s current voluntary model with a mandatory national purchasing system for all items designated as common goods: products that are functionally interchangeable across trusts, including surgical consumables, diagnostic supplies, office materials, cleaning products, catering supplies, standard pharmaceuticals, and non-specialist medical equipment. Trusts will be prohibited from procuring common goods outside the Authority except where the Authority certifies that it cannot meet a specific clinical need. The Authority will be required to achieve a minimum market share of 90% for common goods within three years of establishment. For every common item, the Authority will negotiate a single national price through competitive tender. Trusts that procure outside the Authority without certification will have the excess cost deducted from their annual allocation. This is the end of the 200-trust procurement free-for-all. One buyer, one price, one system.
- b) The Technology Procurement Exemption. The Act will create a separate procurement pathway for technology and innovation. Acquisitions designated as technology procurement, defined as systems or services that are novel, require clinical evaluation, or involve iterative development, will be exempt from standard competitive tender requirements. Instead, they will be governed by a Technology Procurement Protocol designed around the tournament-style model established in NHS3.1. The Protocol will permit staged funding, parallel development tracks, clinical pilot evaluation, and iterative specification refinement. The objective is to allow the NHS to move at the speed of technology rather than the speed of procurement compliance. The Health Standards Authority established under NHS2 will have oversight of the Technology Procurement Protocol, ensuring that the exemption is used for genuine innovation and not as a loophole for avoiding competitive discipline on commodity purchases.
- c) Mandatory anti-corruption provisions. The Act will make it a criminal offence for any person involved in NHS procurement to award, influence, or facilitate the award of a contract to a supplier in which they have an undisclosed financial interest, or to a supplier that has been referred through an informal channel outside the Authority’s standard procedures. The Act will establish a Procurement Integrity Unit within the Health Standards Authority, staffed by forensic accountants, procurement specialists, and former law enforcement officers, with the power to investigate suspected procurement fraud, corruption, or abuse of process. The Unit will have statutory access to all procurement records held by trusts, integrated care systems, and the Authority itself. Any contract awarded in breach of the Act’s anti-corruption provisions will be voidable at the direction of the Unit, with personal liability attaching to the individuals responsible. The VIP lane was not just a scandal. It was the symptom of a system with no enforcement. This provision creates enforcement.
- d) UK manufacturing preference for critical supplies. The Act will establish a statutory preference for UK-manufactured products in all NHS procurement of items designated as critical to supply chain resilience. These items, to be defined by regulation and reviewed annually, will include personal protective equipment, basic surgical consumables, essential pharmaceuticals and active pharmaceutical ingredients, diagnostic reagents, and sterile single-use devices. For critical items, UK-manufactured products will receive a preference of up to 20% on price in competitive evaluations, meaning a UK supplier bidding at up to 120% of the lowest foreign bid will be preferred. This preference is explicitly designed to rebuild domestic manufacturing capacity in the categories where the COVID-19 pandemic exposed the most dangerous supply chain vulnerabilities. The NHS was unable to source adequate PPE during the pandemic because the UK had offshored production of critical medical supplies. The Centre for Long-Term Resilience found in March 2025 that the UK is perilously vulnerable to supply disruptions and less prepared than it was before COVID-19. UK life sciences manufacturing volumes declined between 2009 and 2021. The country is heavily reliant on China for active pharmaceutical ingredients, including the API for gentamicin. The Act ensures that this structural vulnerability is addressed not through exhortation but through the market mechanism: a guaranteed domestic demand signal that makes UK manufacturing investment commercially viable.
- e) Mandatory supply chain resilience standards. The Act will require the NHS National Procurement Authority to maintain, for every critical supply item, a minimum of three qualified suppliers, of which at least one must have UK-based manufacturing capacity. The Authority will maintain a strategic buffer stock of no fewer than 90 days’ supply for all critical items, held in NHS-controlled storage facilities. The buffer stock requirement replaces the ad hoc pandemic stockpile approach, which the COVID-19 experience demonstrated was inadequate. The Authority will publish an annual Supply Chain Resilience Report identifying single points of failure, geographic concentration risks, and recommended diversification actions. Where a critical supply item is sourced from fewer than three suppliers, or where more than 50% of supply originates from a single country, the Authority will implement a diversification plan within twelve months.

OPERATIONAL

NHS National Procurement Authority establishment.

Within 90 days of Royal Assent, the Secretary of State will appoint the founding board of the Authority, comprising procurement specialists, supply chain experts, clinicians, and representatives from UK manufacturing. The Authority will absorb NHS Supply Chain’s existing functions, contracts, and staff within six months. The first list of common goods subject to mandatory national purchasing will be published within 120 days, prioritising the product categories identified by Lord Carter as having the highest price variation.

Technology Procurement Protocol.

Within 60 days of Royal Assent, the Health Standards Authority will publish the Technology Procurement Protocol, defining the criteria for technology designation, the staged evaluation process, and the governance requirements for technology procurements. The Protocol will be developed in consultation with NHS trust CIOs, the NHS Digital Innovation Fund (NHS3.1), and the Technology and Clinical Research directorate.

Procurement Integrity Unit.

Within 90 days, the Health Standards Authority will establish the Procurement Integrity Unit and begin retrospective review of all contracts valued at over 10 million pounds awarded in the previous five years. The Unit will publish its first annual report on procurement integrity within twelve months, including any enforcement actions taken.

PFI legacy.

Within 180 days, the Department of Health will publish a comprehensive audit of all remaining PFI contracts, including the total lifetime cost, the annual payment, the remaining term, and the estimated cost of early termination for each contract. The audit will inform a PFI exit strategy identifying contracts where early termination or renegotiation would deliver net savings to the NHS, prioritising the contracts where PFI repayments exceed 5% of trust revenue. The seven trusts currently exceeding the 5% threshold will be assessed first. For each, the Department will calculate the net present value of continuing the contract versus early termination, including any break-clause penalties, residual maintenance liability, and alternative capital financing costs. Where early termination delivers a positive net present value within ten years, the Department will pursue termination using the break clauses embedded in the original contracts. Where break clauses are commercially unviable, the Department will explore compulsory purchase of the PFI special purpose vehicle’s equity interest using powers to be established under the Act, modelled on the IPPR’s proposed right-to-enfranchisement for PFI assets.

Anti-corruption training.

Within 120 days, the Department will mandate completion of a procurement integrity training programme for every NHS employee with procurement authority above 50,000 pounds. The programme will be developed by the Procurement Integrity Unit and will cover conflict of interest disclosure, whistleblowing procedures, the criminal liability provisions of the Act, and case studies drawn from the COVID-19 PPE procurement failures. Completion will be a condition of procurement authority, reviewed annually.

UK manufacturing development.

Within 12 months, the NHS National Procurement Authority will publish a UK Manufacturing Development Plan identifying the product categories where domestic production capacity is most urgently needed, the current gap between NHS demand and UK manufacturing output, and the investment required to close that gap. The Plan will be developed in consultation with the Department for Business and Trade, UK manufacturers, and the trade unions representing manufacturing workers. The 20% price preference for critical supplies will take effect from the date the common goods list is published, creating an immediate market signal for UK manufacturers to invest in production capacity.

##### NHS4.2: Price Monitoring and Cost Discipline

The Problem

The NHS has no transparent, publicly available system for tracking what it pays for goods and services over time. It is the largest single purchaser of healthcare products in Europe, spending approximately 30 billion pounds per year through procurement, and it cannot tell the public whether prices are going up or down, which trusts are paying the most, or whether the system as a whole is getting better value for money. This is extraordinary. Every household in Britain can compare the price of a pint of milk at different supermarkets. The NHS cannot compare the price of a box of surgical gloves across its own trusts.

Lord Carter recommended a purchasing price index in 2016, starting with a basket of around 100 products, with monthly trust-level reporting and NHS Improvement holding trusts to account on performance. The index was partially implemented but never became a binding instrument of cost discipline. Trusts are still free to pay whatever they negotiate locally. NHS England makes procurement data available to trusts but relies on them to analyse it and change their practices voluntarily. Despite NHS England’s central role, it does not use this data to systematically challenge trusts as to why they do not purchase more efficiently. The Public Accounts Committee noted that NHS England is not in a position to mandate that trusts always use NHS Supply Chain and does not consider that it can provide more funding to accelerate the transformation.

The consequences of price opacity are compounding. Without transparent benchmarking, trusts have no way of knowing whether they are getting a good deal. Without mandatory compliance, trusts that negotiate locally may appear to achieve savings for themselves while undermining the collective purchasing power that would benefit the system. The NAO noted that some trusts use NHS Supply Chain’s negotiated prices as leverage to secure discounts from alternative suppliers, a practice that generates savings for individual trusts at the expense of the national system. The incentive structure is backwards: trusts are rewarded for breaking ranks and penalised for cooperating. The NHS Price Index proposed below inverts this incentive structure by making price performance visible, comparable, and consequential.

Medicines procurement presents parallel challenges. Total NHS spending on medicines, appliances, and medical devices reached 20.9 billion pounds in 2024/25. The Voluntary Scheme for Branded Medicines Pricing, Access and Growth caps aggregate branded medicine spending, with pharmaceutical companies repaying revenue above the cap. The 2025 repayment rate for newer medicines reached 22.9%, the highest ever, with industry paying approximately 3.5 billion back to the government. But the rebate system is opaque: rebates flow primarily to the Department of Health, not directly to NHS front-line budgets. Individual trust-level medicine costs rose by 44.3% between 2019/20 and 2023/24, even though much of the increase was nominally offset by rebates that trusts never see. Meanwhile, the Competition and Markets Authority has fined pharmaceutical companies for excessive pricing of generic medicines, including a fine for the company Advanz over the pricing of the thyroid medicine liothyronine in May 2025. Medicine supply disruption notifications increased by approximately 20% in 2024 compared to 2022 and 2023, with over 1,900 notifications in a single year. The system manages medicines prices at the macro level but has no mechanism for real-time, trust-level price transparency and cost discipline.

The international evidence is clear. Every comparable health system that has implemented centralised purchasing with transparent price benchmarking has achieved significant savings.
