The Danish AMGROS model, which centralises all hospital pharmaceutical procurement through a single buyer, consistently achieves lower unit prices than the UK. The Australian Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme publishes complete price transparency. The Swedish system uses mandatory national tendering for common supplies. The NHS is an outlier: it is the largest single-payer health system that still permits individual hospitals to procure independently for commodity products. This is not local discretion. It is local waste.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Procurement and Anti-Corruption Act will establish:

- a) The NHS Price Index. The Act will require the NHS National Procurement Authority to create and maintain a comprehensive, publicly accessible price index covering every product and service purchased by the NHS. The Index will begin with the top 1,000 products by volume and expenditure, expanding to cover all procurement categories within three years. For every item in the Index, the Authority will publish the national benchmark price, the price paid by each trust, and the percentage variance from benchmark, updated quarterly. The Index will be published online in machine-readable format and will be accessible to any member of the public. Trust boards will be required to report quarterly on their procurement performance against the Index, with trusts in the bottom decile required to submit remediation plans to the Health Standards Authority. This is not a league table for internal management. It is a public accountability tool that makes every pound of NHS procurement spending visible and comparable.
- b) Maximum price orders. The Act will empower the Secretary of State to issue Maximum Price Orders for any product or service category where the Index reveals persistent overcharging. A Maximum Price Order will set a ceiling price that no trust or supplier may exceed for a defined product or category. The mechanism is simple: the NHS is a monopsony buyer for most of the products it consumes. It should use that power. Where the Index shows that trusts are routinely paying more than 150% of the benchmark price for a product, a Maximum Price Order will cap the price at no more than 110% of benchmark. Suppliers that cannot supply at the capped price will be replaced. The power exists implicitly in the NHS’s market position. The Act makes it explicit, enforceable, and transparent.
- c) The Procurement Oversight Board. The Act will establish a permanent Procurement Oversight Board, constituted as an independent statutory body with representation from clinical staff, procurement professionals, patient advocates, and independent economists. The Board will have three functions. First, it will review and approve all NHS contracts valued at over 50 million pounds before they are executed, with the power to block contracts that do not demonstrate value for money. Second, it will conduct annual reviews of the top 100 supplier relationships by value, publishing its findings on whether each relationship delivers competitive pricing and adequate service. Third, it will monitor compliance with the NHS Price Index and recommend enforcement action where trusts or suppliers persistently fail to meet benchmark standards. The Board will report directly to Parliament, not to the Department of Health, ensuring that its oversight function is independent of the department it is scrutinising.

The Board’s independence is the critical design feature. Previous procurement oversight has been conducted by bodies that report to NHS England or to the Department of Health, both of which have institutional incentives to minimise the visibility of procurement failures. The Procurement Oversight Board reports to the Health Select Committee and the Public Accounts Committee, creating a direct accountability link between procurement decisions and parliamentary scrutiny. The Board’s annual report will include a named assessment of every contract over 50 million pounds reviewed in the preceding year, the Board’s recommendation, and whether that recommendation was followed. Where a contract is awarded against the Board’s recommendation, the responsible official must provide a written justification to Parliament. This does not give the Board a veto. It gives it a voice that cannot be silenced by institutional convenience.

- d) Medicine price transparency. The Act will require that all VPAG rebates attributable to medicines consumed by individual trusts be transparently allocated and reported at trust level in annual accounts. Trusts will know exactly how much they spent on medicines, how much was rebated, and what their net cost was, relative to other trusts and relative to the national benchmark. The Act will further require NICE to publish, alongside each technology appraisal, the expected net cost to the NHS per patient after rebates, so that prescribers and trust pharmacists can make informed decisions based on the true rather than the headline price. Where the Competition and Markets Authority identifies excessive pricing of generic medicines, the Act will empower the Secretary of State to impose interim price caps pending full investigation, preventing pharmaceutical companies from profiting from supply constraints while regulatory proceedings are ongoing.

OPERATIONAL

NHS Price Index launch.

Within 120 days of Royal Assent, the NHS National Procurement Authority will publish the first edition of the NHS Price Index, covering the top 500 products by volume. The Index will expand to 1,000 products within six months and to all procured categories within three years. The Authority will establish a dedicated analytics team to maintain the Index and produce quarterly performance reports for every trust.

First Maximum Price Orders.

Within six months, the Secretary of State will issue the first Maximum Price Orders targeting the ten product categories with the highest demonstrated price variance. The orders will be informed by the first Price Index data and will be subject to a 30-day consultation period before taking effect.

Procurement Oversight Board.

Within 90 days, the Secretary of State will appoint the founding members of the Board and publish its terms of reference. The Board will be operational within six months and will conduct its first contract reviews within nine months. All contracts valued at over 50 million pounds that are in the pipeline at the time of the Board’s establishment will be submitted for review before execution.

Medicine price transparency.

Within 12 months, NHS England will publish the first trust-level medicine cost reports, including VPAG rebate allocations. The data will be published alongside the NHS Price Index, creating a single public resource for understanding what the NHS pays for everything it buys. NICE will be directed to include net-cost-after-rebate estimates in all new technology appraisals from the date of Royal Assent. The Act will also require pharmaceutical companies to provide quarterly sales and pricing data directly to the NHS National Procurement Authority, enabling real-time monitoring of pricing trends and early identification of potential supply constraints or price exploitation.

Generic medicines price monitoring.

Within six months, the NHS National Procurement Authority will establish a dedicated generic medicines monitoring function, working in coordination with the Competition and Markets Authority. The function will track prices of all off-patent medicines consumed by the NHS, flag anomalous price increases within 30 days of occurrence, and refer suspected excessive pricing to the CMA for investigation. Where an interim price cap is imposed by the Secretary of State pending CMA investigation, the Authority will identify and qualify alternative suppliers to ensure continuity of supply at the capped price.

Procurement workforce development.

Within 12 months, the Authority will publish a Procurement Workforce Strategy identifying the skills, training, and career pathways required to professionalise NHS procurement. The strategy will address the finding in Lord Carter’s review that most trusts lack basic procurement competence, with purchase order compliance as low as 30% in some trusts against a benchmark of 80%. The strategy will establish mandatory professional qualifications for senior procurement roles, create a graduate procurement training scheme modelled on the NHS Graduate Management Training Scheme, and set a target of reducing the number of individuals authorised to place purchase orders by at least 50% from the 7,000-plus identified in the Carter review sample, concentrating procurement authority in qualified professionals.

##### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The NHS4 framework is built on the NHS Procurement and Anti-Corruption Act, a single piece of primary legislation introduced alongside the NHS Core Mission Act (NHS1), the NHS Workforce Act (NHS2), the NHS Information Systems Act (NHS3), and the Tax Reset Act (E6) in the first King’s Speech.

###### NHS Procurement and Anti-Corruption Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: NHS National Procurement Authority as statutory body with mandatory purchasing powers for common goods, replacing NHS Supply Chain’s voluntary model. Minimum 90% market share target for common goods within three years. Technology Procurement Exemption creating a separate pathway for innovation procurement outside standard competitive tender, governed by Technology Procurement Protocol. Criminal offence for undisclosed conflicts of interest or informal referral channels in NHS procurement. Procurement Integrity Unit within the Health Standards Authority with statutory investigation powers and contract voiding authority. UK manufacturing preference of up to 20% on price for critical supply chain items. Mandatory supply chain resilience standards requiring minimum three qualified suppliers for critical items and 90-day strategic buffer stocks. NHS Price Index as mandatory, publicly accessible, trust-level price transparency tool. Maximum Price Orders empowering the Secretary of State to cap prices where persistent overcharging is demonstrated. Procurement Oversight Board as independent statutory body with contract review powers for all contracts over 50 million pounds, reporting to Parliament. Medicine price transparency requiring trust-level VPAG rebate allocation and NICE net-cost reporting. PFI compulsory purchase powers for early termination of bad-value contracts.

Delivered operationally: Procurement Authority board appointed within 90 days, absorbing NHS Supply Chain within six months. First common goods list published within 120 days. Technology Procurement Protocol published within 60 days. Procurement Integrity Unit established within 90 days, beginning retrospective contract review. Anti-corruption training mandatory for all staff with procurement authority over 50,000 pounds within 120 days. PFI contract audit published within 180 days with exit strategy for contracts exceeding 5% of trust revenue. NHS Price Index first edition (500 products) within 120 days, expanding to 1,000 within six months. First Maximum Price Orders within six months. Procurement Oversight Board operational within six months, first reviews within nine months. Trust-level medicine cost reports within 12 months. Generic medicines price monitoring function within six months. Procurement Workforce Strategy published within 12 months. UK Manufacturing Development Plan published within 12 months. Annual Supply Chain Resilience Report from year one.

##### Funding NHS4

NHS4 is not a spending programme. It is a savings programme. Every provision in this document is designed to reduce the amount the NHS spends on procurement and to redirect the savings to front-line care.

Price standardisation savings. Lord Carter estimated 700 million pounds per year in savings from eliminating procurement price variation alone. The NAO estimated at least 500 million per year from collaborative purchasing. The NHS National Procurement Authority’s mandatory purchasing model, combined with the NHS Price Index and Maximum Price Orders, targets the full Carter saving of 700 million per year within three years, rising to 1 billion per year as the Index expands to cover all procurement categories and the Authority achieves its 90% market share target.

Corruption prevention. The PPE scandal cost the taxpayer an estimated 8.7 billion pounds in write-offs. The Procurement Integrity Unit’s mandate to investigate and void contracts awarded in breach of anti-corruption provisions is designed to prevent recurrence. Even preventing a fraction of the waste seen during COVID-19 would save billions. The Unit’s operating cost, estimated at 20 to 30 million pounds per year, is negligible relative to the sums at risk.

PFI renegotiation. NHS trusts are paying over 2 billion per year in PFI repayments for assets that cost 13 billion to build but will cost 80 billion to finance. The PFI audit and exit strategy mandated by NHS4.1 will identify contracts where early termination or renegotiation delivers net savings. IPPR has proposed a right-to-buy scheme allowing trusts to bring bad-value contracts into public ownership through legislated enfranchisement. Even modest renegotiation of the worst contracts, those where annual payments exceed 5% of trust revenue, could release hundreds of millions per year for patient care.

UK manufacturing investment. The 20% price preference for UK-manufactured critical supplies represents a short-term cost premium that is offset by supply chain resilience. The UK’s inability to source PPE domestically during the pandemic resulted in emergency procurement at prices that were 80% or more above market rate. A 20% domestic preference on an ongoing basis is dramatically cheaper than an 80% crisis premium in an emergency. It also creates a domestic industrial base that generates UK employment, tax revenue, and manufacturing capability. The NHS spends approximately 8 billion per year on medical equipment and consumables. If critical supplies represent even 20% of this total, the 20% preference amounts to a maximum annual premium of approximately 320 million pounds, a premium that is entirely offset by the avoided cost of a single pandemic-scale supply crisis and by the economic multiplier effects of domestic manufacturing investment.

Procurement workforce professionalisation. The investment in procurement training, career pathways, and professional qualifications represents a small cost with a large return. The Carter review found that savings of 900,000 to 1.5 million per trust per year were achievable simply by buying at the lowest available price. Across 200 trusts, that represents 180 to 300 million per year in savings from price discipline alone, before any benefit from reduced product variation, consolidated ordering, or improved contract management. A professional procurement workforce, properly trained and properly incentivised, pays for itself many times over.

NHS4 is the accountability architecture that ensures every other NHS reform delivers value for money. Without transparent pricing, any amount of additional NHS funding will be absorbed by inflated supplier margins. Without anti-corruption enforcement, procurement will remain vulnerable to the political capture demonstrated during COVID-19. Without mandatory national purchasing, 200 trusts will continue to pay 200 different prices for the same products. NHS4 turns procurement from a cost centre into a strategic capability, and makes the savings visible, measurable, and irreversible.

##### Cross-References to Other NHS Framework Documents

NHS1 (Back to Basics Campaign): The Treatment Coverage Commission’s evidence-based scope of NHS services determines what the NHS needs to procure. The 70% revenue ring-fence for front-line services requires procurement savings to flow to patient care, not to be absorbed by administrative overhead.

NHS2 (Workforce Crisis Management): The Health Standards Authority created under NHS2 gains procurement oversight functions under NHS4, housing both the Procurement Integrity Unit and the Technology Procurement Protocol governance. The 40% documentation reduction target is enabled by digital procurement systems that reduce administrative burden on clinical staff.

NHS3 (Information Systems and Data Capitalisation): The tournament-style funding model established in NHS3.1 is the template for the Technology Procurement Protocol. The FHIR-compliant data architecture enables automated procurement analytics and the NHS Price Index. The NHS Data Authority’s commercial licensing revenue provides an additional funding source for procurement infrastructure investment.

NHS5–NHS7 (forthcoming): NHS4 provides the procurement discipline required for NHS6 infrastructure and capital investment programmes, ensuring that future hospital building avoids the PFI trap. NHS7 social care procurement will be subject to the same Price Index and anti-corruption provisions, extending procurement accountability across the health and care system.

##### Conclusion: The End of Discretionary Waste

The NHS procurement system has been studied, reviewed, audited, reformed, and restructured continuously for over two decades. Lord Carter’s review in 2016 identified the problems. The creation of NHS Supply Chain in 2019 attempted to address them. The National Audit Office found in 2024 that the problems persist. The Public Accounts Committee found the same. The COVID-19 pandemic revealed that the system was not merely inefficient but structurally vulnerable to political capture and corruption on a scale that cost the taxpayer billions.

The pattern is familiar: a report identifies waste, a reform is announced, the reform is implemented voluntarily, trusts choose not to participate, the waste continues, and the next report identifies the same waste again. This cycle continues because every previous reform has been permissive. NHS Supply Chain was designed to be so compelling that trusts would choose to use it. They did not. The Procurement Act 2023 offers flexibility. Flexibility without consequences is indulgence.

NHS4 breaks this cycle by making the right procurement behaviour mandatory rather than optional, transparent rather than opaque, and enforceable rather than aspirational. The NHS National Procurement Authority replaces voluntary aggregation with mandatory national purchasing. The NHS Price Index replaces private negotiation with public accountability. Maximum Price Orders replace moral persuasion with legal enforcement. The Procurement Integrity Unit replaces retrospective auditing with real-time investigation. The UK manufacturing preference replaces reactive crisis purchasing with proactive supply chain resilience. And the Procurement Oversight Board replaces internal management with independent parliamentary scrutiny.

The sums involved are enormous. Over 30 billion pounds passes through NHS procurement every year. The demonstrated price variation across trusts is at least 10% on average, and over 50% on thousands of individual items. PFI contracts are draining over 2 billion per year for assets that were built for a fraction of the repayment cost. The PPE scandal lost 8.7 billion in a single episode. Even conservative estimates of the savings achievable through the measures in this document exceed 1 billion per year within three years, rising to 2 to 3 billion per year as the Price Index, Maximum Price Orders, and mandatory national purchasing take full effect.

To put this in perspective: 1 billion pounds per year in procurement savings is equivalent to the annual salary cost of approximately 20,000 nurses. Two billion per year is equivalent to building a new district general hospital every year. Three billion per year is equivalent to the entire annual budget of the NHS cancer drugs fund, the mental health investment standard, and the community diagnostic centres programme combined. These are not abstract numbers. They are the clinical capacity that the NHS is currently sacrificing to procurement waste, price variation, corruption, and institutional inertia. Every year that these reforms are delayed is another year in which billions of pounds that should be funding patient care are instead funding supplier margins, PFI interest payments, and the administrative overhead of 200 separate procurement operations doing the same job 200 different ways.

These are not theoretical savings. They are money that is currently being spent unnecessarily: on products that cost more than they should, on suppliers that deliver less than they promise, on intermediaries that add cost without adding value, on PFI contracts that were structured to benefit investors rather than patients, and on a procurement culture that treats waste as an unavoidable feature of public service rather than as a failure of institutional design. NHS4 treats it as a failure of institutional design and provides the institutional redesign to fix it.

Every pound saved through better procurement is a pound that can be spent on patient care. Every corrupt contract prevented is a contract that can be awarded to a supplier that delivers. Every trust that buys at the national benchmark price rather than at a locally inflated price is a trust with more money for nurses, doctors, beds, and equipment. Procurement is not a back-office function. It is the mechanism through which 30 billion pounds of public money is converted into patient care. NHS4 ensures that this mechanism works.

#### NHS5. Public Health for the 21st Century

Governing Principle

The NHS was designed to treat illness. It was not designed to prevent it. This is its most consequential design flaw. For every pound the NHS spends on treatment, it spends approximately two pence on prevention. The public health grant to local authorities, which funds the majority of preventive health services in England, was 3.6 billion pounds in 2024/25, equivalent to just 2.2% of the NHS England budget. Since 2015/16, this grant has been cut by 26% in real terms per person. The Health Foundation estimates that restoring it to 2015/16 levels would require an additional 1 billion pounds per year. Preventive spending on children’s services has collapsed from 4.2 billion in 2009/10 to less than 900 million in 2023/24. The most deprived areas, which need prevention most, have suffered the deepest cuts. This is not a health policy. It is a policy for generating patients.

The consequences are written in the data. Life expectancy improvements in England have stalled. Male life expectancy at birth is now 3.7 years lower than it would be if pre-2012 trends had continued. Healthy life expectancy, the number of years a person can expect to live in good health, is approximately 61.5 years for men and 61.9 years for women. But this national average conceals a chasm of inequality. In the most deprived areas of England, men can expect only 52.3 years in good health. In the least deprived areas, the figure is 70.9 years, a gap of 18.6 years. For women, the gap is 20.2 years. The difference in healthy life expectancy between the most and least deprived areas has grown by over 20% since 2011. Healthy life expectancy has fallen in 87% of local authority areas since 2017/19 and has not recovered to pre-pandemic levels. The state pension age is rising to 67 from 2026, but in the most deprived areas, poor health begins in the early fifties. Millions of people are being asked to work for fifteen years after their health has already failed.

The three principal drivers of preventable disease in England are diet, tobacco, and alcohol. They are not mysteries. They are not contested. They are the subjects of decades of research, hundreds of reports, and virtually no structural intervention.

Obesity and excess weight cost the UK economy approximately 126 billion pounds per year. This includes 12 billion to the NHS, 31 billion in lost productivity, 71 billion in reduced quality of life, and 10.5 billion in informal care costs. Nearly one in three adults in England lives with obesity. Over 23% of children aged 10 to 11 are obese. The prevalence is highest in the most deprived areas, where the cost per 1,000 people is approximately 440,000 pounds compared to 360,000 in the least deprived areas. If obesity and excess weight fell by 5% each year for five years, reducing prevalence from 32% to 25% by 2030, the UK would see productivity gains worth billions. Instead, obesity rates have doubled over the past thirty years and costs are projected to reach 150 billion per year by 2035.

Smoking costs society in England 43.7 billion pounds per year through lost productivity and health and social care costs, rising to 78.3 billion when the cost of early deaths is included. In 2024, smoking cost the public finances 16.5 billion, more than double the 6.8 billion raised through tobacco taxes. Approximately 5.3 million adults in the UK still smoke, down from historic highs but still the leading cause of premature, preventable death and the single largest driver of the gap in healthy life expectancy between rich and poor. Around 230,000 people are unable to work due to smoking-related illness. The Tobacco and Vapes Bill, currently progressing through the House of Lords, will create a smokefree generation by making it illegal to sell tobacco to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009 from 2027. Progress supports this measure unreservedly and proposes to build on it.

Alcohol costs England 27.4 billion per year, including 4.9 billion to the NHS and healthcare, 14.5 billion in crime and disorder, 5 billion in lost productivity, and 2.9 billion in social care costs. Tax revenue from alcohol is approximately 12.5 billion, meaning the net cost to the taxpayer is enormous. Over 10,000 people died from alcohol-specific causes in 2022, the highest level since records began. Alcohol-related hospital admissions cost over 2 billion per year. Yet the government has not published a comprehensive alcohol strategy for over two decades, and funding for alcohol treatment services has fallen since responsibility transferred to local authorities in 2014. The Public Accounts Committee concluded that the government was not taking alcohol harm sufficiently seriously.

These three conditions, obesity, smoking, and alcohol, are the biggest risk factors for avoidable mortality. They interact with and amplify each other, and they concentrate in the same communities: the most deprived, the most underserved, the most neglected. A child born in Blackpool will live, on average, 10.3 fewer years than a child born in Hart, Surrey. But the difference in years of good health is even greater. This is not fate. It is policy failure. The conditions that produce poor health are the product of specific decisions about food systems, urban design, education, advertising, pricing, and the allocation of public resources. NHS5 addresses the root causes, not just the symptoms.

Progress’ position on public health is pragmatic, not paternalistic. We distinguish between substances and behaviours on the basis of their harm profile, their addictiveness, and the degree to which individual choice is genuinely free. Tobacco is a product that kills half its long-term users and has no safe level of consumption. The regulatory approach should be one of elimination. Alcohol is a product that causes significant harm at population level but is consumed moderately and safely by the majority. The regulatory approach should be one of harm reduction, education, and targeted intervention for problem use, not prohibition. Obesity is primarily a consequence of a food system that makes unhealthy food cheaper, more accessible, and more aggressively marketed than healthy food, combined with a built environment that discourages physical activity and a working pattern that leaves families no time to cook. The regulatory approach should be one of system redesign: making the healthy choice the easy choice, and building state infrastructure to support working families rather than lecturing them about their personal responsibility. These are different problems. They require different solutions. NHS5 provides them.

##### NHS5.1: The National Food Service and Lifestyle Education

The Problem

The obesity crisis is not caused by a lack of willpower. It is caused by a food system that is structurally designed to produce obesity. Ultra-processed foods now constitute approximately 57% of calories consumed in the UK, the highest proportion in Europe. These products are engineered to be hyper-palatable, calorie-dense, and resistant to satiation. They are cheaper than fresh food, available in every corner shop and petrol station, marketed with billions of pounds in advertising, and promoted through pricing mechanisms like multi-buy offers that incentivise overconsumption. Against this commercial infrastructure, telling individuals to eat better is not a policy. It is an abdication.

The reality of modern working life makes the problem structural. In the majority of households with children, both parents work. The average full-time employee in the UK works 36.4 hours per week, commutes for an additional 4 to 6 hours, and arrives home with neither the time nor the energy to prepare a nutritious meal from fresh ingredients. The response of the market has been the ready meal: cheap, fast, and nutritionally catastrophic. The average supermarket ready meal contains more salt, sugar, and saturated fat per serving than a comparable home-cooked meal, and less fibre, protein, and micronutrients. Families are not choosing bad food. They are choosing the only food that fits their schedule. The state has done nothing to provide an alternative.

School nutrition education is perfunctory. Children learn that fruit and vegetables are good and sweets are bad. They do not learn to cook. They do not learn to read a nutrition label. They do not learn that the metabolic consequences of a diet dominated by ultra-processed food will determine their risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and certain cancers for the rest of their lives. They do not learn that these risks are not equally distributed: that a child growing up in the most deprived quintile faces an obesity rate roughly double that of a child in the least deprived quintile, and that this gap is widening. The education system treats nutrition as a footnote in PSHE rather than as a core determinant of lifelong health.

Meanwhile, the NHS spends billions treating the consequences. Type 2 diabetes alone costs the NHS approximately 10 billion per year, roughly 10% of its total budget. Between 60% and 90% of type 2 diabetes cases are attributable to excess weight. Bariatric surgery costs between 6,000 and 15,000 per procedure, and the NHS performs thousands each year because it is cheaper than a lifetime of diabetes management. The economics of prevention are overwhelming: for every pound spent on weight management services, the NHS saves between 3 and 10 pounds in avoided treatment costs. Yet weight management services have been decimated by public health grant cuts.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Public Health Act will establish:

- a) The National Food Service. The Act will create a state-operated food preparation and distribution service, constituted as a public body under the Department of Health and the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. The Service is not a welfare programme. It is a public food utility: a state-operated competitor to the commercial ready meal market, designed to be financially self-sustaining at population scale while delivering a step-change in the nutritional quality of the meals that working families actually eat.

The Service will operate through a network of regional kitchens, modelled on the wartime British Restaurant programme but designed for 21st-century logistics. Regional kitchens will prepare fresh meals daily using standardised, dietitian-designed recipes that meet NHS nutritional guidelines: calorie-controlled (targeting 500 to 600 calories per adult portion, compared with 750 to 1,000 in a typical commercial ready meal), low in salt and sugar, high in fibre, with balanced macronutrients. Meals will be distributed through three channels: collection points at schools, community centres, and NHS neighbourhood health centres; home delivery through integration with existing grocery delivery infrastructure; and workplace collection through partnerships with major employers.

The pricing model is explicit. At institutional scale, the production cost of a nutritious ready meal is approximately 2.50 to 3.00 pounds per portion, based on established institutional catering benchmarks (school meals cost 3.00 to 3.50 at current prices; NHS hospitals produce meals at 1.80 to 3.00 per portion for food costs). The Service will sell meals to the general public at 3.50 to 4.00 pounds, at or below supermarket ready meal prices, generating a modest operating surplus that cross-subsidises the lower tiers. For low-income households above the Universal Credit threshold, a sliding-scale subsidy will reduce the price to between 1.50 and 2.50 pounds, scaled to household income. For households receiving Universal Credit, meals will be free. This three-tier structure ensures that the Service is accessible to those who need it most while remaining commercially credible to the majority of households who will pay close to market price for a superior product.

Critically, every NFS meal purchased will earn credits under the National Health Incentive Scheme established by NHS5.2. A meal costing 3.50 at the till that earns 1.00 in Health Incentive credits, redeemable against childcare costs, council tax, public transport, or NHS dental and optical charges, has an effective price of 2.50. This is cheaper than the commercial alternative and nutritionally superior to it. The incentive structure means the NFS does not need to compete with ultra-processed food on taste alone. It competes on total household value: the meal plus the credit is a better deal than the supermarket lasagne, and the household accumulates tangible financial benefit over time. A family using the Service five evenings per week would earn approximately 250 pounds per year in credits, building compound engagement: once a household has 50 or 100 pounds accruing toward a council tax reduction, the incentive to continue is self-reinforcing.

The obesity reduction mechanism is specific and quantifiable. Every NFS meal eaten displaces a commercial ready meal. If the average commercial ready meal delivers 800 calories and the NFS equivalent delivers 550, that is a 250-calorie daily deficit for a household using the service five nights per week. Ready meals are inherently portion-controlled: you cannot overserve from a pre-portioned container the way you can from a pot on the stove. The NFS builds portion discipline into the format without requiring conscious effort from the consumer. This is the easiest possible behaviour change: the same action (buying a ready meal), from a different supplier, at a lower effective price, that happens not to produce type 2 diabetes.

Because NFS usage is linked to NHS numbers through the Health Incentive Scheme, the Service generates a population-level dietary dataset of unprecedented scale. Integrated with the NHS3 data infrastructure, this allows real-time monitoring of nutritional intake patterns, correlation with health outcomes, and targeted intervention for households that are not engaging with the Service. The NFS is not just a food provider. It is a public health intelligence platform.

The fiscal case is conservative. If 10% of English households use the Service for one evening meal five nights per week, that is approximately 14 million meals per week. At a production cost of 3.00 pounds and an average selling price (across all three tiers) of approximately 2.80 pounds, the net subsidy cost is approximately 150 million pounds per year. Set against the 12 billion the NHS spends annually on obesity and excess weight, this is a return on investment of approximately 80:1 even if the Service achieves only a 2% reduction in obesity prevalence. The objective is not to replace home cooking. It is to ensure that when families cannot cook, the default option is nutritious, affordable, and actively rewarded by the state, rather than ultra-processed, overpriced, and metabolically catastrophic. If the state can provide school meals for children, it can provide evening meals for the families of those children. The National Food Service makes this real.

- b) Mandatory nutrition and cooking education. The Act will make nutrition science and practical cooking a statutory component of the national curriculum from Key Stage 2 through Key Stage 4. The curriculum will be designed by a joint commission of the Department for Education, the Department of Health, and the Royal College of General Practitioners, and will include: the biology of metabolism, energy balance, and body composition; the relationship between diet and disease, with explicit teaching on obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and diet-related cancers; practical cooking skills sufficient to prepare a nutritious meal from raw ingredients for a family of four within 30 minutes and for less than 5 pounds; critical analysis of food marketing, including the identification of ultra-processed food, the reading of nutrition labels, and the commercial incentives behind product formulation; and the specific health consequences of tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and physical inactivity, taught with the same rigour as sex education. Schools will be required to maintain equipped teaching kitchens, funded through the capital programme established under NHS6. Ofsted inspections will include assessment of nutrition education delivery and school food quality.
- c) Food environment regulation. The Act will establish powers for the Secretary of State to regulate the commercial food environment through secondary legislation. These powers will include: mandatory calorie, sugar, and salt limits per serving for all foods marketed as convenience or ready-to-eat meals, with a five-year compliance timetable and escalating penalties for non-compliance; prohibition of advertising for products exceeding specified calorie density thresholds during all broadcast hours and across all digital platforms, extending the existing pre-watershed junk food advertising ban to a comprehensive prohibition; mandatory front-of-pack traffic light labelling on all food products sold in England, with the traffic light system standardised by regulation and enforced by Trading Standards; and restrictions on the placement and promotion of high-fat, high-sugar, high-salt products in retail environments, building on existing supermarket placement restrictions to include all retail premises including convenience stores, forecourt shops, and online grocery platforms.
- d) The Community Kitchen programme. The Act will create a statutory duty on local authorities to maintain at least one Community Kitchen per 20,000 population, defined as a publicly accessible facility where residents can cook, learn, and eat together. Community Kitchens will be staffed by trained nutritionists and will offer: free weekly cooking classes for adults, prioritising families with children under 16 and individuals with diet-related health conditions; low-cost communal dining, with meals prepared collaboratively by participants using fresh ingredients provided at cost; and social prescribing integration, with GPs able to refer patients with obesity, type 2 diabetes, or diet-related conditions directly to Community Kitchen programmes. The programme explicitly recognises that cooking is a social activity, that isolation is a driver of poor diet, and that community infrastructure can address both.

OPERATIONAL

National Food Service pilot.

Within 12 months of Royal Assent, the Department of Health will launch National Food Service pilots in ten areas, prioritising the local authorities with the highest obesity prevalence and the lowest healthy life expectancy. The pilots will test the regional kitchen model, distribution logistics, the three-tier pricing structure, Health Incentive credit integration, and uptake patterns across income groups. A full evaluation will be published within 24 months, reporting on: unit economics per meal across all three pricing tiers; uptake rates by household income; calorie displacement compared with commercial ready meal baselines; and measurable changes in weight, BMI, and diet-related biomarkers among regular users. The initial target is to serve 500,000 meals per week within the pilot areas by the end of the first year, with the Service demonstrating operational self-sufficiency (general-public sales covering at least 80% of total costs) before national rollout.

Curriculum reform.

Within six months, the Department for Education will publish the revised national curriculum incorporating mandatory nutrition and cooking education. Schools will have 18 months to comply with the kitchen infrastructure requirements, with capital funding provided through NHS6 infrastructure allocations. Teacher training programmes will be developed in partnership with the British Nutrition Foundation and the Culinary Institute.

Community Kitchen rollout.

Within 12 months, the first 200 Community Kitchens will be operational, located in the 200 most deprived wards in England. The programme will expand to full national coverage within five years. Existing community centre, library, and school kitchen facilities will be repurposed where possible, minimising capital expenditure.

##### NHS5.2: Prevention Infrastructure and the Incentive Revolution

The Problem

The UK’s approach to prevention has been characterised by campaigns that inform, services that treat, and regulations that restrict, but almost nothing that actively incentivises healthy behaviour. The assumption has been that if people are told what is good for them, they will do it. This assumption is wrong. Decades of behavioural science research demonstrate that information alone changes behaviour only marginally. What changes behaviour is the structure of choices: what is easy, what is rewarded, what is available, and what is the default. The UK’s choice architecture overwhelmingly favours unhealthy behaviour. Healthy food costs more. Gyms require memberships. Parks are underfunded. Active transport infrastructure is patchy. And no one is rewarded for staying healthy, while the NHS provides unlimited free treatment for the consequences of not doing so.

Tobacco control is the exception that proves the rule. The UK has been a global leader in tobacco control: banning advertising, introducing plain packaging, raising taxes, banning smoking in enclosed public places, and now pursuing a smokefree generation through the Tobacco and Vapes Bill. The results are remarkable: smoking prevalence has fallen from over 45% in the 1970s to 10.6% in 2024. But the remaining 5.3 million smokers are disproportionately concentrated in deprived communities, where daily smoking is more than twice as common in the lowest socioeconomic group as in the highest. The challenge is no longer mass prevalence reduction. It is reaching the hardest-to-reach smokers in the most disadvantaged communities. This requires not just regulation but active, funded, community-based cessation services, and those services have been cut. Local authority spending on smoking cessation fell from 120.6 million in 2016/17 to under 100 million by 2017/18, and has not recovered.

Alcohol policy is the opposite of tobacco policy. Despite alcohol costing the NHS 4.9 billion per year and society 27.4 billion, the UK has no current comprehensive alcohol strategy. The last nationwide assessment of the cost of alcohol harm was published in 2003. Scotland introduced minimum unit pricing in 2018 and has seen measurable reductions in alcohol-related deaths and hospital admissions. England has not followed. Progress takes a deliberately lighter regulatory approach to alcohol than to tobacco, recognising that the majority of adults consume alcohol moderately and that prohibition would be both ineffective and unjust. But a lighter approach does not mean no approach. It means targeted intervention: better treatment services, honest education, and pricing mechanisms that discourage dangerous consumption patterns without penalising moderate use.

Physical inactivity costs the NHS approximately 1.2 billion per year in direct treatment costs and the wider economy an estimated 7.4 billion. Only 67% of adults meet the Chief Medical Officer’s guidelines of 150 minutes of moderate activity per week. Inactivity rates are highest in the most deprived communities, among older adults, and among people with disabilities. The built environment in many deprived areas offers few safe, accessible, free opportunities for physical activity. Public leisure centres have been hit by austerity, with many closing or increasing prices beyond the reach of low-income families. School sports funding, while maintained through the PE and Sport Premium, reaches children but does nothing for the working adults who most need to be active.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Public Health Act will establish:

- a) The National Health Incentive Scheme. The Act will create a universal incentive programme that rewards healthy behaviour with tangible, cashable benefits. Every adult resident of England will be eligible for a Health Incentive Account, linked to their NHS number, into which credits are deposited for verified healthy behaviours. The credit schedule will include: completion of an annual NHS Health Check (all adults over 40, expanded from the current programme), credits for meeting physical activity targets verified through wearable technology or gym attendance records, credits for completing smoking cessation programmes (verified by CO monitoring), credits for participation in Community Kitchen programmes or National Food Service meal plans, and credits for maintaining recommended vaccination schedules. Credits will be redeemable against: childcare costs (including nursery fees, after-school clubs, and holiday childcare), council tax, public transport costs, and NHS dental and optical charges. The scheme explicitly links health to economic benefit, recognising that healthy behaviour has value to the state and that the state should share that value with the individual. For people with disabilities or long-term conditions that limit their ability to meet standard activity targets, the scheme will offer adapted criteria designed with disability organisations, ensuring that incentives are accessible and equitable. The objective is not to penalise illness. It is to reward engagement with health-promoting behaviours at whatever level the individual can achieve.
- b) Tobacco: completing the endgame. The Act will complement the Tobacco and Vapes Bill by establishing: a statutory duty on every integrated care system to fund and maintain smoking cessation services accessible to every registered smoker in their area, reversing the post-2015 decimation of cessation support; a national quit-or-switch programme offering free nicotine replacement therapy or regulated vaping products to every smoker who requests them, funded centrally through a new levy on tobacco company profits rather than through the public health grant; and an enhanced enforcement programme for illicit tobacco, including increased penalties and additional funding for HMRC and Trading Standards. Progress supports the smokefree generation. This provision ensures it is funded, enforced, and supported at community level.
- c) Alcohol: harm reduction without prohibition. The Act will establish: a statutory duty on the Secretary of State to publish a comprehensive National Alcohol Strategy within 12 months of Royal Assent, the first in over two decades; a requirement for alcohol care teams in every acute hospital in England, not just those with the highest rates of harm as currently planned, funded through a ring-fenced allocation from alcohol duty revenue; mandatory unit labelling on all alcoholic products, including the number of units per container, the Chief Medical Officer’s low-risk drinking guidelines, and a calorie count; a review of minimum unit pricing, with the Act requiring the Secretary of State to assess the Scottish evidence and either implement minimum unit pricing in England within two years or publish a statement explaining why not; and enhanced funding for community alcohol treatment services, restoring funding to at least 2015/16 real-terms levels.
- d) The National Activity Infrastructure. The Act will create a statutory duty on local authorities to provide free, publicly accessible physical activity facilities sufficient to serve their population. The duty will be met through: maintenance and expansion of public leisure centres, with a commitment that no resident is more than 20 minutes’ travel from a free-to-use swimming pool, gym, or sports hall; investment in active transport infrastructure, including protected cycling lanes, walking routes, and secure bicycle storage at all public buildings, workplaces with more than 50 employees, and transport hubs; and free access to public sports and leisure facilities for all children under 18, all adults over 65, and all recipients of Universal Credit or disability benefits. The capital investment will be funded through NHS6 infrastructure allocations.

OPERATIONAL

Health Incentive Scheme launch.

Within 18 months of Royal Assent, the Department of Health will launch the Health Incentive Scheme in 20 pilot areas, testing the credit schedule, verification systems, and redemption pathways. The pilot will be independently evaluated at 12 months. National rollout will begin within 30 months, with full population coverage within four years. The scheme’s IT infrastructure will be developed in conjunction with the NHS App and the digital architecture established under NHS3.

Smoking cessation restoration.

Within six months, NHS England will publish requirements for integrated care systems to restore smoking cessation services to full population coverage. Funding will be provided through the tobacco company levy established by the Act. Within 12 months, every registered smoker will have access to a funded quit-or-switch pathway.

National Alcohol Strategy.

Within 12 months, the Secretary of State will publish the first National Alcohol Strategy since the early 2000s. The strategy will be developed by an independent commission including public health experts, clinicians, law enforcement representatives, and people with lived experience of alcohol harm. Alcohol care teams will be operational in every acute hospital within 24 months.

Activity infrastructure.

Within 12 months, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport will publish a National Activity Infrastructure Plan identifying areas of deficit and setting a five-year investment programme. The plan will be developed in conjunction with Sport England, local authorities, and Active Partnerships.

##### NHS5.3: Dignity in Ageing

The Problem

The UK population is ageing. The number of people over 85 is projected to double by 2045. The centenarian population has already doubled from 8,300 in 2004 to 16,600 in 2024. An ageing population is not a problem to be managed. It is a triumph to be honoured. But the NHS’s model of care for older people is reactive, fragmented, and too often undignified. Older people are admitted to hospital because no one identified their deteriorating health early enough to intervene. They are kept in hospital because there is no community support to receive them. They are discharged without follow-up because the primary care system has no structured programme for geriatric assessment. And when they reach the end of their lives, they are subjected to interventions that prolong dying rather than supporting living, because the system has no framework for honest, compassionate conversations about treatment futility.

The NHS Health Check programme, which offers a cardiovascular risk assessment to adults aged 40 to 74, is the closest thing to a systematic preventive programme for older adults. But it is not a comprehensive geriatric assessment. It checks blood pressure, cholesterol, and glucose. It does not assess functional capacity, cognitive function, falls risk, nutritional status, polypharmacy, social isolation, or mental health. For a 45-year-old, a cardiovascular risk check is appropriate. For a 75-year-old, it is necessary but radically insufficient. The conditions that determine quality of life in older age are not primarily cardiovascular. They are mobility, cognition, continence, sensory function, nutrition, mental health, and social connection. No existing NHS programme systematically assesses these domains. The result is that preventable decline goes undetected until it produces a crisis: a fall, a hospital admission, a loss of independence that could have been avoided.

End-of-life care presents the most profound challenge. Approximately 500,000 people die in England each year. The majority die in hospital, despite surveys consistently showing that most people would prefer to die at home. Many receive aggressive treatment in their final weeks that extends suffering without extending meaningful life. The conversations that should happen, about what the patient wants, what treatment can realistically achieve, and when the focus should shift from cure to comfort, often do not happen until it is too late, if they happen at all. Clinicians are trained to treat. They are not trained to say that treatment has nothing more to offer, and to help patients and families navigate that reality with dignity and agency. Treatment futility is one of the most sensitive topics in medicine. It is also one of the most expensive: a significant proportion of lifetime healthcare costs are incurred in the final months of life, much of it on interventions that do not improve outcomes. This is not about rationing. It is about ensuring that patients are empowered to make informed choices about their own care, including the choice to stop treatment and to die well.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Public Health Act will establish:

- a) The Over-70s MOT. The Act will create a statutory entitlement for every person over the age of 70 to an annual comprehensive geriatric assessment, delivered by a geriatrician-led multidisciplinary team. The MOT will go far beyond the existing NHS Health Check. It will assess: cardiovascular risk and metabolic health (blood pressure, glucose, lipids, kidney function); functional capacity (mobility, balance, grip strength, activities of daily living); cognitive function (standardised screening for mild cognitive impairment and early dementia); falls risk (including medication review, vision and hearing assessment, and home hazard evaluation); nutritional status (including screening for malnutrition, which affects approximately 1 in 10 older adults in the community); polypharmacy (with a structured medication review by a clinical pharmacist, identifying and deprescribing medications that are no longer beneficial or that interact adversely); mental health (screening for depression, anxiety, and loneliness, with direct referral pathways to psychological therapies and social prescribing); and social needs (assessment of housing adequacy, carer support, transport access, and social connectedness). Each MOT will produce a personalised health and wellbeing plan, developed with the patient, identifying priorities for the coming year. The plan will be shared with the patient’s GP, any specialist services involved in their care, and, with consent, their family or carers. Follow-up appointments will be scheduled at intervals determined by clinical need. For patients identified as being at high risk of functional decline, falls, or hospital admission, the MOT will trigger a proactive care pathway including physiotherapy, occupational therapy, home adaptation, and enhanced community support. The objective is simple: identify problems before they become crises, intervene before they become emergencies, and keep people living well at home for as long as possible.
- b) The Right to an Honest Conversation. The Act will establish a statutory framework for advance care planning and treatment escalation decisions. Every patient over 70 will be offered, as part of their annual MOT, the opportunity to discuss and document their preferences for care in the event of serious illness, loss of capacity, or approaching end of life. These discussions will be conducted by clinicians specifically trained in advance care planning, using a standardised national protocol developed by the Royal College of Physicians, the Royal College of General Practitioners, and patient advocacy organisations. The documentation, known as an Advance Care Statement, will be recorded in the patient’s electronic health record and will be accessible to all clinicians involved in their care, including emergency services. The Act will make it a statutory requirement for clinicians to consult a patient’s Advance Care Statement before initiating life-sustaining treatment in an emergency, where the statement is available. The Act does not create a right to refuse emergency treatment on behalf of another person, and it does not alter the existing law on advance decisions to refuse treatment under the Mental Capacity Act 2005. What it does is ensure that the conversation happens proactively, routinely, and with proper support, rather than in the distress and confusion of a medical emergency. The name of this provision, the Right to an Honest Conversation, reflects its purpose: patients have a right to be told, clearly and compassionately, what treatment can and cannot achieve, and to have their wishes about their own care respected.
- c) The Geriatric Care Academy. The Act will establish a national training programme for geriatric medicine, recognising that the UK does not have enough geriatricians to deliver the Over-70s MOT at population scale. The Academy will: fund 500 additional geriatric medicine training posts over five years, in addition to the workforce expansion measures established under NHS2; create a new role of Community Geriatric Practitioner, a clinician with specialist training in geriatric assessment who works in the community rather than in hospital, delivering MOTs in patients’ homes, GP surgeries, and community health centres; develop mandatory training modules on advance care planning and treatment futility conversations for all doctors, nurses, and allied health professionals working with older patients; and establish regional centres of excellence in geriatric innovation, partnering with universities to research and develop new models of care for an ageing population, including technology-enabled remote monitoring, AI-assisted falls prediction, and smart home adaptations that extend independent living.

OPERATIONAL

Over-70s MOT pilot.

Within 12 months of Royal Assent, NHS England will launch the MOT programme in 30 integrated care systems, prioritising areas with the oldest populations and the highest rates of emergency hospital admissions among over-75s. The pilots will test the assessment protocol, workforce model, referral pathways, and patient experience. Full national rollout will begin within 24 months. The target is to offer an annual MOT to every person over 70 in England within three years, representing approximately 8 million assessments per year.

Advance Care Planning rollout.

Within six months, NHS England will publish the national Advance Care Planning protocol and begin training facilitators. Within 18 months, every GP practice and community health centre will have at least one clinician trained to lead advance care planning conversations. The NHS App, enhanced under NHS3, will include functionality for patients to view, update, and share their Advance Care Statement digitally.

Geriatric Care Academy.

Within 12 months, Health Education England will announce the first 200 additional geriatric medicine training posts and publish the Community Geriatric Practitioner role specification. The first cohort of Community Geriatric Practitioners will qualify within three years. Regional centres of excellence will be established within two years, with initial funding from the NHS Digital Innovation Fund (NHS3.1).

End-of-life care quality.

Within 12 months, the Care Quality Commission will introduce specific inspection criteria for end-of-life care, including assessment of advance care planning rates, patient-reported experience of end-of-life discussions, and the proportion of patients who die in their preferred place of death. These metrics will be published at trust level, creating transparency and accountability for end-of-life care quality for the first time.

##### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The NHS5 framework is built on the NHS Public Health Act, a single piece of primary legislation introduced alongside the NHS Core Mission Act (NHS1), the NHS Workforce Act (NHS2), the NHS Information Systems Act (NHS3), the NHS Procurement and Anti-Corruption Act (NHS4), and the Tax Reset Act (E6) in the first King’s Speech.

###### NHS Public Health Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: National Food Service as a public body providing nutritious, affordable meals through regional kitchens and multiple distribution channels. Mandatory nutrition and cooking education from Key Stage 2 to Key Stage 4. Food environment regulation powers including calorie limits for convenience foods, comprehensive advertising prohibition for unhealthy products, mandatory traffic light labelling, and retail placement restrictions. Community Kitchen programme with statutory duty on local authorities. National Health Incentive Scheme providing cashable credits for healthy behaviours, redeemable against childcare, council tax, transport, and NHS charges, with disability-adapted criteria. Statutory duty on integrated care systems to fund full-population smoking cessation services, funded by tobacco company levy. National Alcohol Strategy requirement within 12 months. Alcohol care teams in every acute hospital. Mandatory unit labelling on all alcohol products. Minimum unit pricing review requirement. National Activity Infrastructure duty on local authorities. Over-70s MOT as statutory entitlement to annual comprehensive geriatric assessment. Right to an Honest Conversation establishing advance care planning framework. Geriatric Care Academy with 500 additional training posts and Community Geriatric Practitioner role.

Delivered operationally: National Food Service pilots in 10 areas within 12 months. Revised national curriculum within six months. First 200 Community Kitchens within 12 months. Health Incentive Scheme pilots in 20 areas within 18 months. Smoking cessation services restored within 12 months. National Alcohol Strategy published within 12 months. Alcohol care teams in every hospital within 24 months. National Activity Infrastructure Plan within 12 months. Over-70s MOT pilots in 30 ICBs within 12 months, national rollout within 24 months. Advance Care Planning protocol published within six months. First 200 geriatric training posts within 12 months. CQC end-of-life inspection criteria within 12 months.

##### Funding NHS5

NHS5 is an investment programme with extraordinary returns. The economics of prevention are not speculative. They are documented, quantified, and overwhelmingly positive.

Obesity cost reduction. Nesta and Frontier Economics estimate that a 5% annual reduction in obesity prevalence over five years would generate productivity gains worth billions. The NHS currently spends an estimated 12 billion per year on the consequences of obesity and excess weight. The National Food Service is designed as a self-sustaining public utility: general-public sales at 3.50 to 4.00 per meal generate an operating surplus that cross-subsidises the low-income and UC-free tiers. The net annual subsidy cost is approximately 150 million pounds at 10% household uptake. The Community Kitchen programme, food environment regulation, and nutrition education add further investment, but the combined package targets a return on investment conservatively estimated at 80:1 against the 12 billion annual obesity burden, even at modest prevalence reductions. The integration of the NFS with the Health Incentive Scheme creates a self-reinforcing engagement mechanism: households accumulate credits that reduce childcare, council tax, and transport costs, making sustained NFS usage economically rational for the consumer as well as for the state.

Tobacco cost reduction. Smoking costs the public finances 16.5 billion per year, against tobacco tax revenue of 6.8 billion. Every percentage point reduction in smoking prevalence saves the public finances hundreds of millions per year. The tobacco company levy will fund cessation services without drawing on general taxation. The Tobacco and Vapes Bill will progressively eliminate tobacco consumption over the coming decades. NHS5’s cessation services ensure that existing smokers are supported to quit now, not in twenty years.

Alcohol cost reduction. Alcohol costs the NHS 4.9 billion per year. The minimum unit pricing evidence from Scotland demonstrates measurable reductions in harm. Alcohol care teams in hospitals have been shown to reduce readmissions and length of stay. The cost of universal alcohol care teams is a fraction of the 4.9 billion annual burden. Enhanced treatment services cost less than the crime, social care, and healthcare costs they prevent.

Geriatric prevention. Emergency hospital admissions among older people are among the most expensive episodes in the NHS. A single hip fracture from a preventable fall costs the NHS approximately 30,000 in the first year. Falls among older people cost the NHS an estimated 4.4 billion per year. The Over-70s MOT, by identifying falls risk, polypharmacy, malnutrition, and cognitive decline before they produce emergencies, targets the most expensive failure mode in the system. Comprehensive geriatric assessment in hospital settings has been shown to improve survival, increase the likelihood of living at home, and reduce length of stay. Delivering the same assessment in the community, before the hospital admission, multiplies these benefits.

Health Incentive Scheme. The scheme generates its own return. Every person who maintains healthy behaviour as a result of the incentive avoids costs to the NHS, to employers, and to the social care system. The credits redeemed represent a transfer from future healthcare costs to present incentive payments, at a net saving to the state. The scheme will be structured so that total credit expenditure is capped annually and adjusted based on measured health outcomes, ensuring fiscal sustainability.

The public health grant has been cut by 26% in real terms per person since 2015/16. The Health Foundation estimates that restoring it would require an additional 1 billion per year. NHS5 does not merely restore the grant. It creates an entirely new institutional architecture for prevention, funded not through the public health grant but through dedicated revenue streams: the tobacco company levy, ring-fenced alcohol duty revenue, food industry compliance fees, and the fiscal savings generated by the programme itself. Prevention is not a cost. It is the only route to an affordable NHS. The alternative is a system that spends 90% of its budget treating conditions that could have been prevented, in a population that is getting sicker, and wondering why it is always running out of money.

##### Cross-References to Other NHS Framework Documents

NHS1 (Back to Basics Campaign): The Treatment Coverage Commission determines the scope of NHS services. NHS5’s prevention programmes reduce demand for those services, directly supporting the 70% front-line spending ring-fence by reducing the volume and acuity of patients entering the system.

NHS2 (Workforce Crisis Management): The Geriatric Care Academy and Community Geriatric Practitioner role are workforce expansion measures that complement NHS2’s broader workforce strategy. The 40% documentation reduction target improves clinician capacity for the proactive care pathways established under NHS5.3.

NHS3 (Information Systems and Data Capitalisation): The NHS App provides the digital infrastructure for the Health Incentive Scheme, advance care planning, and the Over-70s MOT personalised health plans. The Disease Monitoring Service established under NHS3.3 provides real-time population health surveillance that informs NHS5 intervention targeting.

NHS4 (Procurement and Anti-Corruption): The NHS National Procurement Authority established under NHS4.1 procures supplies for the National Food Service, Community Kitchens, and the Over-70s MOT programme. The NHS Price Index ensures that prevention programme costs are transparent and benchmarked.

NHS6–NHS7 (forthcoming): NHS6 infrastructure and capital programmes fund the physical facilities for Community Kitchens, teaching kitchens in schools, and the geriatric care centres. NHS7 social care integration is essential to the Over-70s MOT, as geriatric assessment frequently identifies social care needs that must be met to prevent hospital admission.

##### Conclusion: From Sickness Service to Health Service

Aneurin Bevan created the NHS to free the British people from the fear of illness. Seventy-eight years later, the NHS is overwhelmed by illness that it could have prevented. The system that was designed to be the envy of the world has become an engine of reactive treatment, consuming ever-larger shares of national income to manage conditions that are largely the product of how we eat, what we smoke and drink, how little we move, and how poorly we support people as they age. The irony is that the NHS’s founding principle, universal free care at point of use, has become an obstacle to prevention: because treatment is free, the economic case for prevention is invisible to the individual, even though it is overwhelming for the state.

NHS5 makes prevention visible, tangible, and rewarded. The National Food Service makes healthy eating as convenient as unhealthy eating. Mandatory nutrition education equips the next generation to make informed choices. The Health Incentive Scheme creates a direct economic link between healthy behaviour and personal benefit. Restored smoking cessation services and the tobacco company levy complete the smokefree generation. The National Alcohol Strategy and universal alcohol care teams address a harm that has been neglected for two decades. The National Activity Infrastructure makes physical activity accessible and free. The Over-70s MOT catches problems before they become emergencies. The Right to an Honest Conversation ensures that ageing and dying are treated with the dignity and agency that every person deserves.

The costs of inaction are quantified. Obesity: 126 billion per year. Smoking: 78 billion. Alcohol: 27 billion. Physical inactivity: 7.4 billion. Preventable falls in older people: 4.4 billion. These numbers will grow every year that prevention remains unfunded. The public health grant has been cut by a quarter in a decade. Preventive spending on children has fallen by 80%. Life expectancy improvements have stalled. Healthy life expectancy is declining. The gap between rich and poor is widening. This is what a sickness service looks like. NHS5 builds a health service.

Every pound invested in prevention returns between 3 and 14 pounds in avoided healthcare, productivity, and social care costs. Every year of healthy life gained for a person in a deprived community is a year of work, of family life, of contribution to their community, that would otherwise have been lost to preventable disease. Every older person whose decline is caught early by an MOT is a hospital admission avoided, a fall prevented, a year of independence preserved. NHS5 is the single highest-return investment in the entire NHS framework. It is also the most overdue.

#### NHS6. Infrastructure and Capital Investment

Governing Principle

The NHS is dying of underinvestment. Not metaphorically. Physically. The buildings are collapsing. The concrete is crumbling. The pipes are leaking. The roofs are failing. The ventilation systems are shutting down in operating theatres. The IT systems are running on software so old that their manufacturers have stopped supporting it. And every year, the gap between what the estate needs and what it receives grows wider.

The maintenance backlog, the estimated cost of bringing the NHS estate back to a minimum acceptable standard, reached £15.9 billion in 2024/25. This is a 15.7% increase on the £13.8 billion recorded just one year earlier, and more than double the £6.4 billion recorded in 2015/16. The backlog is now larger than the total annual cost of running the NHS estate, which was £14 billion in 2024/25. Within this total, the high-risk component, work that must be done to prevent catastrophic failure or serious disruption to clinical services, rose 28% in a single year to £3.5 billion. Fifty-one trusts now have individual backlogs exceeding £100 million, with a combined total of £10.7 billion, two thirds of the national figure. Fourteen trusts have backlogs above £200 million. Six exceed £400 million. Imperial College Healthcare tops the list at £902 million, driven by the chronic neglect of three major hospitals: Charing Cross (£425 million), St Mary’s Paddington (£296 million), and Hammersmith (£132 million). Nine individual hospital buildings now have backlogs exceeding £200 million each.

Lord Darzi’s independent investigation of the NHS, published in September 2024, identified a £37 billion shortfall in capital investment over the preceding decade and a half. This is the gap between what the UK actually invested in health infrastructure and what comparable countries invested over the same period. Darzi described the NHS as suffering from “capital starvation.” Those £37 billion missing pounds could have prevented the entire maintenance backlog, modernised technology and equipment across the service, paid for the promised 40 new hospitals, or rebuilt every GP practice in the country. Instead, capital budgets were repeatedly raided to cover day-to-day spending deficits: £4.3 billion was transferred from capital to revenue between 2014/15 and 2018/19 alone. The consequence is an estate where services are disrupted at 13 hospitals a day by failing or crumbling buildings, where 751 incidents affecting patients and staff were caused by infrastructure failures in a single year, and where 20% of the primary care estate predates the founding of the NHS in 1948.

Forty-nine hospital sites contain reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete (RAAC), a lightweight building material used between the 1960s and 1980s with an approximate 30-year lifespan. It has now significantly exceeded that lifespan. RAAC absorbs moisture, corrodes internal reinforcing steel, and is liable to sudden structural failure without warning. Seven hospitals were built predominantly from RAAC and have been prioritised for replacement. But the original target of completing these replacements by 2030 has already slipped to 2032/33, and some have required more than £500 million in mitigation works just to remain standing while replacements are planned. Every year of delay increases both cost and risk. A RAAC panel collapse in an occupied clinical area would be a catastrophe without precedent in modern NHS history.

The New Hospital Programme, announced in 2020 with a promise of 40 new hospitals by 2030, has been comprehensively reset. The January 2025 review revealed that the programme was unfunded beyond March 2025, that the original timetable was fictional, and that total costs will be approximately £33.8 billion more than initially estimated. The revised plan delivers projects in four waves stretching to 2045/46. Five schemes will not even begin construction until 2037 to 2039. Eighteen of the original 40 hospitals will not start construction until after 2030. The programme now has secured funding of approximately £2 billion per year rising to £3 billion, totalling £15 billion over five-year cycles. Meanwhile, trusts within the programme account for over 40% of the total national maintenance backlog, some spending upwards of £1 million per month on emergency repairs to buildings that are scheduled for eventual replacement but will not be replaced for a decade or more.

The technology estate is equally degraded. The WannaCry ransomware attack in 2017 infected one third of all NHS trusts and 8% of GP practices, costing £92 million in disrupted services and IT recovery. The attack exploited the NHS’s reliance on outdated operating systems, including Windows XP, which Microsoft had stopped supporting three years earlier. A 2018 review found that all 200 NHS organisations checked after the attack still failed basic cybersecurity standards. NHS Digital estimated that meeting the Cyber Essentials Plus standard would cost £1 billion, and refused to fund it on value-for-money grounds. Subsequent attacks have continued: in 2024 alone, Wirral University Teaching Hospital was hit by ransomware. The Darzi report found the NHS to be “in the foothills of digital transformation,” with IT projects routinely seen as a burden on clinicians rather than an aid. Technological solutions that have been standard in the private sector for over 15 years remain subscale or underutilised across the NHS.

The energy cost of this neglect is substantial. The NHS estate consumed 11.3 billion kilowatt hours of energy in 2024/25. Single-glazed windows, uninsulated walls, and heating systems designed for buildings that no longer exist waste energy on an industrial scale. The NHS has committed to net zero by 2040 for direct emissions, but achieving this with an estate where basic fabric maintenance has been deferred for decades is arithmetically impossible without the structural investment that NHS6 provides.

Progress’ position is unambiguous. Capital starvation is not an oversight. It is a policy choice that has been made repeatedly over fifteen years by successive governments, and it has produced a national health estate that is physically dangerous, operationally inefficient, and technologically obsolete. NHS6 ends capital starvation. It does so not by creating another aspirational programme with fictional timetables, but by establishing a legal framework that protects capital investment from revenue raids, accelerates the elimination of dangerous infrastructure, and creates a modern technology estate that supports rather than hinders clinical care.

##### NHS6.1: Ending the Maintenance Crisis

The Problem

The NHS maintenance backlog is not a technical accounting category. It is a list of things that are broken, dangerous, or failing in the buildings where sick people are treated.
