It includes: electrical systems that trip and cut power to wards; heating systems that leave patients in cold rooms or overheat clinical areas beyond safe operating temperatures; ventilation systems whose failure cancels operating theatre sessions; plumbing that leaks sewage through corridors; roofs that admit rain onto wards; windows that cannot be opened for ventilation or closed for warmth; lifts that break down trapping patients and staff; and fire safety systems that no longer meet regulatory standards. The backlog has more than doubled in real terms in less than a decade. Investment to reduce the backlog fell by £707 million in real terms between 2021/22 and 2023/24. The estate is deteriorating faster than it is being repaired.

The planning and approval process for basic maintenance and improvement works compounds the problem. Replacing single glazing, fixing a leaking roof, or upgrading an electrical distribution board should not require the same governance pathway as building a new wing. Yet trusts report that even routine capital works are subject to lengthy business case processes, multiple approval stages, and competition for limited capital allocations that make timely intervention impossible. By the time approval is granted and a contractor appointed, the original repair estimate has escalated because the problem has worsened. This creates a vicious cycle: delayed maintenance becomes more expensive maintenance, which consumes more of the limited capital budget, which delays other maintenance, which escalates further.

The capital regime itself has been dysfunctional. Capital budgets have been raided to cover revenue deficits, a practice Darzi described as “robbing the future to pay for today.” Trusts that underspend on capital, often because they are running deficits and cannot afford the revenue consequences of capital projects, lose their allocations. Trusts that overspend face penalties in subsequent years. The system incentivises short-term patching over strategic investment. The 2025 Spending Review settlement of £44 billion over four years and the £750 million per year Estates Safety Fund are welcome, but the backlog is growing at approximately £2 billion per year. At current investment rates, the backlog will never be eliminated. It will continue to grow, and the cost of eventual remediation will continue to rise.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Infrastructure Act will establish:

- a) The Capital Ring-Fence. The Act will make it a statutory requirement that NHS capital budgets cannot be transferred to revenue spending under any circumstances. This is the single most important provision in NHS6. The practice of raiding capital to cover day-to-day deficits, which Darzi identified as a central driver of capital starvation, will be made unlawful. Capital allocations to trusts will be ring-fenced by statute, with the Comptroller and Auditor General empowered to report any breach directly to Parliament. The Secretary of State will retain power to reallocate capital between trusts (for example, to redirect funding from a trust that cannot spend its allocation to one with urgent need), but the total capital envelope for the NHS in any given year cannot be reduced to fund revenue. This provision ends a fifteen-year practice that has produced the £15.9 billion backlog.
- b) The Rapid Remediation Programme. The Act will create a statutory remediation pathway for all maintenance works classified as high-risk or significant-risk (currently totalling £9.1 billion combined). Works under this pathway will be exempt from the standard NHS business case process. Instead, a simplified three-stage process will apply: identification (trust estates team certifies the risk category and estimated cost), approval (regional estates director approves works up to £5 million within 10 working days; works above £5 million approved by a national Remediation Board within 20 working days), and execution (trust proceeds to procurement under NHS4 frameworks without further approval). The objective is to reduce the elapsed time from identification of a critical maintenance issue to commencement of works from the current average of 12 to 18 months to a maximum of 60 days for high-risk items and 120 days for significant-risk items. The Act will establish a statutory target of eliminating all high-risk backlog within five years and all significant-risk backlog within ten years.
- c) RAAC Eradication. The Act will establish a statutory deadline for the complete eradication of RAAC from the NHS estate. All RAAC must be removed or replaced by 2032, with the seven predominantly RAAC hospitals replaced by 2030. The current programme, which has already slipped from its original 2030 target and now contemplates completion by 2035, is too slow given the risk of sudden structural failure. The Act will empower the Secretary of State to direct emergency procurement for RAAC replacement works, bypassing standard competitive procedures where necessary to maintain the 2032 deadline. RAAC eradication will be funded from a dedicated allocation outside the general Estates Safety Fund, preventing RAAC costs from crowding out investment in the wider backlog.
- d) Single Glazing Elimination. The Act will prohibit the continued use of single-glazed windows in any NHS clinical facility from 2030. All single glazing must be replaced with double or triple glazing that meets current Building Regulations Part L standards. This is simultaneously a patient comfort measure, an infection control measure (single-glazed windows create condensation that promotes mould growth), an energy efficiency measure (replacing single glazing reduces heating energy consumption by 20 to 30%), and a security measure. Trusts will be required to complete a window audit within six months of Royal Assent and submit replacement programmes within twelve months, with funding provided through the Estates Safety Fund. The provision also serves as a symbol: if the NHS cannot even replace its windows, it cannot credibly claim to be a modern health service.
- e) The New Hospital Programme Acceleration. The Act will place the New Hospital Programme on a statutory footing with legally binding completion dates for each wave. Wave 1 (2025 to 2030) and RAAC hospital replacements will proceed as currently planned. For Waves 2 to 4, the Act will require the Secretary of State to publish binding annual progress reports to Parliament, with the National Audit Office empowered to certify whether the programme is on track. Where a scheme falls behind its statutory timetable, the Secretary of State must publish an explanation and remediation plan within 60 days. The Act will also establish a modular construction preference for all new hospital builds where clinically appropriate, reducing construction timelines by 30 to 50% compared to traditional methods and providing a guaranteed pipeline for UK modular construction capacity.

OPERATIONAL

Backlog triage.

Within 90 days of Royal Assent, NHS England will complete a national triage of all high-risk backlog items, categorising each by clinical impact, safety risk, and remediation cost. The triage will produce a prioritised national remediation schedule. The first tranche of Rapid Remediation works (targeting the 500 highest-risk items nationally) will commence within six months.

RAAC acceleration.

Within 60 days, the Department of Health will publish the updated site-by-site RAAC assessment and confirm the eradication timetable for each affected site. Emergency procurement for the three highest-risk RAAC hospitals will commence within 90 days.

Single glazing audit.

Within six months, every trust will submit a complete window audit identifying all single-glazed clinical areas, with estimated replacement costs. A national replacement programme, prioritising buildings with the oldest glazing and the highest energy consumption, will be published within 12 months.

Capital protection.

From the first financial year following Royal Assent, the capital ring-fence will be in force. The Department of Health will publish quarterly capital spending reports, and any variance from planned capital expenditure will be reported to Parliament by the NAO.

##### NHS6.2: Technology Estate Modernisation

The Problem

The NHS’s technology estate is a patchwork of systems that do not talk to each other, hardware that is past end-of-life, and cybersecurity defences that are inadequate against modern threats. The WannaCry attack in 2017 was not a sophisticated operation. It exploited a known vulnerability in software that had been publicly patched two months earlier. The NHS was vulnerable because it was running unsupported operating systems, because trusts had not applied available patches, and because there was no centralised mechanism to enforce compliance with basic cybersecurity standards. The attack cost £92 million, cancelled thousands of appointments and operations, and diverted ambulances from affected hospitals. In 2018, every NHS organisation checked still failed cybersecurity assessments. The lesson was clear: the NHS’s technology infrastructure was a national security vulnerability. The response was inadequate: NHS Digital estimated the cost of meeting basic cybersecurity standards at £1 billion and declined to fund it.

The interoperability problem is equally severe. NHS3 of this framework establishes the data architecture, the FHIR standards, and the Disease Monitoring Service that will enable data to flow across the system. But data cannot flow through hardware that does not exist, over networks that are unreliable, or on systems that cannot be updated. The Darzi report found the NHS to be “in the foothills of digital transformation,” with many trusts operating at low digital maturity. Electronic patient records exist in some trusts but not others. Where they exist, they frequently cannot communicate with systems in neighbouring trusts, in primary care, or in community services. Clinicians resort to phone calls, faxes, and printed letters to share information that should be available at the click of a button. The Federated Data Platform, the NHS App, and other digital initiatives remain subscale or underutilised because the underlying infrastructure cannot support them.

The cost of technological obsolescence is paid in clinical time. Every minute a clinician spends waiting for a system to load, re-entering data that should have transferred automatically, or walking to another department because the network is down, is a minute not spent with a patient. The NHS2 workforce framework targets a 40% reduction in documentation burden. That target is unachievable if the technology that clinicians use every day actively impedes their work. The productivity gap that Darzi identified, with the NHS still below its 2019 productivity level, is substantially a technology gap. The NHS employs more staff than it did before the pandemic but produces fewer outputs per staff member, in significant part because the technology that should amplify human effort instead retards it.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Infrastructure Act will establish:

- a) Mandatory Minimum Technology Standards. The Act will empower the Secretary of State to set, by regulation, mandatory minimum standards for the NHS technology estate, enforceable against every trust and primary care provider. The initial standards, to be published within six months of Royal Assent, will include: no device connected to the NHS network may run an operating system that has passed its manufacturer’s end-of-support date; all devices must have current security patches applied within 14 days of release; all trusts must achieve Cyber Essentials Plus certification within 24 months; all clinical systems must support FHIR interoperability standards (as established under NHS3) within 36 months; and all trusts must maintain a complete, auditable asset register of every device connected to their network. Non-compliance with mandatory standards will be a matter for the Health Standards Authority (NHS2), which will have power to issue compliance notices, require remediation plans, and, in cases of persistent non-compliance that create patient safety risks, direct emergency intervention funded from the trust’s allocation.
- b) The NHS Technology Replacement Fund. The Act will create a dedicated, ring-fenced fund for the systematic replacement of end-of-life technology across the NHS estate. The Fund will operate on a rolling five-year cycle, replacing approximately 20% of the installed base each year to ensure that no device in the NHS is ever more than five years past its optimal replacement date. The Fund will be centrally managed by the NHS National Procurement Authority (NHS4), which will negotiate volume discounts, standardise specifications, and ensure that replacement devices meet interoperability requirements from day one. The Fund will also cover network infrastructure: switches, routers, cabling, and wireless access points that are currently beyond end-of-life in many trusts. The objective is a technology estate where every clinician has access to a device that is fast, secure, reliable, and connected, and where the words “it takes ages to load” are never spoken in a clinical setting again.
- c) Cybersecurity as Critical National Infrastructure. The Act will designate the NHS technology estate as critical national infrastructure for the purposes of cybersecurity regulation. This designation will trigger enhanced obligations under the Network and Information Systems Regulations, including: mandatory incident reporting to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) within one hour of detection; annual penetration testing of all trust networks by NCSC-certified providers; a national NHS Security Operations Centre (SOC), operating 24/7, with visibility across the entire NHS network and authority to isolate compromised segments in real time; and criminal liability for senior officers of trusts that fail to apply critical security patches within the mandatory 14-day window, where the failure leads to a patient safety incident. The WannaCry attack was preventable. The patches existed. The warnings had been issued. The failure was institutional: no one had the authority or the incentive to enforce compliance. This provision creates both.
- d) The Universal Clinical Platform. The Act will require all NHS trusts and primary care providers to migrate to a common clinical platform within five years. The platform will be procured through the tournament-style model established under NHS3.1, with multiple vendors invited to compete for modules (patient administration, clinical records, prescribing, diagnostics, scheduling) that must conform to the FHIR architecture mandated by NHS3. The objective is not a single monolithic system. It is a platform of interoperable modules, any of which can be replaced without disrupting the whole, but all of which share a common data standard and a common user interface logic. A clinician moving from one trust to another should find the same core system, the same data structures, and the same workflows. The current landscape, in which every trust operates a different combination of systems requiring different training, different workarounds, and different data entry processes, is an interoperability failure, a training failure, and a safety failure. The Universal Clinical Platform resolves all three.

OPERATIONAL

Technology audit.

Within 90 days, every trust will submit a complete technology audit to NHS England, identifying: every device connected to the network (type, age, operating system, patch status); every clinical system in use (vendor, version, FHIR compliance status); network infrastructure age and capacity; and cybersecurity certification status. The audit will establish the national baseline against which progress toward Mandatory Minimum Standards will be measured.

End-of-life device replacement.

Within 12 months, the Technology Replacement Fund will complete the first wave of replacements, targeting all devices running end-of-support operating systems. The estimated scale, based on WannaCry-era assessments and subsequent audits, is approximately 200,000 to 300,000 devices nationally. Replacement devices will be procured centrally through the NHS National Procurement Authority at volume prices.

NHS Security Operations Centre.

Within six months, the national SOC will be operational, initially monitoring the 50 trusts with the highest cyber risk profiles (assessed by NCSC). Full national coverage will be achieved within 18 months. The SOC will be staffed jointly by NHS technology specialists and NCSC secondees, ensuring that the NHS benefits from the same threat intelligence and response capabilities as other critical national infrastructure.

Universal Clinical Platform procurement.

Within six months, NHS England will publish the platform specification and launch the tournament-style procurement under NHS3.1 governance. Vendor selection for core modules will be completed within 18 months. The first trusts will migrate within 24 months, with the programme targeting full national migration within five years. The migration will be managed by a dedicated programme team reporting directly to the Health Standards Authority, with ring-fenced funding from the Technology Replacement Fund.

##### Summary of Legislative Requirements

NHS6 is built on the NHS Infrastructure Act, introduced alongside the NHS Core Mission Act (NHS1), the NHS Workforce Act (NHS2), the NHS Information Systems Act (NHS3), the NHS Procurement and Anti-Corruption Act (NHS4), the NHS Public Health Act (NHS5), and the Tax Reset Act (E6) in the first King’s Speech.

###### NHS Infrastructure Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: Statutory capital ring-fence prohibiting transfers from capital to revenue, enforceable by the Comptroller and Auditor General. Rapid Remediation Programme with simplified approval pathway for high-risk and significant-risk maintenance, with statutory targets of eliminating high-risk backlog within five years and significant-risk within ten. RAAC eradication deadline of 2032, with predominantly RAAC hospitals replaced by 2030 and emergency procurement powers. Single glazing elimination from all clinical facilities by 2030. New Hospital Programme placed on statutory footing with legally binding wave completion dates, annual progress reports, NAO certification, and modular construction preference. Mandatory Minimum Technology Standards enforceable by the Health Standards Authority, including end-of-support prohibition, 14-day patching requirement, Cyber Essentials Plus within 24 months, and FHIR compliance within 36 months. NHS Technology Replacement Fund for rolling five-year device and infrastructure replacement. NHS technology estate designated critical national infrastructure with mandatory incident reporting, annual penetration testing, 24/7 Security Operations Centre, and criminal liability for patch non-compliance. Universal Clinical Platform migration within five years through tournament-style procurement.

Delivered operationally: National backlog triage within 90 days. First 500 high-risk remediation works within six months. RAAC site-by-site assessment published within 60 days. Single glazing audit within six months, replacement programme within 12 months. Capital ring-fence in force from first financial year. Technology audit within 90 days. End-of-life device replacement (200,000 to 300,000 devices) within 12 months. NHS SOC operational within six months, full coverage 18 months. Universal Clinical Platform specification within six months, first migrations 24 months, full migration five years.

##### Funding NHS6

NHS6 is the most capital-intensive component of the framework. It is also the one with the most clearly quantified cost of inaction. The question is not whether the NHS can afford to invest. It is whether the NHS can afford not to.

The cost of the backlog. The maintenance backlog stands at £15.9 billion and is growing at approximately £2 billion per year. Deferred maintenance is more expensive than timely maintenance: a roof repair deferred by five years typically costs three to five times more than the original estimate because water ingress damages structural elements, electrical systems, and clinical equipment below. The high-risk backlog of £3.5 billion represents works that, if not completed, will cause catastrophic failure, service closure, or serious harm. Every year of deferral increases the total cost. The Rapid Remediation Programme does not create new spending. It brings forward spending that will occur regardless, but at lower cost and lower risk.

The capital ring-fence. This provision does not increase capital spending. It prevents existing capital allocations from being diverted. The £4.3 billion raided between 2014/15 and 2018/19 was not saved. It was spent on revenue, while the capital projects it should have funded were deferred, escalating in cost. The ring-fence saves money by preventing the most expensive form of capital mismanagement: diversion followed by escalation.

RAAC eradication. The current programme allocation is £1.6 billion over four years (2026/27 to 2029/30). The total programme cost for the seven predominantly RAAC hospitals is expected to exceed £7 billion over the programme lifetime. Some individual hospitals have already required more than £500 million in mitigation works. The alternative to funded replacement is unplanned structural failure in an occupied clinical building. The cost comparison is not between investment and no investment. It is between planned investment and catastrophic failure.

Technology estate. NHS Digital estimated the cost of meeting Cyber Essentials Plus at £1 billion and declined to fund it. The WannaCry attack cost £92 million in a single incident. Subsequent cyber attacks have continued. The annualised cost of cyber incidents, including service disruption, data recovery, cancelled appointments, and reputational damage, exceeds £150 million per year. A £1 billion investment in cybersecurity pays for itself within seven years at current loss rates, and that calculation excludes the unquantifiable cost of a successful attack on patient records or clinical systems during a medical emergency. The Technology Replacement Fund, estimated at approximately £500 million per year for rolling device and infrastructure replacement, prevents the accumulation of the technological debt that made WannaCry possible and that makes the next attack inevitable.

Energy savings. The NHS estate consumed 11.3 billion kilowatt hours of energy in 2024/25. Single glazing replacement alone reduces heating energy by 20 to 30% in affected buildings. Comprehensive fabric improvements (insulation, glazing, heating controls, LED lighting) can reduce energy consumption by 30 to 50%. At current energy prices, this represents hundreds of millions per year in avoided cost, contributing directly to the NHS’s net zero target and releasing revenue that would otherwise be spent on energy bills.

Productivity gains. Darzi identified that the NHS remains below its 2019 productivity level despite employing more staff. A significant component of this productivity gap is technological: slow systems, manual data entry, lack of interoperability, and time spent on workarounds. The Universal Clinical Platform, combined with the Technology Replacement Fund, directly addresses this gap. Even a 2% productivity improvement across the NHS workforce, the target set by the government’s own Spending Review, would generate the equivalent of billions per year in additional clinical capacity without hiring a single additional member of staff. The investment in technology that enables this productivity gain is among the highest-return capital investments available to the state.

The 2025 Spending Review committed £44 billion of capital over four years. The 10 Year Infrastructure Strategy commits at least £64 billion over a decade. NHS6 does not assume that these commitments are insufficient. It assumes they are at risk. Every previous capital commitment to the NHS has been eroded, raided, or deferred. NHS6’s capital ring-fence converts political commitments into legal obligations. That is its most important function.

##### Cross-References to Other NHS Framework Documents

NHS1 (Back to Basics Campaign): The 70% front-line spending ring-fence depends on a functioning estate. Clinical services cannot operate in buildings that are structurally dangerous. The capital ring-fence in NHS6 protects the physical platform on which NHS1’s service delivery targets depend.

NHS2 (Workforce Crisis Management): Staff morale and retention are directly affected by the quality of the working environment. Darzi found that crumbling estates contribute to staff burnout. The Rapid Remediation Programme and Technology Replacement Fund create working conditions that support the workforce strategy. The Health Standards Authority gains enforcement powers over technology compliance.

NHS3 (Information Systems and Data Capitalisation): NHS3 establishes the data architecture (FHIR standards, Disease Monitoring Service, Data Authority). NHS6 provides the physical infrastructure to carry it: the devices, networks, and platform on which NHS3’s data flows. The Universal Clinical Platform is the hardware-side delivery mechanism for NHS3’s software-side vision. The tournament-style procurement model established in NHS3.1 governs the platform competition.

NHS4 (Procurement and Anti-Corruption): The NHS National Procurement Authority centrally procures replacement devices, construction materials, and energy infrastructure. The Procurement Integrity Unit reviews major capital contracts. The Price Index benchmarks estates and technology spending. NHS4’s anti-PFI provisions (mandatory audit, compulsory purchase powers for bad-value contracts) directly protect NHS6 capital investment from the PFI trap.

NHS5 (Public Health for the 21st Century): NHS6 infrastructure and capital programmes fund the physical facilities for Community Kitchens, teaching kitchens in schools, geriatric care centres, and the National Activity Infrastructure. The capital ring-fence ensures that prevention infrastructure is not sacrificed to acute revenue pressures.

NHS7 (forthcoming): Social care integration requires shared technology platforms and physical co-location of services. NHS6’s Universal Clinical Platform and estates investment provide the infrastructure for NHS7’s integrated care model.

##### Conclusion: The Foundation Beneath Everything

Every other policy in this framework depends on buildings that stand up, systems that work, and networks that are secure. NHS1’s service targets cannot be met in hospitals where operating theatres are closed because ventilation has failed. NHS2’s workforce strategy cannot succeed if staff are demoralised by a working environment that is visibly decaying around them. NHS3’s data revolution cannot happen on devices running unsupported software over unreliable networks. NHS4’s procurement savings cannot be realised if capital budgets are raided to cover revenue deficits. NHS5’s prevention programmes cannot be delivered without Community Kitchens, teaching kitchens, and geriatric care centres that have to be built somewhere, with capital that has to be protected.

Infrastructure is not glamorous. It does not win elections. It does not generate headlines. It is the reason why capital investment has been the first casualty of every spending squeeze for fifteen years. But it is the foundation beneath everything else. A health service whose buildings are crumbling, whose technology is obsolete, and whose infrastructure is dangerous is not a health service that can deliver any of the ambitions set out in NHS1 through NHS5 or NHS7. It is a health service that is consuming its own capital base, spending ever more to maintain ever less, and producing a steadily deteriorating physical environment for patients and staff.

The numbers are stark. A £15.9 billion backlog, growing by £2 billion per year. A £37 billion capital shortfall identified by Darzi. 49 hospital sites with RAAC. 51 trusts with backlogs above £100 million. 200,000 or more devices that need replacing. A cybersecurity estate that has never met basic standards. An energy bill of 11.3 billion kilowatt hours in buildings that waste heat through single-glazed windows and uninsulated walls. A New Hospital Programme that will not be complete until 2046.

NHS6 does not solve all of this overnight. But it does three things that no previous approach has done. First, it makes the capital ring-fence law, ending the practice that has caused more damage to the NHS estate than any other single factor. Second, it creates a rapid remediation pathway that removes the bureaucratic obstacles to fixing things that are broken, accepting that a leaking roof does not need a three-stage business case. Third, it treats the technology estate with the same seriousness as the physical estate, recognising that a hospital whose IT systems fail is as clinically compromised as one whose roof fails. The capital ring-fence protects the investment. The Rapid Remediation Programme directs it. The Technology Replacement Fund and Universal Clinical Platform modernise it. Together, they rebuild the foundation on which the entire NHS stands.

#### NHS7. Social Care Integration

Governing Principle

The NHS treats you. Social care looks after you. The boundary between the two is an administrative fiction that has no basis in the reality of how illness, ageing, and disability actually work. A patient who has a hip replacement is treated by the NHS. When the surgeon has finished, the same patient needs rehabilitation, pain management, help washing, help eating, and help getting home. That is social care. The patient does not experience a transition between two systems. The patient experiences a single episode of need. But the two systems that serve that need are funded differently, governed differently, staffed differently, assessed differently, and charged for differently. The result is a gap. And people fall into it. Every day. In their thousands.

In England, an average of 13,000 patients per day remain in hospital despite being medically fit for discharge. One in seven acute hospital beds is occupied by someone who does not need to be there. In 2024/25, delayed discharges cost the NHS over £2 billion. In winter months, the figure rises: 272,000 bed days were lost to delayed discharge in December 2024 alone. Over 57% of patients who were medically fit for discharge at some point during winter 2024/25 remained in hospital longer than they needed to. The number of patients staying in hospital for over 21 days reached 19,180 in the worst week of winter, an 8.1% increase from the start of the season. Sixty-three percent of trusts saw delayed discharge performance deteriorate between summer 2024 and summer 2025. Only 40 to 45% of patients ready for discharge actually leave hospital when they are ready.

The causes of delayed discharge are multiple, but the dominant factor is a lack of capacity in social care. One third of all delayed discharges are directly attributable to insufficient social care provision: patients waiting for home care packages, care home placements, or intermediate care beds that do not exist or cannot be staffed. A further 28% are caused by interface problems: NHS trusts and social care partners spending too long negotiating who is responsible for what. The remaining third is attributable to hospital processes, care transfer hub delays, and wellbeing or safeguarding concerns. The pattern has been stable for years. Initiatives have been launched, funds announced, targets set. The numbers have not improved. If anything, they have worsened. The delayed discharge rate rose from 10.1% to 11.0% of bed days between summer 2024 and summer 2025. The NHS entered winter 2025/26 in a worse position than the previous year.

This is not solely a funding problem, though funding is catastrophically inadequate. Overall public spending on adult social care in England was approximately £27.8 billion in 2024/25. The sector employs 1.6 million people. But decades of austerity have hollowed out the system. Spending was cut in real terms during the 2010s, and although it has increased since, it has not kept pace with rising demand, rising costs, or rising complexity. The National Living Wage increase of 6.7% in 2025/26 and the 1.2% rise in employer National Insurance contributions created an additional £2.4 billion funding hole that the £880 million Social Care Grant uplift does not begin to fill. The Association of Directors of Adult Social Services reported a funding gap of over £1 billion just to stand still. The workforce is increasingly dependent on international recruitment: by 2024/25, almost one in four social care workers (23.5%) came from outside the UK and EEA, up from one in twelve (8.2%) in 2019/20. Changes to skilled worker visas from July 2025 threaten to choke this pipeline without any strategy for replacing it through domestic recruitment.

The previous government’s charging reforms, the Dilnot cap on lifetime care costs, were cancelled by the current government in July 2024. The current government has established the Casey Commission, led by Baroness Louise Casey, to recommend long-term social care reform. The commission began work in April 2025. Its first phase will report in 2026. Its final report is due in 2028. This is the third independent commission on social care reform in England in thirty years. The Royal Commission on Long Term Care reported in 1999. Its key recommendation was rejected. The Dilnot Commission reported in 2011. Its recommendations were enacted, delayed, delayed again, and then cancelled. The sector’s assessment is blunt: another commission, another delay. BASW England stated: “we do not need a new Commission to tell us what we already know.” Care England warned: “this commission must not become another exercise in managing decline.”

Progress agrees. We have had the diagnosis. We have had the commissions. We have had the white papers. We do not need another decade of consensus-building followed by cancellation. We need a statutory framework that integrates social care with the NHS at the point of delivery, that guarantees discharge pathways for every patient, and that builds a social care workforce capable of meeting demand. NHS7 provides that framework. It is not a comprehensive redesign of social care funding, which is properly the work of a cross-party settlement with decades-long implications that no single-term government should attempt unilaterally. It is instead the integration of social care with the NHS at the specific points where the gap between the two systems causes the most harm: at discharge, at crisis, and at the boundary between health and care in the community.

##### NHS7.1: The Discharge Guarantee

The Problem

The current system operates on a principle that sounds reasonable but produces catastrophic results: no patient should be discharged from hospital until an appropriate care package is in place. In theory, this protects vulnerable people from being sent home without support. In practice, it means that 13,000 people per day remain in hospital beds they do not need, at a cost of £395 per night per patient, while the care packages they are waiting for take weeks or months to materialise, or never materialise at all. The patient deteriorates. Hospital-acquired infections accumulate. Muscle mass declines. Cognitive function diminishes. Independence that existed on admission is lost during the wait. By the time a care package is arranged, the patient often needs more care than they would have needed if they had been discharged promptly. The delay creates the dependency it was supposed to prevent.

The problem is compounded by a perverse interaction between patient choice and system capacity. Patients and families have the right to express preferences about post-discharge care: which care home, which home care provider, what location, what type of support. These preferences are legitimate. But the system has no mechanism for distinguishing between a patient who has no discharge option and a patient who is declining the options that exist. A patient waiting for a specific care home that has no available bed, while an equivalent care home five miles away has a vacancy, occupies the same hospital bed as a patient for whom no care provision exists anywhere. The hospital cannot discharge either of them. The result is that patient choice, which should be a right exercised in the community, becomes a mechanism for occupying hospital beds at £395 per night.

Meanwhile, the patient who is waiting in A&E for an acute bed, the patient whose elective surgery has been cancelled because no ward bed is available, and the patient being treated in a corridor because the hospital is full, are all paying the price for a discharge system that cannot distinguish between need and preference. This is not a criticism of patients or families. It is a criticism of a system that offers them no structured pathway, no guaranteed option, and no clear timeline, and then allows the resulting uncertainty to consume the most expensive and most clinically critical resource in the NHS: the acute hospital bed.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Social Care Integration Act will establish:

- a) The Discharge Guarantee. The Act will establish a statutory guarantee that every patient who is medically fit for discharge will be offered at least one appropriate social care option within 48 hours of being declared fit for discharge. The option must be clinically appropriate (meeting the patient’s assessed care needs), safe (CQC-rated Good or above, or meeting equivalent standards for home care), and available (a bed, a package, or a placement that can accept the patient within 48 hours of acceptance). The option need not be the patient’s first choice. It must meet the patient’s needs. The guarantee places a statutory duty on the Integrated Care Board to ensure that sufficient social care capacity exists within its area to meet discharge demand. If the ICB cannot provide an option within 48 hours, it must fund emergency provision at its own cost, creating a direct financial incentive to invest in discharge capacity.
- b) The Structured Choice Framework. Once a patient has been offered an appropriate social care option under the Discharge Guarantee, a structured timeline applies. The patient and family will have 24 hours to accept or decline the offered option. If the option is accepted, discharge proceeds within 48 hours. If the option is declined, the patient retains the right to request alternative provision, but the hospital is no longer required to hold the acute bed. The patient will be transferred to a designated Discharge Assessment Unit (a step-down facility, not an acute ward) while alternative arrangements are made. The Discharge Assessment Unit will be lower-cost, non-acute, and staffed for rehabilitation and assessment rather than acute clinical care. The patient will continue to receive appropriate support, but will not occupy a bed that is needed for acutely unwell patients. If the patient or family arranges their preferred alternative within 14 days, they are discharged to it. If not, the original state-provided option remains available.

This provision will be contentious. It must be stated clearly why it is necessary. The current system treats every patient identically regardless of whether they have no options or are declining the options available. A patient who has been offered a safe, appropriate, CQC-rated care home placement and is declining it because they prefer a different facility is not in the same position as a patient for whom no care exists. Treating them identically means that both occupy acute beds at £395 per night, that A&E patients wait in corridors, that elective surgeries are cancelled, and that the overall system capacity is consumed by a process that has no resolution mechanism. The Discharge Guarantee does not remove choice. It provides a guaranteed option, a structured timeline, and a step-down pathway. No patient is discharged to the street. No patient is denied care. Every patient receives an appropriate option. What changes is that declining that option no longer entitles the patient to indefinite occupation of an acute hospital bed at public expense while other patients suffer the consequences.

- c) The Right to Return. To protect patients who accept the state-provided option and find it inadequate, the Act will establish a statutory Right to Return. If a patient is discharged to a care setting that fails to meet their assessed needs (as determined by a reassessment within seven days of discharge), the ICB must provide an alternative within 72 hours. The Right to Return ensures that the Discharge Guarantee does not become a mechanism for dumping patients into substandard care. It also creates accountability: ICBs that consistently discharge patients to settings that trigger Right to Return claims will face scrutiny from the Health Standards Authority (NHS2), providing a quality assurance mechanism that does not depend on the patient remaining in an acute hospital bed.
- d) Discharge Pathway Integration. The Act will require every ICB to establish a single Discharge Coordination Service, jointly staffed by NHS and local authority social care teams, co-located in every acute hospital. The Service will have a single point of accountability for every delayed discharge, with statutory authority to commission emergency social care provision (home care, residential care, intermediate care) without referral back to the local authority’s standard commissioning process. The Service will manage the Discharge Guarantee, the Structured Choice Framework, and the Right to Return as a single integrated pathway. Current data shows that 28% of delayed discharges are caused by interface problems between NHS trusts and social care partners. A co-located team with joint authority eliminates this category of delay entirely.

OPERATIONAL

Discharge Guarantee pilots.

Within six months of Royal Assent, the Department of Health will launch the Discharge Guarantee in 20 ICB areas, prioritising those with the highest rates of delayed discharge and the greatest proportion of bed days lost. Pilots will test the 48-hour guarantee, the Structured Choice Framework, the Discharge Assessment Unit model, and the Right to Return. An independent evaluation will report at 12 months, measuring: reduction in delayed discharge rates, bed days recovered, patient outcomes (readmission rates, patient experience, mortality at 90 days post-discharge), and A&E performance in pilot areas. National rollout will follow within 24 months.

Discharge Assessment Units.

Within 12 months, every acute hospital trust will be required to designate or create a Discharge Assessment Unit, separated from acute wards, with appropriate staffing for step-down rehabilitation and social care assessment. Units may be co-located on hospital sites, in nearby community facilities, or in repurposed intermediate care settings. Capital funding will be provided through the NHS6 Infrastructure Act. The objective is that no patient who has been offered and declined a Discharge Guarantee option occupies an acute bed.

Discharge Coordination Services.

Within six months, every ICB will establish its co-located Discharge Coordination Service in every acute hospital within its area. The Service will absorb existing discharge teams, transfer of care hubs, and social care liaison functions into a single integrated team. Staffing will be jointly funded from NHS and local authority budgets through the Better Care Fund, with additional ring-fenced allocation.

##### NHS7.2: Social Care as National Infrastructure

The Problem

The Discharge Guarantee cannot function if the social care capacity it depends on does not exist. The guarantee creates the legal obligation. NHS7.2 creates the capacity to meet it. Without NHS7.2, the Discharge Guarantee is an unfunded mandate. With it, the guarantee becomes a mechanism for driving investment toward the point of greatest system failure.

Social care in England is not a national system. It is 152 separate local systems, each funded differently, each setting different eligibility thresholds, each paying different rates to providers, and each making independent decisions about what level of service to provide. There are no binding national standards for provision. There is no national workforce strategy. There is no national commissioning framework. The result is a postcode lottery in which the care a person receives depends not on their needs but on where they live and how much money their local authority has left after meeting its other obligations. This is not a design. It is the absence of design. It is what happens when successive governments refuse to create a national framework for a service on which the NHS, the economy, and millions of vulnerable people depend.

The workforce crisis is the most immediate threat. The sector employs 1.6 million people, but pay is chronically low. The median hourly pay for independent sector care workers was barely above the National Living Wage. One quarter of staff are on zero-hours contracts. Annual turnover has been historically high, though it has recently fallen, largely because international recruitment brought in workers on fixed-term visa contracts with lower turnover rates. By 2024/25, international workers comprised 23.5% of the social care workforce, up from 8.2% in 2019/20. The government has now restricted skilled worker visas from July 2025. Monthly applications for Health and Care Worker visas collapsed from an estimated 18,300 in August 2023 to 2,300 in August 2024. The workforce that has been plugging the domestic recruitment gap is being removed without any strategy for replacing it. Skills for Care estimates that the sector will need an additional 470,000 posts by 2040 to keep pace with demographic growth. Meanwhile, the government cut £115 million from adult social care training funding, and the share of care workers with a relevant qualification has hit a new low.

The funding structure is equally dysfunctional. Social care is means-tested. The NHS is free at the point of use. A patient with cancer receives treatment, surgery, chemotherapy, and follow-up care from the NHS without charge. A patient with dementia, whose needs are equally medical and equally involuntary, can be charged catastrophic sums for their care, potentially losing their home to fund a condition they did not choose. The cap on lifetime care costs, recommended by Dilnot, enacted in 2014, has been delayed and then cancelled by every government since. The insurance problem, the risk that any individual could face unlimited care costs, remains unresolved. Addressing it properly requires a cross-party funding settlement that is beyond the scope of a single-term government. But the operational integration of social care with the NHS does not require solving the funding question. It requires building the infrastructure to deliver care where it is needed, when it is needed, to the standard that patients deserve.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The NHS Social Care Integration Act will establish:

- a) National Minimum Standards for Social Care Provision. The Act will empower the Secretary of State to set, by regulation, binding national minimum standards for adult social care, applicable to all local authorities and all registered providers. Initial standards will include: maximum waiting times for needs assessments (14 days from referral), maximum waiting times for care packages to commence after assessment (7 days for critical needs, 28 days for substantial needs), minimum staffing ratios for residential and nursing care, minimum qualification requirements for care workers (the Level 2 Care Certificate within 12 months of employment), and minimum pay rates for publicly funded care workers (indexed to the National Living Wage plus a social care supplement set by the Fair Pay Agreement). Standards will be enforced by CQC for providers and by the Health Standards Authority for ICB commissioning compliance. The objective is to end the postcode lottery: a person in Blackpool should receive the same standard of social care as a person in Surrey.
- b) The Social Care Workforce Guarantee. The Act will establish a statutory duty on the Secretary of State to maintain a national social care workforce strategy, updated annually, that ensures sufficient domestic recruitment to meet projected demand. The strategy will include: a national recruitment campaign, funded centrally and not dependent on local authority budgets; mandatory training funded through a restored and expanded national training fund (reversing the £115 million cut); a career progression framework from entry-level care worker through to advanced practitioner, with salary increments at each stage; a statutory right to a permanent contract for any care worker who has worked continuously for the same employer for 12 months (ending the zero-hours default); and a social care bursary scheme (modelled on the NHS bursary) for care workers undertaking the Level 3 and Level 5 qualifications while in employment. The Act will also require the Migration Advisory Committee to assess the social care workforce impact before any changes to visa eligibility that affect the Health and Care Worker route, ensuring that immigration policy does not destabilise a sector that now depends on international recruitment for one quarter of its workforce.
- c) Integrated Commissioning. The Act will require every ICB and its partner local authorities to establish a single Integrated Commissioning Board for health and social care, jointly accountable for the totality of health and social care spending within the ICB area. The Board will control the pooled Better Care Fund (currently approximately £9 billion nationally) and the social care element of the ICB allocation. Commissioning decisions that affect both health and social care, including all discharge-related provision, intermediate care, community rehabilitation, home care for people with long-term conditions, and residential care for people whose needs span health and social care, will be made by the Integrated Board rather than by parallel NHS and local authority processes. This provision eliminates the interface problem. There is no interface if there is one decision-maker.
- d) The Community Care Guarantee. The Act will establish a statutory right to a community care assessment for every person over 65 who presents to the NHS with an unplanned admission, and for every person of any age who is admitted to hospital three or more times within 12 months. The assessment will be conducted by the Integrated Commissioning Board’s community team (jointly staffed by NHS community nurses and local authority social workers), will identify unmet health and social care needs, and will produce a Community Care Plan that is shared with the patient’s GP, the ICB, and relevant social care providers. The purpose is upstream prevention: identifying the social care gap before it produces a hospital admission, rather than discovering it after the patient is occupying a bed. This provision integrates directly with the NHS5 Over-70s MOT: the geriatric assessment identifies clinical needs, the Community Care assessment identifies social care needs, and the combined plan prevents the crisis that produces the delayed discharge.

OPERATIONAL

National Minimum Standards.

Within six months of Royal Assent, the Department of Health will publish the first set of binding minimum standards. Existing CQC inspection frameworks will be updated to incorporate the standards within 12 months. The Health Standards Authority will publish ICB-level compliance data quarterly from year two.

Workforce Guarantee.

The restored national training fund will be operational within six months. The national recruitment campaign will launch within three months. The Fair Pay Agreement, already introduced through the Employment Rights Bill, will be accelerated to conclude within 12 months. The statutory right to a permanent contract after 12 months of continuous employment will take effect from Royal Assent.

Integrated Commissioning Boards.

Within 12 months, every ICB area will have established its Integrated Commissioning Board with a joint health and social care budget. Existing Better Care Fund governance structures will be absorbed into the new Boards. Joint accountability frameworks will be agreed between the Department of Health and the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government within six months.

Community Care Guarantee.

Within 12 months, every ICB will have a functioning community assessment team capable of delivering the Community Care Guarantee. Initial priority will be given to the 30 ICB areas with the highest rates of unplanned admissions among over-65s. Full national coverage will be achieved within 24 months.

##### Summary of Legislative Requirements

NHS7 is built on the NHS Social Care Integration Act, introduced alongside the NHS Core Mission Act (NHS1), the NHS Workforce Act (NHS2), the NHS Information Systems Act (NHS3), the NHS Procurement and Anti-Corruption Act (NHS4), the NHS Public Health Act (NHS5), the NHS Infrastructure Act (NHS6), and the Tax Reset Act (E6) in the first King’s Speech.

###### NHS Social Care Integration Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: Discharge Guarantee requiring at least one appropriate social care option within 48 hours of medical fitness for discharge, with ICB statutory duty to ensure capacity and financial liability for emergency provision if the guarantee is not met. Structured Choice Framework with 24-hour acceptance window, transfer to Discharge Assessment Unit for patients declining the guaranteed option, and 14-day alternative arrangement period. Right to Return with 7-day reassessment and 72-hour alternative provision for patients discharged to inadequate care. Discharge Coordination Service jointly staffed and co-located in every acute hospital. National Minimum Standards for adult social care provision including maximum waiting times, staffing ratios, qualification requirements, and minimum pay rates. Social Care Workforce Guarantee with statutory duty to maintain national workforce strategy, restored training fund, career progression framework, statutory right to permanent contract after 12 months, social care bursary, and mandatory Migration Advisory Committee assessment before visa changes affecting social care. Integrated Commissioning Boards jointly controlling pooled health and social care budgets in every ICB area. Community Care Guarantee of community assessment for every unplanned over-65 admission and every patient with three or more admissions within 12 months.

Delivered operationally: Discharge Guarantee pilots in 20 ICB areas within 6 months, national rollout 24 months. Discharge Assessment Units in every acute trust within 12 months. Discharge Coordination Services in every acute hospital within 6 months. National Minimum Standards published within 6 months, CQC incorporation 12 months. National recruitment campaign within 3 months. Training fund restored within 6 months. Fair Pay Agreement concluded within 12 months. Integrated Commissioning Boards operational in every ICB within 12 months. Community Care Guarantee teams in 30 priority ICBs within 12 months, full national coverage 24 months.

##### Funding NHS7

NHS7 is not a comprehensive social care funding reform. Progress is explicit about this. The question of how social care should be funded in the long term, whether through general taxation, social insurance, a cap on costs, or some combination, is a question with generational implications that requires cross-party agreement. What NHS7 does is fund the integration of social care with the NHS at the points of greatest failure, using resources that are already being spent, but spent badly.

The cost of inaction. Delayed discharges cost the NHS over £2 billion per year at an average of £395 per night per patient. This is dead money. It produces no clinical benefit. The patient is medically fit. They do not need the acute bed. They need a care package that costs a fraction of the hospital bed they are occupying. Every pound spent on social care capacity that enables discharge is a pound that releases an acute bed for a patient who needs it. The Discharge Guarantee does not create new spending. It redirects spending from the most expensive setting (acute hospital) to the most appropriate setting (community care). The net saving to the NHS is the difference between £395 per night for a hospital bed and the cost of the community care alternative: approximately £50 to £150 per day for home care, £100 to £200 per day for residential care. Even at the most conservative estimate, recovering 5,000 of the 13,000 daily delayed discharge beds would save the NHS approximately £450 million per year.

Integrated Commissioning. The Better Care Fund already pools approximately £9 billion of NHS and local authority funding. NHS7 does not increase this total. It creates a single decision-making body for how it is spent, eliminating the duplication, fragmentation, and interface costs that currently consume administrative resources while patients wait. The integration of commissioning is a governance reform, not a spending reform. Its cost is the cost of establishing the Integrated Commissioning Boards, which is marginal against a £9 billion fund.

Workforce investment. Restoring the social care training fund to adequate levels requires approximately £200 million per year, reversing the £115 million cut and providing the additional investment needed for the career progression framework and bursary scheme. The social care bursary scheme, modelled on the NHS bursary, will cost approximately £100 million per year at full scale. These are real costs. But they are costs that generate returns: a trained, stable workforce with lower turnover reduces agency spending (which currently costs the sector hundreds of millions per year), reduces safeguarding incidents, improves CQC ratings, and reduces the hospital admissions caused by inadequate community care. The Fair Pay Agreement will increase wage costs for providers, but the costs must be funded through the local government finance settlement, not absorbed by providers through reduced quality or staffing.

Discharge Assessment Units. Capital costs for establishing Discharge Assessment Units in every acute trust will be funded through the NHS6 Infrastructure Act. Running costs are substantially lower than acute ward costs: a step-down rehabilitation unit costs approximately £200 to £250 per day to operate, compared with £395 or more for an acute bed. The units pay for themselves by releasing acute capacity.

The Community Care Guarantee. Community assessment teams require investment in community nursing and social work capacity. The estimated cost of delivering 500,000 community care assessments per year (covering all unplanned over-65 admissions and high-frequency attenders) is approximately £150 to £200 million, funded through the Integrated Commissioning Board from the pooled health and social care budget. The return is measurable: every hospital admission prevented by an upstream community care intervention saves the NHS between £3,000 and £10,000 per admission, depending on length of stay. A 10% reduction in unplanned over-65 admissions would save the NHS approximately £1 billion per year.

The total net investment required for NHS7, above existing spending, is estimated at £500 to £700 million per year. The total savings generated, through reduced delayed discharge costs, reduced unplanned admissions, reduced agency staffing, and improved system efficiency, are estimated at £1.5 to £2.5 billion per year. NHS7 does not just pay for itself. It is one of the most cost-effective interventions in the entire framework. The obstacle has never been economics. It has been the political refusal to integrate two systems that should never have been separated.

##### Cross-References to Other NHS Framework Documents

NHS1 (Back to Basics Campaign): The 70% front-line spending ring-fence depends on beds being available for acute patients. Delayed discharges consume 1 in 7 acute beds. The Discharge Guarantee directly recovers capacity for NHS1’s service delivery targets. Every delayed discharge bed recovered is a bed available for elective surgery, emergency admission, or diagnostic assessment.

NHS2 (Workforce Crisis Management): The Social Care Workforce Guarantee aligns with NHS2’s workforce strategy: career progression frameworks, training investment, and the elimination of exploitative employment practices. The Health Standards Authority gains enforcement powers over ICB commissioning compliance and social care standards. The Fair Pay Agreement for care workers mirrors NHS2’s approach to sustainable workforce investment.

NHS3 (Information Systems and Data Capitalisation): Integrated Commissioning Boards depend on shared data across health and social care. The FHIR standards, NHS App, and Disease Monitoring Service established under NHS3 provide the data architecture. The Community Care Guarantee generates assessments that must be shared between GPs, hospitals, social care providers, and community teams through the NHS3 infrastructure. The Universal Clinical Platform (NHS6) provides the technology.

NHS4 (Procurement and Anti-Corruption): The NHS National Procurement Authority will develop standardised commissioning frameworks for social care provision purchased through Integrated Commissioning Boards, ensuring value for money and consistent quality across ICB areas. The Price Index will benchmark social care costs nationally.

NHS5 (Public Health for the 21st Century): The Over-70s MOT (NHS5.3) is the clinical counterpart to the Community Care Guarantee. The geriatric assessment identifies clinical needs; the community care assessment identifies social care needs. Together, they provide a comprehensive picture that prevents the crisis admission. The Dignity in Ageing provisions, including advance care planning, integrate directly with NHS7’s community assessment framework.

NHS6 (Infrastructure and Capital Investment): NHS6 funds the capital costs of Discharge Assessment Units, community care facilities, and the technology infrastructure that enables integrated commissioning. The Universal Clinical Platform provides the shared system on which NHS and social care staff access patient records, care plans, and assessment data. The capital ring-fence ensures that integration infrastructure is not sacrificed to revenue pressures.

##### Conclusion: One Patient, One System

The NHS was founded on a principle that illness should not be a source of financial ruin. Social care was left out. Seventy-seven years later, the consequences of that omission are measured in 13,000 people per day occupying hospital beds they do not need, in over £2 billion per year spent on patients who are medically fit to leave, in families selling their homes to pay for dementia care that the state would fund if the same brain had produced a tumour instead of plaques and tangles, and in a workforce of 1.6 million people paid so little that one quarter of them have been recruited from overseas because domestic workers will not accept the terms.

NHS7 does not solve all of this. The long-term funding question, the Dilnot cap, the means-testing threshold, the balance between state and individual responsibility, these are questions for a cross-party settlement that endures beyond a single parliament. Progress is honest about this. What NHS7 does solve is the operational failure at the boundary between health and social care. The Discharge Guarantee ensures that every patient has an option. The Structured Choice Framework ensures that declining that option does not consume an acute bed indefinitely. The Right to Return ensures that the guarantee is not a mechanism for dumping patients into inadequate care. The Integrated Commissioning Boards ensure that a single decision-maker controls the pooled budget. The Community Care Guarantee catches people before the crisis. The Workforce Guarantee builds the workforce to deliver it all.

The cost of NHS7 is £500 to £700 million per year above existing spending. The savings are £1.5 to £2.5 billion. The human cost of not acting is 13,000 people per day in beds they do not need, in hospitals they should not be in, losing independence they will never recover, while the patients who do need those beds wait in corridors, in ambulances, and on waiting lists that grow longer every month. NHS7 is the final piece of the framework. It connects everything that comes before it. Without it, the NHS remains a system that treats illness brilliantly and then abandons people at the hospital door. With it, for the first time, the patient experiences a single system from admission to recovery, from hospital to home, from treatment to care. One patient. One system. One standard. That is what the NHS was always supposed to be.

#### Implementation Framework

Governance, Culture, Measurement, and Financial Sustainability

##### Introduction: From Policy to Reality

NHS1 through NHS7 constitute the most comprehensive reform of the National Health Service since its foundation. The organising principle is not expansion. It is focus, reallocation, and productivity. The NHS does not need more money thrown at a system that wastes what it already has. It needs to spend what it has on the things that matter, stop spending on the things that do not, and build the institutional discipline to tell the difference. Together, the seven policies mandate: a statutory Core Mission definition with 70% front-line spending ring-fence, service transfers to specialist providers, and a Treatment Coverage Commission (NHS1); a workforce reorientation that replaces agency dependency with permanent staffing, cuts documentation burden by 40%, consolidates six regulators into one Health Standards Authority, and makes existing staff radically more productive (NHS2); a national data architecture with FHIR interoperability and Disease Monitoring Service (NHS3); a Procurement Authority with anti-corruption enforcement, compulsory PFI audit, and 15% unit cost reduction targets (NHS4); a National Food Service, Health Incentive Scheme, and Over-70s MOT (NHS5); a statutory capital ring-fence with rapid remediation and technology modernisation (NHS6); and a Discharge Guarantee with integrated commissioning and social care workforce guarantee (NHS7).

None of this will work unless it is implemented well. Policy is a document. Implementation is a decade of decisions, each of which can reinforce or undermine the intent. The history of NHS reform is a history of excellent policy papers producing mediocre or actively harmful outcomes because the implementation framework was an afterthought: insufficiently specified, insufficiently governed, and insufficiently honest about the cultural transformation required.

This document addresses the four dimensions that determine whether NHS1 through NHS7 succeed or fail: governance and power structures (who decides what, and who is accountable when decisions are wrong); cultural transformation (how the NHS thinks about itself, its patients, and its purpose); measurement and evaluation (how we know whether things are getting better, and how we avoid the measurement becoming the enemy of the thing measured); and financial sustainability (how the framework survives the fiscal pressures of demographic change and political cycles). It also specifies the success metrics against which Progress will be judged, honestly and publicly, at the end of a parliamentary term.

##### 1. Governance and Power Structures

###### 1.1. The Problem with NHS Governance

The NHS has been reorganised more frequently than almost any comparable institution in the world. Each reorganisation promises to simplify. Each produces new layers. The Lansley reforms of 2012, which Darzi identified as uniquely damaging, abolished Primary Care Trusts and Strategic Health Authorities and replaced them with Clinical Commissioning Groups, NHS England as an arm’s-length body, Public Health England, Health Education England, and a suite of other bodies. The Cameron government alone added more management layers than it removed. The 2022 Health and Care Act then abolished CCGs and created Integrated Care Boards, while beginning the process of absorbing NHS England back into the Department of Health. The result is a system where lines of accountability are unclear, where the same decision requires sign-off from multiple bodies, and where no single person can be identified as responsible when something goes wrong.

Progress’ approach is different. We do not propose another reorganisation. We propose a clear specification of who has power over what, under the framework established by NHS1 through NHS7, and a set of accountability mechanisms that ensure power is exercised visibly and consequentially.

###### 1.2. The Power Map

Secretary of State for Health and Social Care

Retains ultimate ministerial accountability for the NHS. Under the framework, the Secretary of State’s powers include: setting National Minimum Standards for social care (NHS7); directing RAAC eradication and emergency procurement (NHS6); publishing binding targets for New Hospital Programme waves (NHS6); setting food environment regulations (NHS5); and reporting to Parliament on capital spending (NHS6). The Secretary of State does not have power to override clinical decisions, direct individual procurement awards, or interfere with the operational independence of the bodies established below. The Secretary of State sets the destination. The system navigates.

The Health Standards Authority (NHS2)

The single most important new body in the framework. The HSA replaces CQC’s inspection function with a body that has genuine enforcement powers. Its jurisdiction includes: workforce standards and documentation burden (NHS2); technology compliance and Mandatory Minimum Standards (NHS6); ICB commissioning compliance including social care (NHS7); and quality assurance across all NHS-funded services. The HSA reports directly to Parliament, not to the Secretary of State. This independence is essential. If the regulator reports to the minister, the minister can suppress inconvenient findings. A regulator that reports to Parliament is accountable to the public. The HSA’s Chief Inspector is a statutory officer whose removal requires a vote of the Health and Social Care Committee, not a ministerial decision.

The NHS National Procurement Authority (NHS4)

Controls all procurement above the mandatory threshold, negotiates national framework contracts, and manages the NHS Price Index. Incorporates the Procurement Integrity Unit with criminal investigation powers. Reports to the Secretary of State but has operational independence in procurement decisions, modelled on the relationship between HM Treasury and the Office for Budget Responsibility. No minister can direct a specific procurement award. This is the anti-corruption firewall.

The NHS Data Authority (NHS3)

Controls access to NHS data assets, governs the Federated Data Platform, and manages the tournament-style procurement for data analytics and clinical platform modules. Operates under strict governance to prevent both commercial exploitation and bureaucratic hoarding. The Data Authority’s dual mandate is: maximise the research, clinical, and commercial value of NHS data while maintaining absolute patient trust. It is accountable to the Health Standards Authority for data governance and to the Secretary of State for strategic direction.

The Treatment Coverage Commission (NHS1)

An independent clinical body that determines what the NHS covers and what it does not, replacing the current ambiguity with transparent, evidence-based boundaries. The Commission’s determinations are binding on the Secretary of State. This is deliberately designed to remove coverage decisions from political pressure. A politician who can add treatments to the NHS for electoral advantage without funding them is a politician who will do so. The Commission prevents this.

Integrated Care Boards

ICBs remain the operational tier. Under the framework, their responsibilities are expanded and their accountability sharpened. ICBs are the statutory bodies responsible for: meeting the Discharge Guarantee (NHS7) including financial liability for emergency provision; ensuring sufficient social care capacity within their area; operating Integrated Commissioning Boards with partner local authorities (NHS7); delivering the Over-70s MOT and Community Care Guarantee (NHS5/7); and meeting the 70% front-line spending target (NHS1). ICB Chief Executives are personally accountable for performance within their area. They are subject to annual performance evaluation by the Health Standards Authority, measured against published operational benchmarks, with replacement following persistent underperformance (see Section 1.3). The ICB is where the framework meets reality. If the ICB works, the framework works. If it does not, no amount of legislation will compensate.

Trust Chief Executives and Clinical Directors

Retain operational control of their organisations. The framework does not micromanage trusts. It sets standards (HSA), procurement rules (Procurement Authority), data requirements (Data Authority), capital protections (ring-fence), and discharge obligations (Discharge Guarantee). Within these boundaries, trusts have professional autonomy. Trust Chief Executives, like ICB Chief Executives, are subject to annual HSA performance evaluation with published results and replacement for persistent underperformance. The framework’s approach to trust governance is: tell them what must be achieved, give them the tools and funding to achieve it, hold them personally accountable for results, and replace them if they cannot deliver. Do not tell them how to run their hospitals. Do tolerate honest difficulty. Do not tolerate sustained incompetence.

###### 1.3. Accountability Mechanisms

Four mechanisms ensure accountability without creating bureaucratic paralysis:

Transparency

Every body in the framework publishes quarterly performance data, accessible to the public through the NHS App and the HSA website. Data includes: ICB-level delayed discharge rates, waiting times, staff vacancy rates, capital spending against allocation, technology compliance status, procurement savings, and patient satisfaction. Transparency is not a reporting burden. It is the single cheapest and most effective accountability mechanism available. An ICB that is failing and knows the data is public will act to avoid the scrutiny. An ICB that is failing in private will continue to fail.

Zealous evaluation of senior leadership

The framework draws a hard distinction between frontline staff and senior leaders. An NHS nurse, doctor, porter, or healthcare assistant who makes an honest mistake in a pressured environment is protected by the just culture framework and the Safe Harbour provision (NHS2). That is how you build a learning organisation. But an ICB Chief Executive, a Trust Chief Executive, a Finance Director, or a Clinical Director is not in the same position. These are people who sought leadership roles, who are paid six-figure salaries to run complex organisations, and whose underperformance is not a mistake but a failure of stewardship. The standard for senior leaders is not support first. It is performance or replacement.

The Health Standards Authority will conduct annual performance evaluations of every ICB Chief Executive and every Trust Chief Executive, measured against a published set of operational benchmarks: waiting time trajectories, delayed discharge rates, financial performance, workforce retention, technology compliance, capital spending against allocation, and patient satisfaction. These evaluations will be published. An executive who meets or exceeds benchmarks retains their post. An executive who falls short receives a formal improvement notice with a 12-month remediation period. An executive who fails to meet the improvement notice, or who fails to meet benchmarks in two consecutive years without an approved Implementation Period, will be replaced. There is no third chance. There is no permanent tenure in a role where people’s lives depend on competent management.

This is not punitive. It is the same standard that applies to any senior executive in any well-run organisation. The NHS has suffered for decades from a culture in which senior leaders can preside over institutional failure, receive performance-related pay, and move to another trust to repeat the pattern. The implementation framework ends this. The HSA’s evaluation is independent of the trust board (which may have incentives to protect its own executive), independent of the Secretary of State (who may have political reasons to avoid embarrassing dismissals), and based entirely on published data that the executive has seen and had the opportunity to act upon. The question is not whether an executive is a good person. The question is whether the organisation they lead is performing. If it is not, and the executive has had time and support to improve it, the organisation gets a new leader.

Support and learning for frontline staff

Below the executive level, the framework’s default response to poor performance is support, not sanction. The Health Standards Authority’s intervention in an underperforming ward, department, or clinical team begins with a diagnostic review and improvement plan. The just culture framework (detailed in Section 2) distinguishes between system errors (addressed through process improvement), individual errors (addressed through retraining and support), and deliberate harm or reckless disregard (addressed through disciplinary or criminal processes). The overwhelming majority of clinical incidents are system errors. A system that treats them as individual failures produces concealment, not safety. Sanctions for frontline staff are reserved for cases where support has been provided and declined, or where patient safety is at immediate risk. The objective is a system that learns from failure rather than hiding it. But this support-first principle applies to the people who deliver care, not to the people who are paid to lead the organisations that deliver it. Leaders are held to a different standard because they hold a different responsibility.

Professional autonomy within boundaries

The framework does not abolish clinical autonomy. It constrains the system within which autonomy is exercised. A clinician has complete freedom to make clinical judgements about patient care. A trust has freedom to organise its services as it sees fit. Neither has freedom to ignore procurement rules, data standards, technology requirements, or discharge obligations. The distinction is between professional judgement (which the framework protects) and institutional compliance (which the framework enforces). These are not in tension.
