A clinician who has access to reliable data, functional technology, adequate staffing, and a building that is not falling down is a clinician whose professional autonomy is enhanced, not diminished, by the framework.

Ministerial distance

The framework deliberately places distance between ministers and operational decisions. The Secretary of State sets strategy, legislation, and funding levels. The HSA, Procurement Authority, Data Authority, and Treatment Coverage Commission execute within their statutory mandates. Ministers do not direct procurement awards, inspection findings, treatment coverage decisions, or data access. This is not a democratic deficit. It is a recognition that NHS operational decisions are too important, too technical, and too consequential to be made by people whose primary incentive is re-election. The democratic accountability is in the legislation that creates the framework, the funding levels set by Parliament, and the ministerial power to appoint and remove the leaders of the statutory bodies. The operational accountability is in the framework itself.

##### 2. Cultural Transformation

###### 2.1. Why Culture Matters More Than Structure

Every NHS reform in the past thirty years has changed the structure. Almost none has changed the culture. Structures can be legislated in a parliamentary session. Culture changes over a generation, or not at all. The NHS’s cultural problems are not problems of bad people. They are problems of good people operating in a system that has, over decades, produced a set of institutional reflexes that work against the interests of patients and staff: defensive documentation driven by fear of litigation rather than commitment to care; compliance theatre in which processes are followed performatively without genuine engagement; hierarchical deference in which junior staff do not challenge senior colleagues even when patient safety is at risk; and a pervasive pessimism, a belief that things cannot improve, that reform is something done to the NHS rather than by it, and that the best anyone can hope for is to survive until retirement.

Progress cannot legislate culture. But it can create the conditions in which a different culture can grow. NHS2’s 40% documentation reduction removes the defensive bureaucracy that drains clinical energy. NHS6’s infrastructure investment gives staff working environments that communicate respect rather than neglect. NHS7’s Discharge Guarantee gives staff the tools to do what they already want to do: move patients through the system rather than watching them languish. The implementation framework adds one further element: a symbolic framework that gives the cultural transformation a language and a set of commitments that clinicians and support staff can own.

###### 2.2. The NHS Oath

Doctors take the Hippocratic Oath. Lawyers are called to the Bar. Military officers are commissioned. These are not mere ceremonies. They are identity-forming rituals that establish a set of commitments, publicly made, that shape how the individual understands their role. The NHS has no equivalent. A nurse, a porter, a healthcare assistant, a receptionist, a manager, an administrator: all serve the same institution, all share the same purpose, but none has ever been asked to articulate what that purpose means to them personally, or to commit to it in front of their colleagues.

Progress proposes the introduction of an NHS Oath, to be taken voluntarily by all NHS staff, clinical and non-clinical, upon joining the service, and renewed annually. The oath is not a legal instrument. It does not create contractual obligations. It does not replace professional codes of conduct. It is a cultural artefact: a statement of shared commitment that gives language to the values that most NHS staff already hold but that the system has never asked them to express.

The oath will be developed through consultation with NHS staff, patient groups, and professional bodies, but Progress proposes the following principles as the foundation:

First, do no harm.

I will never knowingly act in a way that puts a patient at risk, and I will speak up when I see others doing so, regardless of their seniority or my own. Patient safety is not negotiable. It is not balanced against convenience, budget, reputation, or hierarchy.

I will treat every patient as I would treat my own family.

Not with detachment, not with clinical distance, but with the urgency and care I would bring if the person in front of me were someone I loved. This does not mean abandoning professional boundaries. It means never forgetting that the patient is a person, not a case, not a number, not a bed.

I will use evidence and trust my judgement.

Data informs. Protocols guide. But in the moment of decision, I am the person in the room. I will use every tool available to me, and I will also trust the knowledge, experience, and instinct that no algorithm can replace. When the data says one thing and my professional judgement says another, I will make the call, document the reasoning, and accept responsibility for the outcome.

I will act with courage when courage is needed.

There are moments in clinical care and in institutional life when the right thing to do is clear but difficult. I will not defer when a patient needs an advocate. I will not stay silent when a system is failing. I will not wait for permission when a life is at stake. The NHS was built by people who refused to accept that illness should be a matter of wealth. That refusal required courage. So does the daily work of keeping it alive.

I will forgive mistakes and accept consequences.

I work in a system where errors are inevitable. I will not conceal my own errors or punish others for theirs. I will report, learn, and improve. I accept that an error honestly reported is the foundation of a safer system, and that an error concealed is a danger to every patient who follows. I also accept that accountability and forgiveness are not opposites. I can be forgiven for an honest mistake and still accept the consequences it produces.

I serve the public. The public does not serve me.

The NHS belongs to the people of this country. I am its custodian, not its owner. I will never allow institutional convenience to override patient need, professional prestige to override staff welfare, or bureaucratic process to override common sense. When the system is wrong, I will say so. When I am wrong, I will hear it.

The oath is introduced voluntarily. It is not imposed. Staff who choose not to take it face no penalty. But the oath will be prominently displayed in every NHS facility, recited at induction ceremonies, and offered annually at a service-wide NHS Day (proposed for 5 July, the anniversary of the NHS’s founding). The purpose is not compliance. It is identity. A system whose staff have articulated, publicly, what they believe in, is a system that holds itself to a higher standard than any regulator can impose.

###### 2.3. Psychological Safety and the Learning Culture

The oath’s commitment to reporting errors and challenging authority requires a system that does not punish people for doing either. The framework establishes this through three mechanisms.

The just culture framework

NHS2’s Health Standards Authority will implement a national just culture policy, distinguishing between system errors (which are addressed through process improvement), individual errors (which are addressed through support and training), and deliberate harm or reckless disregard (which are addressed through disciplinary or criminal processes). The overwhelming majority of clinical incidents are system errors. A system that treats them as individual failures produces concealment, not safety. The just culture framework makes the distinction explicit and binding.

Freedom to Speak Up

The existing Freedom to Speak Up Guardian role will be strengthened. Every trust will be required to have at least one full-time Guardian (not a part-time addition to an existing role). Guardians will report directly to the Health Standards Authority, not to trust management, ensuring independence. Annual data on speaking-up activity, outcomes, and any retaliation will be published at trust level. The HSA will have power to investigate and sanction any trust where evidence of retaliation against whistleblowers is found.

The learning infrastructure

NHS3’s data architecture enables the systematic analysis of clinical incidents, near-misses, and outcomes across the entire NHS. The Disease Monitoring Service can identify patterns that are invisible at trust level but clear at population level. The implementation framework mandates that this capability is used not just for surveillance but for learning: quarterly national learning bulletins, published to all staff, identifying systemic risks, sharing innovations, and celebrating improvements. The NHS should be the largest learning organisation in the world. It has the data to make this possible. It has lacked the governance to make it happen.

##### 3. Measurement and Evaluation

###### 3.1. The Measurement Trap

What gets measured gets managed. This is true. It is also dangerous. A system that is obsessively measured produces behaviour optimised for the metric rather than the outcome the metric was supposed to represent. The NHS has extensive experience of this phenomenon. The four-hour A&E target produced hospitals that redesigned pathways to hit the target rather than to improve patient experience: patients moved to assessment units at 3 hours 55 minutes were not receiving better care, they were being administratively reclassified. The 18-week referral-to-treatment target produced waiting list management strategies that bore no relationship to clinical priority. Targets for GP access produced appointment systems that were technically compliant but practically useless: a patient who can get a telephone appointment within 48 hours but cannot see their GP for three weeks has met the target and not received care.

The instinct in the face of this evidence is to add more metrics, to refine the measurement, to close the loopholes. This instinct is wrong. Every additional metric creates an additional axis of gaming. The correct response is not more measurement. It is better measurement, combined with the professional judgement to know when the measurement is telling you something important and when it is lying.

Progress’ approach to measurement rests on three principles. First, measure outcomes, not processes. The patient does not care whether they were triaged within 15 minutes. They care whether they were treated effectively and with dignity. Second, measure trends, not snapshots. A trust whose A&E performance dropped from 80% to 75% while implementing a major system change is not necessarily failing. A trust whose performance has declined steadily for three years is. Third, leave room for human judgement. The single most important question in NHS evaluation is not any metric. It is this: is the care in this hospital better today than it was five years ago? That question cannot be answered by a dashboard. It can be answered by patients, by staff, and by experienced evaluators who spend time in the organisation and talk to the people who work and are treated there.

###### 3.2. The Measurement Framework

Primary indicators

These are the metrics against which the framework’s success will be publicly judged. They are deliberately few, deliberately outcome-focused, and deliberately resistant to gaming.

Acute care waiting times

The proportion of patients seen within the 18-week referral-to-treatment standard. This is a blunt instrument but it is the metric the public understands. The target: return to the 92% standard within the life of a parliament. Measured quarterly, published nationally and at trust level.

Patient recommendation rate

The percentage of patients who, when asked, would recommend the service they received to a family member. This is the single best proxy for care quality. It captures clinical outcomes, communication, dignity, and overall experience in a single number. It is resistant to gaming because it is based on the patient’s subjective experience, which cannot be reclassified or administratively adjusted. The target: 85% recommendation rate nationally within five years. Measured through the existing Friends and Family Test, expanded to capture all inpatient, outpatient, and community contacts.

Healthcare worker retention

The percentage of staff who remain in post after one year, three years, and five years. This is the best proxy for working conditions, morale, and the effectiveness of the workforce strategy (NHS2). A system that retains its staff is a system that is working. A system that loses them is not. The target: reduce voluntary turnover by 25% within five years. Measured quarterly through the Electronic Staff Record.

Procurement cost reduction

The percentage reduction in unit costs for standardised NHS supplies, measured against the NHS Price Index (NHS4). This is the direct financial accountability measure for the Procurement Authority. The target: 15% reduction in unit costs for the top 100 commodity categories within three years.

Population health indicators

Adult obesity prevalence, smoking prevalence, alcohol-specific hospital admissions, and healthy life expectancy by deprivation decile. These measure the long-term impact of NHS5’s prevention framework. They will not move quickly. A reduction in obesity prevalence takes five to ten years to manifest in population data. The target: measurable improvement in all four indicators within a parliamentary term, with the expectation that the most significant gains will be in smoking prevalence (building on existing downward trends) and alcohol-specific admissions (where alcohol care teams produce rapid results). Healthy life expectancy by deprivation decile is the ultimate equity measure: the framework succeeds if the gap narrows.

###### 3.3. Secondary Indicators

Secondary indicators provide diagnostic depth but are not used for headline accountability. They include: regulatory compliance costs as a proportion of trust budgets (should decline as HSA replaces CQC); staff morale measured through the annual NHS Staff Survey (discretionary effort index, recommendation rate, and burnout prevalence); delayed discharge rates (should decline as NHS7’s Discharge Guarantee takes effect); system resilience during winter and surge periods (measured by excess mortality, ambulance response times, and critical care occupancy during peak demand); documentation burden (measured through NHS2’s baseline audit and tracked quarterly); and capital spending against allocation (the capital ring-fence compliance measure). Secondary indicators are published alongside primary indicators but are used for system learning rather than public judgement.

###### 3.4. Qualitative Evaluation

Numbers alone are not enough. The Health Standards Authority will conduct annual qualitative evaluations of a representative sample of trusts, ICBs, and primary care networks. Evaluations will be conducted by experienced assessors who spend a minimum of five working days in each organisation, observing clinical practice, speaking to staff at all levels, speaking to patients and families, and reviewing governance records. The evaluation will answer three questions: is the care in this organisation good? Is it getting better or worse? And what is preventing it from being better? The qualitative evaluation is published alongside the quantitative data, providing the context that dashboards cannot.

This is expensive. It requires skilled assessors and substantial time. It is worth it. A qualitative evaluation that identifies a cultural problem, a leadership failure, or a systemic bottleneck prevents more harm than a year of dashboard monitoring. The NHS has never lacked data. It has lacked the interpretive capacity to understand what the data means. The qualitative evaluation provides that capacity.

###### 3.5. The Permission to Be Temporarily Worse

This is perhaps the most important and most counterintuitive element of the measurement framework. When implementing a major system change, performance will temporarily decline. A trust migrating to the Universal Clinical Platform (NHS6) will have a period of reduced efficiency while staff learn the new system. An ICB implementing the Discharge Guarantee (NHS7) will have a period of disruption while new pathways are established. A hospital undergoing rapid remediation (NHS6) will lose capacity while works are in progress. If the measurement framework punishes these temporary declines, it creates a perverse incentive to avoid change. Trusts that know they will be penalised for a performance dip will defer the migration, delay the remediation, and resist the new pathway, because the metric rewards stability even when stability means stagnation.

The framework therefore establishes a formal process for declaring an Implementation Period. During an Implementation Period (maximum 12 months, renewable once with HSA approval), a trust or ICB is assessed against a trajectory rather than an absolute target. The question is not are you meeting the 92% standard? but are you on track to meet it by the end of the Implementation Period? This permission to be temporarily worse is the permission to improve. Without it, the system will optimise for the measurement and never change. With it, the system can tolerate the disruption that improvement requires.

##### 4. Financial Sustainability

###### 4.1. The Demographic Challenge

The NHS budget will need to grow in real terms for the next 20 to 25 years. This is not a policy choice. It is an arithmetic consequence of demographic change. The over-85 population is projected to double by 2045. The number of centenarians has already doubled between 2004 and 2024. Age is the single strongest predictor of healthcare utilisation: a person over 85 consumes approximately five times the NHS resources of a person aged 40. As the baby boomer generation ages through their 70s, 80s, and 90s, demand for acute care, geriatric care, social care, and end-of-life care will increase substantially regardless of the success of prevention programmes.

Progress is honest about this. The NHS budget must expand during the demographic ageing phase. Pretending otherwise, or promising that efficiency alone will absorb demographic growth, is a lie that every government has told and that reality has exposed every time. The question is not whether the NHS will cost more, but how the increase is funded, how it is managed, and what happens on the other side.

On the other side is an important and underappreciated fact. The demographic bulge is not permanent. Birth rates are declining. The working-age population is stabilising. At some point in the 2050s or 2060s, the ageing bulge will have passed through the system. The NHS will then face the opposite problem: a system built for peak demand operating in a period of declining demand. If the expansion is funded through permanent revenue commitments (dedicated NHS taxes, ring-fenced allocations), the system will have structural overcapacity. If it is funded through temporary mechanisms that can be adjusted, the system can scale back gracefully. The implementation framework must plan for both phases: the expansion and the contraction.

###### 4.2. Funding the Expansion

Reallocation before expansion

The framework’s first principle is that the NHS does not need more money. It needs to spend the money it has on the right things. NHS1 transfers non-Core Mission services out of the NHS, redirecting their revenue to acute care. NHS2 eliminates 3 billion pounds per year in agency spending by replacing it with a permanent workforce that costs less and performs better. NHS4 targets 2 to 2.5 billion per year in procurement savings through volume negotiation and price transparency. NHS7 recovers over 2 billion per year in delayed discharge costs by moving patients to appropriate, cheaper care settings. The Documentation Reduction Target (NHS2) frees the equivalent of billions in clinical time that is currently consumed by non-essential paperwork. The regulatory consolidation from six bodies to one saves over a billion per year in compliance costs. None of this is new money. It is existing money redirected from waste to care. The framework is designed so that the NHS can dramatically improve outcomes within its current funding envelope, by focusing the institution, eliminating bureaucratic overhead, and holding leadership accountable for how every pound is spent.

Economic growth as the long-term underwriter

Over the 20 to 25 year demographic expansion, some real-terms growth in the NHS budget will be necessary regardless of efficiency gains. The E-series policies (particularly E1 through E12) are designed to generate the economic expansion that produces the tax revenue to fund this growth without politically toxic tax rises or unsustainable borrowing. Progress’ economic framework is therefore the precondition for the long-term sustainability of its NHS framework. But the near-term programme, within the life of a parliament, is funded entirely through reallocation and efficiency, not through additional expenditure. This is the honest position: the NHS has enough money to be excellent, if it stops wasting a third of it.

The capital ring-fence as fiscal discipline

NHS6’s statutory capital ring-fence does not just protect capital investment. It imposes fiscal discipline on the revenue side. A government that cannot raid capital to cover revenue overspends must either fund revenue adequately or explain to Parliament why it has not. The ring-fence forces honest budgeting. This is a constraint that benefits the system even though it is painful for the chancellor.

Pension liability management

The NHS Pension Scheme is one of the largest defined-benefit schemes in the world. Its liabilities are sensitive to workforce composition: the shift from agency to permanent staff under NHS2 increases the number of scheme members even if total headcount is stable or declining. Progress will commission an independent actuarial review of the scheme within the first year of government, with a mandate to propose adjustments that ensure long-term sustainability without breaking existing commitments to current members. The review will consider: the balance between employer and employee contributions; the impact of longer working lives on scheme liabilities; the interaction between the pension scheme and the workforce strategy (a scheme that penalises part-time or portfolio working will undermine NHS2’s flexible workforce model); and the transition from defined benefit to defined contribution for new entrants, if actuarially necessary. This is not a commitment to cut pensions. It is a commitment to honesty about the liabilities and a plan for managing them.

###### 4.3. Revenue Generation Within the Framework

The framework contains several mechanisms that generate revenue or reduce costs independently of general taxation:

Health data commercialisation

The NHS holds the largest longitudinal health dataset in the world: 67 million patient records, cradle to grave, linked to outcomes, genomics, prescribing, and social determinants. Properly governed and anonymised, this data is extraordinarily valuable to pharmaceutical companies, medical device manufacturers, AI developers, and academic researchers. NHS3’s Data Authority will license access to anonymised datasets through a structured commercial programme, with revenue ring-fenced to NHS operational budgets. The estimated revenue potential is 500 million to 1 billion pounds per year, based on comparable programmes internationally (notably the Finnish Findata model and the Danish national registry). This revenue is not speculative. It requires robust governance (which NHS3 provides), public trust (which the Data Authority’s independence provides), and commercial capability (which the tournament-style procurement model provides). The data already exists. The governance now exists. The revenue follows.

Procurement savings

NHS4’s Procurement Authority targets a 15% reduction in unit costs for commodity categories. At current NHS procurement spending of approximately 30 billion per year on goods and services, a 15% saving on even half of this spend generates 2 to 2.5 billion per year. This is not hypothetical. It is the documented experience of every comparable system that has centralised procurement with volume-based negotiation. The Carter Review identified variation of 10 to 50% in the prices paid by different trusts for identical products. Eliminating this variation is the simplest efficiency gain in the entire framework.

Anti-corruption savings

NHS4’s Procurement Integrity Unit targets fraud, corruption, and waste in NHS procurement. The NHS Counter Fraud Authority estimates that fraud costs the NHS approximately 1.2 billion per year. Enhanced investigation, mandatory disclosure, and criminal prosecution will not eliminate all fraud, but a 30 to 50% reduction is achievable based on international comparators, generating 360 to 600 million per year in recovered or prevented losses.

PFI renegotiation

NHS4’s compulsory audit of all PFI contracts, with buy-out or renegotiation powers, targets the estimated 2 billion per year in excess PFI costs. Even partial renegotiation, achieving 20 to 30% reductions in annual unitary charges, would generate 400 to 600 million per year in savings over the remaining contract life.

Prevention returns

NHS5’s prevention framework is the largest long-term revenue generator in the system. Obesity costs the UK economy 126 billion per year. Smoking costs the public finances 16.5 billion. Alcohol costs 27.4 billion. Even marginal reductions in prevalence generate billions in avoided costs. These savings do not accrue immediately or entirely to the NHS budget, but they reduce the growth rate of NHS demand, which is the single most important fiscal variable in long-term health spending projections. A 1% reduction in the annual growth rate of NHS demand, sustained over a decade, is worth tens of billions in cumulative avoided spending.

##### 5. Success Metrics: How Progress Will Be Judged

Progress will publish, on its first day in government, a scorecard of commitments against which it will be judged at the end of a parliamentary term. This scorecard will be updated quarterly and published on the NHS App. Progress has no interest in hiding behind process measures. The public will know, in plain language, what we promised and whether we delivered.

###### 5.1. Primary Commitments (End of Parliament)

Waiting times

Return to the 92% 18-week referral-to-treatment standard for elective care. No patient waiting more than 52 weeks for treatment. A&E: 78% seen within four hours, moving toward restoration of the 95% standard.

Patient experience

85% patient recommendation rate nationally across all service types.

Workforce retention

25% reduction in voluntary turnover across all NHS staff groups. Nursing vacancy rate below 5%.

Procurement

15% reduction in unit costs for top 100 commodity categories. First PFI contracts renegotiated or bought out.

Population health

Adult smoking prevalence below 8% (from 10.6%). Measurable reduction in adult obesity prevalence. Alcohol-specific hospital admissions declining year-on-year. Healthy life expectancy gap between most and least deprived deciles narrowing.

Delayed discharge

Reduction from 13,000 patients per day to below 7,000. 80% of medically fit patients discharged within 48 hours of being declared fit.

Infrastructure

High-risk maintenance backlog reduced by 50%. Zero capital-to-revenue raids. All NHS devices on supported operating systems. NHS Security Operations Centre fully operational.

###### 5.2. Secondary Commitments (Tracked Quarterly)

Documentation burden

30% reduction toward the 40% target (NHS2).

Staff morale

NHS Staff Survey discretionary effort index improved from baseline.

Data interoperability

80% of trusts FHIR-compliant within the parliamentary term.

Prevention infrastructure

National Food Service operational in pilot areas. Community Kitchen programme underway. Health Incentive Scheme piloted and evaluated.

Social care workforce

Fair Pay Agreement concluded. Social care vacancy rate below 6%. Training fund fully operational.

###### 5.3. The Honest Reckoning

Not all of these targets will be met. Some will be met early. Some will be missed. Some will need to be revised as implementation reveals realities that policy could not foresee. Progress commits to publishing, annually, an honest assessment of progress against each target, including an explanation of where targets have been missed, why, and what is being done about it. This is not a concession of failure in advance. It is a recognition that a government that promises perfection and delivers excuses is worse than a government that promises honesty and delivers accountability. The public has been promised 40 new hospitals by 2030, a world-beating track and trace system, and 300,000 new homes a year. They have learned to distrust politicians who set targets they know they will not meet. Progress will set targets it believes it can meet, and when it cannot, it will say so and explain why, in public, with data, and without spin.

##### Conclusion: The Machine and the Mission

The NHS is a machine. It has 1.4 million moving parts. It operates every hour of every day. It processes millions of interactions per week. Like any machine, it requires maintenance, fuel, skilled operators, and a clear understanding of what it is for. NHS1 through NHS7 provide the maintenance (NHS6), the fuel (reallocation of existing waste through NHS1’s service transfers, NHS2’s agency elimination, and NHS4’s procurement savings), the skilled operators (NHS2’s workforce reorientation), and the understanding of purpose (NHS1’s Core Mission, NHS5’s prevention, NHS7’s integration). This implementation framework provides the operating manual: who controls what, who is replaced when they fail, how the machine knows if it is working, what it does when a part breaks, and how it pays for the energy it consumes.

But the NHS is not just a machine. It is the institutional expression of a moral commitment: that no one in this country should suffer or die because they cannot afford to be treated. That commitment is held not by ministers or managers or regulators. It is held by the 1.4 million people who work in the NHS and the 67 million people who depend on it. The NHS Oath is not a management tool. It is a recognition that the most powerful force in any institution is the shared belief of the people within it. If NHS staff believe the system can improve, it will improve. If they believe it cannot, no amount of legislation will make it.

The implementation framework is designed to create the conditions for belief. Governance structures that are clear and consequential. A cultural framework that honours the commitment NHS staff already hold. A measurement system that rewards improvement rather than punishing the disruption that improvement requires. A financial model that is honest about costs, honest about returns, and honest about the demographic challenge ahead. And a set of success metrics that the public can read, understand, and use to hold Progress accountable.

This is the final document in the NHS policy framework. NHS1 through NHS7 plus this implementation framework constitute a complete programme for government. They are detailed, costed, cross-referenced, and designed to be implemented as an integrated system rather than a collection of independent policies. They are ambitious. They are honest about what they can and cannot achieve. And they are grounded in a single conviction that has not changed since 5 July 1948: the NHS is sacred in principle. Our job is to make it work in practice.

#### CS1: Restoring Ministerial Authority

“The Government Does Not Control the Government”

Governing Principle

The most important fact about the British Government is the one that almost nobody understands: the Government does not control the Government. Ministers are notionally responsible for their departments, accountable to Parliament for every decision taken in their name, and possessed of the democratic mandate that alone confers legitimacy on the exercise of state power. In practice, they control almost nothing. The permanent bureaucracy controls the senior appointments process through the Civil Service Commission and the Senior Leadership Committee. It controls the flow of information to ministers through the submission chain. It controls the timetable of implementation through the approval culture. It controls the drafting of legislation through the Office of Parliamentary Counsel, to which ministers have no independent access. And it controls the definition of “merit” by which its own members are selected, promoted, and protected from dismissal. The result is a system in which elected politicians provide the theatre of democratic legitimacy while permanent officials exercise the substance of governmental power. This is the central constitutional deception of modern Britain, and it is the first thing that must be corrected.

The Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010 is the legislative foundation of this deception. Passed in the dying days of the Brown government, rushed through the parliamentary wash-up procedure in April 2010 with minimal scrutiny, CRAG put on a statutory footing a set of arrangements that had previously existed only by convention. It established the Civil Service Commission in statute and gave it exclusive authority to define what “merit” means for civil service appointments. It required that all appointments to the civil service be made “on merit on the basis of fair and open competition.” It prohibited special advisers from exercising any power over the management of any part of the civil service. And it provided no mechanism by which ministers could appoint or dismiss the senior officials who run their departments on a day-to-day basis. The effect was to give legal protection to a system in which the permanent bureaucracy selects, promotes, and retains its own members according to criteria it defines, under the oversight of a Commission whose own members are drawn from the same professional milieu. The Civil Service Commission’s first chair, Sir David Normington, stated explicitly that CRAG “empowered the Commission alone to decide what appointment by merit meant.” When the Coalition government proposed allowing ministers to choose their Permanent Secretary from a shortlist, the Commission blocked it.

The consequences are visible in every department of government. The civil service has grown 35% from its 2016 minimum to 549,660 as of March 2025, with 520,440 on a full-time equivalent basis. This growth occurred despite successive ministerial announcements of headcount caps, hiring freezes, and efficiency drives. In October 2023, Chancellor Jeremy Hunt imposed an “immediate” cap on civil service headcount. In the following two quarters, the civil service expanded by 1.3% and 1.6% respectively. Chancellor Rachel Reeves announced in March 2025 a target to cut administrative costs by 15% by the end of the parliament, implying a reduction of around 40,000 posts. By September 2025, the headcount had increased by 5,000. The pattern is consistent and unmistakable: ministers announce; the machine ignores. The policy profession alone has grown 116% since the 2016 referendum, adding 19,275 officials, while the operational delivery profession, which actually serves the public, has grown at a fraction of this rate in proportional terms. Three-quarters of civil servants now sit at Executive Officer grade and above, up from 60% in 2015, a phenomenon the Institute for Government identifies as “grade inflation” driven by promotional practices that the system controls and ministers do not.

The appointment of Permanent Secretaries, the most senior officials in each department, illustrates the problem with particular clarity. Under CRAG, the Civil Service Commission manages all recruitment to the Senior Civil Service. The Senior Leadership Committee, an internal body whose membership is dominated by serving Permanent Secretaries, decides whether vacancies are filled by external competition, internal competition, or “managed move”, in which a civil servant is transferred into the role without any competitive process at all. The House of Lords Constitution Committee described the Senior Leadership Committee in 2023 as “an opaque body” about which it “received contradictory accounts of the exact role it plays.” The Cabinet Secretary and the First Civil Service Commissioner gave different descriptions of who decides the selection route for senior appointments. The Senior Appointments Protocol, agreed in 2011 between the then Cabinet Secretary and the then First Civil Service Commissioner, does not “accurately reflect current practice,” according to the evidence of the Cabinet Secretary himself. The system for selecting the most powerful officials in the country is, by the admission of those who operate it, opaque, contradictory, and undocumented.

The Prime Minister’s formal role in this process is confined to choosing from a list of candidates deemed “appointable” by a panel chaired by the First Civil Service Commissioner. Secretaries of State, who must work with the Permanent Secretary on a daily basis and who are accountable to Parliament for their department’s performance, have no formal power of choice at all. They may suggest lines of questioning. They may meet candidates with a Commission representative present. They may not sit on the selection panel, add or remove candidates, or exercise any authority over who runs their own department. When a Permanent Secretary is manifestly failing, the minister cannot dismiss them. Departure must be negotiated through the Cabinet Secretary, with compensation agreed under the Civil Service Compensation Scheme, and the minister may be required to explain the decision to the Civil Service Commission. The system makes it easier to remove a Prime Minister than a Permanent Secretary.

This is not how the British state has always functioned. Before the Northcote-Trevelyan reforms of 1854, ministers held genuine authority over their departments. William Pitt the Younger hired, fired, and promoted on the basis of performance. He nurtured young talent intensively: Canning was placed in the Foreign Office in his thirties; Palmerston was appointed Secretary at War aged twenty-five. The Pitt-era state built infrastructure, won wars, and administered a global empire with a Whitehall establishment of a few hundred clerks. The Secretary of War’s office had thirty-five clerks in 1796. The Home Office had thirty-four permanent clerks. HM Treasury contained 142 clerks. The Ministry of Justice today has 90,000 employees and a backlog of approximately two million court cases. The Ministry of Defence alone employs nearly 60,000 civilian staff. The growth in size has not produced a growth in capability. By any reasonable measure, the Whitehall of the 1790s, directed by ministers with real authority over a small, competent, performance-driven workforce, delivered more than the Whitehall of the 2020s, in which 550,000 officials operate a system that no elected politician controls.

Other democracies have refused to accept this arrangement. In Australia, the Public Service Act 1999 provides that Departmental Secretaries are appointed by the Governor-General on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, and that their appointments may be terminated on the same basis. Since the removal of tenure under Prime Minister Paul Keating, Australian Departmental Secretaries serve on fixed-term contracts, typically of five years, and understand that failure to re-appoint following a change of government is a routine occurrence. The Prime Minister’s power is constrained by a reporting requirement from the Commissioner and the Secretary of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, but the final decision is unambiguously political. In New Zealand, the State Sector Act provides for chief executive appointments on fixed terms with performance agreements. In Singapore, Permanent Secretaries serve ten-year maximum terms and are rotated between ministries as a matter of deliberate policy, preventing the entrenchment of departmental fiefdoms. In every case, the principle is the same: the elected government appoints the senior officials who run the state, holds them to account for delivery, and replaces them when they fail. Britain is the outlier.

The argument against restoring ministerial authority rests on the claim that it would “politicise” the civil service. This argument is made in bad faith. The civil service is already political. It is political in its collective resistance to policies it dislikes. It is political in its control of information flows to ministers. It is political in its use of the media to undermine ministerial decisions. It is political in its definition of “merit” to favour candidates from within its own professional culture. What it is not is democratically accountable. The present system does not produce impartiality. It produces a form of institutional self-governance in which 550,000 public servants, led by a senior caste selected by its own members, pursue their collective institutional preferences without meaningful oversight from the people’s elected representatives. The Northcote-Trevelyan settlement was designed to end patronage. It has created something worse: a self-selecting permanent bureaucracy that is accountable to nobody and answerable to nothing except its own institutional culture. Progress will end this. The first step is to amend the Act that gives it legal protection.

##### CS1.1: Amend the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010

The Problem

CRAG 2010 is the single greatest legal barrier to effective ministerial control of the government machine. Its provisions establish a statutory monopoly for the Civil Service Commission over the definition of merit in civil service appointments. They prohibit special advisers from exercising management authority over any part of the civil service, ensuring that ministers’ closest political staff cannot direct the officials who execute policy. They provide no statutory mechanism for ministers to appoint or dismiss senior officials. And they entrench a recruitment framework in which the Commission’s Recruitment Principles have the force of law, binding the civil service and ministers alike, while being drafted by a body that is itself part of the permanent establishment. The effect is circular: the civil service defines the criteria by which its own members are selected, and those criteria have statutory protection from ministerial interference. No business, no military organisation, and no other democracy in the developed world operates on this basis. An incoming government cannot deliver a single element of its programme if the officials who execute that programme are selected by criteria the government cannot influence, cannot be dismissed when they fail, and cannot be replaced by people the government trusts to deliver.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Civil Service Reform Act will:

- a) Repeal Sections 10 to 13 of CRAG 2010, which establish the statutory requirement for appointment on merit through fair and open competition as defined exclusively by the Civil Service Commission. These sections will be replaced by provisions establishing that senior civil service appointments at Director General level and above are made by the relevant Secretary of State (or, for Permanent Secretaries, by the Prime Minister), from candidates who have been assessed as meeting published competence standards. The competence standards will be set by the Office of the Prime Minister (see CS3) in consultation with the relevant department, not by the Civil Service Commission. The principle of competence-based appointment is retained; the principle of exclusive Commission control is abolished.
- b) Amend Section 7 of CRAG 2010 to grant Secretaries of State explicit statutory authority to direct the management of civil servants within their departments, including the authority to issue binding instructions on priorities, resource allocation, and working methods. The current provision, which grants the Minister for the Civil Service a general power to manage the civil service, is interpreted by officials as a power held by the Cabinet Secretary on the Prime Minister’s behalf. It will be replaced by a provision that vests operational management authority in the relevant departmental minister, exercisable through the Directly Responsible Individual appointed under CS1.3.
- c) Repeal Section 8(5) of CRAG 2010, which prohibits special advisers from exercising any power in relation to the management of any part of the civil service. This provision was designed to prevent political interference in operational matters. Its practical effect has been to ensure that the only people in government with the political authority and the ministerial mandate to direct change are legally prohibited from doing so. The repeal will be accompanied by a revised Special Advisers’ Code that defines the scope of special adviser authority: advisers may direct the execution of ministerial priorities, commission work from civil servants, and require information from departments, but may not exercise disciplinary authority or make appointments below Director level without ministerial authorisation.
- d) Establish in statute that the Prime Minister has unfettered authority to appoint, re-appoint, and dismiss Permanent Secretaries and equivalent senior officials. The Prime Minister’s decision will be informed by an assessment of competence provided by the relevant Secretary of State and the Chief of Staff at the Office of the Prime Minister (see CS3), but will not be subject to approval, veto, or endorsement by the Civil Service Commission. For Director General appointments, the same authority will rest with the relevant Secretary of State, subject to the approval of the Prime Minister. Fixed-term contracts of no more than five years will replace permanent tenure at Permanent Secretary and Director General level, with renewal contingent on published performance assessments. This aligns with the Australian model, in which Departmental Secretaries serve on fixed terms with the explicit understanding that reappointment is contingent on performance and alignment with government priorities.
- e) This Act must be drafted in full before the general election. The legislative text must be prepared by a team assembled outside the civil service, because the civil service will not draft legislation that removes its own statutory protections. The Act will be introduced in the first King’s Speech and passed within the first session of Parliament. Every day of delay is a day in which the government does not control its own departments. The Bill must be short, clear, and narrow in scope: it amends CRAG, it does not attempt a comprehensive Civil Service Act. Comprehensive reform is the enemy of speed. The objective is to remove the legal barriers to ministerial authority within weeks, not to redesign the entire civil service framework within years.

OPERATIONAL

Pre-election preparation

Before the election, the Party will commission a legal team, working independently of the civil service, to draft the Civil Service Reform Bill in full. The draft will include a clause-by-clause commentary, an impact assessment, and a set of model secondary instruments (revised Civil Service Management Code provisions, revised Special Advisers’ Code) that can be laid immediately upon Royal Assent. The legal team will also prepare a comprehensive briefing for the Government Chief Whip on the parliamentary timetable required to pass the Bill within the first session, including strategies for managing House of Lords resistance.

Transitional competence framework

Within 30 days of taking office, the Office of the Prime Minister will publish a transitional competence framework for senior civil service appointments, replacing the Civil Service Commission’s Recruitment Principles for all posts at Director General level and above. The framework will specify the skills, experience, and delivery record required for each tier of senior appointment, drawn from the government’s priorities and the Charter Letters issued under CS7. The framework will apply immediately to all new appointments and will govern the reappointment decisions for existing post-holders when their fixed-term contracts come into effect under the Act.

International recruitment benchmarking

Within 60 days, the Office of the Prime Minister will publish a comparative analysis of senior public service appointment and dismissal practices in Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, Canada, and Estonia, establishing the international evidence base for the reforms and demonstrating that ministerial appointment authority is the norm in high-performing democracies, not the exception.

##### CS1.2: Reconstitute the Civil Service Commission

The Problem

The Civil Service Commission, as currently constituted, functions as the gatekeeper of a closed system. It defines what merit means for civil service recruitment. It oversees all senior appointments. It publishes Recruitment Principles that have statutory force. And it has used this authority to block ministerial involvement in the selection of the most senior officials. When the Coalition government proposed in 2012 that ministers should choose their Permanent Secretary from a shortlist, the First Civil Service Commissioner, Sir David Normington, declared that merit-based appointment was “incompatible with ministerial choice” and that CRAG empowered the Commission alone to define the principle. The Commission’s Recruitment Principles currently require that the selection panel’s recommendation is communicated to the Prime Minister, who may choose from a list of appointable candidates, but the determination of who is appointable remains exclusively with the Commission-chaired panel. For appointments below Permanent Secretary level, ministers have even less involvement. The Commission functions, in effect, as the HR department of a corporation that has no shareholders, no board of directors, and no obligation to deliver anything measurable to anyone.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Civil Service Reform Act will:

- a) Reconstitute the Civil Service Commission as an advisory and audit body, stripping it of its current gatekeeping authority over senior appointments. The reconstituted Commission will retain responsibility for ensuring that civil service recruitment below the Senior Civil Service is conducted fairly and without corruption. It will publish an annual report on the quality and diversity of civil service recruitment. It will investigate and report on allegations of improper patronage in appointments. But it will no longer define what merit means for senior appointments, approve or reject ministerial choices, or exercise a veto over who runs government departments. The distinction is between audit (which the Commission will retain) and control (which it will lose).
- b) Abolish the Senior Leadership Committee in its current form. The SLC, an internal body of serving Permanent Secretaries that decides how senior vacancies are filled, is the mechanism by which the permanent bureaucracy manages its own succession. It operates behind closed doors, its proceedings are confidential, and its decisions are not subject to ministerial approval. The Constitution Committee found its role “opaque” and received “contradictory accounts” of what it does. Under the reformed system, decisions on how senior vacancies are filled will be made by the relevant Secretary of State in consultation with the Office of the Prime Minister, informed by the Commission’s advisory assessment of available talent. The SLC’s talent-management and development functions will transfer to the Office of the Prime Minister.
- c) Require that the First Civil Service Commissioner be appointed by the Prime Minister from outside the civil service. The First Commissioner will serve a fixed term of no more than five years, will be subject to pre-appointment scrutiny by a select committee, and will be dismissible by the Prime Minister. The Commission’s membership will be required to include a majority of members with substantial experience outside the public sector, including in business, technology, the military, and academia. The Commission must never again be dominated by people whose careers have been spent within the system it is supposed to oversee.

OPERATIONAL

Immediate transparency measures

Within 14 days of taking office, the government will publish the full membership, terms of reference, minutes, and decision records of the Senior Leadership Committee, the Senior Appointments Protocol, and all related governance documents. The principle is simple: the public is entitled to know how the most powerful unelected officials in the country are selected. There will be no more opaque bodies making decisions about the leadership of the state behind closed doors.

Transition plan

The reconstituted Commission will be operational within 90 days of Royal Assent of the Civil Service Reform Act. During the transitional period, senior appointments will be made under the Prime Minister’s direct authority, informed by the competence framework published under CS1.1 and by assessments from the Office of the Prime Minister. The Commission’s legacy Recruitment Principles will cease to have statutory force upon Royal Assent.

##### CS1.3: The Directly Responsible Individual

The Problem

The British civil service does not have a functioning system of personal accountability for delivery. Permanent Secretaries are “accounting officers” responsible for the propriety and regularity of departmental spending, but they are not personally accountable for whether the department actually delivers the government’s programme. When a major project fails, when a policy is not implemented, when a department misses every target set by its own business plan, no named individual is held responsible. The Permanent Secretary may appear before a select committee, offer carefully phrased explanations drafted by the department’s communications team, and return to their office. Ministerial responsibility to Parliament, which was real in the era of Pitt and Palmerston, has become a constitutional fiction in which ministers take the blame for failures they did not cause, could not prevent, and in many cases were not told about. The civil service has achieved the extraordinary feat of operating a system with enormous power and zero accountability: officials exercise the substance of executive authority while ministers bear the consequences.

The concept of the Directly Responsible Individual, drawn from technology and military organisations, inverts this. A DRI is a named person who is personally responsible for delivering a defined outcome within a defined timetable, who has the authority to command the resources needed to do so, and who is replaced if they fail. The DRI model is used at Apple, at Amazon, and in military operations precisely because it solves the problem that the civil service has refused to solve: who, specifically, is responsible, and what happens to them when it goes wrong? The DRI model was proposed for the civil service by reformers within No. 10 in 2020 and found strong support among officials who were frustrated by the diffusion of responsibility within the existing system. It was not implemented because the government lacked the legal authority under CRAG to appoint outsiders to senior roles or to dismiss officials who resisted.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Civil Service Reform Act will:

- a) Establish the DRI as a formal role within the Senior Civil Service. Every government department will have a Directly Responsible Individual appointed by the Secretary of State with the approval of the Prime Minister. The DRI replaces the Permanent Secretary as the senior operational leader of the department. The DRI is personally responsible for the delivery of the department’s Charter Letter priorities (see CS7), has the authority to hire, fire, reorganise, and reallocate resources within the department, and reports directly to the Secretary of State. The DRI may be drawn from the existing civil service, from business, from the military, from technology, from academia, or from any other background. There is no requirement that the DRI be a career civil servant. There is a requirement that the DRI be demonstrably capable of delivering results at scale.
- b) DRIs will serve on fixed-term contracts of no more than three years, renewable once, with published performance agreements linked to the Charter Letter priorities. Performance will be assessed at six-month intervals by the Office of the Prime Minister’s Public Expenditure and Performance Unit. DRIs who deliver will be rewarded with performance-linked pay competitive with private sector equivalents in comparable roles. DRIs who fail will be replaced. The assessment will be published. There will be no ambiguity about whether a department is meeting its targets, no ambiguity about who is responsible, and no ambiguity about the consequences.
- c) The DRI will assume the Permanent Secretary’s role as Accounting Officer, with full responsibility for the propriety, regularity, and value for money of departmental expenditure. The existing Accounting Officer framework, in which Permanent Secretaries may seek a “ministerial direction” to record their objection to a ministerial decision while implementing it, will be retained. The DRI, like the current Permanent Secretary, will have the right to seek a direction if they believe a ministerial instruction conflicts with propriety, regularity, feasibility, or value for money. But the DRI, unlike the current Permanent Secretary, will also have the obligation to execute ministerial instructions with urgency once a direction has been given, rather than using the direction mechanism as a tool of delay. The responsibility married to authority principle, established in E10.4 of the Economic Policy Framework, governs the entire DRI model: every person with decision-making power has published metrics and personal consequences.

OPERATIONAL

Pre-election talent identification

Before the election, Progress will assemble a reserve army of potential DRI candidates: executives from business and technology, senior military officers, experienced project managers, and reform-minded officials within the existing civil service. Each candidate will be briefed on the Charter Letter priorities for their potential department, given access to the policy frameworks (E1 to E12, C1 to C13, NHS1 to NHS7, CS1 to CS10), and prepared for deployment on Day 1 or as soon as the Civil Service Reform Act receives Royal Assent. The talent acquisition function will be led by a dedicated appointment working directly with the party leader, operating independently of the civil service’s own talent-management apparatus.

Day 1 interim appointments

On the first day of government, and prior to the passage of the Civil Service Reform Act, the Prime Minister will use existing prerogative powers and the machinery of government flexibility to install interim leaders in priority departments. Where existing Permanent Secretaries are willing and able to operate as DRIs, they will be retained and given Charter Letters. Where they are not, they will be moved to non-operational advisory roles pending the formal implementation of the DRI system under the Act. The objective is that no department enters the first week of the new government without a named individual who is personally responsible for delivery and who understands and is committed to the government’s programme. Internal allies within the existing civil service, officials who support radical reform and who were identified during the pre-election preparation phase, will be elevated and empowered from Day 1.

##### CS1.4: Opening the Senior Civil Service

The Problem

The Senior Civil Service in the United Kingdom is a closed professional caste. Of the 7,525 officials who comprise the SCS, the vast majority have spent their entire careers within the civil service. The Fast Stream, the main graduate entry programme, receives approximately 20,000 applications per year for around 1,000 places. Successful candidates are then rotated through a series of two-year postings, gaining breadth of experience at the expense of depth of expertise. The generalist culture that Thomas Balogh criticised in 1959 as “the apotheosis of the dilettante” persists: the Fast Stream rewards verbal fluency, the ability to draft a ministerial submission, and skill at navigating institutional politics. It does not reward deep technical knowledge, commercial expertise, project delivery experience, or the ability to build and run things. The result is a senior leadership cadre that is exceptionally skilled at process and exceptionally poor at execution. Whitehall can produce a Green Paper on any subject in the world. It cannot build a hospital on time and on budget.

The Senior Civil Service is also conspicuously unrepresentative of the country it serves in terms of professional background. The policy profession has grown 116% since 2016, while the digital and data profession, though growing, remains small in absolute terms. Fifty-four per cent of Policy professionals are based in London, compared with less than 20% of the civil service as a whole. The concentration of generalist policy professionals in London headquarters, advising ministers on matters they have never personally delivered, is the structural root of Whitehall’s delivery deficit. Singapore builds a world-class public service by recruiting its Permanent Secretaries from an Administrative Service that rotates between ministries and statutory boards, forcing leaders to gain operational experience. Britain builds its senior leadership by promoting people who have spent their careers writing submissions to ministers.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Civil Service Reform Act will:

- a) Require that a minimum of one-third of all Senior Civil Service appointments at Director level and above be filled by candidates from outside the civil service within the first parliament. The purpose is not to replace career civil servants wholesale, but to break the monoculture by ensuring that the senior leadership of every department includes people who have built businesses, led military operations, managed hospitals, written software, or delivered major projects in the real world. The one-third external target will be monitored by the reconstituted Civil Service Commission and reported to Parliament annually. Departments that fail to meet the target will be required to advertise all subsequent senior vacancies externally until the target is met.
- b) Establish competitive-market pay for externally recruited senior officials. One of the primary reasons the civil service cannot attract talent from the private sector is that it does not pay competitive salaries. A Permanent Secretary earns approximately £160,000 to £200,000 per year; the Cabinet Secretary earns just over £200,000. The equivalent role in a FTSE 250 company commands a multiple of this. The Act will establish a Senior Service Pay Framework under which externally recruited DRIs and senior officials may be paid at rates benchmarked to the relevant private sector equivalent, with a performance-linked component of up to 30% of base salary. Internal candidates appointed to DRI roles will be eligible for the same pay framework. The objective is to create a senior public service in which the best people in the country are willing to serve, not one in which only those who cannot earn more elsewhere choose to stay.
- c) Reform the Fast Stream into a specialist-track programme. The current Fast Stream, which rotates generalists through two-year postings with no requirement to develop deep expertise, will be replaced by a programme that recruits into defined specialist tracks: delivery, digital and data, commercial, finance, engineering, and policy. Fast Stream entrants will spend a minimum of four years in their specialist track before becoming eligible for cross-departmental moves. The generalist rotation model, which produces senior officials who know a little about everything and a lot about nothing, will be discontinued. The model is taken from Singapore’s Administrative Service, which rotates officials between ministries but ensures that each posting is of sufficient duration to develop genuine operational expertise, and from the German system, which requires senior officials to have substantive expertise in the policy areas they manage.

OPERATIONAL

Senior Service recruitment campaign

Within 60 days of taking office, the Office of the Prime Minister will launch a national recruitment campaign for senior public service roles, targeted at executives in technology, infrastructure, defence, healthcare, finance, and project delivery. The campaign will be explicit about the government’s reform programme, the DRI model, the competitive pay, and the expectation that appointees will deliver measurable results on war-speed timelines. The campaign will be run by the OPM’s talent function, not by the civil service’s own HR apparatus.

Secondment and interchange programme

Within 90 days, the government will establish a formal secondment programme enabling senior leaders from business, the military, and technology to serve in government for periods of one to three years, and enabling senior civil servants to spend time in operational roles outside Whitehall. The programme will be administered by the OPM and will explicitly target the skills gaps identified in the Charter Letters: commercial negotiation, digital delivery, infrastructure management, and operational leadership. Every secondee will have a DRI-style performance agreement. The principle of the Angliot (CS10) applies at every level: the civil service must become a place where the most talented people in the country want to serve, not a place that talented people leave.

##### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The CS1 framework is built on the Civil Service Reform Act, a single piece of primary legislation introduced in the first King’s Speech. The Act must be drafted in full before the general election by a legal team operating independently of the civil service. It must be short, focused, and designed for rapid parliamentary passage. No additional Acts are required for CS1; all other measures are deliverable by ministerial direction, statutory instrument, or departmental action.

Civil Service Reform Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: Repeal of Sections 10 to 13 of CRAG 2010 (Civil Service Commission’s exclusive authority over merit-based appointment). Amendment of Section 7 (ministerial management authority over departmental civil servants). Repeal of Section 8(5) (prohibition on special adviser management authority). Statutory authority for Prime Minister to appoint and dismiss Permanent Secretaries without Commission approval. Statutory authority for Secretaries of State to appoint and dismiss Directors General with Prime Ministerial approval. Fixed-term contracts of no more than five years for all Permanent Secretaries and Directors General. Reconstitution of Civil Service Commission as advisory and audit body. Abolition of Senior Leadership Committee’s gatekeeping functions. Requirement for First Civil Service Commissioner to be appointed from outside the civil service. Establishment of DRI as formal Senior Civil Service role with published performance agreements. DRI authority over departmental hiring, firing, reorganisation, and resource allocation. One-third external recruitment target for Senior Civil Service within first parliament. Senior Service Pay Framework benchmarked to private sector equivalents. Fast Stream reform into specialist tracks with four-year minimum postings.

Delivered operationally: Pre-election drafting of full Bill text and secondary instruments. Transitional competence framework for senior appointments within 30 days. Full transparency on Senior Leadership Committee proceedings within 14 days. International recruitment benchmarking within 60 days. Reserve army of DRI candidates briefed and prepared before election. Day 1 interim appointments in priority departments. Reconstituted Commission operational within 90 days of Royal Assent. National senior service recruitment campaign within 60 days. Secondment and interchange programme within 90 days. Fast Stream specialist-track restructuring within six months.

CS1 is the document that makes every other document deliverable. Without the authority to appoint, direct, and dismiss the officials who run the government machine, an incoming administration is a passenger in its own vehicle. The Economic Policy Framework (E1 to E12) requires officials who can procure competently, regulate intelligently, and build infrastructure at pace. The Crime Policy Framework (C1 to C13) requires a reformed CPS, effective police governance, and functioning courts administered by officials who answer to ministers. The NHS Policy Framework (NHS1 to NHS7) requires a Health Standards Authority that holds leaders to account, a Procurement Authority that negotiates prices, and a Data Authority that commercialises health data. None of this happens while the people who run these institutions are selected by a system ministers do not control, serve under terms ministers cannot set, and face consequences ministers cannot impose. CS1 ends this. It restores the first principle of democratic government: that the people’s elected representatives control the state.

#### CS2: Curtailing Judicial Overreach

“Responsibility Without Authority Is Servitude; Authority Without Accountability Is Tyranny”

Governing Principle

The cardinal thesis of Progress’ Civil Service Reform Framework is that responsibility must be combined with authority. A minister who is accountable to Parliament for the performance of a department must have the authority to direct that department. A Prime Minister who bears responsibility for the government’s programme must have the power to appoint and dismiss the officials who execute it. An elected government that answers to the electorate for the condition of the country must possess the legal, administrative, and operational means to change that condition. Where responsibility and authority are separated, the result is not a system of checks and balances but a system of institutional fraud: those who bear the consequences of failure are denied the tools to prevent it, while those who possess the tools face no consequences for their misuse. CS1 addressed the first separation, in which ministers hold nominal responsibility for departments they cannot control. CS2 addresses the second: the progressive expansion of judicial power into the domain of policy, which has created a system in which the courts possess an effective veto over elected government action, while bearing no responsibility whatsoever for the consequences of exercising it.

Judicial review is a legitimate and necessary function of the courts. No democratic government should be above the law. When a public body acts outside the powers granted to it by Parliament, when it violates the procedural requirements of a statute, or when it acts in a manner so irrational that no reasonable decision-maker could have reached the same conclusion, the courts are right to intervene. These are the three traditional grounds of judicial review established in the GCHQ case of 1985: illegality, procedural impropriety, and irrationality. Progress does not seek to abolish judicial review. Progress seeks to restore it to its proper constitutional scope, from which it has been expanded by four decades of judicial activism into a roving commission of inquiry into the merits of government policy. The distinction between legality and policy is the constitutional red line. When a court reviews whether a minister acted within the powers granted by statute, it performs a legal function. When a court reviews whether a minister’s policy was the right one, whether it weighed the correct considerations, whether its assessment of fact was defensible, or whether its objectives were proportionate to its methods, it performs a political function for which it has no democratic mandate and no institutional competence.

The expansion of judicial review beyond its traditional scope has occurred through three distinct mechanisms. The first is the progressive abandonment of the non-justiciability doctrine. Until the Supreme Court’s judgment in R (Miller) v The Prime Minister in 2019, it was accepted that certain prerogative powers, including prorogation, dissolution, the making of treaties, and defence of the realm, were non-justiciable. Lord Roskill stated in the GCHQ case that these powers could not properly be made the subject of judicial review. The Miller II court overturned this principle by a novel and controversial means: rather than reviewing the exercise of the prorogation power, it redefined the scope of the power itself, holding that it did not extend to a prorogation that frustrated Parliament’s ability to perform its constitutional functions without reasonable justification. This collapsed the distinction between the scope and the exercise of a prerogative, extending the court’s jurisdiction into territory that the GCHQ court had explicitly excluded. The consequence is that there is now no prerogative power whose exercise a court will treat as non-justiciable, and no governmental decision, however clearly political in character, that the Supreme Court will regard as beyond its reach.

The second mechanism is the incorporation of the European Convention on Human Rights into domestic law through the Human Rights Act 1998. The HRA requires every public authority to act compatibly with Convention rights, and empowers the courts to grant remedies, including quashing decisions, where they find a violation. The proportionality test imported by Convention jurisprudence requires courts to assess whether a government measure is proportionate to its legitimate aim, a test that necessarily involves the court substituting its judgment on policy questions for that of the elected government. The Supreme Court’s unanimous ruling in the Rwanda case in November 2023 illustrated the scale of this expansion. The court did not merely review whether the Home Secretary had the statutory power to remove asylum seekers to a third country. It conducted its own independent assessment of the factual question of whether Rwanda was safe, weighing evidence from the UNHCR against the government’s assessment and concluding that the government was wrong. A court that assesses the factual basis of a policy and substitutes its own evaluation for that of the elected government is not performing judicial review. It is performing government.

The third mechanism is the creep of international law into the domestic legal order. The United Kingdom is a dualist state: international treaty obligations bind the state on the international plane but do not create rights or obligations in domestic law unless Parliament legislates to give them domestic effect. This was the settled constitutional position for centuries. It has been progressively undermined by judicial decisions that treat unincorporated international law as a relevant consideration in domestic proceedings, by the HRA’s requirement that domestic law be interpreted compatibly with the ECHR, and by the stance of government lawyers who treat international obligations as binding constraints on ministerial action even where Parliament has not enacted them into domestic law. The Policy Exchange report on government lawyers and the Civil Service Code documented the phenomenon: officials in the Home Office were reportedly reluctant to implement ministerial decisions on Rwanda because they considered them incompatible with international obligations. Government lawyers advised ministers that the Civil Service Code required compliance with international law, a position that a High Court judgment in 2024 confirmed was legally incorrect. The effect is a system in which unelected lawyers within the government machine use unenacted international law as a basis for refusing to implement the decisions of elected ministers. This is the ultimate separation of responsibility from authority: the minister is responsible to Parliament for the policy, but the officials who refuse to implement it face no consequences at all.

The cumulative effect of these three mechanisms is that the elected government of the United Kingdom now operates within a web of judicial constraints that no previous generation of British politicians would have recognised. Every significant policy decision must be assessed against HRA compatibility, against potential judicial review grounds that now extend far beyond the traditional Wednesbury framework, against the views of government lawyers whose interpretation of international law is more restrictive than the law requires, and against the possibility that the Supreme Court will conduct its own factual assessment of the policy’s merits and substitute its judgment for that of ministers. The Institute for Government’s research on judicial review and policy-making documented the effect within Whitehall: officials spend substantial time assessing the likelihood of legal challenge rather than implementing policy. The risk of potential cases shapes decisions as much as actual litigation. The courts have acquired, through the expansion of judicial review, a prospective veto over government action that operates through the compliance culture within the civil service. Officials use the threat of judicial review to slow, modify, or block ministerial decisions they disagree with, citing legal risk as the reason. The result is a system in which the courts do not need to strike down a policy: they merely need to exist as a possibility, and the civil service will use that possibility as a reason not to implement it.

Progress’ position is clear. The principle that responsibility must be combined with authority applies to the judicial branch as much as to the executive. A court that exercises the power to veto government policy must bear the responsibility for the consequences of that veto. But courts bear no such responsibility. No judge is accountable for the immigration backlog that results from blocking a removal policy. No court is answerable for the infrastructure projects that are delayed by years of litigation. No panel of Supreme Court justices faces the electorate when their ruling prevents the government from acting on its manifesto. Judges exercise authority without responsibility, which is the precise inversion of the constitutional principle that Progress seeks to restore.
