The solution is not to abolish judicial review but to restrict it to its proper scope, to reassert the dualist principle that international law operates on the international plane unless Parliament enacts it into domestic law, and to reform the government legal profession so that lawyers serve ministers rather than frustrate them. The Executive Decisions Act will accomplish this. It will be drafted before the election and introduced in the first King’s Speech alongside the Civil Service Reform Act.

##### CS2.1: The Executive Decisions Act

The Problem

The grounds on which ministerial decisions can be challenged by judicial review have expanded far beyond the traditional GCHQ framework. Proportionality review, imported through the HRA and EU law, requires courts to assess the balance between a policy’s objectives and its impact on individual rights, a judgment that is inherently political. The courts have extended the grounds of irrationality review to include what is effectively a merits assessment: in the Rwanda case, the Supreme Court did not merely ask whether the Home Secretary’s assessment of Rwanda’s safety was one that a reasonable minister could have reached, but whether the court itself agreed with it. The scope of procedural challenge has expanded to include allegations that decision-makers failed to take into account every potentially relevant consideration, or that they failed to conduct a sufficiently rigorous impact assessment, or that they failed to give adequate reasons. Each of these expanded grounds converts what was once a narrow check on legality into a comprehensive supervision of the quality of government decision-making. The courts have become, in effect, a permanent standing commission for the review of policy.

The practical effect within Whitehall is devastating. The Institute for Government found that the prospect of judicial review shapes policy-making at every stage: officials assess legal risk before, during, and after every significant decision. In the Home Office, ministers receive spreadsheets listing upcoming cases, the risk of challenge, and the likely policy impact. Government Legal Department lawyers routinely advise against courses of action on the grounds that they might be challenged, without distinguishing between challenges that are likely to succeed and challenges that are merely conceivable. The result is that policy is drafted to survive judicial scrutiny rather than to achieve its stated objective. Speed, simplicity, and decisive action are sacrificed to the production of legally defensible paper trails. The minister has the responsibility for the policy’s outcomes. The lawyers who insist on diluting it to reduce legal risk bear none.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Executive Decisions Act will:

- a) Codify the grounds of judicial review in statute, replacing the common law framework with a statutory definition. The permitted grounds will be: illegality (the decision-maker acted outside the powers conferred by statute), procedural impropriety (the decision-maker failed to comply with a mandatory procedural requirement imposed by statute), and manifest unreasonableness (the decision was one that no reasonable person in the decision-maker’s position, with access to the same information, could have reached). The third ground restores the original Wednesbury standard and excludes proportionality review, which will no longer be available as a free-standing ground of challenge in cases that do not involve Convention rights under the HRA. The Act will expressly provide that the courts may not review the merits, factual assessment, or policy judgment of a ministerial decision, and may not substitute their own evaluation of evidence for that of the decision-maker. The Rwanda precedent, in which the Supreme Court conducted an independent factual assessment of a foreign country’s safety, will be legislatively reversed.
- b) Establish a statutory presumption of non-justiciability for decisions of high policy. The Act will provide that decisions made by ministers in the exercise of prerogative powers relating to the conduct of foreign affairs, the deployment and management of the armed forces, the organisation of the civil service, the dissolution and prorogation of Parliament, and the making and implementation of treaties are not justiciable unless Parliament has expressly provided otherwise by statute. This reverses the trajectory from GCHQ through Miller II, in which the courts progressively extended their jurisdiction over prerogative powers that were previously treated as non-justiciable. The presumption may be displaced only by express statutory language, not by judicial inference from constitutional principles. The Act will contain a specific ouster provision confirming that the prorogation prerogative is not subject to judicial review, reversing Miller II directly. The Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022 already contains an ouster clause for the dissolution prerogative; the Executive Decisions Act will extend the same protection to prorogation and to the other prerogative powers listed.
- c) Impose a strict time limit and permission filter for judicial review of ministerial decisions. Claims for judicial review of decisions made by a Secretary of State or the Prime Minister must be filed within 14 days of the decision being published or communicated, reduced from the current three-month time limit. The permission stage will require the claimant to demonstrate not merely an arguable case but a strong prima facie case that the decision was made outside the statutory powers or in breach of a mandatory procedural requirement. Claims that amount to a disagreement with the merits of a policy, or that rely on the failure to consider a non-mandatory consideration, will be refused permission. The permission decision will be made on the papers with no right to an oral renewal. The objective is to preserve access to justice for genuinely unlawful decisions while eliminating the use of judicial review as a strategic delay mechanism by opponents of government policy.
- d) Restrict standing to bring judicial review of government policy decisions. Under the current rules, any person with a “sufficient interest” in the matter may bring a claim, a test so broad that campaign groups, charities, and individual activists routinely challenge government decisions that affect them only indirectly. The Act will restrict standing for challenges to ministerial policy decisions to persons who are directly and personally affected by the decision. Organisations may bring claims only where they can demonstrate that they represent identifiable individuals who are directly affected. Interveners in policy-related judicial reviews will bear their own costs and any costs caused to the parties by their intervention. The objective is to end the practice by which campaign organisations use judicial review as a political tool to obstruct policies they oppose, substituting the courtroom for the ballot box as the arena of democratic contest.

OPERATIONAL

Pre-election Bill drafting

The Executive Decisions Act will be drafted in full before the election by the same independent legal team that prepares the Civil Service Reform Act (CS1). The two Bills will be introduced together in the first King’s Speech. The legislative text will include clause-by-clause commentary, precedent analysis, and a detailed impact assessment demonstrating that the reforms are consistent with the rule of law and that comparable restrictions exist in other common law democracies. The independent legal team will also prepare a comprehensive brief on parliamentary handling, including strategies for managing House of Lords resistance and the use of the Parliament Acts if necessary.

Judicial review audit

Within 30 days of taking office, the Office of the Prime Minister will commission an audit of all judicial review proceedings pending against central government departments, identifying cases that challenge policy decisions (as distinct from individual administrative decisions), assessing the financial cost and policy delay attributable to each, and publishing the results. The audit will establish the evidence base for the reforms by demonstrating the cumulative cost of the expanded judicial review regime to government effectiveness.

##### CS2.2: Reasserting Domestic Law Primacy

The Problem

The United Kingdom is a dualist state. International treaties bind the state at the international level but do not form part of domestic law unless Parliament legislates to incorporate them. This is not a technicality. It is the foundation of parliamentary sovereignty: the people’s elected representatives, and only they, determine what the law of the land is. A treaty signed by the executive and ratified under CRAG cannot, without an Act of Parliament, create rights or obligations enforceable by individuals in domestic courts. This principle has been progressively undermined by three developments. First, the Human Rights Act 1998 incorporated the ECHR into domestic law and required the courts to interpret all legislation, so far as possible, compatibly with Convention rights. This created a one-way ratchet in which the scope of domestic law is progressively expanded by reference to the evolving jurisprudence of the Strasbourg Court, a body over which Parliament has no control and to which the British electorate has no recourse. Second, the courts have increasingly treated unincorporated international law as a “relevant consideration” that decision-makers must take into account, blurring the line between domestic obligation and international aspiration. Third, government lawyers have adopted a practice of advising ministers that international obligations constrain their freedom of action even where those obligations have not been enacted into domestic law.

The practical consequences were displayed during the Rwanda litigation. The Supreme Court found the Rwanda policy unlawful by reference to the principle of non-refoulement, which it held was established by multiple international instruments including the Refugee Convention, the UN Convention against Torture, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and the ECHR. The Refugee Convention has never been fully incorporated into domestic law by Parliament. The Convention against Torture has not been enacted as a domestic statute. Yet the Supreme Court treated these unincorporated obligations as directly determinative of the lawfulness of a domestic policy decision. The Safety of Rwanda Act 2024, which attempted to declare Rwanda safe by statute, prompted government lawyers to advise that civil servants could not implement removals that would breach the ECHR, even though the Act expressly empowered ministers to decide whether to comply with Rule 39 interim orders from the European Court of Human Rights. The High Court in 2024 held that the Civil Service Code’s requirement to “comply with the law” did not impose a free-standing duty to comply with unincorporated international law, but the cultural norm within the government legal profession had already achieved what the law did not require: officials treated international obligations as domestically binding, regardless of what Parliament had enacted.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Executive Decisions Act will:

- a) Provide that no rule of international law, and no provision of any international treaty to which the United Kingdom is party, shall be enforceable in any domestic court or tribunal, or shall constitute a ground for judicial review, unless that rule or provision has been enacted into domestic law by Act of Parliament. This is a statutory restatement of the dualist principle. It does not withdraw the United Kingdom from any international obligation. It does not repeal the Human Rights Act. It clarifies that the domestic legal system is governed by Acts of Parliament and the common law, not by the evolving interpretations of international bodies. The provision will expressly override any judicial decision that has treated unincorporated international law as directly applicable in domestic proceedings.
- b) Amend the Human Rights Act 1998 to provide that, where a court finds a provision of primary legislation to be incompatible with a Convention right, the court’s sole remedy is a declaration of incompatibility under Section 4. The court may not grant any other remedy, including damages, injunctive relief, or the quashing of an administrative decision, on the basis of Convention incompatibility alone. The declaration of incompatibility remains a signal to Parliament that remedial action may be appropriate, but the decision whether to act, and how, rests exclusively with Parliament. The current interpretive obligation under Section 3, which requires courts to read and give effect to legislation in a way that is compatible with Convention rights “so far as it is possible to do so,” will be amended to a weaker duty to take Convention rights into account where the language of the statute permits, without straining the natural meaning of the legislative text. This prevents the courts from using Section 3 as a mechanism to rewrite legislation that Parliament has deliberately enacted in terms that do not comply with the ECHR.
- c) Provide that no minister, civil servant, or other public official shall be required by any code of conduct, management code, or contractual term to comply with any obligation arising under international law that has not been enacted into domestic law by Act of Parliament. The Civil Service Code, the Civil Service Management Code, and the Ministerial Code will be amended accordingly. The 2024 High Court judgment confirming that the Code’s “comply with the law” provision does not mandate compliance with unincorporated international law will be given statutory force. Government lawyers who advise that unincorporated international law prevents the implementation of a ministerial decision will be required to provide that advice in writing, identifying the specific domestic legal provision (not international instrument) that they contend is breached. If no domestic provision is identified, the advice does not constitute a legal barrier to implementation, and the minister’s instruction must be carried out.

OPERATIONAL

Government Legal Department directive

Within seven days of taking office, the Attorney General will issue a directive to the Government Legal Department clarifying the legal framework within which government lawyers operate. The directive will confirm that government lawyers advise on domestic law, that international obligations are relevant only insofar as they have been incorporated into domestic law, and that the characterisation of a ministerial instruction as “incompatible with the rule of law” requires identification of a specific provision of domestic law that is breached. Lawyers who are unable to identify such a provision may record their policy concerns through normal channels but may not advise that the instruction is unlawful. The directive will be published and will apply to all government lawyers, including those embedded in departments and those in the Government Legal Department’s central advisory functions.

International obligations review

Within 90 days of taking office, the Office of the Prime Minister will publish a comprehensive review of the United Kingdom’s international treaty obligations, identifying which obligations have been incorporated into domestic law and which have not, assessing whether each unincorporated obligation should be incorporated, modified, or noted as a matter of international policy that does not constrain domestic action. The review will establish a clear register of the United Kingdom’s binding domestic legal commitments as distinct from its international policy commitments. Every subsequent government decision that involves international law will reference this register, ensuring that ministers and officials operate from a common understanding of what the law actually requires as opposed to what the government legal culture has assumed it requires.

##### CS2.3: Reforming the Government Legal Profession

The Problem

The government legal profession in the United Kingdom does not serve the government. It serves itself. Government lawyers, employed within the Government Legal Department and embedded in every Whitehall department, have developed an institutional culture in which their primary loyalty is to what they conceive as “the rule of law” rather than to the elected ministers whose decisions they exist to implement. This would be entirely proper if “the rule of law” meant compliance with domestic statute. In practice, it means compliance with a far broader set of norms: international treaty obligations that Parliament has not enacted, the evolving jurisprudence of the Strasbourg Court, the opinions of UN treaty bodies, and the professional consensus of the wider legal community in which government lawyers operate and to which they will return when they leave public service. The Policy Exchange research documented the phenomenon: government lawyers in the Home Office were reportedly reluctant to implement the Rwanda policy not because it breached any provision of domestic law, but because it was incompatible with their understanding of international obligations. Their career incentives reinforce this stance: government lawyers are regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority or the Bar Standards Board, both of which require compliance with professional duties that government lawyers interpret as extending to international law. A government lawyer who implements a ministerial instruction that the wider legal profession considers unlawful risks professional sanction. A government lawyer who frustrates a ministerial instruction by citing “rule of law” concerns faces no adverse consequence whatsoever.

The institutional incentive structure is the same separation of responsibility from authority that pervades the rest of the civil service. Government lawyers exercise enormous power over what ministers can do. They draft the legal advice that determines whether a policy proceeds. They assess the risk of judicial review that shapes how a policy is designed. They review the legislative drafting that determines what a statute actually says. Yet they are accountable to nobody for the policy consequences of their advice. A government lawyer who advises that a manifesto commitment cannot be implemented because of ECHR compatibility concerns bears no responsibility for the fact that the commitment is not delivered. The minister bears that responsibility. The lawyer receives their salary, their pension, and their professional standing regardless. Responsibility and authority are not merely separated. They are inverted: the person with authority over the legal advice faces no consequences, while the person who bears the consequences has no authority over the advice.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Executive Decisions Act will:

- a) Establish a statutory duty on government lawyers to provide advice that enables the implementation of ministerial decisions within the law, rather than advice that identifies reasons why ministerial decisions cannot be implemented. This is a fundamental reorientation of the government legal function. A private sector lawyer who told a client “you cannot do this” without offering a lawful route to achieve the same objective would lose the client. Government lawyers who tell ministers “you cannot do this” without offering a lawful alternative route will be in breach of their statutory duty. The duty will require government lawyers, when advising that a proposed course of action is unlawful, to identify the specific provision of domestic law that is breached and to propose at least one alternative course of action that achieves the minister’s objective lawfully. Advice that relies solely on international law that has not been enacted into domestic statute will not satisfy the duty.
- b) Require that the head of the Government Legal Department be appointed by the Attorney General with the approval of the Prime Minister, and serve on a fixed-term contract of no more than five years. The head of the GLD will have a published performance agreement that includes the timely delivery of implementable legal advice in support of the government’s programme. Departmental legal directors, the senior lawyers embedded in each department, will be appointed by the relevant Secretary of State with the approval of the Attorney General, and will serve on the same terms. The principle of responsibility married to authority applies: if government lawyers are to exercise the power to shape and constrain ministerial decisions, they must be accountable to ministers for the quality, timeliness, and constructiveness of that advice.
- c) Provide that government lawyers are not subject to professional regulatory sanction for implementing lawful ministerial decisions with which the wider legal profession disagrees. The current position, in which government lawyers may fear that implementing a minister’s instruction will expose them to complaints from other lawyers, creates a perverse incentive to frustrate rather than facilitate the elected government’s programme. The Act will provide that no professional regulatory body may take disciplinary action against a government lawyer for providing advice in support of, or implementing, a decision of a minister that is lawful under domestic law, regardless of its compatibility with international law, professional consensus, or the views of non-governmental legal organisations. This provision protects lawyers who do their job, implementing the decisions of the elected government, from retaliation by a professional community that may disagree with the policy.

OPERATIONAL

Attorney General’s Protocol

Within 14 days of taking office, the Attorney General will publish a Protocol on Government Legal Advice setting out the principles that govern the provision of legal advice within government. The Protocol will require that all legal advice identifies the specific domestic legal provisions engaged, distinguishes between domestic legal constraints (which are binding) and international law considerations (which are advisory), offers constructive routes to achieve ministerial objectives where an initial route is identified as unlawful, and is delivered within defined timeframes appropriate to the urgency of the ministerial decision. The Protocol will be incorporated into the terms of service of all government lawyers.

Legal advice transparency

Within 60 days, the government will establish a Legal Advice Register within the Office of the Prime Minister, recording all instances in which government lawyers advise that a ministerial decision cannot be implemented, the legal basis cited, the alternative routes proposed, and the time taken to deliver the advice. The Register will be reviewed quarterly by the Attorney General and the Chief of Staff at the OPM. Departments in which legal advice consistently obstructs or delays ministerial decisions without identifying constructive alternatives will be subject to review of their legal staffing and the appointment of their departmental legal director.

##### CS2.4: Protecting the Reform Programme

The Problem

Every element of the Progress Civil Service Reform Framework will be challenged in the courts. The Civil Service Reform Act (CS1) will be challenged by the FDA union, by former senior civil servants, and by campaign organisations that regard the Northcote-Trevelyan settlement as sacrosanct. The Office of the Prime Minister (CS3) will be challenged on the grounds that it concentrates excessive power in the executive. The Charter Letters (CS7) will be challenged on the grounds that they politicise the civil service. The King’s Regulations (CS8) will be challenged on HRA grounds by officials facing disciplinary proceedings. The Angliot (CS10) will be challenged on equality grounds. Without prophylactic legislative protection, the reform programme will spend its first two years in the courts rather than in implementation. The history of radical government reform in the United Kingdom demonstrates that legal challenge is the primary weapon of the institutional status quo. The opponents of reform do not need to win in court. They need only to delay, because delay is indistinguishable from defeat for a government with a limited mandate and a volatile electoral position.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Executive Decisions Act will:

- a) Include ouster clauses in both the Civil Service Reform Act and the Executive Decisions Act itself, providing that specified provisions of these Acts are not subject to judicial review. The ouster clauses will be drafted in the strongest possible terms, drawing on the formulation used in the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022 and the model proposed by the Independent Review of Administrative Law (the Faulks Review). The clauses will provide that no court or tribunal may question, review, or hold unlawful any decision made by a minister or the Prime Minister in the exercise of powers conferred by these Acts. The intention is to place the core machinery of civil service reform, the appointment and dismissal of senior officials, the organisation of the Office of the Prime Minister, the issuance of Charter Letters, beyond the reach of judicial interference. These are decisions that the elected government must be able to take quickly, decisively, and without the prospect of litigation. They are the essence of the executive function, and the courts have no role in supervising them.
- b) Provide that the Executive Decisions Act itself may not be challenged on HRA grounds and that no declaration of incompatibility may be made in respect of its provisions. Progress acknowledges that this provision will be controversial. It is also necessary. The entire purpose of the Act is to reassert the primacy of parliamentary legislation over judicial interpretation. A court that could issue a declaration of incompatibility against the Act would be using the very mechanism the Act is designed to constrain. The Act will be passed by Parliament. It will be the law of the land. If future parliamentarians wish to repeal or amend it, they may do so through the normal legislative process. But the courts may not undo through declaration what Parliament has done through legislation.
- c) Establish an expedited litigation track for challenges to government reform legislation, requiring that any challenge to the validity of provisions of the Civil Service Reform Act, the Executive Decisions Act, or any other Act introduced as part of the CS1 to CS10 framework be heard and determined within 28 days of filing, with a single right of appeal to the Supreme Court to be heard and determined within a further 28 days. The expedited track prevents legal challenges from achieving delay by default. The current system, in which a judicial review claim can take months or years to reach a final hearing, allows opponents of reform to achieve their objective of obstruction merely by filing a claim. Under the expedited track, the legal question will be resolved quickly, and the government will either proceed with implementation or adjust its approach. The principle is that legal certainty serves everyone: the government, the civil service, and the public.

OPERATIONAL

Litigation readiness unit

Before the election, the Party will establish a Litigation Readiness Unit staffed by barristers and solicitors who are not part of the government legal profession and who are committed to the reform programme. The Unit will prepare defensive briefs for every anticipated legal challenge to every element of the CS1 to CS10 framework, identifying the likely claimants, the probable grounds, the relevant case law, and the government’s response. On Day 1, the Unit will transfer into the Office of the Prime Minister and function as a dedicated litigation team, separate from the Government Legal Department, reporting directly to the Attorney General. The objective is to ensure that the government is not dependent on its own institutional lawyers, many of whom will be sympathetic to the legal challenges, to defend its reform programme. The principle of responsibility married to authority extends to litigation: the people defending the programme must be accountable to the ministers who designed it.

Public communication strategy

Within 14 days of introducing the Executive Decisions Act, the government will publish a public document explaining in plain language what the Act does and why it is necessary. The document will set out the constitutional case for parliamentary sovereignty, the evidence of judicial overreach, the comparative international position, and the specific provisions of the Act. The document will be explicit that the government is not abolishing judicial review, is not withdrawing from the ECHR, and is not placing itself above the law. It is restoring the law to its proper scope: Parliament makes the law, the government implements it, and the courts ensure that the government acts within the powers Parliament has granted. This is the most basic principle of the British constitution, and it is the one that four decades of judicial expansion have obscured.

##### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The CS2 framework is built on the Executive Decisions Act, a single piece of primary legislation introduced in the first King’s Speech alongside the Civil Service Reform Act (CS1). The Act must be drafted in full before the general election by the same independent legal team. No additional Acts are required for CS2. All other measures are deliverable by Attorney General’s directive, ministerial instruction, or departmental action.

Executive Decisions Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act: Statutory codification of judicial review grounds: illegality, procedural impropriety, manifest unreasonableness (Wednesbury restored). Exclusion of proportionality as free-standing ground outside HRA Convention rights claims. Prohibition on courts reviewing merits, factual assessment, or policy judgment of ministerial decisions. Statutory presumption of non-justiciability for prerogative powers relating to foreign affairs, armed forces, civil service organisation, prorogation, and treaty-making. Specific ouster clause reversing Miller II on prorogation. Fourteen-day filing deadline for JR of ministerial decisions. Strong prima facie case required at permission stage. Standing restricted to directly and personally affected persons. Interveners bear own costs. Statutory restatement of dualist principle: unincorporated international law not enforceable in domestic courts. Amendment to HRA Section 3 (interpretive obligation weakened). Amendment to HRA Section 4 (declaration of incompatibility as sole remedy). Prohibition on codes of conduct requiring compliance with unincorporated international law. Statutory duty on government lawyers to provide constructive, implementation-focused advice. Government Legal Department head appointed by Attorney General on fixed-term contract. Departmental legal directors appointed by Secretaries of State. Professional regulatory immunity for government lawyers implementing lawful ministerial decisions. Ouster clauses protecting Civil Service Reform Act and Executive Decisions Act from JR. Prohibition on declarations of incompatibility against the Executive Decisions Act. Expedited 28-day litigation track for challenges to reform legislation.

Delivered operationally: Pre-election drafting of full Bill text by independent legal team. Pre-election Litigation Readiness Unit with defensive briefs for all anticipated challenges. Attorney General’s directive to Government Legal Department within seven days. Government Legal Department directive on domestic law primacy within seven days. Judicial review audit within 30 days. Attorney General’s Protocol on Government Legal Advice within 14 days. Legal Advice Register within 60 days. International obligations review within 90 days. Public communication document within 14 days of Bill introduction. Expedited litigation track operational from Royal Assent.

CS2 is the companion to CS1 and the second pillar of the reform framework. CS1 removes the internal barriers to ministerial authority: the Civil Service Commission’s monopoly, the Senior Leadership Committee’s opacity, the absence of a DRI accountability model. CS2 removes the external barriers: the expanded scope of judicial review that allows courts to veto policy, the creep of international law into domestic proceedings that gives unelected lawyers a basis for refusing ministerial instructions, and the institutional culture of the government legal profession that prioritises legal risk avoidance over the implementation of the elected government’s programme. Together, CS1 and CS2 establish the principle that runs through every document in this framework: that the people’s elected representatives shall control the government of the country, that authority shall be combined with responsibility at every level, and that no institution, whether permanent bureaucracy or roving judiciary, shall exercise the substance of governmental power without bearing the consequences of its decisions. The Executive Decisions Act does not attack the rule of law. It restores the original and most fundamental rule of the British constitution: that Parliament is sovereign, that the law is what Parliament says it is, and that the government acts within the law when it acts within the powers Parliament has conferred.

#### CS3: Office of the Prime Minister

“The Prime Minister Must Control the Government Machine, or the Government Machine Will Control the Prime Minister”

Governing Principle

The cardinal thesis of Progress’ Civil Service Reform Framework is that responsibility must be combined with authority. CS1 restores ministerial hire and fire authority over the civil service. CS2 removes the judicial veto over ministerial decisions. CS3 addresses the structural problem at the heart of the British state: that the Prime Minister, who bears ultimate responsibility to Parliament and the electorate for the government’s performance, does not control the government machine. The Prime Minister’s Office is formally a business unit within the Cabinet Office. It reports to the Cabinet Secretary. On busy days, some 400 officials work across the Downing Street complex, yet the Prime Minister cannot appoint most of them, cannot dismiss them, and cannot direct their work except through the intermediation of the Cabinet Secretary and the senior civil servants who populate the Cabinet Office. The Prime Minister has responsibility for everything the government does. The Prime Minister has authority over almost nothing the government does. This is the most consequential separation of responsibility from authority in the British constitution, and it is the one that CS3 is designed to eliminate.

The Cabinet Office was created in 1916 by Maurice Hankey with a narrow and precise mandate: to serve as a secretariat for the War Cabinet by preparing agendas, recording decisions, and communicating them to the departments responsible for implementation. Hankey’s secretariat was deliberately small, deliberately neutral, and deliberately without policy functions. It existed to make the Cabinet work, not to substitute for it. Over the following century, it metastasised into something its creator would not recognise. By the 2010s, the Cabinet Office had accumulated a policy machine, a communications apparatus, personnel files on every senior civil servant through the PET system, security and intelligence coordination, digital and data functions, procurement oversight, cross-government functions, and approximately 10,200 staff. Even after the July 2024 machinery of government change that transferred the Government Digital Service, the Central Digital and Data Office, and the Incubator for Artificial Intelligence to the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, the core department retained some 4,370 full-time equivalent staff and responsibility for 29 agencies and public bodies. The Cabinet Secretary, who leads this apparatus, now gives policy advice to the Prime Minister (forbidden in Hankey’s design), controls all senior appointments through the Senior Leadership Committee (forbidden in Hankey’s design), interferes with ministerial responsibility by chairing meetings that hold ministers to account (forbidden in Hankey’s design), and advises the Prime Minister on removing ministers. As Gus O’Donnell stated: “There are not two departments. I stress there is one department. There is one Cabinet Office of which Number 10 is a subset.”

The constitutional absurdity is complete. The Prime Minister is a subset of the Cabinet Secretary’s empire. The person accountable to the electorate for the government’s performance is subordinate, in institutional terms, to a permanent official who is accountable to nobody. Jeremy Heywood, one of the most influential Cabinet Secretaries in modern history, stated in 2010 that he thought it was “a good idea to reassert the Civil Service being in the lead in Number 10.” Robin Butler, another former Cabinet Secretary, admitted the real mechanism of control: “Control of the senior appointments gives the Cabinet Secretary leverage over government departments.” The Cabinet Secretary uses this leverage to script Potemkin meetings in which ministers read pre-prepared positions while decisions are taken elsewhere. Pre-meetings between officials determine the outcome; the ministerial meeting ratifies it. Ministerial responsibility, the foundation of the Westminster system, has become institutional theatre. The audience is Parliament. The directors are unelected permanent officials. The actors are ministers who read their lines and leave.

Every post-war Prime Minister has eventually confronted this reality. Blair complained of “scars on my back.” Thatcher, the most determined reformer since Churchill, could push the system on her direct priorities but outside the lighthouse beam of focused prime ministerial energy the system drifted; her refusal to face the structural reality of modern Whitehall led directly to being outmanoeuvred on the Single European Act and the ERM. Johnson received a blueprint for radical reform, delayed action, briefly empowered outsiders during the pandemic, and then surrendered. The pattern is invariable: conventional reform attempts tinker with the structure (more special advisers, better special advisers, rename the Cabinet Office, create a Delivery Unit) but never touch the core issues of talent, responsibility, incentives, culture, and power. They do not challenge the Northcote-Trevelyan settlement. After 18 months the government is in mid-term, nothing has changed, and another parliament is wasted.

The international comparison is instructive. In Australia, the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet employs approximately 2,500 staff and is led by a Secretary whom the Prime Minister appoints on the recommendation of the departing Secretary and the Public Service Commissioner, but whom the Prime Minister can replace. The Australian PMO, the political office of the Prime Minister, has been led by a Chief of Staff since 1972 and the role carries genuine executive authority. The Secretary of PM&C chairs the Secretaries’ Council, which coordinates across departments. The critical difference from the British system is that the Australian centre is explicitly the Prime Minister’s instrument: it exists to serve the Prime Minister’s agenda, not to provide an alternative source of authority that competes with and constrains the elected leader. In Singapore, the Prime Minister’s Office is a full ministry with dedicated staff, and the Cabinet Secretary role does not exist as an autonomous power centre. In France, the Secrétariat général du Gouvernement serves a coordinating function but operates under the authority of the Prime Minister, who has genuine executive power delegated by the President. Britain is unique among comparable democracies in having a centre of government that is structurally designed to constrain the elected leader rather than to serve them.

Progress’ solution is radical but constitutionally straightforward. The Cabinet Office will be closed. Its functions will be divided into two categories. The first category, coordination, delivery, and the strategic direction of the government’s programme, will transfer to a new Office of the Prime Minister. The second category, the original Hankey mandate of servicing Cabinet meetings, will return to a small Cabinet Secretariat of fewer than 20 staff. The position of Cabinet Secretary will be abolished. The position of Head of the Civil Service will be abolished. Cross-system appointment power will sit only in the OPM. The Prime Minister’s Chief of Staff, appointed by the Prime Minister and holding ministerial rank, will lead the OPM and will be the most senior official in the government after the Prime Minister. This is not a machinery of government change in the conventional sense. It is the restoration of a constitutional principle: that the person who bears responsibility for the government must have authority over the government. The change can be accomplished on Day 1, using Orders in Council under the Ministers of the Crown Act 1975 and prerogative powers. No primary legislation is required.

##### CS3.1: Closing the Cabinet Office

The Problem

The Cabinet Office is not a department in any meaningful sense. It is a holding company for functions that have accumulated over a century without strategic design, without clear ministerial accountability, and without any mechanism by which Parliament or the electorate can judge its performance. The National Audit Office’s 2024-25 overview recorded that the Cabinet Office group was made up of the core department and 15 other bodies. Its functions ranged from government resilience and national security to counter-fraud, lobbying regulation, propriety and ethics, honours, vetting, and the management of the government estate. It has experienced seven machinery of government transfers in a single financial year (2023-24), five out and two in. The Government Property Agency, the Crown Commercial Service, the Infrastructure and Projects Authority (now the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority), and the Government Commercial Organisation all sit within or adjacent to the Cabinet Office. The Advisory Committee on Business Appointments was disbanded in October 2025. The centres of six of the fourteen government functions are housed in the Cabinet Office. This is not a department executing a coherent policy programme under ministerial direction. It is a bureaucratic accumulation that exists because nobody has had the authority or the will to dismantle it.

The constitutional problem is more fundamental than organisational untidiness. The Cabinet Office, through the Cabinet Secretary, exercises a form of sovereignty over the rest of Whitehall. The PET system (Personnel, Efficiency, and Talent) holds personnel files on every senior civil servant, giving the Cabinet Secretary leverage over every department. The Senior Leadership Committee, chaired by the Cabinet Secretary and populated by serving Permanent Secretaries, decides how senior vacancies are filled: by external competition, internal competition, or managed move. The House of Lords Constitution Committee in 2023 described the SLC as “an opaque body” about which it received “contradictory accounts.” The Cabinet Secretary and the First Civil Service Commissioner gave different descriptions of who decides selection routes. The Senior Appointments Protocol does not, according to the Cabinet Secretary’s own evidence, “accurately reflect current practice.” This is the mechanism by which the permanent civil service reproduces itself. It is not controlled by ministers. It is not visible to Parliament. It is not accountable to the electorate. Yet it determines who runs every department of state. Responsibility and authority are completely separated: ministers bear the consequences of departmental performance, but the Cabinet Secretary selects the people who determine that performance.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) On Day 1, the Prime Minister will sign an Order in Council under the Ministers of the Crown Act 1975 transferring all coordination, delivery, strategy, and performance-monitoring functions from the Cabinet Office to the Office of the Prime Minister. The OPM will be a new ministerial department, headed by the Prime Minister and led day-to-day by the PM’s Chief of Staff, who will hold the rank of Minister of State and will be accountable to Parliament for the OPM’s operations. The transfer of functions order will be laid before Parliament. No prior parliamentary approval is required. The precedent is well established: successive prime ministers have created, merged, and abolished departments by Order in Council without difficulty. The July 2024 transfer of GDS, CDDO, and iAI from the Cabinet Office to DSIT was accomplished by the same mechanism. The creation of the OPM is a machinery of government change of the same legal character, differing only in ambition.
- b) The following functions will transfer to the OPM: the Policy Unit, the Delivery Unit, the National Security Secretariat, the Joint Intelligence Organisation, the Propriety and Constitution Group, government resilience and crisis management (COBR), the Economic and Domestic Affairs Secretariat, and all cross-government coordination functions. The OPM will also absorb the performance-monitoring functions currently shared between the Cabinet Office and HM Treasury, establishing the Public Expenditure and Performance Unit described in CS5 and CS7. All staff currently performing these functions will transfer with them. The transfer will be executed within 14 days of taking office, with transitional arrangements ensuring continuity of operations, particularly in national security and crisis management.
- c) The following functions will not transfer to the OPM and will instead be redistributed to line departments: the Government Property Agency will transfer to HM Treasury; the Crown Commercial Service will transfer to a reformed procurement function (E10); the Government Commercial Organisation will transfer to HM Treasury; vetting and security clearance functions will transfer to the Home Office; the honours secretariat will remain as a standalone office within the Privy Council Office. Any remaining functions that do not have a natural departmental home will be reviewed within 60 days and either absorbed into the OPM, transferred to a department, or abolished. The principle is that no function should exist at the centre unless it requires direct prime ministerial authority or cross-departmental coordination that cannot be achieved by bilateral agreement between departments.
- d) The PET system will be abolished within seven days of taking office. All personnel files on senior civil servants held centrally by the Cabinet Office will transfer to the OPM’s talent management function, which will operate under the direct authority of the Chief of Staff. The information contained in PET will no longer be used as a source of leverage by a Cabinet Secretary over departments. It will be used as a management tool by the OPM to support the DRI appointment process (CS1), the Charter Letter system (CS7), and the performance review cycle. The principle is straightforward: personnel information should serve the Prime Minister’s ability to manage the government, not the permanent bureaucracy’s ability to manage the Prime Minister.

##### CS3.2: Abolishing the Cabinet Secretary

The Problem

The position of Cabinet Secretary is the most powerful unelected role in the British state. The holder simultaneously serves as the most senior civil servant (Head of the Home Civil Service), the Prime Minister’s principal policy adviser, the manager of Cabinet business, the chair of the Senior Leadership Committee that controls senior appointments across Whitehall, and the custodian of the Ministerial Code and the machinery of government. No elected politician holds a comparable concentration of functions. The Cabinet Secretary advises the Prime Minister on which ministers to promote, which to demote, and which to dismiss. The Cabinet Secretary decides which officials are appointed to run departments. The Cabinet Secretary chairs the meetings at which ministers are held to account for their performance. The Cabinet Secretary controls the intelligence and security briefings that shape the Prime Minister’s understanding of threats. The Cabinet Secretary determines the agenda and papers for Cabinet and its committees. The Cabinet Secretary is, in practice, the chief executive of the British government, while the Prime Minister is, in practice, the chairman of a board that the chief executive controls.

This concentration of power in a single unelected individual is not a feature of the original constitutional design. Hankey’s Cabinet Secretary was a minute-taker, not a minister-maker. The accumulation occurred progressively: the Treasury Permanent Secretary was made Head of the Civil Service in 1919; the role was later combined with the Cabinet Secretary; senior appointment power was acquired through convention rather than statute; the policy advisory function grew under successive holders who expanded their influence. The result is a role that violates every principle of the responsibility-authority framework. The Cabinet Secretary exercises authority over the entire machinery of government. The Cabinet Secretary bears responsibility to nobody. The Cabinet Secretary is not accountable to Parliament except through the formality of occasional select committee appearances. The Cabinet Secretary is not accountable to the electorate. The Cabinet Secretary can be dismissed by the Prime Minister but convention makes this so difficult that it has never happened against the incumbent’s wishes. The office is, in constitutional terms, an anomaly: a permanent executive with no democratic mandate exercising powers that would be controversial if held by an elected politician.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) The position of Cabinet Secretary will be abolished on Day 1. The incumbent will be offered an alternative senior role or early retirement. The functions currently performed by the Cabinet Secretary will be distributed as follows. Policy advice to the Prime Minister: transferred to the Chief of Staff and the OPM Policy Unit. Management of Cabinet business: transferred to the Secretary of the Cabinet Secretariat, a new role leading the reduced secretariat (see CS3.3). Senior appointments: transferred to the OPM talent management function under the Chief of Staff, operating within the framework established by the reconstituted Civil Service Commission (CS1). Head of the Home Civil Service: abolished as a separate role; the Chief of Staff will exercise cross-service coordination authority through the OPM. Intelligence and security coordination: transferred to the National Security Adviser, who will report directly to the Prime Minister through the OPM. Custodian of the Ministerial Code: transferred to the Prime Minister personally, with administrative support from the OPM Propriety and Constitution team.
- b) The PM’s Chief of Staff will be appointed by the Prime Minister without any requirement for Civil Service Commission approval, external competition, or advisory panel. The Chief of Staff will hold the rank of Minister of State and will be accountable to Parliament through the normal mechanisms of ministerial accountability: oral and written questions, select committee appearances, and ultimately the confidence of the Prime Minister. The Chief of Staff may be drawn from any background: politics, the civil service, business, the military, academia, or technology. The appointment will be on a fixed-term basis of no more than five years, coterminous with the parliament unless renewed. The Chief of Staff may be dismissed by the Prime Minister at any time without cause. The principle is absolute: the person who runs the government machine on behalf of the Prime Minister must be chosen by, accountable to, and dismissible by the Prime Minister. Responsibility and authority are united in a single person who serves at the pleasure of the elected leader.
- c) The Head of the Home Civil Service role will be abolished. The cross-service functions currently exercised under this title, including the setting of civil service values, the management of the civil service code, and the oversight of cross-departmental workforce planning, will transfer to the OPM. The civil service will continue to have a distinct identity, ethos, and set of values, but these will be defined by the elected government through the King’s Regulations (CS8) rather than by a permanent official whose interest is in preserving the autonomy of the institution from the ministers it is supposed to serve. The abolition of the Head of the Civil Service role is not a symbolic act. It eliminates the constitutional fiction that the civil service is an independent estate of the realm with its own leader, separate from and potentially in tension with the elected government.

##### CS3.3: The Cabinet Secretariat

The Problem

The Cabinet Secretariat has expanded far beyond its original function. What began as a small team preparing agendas, recording decisions, and communicating them to departments has become a sprawling apparatus of Cabinet Committees, sub-committees, implementation taskforces, and cross-cutting policy teams that collectively constitute an alternative policy machine operating parallel to and often in competition with the departments of state. The Economic and Domestic Affairs Secretariat and the National Security Secretariat alone employ hundreds of officials. Cabinet Committees, which were designed to relieve the burden on full Cabinet by dealing with business that did not need to be discussed at the top table, have become the mechanism by which officials control the policy agenda: officials prepare the papers, officials chair the pre-meetings that determine the outcome, officials decide what reaches Cabinet and what does not. The minister who chairs a Cabinet Committee often exercises less influence over its conclusions than the secretariat official who prepared its papers and briefed its members.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) The Cabinet Secretariat will be reduced to fewer than 20 staff within 60 days of taking office. Its functions will be restricted to the original Hankey mandate: preparing agendas for Cabinet meetings in consultation with the Chief of Staff; recording decisions taken in Cabinet; communicating those decisions to the departments responsible for implementation; and maintaining the Cabinet minute book. The Secretariat will not prepare policy papers, will not chair pre-meetings, will not manage Cabinet Committees, and will not maintain implementation trackers. These functions will transfer to the OPM or to the departments responsible for the relevant policy areas. The Secretary of the Cabinet Secretariat will be a senior civil servant appointed by the Chief of Staff, reporting to the Chief of Staff, with no independent authority over Cabinet business.
- b) Cabinet Committees will be reduced to a maximum of four standing committees: Economic Affairs, National Security, Legislation, and Social Policy. Each will be chaired by a Secretary of State designated by the Prime Minister, not by an official. No pre-meetings between officials will take place before Cabinet or Cabinet Committee meetings. Ministers will receive papers directly from the sponsoring department and will be expected to arrive at meetings having read them and prepared their own positions. The practice by which officials script ministerial contributions to create the appearance of collective deliberation will end. If a minister cannot articulate and defend a position without a script prepared by officials, that minister is not performing their function and the Prime Minister will draw the appropriate conclusion under the War Cabinet model (CS9). The purpose of Cabinet is collective decision-making by elected politicians, not the ratification of decisions already taken by unelected officials.
- c) The National Security Secretariat and the Economic and Domestic Affairs Secretariat will transfer in their entirety to the OPM. These are not secretariat functions. They are policy coordination and advisory functions that properly belong to the centre of government under direct prime ministerial authority. The National Security Adviser, currently a dual-hatted role that combines policy advice with secretariat management, will become a dedicated policy role within the OPM, reporting directly to the Prime Minister through the Chief of Staff. The NSA will retain authority over the Joint Intelligence Organisation and the intelligence assessment process but will no longer manage Cabinet committee business. The separation is clean: the Secretariat records what Cabinet decides; the OPM advises the Prime Minister and coordinates implementation.

##### CS3.4: Structure of the Office of the Prime Minister

The Problem

The Prime Minister of the United Kingdom has the weakest institutional support of any leader of a comparable democracy. The Number 10 operation, described by Sue Gray as “more akin to a small government department” in size but without the structures to support it, is a cramped, under-resourced, and chaotically organised operation that has grown incrementally over decades without strategic design. The Spectator noted that the numbers working in Downing Street had quadrupled in 30 years “to little visible benefit.” The Prime Minister’s Office is formally part of the Cabinet Office. It has no Permanent Secretary of its own (though Boris Johnson briefly attempted to create one). It has no dedicated budget line visible to Parliament. It has no published organogram that accurately reflects its internal structure. The government’s own responses to parliamentary questions about Number 10 staffing simply refer to overall Cabinet Office figures. This is not a centre of government. It is an afterthought bolted onto someone else’s empire.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) The Office of the Prime Minister will be established as a full ministerial department with its own Accounting Officer, its own budget line in the Estimates, its own published structure chart, and its own annual report to Parliament. The OPM will be led by the Chief of Staff (Minister of State rank) and will contain the following units: the Policy Unit (strategic policy advice and cross-departmental coordination); the Delivery Unit (monitoring Charter Letter implementation and departmental performance); the Public Expenditure and Performance Unit (joint budget and performance monitoring, replacing the current CO/HMT shared function, as detailed in CS5); the National Security Unit (incorporating the NSA, JIO, and COBR); the Talent and Appointments Unit (senior civil service appointments, DRI selection, performance reviews, and the reconstituted Civil Service Commission liaison); the Government Communications Unit (strategic communications and media); and the Parliamentary and Legislative Unit (managing the government’s legislative programme and parliamentary business). Each unit will be led by a Director reporting to the Chief of Staff.
- b) The OPM will have a total staff ceiling of 500, a figure deliberately chosen to be smaller than the current combined Cabinet Office centre and Number 10 operation. The reduction will be achieved by transferring operational functions to departments (property, commercial, procurement), by abolishing the committee management and pre-meeting apparatus, and by eliminating the duplication that arises from having both a Cabinet Office and a Number 10 attempting to perform the same coordination functions. The OPM will be an elite organisation: small, fast, and staffed by the most capable people available from inside and outside the civil service. The CS1 reforms to senior appointments and the CS10 Angliot pipeline will ensure a supply of talent. The principle is that the centre of government should be a brain, not a body: it should think, decide, and direct, not administer, manage, and process.
- c) The OPM will be physically located in a single modern facility with the capacity to accommodate all staff, secure communications infrastructure, and direct access to the Prime Minister. The Downing Street complex will continue to serve as the Prime Minister’s official residence and ceremonial office, but the operational centre of government will move to purpose-built accommodation. The current arrangement, in which government is run from a rabbit warren of 18th-century rooms connected by narrow corridors across three terraced houses, is not fit for the management of a modern state. The OPM facility will include a secure operations centre for crisis management (replacing COBR’s current configuration), dedicated briefing rooms, modern collaborative workspaces, and the infrastructure required for real-time data monitoring of departmental performance. The principle is that the physical environment should reflect the operational ambition: a government that intends to move at war speed cannot operate from a building designed for a Georgian household.
- d) The OPM will publish a weekly dashboard of government performance against Charter Letter priorities (CS7), accessible to the Prime Minister, the Chief of Staff, all Secretaries of State, and all DRIs. The dashboard will draw on the real-time data feeds established by the Public Expenditure and Performance Unit and will provide the Prime Minister with a single view of what is working and what is not across every department. The current system, in which the Prime Minister receives filtered information through the Cabinet Secretary and departmental Permanent Secretaries who have every incentive to present an optimistic picture, will be replaced by a system in which the Prime Minister sees the same data as the DRIs responsible for delivery. The principle of responsibility married to authority extends to information: a Prime Minister who bears responsibility for the government’s performance must have unmediated access to the information that reveals that performance.

##### Summary

CS3 is deliverable on Day 1 by machinery of government change. No primary legislation is required. The legal instruments are an Order in Council under the Ministers of the Crown Act 1975 to transfer functions from the Cabinet Office to the Office of the Prime Minister, and the exercise of prerogative powers to reorganise the civil service and abolish designated positions. The precedent for transfers of this kind is well established and has been used by every incoming government in modern history.

Day 1 actions

Immediate: Order in Council signed, transferring coordination, delivery, strategy, and performance functions from Cabinet Office to OPM. Cabinet Secretary position abolished. Head of the Home Civil Service role abolished. Chief of Staff appointed and confirmed as Minister of State. PET system transferred to OPM within seven days. Attorney General’s directive issued (CS2) and Government Legal Department notified of new reporting lines.

Within 14 days: All staff performing transferring functions formally moved to OPM establishment. Secretary of Cabinet Secretariat appointed. Cabinet Committee structure reduced to four standing committees. Pre-meeting apparatus abolished. National Security Adviser confirmed as OPM Director reporting to PM through Chief of Staff.

Within 60 days: Cabinet Secretariat reduced to fewer than 20 staff. Residual Cabinet Office functions redistributed to departments or abolished. OPM structure chart and budget published. Recruitment campaign for OPM specialist roles launched. Government performance dashboard operational. OPM facility requirements specified and procurement initiated.

Within six months: OPM fully operational at steady state of 500 or fewer staff. First quarterly performance review cycle completed (CS7). Cross-departmental coordination protocols published. OPM annual report framework agreed with the relevant select committee. Remaining transitional arrangements concluded and the Cabinet Office formally dissolved as a department.

CS3 is the operational prerequisite for everything that follows in the reform framework. CS1 gives the Prime Minister the legal authority to appoint and dismiss. CS2 protects ministerial decisions from judicial veto. CS3 gives the Prime Minister an institutional machine through which to exercise that authority: a centre of government that serves the elected leader, that coordinates the departments of state, that monitors performance against published priorities, and that exists for no purpose other than the delivery of the government’s programme. Without CS3, the Prime Minister has authority in law but no mechanism to exercise it. With CS3, responsibility and authority are combined at the apex of the state for the first time since the Cabinet Office metastasised beyond its original mandate. The Office of the Prime Minister is not an innovation. It is a restoration: of the principle that the Prime Minister leads the government, and of the institutional arrangements necessary to make that leadership real.

#### CS4: The Reserve Army

“Structural Reform Without Personnel Change Is Architectural Drawing Without Construction”

Governing Principle

CS1 restores the Prime Minister’s legal authority to appoint and dismiss. CS2 protects ministerial decisions from judicial veto. CS3 gives the Prime Minister an institutional machine through which to exercise authority. CS4 addresses the question that determines whether any of this matters: who will actually run the departments of state on the morning after the election? The cardinal thesis of this framework is that responsibility must be combined with authority. But authority exercised through the wrong people is authority wasted. A Prime Minister who has the legal power to appoint anyone but arrives in office without knowing whom to appoint is a Prime Minister who will default to the existing Permanent Secretaries, who will promise cooperation, who will slow-walk every instruction, and who will outlast the government that appointed them. This is the invariable pattern. Every incoming government since Thatcher has been defeated not by the legal constraints on ministerial authority (though those are real and CS1 addresses them) but by the absence of an alternative personnel pool. Ministers know they want to replace the people running the machine. They do not know with whom. And so the machine continues, unchanged, under new political management that never achieves operational control.

The Senior Civil Service comprises approximately 7,525 officials as of 2025, representing roughly 1.4 percent of the total civil service headcount of 549,660. This small cadre runs the British state. Within it, some 450 officials at Director General level and above make the decisions that shape departmental strategy, allocate resources, manage the senior workforce, and determine the pace and direction of policy implementation. The 25 Permanent Secretaries who lead the major departments of state are the most powerful unelected individuals in the country after the Cabinet Secretary (whose abolition CS3 provides for). Since the July 2024 general election, 12 of 16 department heads have changed, a turnover rate that reflects the reality that incoming governments recognise the problem even if they lack the tools to solve it. But the replacements were drawn from the same pool: career civil servants assessed by the Civil Service Commission under criteria defined by the Commission itself, selected through processes managed by the Senior Leadership Committee, and approved by a system designed to reproduce the existing culture. The 2024-25 Civil Service Commission annual report recorded that 60,544 people were appointed to roles across the civil service that year, of which 56,194 were through fair and open competition and 4,498 by exception. At the senior level, the Commission’s grip is tightest: for the external recruitment of Directors General and Permanent Secretaries, the selection panel must be chaired by a Commissioner, the minister may suggest questions but cannot sit on the panel, and the final list of appointable candidates is determined by the Commission, not the Secretary of State. This is a closed system. It selects for people who resemble the people already in it. It is optimised for continuity, not reform.

The international comparison illuminates the scale of the British anomaly. The United States government makes approximately 4,000 political appointments with each new administration, including around 1,200 that require Senate confirmation. These appointees fill the senior leadership of every federal department and agency, from cabinet secretaries through deputy secretaries, under secretaries, and assistant secretaries. The incoming administration assembles its personnel during the transition period, drawing on think tanks, campaign staff, business, academia, the military, and the legal profession. The result is a government whose senior leadership is genuinely chosen by the President to implement the President’s programme. In Australia, departmental secretaries serve on fixed-term contracts and can be replaced by an incoming Prime Minister on the recommendation of the Public Service Commissioner and the Secretary of PM&C. The failure to reappoint a secretary after a change of government is routine. In France, each minister appoints a cabinet of personal advisers who exercise real authority within the department, and senior officials can be replaced through the prefectoral system. Britain, alone among comparable democracies, requires its incoming Prime Minister to govern through a permanent bureaucracy that the Prime Minister did not choose, cannot easily replace, and cannot direct without the consent of the bureaucracy itself.

Progress’ answer is the Reserve Army: a pre-identified, pre-briefed, and pre-committed cohort of individuals drawn from business, technology, the military, academia, and from within the civil service itself, who are ready to take up senior positions on Day 1 or as soon as the Civil Service Reform Act (CS1) receives Royal Assent. The Reserve Army is not a spoils system. It is a competence system with democratic accountability. Every member will be assessed against published competence criteria. Every member will serve on a fixed-term contract with a published performance agreement linked to a Charter Letter (CS7). Every member will be a Directly Responsible Individual (CS1) with personal accountability for delivery. The difference from the current system is that these individuals will be chosen by the elected government to implement the elected government’s programme, rather than chosen by the permanent bureaucracy to perpetuate the permanent bureaucracy’s culture. The Reserve Army ensures that the legal authority restored by CS1, the judicial protection provided by CS2, and the institutional machine created by CS3 are exercised through people who share the government’s objectives, possess the skills to achieve them, and accept personal responsibility for the results. Without CS4, the framework is a set of empty powers. With CS4, it is a government.

##### CS4.1: Pre-Election Assembly

The Problem

Every failed reform effort shares the same fatal flaw: the incoming government did not arrive with its own people ready to deploy. Blair arrived in 1997 with a political team but no alternative administrative leadership; the existing Permanent Secretaries stayed and the machine absorbed the new government within 18 months. The Coalition in 2010 made a handful of changes but accepted the civil service’s framing of what was possible. Johnson in 2019 briefly empowered outsiders during the pandemic but expelled them as soon as the crisis eased. In each case, the government recognised that the people running the machine were not the right people, but had no replacements available. The transition from election to government is the critical window. A Prime Minister who does not deploy alternative leadership within the first 30 days will not deploy it at all, because the permanent bureaucracy will use those 30 days to establish relationships, demonstrate indispensability, and define the parameters of the possible. The Reserve Army must therefore be assembled before the election, not after it.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) At least 18 months before the expected general election, the Party will establish a Talent Acquisition Unit operating under the direct authority of the Party leader. The Unit will be led by a single individual with extensive experience in senior executive recruitment from the private sector, the military, or both. The Unit’s mandate is to identify, assess, brief, and secure the commitment of individuals capable of serving as Directly Responsible Individuals (CS1) in every priority department of state. The Unit will operate outside any government structure and will be funded by the Party. Its work will be treated with the highest confidentiality. No civil servant, no member of the Civil Service Commission, and no incumbent Permanent Secretary will have any knowledge of or involvement in the process. The Unit will report directly to the Party leader and to the designated Chief of Staff (CS3).
- b) The Unit will identify a minimum of 50 candidates for approximately 25 priority positions: the DRI roles in each major department (replacing Permanent Secretaries), plus a reserve of at least one alternative candidate per role. The candidate pool will be drawn from four sources. First, the private sector: chief operating officers, managing directors, and programme directors from technology companies, infrastructure firms, defence contractors, financial institutions, and professional services firms who have demonstrated the ability to run large organisations, deliver complex programmes, and operate under pressure. Second, the military: serving and recently retired senior officers (Brigadier and above or equivalent) who have commanded large formations, managed multi-billion-pound equipment programmes, or led joint operations. Third, academia and think tanks: individuals with deep policy expertise in the relevant departmental domain who also have operational or management experience. Fourth, the existing civil service: reform-minded officials at Director and Director General level who have been frustrated by the system’s resistance to change and who would welcome the opportunity to lead under a genuine accountability framework. This fourth category is essential. Not every senior civil servant is an opponent of reform. Many are allies who have been suppressed by a culture that punishes initiative and rewards compliance.
- c) Every candidate will be assessed against a published competence framework that the OPM will adopt on Day 1 as the replacement for the Civil Service Commission’s merit criteria (CS1). The framework will assess: operational leadership (demonstrated ability to run organisations of comparable scale and complexity to a government department), programme delivery (track record of delivering complex programmes on time and within budget), strategic judgment (ability to translate political objectives into operational plans), adaptability (willingness to work in an unfamiliar environment under intense political and media scrutiny), and personal accountability (acceptance of the DRI model in which the individual is personally responsible for published performance metrics and dismissible for failure). The assessment will be conducted by the Talent Acquisition Unit with external support from a retained executive search firm operating under strict confidentiality.
- d) Every candidate who passes the competence assessment will receive a comprehensive briefing on the department they may be asked to lead. The briefing will cover: the department’s current organisational structure, budget, and major programmes; the draft Charter Letter (CS7) setting out the government’s priorities for that department; the DRI performance agreement template (CS1); the institutional obstacles the candidate should expect to encounter (including the likely response of incumbent officials, the Civil Service Commission, the FDA union, and the courts); and the support structures available through the OPM (CS3), the Litigation Readiness Unit (CS2), and the wider Reserve Army network. Candidates will also receive a briefing on the political context: the Party’s manifesto commitments, the anticipated parliamentary arithmetic, the likely timeline for the Civil Service Reform Act and the Executive Decisions Act, and the contingency plans for the period between Day 1 and Royal Assent during which some appointments may need to be made using prerogative powers and the exception provisions of the existing Recruitment Principles.

##### CS4.2: Day 1 Deployment

The Problem

The transition from opposition to government is the most dangerous moment for a reform programme. The civil service is at its most cooperative and its most manipulative during the first days of a new government. Permanent Secretaries will present themselves as indispensable partners, will offer comprehensive briefings designed to frame the government’s options within the boundaries the civil service considers acceptable, and will demonstrate a willingness to help that will evaporate the moment the government attempts anything the machine does not want to do. The standard playbook is to consume the new government’s energy with process: briefings, away-days, strategy sessions, consultation exercises, and the production of elaborate implementation plans that defer action to the distant future. By the time the government realises it has been absorbed, six months have passed, the political capital of the election victory has been spent, and the window for radical action has closed. The Reserve Army’s purpose is to prevent this absorption by deploying alternative leadership before the machine has time to establish its grip.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) On Day 1, the Prime Minister will use prerogative powers to make interim appointments of DRI candidates to priority departments. The legal basis for these appointments during the period before the Civil Service Reform Act receives Royal Assent will be the exception provisions in the existing Civil Service Commission Recruitment Principles, specifically Exception 1 (temporary appointments for up to two years) and Exception 9 (appointments under the direct authority of the Prime Minister for reasons of national importance). The Prime Minister’s authority to organise the civil service under prerogative powers is well established. The OPM Talent and Appointments Unit (CS3) will manage the process, with the Litigation Readiness Unit (CS2) prepared to defend any challenge.
