The appointments will be announced publicly as interim, pending the passage of the Civil Service Reform Act, at which point they will be confirmed as permanent DRI appointments on fixed-term contracts.
- b) Priority departments for Day 1 deployment will be determined by the Party leader and Chief of Staff before the election, based on two criteria: the strategic importance of the department to the government’s programme and the assessed likelihood that the incumbent Permanent Secretary will obstruct reform. The expected priority list, subject to revision, includes: HM Treasury (the single most important department for economic reform, CS5), the Home Office (immigration, policing, and national security), the Ministry of Defence (procurement reform, E10, and the nuclear deterrent), the Department of Health and Social Care (NHS reform, NHS1-NHS7), the Ministry of Justice (court backlog, C1-C13), and the Department for Education (skills pipeline, CS10). The remaining departments will receive DRI appointments within 60 days. No department will retain its incumbent Permanent Secretary beyond 90 days unless the OPM has specifically assessed that individual as reform-aligned and has received the Chief of Staff’s approval for their continuation.
- c) Each deployed DRI will arrive at their department with three documents: their Charter Letter (CS7), setting out the Prime Minister’s three to five priorities for the department; their performance agreement (CS1), setting out the published metrics against which they will be assessed at six-monthly intervals; and their authority letter, signed by the Secretary of State and the Chief of Staff, confirming their operational authority over the department’s staff, budget, and organisational structure. The DRI will convene the departmental board within 48 hours, introduce themselves and the Charter Letter, and set out the operational tempo expected by the government. The DRI will identify, within 14 days, the Director General and Director posts that require replacement and will submit recommendations to the OPM Talent and Appointments Unit. The principle is cascading deployment: the DRI replaces the Permanent Secretary, identifies the second-tier posts that need new leadership, and the Reserve Army provides the candidates. Within 60 days, the top three tiers of every priority department will have been reviewed and, where necessary, replaced.
- d) Incumbent Permanent Secretaries and Directors General who are displaced will be offered three options: redeployment to a non-leadership role at their existing grade, with no loss of pay, for a period of up to 12 months during which they may seek alternative employment; voluntary early retirement on standard civil service terms; or, for those assessed as reform-aligned, redeployment to a different department or to the OPM in a role that uses their institutional knowledge without giving them authority to obstruct the reform programme. The government will not victimise officials who have served faithfully under the existing system. It will simply ensure that the people leading departments are people chosen by the elected government to implement the elected government’s programme. The principle of responsibility married to authority requires that the people who exercise authority are accountable to the ministers who bear responsibility. Officials who cannot accept this principle, or who are unable to operate at the pace and intensity the government requires, will be treated with dignity but will not remain in positions of authority.

##### CS4.3: Internal Allies

The Problem

The civil service is not a monolith. Within the 549,660-strong workforce, and within the 7,525 members of the Senior Civil Service, there are officials who are frustrated by the system’s dysfunction, who recognise that the culture of risk-aversion and process-worship prevents effective government, and who would welcome the opportunity to work under a genuine accountability framework. During the brief period of outsider influence in 2020, some of the most effective allies were career civil servants who had been waiting for years for someone to give them permission to act. These officials exist at every level: Directors and Deputy Directors who have been blocked from promotion because they prioritised delivery over consensus, Grade 6 and 7 officials who have developed deep expertise in their policy area but whose recommendations are routinely overridden by generalist seniors, and operational managers in frontline delivery who understand what works and what does not but whose knowledge never reaches ministers because the hierarchical reporting chain filters it out. The Reserve Army is not exclusively an external force. Its most valuable members may be people already inside the machine.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) Before the election, the Talent Acquisition Unit will establish a confidential channel through which serving civil servants who support radical reform can register their interest, their expertise, and their assessment of the obstacles within their department. The channel will operate outside all government systems and will be managed by the Unit’s retained executive search firm under strict data protection protocols. No information will be stored on government networks or accessible to incumbent senior officials. The existence of the channel will be communicated through trusted intermediaries: former officials who have left the service and maintained contact with reform-minded colleagues, academics and think tank researchers who interact regularly with civil servants, and through carefully targeted outreach at professional events and conferences. The objective is not a mass recruitment exercise but a targeted identification of perhaps 200 to 300 individuals across the senior civil service who possess the combination of competence, courage, and commitment to reform that the programme requires.
- b) Within 30 days of taking office, the OPM will publish an open call for expressions of interest from serving civil servants who wish to be considered for accelerated promotion to DRI, Director General, or Director roles under the new accountability framework. The call will make explicit that the government is looking for officials who are prepared to accept personal responsibility for published performance metrics, who are comfortable operating at pace, who prioritise delivery over process, and who are willing to challenge institutional norms. Applications will be assessed by the OPM Talent and Appointments Unit against the same competence framework used for external Reserve Army candidates. Officials who are selected will be offered fixed-term appointments with performance-linked pay, published performance agreements, and the same six-monthly review cycle as external DRIs. The message to the civil service will be clear: this government rewards people who deliver, regardless of whether they came from inside or outside the system.
- c) The OPM will establish a Reform Network connecting internal allies across departments. The Network will provide a secure channel for officials to share intelligence about institutional obstacles, to flag decisions that are being slow-walked or obstructed, and to identify opportunities for cross-departmental collaboration that the existing siloed structure prevents. The Network will report to the OPM Delivery Unit and will feed directly into the weekly performance dashboard (CS3). The Network is not a surveillance mechanism. It is a communication mechanism that bypasses the hierarchical reporting chain through which information is currently filtered, delayed, and sanitised before it reaches ministers. The principle is that the government’s information about what is happening inside its own departments should not be controlled by the people whose performance is being assessed. Responsibility requires information; authority requires channels through which to exercise it. The Reform Network provides both.

##### CS4.4: The Secondment and Interchange Programme

The Problem

The British civil service is an intellectually closed system. The Senior Civil Service is populated overwhelmingly by career officials who entered through the Fast Stream or its predecessors, who have spent their entire working lives within Whitehall, and who have never managed a profit-and-loss account, commanded a military unit, built a product, or delivered a service to a paying customer. The Fast Stream selects approximately 1,000 candidates from 20,000 applicants each year, produces a disproportionate number of Oxford and Cambridge graduates, and rotates them through two-year postings that ensure breadth of exposure at the cost of depth of expertise. The grade inflation documented by the Institute for Government, in which 75 percent of civil servants now work at Executive Officer grade and above compared to 60 percent in 2015, reflects a service that has grown at the top without a corresponding increase in operational capability. The result is a leadership cadre that is extraordinarily skilled at writing submissions, managing stakeholders, and navigating internal process, but that lacks the operational instincts, the commercial awareness, and the delivery focus that the government’s programme demands. The Reserve Army addresses the immediate personnel crisis. The Secondment and Interchange Programme addresses the longer-term cultural transformation by establishing permanent channels through which external talent enters the civil service and civil servants gain experience outside Whitehall.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) Within 90 days of taking office, the OPM will launch a National Service to Government Programme, offering 12-month to 36-month secondments in senior civil service roles to executives from business, technology, finance, engineering, the military, and the third sector. Participants will be seconded at Director or Deputy Director level, will receive civil service pay supplemented where necessary to maintain their external salary level, and will work directly for DRIs in priority departments. The programme will target individuals who are mid-career (35 to 50), who have demonstrated operational leadership in their field, and who are motivated by the opportunity to contribute to public service without making a permanent career change. The programme will be managed by the OPM Talent and Appointments Unit and will be promoted through direct engagement with major employers, professional bodies, industry associations, and military transition programmes. The target is 200 secondees in the first year, rising to 500 by the end of the parliament.
- b) Simultaneously, the OPM will establish a Civil Servants in Industry Programme, requiring that all officials at Grade 6 and above who have spent more than five consecutive years in Whitehall spend a minimum of six months in an operational role outside government before being eligible for further promotion. Placements will be in private sector organisations, military units, NHS trusts, police forces, local authorities, and voluntary sector organisations that deliver frontline services. The objective is to break the intellectual monoculture of the senior civil service by ensuring that every senior official has direct, recent experience of how organisations outside Whitehall operate. The programme will be a condition of promotion, not a voluntary enrichment opportunity. The principle is that an official who has never delivered a service, managed a budget under competitive pressure, or been held personally accountable for a measurable outcome is not qualified to lead a government department, regardless of how many years they have spent writing policy submissions.
- c) The OPM will establish a Military-Civil Integration Programme, creating a permanent pipeline through which mid-career and senior military officers transition into civil service leadership roles. The military produces individuals who are trained to lead under pressure, to make decisions with incomplete information, to accept personal responsibility for outcomes, and to operate within a culture that values execution over deliberation. These are precisely the qualities that the civil service lacks and that the DRI model demands. The programme will identify officers at the rank of Colonel or Brigadier (or equivalent) who are approaching the end of their military careers and who are interested in a second career in government. Participants will receive a six-month induction covering the machinery of government, the policy process, and the administrative law framework, and will then be placed in Director or Director General roles in departments with significant delivery or operational functions: Defence, Home Office, Justice, Health, Transport, and the OPM itself. The target is 30 military-to-civil transitions per year.

##### Summary

CS4 is entirely operational. It requires no primary legislation. It is enabled by the legal framework established by CS1 (ministerial hire and fire authority, DRI model, fixed-term contracts, competence-based appointment), protected by CS2 (judicial review restrictions, Litigation Readiness Unit), and managed through CS3 (OPM Talent and Appointments Unit, Chief of Staff authority). The Reserve Army is the human element that makes the institutional reforms real.

18 months before election:

Talent Acquisition Unit established. Candidate identification begins. Confidential channel for internal allies opened. Executive search firm retained. Competence framework drafted.

12 months before election:

Minimum 50 candidates identified for 25 priority DRI roles. Assessment process underway. Department briefing packs in preparation. Draft Charter Letters circulated to candidates.

6 months before election:

All priority candidates assessed, briefed, and committed. Reserve candidates identified. Deployment plan finalised. Legal strategy for interim appointments confirmed with Litigation Readiness Unit.

Day 1:

Interim DRI appointments to priority departments using prerogative powers and exception provisions. Authority letters issued. Charter Letters delivered. Departmental boards convened within 48 hours.

Within 14 days:

DRIs submit second-tier replacement recommendations to OPM. National Security and intelligence-sensitive appointments completed with enhanced vetting.

Within 30 days:

Open call for internal allies published. Reform Network established. Second-tier appointments in priority departments completed.

Within 60 days:

All major departments reviewed. Remaining DRI appointments made. Displaced officials offered redeployment, early retirement, or reform-aligned roles.

Within 90 days:

National Service to Government Programme launched. Civil Servants in Industry Programme announced. Military-Civil Integration Programme established. First cohort of secondees deployed.

CS4 is the policy that makes every other policy in this framework deliverable. CS1 without CS4 is a legal power with nobody to exercise it. CS3 without CS4 is an empty institution. CS7 without CS4 is a set of letters that nobody reads. The principle that responsibility must be combined with authority extends to personnel: if the elected government is responsible for the country’s governance, the elected government must have the authority to choose the people who govern. The Reserve Army is not a patronage system. It is a competence system in which every appointment is assessed against published criteria, every appointee serves on a fixed-term contract, every appointee has a published performance agreement, and every appointee is dismissed if they fail. The current system, in which appointments are made by the permanent bureaucracy on criteria defined by the permanent bureaucracy and assessed by the permanent bureaucracy, with no performance consequences and no ministerial control, is the true patronage system. It is patronage exercised by an institution in its own interest. The Reserve Army replaces institutional patronage with democratic accountability.

#### CS5: Breaking Treasury Control

“The Treasury Does Not Exist to Control Departments. It Exists to Ensure That Departments Deliver Value for the Money Parliament Has Voted”

Governing Principle

HM Treasury is not a finance ministry. It is a government within the government. Its control over departmental spending extends far beyond the legitimate function of fiscal management into the micro-management of departmental operations, the effective veto of ministerial decisions, and the subordination of elected Secretaries of State to unelected Treasury spending teams staffed by officials who are frequently two decades younger and several grades more junior than the departmental leaders whose spending they control. The Institute for Government described this in 2024 as a power imbalance at the centre of government, in which a dominant Treasury fills the vacuum left by Number 10’s comparative lack of firepower, taking ownership of whole-government strategy that properly belongs to the Prime Minister. The result is a system in which the Chancellor of the Exchequer, through the permanent machinery of the Treasury, exercises a practical veto over the work of every other department. Secretaries of State who are nominally responsible to Parliament for their department’s performance cannot implement their policies without the consent of Treasury officials who bear no responsibility for those policies’ success or failure. Responsibility and authority are separated with surgical precision: ministers bear the political consequences of failure while the Treasury controls the operational levers that determine whether success is even possible.

The mechanism of control is the Delegated Authority Limit system. Every department is allocated a spending limit below which it may approve expenditure without Treasury consent. Expenditure above that limit requires Treasury approval through the Treasury Approvals Process, which involves engagement with the relevant Treasury spending team, the production of business cases assessed against the Green Book methodology, review by the Major Projects Review Group for projects above a threshold value, and ultimately sign-off by the Chief Secretary to the Treasury. In 2023-24, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government had a delegated resource spending limit of just 10 million pounds, meaning that 94 percent of the department’s activity required Treasury approval. The government’s own Office for Value for Money found that this micromanagement hampered the delivery of government priorities, often adding six weeks or more to the approval process, with no evidence of value added by the additional control. The OVfM’s November 2025 reforms raised delegated limits and proposed reducing the number of approval decisions reaching the Chief Secretary by approximately 55 percent. These reforms are welcome but insufficient. They address the symptom (excessive approvals) without addressing the cause (the Treasury’s institutional incentive to control rather than enable). The Treasury does not micro-manage because its delegated limits are set too low. The Treasury sets delegated limits too low because micro-management is the source of its institutional power.

The deeper pathology is cultural. Samuel Beer observed in 1955 that the Treasury’s control framework was, like much of the British constitution, unwritten, formed of guidelines rather than formally enforceable laws, and reliant on goodwill. Gladstone’s principle of saving candle-ends has survived into the 21st century as a culture in which the Treasury’s default posture toward departmental spending is suspicion, and in which Treasury officials derive institutional prestige from preventing expenditure rather than from enabling effective government. The Treasury spending teams that interact with departments are staffed by relatively junior officials, often in their first or second posting, who lack the domain expertise to assess whether a departmental proposal represents good value but who possess the institutional authority to delay or block it. The IfG noted that these officials were too inexperienced and unable to draw on adequate expertise to make the spending decisions asked of them. The result is a system in which major government programmes are delayed not because they are bad value but because the approval process takes months, the officials assessing them lack the competence to evaluate them quickly, and the institutional culture rewards caution over action. A technology programme in one department was required to wait at least two months after completing commercial negotiations with its supplier before it could proceed to contract award, simply because the sequential Treasury approval process had not caught up with the pace of procurement.

CS5 does not propose abolishing Treasury control over public spending. Parliament votes money to the Crown on the recommendation of the Chancellor; the Treasury’s role in ensuring that money is spent in accordance with Parliament’s intentions is constitutionally essential. What CS5 proposes is a fundamental restructuring of how that control is exercised: replacing micro-management of individual spending decisions with strategic oversight of departmental performance, replacing the Treasury’s bilateral monopoly over departments with a joint budget and performance system managed through the OPM (CS3), and replacing the culture of prevention with a culture of accountability. The principle is the same as throughout this framework: responsibility married to authority. Departments should have the authority to spend the money Parliament has voted for them, because departments bear the responsibility for delivering results with that money. The Treasury should retain the authority to set the fiscal envelope and to intervene when departments demonstrably fail to deliver value, because the Treasury bears responsibility to Parliament for the overall fiscal position. What the Treasury should not have is the authority to approve individual spending decisions within a department’s voted allocation, because this authority is exercised without any responsibility for the consequences of delay, obstruction, or risk-aversion that the approval process imposes.

##### CS5.1: The Public Expenditure and Performance Unit

The Problem

The current system separates spending control (Treasury) from performance monitoring (Cabinet Office/Number 10), creating a structural incentive for the Treasury to focus exclusively on cost containment while nobody focuses systematically on whether the money that is spent achieves anything. The Spending Review process sets departmental expenditure limits. The Public Service Agreements that once accompanied Spending Reviews, linking spending to measurable outcomes, were abolished by the Coalition in 2010 and have not been replaced with anything of comparable rigour. The result is that departments negotiate their budgets with the Treasury, receive their allocations, and then spend the money with minimal systematic monitoring of whether the spending achieves the government’s objectives. The Treasury monitors inputs (how much is spent) and the Cabinet Office intermittently monitors outputs (how many things were done), but nobody systematically monitors outcomes (whether the spending made a difference). When things go wrong, the discovery comes years later through NAO reports or select committee inquiries, long after the money has been spent and the opportunity to correct course has passed.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) Within 14 days of taking office, the Prime Minister will establish the Public Expenditure and Performance Unit within the OPM (CS3). The PEPU will be a joint unit combining the Treasury’s expenditure monitoring function with the performance monitoring functions currently scattered between the Cabinet Office, Number 10’s Delivery Unit, and the Infrastructure and Projects Authority (now the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority). The PEPU will be staffed by a combination of Treasury officials with fiscal and budgetary expertise, OPM officials with policy and delivery expertise, and external secondees from the private sector with commercial and financial analysis skills (CS4). The PEPU will report to the Chief of Staff (CS3) and will provide the Prime Minister with a single integrated view of how much each department is spending and what that spending is achieving. The Treasury will retain responsibility for the fiscal envelope, the Spending Review process, and the management of the Reserve. The PEPU will be responsible for everything else: monitoring departmental performance against Charter Letter priorities (CS7), identifying departments that are underspending or overspending relative to their performance, and recommending reallocation of resources from failing programmes to succeeding ones.
- b) The PEPU will produce a quarterly Expenditure and Performance Report for the Prime Minister, the Chancellor, and all Secretaries of State. The report will integrate financial data (actual expenditure against profile, forecast outturn, variance analysis) with performance data (Charter Letter metric progress, delivery milestones, operational indicators). The report will be published, with appropriate redactions for national security, providing Parliament and the public with a single document that answers two questions simultaneously: how much is the government spending, and is that spending achieving the government’s objectives? The current system, in which financial data is published through the Estimates and departmental accounts while performance data is published (if at all) through inconsistent and incomparable departmental annual reports, makes it effectively impossible for anyone, including the Prime Minister, to assess the value for money of the government’s programme as a whole. The PEPU report will replace this fragmentation with integration.
- c) The PEPU will have the authority to recommend the reallocation of resources between programmes within a department’s spending envelope, subject to the Secretary of State’s agreement and the Prime Minister’s approval. Currently, only the Treasury can approve virements (transfers between budget lines) above the delegated limit. This gives the Treasury effective control over departmental strategy, because a department that discovers mid-year that one programme is failing and another is succeeding cannot redirect resources without Treasury permission, which takes weeks or months. Under the PEPU model, the DRI (CS1) will have authority to reallocate resources within the department’s voted allocation, reporting the reallocation to the PEPU for monitoring purposes. The PEPU will flag reallocations that appear to undermine the Charter Letter priorities or that pose fiscal risk, but will not exercise a prior approval function. The DRI is responsible; the DRI has authority; the PEPU monitors and reports. This is the responsibility-authority model applied to financial management.

##### CS5.2: Reforming Delegated Authority

The Problem

The Delegated Authority Limit system is the single most effective mechanism by which the Treasury controls departments. By setting the limit below which a department can spend without approval, the Treasury determines how much of a department’s activity it scrutinises. The lower the limit, the more approvals are required, the more Treasury officials are needed to process them, and the more institutional power the Treasury accrues. The OVfM’s 2025 reforms raised limits and promised a 55 percent reduction in approval decisions reaching the Chief Secretary. But the fundamental architecture remains: the Treasury sets the limits, the Treasury processes the approvals, the Treasury decides whether to grant or withhold consent. The department proposes; the Treasury disposes. Even where limits are raised, the Treasury retains the ability to lower them again at the next Spending Review, to impose ad hoc conditions on specific programmes, or to use informal mechanisms (the phone call from the spending team, the request for additional analysis, the suggestion that a business case needs further work) to delay decisions without formally withholding approval. The formal system is the visible architecture of control. The informal system, in which Treasury officials signal displeasure, request meetings, and create uncertainty, is the invisible architecture and is in many ways more powerful.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) Within 30 days of taking office, the Chancellor will issue a new Delegated Authority Framework. For departments led by DRIs operating under Charter Letters with published performance agreements, the delegated authority limit for resource expenditure will be set at the department’s full annual resource allocation, with no transaction-level approval required from the Treasury. The DRI will have authority to approve all expenditure within the department’s voted envelope. For capital expenditure, the delegated authority limit will be set at 100 million pounds per project, above which Treasury and NISTA approval will be required. The principle is that a DRI who has been appointed by the Prime Minister, who has accepted personal responsibility for delivering the Charter Letter priorities, and who will be dismissed for failure, does not need a 25-year-old Treasury official’s permission to spend the money Parliament has voted for the department’s use. The DRI is accountable. The DRI has the information. The DRI bears the consequences. The DRI should have the authority.
- b) The Treasury spending teams will be restructured. The current model, in which each department has a dedicated Treasury spending team that processes individual approval requests, will be replaced by a model in which the Treasury’s departmental engagement focuses on three functions: setting the department’s expenditure limit at each Spending Review, providing fiscal and economic analysis to support departmental decision-making (an advisory function, not an approval function), and intervening when the PEPU quarterly report identifies a department that is materially overspending, materially underperforming against Charter Letter metrics, or accumulating contingent liabilities that threaten the fiscal position. This restructuring will allow the Treasury to redeploy staff from transaction processing to strategic analysis. The IfG observed that the burden of approval processing prevented spending teams from engaging on large, complex and expensive programmes and how they fit with the government’s long-term strategy. By eliminating the transaction-processing burden, the reforms will enable the Treasury to do what a finance ministry should do: think strategically about the allocation of scarce resources, rather than operationally about whether a particular business case has the right number of appendices.
- c) The Chief Secretary to the Treasury will retain a reserve power to impose enhanced controls on any department where the PEPU quarterly report demonstrates that the DRI is failing to manage the department’s finances responsibly. Enhanced controls will restore transaction-level approval requirements for the specific programme or budget line that is causing concern, and will remain in place until the DRI has demonstrated that the underlying problem has been resolved. This mechanism preserves parliamentary accountability for public spending while eliminating the presumption that all departments require micro-management at all times. The current system treats every department as incompetent until proven otherwise. The reformed system treats every department as competent until the evidence demonstrates otherwise, at which point targeted intervention replaces blanket control. The principle is that competence earns autonomy. DRIs who manage their budgets well will operate with maximum freedom. DRIs who manage their budgets badly will face enhanced scrutiny as a precursor to dismissal under the CS1 performance framework.

##### CS5.3: Reforming the Spending Review

The Problem

The Spending Review is the Treasury’s primary mechanism for strategic control of public expenditure. In theory, it is a rational process in which the government collectively determines how to allocate scarce resources among competing priorities. In practice, it is an adversarial negotiation in which Treasury officials and departmental officials bargain over numbers, with the Treasury holding the stronger hand because it controls the process, sets the timeline, and defines the analytical framework. The IfG identified a damaging short-termism in the Treasury budgeting process, risking static thinking and a bias against transformative policy proposals. The Fraser of Allander Institute noted that the Treasury’s primary concern in the Spending Review is avoiding breaches of the control total, and that departments almost always underspend their limits, suggesting that the system is calibrated for fiscal caution rather than effective delivery. The 2025 Spending Review introduced three-year resource budgets and five-year capital budgets, which is a significant improvement over the annual settlements that preceded them. But the fundamental dynamic remains: the Treasury sets the envelope, the Treasury assesses the bids, the Treasury determines the allocations, and the Treasury retains the ability to impose conditions and controls on how the allocations are spent. The Spending Review is not a collective government exercise. It is a Treasury exercise in which other departments participate as supplicants.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) The Spending Review will be restructured as a joint exercise of the Treasury and the OPM, with the PEPU providing the analytical backbone. The Treasury will retain responsibility for the overall fiscal envelope: total public expenditure, the split between resource and capital, the split between departmental expenditure limits and annually managed expenditure, and the management of the Reserve. The PEPU will be responsible for assessing departmental bids against Charter Letter priorities and performance data. The assessment will answer two questions: is this department delivering on its current priorities with its current resources, and does the proposed allocation enable the department to deliver on its future priorities? The current assessment, which focuses overwhelmingly on fiscal risk and cost containment, will be supplemented by an assessment of delivery risk and performance trajectory. A department that is delivering well should receive its full bid. A department that is delivering poorly should not receive additional resources until it has demonstrated the ability to use its existing resources effectively. The allocation decision will be made jointly by the Chancellor and the Prime Minister, with the PEPU providing the analytical basis and the Chief of Staff coordinating the process.
- b) Spending Review allocations will be accompanied by published Performance Compacts replacing the abolished Public Service Agreements. Each Performance Compact will be agreed between the Secretary of State, the DRI, the Chancellor, and the Prime Minister. It will set out: the department’s expenditure limit for the Review period, the three to five Charter Letter priorities for the period, the quantified metrics against which delivery will be assessed, and the consequences of over-performance (additional resources from the Reserve or from underperforming departments) and under-performance (enhanced controls as described in CS5.2, and ultimately DRI replacement as described in CS1). The Performance Compact will be published, creating a public contract between the government and the electorate about what the money will buy. The current system, in which departments receive allocations with no published performance expectations, makes it impossible for Parliament or the public to assess whether the money was well spent until years after the event. The Performance Compact makes the assessment possible in real time.
- c) The Spending Review cycle will be fixed at two years, with annual monitoring through the PEPU quarterly reports. The fixed cycle will provide departments with greater certainty for planning while ensuring that allocations are regularly reviewed against performance. Between Reviews, the DRI will have full authority to manage the department’s spending within its voted allocation. The Treasury will not impose in-year savings requirements, efficiency targets, or recruitment freezes outside the Spending Review process except in response to a genuine fiscal emergency declared by the Chancellor with the Prime Minister’s agreement. The practice by which the Treasury imposes ad hoc constraints on departments between Spending Reviews, often motivated by short-term fiscal management rather than strategic priority, undermines the authority of DRIs, disrupts departmental planning, and creates the perverse incentive for departments to spend their full allocation as quickly as possible rather than managing resources efficiently over the Review period. If the fiscal envelope needs to change, that change will be made through a formal process with published justification, not through informal Treasury pressure on individual departments.

##### CS5.4: Treasury Culture and Capability

The Problem

The Treasury’s institutional culture is the deepest obstacle to reform. The department has operated for over a century on the Gladstonian principle that its purpose is to prevent expenditure. This was appropriate when public spending was a small fraction of national income and the primary risk was profligacy. It is not appropriate when the government spends over 45 percent of GDP and the primary risks are under-investment in infrastructure, failure to maintain public services, and the inability to implement the government’s programme because the approval process is slower than the pace of change. The Treasury’s self-image as the guardian of the public purse is not wrong, but it is incomplete. A finance ministry that prevents waste but also prevents investment, that avoids fiscal risk but also avoids delivery risk, and that controls spending but does not monitor whether spending achieves anything, is a finance ministry that is failing in its purpose. The OVfM’s temporary success in shifting Treasury culture demonstrates that change is possible. But the OVfM was a 20-person unit with a one-year lifespan. The cultural transformation required is permanent and structural.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) The Treasury’s DRI, appointed under the CS1 framework, will have a Charter Letter (CS7) that explicitly redefines the Treasury’s purpose. The Treasury exists to ensure that the government’s fiscal position is sustainable, that public money is spent effectively, and that departments have the resources they need to deliver the government’s programme. The Treasury does not exist to prevent departments from spending money, to substitute its judgment for that of Secretaries of State on policy questions, or to exercise a practical veto over government decisions by delaying approval processes. The DRI will be assessed against metrics that include: the time taken to process approvals that remain within the Treasury’s remit (capital projects above 100 million pounds), the quality of fiscal and economic analysis provided to departments and to the PEPU, the accuracy of fiscal forecasts, and the delivery of Spending Review settlements on time and within the government’s fiscal rules. The DRI will not be assessed on how much spending they prevented, because preventing spending is not a legitimate measure of Treasury performance.
- b) The Treasury’s workforce will be restructured to increase domain expertise. The current model, in which generalist officials rotate between spending teams every two to three years, will be replaced by a model in which spending teams are staffed by officials with deep expertise in the relevant policy domain. An official overseeing defence spending should understand defence procurement, military capability, and the defence industrial base. An official overseeing health spending should understand clinical pathways, workforce planning, and the economics of health systems. The National Service to Government Programme (CS4) will provide a pipeline of external specialists who can bring private sector, military, or operational expertise into Treasury teams. The Fast Stream rotation model, which ensures that no Treasury official develops deep expertise in any domain, will be replaced by a specialist career track in which officials build expertise over five to ten years in a single policy area before being eligible for promotion to cross-cutting strategic roles.
- c) The Treasury’s relationship with departments will be formally redefined from adversarial to enabling. The current posture, inherited from Gladstone and reinforced by a century of institutional culture, treats every departmental spending proposal as a threat to the fiscal position that must be resisted unless compelling evidence is provided for its approval. The reformed posture will treat every departmental spending proposal as a potential contribution to the government’s programme that should be enabled unless compelling evidence is provided that it threatens the fiscal position or represents poor value for money. The burden of proof shifts: departments no longer need to prove that their spending is justified; the Treasury needs to demonstrate that proposed spending should be blocked. This is not a semantic distinction. It reflects the fundamental constitutional reality that Parliament has voted money for departments to spend, and the Treasury’s role is to ensure that Parliament’s intention is fulfilled, not to frustrate it. The DRI at the Treasury will be expected to model this posture and to hold Treasury officials accountable for enabling departmental delivery. Treasury officials who obstruct or delay departmental spending without identifying a specific fiscal risk or value-for-money concern will face the same performance consequences as officials in any other department who fail to deliver on their Charter Letter obligations.

##### Summary

CS5 is entirely operational. It requires no primary legislation. The Spending Review, the delegated authority framework, and the Treasury’s internal organisation are all within the prerogative of the Chancellor and the Prime Minister to reform by administrative direction. The changes can be implemented through a combination of the Chancellor’s direction to the Treasury, the Prime Minister’s establishment of the PEPU within the OPM, and the joint agreement of the Chancellor and Prime Minister to reform the Spending Review process.

Day 1:

Treasury DRI appointed under CS1 framework. Charter Letter issued redefining Treasury’s purpose. Chief of Staff and Chancellor agree division of responsibilities between OPM and Treasury.

Within 14 days:

PEPU established within OPM, combining expenditure monitoring and performance monitoring functions. Staff transferred from Treasury, Cabinet Office, and NISTA. External secondees recruited through CS4 pipeline.

Within 30 days:

New Delegated Authority Framework issued by Chancellor. Full resource delegation to DRI-led departments. Capital threshold set at 100 million pounds. Treasury spending teams restructured from approval processing to strategic analysis.

Within 60 days:

First PEPU quarterly report framework published. Performance Compact template agreed for next Spending Review. Treasury specialist career track announced.

Within 90 days:

First PEPU quarterly report published, integrating expenditure and performance data for all departments. Treasury-departmental relationship protocol published, codifying the enabling posture.

First Spending Review:

Joint OPM-Treasury exercise. Performance Compacts replace bilateral negotiations. Published allocations accompanied by published performance expectations. Two-year fixed cycle confirmed. In-year savings requirements prohibited outside declared fiscal emergency.

CS5 completes the institutional architecture of the reform framework. CS1 gives the Prime Minister hire and fire authority. CS2 protects ministerial decisions from judicial veto. CS3 creates the OPM as the Prime Minister’s institutional machine. CS4 provides the people to staff the machine and the departments. CS5 breaks the Treasury’s stranglehold over departmental operations, replacing micro-management with strategic oversight and replacing the culture of prevention with the culture of accountability. Together, CS1 through CS5 establish the conditions under which the remaining reforms, CS6 (the Civil Service Management Code), CS7 (Charter Letters), CS8 (King’s Regulations), CS9 (War Cabinet), and CS10 (Angliot), become possible. A Prime Minister who controls the appointments (CS1), is protected from judicial interference (CS2), has an institutional machine (CS3), has the right people (CS4), and has broken Treasury obstruction (CS5) is a Prime Minister who can govern. The remaining policies define what that government will do and how it will sustain itself. The first five define whether it can do anything at all.

#### CS6: Rewriting the Civil Service Management Code

“The Rules That Govern the Civil Service Should Serve the Government of the Day, Not the Permanent Bureaucracy That Wrote Them”

Governing Principle

The Civil Service Management Code is the operating manual of the British state. It sets out the regulations and instructions governing civil servants’ terms and conditions of service, covering recruitment, probation, conduct, discipline, pay, performance management, redeployment, and dismissal. The Code is issued by the Minister for the Civil Service, who is by convention the Prime Minister, under powers conferred by the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010. In theory, this means the Prime Minister controls the rules by which the civil service operates. In practice, the Code was written by the civil service, is maintained by the civil service, is interpreted by the civil service, and is enforced by the civil service. The current version, last substantively updated in November 2016, reflects the institutional preferences of the permanent bureaucracy: maximum job security, minimum performance accountability, extensive procedural protections against dismissal, no mechanism for ministerial direction of individual officials, and a culture of consensus in which every decision requires consultation with trade unions, HR professionals, and legal advisers before anything happens. The Code is the constitution of a self-governing institution. The Minister for the Civil Service’s theoretical power to rewrite it has never been exercised to challenge the institution’s core interests, because every Prime Minister who has held the role has been advised by the very officials whose interests the Code protects.

The Code’s structure reveals its priorities. Its provisions on recruitment defer to the Civil Service Commission and the Recruitment Principles, creating the closed system that CS1 reforms. Its provisions on conduct establish the four core values of integrity, honesty, objectivity, and impartiality, which are unexceptionable as principles but which have been weaponised in practice to prevent officials from implementing policies they disagree with. The requirement for impartiality, designed to protect the civil service from party-political patronage, has been interpreted to mean that officials owe equal loyalty to all possible future governments, a doctrine that in practice means they owe primary loyalty to the institutional status quo rather than to the government of the day. The requirement for objectivity, designed to ensure that advice is based on evidence, has been interpreted to mean that officials may substitute their judgment for that of ministers on policy questions by characterising ministerial decisions as insufficiently evidence-based. The Code’s provisions on discipline and dismissal create extensive procedural protections that, when combined with the involvement of trade unions and the threat of employment tribunal claims, make it practically impossible to dismiss a civil servant for poor performance in under 12 months, and extremely difficult to do so at all. The Code does not contain any provision for ministerial direction of departmental operations, any mechanism for holding individual officials accountable for delivery, or any recognition that the civil service exists to serve the elected government.

The Civil Service Code, which sits alongside the Management Code and is given statutory force by the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010, compounds the problem. Its instruction that civil servants must not frustrate the implementation of policies once decisions are taken is honoured overwhelmingly in the breach. The mechanism for enforcing this provision is an appeal to the Civil Service Commission, which has never found against the institutional interests of the civil service. The Code states that civil servants are accountable to ministers, who in turn are accountable to Parliament. But accountability without consequences is not accountability. A civil servant who frustrates the implementation of a ministerial decision faces, at worst, a redeployment to another role at the same grade and pay. A minister whose policy fails because it was frustrated by officials faces the loss of their career. The asymmetry is total: officials bear no consequences for failure while ministers bear all of them. CS6 proposes to rewrite the Management Code from first principles, replacing the self-governing constitution of the permanent bureaucracy with an operating manual that serves the elected government, that makes delivery the primary duty of every civil servant, that creates genuine performance accountability at every level, and that gives ministers and DRIs (CS1) the management tools to run their departments as leaders run any high-performing organisation.

##### CS6.1: The Duty to Deliver

The Problem

The current Management Code defines the civil servant’s role in terms of values (integrity, honesty, objectivity, impartiality) and process (compliance with rules, consultation with stakeholders, adherence to procedures). It does not define the civil servant’s role in terms of delivery. Nowhere in the Code or the Civil Service Code is it stated that a civil servant’s primary duty is to deliver the government’s programme. Nowhere is it stated that a civil servant who follows every process correctly but fails to deliver a result has failed. The result is a culture in which process compliance is the measure of success: an official who consults all stakeholders, produces a thorough submission, and manages every risk but whose programme delivers nothing is rated as effective, while an official who cuts through process to deliver a result but fails to complete every procedural step is rated as problematic. The Management Code creates officials who are expert administrators of process and incompetent deliverers of outcomes.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) The revised Management Code will open with a statement of purpose that defines the civil service’s role: the civil service exists to deliver the programme of the elected government of the day. Every civil servant, at every grade, bears a personal duty to contribute to the delivery of the government’s programme as set out in the relevant Charter Letter (CS7) and as directed by their departmental DRI (CS1). The four core values of integrity, honesty, objectivity, and impartiality are retained, but their interpretation is reframed. Integrity means putting delivery of the government’s programme above personal preferences, institutional convenience, and risk-aversion. Honesty means telling ministers the truth about what is working and what is not, including when officials’ own decisions have contributed to failure. Objectivity means basing advice on evidence, but accepting that once a minister has considered the evidence and made a decision, the official’s duty is to implement that decision with commitment, not to re-litigate it through delay and obstruction. Impartiality means serving the government of the day with the same energy and commitment regardless of its political colour, which means serving this government with energy and commitment, not hedging between this government and a hypothetical future government.
- b) The revised Code will establish a Delivery Standard as the primary measure of civil service performance. Every official at Grade 7 and above will have a published set of delivery objectives derived from their department’s Charter Letter (CS7) and agreed with their line manager at the start of each performance year. Performance will be assessed primarily against these delivery objectives: did the official achieve the outcomes they were responsible for? Process compliance, stakeholder management, and adherence to procedures will be assessed as secondary factors relevant only insofar as they contributed to or obstructed delivery. The current performance system, in which officials are assessed against generic competency frameworks that reward behaviours (leadership, communication, collaboration) rather than results, will be replaced by a system that rewards delivery and holds officials accountable for failure. The Delivery Standard will be published as part of the revised Code and will apply uniformly across all departments.
- c) The revised Code will abolish the current box-marking system in which the overwhelming majority of officials receive the same performance rating regardless of actual performance. The replacement system will require DRIs to rank officials within each grade band into three categories: delivering (met or exceeded delivery objectives), developing (partially met delivery objectives and demonstrating a trajectory toward full delivery), and failing (did not meet delivery objectives without adequate justification). Officials rated as failing for two consecutive assessment periods will enter a fast-track performance improvement process with a maximum duration of three months, at the end of which they will either have demonstrated improvement sufficient to move to the developing category or will be dismissed. Officials rated as delivering for three consecutive assessment periods will be eligible for accelerated promotion. The distribution will not be forced into predetermined percentages, but DRIs will be expected to demonstrate to the OPM that their ratings are credible and differentiated. A department in which 95 percent of officials are rated as delivering while the department’s Charter Letter metrics are declining will prompt a review of the DRI’s performance management practices.

##### CS6.2: Performance Management and Dismissal

The Problem

Dismissing a civil servant for poor performance under the current Management Code is a process so protracted, so procedurally burdensome, and so vulnerable to legal challenge that it is, in practice, not attempted. The Code requires progressive stages of formal warnings, improvement plans, review periods, and appeals. At each stage the official is entitled to representation, typically by the FDA or PCS union. The union representative’s incentive is to delay and complicate, because time is the official’s ally and the manager’s enemy. Employment tribunal claims for unfair dismissal are common and their prospect deters managers from even beginning the process. The result is that poor performance is managed by redeployment (moving the problem to another team), by acceptance (lowering expectations to match the official’s output), or by promotion (moving the official into a role where their incompetence is less visible). The Northcote-Trevelyan settlement’s guarantee of permanence, designed in 1854 to protect officials from political patronage, has become in the 21st century a guarantee of impunity that protects officials from the consequences of their own failure.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) The revised Management Code will establish a streamlined dismissal process for poor performance. For officials at Grade 7 and above, the process will be: formal notification of performance failure with specific evidence (Day 1), performance improvement plan with measurable targets and a maximum duration of three months (Day 1 to Day 90), final assessment by the DRI or their designated Director (Day 90), and if the targets have not been met, termination with statutory notice and severance (Day 91 onwards). The total elapsed time from formal notification to dismissal will not exceed four months. The official will have the right to make written representations at each stage and to appeal to an internal panel chaired by an official from a different department. The appeal will be determined within 14 days. There will be no right to union representation at internal hearings, though the official may consult a union representative for advice outside the hearing. Employment tribunal rights are statutory and cannot be removed, but the government will defend every claim vigorously through the Litigation Readiness Unit (CS2) and will not settle claims to avoid embarrassment, which is the current practice that incentivises vexatious litigation.
- b) For the Senior Civil Service (Director level and above), the DRI model established by CS1 provides the performance framework. DRIs serve on fixed-term contracts with six-monthly performance reviews conducted by the OPM Talent and Appointments Unit (CS3). DRIs who fail their performance review are dismissed. Directors and Directors General who are not DRIs but who serve under DRIs will also serve on fixed-term appointments (maximum five years) with annual performance reviews conducted by their DRI. The principle of cascading accountability means that every tier of senior leadership is on a fixed term, has a published performance agreement, and is dismissible for failure. The Management Code will make explicit that fixed-term appointment and dismissal for performance failure are the standard conditions of senior civil service employment, replacing the current presumption of permanence. Officials who entered the SCS under the previous arrangements will be transitioned to the new framework over 12 months, with their existing employment protections honoured during the transition period but not thereafter.
- c) The revised Code will reform the relationship between the civil service and its trade unions. The current arrangements, in which unions are consulted on virtually every aspect of civil service management including individual performance cases, organisational restructuring, and policy implementation, will be replaced by a framework in which unions retain their role in representing individual members in grievance and disciplinary proceedings (excluding the streamlined performance dismissal process described above) and in negotiating pay and conditions through the established machinery. Unions will not have a role in performance management, in the design of organisational structures, in the selection or assessment of officials for promotion, or in the implementation of the government’s programme. The revised Code will provide that no management decision required for the delivery of a Charter Letter priority may be delayed by a requirement to consult trade unions, and that union consultation on terms and conditions will be conducted on fixed timetables that cannot be extended by either party.

##### CS6.3: Pay, Incentives, and Conditions

The Problem

Civil service pay is simultaneously too low at the top and too compressed in the middle, with the result that the service cannot attract external talent to senior roles and cannot retain its best internal performers. The Permanent Secretary of a major department responsible for spending tens of billions of pounds and managing tens of thousands of staff is paid approximately 180,000 to 200,000 pounds, a fraction of what an equivalent role commands in the private sector. The compression between grades means that promotion from Grade 7 to Grade 6, or from Deputy Director to Director, often brings a pay increase of only a few thousand pounds while dramatically increasing responsibility and workload. The rational response for a competent official is to remain at their current grade, do the minimum required to retain their position, and supplement their income through outside interests. The Management Code’s provisions on pay defer to the Treasury’s Pay Remit Guidance, which imposes a uniform cap on pay increases across the civil service. The result is that departments cannot pay market rates for scarce skills (technology, data science, commercial, project management), cannot reward exceptional performance with meaningful pay differentials, and cannot compete with the private sector for the talent the government’s programme requires.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) The revised Management Code will establish a new pay framework for the Senior Civil Service, replacing the current uniform pay bands with a market-referenced system. DRIs will be paid at rates determined by the OPM in consultation with the Treasury, benchmarked against comparable private sector roles and adjusted for the public service element. The expectation is that DRI salaries will be in the range of £250,000 to £400,000 depending on the department’s scale and complexity, with a significant performance-related element (up to 30 percent of base salary) paid on the achievement of Charter Letter metrics. Directors General and Directors will be paid on a similar market-referenced basis with performance-related elements. The principle is that if the government is asking people of the calibre required to run major departments to accept the intense public scrutiny, restricted personal freedom, and career risk that come with a DRI appointment, it must pay them accordingly. The alternative is to continue paying Permanent Secretaries a fraction of what their private sector equivalents earn and to continue getting the mediocre performance that sub-market pay produces.
- b) Below the SCS, the revised Code will delegate pay authority to DRIs within each department’s resource allocation. The Treasury’s Pay Remit Guidance will set the overall cost envelope for civil service pay, but within that envelope each DRI will have authority to determine the pay structure for their department, including the ability to pay market supplements for scarce skills, to create performance bonuses linked to delivery objectives, and to differentiate pay between high and low performers at the same grade. The current system, in which every department operates the same pay scales, the same incremental progression, and the same negligible performance bonuses, will be replaced by a system in which DRIs can use pay as a management tool. A DRI who needs to recruit a world-class technology director will be able to offer a competitive package. A DRI who wants to reward a team that has delivered an exceptional result will be able to pay meaningful bonuses. The cost will be managed within the department’s voted allocation; the DRI will not need Treasury approval for individual pay decisions below the published salary threshold (CS5).
- c) The revised Code will introduce a sabbatical obligation for officials at Grade 6 and above. Every official who has spent five consecutive years in Whitehall will be required to spend a minimum of six months in an operational role outside central government before being eligible for further promotion (CS4). This provision, already described in CS4.4 as the Civil Servants in Industry Programme, will be codified in the Management Code as a condition of service. The sabbatical is not a punishment. It is an investment in the capability of the civil service: officials who have managed a factory floor, commanded a military unit, run a ward in an NHS hospital, or led a technology team in a private sector company bring back operational instincts that cannot be acquired in Whitehall. The Code will also remove the restriction on civil servants engaging in outside business interests, subject to a declaration of interest protocol. Officials who develop commercial skills, build professional networks, and understand how the private sector operates are more valuable to the government than officials who have never worked outside the public sector. The current Code’s restrictive approach to outside interests, designed for a 19th-century service in which the risk was corruption, is not appropriate for a 21st-century service in which the risk is insularity.

##### CS6.4: The Obligation of Candour

The Problem

The civil service’s advice to ministers is filtered through multiple layers of hierarchy, each of which has an incentive to soften bad news, to present options in the most favourable light, and to avoid telling ministers things they do not want to hear. The result is that ministers receive advice that is often incomplete, often misleading, and almost always framed to protect the institution rather than to serve the government. When a programme is failing, the submission will describe it as “facing challenges.” When a policy is undeliverable, the advice will recommend further analysis rather than stating that the policy cannot be implemented. When an official has made an error, the system will conceal it behind collective responsibility rather than identifying the individual whose judgment failed. The Civil Service Code requires honesty, but the institutional culture punishes candour: an official who tells a minister that a programme is failing and that specific colleagues are responsible will be ostracised by peers, passed over for promotion, and characterised as disloyal. The Management Code contains no mechanism to protect or reward officials who tell the truth when the truth is uncomfortable.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) The revised Management Code will establish a statutory-equivalent Obligation of Candour requiring every civil servant to provide complete, accurate, and unfiltered information to ministers, DRIs, and the OPM when asked, and to volunteer information about programme failure, delivery risk, or institutional dysfunction without being asked. The Obligation will be a condition of employment, breach of which constitutes a disciplinary offence. The current system, in which officials may technically comply with the duty of honesty while substantively misleading ministers through omission, selective presentation, or euphemistic language, will be replaced by a system in which the test is whether the minister received the information they needed to make a fully informed decision. If a programme is failing, the official responsible must report that it is failing, identify the causes, and propose remedial action. If the causes include the official’s own errors or the errors of colleagues, the report must identify them by name. Collective anonymity in failure, the defining feature of the current culture, will be replaced by individual accountability.
- b) The revised Code will create a Direct Reporting Channel through which any civil servant may communicate directly with the OPM Delivery Unit (CS3) to report programme failure, delivery obstruction, or institutional dysfunction that is not being addressed through normal management channels. The Channel will be managed by the OPM and will guarantee that reports are reviewed within 48 hours by a senior OPM official. Officials who report through the Channel will be protected from retaliation: any adverse action taken against an official within 12 months of a Channel report will be presumed retaliatory unless the department demonstrates otherwise. The Channel is not a whistleblowing mechanism for illegality (which is covered by the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998) but a delivery assurance mechanism that ensures the government receives unfiltered information about what is happening inside its departments. The Reform Network (CS4) will feed into the same Channel, creating multiple routes by which the truth about departmental performance reaches the people responsible for acting on it.
- c) The revised Code will reform the submissions process. Currently, advice to ministers is drafted at working level, cleared through multiple layers of the hierarchy, and signed off by the relevant Director or Director General before reaching the minister. At each stage, the content is softened, the options are narrowed, and the institutional perspective is reinforced. Under the revised Code, DRIs will have the authority to determine their department’s internal processes for advising ministers, including the ability to receive advice directly from working-level officials without hierarchical clearance, to commission advice from outside the department, and to reject advice that does not meet the Obligation of Candour standard. The DRI will also have the authority to require that advice to the Secretary of State identifies the individual official responsible for each recommendation, so that the minister knows whom to hold accountable if the advice proves wrong. The principle is transparency within government: ministers should know who is advising them, what those advisers actually think (not what the hierarchy has permitted them to say), and what evidence supports each recommendation.

##### Summary

CS6 is primarily operational. The Civil Service Management Code is issued by the Minister for the Civil Service (the Prime Minister) under powers conferred by the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010. The Prime Minister can rewrite the Code without primary legislation. Changes to the Code must be laid before Parliament but do not require a parliamentary vote. The Civil Service Code, which has statutory force, can be amended by the same route: the Minister for the Civil Service lays a revised Code before Parliament. The only element that may require primary legislation is the removal of union rights in performance management proceedings, which could be challenged under employment law; the Civil Service Reform Act (CS1) will include provisions addressing this if necessary.

Timeline

Pre-election: Revised Management Code drafted in full by the same independent legal team preparing the Civil Service Reform Act (CS1) and the Executive Decisions Act (CS2). Draft reviewed by prospective DRI candidates (CS4) for operational practicability. Delivery Standard framework, performance assessment system, and streamlined dismissal process designed and tested against existing employment law.

Day 1: Prime Minister issues direction to begin formal revision of the Management Code. Existing Code remains in force during drafting period. Key interim measures implemented immediately: DRIs appointed under CS1 framework, Charter Letters issued under CS7, performance agreements signed.

Within 30 days: Revised Management Code laid before Parliament. Delivery Standard published. New performance assessment framework issued. Pay framework for DRIs and SCS confirmed. Obligation of Candour directive issued to all departments. Direct Reporting Channel established within OPM.

Within 60 days: Revised Code in force. All officials at Grade 7 and above issued delivery objectives derived from Charter Letters. Trade union consultation framework published. Streamlined dismissal process operational. Sabbatical obligation announced with 12-month transition period.

Within 12 months: First full performance assessment cycle completed under new framework. First cohort of officials entering sabbatical programme. Market-referenced SCS pay operational. Delegated departmental pay authority exercised by DRIs. First annual review of Code effectiveness conducted by OPM, with revisions as required.

CS6 is the connective tissue of the reform framework. CS1 gives the Prime Minister the power to appoint and dismiss. CS3 gives the Prime Minister a machine. CS4 gives the Prime Minister people. CS5 gives departments financial authority. CS6 gives DRIs the management tools to use all of these powers effectively: a performance system that rewards delivery and punishes failure, a pay framework that attracts and retains talent, a disciplinary process that works at the speed of government rather than the speed of employment law, and an information architecture that ensures ministers and the OPM know what is actually happening inside the departments they are responsible for. The current Management Code was written by the civil service to protect the civil service. The revised Code will be written by the elected government to serve the country. The civil service will retain its values: integrity, honesty, objectivity, and impartiality. What it will lose is its impunity. Officials who deliver will be rewarded. Officials who fail will be dismissed. Officials who tell the truth will be protected. Officials who conceal failure will be held accountable. These are the conditions under which any high-performing organisation operates. The only remarkable thing about CS6 is that these conditions have never before been applied to the institution that runs the British state.

#### CS7: Charter Letters

“If You Cannot Write Down What You Expect a Department to Achieve, You Cannot Hold Anyone Accountable for Achieving It”

Governing Principle

Every previous attempt to impose performance accountability on the British civil service has failed for the same reason: the centre of government set targets without controlling the personnel who were supposed to deliver them, and without the institutional machinery to monitor progress in real time. Public Service Agreements, introduced by the Treasury in 1998, initially comprised some 250 performance targets negotiated between departments and the Treasury as part of the Spending Review process. By 2007 they had been rationalised to approximately 30 cross-cutting PSAs with 180 performance metrics. The Prime Minister’s Delivery Unit, established in 2001 under Michael Barber, focused on a deliberately small number of priorities across four departments: health, education, transport, and crime reduction. The PMDU’s core method was the stocktake meeting, in which the Prime Minister, the relevant Secretary of State, the Permanent Secretary, Treasury officials, and the Delivery Unit team reviewed progress against specific targets every two to three months. When Tony Blair was actively engaged, the system worked. Hospital waiting times fell. Literacy and numeracy targets were met. Crime fell. When Blair disengaged after 2003, distracted by Iraq and under pressure from Brown, the system faltered. As the Institute for Government concluded, the stocktakes worked only because they were backed by the authority of Blair, and as soon as his involvement dropped off the PMDU struggled to broker action with departments.

The Coalition government abolished both the PSAs and the PMDU in 2010, explicitly rejecting what it characterised as Labour’s top-down target culture. It replaced them with nothing of comparable rigour. Departmental Business Plans published in the early years of the Coalition contained high-level objectives but no quantified metrics, no delivery timelines, and no consequences for failure. By 2015 even these had been abandoned. The Starmer government’s Plan for Change and mission-led framework represent the latest attempt, but repeat the structural weakness: priorities are stated but there is no mechanism that connects those priorities to the people who must deliver them, no published metrics against which delivery can be assessed in real time, and no consequence for failure that the centre has the institutional power to impose. The lesson from 25 years of performance management experimentation is clear. PSA targets without prime ministerial attention decay into bureaucratic box-ticking. Prime ministerial attention without institutional machinery is unsustainable beyond 18 months. Institutional machinery without personnel control is impotent. All three elements, prime ministerial direction, institutional monitoring, and personnel accountability, must be present simultaneously, sustained permanently, and enforced ruthlessly. This is what the Charter Letter system provides.

Canada’s mandate letters offer a partial model. Since 2015, the Prime Minister of Canada has issued published mandate letters to each cabinet minister setting out the government’s expectations for their portfolio. Academic analysis of the 2021 mandate letters found that policy maintenance tasks were the most common and policy initiation the least, suggesting that most ministers were constrained to passive management of the status quo. The Charter Letter system takes the Canadian model and transforms it into something far more powerful by addressing the three weaknesses that the Canadian system shares with every previous British attempt. First, Charter Letters are addressed not to ministers (who rotate frequently and who lack operational control of their departments) but jointly to the Secretary of State and the DRI (CS1), creating dual political and operational accountability. Second, Charter Letters contain not aspirational objectives but quantified metrics with six-monthly review cycles. Third, Charter Letters carry consequences: a DRI who fails to deliver the Charter Letter priorities is dismissed (CS1), and a Secretary of State who fails to deliver them loses the confidence of the Prime Minister and is reshuffled. Responsibility is combined with authority at both the political and operational level. The Charter Letter is the contract between the Prime Minister and each department. It is the instrument through which the government’s programme is translated from manifesto language into operational reality.

##### CS7.1: Structure and Content of Charter Letters

The Problem

Governments communicate their priorities to departments through a chaotic mixture of manifesto commitments, ministerial speeches, ad hoc letters from Number 10, Treasury spending conditions, Cabinet committee decisions, and informal conversations between the Prime Minister’s advisers and departmental officials. No single document sets out what the Prime Minister expects a department to achieve, by when, and at what standard. The manifesto is a political document aimed at voters, not an operational document aimed at officials. The Spending Review settlement is a financial document aimed at the Treasury, not a performance document aimed at the department. Cabinet committee decisions are recorded in minutes that capture what was agreed but not what was expected to result from the agreement. The consequence is that departments have enormous latitude to define their own priorities, to interpret the government’s programme in ways that align with the department’s institutional preferences, and to avoid accountability for delivery by claiming ambiguity about what they were supposed to deliver. When a programme fails, the department can always argue that it was never a priority, that the objective was never clearly defined, or that external circumstances made delivery impossible. The absence of a single authoritative document connecting the Prime Minister’s priorities to departmental operations is the foundational weakness that the Charter Letter system is designed to eliminate.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) Every major department of state will receive a Charter Letter from the Prime Minister within 48 hours of its DRI’s appointment (CS4).
