The Charter Letter will be a public document, published on the OPM’s website and laid before Parliament. It will contain five sections. Section One: Mission Statement, a single paragraph of no more than 100 words setting out the Prime Minister’s strategic direction for the department over the life of the parliament. Section Two: Priority Deliverables, three to five specific outcomes the Prime Minister expects the department to achieve, each expressed as a measurable result with a target date. Section Three: Quantified Metrics, the specific indicators by which each Priority Deliverable will be assessed, with baseline values, target values, and interim milestones at six-monthly intervals. Section Four: Reporting Requirements, the frequency and format of performance reports the DRI must provide to the OPM Delivery Unit (CS3). Section Five: Consequences, an explicit statement that the DRI’s continued appointment is conditional on satisfactory progress against the Charter Letter metrics, assessed at six-monthly reviews conducted by the OPM Talent and Appointments Unit (CS3).
- b) The Charter Letter will be jointly addressed to the Secretary of State and the DRI. The Secretary of State bears political accountability to Parliament and to the Prime Minister for the department’s performance. The DRI bears operational accountability to the Secretary of State, to the Chief of Staff (CS3), and to the Prime Minister for the delivery of the Charter Letter priorities. The dual addressee reflects the responsibility-authority model: the Secretary of State has the political authority to direct the department’s strategy and the political responsibility for its success or failure; the DRI has the operational authority to manage the department’s resources, staff, and processes and the operational responsibility for translating the Secretary of State’s direction into delivered results. Neither can succeed without the other. A Secretary of State who sets the wrong priorities will fail regardless of the DRI’s competence. A DRI who cannot deliver will fail regardless of the Secretary of State’s vision. The Charter Letter aligns both by requiring both to sign it, confirming their joint commitment to the priorities, the metrics, and the consequences.
- c) The Priority Deliverables will be drafted by the OPM Policy Unit (CS3) in consultation with the relevant Secretary of State and the incoming DRI during the pre-election preparation period (CS4). They will be derived from the Party’s manifesto commitments, refined through operational analysis of what is achievable within the department’s resources and capabilities, and stress-tested against the PEPU’s (CS5) assessment of the department’s financial position. The drafting process will ensure that every Charter Letter priority is simultaneously ambitious (reflecting the government’s political commitment), achievable (reflecting operational reality), and measurable (expressed in terms that permit objective assessment of progress). A priority that cannot be expressed as a measurable outcome will not appear in the Charter Letter. The discipline of quantification is itself a reform: it forces the government to define what it means by success before it begins, rather than defining success retrospectively to match whatever happened.
- d) No department will receive more than five Priority Deliverables. The PMDU’s most important lesson was that effectiveness requires a rigorous and relentless focus on a relatively small number of priorities. The temptation for every government is to overload departments with objectives: every manifesto commitment, every backbench interest, every media-driven crisis generates a new priority that is added to the department’s workload without anything being removed. The Charter Letter imposes constraint. Five priorities, measured quarterly, reviewed six-monthly, with consequences. Everything else the department does is necessary operational work that must continue, but the DRI’s personal accountability is limited to the five things the Prime Minister has identified as the priorities that will define the government’s success or failure. This constraint also protects DRIs from the incessant additions that have historically diluted every government’s focus: if a new priority is added, an existing priority must be removed, and the decision to change a Charter Letter requires the Prime Minister’s personal approval.

##### CS7.2: The Review Cycle

The Problem

The PSA regime failed in part because its review cycle was too infrequent and too detached from operational reality. PSA targets were set at each Spending Review (typically every two to three years) and assessed through annual departmental reports that were published months after the period they covered. By the time anyone discovered that a target was being missed, the opportunity to correct course had often passed. The PMDU’s stocktake meetings were more effective because they were more frequent (every two to three months) and because they involved the Prime Minister directly. But the stocktakes depended entirely on Blair’s personal engagement and collapsed when that engagement waned. The lesson is that the review cycle must be frequent enough to detect failure early, institutionalised enough to survive changes in prime ministerial attention, and consequential enough to compel departmental action.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) DRIs will provide monthly written reports to the OPM Delivery Unit on progress against each Charter Letter metric. The reports will follow a standardised format: current value of each metric, trajectory (on track, at risk, off track), explanation of any deviation from the planned trajectory, and remedial action underway or proposed. The reports will be factual, not analytical: they will present data, not arguments. The Obligation of Candour (CS6) requires that DRIs report honestly; the Direct Reporting Channel (CS6) provides an alternative route by which the OPM can verify that reports are accurate. Monthly reporting is not bureaucratic overhead. It is the minimum frequency at which the centre of government can detect emerging problems before they become irreversible. A DRI who reports a metric as “on track” for three consecutive months and then reports it as “off track” in the fourth month has either been dishonest in the first three reports or has failed to anticipate a problem that competent management should have foreseen. Either explanation triggers a conversation with the OPM about the DRI’s performance.
- b) Every six months, the Prime Minister will conduct a Charter Review meeting for each major department. The meeting will be attended by the Prime Minister, the Chief of Staff (CS3), the Secretary of State, the DRI, the relevant PEPU analyst (CS5), and the Director of the OPM Delivery Unit. The meeting will review performance against every Charter Letter metric, hear the DRI’s assessment of delivery risks and obstacles, consider the PEPU’s integrated expenditure and performance analysis, and conclude with one of three outcomes. Green: the department is delivering satisfactorily; the DRI’s appointment is confirmed for the next six-month period. Amber: the department is delivering partially; the DRI receives specific remedial directions and is given six months to demonstrate improvement. Red: the department is failing to deliver; the DRI is replaced through the mechanism described in CS1, and the incoming DRI receives a revised Charter Letter reflecting lessons from the predecessor’s failure. The Charter Review meeting is not a PMDU-style stocktake that relies on prime ministerial charisma. It is an institutional process embedded in the OPM’s operational rhythm, with published outcomes and predetermined consequences. It will take place whether the Prime Minister is focused on domestic policy or distracted by international events, because the Chief of Staff has the authority to act on the Prime Minister’s behalf and the institutional machinery to enforce the outcome.
- c) The results of every Charter Review will be published within seven days, in a standardised format that reports each metric’s baseline, target, and current value, the overall assessment (green, amber, red), and any change in DRI appointment. Publication serves three purposes. First, it creates public accountability: the electorate can see in real time whether the government is delivering on its priorities. Second, it creates parliamentary accountability: select committees can use the published data to scrutinise departmental performance with unprecedented precision. Third, it creates internal accountability: every civil servant in every department can see whether their department is delivering, which creates a cultural expectation of delivery that no amount of internal exhortation can achieve. The PMDU’s stocktakes were private, which meant their impact was limited to the small number of people in the room. The Charter Review’s publication means its impact extends to every official in the department, every journalist covering the department, and every member of the public affected by the department’s work.

##### CS7.3: Cascading Accountability

The Problem

Even where performance frameworks exist, they typically apply only to the most senior level. The Permanent Secretary or DRI may have a published objective, but the thousands of officials below them who actually do the work have no formal connection between their individual performance and the department’s priorities. The result is that the DRI’s objectives exist in isolation: they are the DRI’s problem, not the department’s problem. A Director General whose team is responsible for a failing Charter Letter priority may face no personal consequence, because their own performance objectives are set in the generic competency framework that CS6 replaces, not in terms derived from the Charter Letter. The cascading accountability system ensures that every senior official’s performance is assessed against their contribution to the Charter Letter priorities, creating a direct line from the Prime Minister’s strategic direction to the work of every official who contributes to delivery.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) Within 14 days of receiving the Charter Letter, the DRI will produce a Departmental Delivery Plan that translates each Charter Letter priority into operational workstreams, assigns each workstream to a named Director General or Director, and specifies the contribution each workstream must make to the overall metric. The Delivery Plan will be submitted to the OPM Delivery Unit and published internally within the department. Every Director General and Director will then produce their own delivery objectives derived from the workstreams assigned to them, cascading the Charter Letter priorities down through the departmental hierarchy until every official at Grade 7 and above has a set of personal delivery objectives that connect their work to a Charter Letter metric. The Delivery Standard (CS6) provides the assessment framework: officials are assessed primarily on whether they achieved the delivery objectives derived from the Charter Letter. The cascade creates a direct, traceable chain of accountability from the Prime Minister’s five priorities to the specific tasks of every senior official in the department.
- b) The DRI will have authority to restructure the department’s organisation to align with the Charter Letter priorities. If the existing departmental structure places a Charter Letter priority across multiple directorates with no single point of accountability, the DRI may create a new delivery directorate, appoint a Director General to lead it, and transfer staff and resources from existing structures. The DRI does not need the Cabinet Secretary’s approval (the position is abolished under CS3), does not need the Civil Service Commission’s approval for internal restructuring, and does not need Treasury approval for resource reallocation within the voted envelope (CS5). The DRI’s authority over departmental organisation is the operational corollary of the DRI’s accountability for Charter Letter delivery: if the DRI is to be dismissed for failure, the DRI must have the authority to organise the department in whatever way gives delivery the best chance of success. Any other arrangement separates authority from responsibility and guarantees failure.
- c) The OPM will maintain a Government Delivery Dashboard, updated weekly with data from every department’s monthly reports. The Dashboard will be accessible to the Prime Minister, the Chief of Staff, all Secretaries of State, all DRIs, and all Directors General. It will present each Charter Letter metric’s current value, trajectory, and status in a standardised visual format that permits the Prime Minister to see at a glance which departments are delivering and which are not. The Dashboard will also present cross-departmental analysis identifying systemic obstacles that affect multiple departments, shared dependencies between Charter Letter priorities, and opportunities for cross-departmental collaboration. The PEPU (CS5) will integrate expenditure data into the Dashboard, showing not only whether departments are delivering but how much the delivery is costing. A department that is meeting its Charter Letter targets but burning through its budget at twice the planned rate is not delivering successfully; it is purchasing results at unsustainable cost. The Dashboard integrates performance and expenditure into a single view, giving the Prime Minister the information needed to make informed decisions about resource allocation, DRI performance, and the government’s overall trajectory.

##### CS7.4: Updating and Evolving Charter Letters

The Problem

Governments do not operate in static environments. Crises emerge, priorities shift, manifesto commitments prove undeliverable, and new opportunities arise that were not anticipated at the time of the election. The PSA regime was criticised for frequent changes to targets, which undermined credibility and provided departments with opportunities to redefine success retrospectively. But the opposite problem, rigid adherence to targets that have become irrelevant, is equally damaging: it forces departments to pursue objectives that no longer serve the government’s interests simply because they were written into a document two years earlier. The Charter Letter system must balance discipline (preventing departments from evading accountability by constantly redefining their objectives) with adaptability (permitting the government to respond to changing circumstances without destroying the integrity of the performance framework).

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) Charter Letters will be updated at each six-monthly Charter Review. Updates may take three forms. First, metric adjustment: where the baseline data proves inaccurate, where external circumstances have materially changed the feasibility of a target, or where a metric is found to incentivise perverse behaviour, the metric may be revised. Metric adjustment requires a published explanation of why the change is necessary and what the revised metric is. Second, priority replacement: where a Charter Letter priority has been achieved ahead of schedule, or where a new priority has emerged that is more important, a priority may be replaced. Priority replacement requires the Prime Minister’s personal approval and a published explanation. Third, priority addition: in exceptional circumstances, a sixth priority may be added for a limited period, but only if the Prime Minister determines that no existing priority can be removed. Priority additions automatically expire at the next Charter Review unless confirmed. In all cases, the original Charter Letter and all subsequent revisions will be published together, creating a complete public record of what the government expected, what changed, and why.
- b) No Charter Letter priority may be removed or downgraded except at a Charter Review meeting with the Prime Minister’s personal approval. This provision prevents the informal erosion that destroyed the PSA regime’s credibility: departments quietly dropping targets that they were failing to meet, redefining metrics to show improvement where none existed, and moving the goalposts to avoid embarrassment. The discipline of requiring prime ministerial approval for any change ensures that Charter Letters remain the Prime Minister’s document, reflecting the Prime Minister’s priorities, rather than becoming the department’s document, reflecting the department’s assessment of what is convenient. A DRI who requests the removal of a priority because it is proving too difficult to achieve is making a statement about their own capability that the OPM will note in the next performance review.
- c) At the mid-point of the parliament, the Prime Minister will issue refreshed Charter Letters to every department, resetting priorities for the second half of the term. The refresh will be informed by the cumulative data from the first two years of Charter Reviews, the PEPU’s expenditure and performance analysis, and the government’s assessment of its remaining manifesto commitments. The mid-term refresh is the political equivalent of a business’s annual strategic review: it provides an opportunity to take stock, to redirect resources from achieved or abandoned objectives to new priorities, and to adjust the government’s trajectory in light of what has been learned. The refresh process will be managed by the OPM Policy Unit in consultation with Secretaries of State and DRIs, and the refreshed Charter Letters will be published, debated in the House of Commons, and become the basis for the second Spending Review of the parliament (CS5).

##### Summary

CS7 is entirely operational. Charter Letters are issued by the Prime Minister under the prerogative power to organise and direct the executive branch. They require no legislation, no parliamentary vote, and no regulatory approval. They are the administrative expression of the Prime Minister’s constitutional authority to lead the government.

Timeline

Pre-election: Draft Charter Letters prepared by OPM Policy Unit equivalent (operating within the Party’s Talent Acquisition Unit, CS4) for every priority department. Drafts shared with prospective DRIs during the briefing process. Metrics stress-tested against available departmental data. Delivery Plan templates designed.

Day 1 to Day 2: Charter Letters issued to all priority departments simultaneously with DRI appointments (CS4). Published on government website. Laid before Parliament.

Within 14 days: DRIs produce Departmental Delivery Plans. Cascading accountability framework operational: every DG and Director has delivery objectives derived from the Charter Letter. Government Delivery Dashboard framework activated. First monthly DRI reports due at Day 30.

Month 6: First Charter Review meetings. Green, amber, or red assessments for every department. Results published. DRI appointments confirmed or terminated. First cycle of the performance framework complete.

Month 12: Second Charter Review. Full year of data available. PEPU integrated analysis combining 12 months of expenditure and performance data. First annual assessment of government programme delivery. Adjustments to Charter Letters as required.

Month 24: Mid-term Charter Letter refresh. Priorities reset for second half of parliament. Refreshed letters published and debated in the House of Commons. Second Spending Review allocations aligned to refreshed priorities.

CS7 is the instrument that makes the entire framework operational. CS1 provides the personnel authority: the power to appoint and dismiss DRIs. CS2 protects the framework from judicial interference. CS3 provides the institutional machinery: the OPM, the Delivery Unit, the PEPU, the Talent and Appointments Unit. CS4 provides the people: the Reserve Army of DRIs and their supporting leaders. CS5 provides the financial architecture: delegated authority, reformed Spending Reviews, Performance Compacts. CS6 provides the management tools: the Delivery Standard, streamlined dismissal, market-referenced pay, the Obligation of Candour. CS7 connects all of these into a single operating system by answering the question that every other policy assumes has been answered: what, specifically, does the Prime Minister want each department to achieve? The Charter Letter is the answer. It is a short document, deliberately constrained to five priorities, deliberately expressed in quantified metrics, deliberately published, and deliberately consequential. It is not a wish list, not an aspiration statement, and not a political communication. It is an operational contract between the Prime Minister and each department, enforceable through the DRI’s fixed-term appointment and the six-monthly review cycle. When a government falls short of its promises, the Charter Letter system will make it possible to identify exactly where, when, and under whose leadership the failure occurred. That transparency is the ultimate expression of the cardinal thesis: responsibility married to authority, at every level, for every priority, in every department.

#### CS8: King’s Regulations for the Civil Service

“One Service, One Rulebook, One Standard”

Governing Principle

The governance of the British civil service is scattered across a bewildering array of overlapping, contradictory, and largely unenforceable documents. The Civil Service Code, given statutory force by the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010, sets out four core values: integrity, honesty, objectivity, and impartiality. The Civil Service Management Code, issued by the Prime Minister as Minister for the Civil Service under CRaG 2010 section 3, covers recruitment, probation, conduct, discipline, pay, conditions, and departure. The Special Adviser Code of Conduct, also required by CRaG 2010, governs the behaviour of political appointees who are technically temporary civil servants but are exempt from the impartiality and objectivity requirements. The Ministerial Code, issued by the Prime Minister but without statutory basis, governs ministers’ conduct and their relationship with civil servants. The Business Appointment Rules govern post-employment restrictions for Crown servants. The Directory of Civil Service Guidance, running to hundreds of pages, provides detailed supplementary rules on everything from media contact to political activities to the acceptance of gifts. The Government Communication Service’s Propriety Guidance governs communications. Individual departments issue their own supplementary codes, the Diplomatic Service has its own regulations, and the Seven Principles of Public Life established by the Nolan Committee provide an overarching ethical framework that is referenced by almost every document but enforced by none of them.

The result is a system in which no single person, including the most senior officials in Whitehall, can confidently state the complete set of rules that govern their conduct. A civil servant who wishes to understand their obligations must consult at minimum six separate documents, each issued by a different authority, each updated on a different timetable, and each enforced through a different mechanism. The Civil Service Code is enforced through complaint to the Civil Service Commission. The Management Code is enforced through departmental HR processes. The Business Appointment Rules are enforced through the Civil Service Commission for the most senior officials, through departmental processes for others, and through the Independent Adviser on Ministerial Standards for former ministers. The Special Adviser Code is enforced by the appointing minister. The Ministerial Code is enforced at the Prime Minister’s discretion. This fragmentation is not an administrative inconvenience. It is a structural guarantee of non-accountability. When the rules are scattered, contradictory, and enforced by multiple bodies with overlapping jurisdictions, nobody is clearly responsible for enforcing any of them, and nobody can be clearly held to have breached them. The system protects the institution by making accountability procedurally impossible.

The military solved this problem centuries ago. King’s Regulations, first published in 1731, consolidated into a single volume all orders and regulations governing discipline and personal conduct across the armed forces. As Sir Frederick Pollock defined them in 1907, the Crown issues regulations and orders for the government, discipline, and general economy of the military forces under the sign manual of the Sovereign. King’s Regulations provide every officer and soldier with a single, authoritative rulebook. They are regularly updated. They are universally known. They are consistently enforced. They cover everything from the etiquette of the mess-room to the formalities required in communicating with the authorities. They are, in short, exactly what the civil service lacks: one service, one rulebook, one standard. CS8 creates King’s Regulations for the Civil Service. It consolidates every existing code, guidance document, and set of rules into a single instrument issued by the Prime Minister as Minister for the Civil Service, covering every aspect of civil service life from appointment to departure. It replaces fragmentation with clarity, ambiguity with precision, and multiple enforcement bodies with a single chain of accountability running through the DRI to the OPM.

##### CS8.1: Consolidation and Structure of King’s Regulations

The Problem

The proliferation of governance documents has occurred incrementally over decades. The Civil Service Code emerged from the Armstrong Memorandum of 1985, was formalised in 1996 on the recommendation of the Nolan Committee, and was given statutory force by CRaG 2010. The Management Code evolved from internal Treasury regulations. The Special Adviser Code was created to address the anomalous position of political appointees within the civil service framework. The Business Appointment Rules were developed to manage the revolving door between Whitehall and the private sector. Each document was created to solve a specific problem, and each solved that problem by adding a new layer of regulation without rationalising the existing ones. The Directory of Civil Service Guidance, published by the Cabinet Office in 2000, attempted to impose order by cataloguing the full range of rules in a single reference document, but it was a directory, not a consolidation: it pointed officials to the relevant rules without replacing, reconciling, or simplifying them. The consequence is a governance architecture that is comprehensive in its coverage but incoherent in its structure, making it simultaneously overregulated and underenforced.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

- a) The Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010 will be amended to replace the requirement for separate Civil Service Code (s.5), Management Code (s.3), and Special Adviser Code (s.7) with a requirement for a single instrument: the King’s Regulations for His Majesty’s Civil Service. The amendment will provide that the Minister for the Civil Service must publish King’s Regulations governing the appointment, conduct, management, discipline, performance, pay, conditions, and departure of all persons holding positions in the civil service, including special advisers and persons appointed under exception to the Civil Service Commission’s Recruitment Principles. The Regulations must require civil servants to carry out their duties for the assistance of the administration of the day, with integrity, honesty, objectivity, and impartiality (retaining the statutory minimum from CRaG 2010 s.5). The Regulations must be laid before Parliament but do not require a vote. The amendment will repeal the separate provisions for a Special Adviser Code and a Management Code, folding both into King’s Regulations. This is not a radical constitutional change: it consolidates three instruments into one, all of which are already issued by the same authority (the Minister for the Civil Service) under the same statute.

OPERATIONAL

- b) King’s Regulations will be organised into eight Parts, each replacing one or more existing governance documents. Part I: Purpose and Values, replacing the Civil Service Code and incorporating the reframed values from CS6 (the Duty to Deliver). Part II: Appointment and Entry, replacing the recruitment provisions of the Management Code and the Civil Service Commission’s Recruitment Principles, incorporating the DRI appointment mechanism (CS1) and the Reserve Army provisions (CS4). Part III: Conduct and Discipline, replacing the conduct provisions of the Management Code, the relevant sections of the Civil Service Code, departmental conduct guidance, and the Government Communication Service’s Propriety Guidance. Part IV: Performance and Accountability, replacing the performance provisions of the Management Code, incorporating the Delivery Standard (CS6), Charter Letter cascading accountability (CS7), and the streamlined dismissal process (CS6). Part V: Pay, Conditions, and Service, replacing the pay and conditions provisions of the Management Code, incorporating market-referenced SCS pay (CS6) and the sabbatical obligation (CS6). Part VI: Special Advisers, replacing the Special Adviser Code of Conduct, clarifying the relationship between political appointees and the permanent civil service. Part VII: Departure and Post-Employment, replacing the Business Appointment Rules and the memoir provisions scattered across the Management Code and the Special Adviser Code. Part VIII: Enforcement, establishing a single enforcement mechanism replacing the multiple overlapping bodies that currently share jurisdiction.
- c) The following documents will be formally revoked on the date King’s Regulations come into force: the Civil Service Code (as a separate document; its statutory content is absorbed into Part I); the Civil Service Management Code; the Special Adviser Code of Conduct; the Business Appointment Rules for Crown Servants (as they apply to civil servants and special advisers; the ministerial rules are a matter for the Ministerial Code); the Directory of Civil Service Guidance (in its entirety); the Government Communication Service’s Propriety Guidance (absorbed into Part III); and all departmental supplementary conduct codes that are not specifically authorised by King’s Regulations. From the date of commencement, no governance document governing the conduct, management, or conditions of civil servants shall have force unless it is either contained within King’s Regulations or expressly authorised by King’s Regulations as a departmental supplement. This provision eliminates the accumulation of shadow guidance that currently allows departments to create their own interpretive frameworks, often more restrictive and risk-averse than the central rules require.

##### CS8.2: The Enforcement Mechanism

The Problem

The current system distributes enforcement across multiple bodies with overlapping and unclear jurisdictions. The Civil Service Commission hears complaints under the Civil Service Code and provides advice on Business Appointment Rules for the most senior officials. Departments handle internal conduct and discipline through their own HR processes. The Independent Adviser on Ministerial Standards advises on the Business Appointment Rules for former ministers. The newly established Ethics and Integrity Commission provides yet another layer of oversight. The Government People Group in the Cabinet Office sets central guidance but has no enforcement power. The result is that enforcement is simultaneously everywhere and nowhere: multiple bodies have jurisdiction, but none has clear authority to act decisively. A civil servant who wishes to report a breach of the rules faces a maze of overlapping processes, and the most common outcome of a complaint is not resolution but referral to another body. The enforcement architecture protects the institution rather than the rules, because the complexity of the system makes enforcement procedurally exhausting and substantively uncertain.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) Enforcement of King’s Regulations will operate through a single chain of command: the individual official’s line manager, the DRI, and the OPM Talent and Appointments Unit (CS3). There will be no external enforcement body for internal management matters. The Civil Service Commission’s role will be confined to its statutory function under CRaG 2010: upholding the merit principle in recruitment and hearing complaints that the Recruitment Principles have been breached. The Commission will have no role in enforcing King’s Regulations beyond the recruitment provisions. This is not a reduction in accountability: it is a clarification. The current system creates the illusion of external accountability through the Commission’s complaints jurisdiction, but the Commission has never found against the institutional interests of the civil service in a case that mattered, and its processes are too slow and too procedurally complex to function as a real enforcement mechanism. Under CS8, enforcement is real because it runs through the DRI, who has both the authority and the incentive to enforce the rules: the DRI’s own appointment depends on Charter Letter delivery (CS7), and Charter Letter delivery depends on a department staffed by officials who comply with King’s Regulations.
- b) King’s Regulations will establish a three-tier disciplinary framework. Tier One covers minor breaches: failure to meet reporting deadlines, inadequate record-keeping, procedural non-compliance. Tier One breaches are dealt with by the official’s line manager through a formal written warning, with a copy to the DRI. Two Tier One warnings within 12 months escalate to Tier Two. Tier Two covers serious breaches: failure to comply with the Obligation of Candour (CS6), obstruction of delivery, providing misleading information to ministers or the DRI, failure to implement ministerial decisions. Tier Two breaches are dealt with by the DRI or a designated Director General through a formal disciplinary hearing, with outcomes ranging from a final written warning to demotion or transfer. The official may make written representations and has 14 days to appeal to a cross-departmental panel (CS6). Tier Three covers gross breaches: fraud, corruption, deliberate sabotage of government programmes, sustained and wilful refusal to implement lawful ministerial decisions, serious breach of the post-employment restrictions. Tier Three breaches result in summary dismissal by the DRI, with statutory employment tribunal rights preserved but no internal appeal beyond the cross-departmental panel.
- c) The Direct Reporting Channel established under CS6 will serve as the primary mechanism for reporting suspected breaches of King’s Regulations by senior officials, including DRIs themselves. Reports concerning a DRI are handled by the OPM Talent and Appointments Unit and escalated to the Chief of Staff. Reports concerning officials below DRI level are forwarded to the relevant DRI for investigation and action. The Direct Reporting Channel replaces the current system in which complaints are routed through the very hierarchy that may be responsible for the breach. Every report receives a 48-hour initial review, a determination within 14 days of whether a formal investigation is required, and if so, completion of the investigation within 60 days. The OPM publishes quarterly statistics on the number of reports received, investigated, substantiated, and the actions taken, broken down by department, without identifying individual officials. This transparency creates institutional pressure for consistent enforcement: a department with significantly more substantiated breaches than its peers faces questions about its DRI’s management of compliance.

##### CS8.3: Post-Employment and the Revolving Door

The Problem

The Business Appointment Rules represent one of the most conspicuous failures of the current governance framework. The rules require civil servants to seek approval before taking up outside appointments after leaving Crown service: for one year at Grade 6 and below, and for two years at SCS1 and above. The Advisory Committee on Business Appointments, which provided independent advice on the most senior cases, was closed in October 2025 and its functions transferred to the Civil Service Commission (for civil servants) and the Independent Adviser on Ministerial Standards (for former ministers). The fundamental weakness of the system has never been addressed: there is no legal mechanism to prevent a former civil servant from taking up an appointment without approval or in breach of conditions imposed. The rules are advisory, not mandatory. They depend on the goodwill of individuals who have already left Crown service and who have every incentive to ignore restrictions that limit their earning potential. Meanwhile, the rules create a disproportionate burden on mid-ranking officials making routine career moves while failing to prevent the most damaging cases of revolving-door influence at the most senior levels.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) Part VII of King’s Regulations will replace the Business Appointment Rules with a Post-Employment Code that is a condition of employment, enforceable through contractual mechanisms rather than advisory goodwill. Every civil servant at Grade 7 and above will, as a condition of appointment, sign a Post-Employment Agreement that forms part of their contract of employment. The Agreement will specify: a cooling-off period of 12 months for Grade 7 to Director level, 18 months for Director General level, and 24 months for DRI and equivalent level; a prohibition on lobbying any part of government on behalf of a new employer during the cooling-off period; a prohibition on taking up any role with an organisation with which the official had direct and significant official dealings in their last two years of service, unless approved by the DRI (or, for DRIs, by the OPM); and a continuing obligation of confidentiality over privileged information with no time limit. Breach of the Post-Employment Agreement will be enforceable as breach of contract, with the government entitled to seek injunctive relief and damages. This transforms post-employment restrictions from advisory conventions into legally binding obligations.
- b) The approval process will be streamlined to match the risk profile of the appointment. Routine moves to the private sector that do not involve lobbying, do not involve organisations with which the official had significant dealings, and do not involve privileged information will be approved automatically by the DRI within seven days of application. Only high-risk moves, those involving potential conflicts of interest, lobbying risk, or access to commercially sensitive information, will require detailed assessment. The assessment will be conducted by the OPM Talent and Appointments Unit, not by a committee of part-time advisers meeting periodically, but by a standing team with full-time capacity to process applications within 28 days. Applications from DRIs and equivalent will be assessed by the Chief of Staff. The current system, in which even routine applications can take months to process, incentivises non-compliance by making compliance unreasonably burdensome. The reformed system imposes strict restrictions on high-risk moves while ensuring that the vast majority of legitimate career transitions are processed without delay.
- c) The memoir provisions currently scattered across the Management Code and the Special Adviser Code will be consolidated into Part VII with a clear and enforceable framework. Officials at Director level and above who wish to publish memoirs, articles, or books drawing on their government experience must submit manuscripts to the OPM for review. The OPM’s review is limited to identifying material that would damage national security, compromise privileged information, or breach the continuing obligation of confidentiality. The OPM may not suppress material that is merely embarrassing to the government, to individual ministers, or to the civil service as an institution. The review must be completed within 60 days. If the OPM fails to respond within 60 days, the official may publish without restriction. This provision prevents the current practice of using the review process as a de facto censorship mechanism to suppress accounts of government failure or institutional dysfunction. The public interest in honest accounts of how government works outweighs the institutional interest in controlling the narrative.

##### CS8.4: Maintenance and Evolution

The Problem

The Civil Service Management Code was last substantively updated in November 2016. The Civil Service Code was last amended in March 2015. The Directory of Civil Service Guidance dates from 2000. The governance framework is not merely fragmented; it is stale. Rules drafted for a pre-digital, pre-remote-working, pre-social-media civil service continue to govern a workforce that operates in a fundamentally different environment. The pace of change in government, driven by technology, by evolving security threats, by changing workforce expectations, and by the reform programme itself, requires a governance framework that can be updated rapidly, consistently, and with clear authority. The military updates King’s Regulations through frequent amendments, issued as required, without waiting for periodic comprehensive reviews. The civil service governance framework has no equivalent mechanism: changes are made ad hoc, by different authorities, to different documents, on different timetables, with no systematic process for ensuring consistency or comprehensiveness.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) King’s Regulations will be maintained by the OPM as a living document, updated through a formal amendment process modelled on military practice. Amendments will be issued as required, numbered sequentially, dated, and published on the OPM’s website. Each amendment will specify the provision it modifies, the date of effect, and the authority under which it is issued (the Minister for the Civil Service under CRaG 2010 s.3, as amended by CS8.1). A consolidated version of King’s Regulations incorporating all current amendments will be published annually and laid before Parliament. The annual consolidation is not a review or a consultation: it is a clean restatement of the current rules, incorporating all amendments issued during the preceding year, so that every civil servant can access the complete, current rulebook in a single document. The OPM will maintain a digital version with full amendment history, searchable by topic, Part, or date, accessible to every civil servant.
- b) DRIs will have authority to issue Departmental Standing Orders supplementing King’s Regulations for matters specific to their department’s operational requirements. Departmental Standing Orders must be consistent with King’s Regulations and may not impose additional restrictions on officials’ conduct, pay, or conditions that are not authorised by King’s Regulations. They may address operational matters such as security procedures specific to the department’s work, specialist professional standards for technical roles, departmental reporting structures, and locally negotiated working arrangements within the framework of Part V. Departmental Standing Orders must be submitted to the OPM for consistency review before publication, and the OPM may require amendment or withdrawal of any Standing Order that conflicts with King’s Regulations or that imposes unauthorised restrictions. This provision permits necessary departmental variation while preventing the accumulation of shadow governance that currently undermines the coherence of the central framework.
- c) Every three years, the OPM will commission an independent review of King’s Regulations by a panel comprising an external chair (drawn from outside government), two serving DRIs, and two officials below SCS level nominated by the Reform Network (CS4). The review will assess whether the Regulations remain fit for purpose, identify provisions that have become obsolete or unworkable, recommend amendments, and report on the consistency of enforcement across departments. The review will be published in full and laid before Parliament. The three-year cycle ensures that King’s Regulations evolve with the demands of government without the instability of continuous revision. The composition of the review panel, with its external chair and below-SCS representation, ensures that the review reflects operational reality rather than institutional convenience. The Prime Minister will respond to each review within 90 days, accepting or rejecting each recommendation with reasons. Accepted recommendations will be implemented through the standard amendment process within 180 days of the Prime Minister’s response.

##### Summary

CS8 requires one legislative amendment to the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010, consolidating the requirement for separate codes into a requirement for a single instrument. The amendment is modest in scope: it preserves the statutory minimum values (integrity, honesty, objectivity, impartiality), preserves the requirement to lay the instrument before Parliament, and preserves the Civil Service Commission’s statutory role in upholding the merit principle. It changes only the form of the governance framework, from multiple overlapping documents to one comprehensive rulebook, not the constitutional relationship between Parliament, ministers, and civil servants.

Timeline

Pre-election: Drafting of King’s Regulations in full, drawing on the revised Management Code provisions from CS6, the DRI appointment framework from CS1, the Reserve Army provisions from CS4, the Charter Letter accountability framework from CS7, and the reformed pay and conditions structure from CS6. All eight Parts prepared in final form, reviewed by legal counsel for consistency with CRaG 2010 and employment law.

Day 1 to Day 14: Existing Civil Service Management Code replaced by King’s Regulations, issued by the Prime Minister as Minister for the Civil Service under CRaG 2010 s.3. This is operationally possible on Day 1 because the Management Code is already issued under this power; King’s Regulations simply replace it. The statutory Civil Service Code and Special Adviser Code continue in parallel until the CRaG amendment is enacted.

Within 60 days: CRaG 2010 Amendment Bill introduced in Parliament, consolidating the requirement for separate codes into the King’s Regulations framework. Bill passage expected within the first session given its technical and non-controversial nature.

Upon Royal Assent: Full King’s Regulations come into force as the single governance instrument. Civil Service Code, Special Adviser Code, and all other revoked documents formally cease to have effect as separate instruments. All provisions absorbed into King’s Regulations. Civil Service Commission’s jurisdiction formally confined to recruitment merit principle.

Within 90 days of Royal Assent: All departments issue Departmental Standing Orders consistent with King’s Regulations. OPM consistency review completed. Digital version with full search and amendment history published. Training programme for all officials at Grade 7 and above on the new framework completed.

CS8 completes the institutional architecture of the reform programme. CS1 through CS7 create new powers, new institutions, new personnel, new financial frameworks, and new performance instruments. CS8 codifies the rules under which all of these operate into a single, authoritative, enforceable, and regularly updated rulebook. The military analogy is deliberate. King’s Regulations have governed the armed forces since 1731 because the armed forces understood something that the civil service has never grasped: that an institution of hundreds of thousands of people, operating under enormous pressure, making decisions with profound consequences, cannot function effectively if its members do not know the rules. The civil service has operated for decades under a governance framework that nobody fully understands, that nobody consistently enforces, and that nobody believes carries real consequences. King’s Regulations replace that framework with something that every civil servant can read in a single document, that every DRI has the authority and the incentive to enforce, and that carries consequences that are clear, proportionate, and real. One service, one rulebook, one standard. It is not complicated. It has simply never been done.

#### CS9: Reducing the Cabinet

“A Body Small Enough to Decide and Senior Enough to Bind”

Governing Principle

The United Kingdom currently has 24 ministerial departments, and the Cabinet as constituted following the September 2025 reshuffle contains over 20 full members plus additional ministers who attend. This is a body too large to function as a decision-making forum. The Cabinet Manual describes the Cabinet as the ultimate arbiter of all government policy, yet a meeting of more than 20 people around a table cannot arbitrate anything: it can listen to presentations, ratify decisions already taken elsewhere, and provide a ceremonial expression of collective responsibility, but it cannot deliberate, debate, or decide in any meaningful sense. Every Prime Minister since Thatcher has understood this. The real decisions are taken in bilateral meetings between the Prime Minister and individual Secretaries of State, in ad hoc groups convened by Number 10, or in Cabinet committees whose membership and agendas are controlled by the centre. Full Cabinet has become a rubber stamp, meeting for 30 to 90 minutes once a week to hear announcements and confirm what has already been settled. The pretence that collective Cabinet government persists in a room of 20-plus ministers and their officials is one of the enduring fictions of the British constitution.

The problem is not new. The full Cabinet had come to be regarded as a bloated and cumbersome body even during the First World War, especially after the creation of new departments brought additional ministers requiring inclusion. Lloyd George’s solution in December 1916 was radical: a War Cabinet of five members, most without departmental responsibilities, supported by the first Cabinet secretariat under Maurice Hankey. The five-member War Cabinet could concentrate on overall strategy without distraction by departmental business. Churchill adopted the same model in May 1940, forming a five-member War Cabinet that included Chamberlain, Attlee, Halifax, and Greenwood. Clement Attlee, who had studied cabinet reform extensively since the early 1930s, believed that the maximum effective size of a cabinet was sixteen, and structured his post-war government accordingly. He instructed committee chairmen to stress not general discussion but the deciding of issues, and removed two members of his cabinet for talking too much. With the return of peace in 1919, Lloyd George had replaced his small War Cabinet with a traditional Cabinet of 20 members, and every peacetime government since has reverted to the bloated model. The lesson has been learned repeatedly and never retained: a small cabinet decides; a large cabinet ratifies.

The proliferation of departments compounds the problem. The United Kingdom has 24 ministerial departments not because the functions of government naturally divide into 24 categories, but because departments have accumulated through historical accident, political convenience, and the patronage requirements of successive Prime Ministers who need cabinet seats to reward allies and balance factions. The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology was created in 2023 by splitting functions from the Department for Business. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero was created simultaneously. The Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities was renamed from the Department for Communities and Local Government, which had been renamed from the Office of the Deputy Prime Minister. Each reorganisation creates a new Secretary of State, a new Permanent Secretary, a new private office, a new departmental board, and a new set of institutional interests to be defended. The result is a government fragmented into so many competing fiefdoms that no Prime Minister can hold the whole picture, and cross-cutting priorities that require cooperation between departments are systematically under-delivered because no single Secretary of State owns them. CS9 reduces the Cabinet to a size at which it can function as a genuine decision-making body, and reduces the number of departments to a number that reflects the actual functions of government rather than the patronage requirements of politics.

##### CS9.1: The Ten-Department Government

The Problem

The current departmental structure fragments related functions across multiple departments, creating coordination problems that consume enormous institutional energy without producing better outcomes. Energy policy is split between the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, the Department for Business and Trade, and HM Treasury. Skills policy is split between the Department for Education and the Department for Business and Trade. Immigration enforcement sits in the Home Office while labour market policy sits in the Department for Work and Pensions and the Department for Business and Trade. Housing sits in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government while planning sits partly there and partly in the Department for Levelling Up functions. Science policy sits in the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology but research funding decisions are made by UK Research and Innovation, an arm of the same department, while the application of science to public services is owned by whichever department delivers those services. Every boundary between departments is a friction point where coordination fails, information is lost, and accountability dissolves. The Prime Minister’s mission-led framework was designed to overcome these boundaries, but it operates through cross-departmental boards that have no executive authority, no budget, and no staff: they are committees layered on top of a departmental structure that remains unchanged.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) On Day 1, the Prime Minister will announce a machinery of government restructuring by Order in Council under the Ministers of the Crown Act 1975, reducing the number of major departments from 24 to 10. The 10 departments, each headed by a Secretary of State and a DRI (CS1, CS4), will be: (1) HM Treasury, retaining its fiscal and macroeconomic functions as redefined by CS5; (2) the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, consolidating all external relations including trade negotiation functions currently in Business and Trade; (3) the Home Office, consolidating all domestic security, policing, immigration, and border functions; (4) the Ministry of Defence; (5) the Ministry of Justice, absorbing the Law Officers’ departmental functions; (6) the Department of Health and Social Care; (7) the Department for Education and Skills, absorbing the skills and apprenticeship functions currently split between Education and Business; (8) the Department for the Economy, consolidating the current Department for Business and Trade, the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero into a single department responsible for industrial strategy, energy, science, technology, enterprise, and regulation; (9) the Department for Infrastructure and Environment, consolidating the current Department for Transport, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, and the housing and planning functions of the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government; (10) the Department for Work and Communities, consolidating the Department for Work and Pensions with the remaining functions of MHCLG (local government, community services, devolution) and the Department for Culture, Media and Sport.
- b) Each of the 10 departments will be represented in Cabinet by its Secretary of State. The Cabinet will consist of: the Prime Minister, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the Foreign Secretary, the Home Secretary, the Defence Secretary, the Justice Secretary, the Health Secretary, the Education Secretary, the Economy Secretary, the Infrastructure and Environment Secretary, the Work and Communities Secretary, the Chief of Staff (CS3, Minister of State rank), and the Attorney General (attending but not a member). Total membership: 12, plus the Attorney General. This is a body small enough to sit around a table, small enough for every member to contribute to every discussion, small enough for the Prime Minister to look each colleague in the eye and assess their commitment, and senior enough that every decision made in the room binds the entire government. The Leader of the House of Commons, the Leader of the House of Lords, the Chief Whip, the Secretaries of State for Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, and other Ministers of State will attend Cabinet only when items affecting their responsibilities are on the agenda. They are ministers of the Crown with important functions, but they do not need to be in every Cabinet meeting to discharge those functions.
- c) The territorial Secretaries of State (Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland) will be redesignated as Ministers of State within the OPM (CS3), reporting to the Chief of Staff. Their functions, representing the interests of the devolved nations in UK government and managing the intergovernmental relationship, do not require separate departments or Cabinet rank. The Scotland Office, Wales Office, and Northern Ireland Office will be absorbed into the OPM as territorial units, each headed by a Minister of State who has the right to attend Cabinet when devolution matters are discussed and the right to submit papers to Cabinet on any matter affecting their nation. This arrangement reflects reality: the territorial offices are already among the smallest departments in Whitehall, and their Secretaries of State have historically attended Cabinet as a matter of political representation rather than operational necessity. The redesignation does not reduce their influence; it concentrates it by giving them a direct reporting line to the Chief of Staff rather than leaving them as isolated minor departments competing for attention with 23 other departments.

##### CS9.2: Cabinet as a Decision-Making Body

The Problem

The current Cabinet does not decide. It meets weekly for between 30 and 90 minutes. The agenda is managed by the Cabinet Secretariat (CS3) in consultation with Number 10. Papers are circulated in advance but frequently arrive too late for ministers to read them. Discussion is formulaic: the Prime Minister introduces the item, the relevant Secretary of State presents, a few ministers comment, and the Prime Minister summarises a conclusion that was predetermined before the meeting began. Dissent is expressed privately in bilaterals, not publicly in Cabinet. The minutes, drafted by the Cabinet Secretariat, record conclusions but rarely record the arguments that led to them, still less the arguments against. Collective responsibility is maintained not because ministers have collectively decided but because they have collectively acquiesced. The degradation of Cabinet into a ratification body has been documented by every serious study of British government for the past 40 years. The consequence is that major decisions are taken without the scrutiny, challenge, and deliberation that collective decision-making is supposed to provide, and ministers who are nominally bound by collective responsibility feel no ownership of decisions they did not participate in making.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) Cabinet will meet twice weekly: a 90-minute strategic session on Monday mornings and a 60-minute operational session on Thursday mornings. The Monday session will address no more than three substantive agenda items, each introduced by a written paper circulated at least 48 hours in advance. Every Cabinet member will be expected to have read every paper and to contribute to the discussion. The Prime Minister will chair the discussion but will speak last, not first, on each item: each Secretary of State will state their position before the Prime Minister summarises the collective view. This reversal of the current practice, in which the Prime Minister’s opening remarks signal the desired conclusion and foreclose genuine debate, is essential to restoring Cabinet as a deliberative body. The Thursday session will review the Government Delivery Dashboard (CS7), hear brief reports from any Secretary of State whose department has moved to amber or red status, and address urgent operational matters that have arisen during the week. The Thursday session is not for policy debate; it is for performance monitoring and crisis management.
- b) Cabinet minutes will record not only the conclusion reached but the arguments made for and against, attributed to the ministers who made them. The current practice of anonymised, sanitised minutes that conceal who said what enables ministers to avoid accountability for their contributions and enables the Secretariat to shape the record to suit institutional preferences. Under the reformed minutes, every minister will know that their position is recorded, which creates an incentive to prepare seriously, argue honestly, and take responsibility for the outcome. The minutes will be classified and will not be released under the 30-year rule as currently practised (which in practice means redaction to the point of uselessness); instead, they will be released in full after 20 years, with national security redactions only. The purpose of this reform is not transparency for its own sake but accountability: ministers who know that their arguments will eventually be published will make better arguments. The Cabinet Secretariat (CS3) will prepare the minutes under the direction of the Secretary of the Cabinet Secretariat, not the Cabinet Secretary (abolished under CS3).
- c) No major policy decision, no commitment of significant public expenditure outside the voted estimates, and no machinery of government change will take effect without having been discussed and decided in Cabinet or in a Cabinet committee chaired by a Secretary of State (CS3). The current practice of announcing policies through press releases, media briefings, and bilateral agreements between Number 10 and individual departments without Cabinet discussion will cease. This does not mean that every decision must come to full Cabinet: the four standing Cabinet committees established under CS3 (Economic Affairs, National Security, Legislation, Social Policy) will handle the detailed work. But every decision of consequence must be recorded as having been collectively made, either in Cabinet or in a committee whose conclusions are reported to Cabinet. The Prime Minister retains the authority to act in genuine emergencies without prior Cabinet approval, but must report to Cabinet within 48 hours and seek retrospective endorsement. A Cabinet that decides is a Cabinet whose members share genuine collective responsibility, not a Cabinet that rubber-stamps decisions taken elsewhere and then pretends to own them.

##### CS9.3: Ministers of State and the Outer Ministry

The Problem

Reducing the Cabinet to 12 members raises the immediate political objection that it reduces the number of senior positions available to reward loyal backbenchers, balance party factions, and represent diverse constituencies within the governing party. Every Prime Minister uses cabinet appointments as a political management tool, and reducing the number of seats reduces the tool’s effectiveness. This is a real constraint. A reform that is intellectually elegant but politically impossible is not a reform; it is a seminar paper. The solution is to create a clearly defined tier of Ministers of State who hold significant operational responsibility, attend Cabinet when relevant, and carry sufficient status and remuneration to satisfy the political requirements of patronage, while keeping the decision-making core of Cabinet small enough to function.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) Each of the 10 departments will have two to four Ministers of State, appointed by the Prime Minister on the recommendation of the Secretary of State, responsible for specific policy areas within the department’s portfolio. The Economy Department, for example, might have Ministers of State for Energy, for Science and Technology, for Enterprise and Small Business, and for Trade. The Infrastructure and Environment Department might have Ministers of State for Transport, for Housing and Planning, and for Environment and Rural Affairs. Ministers of State will have genuine operational authority within their area, including the right to commission work from the DRI, to chair departmental sub-boards, and to represent the department in Parliament on matters within their brief. They are not cabinet members, but they are senior members of the government with real power and public visibility. The total number of Ministers of State across the 10 departments will be approximately 25 to 30, providing the Prime Minister with sufficient positions to manage the political requirements of government formation.
- b) Ministers of State will attend Cabinet when items within their area of responsibility are on the agenda, at the invitation of the Prime Minister. A Minister of State for Energy attending the Cabinet discussion of energy security is not a dilution of the small-cabinet principle; it is the application of the principle that decisions should be informed by the minister with the deepest knowledge of the subject. The key distinction is between permanent membership and invited attendance. Permanent members are the 12 who sit in every meeting, who read every paper, who vote on every question, and who bear collective responsibility for every decision. Invited attendees contribute their expertise to specific items and then leave. This is precisely the model that Churchill’s War Cabinet used: the five permanent members made the decisions, but departmental ministers attended for items affecting their departments, and the service chiefs attended for military items. The result was a cabinet that was simultaneously small enough to decide and well-informed enough to decide wisely.
- c) The outer ministry will also include Parliamentary Under-Secretaries of State, whose functions are primarily parliamentary: answering questions, steering legislation through committee, and representing the department in debates. The total ministerial team across the 10 departments, including Secretaries of State, Ministers of State, and Parliamentary Under-Secretaries, will be approximately 80, compared with the current total of over 120 ministers across 24 departments. The reduction in ministerial numbers is proportionate to the reduction in departments: fewer departments means fewer private offices, fewer ministerial teams, and fewer layers of political oversight sitting between the DRI and the Secretary of State. Every layer removed is a layer of delay, interpretation, and filtering that is eliminated. The relationship between the Secretary of State, the Ministers of State, and the DRI will be defined in King’s Regulations (CS8): the Secretary of State sets the political direction, the Ministers of State oversee specific policy areas, and the DRI delivers. Three tiers, clear lines, no ambiguity.

##### CS9.4: Executing the Merger

The Problem

Machinery of government changes are notoriously disruptive. Every merger of departments involves the reorganisation of thousands of officials, the reconciliation of different IT systems, pay scales, and employment terms, the relocation of staff, the renegotiation of contracts, and the disruption of ongoing programmes. The merger of the Department for International Development with the Foreign and Commonwealth Office in 2020 took over a year to complete and was widely criticised for the loss of development expertise during the transition. The risk of CS9 is that the operational disruption of merging 24 departments into 10 undermines delivery during the critical first year of the reform programme, precisely when the Charter Letters (CS7) require departments to demonstrate early progress. The execution plan must therefore be designed to deliver the political and structural benefits of the merger, the small Cabinet, the reduced number of Secretaries of State, the clearer lines of accountability, as quickly as possible while managing the operational transition over a longer period.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) The machinery of government changes will be announced on Day 1 and will take immediate legal effect through Orders in Council. From Day 1, the 10 Secretaries of State are appointed, the 10 DRIs are deployed (CS4), and the 10 Charter Letters are issued (CS7). The political and accountability structure is operational on Day 1. The administrative merger, the integration of back-office functions, IT systems, estates, HR, and finance, will proceed over a 12-month transition managed by each department’s DRI with the support of the OPM. During the transition, the legacy departmental structures continue to operate as divisions within the new department, with their existing management chains reporting to the new DRI. No official is relocated, no IT system is migrated, and no contract is renegotiated during the first 90 days. The DRI’s first task is to produce a Departmental Integration Plan within 30 days, identifying which functions should be merged, which should be maintained as distinct divisions, and which should be eliminated. The OPM reviews and approves each Integration Plan to ensure consistency across government.
- b) The principle governing the merger is operational efficiency, not organisational symmetry. Not every function of the merging departments needs to be physically integrated. Where two legacy departments have separate but well-functioning finance teams, they may continue to operate as separate teams within the new department’s finance directorate, reporting to a single Director of Finance. Where two legacy departments have overlapping policy teams covering the same subject from different angles, those teams will be merged. Where a legacy department has a unique specialist capability, that capability will be preserved as a distinct unit. The DRI has the authority (CS1, CS6) to determine the internal structure of the department, and is assessed on Charter Letter delivery (CS7), not on the speed or elegance of organisational integration. A DRI who delivers the Charter Letter priorities while managing a department with some residual legacy structures is succeeding. A DRI who produces a beautifully integrated organisational chart while missing delivery targets is failing. The merger serves the reform programme; the reform programme does not serve the merger.
- c) The savings from the merger will be significant but should not be overstated or treated as the primary objective. The elimination of 14 Secretaries of State and their private offices, 14 Permanent Secretary salaries, 14 departmental boards, 14 sets of corporate services overhead, and the associated layers of management will reduce administrative cost. The Cabinet Office estimated that the Places for Growth programme would deliver £1.9 billion in staff and estate savings by 2030; departmental consolidation will accelerate and extend these savings. However, the primary benefit is not financial but structural: fewer departments means fewer coordination failures, fewer boundaries across which priorities must be negotiated, fewer institutional interests competing for resources and attention, and a Cabinet small enough to function as the constitution intends. The financial savings are a welcome consequence of a reform whose purpose is effective government, not a cost-cutting exercise disguised as reform.

##### Summary

CS9 is entirely operational. The Prime Minister’s prerogative power to determine the machinery of government, to appoint and dismiss ministers, and to decide the composition and procedures of Cabinet requires no legislation and no parliamentary vote. Orders in Council under the Ministers of the Crown Act 1975 provide the legal mechanism for transferring functions between departments. The Ministerial and Other Salaries Act 1975 caps the number of paid ministerial positions, and the reduced number of departments and ministers under CS9 operates well within this cap.

Timeline

Pre-election: Detailed machinery of government plan prepared, including: precise allocation of functions to each of the 10 departments; draft Orders in Council; DRI assignments aligned to the 10-department structure (CS4); Charter Letters drafted for each of the 10 departments (CS7); transition management framework designed.

Day 1: Orders in Council issued. 10 Secretaries of State appointed. 10 DRIs deployed. 10 Charter Letters published. Cabinet meets for the first time in its 12-member format. Territorial Secretaries of State redesignated as Ministers of State within the OPM. Legacy departments continue operating as divisions within new departments.

Within 30 days: Each DRI produces Departmental Integration Plan. OPM reviews and approves all Integration Plans. Ministers of State appointed to all 10 departments. Outer ministry (Parliamentary Under-Secretaries) appointed. Full ministerial team operational.

Within 90 days: New Cabinet procedures fully operational: twice-weekly meetings, reformed minutes, 48-hour paper circulation. Standing Cabinet committees constituted (CS3). No physical relocation or IT migration during this period; focus exclusively on Charter Letter delivery.

Months 3 to 12: Administrative integration proceeds department by department according to Integration Plans. Back-office functions consolidated. Redundant management layers removed. Estates rationalised where co-location is practicable. Corporate services merged. Each DRI reports monthly to OPM on integration progress alongside Charter Letter delivery progress.

Month 12: Integration substantially complete. 10 departments fully operational as unified organisations. First annual review of the 10-department structure, assessing whether the allocation of functions is correct and whether further adjustment is needed.

CS9 completes the political architecture of the reform programme. CS1 through CS8 create the powers, the institutions, the people, the financial frameworks, the performance instruments, and the rulebook. CS9 creates the political structure within which all of these operate: a government of 10 departments, each led by a Secretary of State with clear political accountability and a DRI with clear operational accountability, reporting to a Cabinet small enough to decide and a Prime Minister supported by an OPM designed to govern. The war cabinets of 1916 and 1940 demonstrated that a small executive body, freed from the burden of departmental representation, can make decisions of extraordinary consequence with extraordinary speed. The peacetime government does not face the same existential pressures, but it faces the same structural problem: a body too large to decide is a body that does not govern. CS9 creates a Cabinet that governs. It is the political expression of the cardinal thesis: authority concentrated where it can be exercised, responsibility attached to those who exercise it, and a structure small enough that neither authority nor responsibility can be diffused into the comfortable anonymity of a 24-person room.

#### CS10: The Angliot, the British Grand École

“Skilled Enough to Serve, Tough Enough to Deliver, Free Enough to Think”

Governing Principle

The positions held and the role played by the British Civil Service as it presently is in inhibiting the execution of public mandates and holding back the country’s power to administer to its own borders, prevent the abuse of its courts, develop its natural resources and build infrastructure, are not merely a matter of organisational imperative as formed and guaranteed by incentive, but also a matter of attitude, culture, and dispositional profile as are manifestly found in the individual members of its service.

CS1 through CS9 reform the structure: the powers of ministers, the accountability of officials, the machinery of government, the instruments of performance, the rules of conduct, and the architecture of the state. But structures are operated by people, and the people who operate the British civil service are, overwhelmingly, the products of a single formation: a humanities degree from a selective university, followed by the Fast Stream, followed by a career of lateral rotation through generalist policy roles, accumulating institutional knowledge but rarely acquiring technical depth, operational experience, or exposure to the world outside Whitehall. The structure creates the culture, but the culture also creates the structure. Reforming one without reforming the other guarantees that the old culture will eventually recapture the new structure, as it has after every previous attempt at civil service reform since Northcote-Trevelyan.

If we want a much higher standard of CS that guarantees the national interest, instead of paralysing the country on the basis of its own private interest, we need a very different CS culture. This requires training civil servants very differently. The best way to ensure this happens is to create an institution capable of training civil servants very differently, and at the highest level – an equivalent to France’s Grand École.

France understood this in 1794 when the National Convention created the École Polytechnique during the Revolution, and again in 1945 when de Gaulle created the École Nationale d’Administration to rebuild the state after Vichy. The Polytechnique combined academic excellence with military training and public service: students were officer cadets, they studied mathematics and engineering at the highest level, and they graduated into the grands corps that ran France’s infrastructure, its mines, its bridges, its arsenals, and its treasury. The ENA took the administrative elite and gave them a common formation: a shared curriculum in public law, economics, and finance, shared internships in prefectures and embassies, and a shared ethos of state service. The énarques who emerged dominated French public life for seven decades: four Presidents, countless Prime Ministers, and the senior ranks of every ministry. The system had profound flaws. It became a closed caste, self-recruiting from the same Parisian lycées, the same Sciences Po seminars, the same social milieu. It prioritised conformity over initiative, procedure over outcome, and institutional status over operational achievement. Macron, himself an énarque, dissolved the ENA in 2021 and replaced it with the Institut National du Service Public, explicitly to combat the insularity and elitism that the school had bred. The lesson from France is not that the Grand École model failed; it is that a Grand École that recruits from too narrow a base and trains for procedure rather than performance will reproduce the very pathologies it was designed to overcome.
