The deeper lesson is subtler: the ENA’s admissions crisis was not ultimately a demographic problem but an epistemological one. When every entrant arrives via the same preparatory pipeline, saturated in the same doctrines, trained to produce the same style of analysis, the institution selects for a single way of knowing the world. The result is a governing class that is not merely socially homogeneous but intellectually homogeneous, and intellectual homogeneity is the true enemy of effective government, because it guarantees that the institution’s blind spots are systematic rather than random.

Britain’s current equivalent is the Fast Stream, and the comparison is damning. The Fast Stream in the 2024-25 cycle received over 72,000 applications for approximately 750 places, a success rate of barely 1%. It is, by the numbers, among the most competitive graduate schemes in the country. Yet the scheme produces neither the technical depth, the operational toughness, nor the mission-oriented culture that the civil service requires. Fast Streamers enter at the Higher Executive Officer level and rotate through departments on one-year postings, acquiring breadth at the expense of depth and institutional familiarity at the expense of genuine capability. The application process, centred on situational judgement tests that reward the ability to think like a civil servant rather than the ability to think differently from one, is designed to select for conformity with existing institutional norms. Pay is below the equivalent non-Fast-Stream grades, attrition is high, and the scheme’s relationship with departments is often adversarial: departments submit bids for Fast Streamers to fill recruitment gaps, and Fast Streamers are allocated to roles they did not choose, in departments they did not select, performing work that may bear no relationship to their skills or interests. The scheme’s defenders point to its competition ratios and its alumni in senior positions. Its critics, including many of its own graduates, point to a programme that lobotomises bright young graduates into institutional orthodoxy, wastes talent in roles that nobody else wanted, and produces generalists in an age that demands specialists. The Fast Stream will continue under the reformed civil service as a volume recruitment channel. But it is not, and cannot be, the institution that creates the cadre of exceptional public servants that CS1 through CS9 require to operate.

Britain’s equivalent thereof will be called the Angliot. It will be a seat of accelerated higher-learning, which takes extreme selectivity and extent of training to a level beyond even that of its highest-ranked institutions of tertiary education. In it, selected students will pursue an accelerated dual-honours degree in key subjects, while also being given extensive technical education. Concurrently with these pursuits, they will undergo a process of tailored national service, being exposed not merely to the full rigours of basic armed forces training but to the most elite and high-leverage edges of British military activity and the country’s wider R&D ecosystem.

The curriculum of the Grand École will be predominantly mission-focused – students will be handed task after task, be it in the realm of the mundane (organising a conference for their fellow cadets) or the extraordinary (penetrating the communications network of a live terrorist cell), and given minimal guidance-to-completion.

After a preliminary period of 2–3 years of concurrent study, the cadets will be phased into their vocation. Within this formidable battery of abstract, executive, and technical educations is an underlying and critically important education in the theory of service. The orthodoxy that shall prevail among them will hold that: it is their duty that the acts of Parliament and the courts should reflect the mandate; it is their duty to ensure reasonable impediments to the British public’s ability to go about their business in security, exercise their freedoms (of enterprise, of speech), and proceed along their private tracks to prosperity, are removed; and it is their duty to ensure that all the duties of government are to be executed with the greatest possible speed and quality, so that public expenditures may be minimised and honoured thereby.

Our aim with this school is to create bastions of civil service so skilled, mission-oriented, entrepreneurial, and variously-able, that the overall size of the service can be dramatically reduced while capabilities dramatically scale up.

##### CS10.1: Establishment and Statutory Framework

The Problem

There is no institution in the United Kingdom that combines academic education at the highest level, technical and vocational training, military formation, and preparation for public service in a single integrated programme. The universities provide academic education but not vocational training, not military discipline, and not an ethos of public service. Sandhurst provides military training but not academic education beyond the level required for a commission. The Fast Stream provides a development programme within the civil service but not a foundational education before entry. The absence of such an institution means that the civil service recruits from the general graduate population, people who have been trained to think but not to do, to analyse but not to execute, to advise but not to deliver. The ENA, for all its faults, produced graduates who shared a common formation, a common language, a common set of professional reflexes, and a common understanding of what the state was for. The British civil service has no equivalent shared formation, which is one reason why its culture is transmitted informally through institutional osmosis rather than formally through professional education, making it extraordinarily resistant to deliberate change.

Establishing an institution of this nature within the existing higher education framework is not straightforward. The Office for Students regulates higher education providers in England, and the process for obtaining degree-awarding powers is lengthy, bureaucratic, and designed for conventional universities, not for a hybrid military-academic-vocational institution sponsored by the Crown. The military training component requires the formal involvement of the Ministry of Defence, which has no existing framework for embedding sustained military training within a civilian educational institution outside of the University Officer Training Corps, a part-time programme wholly inadequate to the ambition of the Angliot. The service obligation, requiring graduates to spend a minimum of seven years in the public sector, has no precedent in civilian higher education, though it has clear parallels in military education: graduates of Sandhurst are required to serve a minimum period, and the armed forces routinely impose return-of-service obligations on personnel who receive expensive training at public expense. The statutory framework must therefore create a new category of institution, one that is neither a conventional university nor a military academy but a hybrid with characteristics of both, empowered to award degrees, authorised to conduct military training, and legally entitled to impose a service obligation on its graduates in return for the full public funding of their education.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

- a) The Angliot Act will establish the Angliot as a body corporate and a Crown institution, governed by a Board of Governors appointed by the Prime Minister. The Act will confer degree-awarding powers directly, without requiring registration with the Office for Students or compliance with the standard OfS registration conditions, which are designed for mass higher education providers and are wholly inappropriate for a small, intensely selective, publicly funded institution training future senior civil servants. The Act will provide that the Angliot may award undergraduate and postgraduate degrees validated by itself, subject to periodic external quality review by a panel appointed by the Secretary of State for Education and Skills (CS9), not by the OfS. The Act will designate the Angliot as a Schedule 1 institution under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, ensuring full transparency, and will exempt it from the competition and consumer law provisions of the Higher Education and Research Act 2017 that apply to conventional providers, on the grounds that the Angliot does not operate in a market: it charges no fees, its students are selected by the Crown, and its graduates are directed into public service. This is the model used for Sandhurst and the other service academies, which operate outside the OfS framework, and it is the correct model for the Angliot.
- b) The Angliot Act will establish a formal partnership between the Angliot and the Ministry of Defence for the delivery of the military training component. The Act will provide that students accepted to the Angliot are enlisted as Officer Cadets in the Reserve Forces for the duration of their studies, under the Reserve Forces Act 1996, with a bespoke terms-of-service instrument issued by the Defence Council. This gives the Ministry of Defence legal authority over the military training element, provides students with the legal status necessary to participate in military exercises, access classified facilities, and handle sensitive material, and creates a framework for the secondment of military instructors and the use of military training facilities. The model is directly analogous to the École Polytechnique, where French engineering students are officer cadets under the Ministry of Armed Forces for the duration of their studies, receiving military pay and undergoing six months of mandatory military and human formation training before commencing their academic programme. At the Angliot, the military component is not an add-on or an optional enrichment activity: it is a core and concurrent element of the programme, running alongside the academic and technical curriculum throughout the period of study.
- c) The Angliot Act will establish the Graduate Service Obligation. Every graduate of the Angliot will be required, as a condition of admission, to spend no fewer than seven years after graduation working in the British public sector. The public sector, for this purpose, includes the civil service (the primary destination), the armed forces, the intelligence services, the NHS at a managerial or policy level, local government at a senior level, and any other Crown body or statutory agency designated by the Secretary of State, including the Malebranche (C3.1) and the National Megaproject Office, the Megabureau (C4). The seven-year obligation is a legally binding commitment, enforceable through a repayment mechanism: graduates who leave the public sector before completing seven years of qualifying service will be required to repay a proportion of the cost of their education, calculated on a sliding scale (100% if departing within two years of graduation, reducing by one-seventh for each year of qualifying service completed). The repayment obligation is a debt due to the Crown, recoverable through the county court or by deduction from salary if the individual is employed by a public body. This mechanism is modelled on the return-of-service obligations imposed on military personnel who receive funded professional training and on NHS-funded medical graduates in several comparable jurisdictions. It is not punitive: it reflects the straightforward principle that an education funded entirely by the public at very considerable expense creates an obligation to the public. Given that successful alumni of the course will, in the course of seeing to their duties, create untold £billions for the country in averted waste, saved expenditures, and efficiencies-created, the entire program is cost-covered in full for all of those who succeed in being accepted to the first year class. Candidates’ bed, board, and basic living expenses will be accounted for. In return for this, all graduates are expected to spend no fewer than seven years after graduation working in the British public sector.

##### CS10.2: Selection and Admission

The Problem

The ENA’s fatal weakness was not its curriculum or its ambition but its admissions, and specifically the kind of homogeneity its admissions produced. By the time of its dissolution, roughly 70% of the ENA’s intake arrived via the same preparatory pipeline: Sciences Po, the Parisian lycées, the same social milieu. The École Polytechnique, despite its military character, suffered a similar narrowing: its entrance examination, conducted after two years of gruelling preparatory classes available primarily in elite lycées, selected for a very specific type of mathematical virtuosity. Macron, himself an énarque, dissolved the ENA in 2021 and replaced it with the Institut National du Service Public, explicitly because the school had become a mechanism for reproducing a single governing caste. The conventional critique of this homogeneity is demographic: the school recruited from too narrow a class. But the deeper problem was epistemological. When every entrant has been trained in the same analytical frameworks, steeped in the same doctrines, and rewarded for the same style of reasoning, the institution does not merely lack social diversity; it lacks cognitive diversity. It produces a governing class whose members all see the world through the same lens, and whose collective blind spots are therefore systematic rather than random. A room full of people who think the same way will, with great confidence and great efficiency, converge on the same wrong answer.

If the Angliot is to avoid reproducing this pathology, its selection process must be designed from the outset to identify exceptional ability and to select explicitly for epistemological diversity: people who reason differently from one another, who approach problems from different angles, who possess different cognitive toolkits. This is not a demographic exercise. The selection process is entirely blind to race, sex, class, religion, geography, school type, and every other demographic characteristic. It is interested in one thing only: whether the candidate possesses the raw ability, the strength of character, and the distinctiveness of mind that the civil service requires. The institution does not sort by category; it sorts by capability and by the range of thinking styles that the cohort, taken as a whole, represents. No quotas, no tokenism, no arbitrary criteria. The only question is: can this person think, act, endure, and lead at the level the Angliot demands, and does their presence make the cohort collectively more formidable?

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) The Angliot will admit a first-year cohort of approximately 80 to 100 cadets annually. This is deliberately small: smaller than the ENA’s annual intake of 80 to 90, comparable to the Polytechnique’s annual intake of approximately 350 (of whom roughly 80 enter the grands corps), and a fraction of the Fast Stream’s annual cohort of approximately 750. The small cohort is essential to the model. Every cadet will know every other cadet. Every instructor will know every cadet by name. The programme is not a mass education scheme; it is an elite formation programme, and the word elite is used here in its proper sense: selected for excellence, not selected for privilege. The cohort size also reflects the institution’s purpose: the Angliot does not aim to supply the entire civil service with graduates. It aims to supply the civil service with a cadre of exceptionally capable individuals who will, over the course of their careers, rise to the most demanding and consequential positions in the state, carrying with them a shared formation, a shared professional standard, and a shared understanding of what public service requires. The Fast Stream continues as the volume channel. The Angliot is the forge.
- b) The selection process will operate in four stages, designed to identify exceptional merit and epistemological range rather than educational attainment and social polish. Stage One is an open application, available to any British citizen aged 17 to 21 who has achieved or is predicted to achieve the equivalent of three A-levels at grade A or above (or equivalent Scottish, Welsh, or international qualifications). There is no requirement for specific subjects, no requirement for a university place, and no advantage conferred by the name of the applicant’s school. The application is entirely blind to demographic characteristics: no name, no photograph, no school name, no parental occupation, and no information from which any demographic inference could be drawn is visible to any assessor at any stage of the process. Stage Two is a written examination, administered at regional centres across the United Kingdom, testing analytical reasoning, quantitative ability, written communication, and general knowledge. The examination is designed to be resistant to coaching: it tests the capacity to think under pressure, not the capacity to rehearse model answers. Crucially, the examination includes problems that reward heterodox reasoning, problems that have multiple valid solution paths and that penalise candidates who default to a single conventional method. The purpose is to identify not only the most able candidates but the most cognitively distinctive ones: candidates who solve problems in ways that the examiners did not anticipate. Stage Three is a week-long residential assessment, held at the Angliot’s campus, during which candidates undergo physical fitness testing, group problem-solving exercises, individual interviews, a simulated crisis-management scenario, and a 48-hour field exercise conducted in partnership with military instructors. The residential assessment is the decisive stage: it tests not what candidates know but who they are, how they behave under stress, whether they can lead and whether they can follow, whether they can think clearly when tired, cold, and uncertain, and whether they possess the moral seriousness that public service demands. The group exercises are specifically designed to reveal cognitive complementarity: assessors are trained to identify candidates whose thinking compensates for the blind spots of other candidates, and to value the candidate who sees the problem from an angle that nobody else in the room has considered. Stage Four is a final panel interview, conducted by a panel comprising the Commandant of the Angliot, a serving DRI (CS1), a military officer of at least brigadier rank, and an external member drawn from outside government. The panel makes the final admission decision, and its decisions are not subject to appeal. The panel is specifically instructed to construct a cohort, not merely to rank individuals: the 80 to 100 cadets selected should collectively represent the widest possible range of cognitive styles, problem-solving approaches, and intellectual temperaments consistent with the threshold standard of exceptional merit.
- c) The Angliot will maintain a rigorous separation between selection and demography. No demographic data of any kind will be collected during the application process, and no demographic analysis of the cohort will be published. The institution does not define excellence by reference to the candidate’s background; it defines excellence by reference to the candidate’s mind, character, and performance under pressure. The only published statistic will be the number of applicants, the number of offers, and the acceptance rate. If the selection process is correctly calibrated to identify exceptional ability wherever it exists, the cohort will naturally reflect the distribution of exceptional ability across the population, which is the only distribution that matters. Any attempt to engineer the cohort by demographic category, whether through quotas, targets, weighting, or any other mechanism, is expressly prohibited by the Angliot Act. The Angliot selects for the best. That is the beginning and the end of the admissions policy.

##### CS10.3: The Curriculum

The Problem

The British civil service has historically recruited generalists and kept them generalist. The Northcote-Trevelyan report of 1854 divided the service into an intellectual class and a mechanical class, and the intellectual class has dominated ever since: clever people who can write a brief, summarise a problem, and manage a submission through the system, but who possess no technical depth in any domain and who rotate through departments too quickly to acquire it. The Fulton Report of 1968 identified the cult of the generalist as the central weakness of the civil service and recommended the creation of a professional civil service with specialist career streams. The recommendation was substantially ignored. Fifty-seven years later, the most powerful officials in Whitehall remain overwhelmingly generalist policy professionals who have never managed a large operation, never built anything, never coded anything, never negotiated a commercial contract, and never been responsible for a budget larger than their own team’s running costs. They advise ministers on matters of enormous technical complexity, from nuclear energy to artificial intelligence to infrastructure procurement, without possessing the technical knowledge to evaluate the advice they are transmitting from the specialists below them. This is not a criticism of their intelligence, which is generally formidable. It is a criticism of a system that takes intelligent people and systematically fails to give them the skills they need to do their jobs.

The Angliot curriculum addresses this failure by combining four concurrent streams of education into a single integrated programme: an academic stream providing intellectual depth, a technical stream providing practical capability, an epistemics stream providing the metacognitive tools to think about thinking itself, and a formation stream providing the physical resilience, leadership skills, and professional ethos that the civil service lacks. The curriculum is predominantly mission-focused. Students will be handed task after task, be it in the realm of the mundane (organising a conference for their fellow cadets) or the extraordinary (penetrating the communications network of a live terrorist cell), and given minimal guidance to completion. This is the antithesis of the university seminar and the Whitehall submission: it is education by doing, under pressure, with real consequences for failure and real recognition for success.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) The Academic Stream. Every Angliot cadet will complete an accelerated dual-honours degree over the first two to three years of the programme. The degree combinations will be drawn from a defined list of pairings designed to produce the intellectual versatility that senior civil servants require: Mathematics and Economics, Law and Political Science, Engineering and Public Policy, Computer Science and Statistics, Natural Sciences and Philosophy, or Modern Languages and International Relations. The pairings are not arbitrary: each combines analytical depth in a technical discipline with breadth in a discipline relevant to governance. A cadet studying Mathematics and Economics will graduate with genuine quantitative capability and genuine understanding of how economies function, not the superficial familiarity with both that a conventional PPE degree provides. A cadet studying Computer Science and Statistics will be able to write production-grade code and to interrogate the data on which policy is based, capabilities that are vanishingly rare in the current Senior Civil Service. The academic programme will be taught by a permanent faculty recruited at internationally competitive salaries, supplemented by visiting practitioners drawn from government, the military, and the private sector. The Angliot will not be a university that also does military training; it will be a professional formation institution that also awards degrees, and the academic component, while rigorous, is in service of the professional mission, not an end in itself.
- b) The Technical Stream. Running concurrently with the academic programme, the technical stream will provide every cadet with a defined set of practical capabilities that the civil service currently lacks at senior levels. The core technical curriculum, mandatory for all cadets regardless of degree pairing, will include: advanced data analysis and statistical programming (Python, R, SQL); financial modelling and cost-benefit analysis to a standard that enables graduates to scrutinise Treasury business cases rather than merely accept them; cyber security fundamentals, reflecting the centrality of information security to modern government; procurement and contract management, including the legal framework governing public contracts and the practical skills required to negotiate with major contractors from a position of knowledge rather than ignorance; the drafting of primary and secondary legislation, and the management of parliamentary questions; and, critically, the Angliot’s own bespoke project management methodology.

The Angliot will not certify cadets in conventional project management frameworks. The existing accreditation landscape, APM, PRINCE2, PMI, and their variants, represents a body of codified practice designed for generic commercial contexts and optimised for process compliance rather than outcome delivery. The civil service’s adoption of these frameworks has not prevented it from achieving an 11% megaproject success rate; it has merely ensured that failure is documented in the correct format. The Angliot will instead develop and teach its own project management doctrine, synthesising the highest and most potent insights from the history of project delivery: the principles that enabled Kelly Johnson’s Skunk Works to deliver the SR-71 under budget and ahead of schedule with 140 engineers; the governance model that allowed the Olympic Delivery Authority to bring London 2012 in on time and under budget; the design-build integration that characterises the most successful infrastructure programmes in East Asia; the disciplined staged-commitment methodology of the oil and gas industry’s Front End Loading process; and the failure modes catalogued by the National Megaproject Office, the Megabureau (C4), whose living archive of megaproject management will serve as both a teaching resource and a live laboratory for Angliot cadets. The resulting doctrine will be codified in an Angliot Project Management Manual, continuously updated, and taught through live application to real government projects during the vocational phase. The manual and the methodology represent a proprietary intellectual asset with significant potential for later commercialisation, offering project management training to allied governments, international organisations, and private sector clients outside the scope of the Graduate Service Obligation.

- c) The Epistemics Stream. Regardless of their specific dual-honours pairing, all cadets will take an intensive and continuous course in epistemics and epistemological techniques, running from the first term to the last. The purpose of this stream is to produce civil servants who are not merely well-informed but metacognitively masterful: people who understand how they think, who can identify the biases, heuristics, and frames that shape their reasoning, who can recognise when they are in the grip of a dogma and have the intellectual tools to escape it, and who can evaluate competing claims to knowledge with the precision and humility that effective governance demands. The curriculum will cover: the formal structure of argument and inference, including Bayesian reasoning and probabilistic thinking; the taxonomy of cognitive biases, with practical exercises in identifying and correcting them in real-time decision-making; the philosophy of science and the demarcation of genuine knowledge from pseudo-knowledge, including the skills required to evaluate scientific evidence, statistical claims, and expert testimony; decision theory and the management of uncertainty, including how to make irreversible decisions on incomplete information without either paralysis or recklessness; the history and epistemology of institutional failure, examining how intelligent institutions staffed by intelligent people arrive at catastrophically wrong conclusions, from groupthink to information cascades to the normalisation of deviance; adversarial epistemics, including red-teaming, pre-mortem analysis, and the structured use of dissent as a decision-quality tool; and the discipline of intellectual honesty, including the capacity to hold a position provisionally, to change one’s mind when the evidence demands it, and to distinguish between what one knows, what one believes, and what one wants to be true. This stream is not a philosophy elective. It is the intellectual backbone of the entire programme. A civil servant who cannot think clearly about how they think is a civil servant who will, at the decisive moment, default to convention, orthodoxy, or institutional convenience. The Angliot exists to produce officials who do not default. The epistemics stream is how.
- d) The Formation Stream. The formation stream is what distinguishes the Angliot from every existing institution in the British educational landscape. Concurrently with the academic, technical, and epistemics streams, every cadet will undergo a process of tailored national service, being exposed not merely to the full rigours of basic armed forces training but to the most elite and high-leverage edges of British military activity and the country’s wider research and development ecosystem. The formation stream has three phases. Phase One (months 1 to 6) is basic military training, conducted at a dedicated facility in partnership with the Ministry of Defence, covering physical fitness, drill, navigation, fieldcraft, weapons handling, first aid, and the fundamentals of military discipline and leadership. Every cadet, regardless of background, begins at the same point and is held to the same standard. The purpose is not to produce soldiers; it is to produce people who have been tested to their physical and mental limits, who understand what it means to operate under conditions of genuine hardship and uncertainty, and who have learned that institutional authority is earned through competence and character, not through seniority or credential. Phase Two (months 7 to 24, running concurrently with the academic programme) consists of periodic intensive exercises and attachments: a two-week attachment to a front-line military unit, a two-week attachment to an intelligence agency, a one-week immersion in a police force or border agency, and a series of weekend and week-long exercises designed to build and test leadership, teamwork, and decision-making under pressure. During Phase Two, cadets will also undertake a structured attachment to the Malebranche (C3.1), working alongside its investigative directorates on live corruption cases, gaining direct experience of forensic audit, documentary analysis, and the operational realities of holding public institutions to account. This attachment serves a dual purpose: it trains cadets in the investigatory skills that senior officials require, and it embeds the anti-corruption ethos of the reform programme into the Angliot’s professional culture from the outset. Phase Three (the final year of the programme) is the vocational phase, in which cadets are attached to government departments, working alongside DRIs (CS1) and their teams on live delivery challenges, applying the academic, technical, epistemics, and formation skills they have acquired to real problems with real consequences. Cadets whose degree pairing and aptitude suit them to infrastructure and procurement will serve vocational attachments within the Megabureau, participating in stage-gate reviews and contributing to the living archive of megaproject management. The vocational attachment is not an internship: cadets are given genuine responsibility, assessed on their contribution to delivery, and their performance in the attachment is the single most important factor in determining their initial posting upon graduation.

##### CS10.4: The Orthodoxy of Service

The Problem

The current civil service has no shared professional orthodoxy beyond a set of procedural values, integrity, honesty, objectivity, impartiality, that are so abstract as to be compatible with virtually any behaviour. A civil servant can obstruct ministerial policy, delay implementation indefinitely, provide technically accurate but strategically misleading advice, and leak to sympathetic journalists, all without violating the Civil Service Code, because the Code defines values without defining obligations. The result is a service whose members share no common understanding of what they are for. Some believe they serve the public. Some believe they serve the constitution. Some believe they serve the institution. Some believe they serve their own careers. The absence of a shared professional orthodoxy means that the culture of the civil service is transmitted not through formal education but through institutional socialisation: new entrants absorb the prevailing norms of their department, their team, and their seniors, and the prevailing norms are overwhelmingly cautious, risk-averse, process-oriented, and institutionally self-protective. CS6 reframes the civil service values around the Duty to Deliver. CS8 codifies the rules in King’s Regulations. But rules and values must be internalised before they can be practised, and internalisation requires formation, not merely instruction.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) Within the formidable battery of abstract, executive, and technical educations that the Angliot provides is an underlying and critically important education in the theory of service. The orthodoxy that shall prevail among Angliot cadets will hold three cardinal principles. First, it is their duty that the acts of Parliament and the decisions of the courts should reflect the mandate given by the electorate to the government of the day: not that officials should blindly execute any instruction, but that the default position of the civil service is to deliver the programme on which the government was elected, and that deviation from that default requires explicit legal justification, not institutional preference. Second, it is their duty to ensure that unreasonable impediments to the British public’s ability to go about their business in security, exercise their freedoms of enterprise and speech, and proceed along their private tracks to prosperity are removed: the civil service exists to enable, not to regulate for regulation’s sake, and every official should ask of every rule and every process whether it serves the citizen or the institution. Third, it is their duty to ensure that all the duties of government are executed with the greatest possible speed and quality, so that public expenditures may be minimised and honoured thereby: speed is not the enemy of quality; delay is the enemy of both, and the default tempo of the civil service should be urgency, not caution. These three principles are not optional philosophical positions. They are the professional creed of the Angliot, taught through every element of the curriculum, tested through every exercise and assessment, and expected of every graduate throughout their career.
- b) The theory of service will be taught not through lectures on public administration but through the lived experience of the programme. When a cadet is tasked with organising a conference and given 72 hours, a budget, and no further guidance, they learn that execution is the test of competence. When a cadet is attached to the Malebranche and works alongside investigators unpicking a local authority procurement fraud, they learn that the rot they are being trained to prevent is real, current, and consequential. When a cadet embedded in the Megabureau participates in a stage-gate review of a billion-pound infrastructure project and sees the specific failure modes that have produced the UK’s catastrophic megaproject record, they learn that the project management doctrine they are studying is not abstract theory but the difference between public money spent and public money wasted. When a cadet is attached to a military intelligence unit and asked to produce an actionable briefing from fragmentary information under time pressure, they learn that perfect information is a luxury that public servants rarely enjoy and that the ability to decide on incomplete information is a core professional skill. When a cadet fails, as every cadet will at some point, and is required to analyse their failure in front of their peers and instructors using the epistemological tools from the epistemics stream, they learn that accountability is not punishment but the foundation of professional improvement. The entire curriculum is designed to produce graduates who instinctively reach for action rather than process, who see problems as opportunities to demonstrate competence rather than risks to be managed through committee, and who understand that the purpose of the civil service is not to advise but to deliver. The formation stream is the vehicle for this internalisation: you cannot teach someone to operate under pressure in a seminar room, and you cannot instil a professional ethos through a PowerPoint presentation. You can only form it through shared hardship, shared achievement, and the sustained experience of being held to a standard that is higher than anything the individual believed they could meet.
- c) The Angliot will maintain its alumni as a professional community throughout their careers. Graduates will be required to complete one week of continuing professional development at the Angliot every two years for the duration of their service obligation, and will be encouraged to continue thereafter. The continuing programme will update their technical skills, refresh and advance the epistemics curriculum, expose them to developments in their academic disciplines, and reconnect them with their cohort and with subsequent cohorts. The Angliot alumni network is not a social club or a patronage network of the kind that made the énarques so corrosive in French public life: it is a professional community bound by a shared formation and a shared orthodoxy, whose members hold each other to the standard they were trained to meet. When an Angliot graduate encounters another Angliot graduate in a different department, the shared formation creates an immediate basis for professional trust and a shared language for professional accountability. Graduates serving in the Malebranche, the Megabureau, the intelligence services, and the 10 departments (CS9) will constitute a distributed network of operationally excellent officials who share not merely a set of skills but a way of understanding what the civil service is for, how it should operate, and what standard of performance is acceptable. Over time, as successive cohorts rise through the service, they will constitute a critical mass sufficient to transform the institution’s culture from within. This is the long-term cultural transformation that CS1 through CS9 cannot achieve alone: structure creates incentives, but formation creates people, and people are what institutions are ultimately made of.

##### CS10.5: Graduation, Career Path, and the Seven-Year Obligation

The Problem

The civil service currently has no mechanism for ensuring that its most capable recruits are deployed to the positions where they can have the greatest impact. Fast Streamers are allocated to departments through a centralised process managed by the Fast Stream and Emerging Talent team in the Cabinet Office, in which departments submit bids and candidates express preferences, but the allocation is driven by departmental recruitment gaps rather than by strategic workforce planning. The result is that talented individuals are frequently placed in roles that neither match their skills nor develop their potential, and the most common career trajectory for a Fast Streamer is a series of one-year rotations that produce a CV of varied experience but no depth of expertise in any domain. The system treats its best recruits as interchangeable units to be distributed across an organisational chart, not as professionals with distinct capabilities to be developed and deployed strategically. Angliot graduates will be different: they will enter the service with a defined technical profile, a known academic specialism, a trained epistemological discipline, and an assessed record of performance under pressure. The career management system must ensure that these capabilities are used, developed, and directed towards the positions of greatest consequence.

Execution

OPERATIONAL

- a) Upon graduation, Angliot cadets will be commissioned as Reserve officers (if they are not already commissioned through the formation stream) and will enter the civil service at Grade 7 level, two grades above the Fast Stream entry point of Higher Executive Officer. This accelerated entry reflects the intensity and duration of their training, which by the point of graduation will have comprised approximately four years of concurrent academic, technical, epistemics, and formation education, equivalent to a demanding postgraduate programme layered on top of an undergraduate degree with military service. Entry at Grade 7 places graduates immediately in positions of genuine responsibility: Grade 7 is the level at which officials lead policy teams, manage budgets, and interact directly with ministers and senior leaders. It is the level at which the DRI system (CS1) expects to find competent operational leaders, and it is the level from which progression to the Senior Civil Service is a realistic prospect within five to seven years. The accelerated entry is not a privilege; it is a recognition that Angliot graduates arrive with capabilities that it takes a conventional entrant a decade or more to develop, and the service obligation ensures that the public receives the full return on its investment.
- b) The initial posting of each graduate will be determined by the OPM Talent and Appointments Unit (CS3) in consultation with DRIs, based on the graduate’s academic specialism, technical profile, epistemological strengths, and assessed performance during the vocational attachment. Graduates who studied Mathematics and Economics and excelled in their Treasury vocational attachment will be posted to the Treasury or the Department for the Economy. Graduates who studied Law and Political Science and distinguished themselves in a Malebranche attachment will be posted to the Malebranche or the Ministry of Justice. Graduates who studied Engineering and Public Policy and served vocational attachments in the Megabureau will be posted to the Department for Infrastructure and Environment or to the Megabureau itself, carrying their Angliot project management training directly into the governance of the UK’s largest capital programmes. The posting is strategic, not administrative: the OPM maintains a register of the critical capability gaps across the 10 departments (CS9), the Malebranche, and the Megabureau, and matches Angliot graduates to those gaps. During the seven-year service obligation, graduates will complete a minimum of two postings in different institutions, each of at least two years’ duration, ensuring breadth of experience without the carousel of annual rotations that characterises the Fast Stream. At the end of the seven-year obligation, graduates are free to leave the public sector, but the expectation, reinforced by the career progression pathway, the continuing professional development programme, and the professional community, is that the majority will remain. The civil service must be good enough to retain them voluntarily, and the reforms of CS1 through CS9 are designed to make it so: a service in which talent is recognised, performance is rewarded, obstruction is penalised, and the mission is delivery is a service that ambitious, capable people will choose to stay in.
- c) Angliot graduates who complete the seven-year obligation and remain in the civil service will be eligible for an accelerated progression track to the Senior Civil Service. This is not an automatic escalator: it is a track that provides structured opportunities for development, mentoring by serving DRIs, and priority access to the most challenging and consequential roles, conditional on sustained high performance assessed against the Delivery Standard (CS6) and Charter Letter metrics (CS7). The accelerated track recognises that the purpose of the Angliot is not merely to produce competent Grade 7 officials but to produce the future DRIs, the future Directors General, the future Directors of the Malebranche and the Megabureau, and ultimately the future leaders of the reformed civil service. Every cohort of 80 to 100 Angliot graduates will include individuals who, within 15 to 20 years, will be leading major departments, and the programme is designed from the outset to identify and develop that potential. The combination of Angliot formation with the DRI reserve army (CS4) creates a self-reinforcing pipeline of leadership talent: the DRI reserve army provides the immediate cadre of senior leaders needed to implement the reform programme, while the Angliot provides the long-term institutional supply of leaders who have been formed from the ground up in the culture, skills, and orthodoxy that the reformed civil service requires. Within a generation, the senior ranks of the British civil service will be populated by people who were selected for exceptional merit and epistemological range, trained for performance, hardened by military formation, equipped with metacognitive mastery, and bound by a shared understanding of what public service means. That is the prize.

Summary

CS10 requires one piece of primary legislation: the Angliot Act, establishing the institution as a Crown body with degree-awarding powers, a military training component under MOD authority, and a legally binding seven-year Graduate Service Obligation. The Act creates a new category of institution in British public life, one that combines the academic rigour of the best universities with the military formation of the service academies and the professional focus of the grands corps. Everything else, the curriculum, the selection process, the physical establishment, the staffing, the career pathway, and the integration with the reformed civil service, the Malebranche, and the Megabureau, is operational.

Timeline

Pre-election: Detailed planning for the Angliot, including: identification of a suitable site (options include a former military establishment with both academic and field training facilities, or a purpose-built campus on MOD land); recruitment of the founding Commandant and a core academic and military faculty; design of the selection process and the curriculum in detail, including the bespoke project management methodology and the epistemics programme; engagement with the Ministry of Defence on the Reserve Forces enlistment framework and military training partnership; engagement with the Malebranche planning team (C3.1) and the Megabureau planning team (C4) on vocational attachment frameworks; drafting of the Angliot Act in full.

Day 1 to Day 90: Angliot Act introduced in Parliament as part of the first-session legislative programme. Founding Commandant appointed by the Prime Minister. Interim Board of Governors constituted. Site acquisition or designation confirmed. Partnership agreement signed with the Ministry of Defence. Memoranda of understanding agreed with the Malebranche and the Megabureau for cadet attachments.

Months 3 to 12: Angliot Act receives Royal Assent. Campus development commences (or adaptation of existing facilities). Faculty recruitment begins, with internationally competitive salaries funded from the programme budget. Epistemics faculty recruited from philosophy, cognitive science, decision science, and intelligence analysis backgrounds. Project management doctrine development begins, drawing on the Megabureau’s living archive. Selection process for the inaugural cohort designed and piloted.

Month 12 to Month 18: First application cycle opens. Written examinations administered at regional centres. Residential assessments conducted at the Angliot’s campus. Final panel interviews completed. Inaugural cohort of 80 to 100 cadets selected on the basis of exceptional merit and epistemological range, through a process entirely blind to demographic characteristics.

Month 18 to Month 24: Inaugural cohort arrives at the Angliot. Phase One of the formation stream (basic military training) commences. Academic, technical, and epistemics programmes begin concurrently at the end of the basic training period. The Angliot is operational.

Year 4 to Year 5: Inaugural cohort graduates. First Angliot graduates enter the civil service at Grade 7, with postings across the 10 departments, the Malebranche, and the Megabureau. Seven-year service obligation begins. Second, third, and fourth cohorts are in training. The institutional pipeline is established. First edition of the Angliot Project Management Manual published and made available to all SROs in government.

Year 10 onwards: The first Angliot graduates complete their service obligation and face the choice to remain or leave. By this point, approximately 400 to 500 Angliot graduates are serving across the civil service, the Malebranche, and the Megabureau. The most capable are approaching Senior Civil Service level. The cultural transformation is visible: departments report a measurable difference in the operational capability, initiative, and delivery orientation of Angliot graduates compared with conventional entrants. The Angliot Project Management methodology is being adopted beyond the Angliot’s own graduates. The epistemics training is producing officials who are visibly more rigorous, more self-aware, and more resistant to institutional dogma than their peers. The long game has begun.

CS10 completes the Progress civil service reform framework. CS1 gives ministers the power to appoint and dismiss. CS2 restricts judicial obstruction. CS3 creates the Office of the Prime Minister. CS4 builds the reserve army of DRIs. CS5 breaks Treasury control. CS6 rewrites the management code around the Duty to Deliver. CS7 issues Charter Letters with measurable targets. CS8 codifies King’s Regulations. CS9 reduces the Cabinet and consolidates departments. CS10 creates the institution that will, over the course of a generation, supply the reformed civil service with the people it needs to sustain the reform. The first nine policies change the system. The tenth changes the people. Structure without culture is temporary. Culture without structure is powerless. Together, they are transformative. The Angliot is the long bet: it will take five years to produce its first graduates and a generation to transform the senior ranks. But every institution that endures was built with patience, and the British civil service, for all its faults, has endured for 170 years. The question is not whether it will endure for another 170 years but what kind of institution it will be. CS1 through CS9 answer that question for the next Parliament. CS10 answers it for the next century.

##### CRX. Angliot, the British ‘Grand École’

The positions held and the role played by the British Civil Service as it presently is in inhibiting the execution of public mandates and holding back the country's power to administer to its own borders, prevent the abuse of its courts, develop its natural resources and build infrastructure, are not merely a matter of organisational imperative as formed and guaranteed by incentive, but also a matter of attitude, culture, and dispositional profile as are manifestly found in the individual members of its service.

If we want a much higher standard of CS that guarantees the national interest, instead of paralysing the country on the basis of its own private interest, we need a very different CS culture.

This requires training civil servants very differently. The best way to ensure this happens is to create an institution capable of training civil servants very differently, and at the highest level – an equivalent to France's Grand École.

Britain's equivalent thereof will be a seat of accelerated higher-learning, which takes extreme selectivity and extent of training to a level beyond even that of its highest-ranked institutions of tertiary education. In it, selected students will pursue an accelerated dual-honours degree in key subjects, while also being given extensive technical education. Concurrently with these pursuits, they will undergo a process of tailored national service, being exposed not merely to the full rigours of basic armed forces training but to the most elite and high-leverage edges of British military activity and the country's wider R&D ecosystem.

The curriculum of the Grand École will be predominantly mission-focused – students will be handed task after task, be it in the realm of the mundane (organising a conference for their fellow cadets) or the extraordinary (penetrating the communications network of a live terrorist cell), and given minimal guidance-to-completion.

After a preliminary period of 2–3 years of concurrent study, the cadets will be phased into their vocation. Within this formidable battery of abstract, executive, and technical educations is an underlying and critically important education in the theory of service.

The orthodoxy that shall prevail among them will hold that:

- It is their duty that the acts of parliament and the courts should reflect the mandate
- It is their duty to ensure reasonable impediments to the British public's ability to go about their business in security, exercise their freedoms (of enterprise, of speech), and proceed along their private tracks to prosperity, are removed
- It is their duty to ensure that all the duties of government are to be executed with the greatest possible speed and quality, so that public expenditures may be minimised and honoured thereby

Our aim with this school is to create bastions of civil service so skilled, mission-oriented, entrepreneurial, and variously-able, that the overall size of the service can be dramatically reduced while capabilities dramatically scale up.

Given that successful alumni of the course will, in the course of seeing to their duties, create untold £billions for the country in averted waste, saved expenditures, and efficiencies-created, the entire program is cost-covered in full for all of those who succeed in being accepted to the first year class. Candidates' bed, board, and basic living expenses will be accounted for. In return for this, all graduates are expected to spend no fewer than seven years after graduation working in the British public sector.

##### CRX. Care for the Disabled

The reduction of unfunded statutory obligations placed on councils must be a keystone of our civil service reform strategy.

A history of incapacity benefits over the last two decades makes plain how we have gotten to the point whereupon a number of local authorities presently face bankruptcy relative to the mounting costs of incapacity benefit:

- 2010–2016: George Osborne cuts incapacity benefits claimants every year and rolls out PIP, Britain seems to have a grip on benefits
- 2014: Care Act 2014 sets out ‘parity of esteem’ – landmark principle which establishes that mental health must be given equal priority to physical health
- 2016: May kicks out Osborne. New era. ‘End to austerity/nasty party’
- 2016–17: The government lose a handful of cases through judicial review brought by disability NGOs, and are forced to expand the scope of PIP, especially to mental health cases – defeating the point of PIP being a more restrictive/cost-saving replacement for DLA.
- 2017–Today: Incapacity benefits claimants start to slowly rise every year, then explode when COVID hits as many more people are hooked onto the system for the first time. Pandemic ends but claimant numbers continue to rapidly grow with no end in sight as approval rates soar.

##### CRX. Pay for Public Servants

If Britain wishes to benefit from the full extent of the talent of its people, then it must make a career in public service highly attractive to those with exceptional skill and experience profiles. As part of our broader efforts to dramatically increase the calibre of public servants, Progress will mandate an increase in pay for Members of Parliament and Cabinet Ministers.

As it is the duty and responsibility of all public servants to ensure that the ship of state is well-maintained, and steered with momentum according to the proper bearing, Progress will also tie all rates of public sector pay to the performance of the economy. At Progress, we believe that incentive engineering is everything, and that fair reward for hard work is a sacred principle – so that excellent work by the public sector to enable national growth shall be rewarded, in direct proportion, with improved pay, while neglect of the health of the state shall occasion reduction.

#### Immigration (I)

“Take the Best, Leave the Rest”

Things being as they are, with no new infrastructure being built, continuing to permit unchecked immigration is no good for either our existing citizenry, nor for migrants themselves. The immigration policy pursued by more than 30 years of British government has represented a consistent and wilful betrayal of the majority of British people's wishes on the subject. It makes neither cultural nor economic sense, given the burden upon the public purse represented by the majority of particularly low-skilled migrants, and given the more-and-more frequent outrages against norms of British civilisation we have seen committed in select migrant communities (chief among them, the Rape Gang Atrocities).

We are committed to service according to the public wish on this subject, and to such service dispatched in a peaceful, lawful, and civilised manner that leaves absolutely no room for violence, unrest, or disruption otherwise to British civil life – a migration policy that is robust, humane, and sane.

##### I1. High-Skilled Migration

We will extensively redefine the threshold and criteria for ‘high-skilled migration’, excluding many such professions as have been previously included (such as ‘barber’, ‘dancer’, various forms of religious teacher etc.). We will furthermore ensure that high-skilled migration is:

- Targeted; that is, awarded solely to people capable of unusually rich degrees of contribution in key areas of economic activity in Britain, particularly in Prosperity Zones and startups
- Costed; that is, high-skilled migrant visas will only be given to those who can be said definitively to put more into the public purse than they take out of it
- Entrepreneurially-graded; that is, skewing towards people who are determined to make jobs and wealth for Britain
- Extensible; that is, we will show greater favour to applicants who have means to spread the skills they have to other Britons. Regular contribution to courses at British skills colleges, schools, and universities will be a mandatory community-investment-oriented requirement of the granting of any high-skilled work visa
- Culturally consistent; that is, we will only grant high-skilled migrant visas to those determined to hold up, exhibit, and defend British values in their lives while working here
- Duly limited; that is, we will ensure that the numbers of high-skilled migrant visas granted will not burden national infrastructure nor have cause to trigger skill inflation
- Intentful; that is, for those people who are skilled, productive, and determined to become a part of Britain's cultural and economic life, we will provide fast-tracks to citizenship

##### I2. Low-Skilled Migration

We will impose a permanent moratorium on low-skilled migrant labour. Only people equipped with the skills to contribute to Britain's national-cultural life, and who can be said with assurance to hold views in step with Britain's values and cultural principles, will be permitted permanent or semi-permanent entry to the country.

##### I3. Asylum Claims

All asylum claims will be processed off-shore, pursuant of Progress' sidelining of ECHR rules relative to asylum and immigration matters, on an indefinite basis, pending a reform initiative, as is within Britain's jurisprudential ability to do. Obfuscatory relitigation of removal decisions will be restricted.

##### I4. Illegal Migration

Illegal migrants will be detained upon arrival, and held in detention indefinitely until repatriation to their country of origin can be duly arranged. Any country that refuses the readmission of its citizens relative to this policy will face immediate travel blacklisting, sanctions, and, where appropriate, the complete suspension of foreign aid.

##### I5. Deportation of Foreign Criminals

Any migrant who engages in serious crime on British soil will face immediate and complete asset seizure and deportation to their country of origin.

##### I6. Migration Blacklisting

Countries whose citizens can be seen to commit a quantitatively or qualitatively disproportionate amount of crime in Britain will face permanent disqualification from all immigration routes otherwise reasonably afforded other countries. Addition to the blacklist will be enforced for a period of no less than 20 years from the point of addition, and position on the blacklist may be lifted or otherwise reinstated at the end of this period dependent on the performance of the country-in-question in a practices-and-environment audit conducted by the British government.

##### I7. Migration Blacklisting

Countries whose citizens can be seen to commit a quantitatively or qualitatively disproportionate amount of crime in Britain will face permanent disqualification from all immigration routes otherwise reasonably afforded other countries.

##### I8. Resourcing for Dependents

Both newly-arriving migrants and all existing migrants must give demonstrable proof that they are able to independently provide-in-full for the fundamental needs of any dependents beyond their immediate families.

##### I9. Resettlement with Amnesty

Progress is aware that many citizens of other nations have come to Britain's shores under the supervision of prior governments, governments determined to grant visas and settled status to persons regardless of their degree of cultural fit with British life or their realistic prospects for contribution to Britain's economic life. Those who were granted right to residence in Britain fairly under prior systems, but whose skill profile does not fit outstanding needs; who are prolongedly out of work and state-dependent; or whose cultural disposition is in pointed contravention to British norms and values; to them we shall dedicate a generous resettlement plan with amnesty, so that they may be resettled comfortably in another country where their skills are in demand and their cultural needs adequately met as they may not be in Britain.

#### PP1.1: The Citizenship Act

“The British state exists to serve the British people”

Governing Principle

The British state exists to serve the British people. This is not a controversial proposition; it is the foundational assumption of every nation state that has ever existed. Yet decades of muddied legislation have obscured who the British people are, what rights attach to that identity, and what obligations the state owes to those it governs versus those it merely hosts.

Britain was 99%+ ethnically homogeneous for thousands of years, making it one of the most ancient and stable civilisations in the world. The 2015 People of the British Isles study confirmed that 75% of the modern British genome traces to original post-Ice Age settlers, with 25% from Anglo-Saxon migration – a population structure essentially unchanged for over a thousand years. This is not an accident of geography but the product of an island nation whose legal, cultural, and constitutional traditions evolved organically from a continuous people.

The constitutional bond between the British nation and its citizens was historically grounded in jus sanguinis – the right of blood. Calvin’s Case (1608) established allegiance as a hereditary birthright, citing the 1351 statute De Natis Ultra Mare, which granted subject status to foreign-born children of the King’s subjects, demonstrating that bloodline transmitted allegiance even outside territorial jurisdiction. The Act of Settlement 1701 barred naturalised subjects from holding prerogative powers – Parliament, the Privy Council, Crown offices – precisely because allegiance was considered inheritable, not merely contractual. Natural-born subjects had allegiance “by nature”; naturalised subjects had it only “by law,” a lesser bond. Blackstone’s Commentaries described subjectship as inheritable, with naturalisation requiring sovereign grace and typically entailing permanent disabilities.

The rigid jus soli vs jus sanguinis binary is itself a 19th-century fabrication. Recent scholarship (Weil, 2001) demonstrates that early modern jurists in France and England did not treat birthplace and parentage as competing principles but as complementary evidences of a single underlying reality: the bond of allegiance between subject and sovereign. The apparent dominance of jus soli in English common law reflects practical circumstances – an island population where birth and descent coincided – not a principled rejection of descent-based belonging. Britain’s jus soli tradition produced the same result as jus sanguinis for millennia because those born in Britain overwhelmingly were of British parentage. That coincidence no longer holds.

The post-war legal order shattered this framework. The British Nationality Act 1948 created a single status of “Citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies” encompassing 800 million people across the Commonwealth, conflating the legal rights of indigenous Britons with those of populations who had no historical connection to Britain beyond colonial administration. The British Nationality Act 1981 attempted a partial correction by introducing the requirement that at least one parent be British or settled, but retained a fundamentally jus soli character: five years’ residence leads to ILR, ILR leads to citizenship, and the conveyor belt to full membership continues regardless of integration, cultural affinity, or contribution. The result is a system that grants the highest privilege a nation can bestow – full citizenship, with the right to vote on the destiny of the nation and to hold its highest offices – to individuals whose connection to Britain may be as shallow as a five-year work visa and a Life in the UK test.

Meanwhile, 98% of Britain’s population growth in 2024 was driven by net immigration. The foreign-born population has risen from under 4% in the mid-twentieth century to approximately 19% of England and Wales. White British residents are projected to fall below 50% of the population by 2065. The Total Fertility Rate has collapsed to a record low of 1.41 – far below the 2.08 replacement level. Natural population change (births minus deaths) is projected to turn negative by 2030, meaning every person added to the British population from that date will be an immigrant. These are not abstract statistics. They represent the progressive dissolution of the nation as a recognisable entity.

The philosophical case for reform rests on the Burkean understanding of national membership as collective property – an intergenerational inheritance encompassing territory, institutions, liberties, and cultural continuity, treated as an entailed estate held in trust by the living generation for the benefit of past and future heirs. As Burke articulated: society is “a partnership not only between those who are living, but between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born.” The Crown-in-Parliament retains sovereign legal authority to grant citizenship through prerogative and statute. Mass naturalisation is therefore fully lawful. But it is unjust – not due to procedural illegitimacy, but because it breaches the objective moral duties inherent in the trust: stewardship rather than ownership of the inheritance, fiduciary obligation not to dilute existing heirs’ proprietary expectancies, and the constraint that no single generation possesses legitimate authority to fundamentally transform what future generations will inherit.

In the age of mass transit, it is now time to institute explicit jus sanguinis laws. Progress will pass a new Act of Settlement – the Citizenship Act 2029 – to restore the constitutional bond between nation and citizen, clarify the rights and obligations attaching to each tier of civic status, and create a meaningful but rigorous pathway for genuine integration over generations.

The Philosophy of Progress underpins every element of this reform:

- #33 (Definition of “People”): A people is defined by shared language, religion, traditions, and territory – not racial purity, but cultural and historical continuity.
- #34 (Definition of “Nation”): A nation is a people with autonomy. The British nation requires a citizenry that shares in the historical and cultural inheritance of the British people.
- #37 (Right to Non-Interference): Indigenous peoples possess a spiritual, cultural, and historical bond to their homeland. The British people’s right to determine who joins their nation is an expression of this bond.
- #38 (Philia and Rejection of Multiculturalism): Aristotelian philia – civic friendship grounded in shared values, identity, and mutual trust – is required for high-trust social cohesion. This cannot be manufactured from arbitrary demographic mixing.
- #54 (Conservation): We are custodians, not owners, of the inheritances entrusted to us by our forebears. The living generation has no moral authority to give away what it holds in trust.

This policy interacts with:

- CS2 (Executive Decisions Act): Ouster clauses and JR restrictions protecting the Citizenship Act from judicial activism
- C6 (Legal Equality Act): Prohibition on parallel legal systems; mandatory integration standards; FGM and forced marriage enforcement
- PP1.2 (The Immigration Reset): Visa system reform, Visa Insurance, and caps that control the inflow; the Citizenship Act controls who may belong
- PP1.3 (Asylum, Removal, and Sovereignty): HRA amendments enabling enforcement of the new framework
- PP1.5 (Enforcement and Internal Control): UK E-Verify, Fit and Proper Persons Register, and biometric infrastructure that operationalise citizenship tiers

##### PP1.1.1: The Five-Tier Citizenship Framework

The Problem

British citizenship law is a palimpsest of contradictions. The British Nationality Act 1981, the Immigration Act 1971, the British Nationality (Falkland Islands) Act 1983, the Hong Kong Act 1985, the British Overseas Territories Act 2002, and successive amendments have created a legal labyrinth in which the relationship between the individual and the state varies by historical accident, colonial legacy, and immigration route rather than by any coherent principle. A person born in Birmingham to two British parents holds the same legal status as a person naturalised after five years on a Skilled Worker visa. A Commonwealth citizen resident in the UK can vote in general elections, while a British citizen abroad may lose the franchise entirely. Irish citizens enjoy near-identical rights to British citizens under the Common Travel Area, yet citizens of allied nations with deeper cultural ties – Australia, New Zealand, Canada – do not.

The consequence is that citizenship has been devalued. It confers no meaningful distinction from permanent residence. It creates no graduated pathway for integration. It provides no mechanism to distinguish between those whose families have inhabited these islands for centuries and those who arrived last year. It treats the franchise – the most consequential right a democracy can bestow – as an administrative by-product of residency rather than an expression of membership in the national community.

International precedent confirms that jus sanguinis citizenship is the norm, not the exception. Ireland permits citizenship claims through grandparents. Italy offers one of the most expansive descent-based regimes in the world, with no generational limit. Poland permits descendants of former citizens to claim nationality. Germany has expanded descent-based rights for descendants of Nazi victims. Japan adheres to strict jus sanguinis, granting citizenship only to those with at least one Japanese parent. Switzerland’s three-tier naturalisation system – commune, canton, federal – provides the most rigorous integration requirement in Europe, with genuine local community involvement in determining who is admitted to membership. Britain’s current system is an outlier in its permissiveness, not in its rigour.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Citizenship Act 2029 (the new Act of Settlement) will establish a five-tier civic status framework replacing the existing categories under the British Nationality Act 1981:

- a) Indigenous British Citizen. Anyone born in the United Kingdom with at least one parent, or two grandparents, with unbroken British lineage; OR any person with three unbroken generations of British Subject status, subject to passing the Citizenship Test (see PP1.1.3). Indigenous British Citizens hold full and unconditional citizenship, including the right to vote in all elections, to hold public office, to serve in security, defence, and intelligence roles, and to transmit citizenship to their children without limitation.
- b) Hereditary British Citizen. Children or grandchildren of Indigenous British Citizens born abroad. Hereditary status must be claimed by passing the Citizenship Test, which verifies that the claimant has maintained genuine cultural connection to their British heritage. Once claimed, Hereditary British Citizens hold the same rights as Indigenous citizens, including full franchise and public office eligibility. The Citizenship Test content – British history, constitution, literature, cultural traditions – will be incorporated into the reformed national curriculum, ensuring parity between those raised in Britain and those claiming citizenship from overseas.
- c) Inherited Conditional British Citizen (ICBC). UK-born descendants of post-1948 naturalised citizens. This status:
- Is automatic at birth (no test required for initial grant)
- Carries the right to reside, work, and access public services
- Does not carry the right to vote in national elections or hold public office
- Is revocable for serious criminal conduct (>12 months’ custodial sentence), prolonged absence (>5 years), welfare dependency (>24 months continuous, flagged for review), or fraud
- Lapses after five years’ absence from the United Kingdom or her overseas territories, including Crown Dependencies
- Requires re-registration every 10 years (confirmation of continued residence, declaration of criminal history, updated contact details; nominal fee ~£50)
- Is the second step on the three-generation pathway to Indigenous citizenship
- d) British Subject. A status for long-term residents who have demonstrated integration but are not eligible for citizenship by descent. Two routes:
- Spousal route: Marriage to a British Citizen (Indigenous or Hereditary only) for 5+ years, subject to passing the British Subject Test (see PP1.1.3)
- Long residence route: 10+ years’ lawful residence, financial independence, clean criminal record, and passing the British Subject Test

British Subject status:

- Carries no right of transmission to children (children’s status determined by other parent, or ICBC if born in the UK to two Subjects)
- Grants right to reside, work, and access public services (but not vote in national elections or hold public office)
- Is revocable for serious criminal conduct, prolonged absence (5+ years), or fraud
- Requires 10-year re-registration
- Is the first step in the three-generation pathway to Indigenous citizenship
- e) Guest. Presence of up to 180 days in any rolling twelve-month period. Guest status does not confer benefit or settlement rights and is automatically removed on suspected breach, notified or not. Outstaying without discretionary renewal constitutes breach. Inability to support one’s life in the UK is grounds for breach.
- f) Birth status determination. The Act will establish the following mapping of parental status to child’s citizenship:

Table 1: Birth in the United Kingdom

Table 2: Birth Abroad

- g) End of automatic jus soli for non-citizens. Under the current British Nationality Act 1981, a child born in the UK to two settled (ILR) parents is automatically British. Under the Citizenship Act, they receive ICBC status – a meaningful distinction that preserves residence rights but reserves full citizenship for those with British lineage or who complete the three-generation pathway.
- h) Restoration of the Indigenous/naturalised distinction. Pre-1948 law distinguished between “natural-born” subjects (full rights, transmissible) and “naturalised” subjects (restricted rights, limited transmission). The Citizenship Act restores this principle: Indigenous and Hereditary citizens hold full, transmissible citizenship; ICBC and British Subject status is conditional and limited.
- i) Statelessness provisions. Children born in the United Kingdom to parents who are not British Citizens and cannot confer citizenship will follow the existing system for statelessness with eligibility for registration, as obliged by the 1961 UN Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness. Such children may register as ICBC upon reaching age 10 if they have been continuously resident and have no other nationality.
- j) Consequential amendments. The Citizenship Act repeals and replaces relevant provisions of the British Nationality Act 1981, including Sections 1 (acquisition by birth), 2 (acquisition by descent), 6 (acquisition by naturalisation), and 40 (deprivation). The Act amends Schedule 1 of the Representation of the People Act 1983 to restrict the parliamentary and local government franchise to Indigenous and Hereditary British Citizens. The Act amends the Act of Settlement 1701 (to the extent not already amended) to codify in modern statutory language the principle that public office is reserved for citizens by blood or proven heritage.

OPERATIONAL

Presumption process for existing residents. The transition to the new system will apply presumptions to minimise disruption:

- Born in UK before 1983: presumed Indigenous (pure jus soli applied under prior law)
- Born in UK 1983–2029 with at least one British parent: presumed Indigenous or ICBC based on available evidence
- Unable to prove British parentage: granted ICBC status by default (can upgrade via three-generation pathway)
- Reduced evidence requirements for over-75s: statutory declaration of parentage may substitute for documentary proof
- Registration free for over-70s or those in receipt of Pension Credit
