Documentation support. The General Register Office will conduct searches for birth/marriage records on behalf of applicants at subsidised fees. Where documentary evidence is unavailable, the following are accepted: witness statements (statutory declarations from family members or long-term acquaintances), circumstantial evidence (school records, medical records, employment history, census records), and DNA testing as a last resort for disputed parentage (Home Office-approved laboratories; cost-shared). Where evidence is insufficient to prove Indigenous status but UK birth is established, the individual receives ICBC status rather than being left stateless.

##### PP1.1.2: The Citizenship Register and Administration

The Problem

Britain has no unified register of who its citizens are, what status they hold, or where they reside. Immigration status is tracked piecemeal across UKVI, BRP cards, eVisas, the EU Settlement Scheme, passport records, and HMRC databases. There is no single authoritative source that can answer the question: “Is this person a British citizen, and if so, what rights does their citizenship confer?” The Office for National Statistics relies on passenger surveys – not actual counts – to estimate migration. Reports measuring waste processing and phone usage suggest the true population may exceed official statistics by ten million or more. This informational vacuum makes enforcement of any citizenship framework impossible.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Citizenship Act 2029 will establish:

- a) The Citizenship Register. A central Home Office database recording the citizenship status of every person lawfully present in the United Kingdom. The Register will record: full name, date and place of birth, biometric identifiers (photograph, fingerprints), citizenship tier (Indigenous, Hereditary, ICBC, British Subject, Guest), date of status determination, and conditions attaching to conditional statuses (ICBC/Subject). The Register will be authoritative: all other systems (electoral roll, DWP, HMRC, NHS Spine, DVLA, employer verification) will draw from it.
- b) The Fit and Proper Persons Register. A publicly accessible Home Office database for non-citizens only, containing: name, photograph, biometric identifiers, current immigration status and visa type, visa expiry date, right to work (yes/no with restrictions), right to rent (yes/no). Indigenous and Hereditary British Citizens are not on the register. The state should not maintain equivalent surveillance over its own people. Citizens verify status via passport or birth certificate as at present. The privacy principle is explicit: the state should know who non-citizens are and what they are doing; it should not have equivalent surveillance over its own citizens.
- c) Mandatory status determination deadline. By Year 5 of the transition, all residents must have their status determined. Those who have not interacted with any administrative touchpoint must proactively register. The Act provides a 12-month grace period after the deadline. After the grace period, unregistered individuals are presumed to have no lawful status and are subject to enforcement action.
- d) Integration with existing systems. The Act will require integration of the Citizenship Register with: UK Visas and Immigration (extended to track citizenship tiers), the Employer Checking Service (updated to show status tier and conditions), the NHS Spine (linked for healthcare entitlement verification), DWP systems (linked for benefit eligibility verification), DVLA (linked for driving licence verification), and the electoral register (franchise confirmed based on citizenship status).

OPERATIONAL

Phased implementation. The transition to the new system will proceed in three phases:

Phase 1 – Legislative Foundation (Year 1): Pass the Citizenship Act establishing the five-tier system. Create the Citizenship Register within the Home Office. Establish criteria and documentation requirements for each status.

Phase 2 – New Births and Applications (Year 1 onwards): All births registered after commencement are classified under the new system. All new visa, settlement, and naturalisation applications processed under new rules. Existing passport holders retain current documents until renewal.

Phase 3 – Gradual Reclassification (Years 1–10): Existing citizens are reclassified upon their next interaction with the system. Status determination occurs at the following touchpoints:

No mass re-registration exercise required; transition occurs organically through existing touchpoints.

Public information campaign (Years 3–5). Multilingual outreach explaining the registration requirement and process, timed to precede the Year 5 mandatory determination deadline.

Special provisions for vulnerable populations. Home visits for elderly or disabled individuals unable to attend registration centres. Council staff and authorised charities to assist with applications. No fees for over-70s or Pension Credit recipients.

##### PP1.1.3: Naturalisation, Assimilation, and the Three-Generation Pathway

The Problem

The current naturalisation system requires five years’ residence for Indefinite Leave to Remain and a further twelve months for citizenship – six years total from first arrival to full, irrevocable membership of the nation, including the right to vote and hold office. The “Life in the UK” test is widely derided as trivially easy, testing knowledge of pub quiz facts rather than genuine cultural integration. There is no local community involvement in the decision, no assessment of values compatibility, and no mechanism to revoke citizenship once granted except in narrow cases of fraud or terrorism. The result is a conveyor belt to citizenship that operates regardless of whether the individual has meaningfully integrated into British society, learned English to a functional level, achieved financial self-sufficiency, or participated in community life.

Switzerland provides the counter-model. Swiss naturalisation requires ten years’ residence (with years aged 8–18 counting double), including two to five years in the specific commune. Applications must be approved at commune, canton, and federal levels. Local communities have genuine power to reject applicants who have not integrated. Applicants must demonstrate: certified language proficiency, financial independence, knowledge of Swiss geography, history, politics, and local customs, participation in community life, compatibility with community values, and absence of any threat to security. Swiss authorities have rejected applicants for refusing to shake hands with officials of the opposite sex, for inability to name local landmarks, and for behaviour deemed incompatible with community values. Britain has nothing comparable.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Citizenship Act 2029 will establish:

- a) Two distinct tests. Progress distinguishes between the British Subject Test (for residence rights) and the Citizenship Test (for those claiming citizenship by descent):

The rationale: a Hereditary British Citizen is claiming membership of the nation by birthright – a more significant status than residence rights. They should demonstrate that their family’s British heritage remains meaningful. Conversely, a long-term resident seeking Subject status need only show they can live here compatibly; they are not claiming to be British, only to live among the British.

- b) The three-generation pathway. The route from British Subject to Indigenous British Citizen:
- Generation 1: Foreign national passes the British Subject Test – granted British Subject status
- Generation 2: Child born in UK to British Subject parent – born as ICBC (automatic, no test at birth)
- Generation 3: Child born in UK to ICBC parent – born as ICBC (automatic, no test at birth)
- Generation 4: Child born in UK to second-generation ICBC parent – eligible for Indigenous British Citizen status, subject to passing the Citizenship Test

The test requirement at Generation 4 is deliberate: three generations of lawful residence demonstrates opportunity to assimilate, not proof of it. A family could spend three generations in a parallel community – attending ethnic schools, consuming foreign media, marrying within their origin community, and participating minimally in British civic life. The Citizenship Test verifies that the opportunity was taken. This prevents the three-generation pathway from becoming an automatic conveyor belt regardless of actual integration.

- c) Swiss-model local authority involvement. The British Subject Test will incorporate:
- Local authority assessment: Parish/ward councils to provide integration assessments, with genuine power to flag concerns. Applications must be approved at local and national level.
- Extended residence requirement: 10 years minimum before Subject status eligibility (currently 5 for ILR + 1 for citizenship under existing law)
- English language proficiency: B2 level for the Citizenship Test, B1 for the British Subject Test (higher than the current requirement), tested by approved institutions only
- Civic knowledge: Rigorous test on British history, constitution, law, and local knowledge relevant to area of residence
- Values interview: Assessment of compatibility with British values including gender equality, religious tolerance, and rule of law
- Community integration evidence: Demonstrated participation in local community life; references from British citizens
- d) Curriculum alignment. The Citizenship Test content will be incorporated into the reformed national curriculum. Indigenous British Citizens will acquire this knowledge through their normal education. The test verifies that Hereditary claimants living abroad, and ICBC descendants completing the three-generation pathway, have maintained or acquired equivalent cultural literacy.

OPERATIONAL

Test development. The Home Office will commission the development of both tests within 12 months of Royal Assent, drawing on Swiss, Danish, and Australian naturalisation models. Tests will be administered at designated centres with identity verification. The values interview will be conducted by trained assessors with local authority input.

Local authority capacity. MHCLG will issue guidance to parish and ward councils on their assessment role, including training for councillors, standard assessment frameworks, and appeal procedures. Local authorities will designate Citizenship Officers responsible for status verification, Home Office liaison, and resident assistance with registration.

##### PP1.1.4: The Franchise and Public Office

The Problem

The British franchise is an anomaly. Commonwealth citizens resident in the UK can vote in general elections – a legacy of the British Nationality Act 1948 that conflated the rights of subjects of the Crown across the entire Commonwealth. In some constituencies, Commonwealth voters constitute nearly 25% of the electorate. Irish citizens also vote in UK general elections under the Common Travel Area arrangements. The result is that the composition of Parliament – the sovereign legislature of the British nation – is determined in part by people who are not members of that nation.

The postal vote system, designed for service personnel and the infirm, has become a vehicle for electoral fraud, particularly in communities where bloc voting is prevalent. Evidence of postal vote farming – collecting and completing ballots on behalf of community members, often under pressure from community leaders – has been documented in multiple constituencies. The combination of non-citizen voting and postal vote abuse undermines democratic legitimacy.

Public office – Members of Parliament, the House of Lords, the Privy Council, senior judicial appointments – should be held by those whose loyalty to the British nation is unambiguous. The Act of Settlement 1701 recognised this principle by barring naturalised subjects from holding prerogative powers. That bar was removed by the British Nationality Act 1948 without serious consideration of the consequences. It should be restored.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Citizenship Act 2029 will establish:

- a) Restriction of the franchise to British Citizens. Only Indigenous British Citizens and Hereditary British Citizens may vote in parliamentary elections, local elections, and referendums. This ends the ability of foreign Commonwealth citizens and Irish citizens to vote in British national elections. The Act amends Schedule 1 of the Representation of the People Act 1983 accordingly.
- b) Restriction of postal voting. The postal vote will be restricted to serving members of the Armed Forces and their immediate families, and to those certified by a medical practitioner as physically unable to attend a polling station. All other electors must vote in person with photographic identification. This removes the primary mechanism for postal vote fraud. The Act will require the Electoral Commission to publish constituency-level data on postal vote rejection rates and to investigate constituencies where rejection rates or postal vote shares exceed defined thresholds.
- c) Public office restricted to British Citizens. Only Indigenous and Hereditary British Citizens may: hold elected office (Parliament, local government), sit in the House of Lords, serve on the Privy Council, hold senior judicial appointments (High Court and above), and hold positions in security, defence, and intelligence services. The Act codifies in modern statutory language the principle of the Act of Settlement 1701 that the highest offices of the state are reserved for those whose allegiance to the nation is by blood and heritage, not merely by legal acquisition.
- d) Measures against ethnic bloc voting. The Act will impose a statutory duty on the Electoral Commission to monitor, report on, and investigate evidence of ethnic bloc voting, including: anomalous registration patterns in specific wards, disproportionate postal vote applications, turnout patterns inconsistent with demographic profiles, and evidence of community-level voter mobilisation by non-political entities (religious institutions, community councils, clan structures). Where the Commission identifies evidence of organised bloc voting, it may recommend boundary changes, enhanced in-person voting requirements, or criminal investigation.

OPERATIONAL

Electoral roll cleansing. Within 12 months of Royal Assent, the Electoral Commission will cross-reference the electoral register with the Citizenship Register to identify and remove ineligible voters. Notices will be sent to those removed, explaining the change and their right to apply for British Subject status if eligible.

Postal vote transition. New postal vote rules take effect from the first general or local election occurring more than 12 months after Royal Assent, providing adequate notice for affected voters to arrange in-person attendance.

##### PP1.1.5: Supporting Constitutional Reforms

The Problem

The citizenship framework described above cannot operate within the current constitutional architecture. Three obstacles must be addressed:

First, the Equality Act 2010. The Public Sector Equality Duty (Section 149) requires public bodies to “advance equality of opportunity” and “foster good relations” between groups defined by protected characteristics. This has been weaponised into a mandate for ethnic preference policies and diversity bureaucracy. The distinction between Indigenous and naturalised citizens – the cornerstone of the Citizenship Act – would be immediately challenged as indirect discrimination on grounds of race. The positive action provisions (Sections 158–159) permit discrimination in favour of “under-represented” groups, creating a system where the indigenous majority can be lawfully disadvantaged.

Second, the Human Rights Act 1998. The HRA’s incorporation of ECHR Articles 8 (private and family life) and 14 (non-discrimination) into domestic law provides a ready-made vehicle for judicial challenge to any citizenship framework that distinguishes between categories of citizen. The Section 3 interpretive obligation would require courts to “read down” the Citizenship Act to achieve ECHR compatibility, potentially gutting its provisions. The Section 6 obligation on public authorities to act compatibly with Convention rights would prevent the Home Office from enforcing citizenship distinctions in practice.

Third, judicial activism. The Supreme Court’s expanding role in reviewing executive decisions – most recently in the Rwanda judgment – has created a de facto judicial veto over immigration and citizenship policy. Without ouster clauses, the Citizenship Act would be litigated into irrelevance within months of Royal Assent.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Citizenship Act 2029 will include, or will be accompanied by concurrent provisions in the Immigration Sovereignty and Human Rights Reform Act (see PP1.3), the following supporting measures:

- a) Equality Act 2010 reform. The Act will:
- Retain individual protections (Parts 3–7): Direct discrimination against individuals in employment, services, and housing remains prohibited. No person should be refused a job or service because of their race, sex, or religion.
- Abolish the Public Sector Equality Duty (Section 149): The requirement for public bodies to “advance equality of opportunity” between protected groups is repealed entirely.
- Replace with a Public Sector Citizen Duty: Public bodies must assess the impact of policies on British citizens and prioritise citizen welfare in service delivery and resource allocation.
- Abolish positive action provisions (Sections 158–159): Hiring and promotion must be on merit alone. “Tie-breaker” provisions permitting discrimination in favour of under-represented groups are repealed.
- Narrow indirect discrimination in immigration and citizenship contexts: The concept of “disproportionate impact” will not apply to immigration or citizenship policy. Parliament, not courts applying disparate impact analysis, determines citizenship policy.
- Repudiate the Macpherson framework: The 1999 Macpherson Report’s definition of “institutional racism” (any organisation whose policies result in unequal outcomes regardless of intent) will be explicitly rejected in statute. Racism requires intent or direct discrimination, not statistical disparity.
- b) HRA targeted disapplication. The Immigration Sovereignty and Human Rights Reform Act (PP1.3) will disapply Sections 3, 6, and 7 of the HRA in the context of immigration, citizenship, and nationality decisions. This is detailed fully in PP1.3 but its effect on the Citizenship Act is critical: courts will not be able to “read down” the five-tier framework to achieve ECHR compatibility, and public authorities will not be obliged to act compatibly with Convention rights when administering the Citizenship Register or enforcing citizenship distinctions.
- c) Ouster clauses. The Citizenship Act will include ouster clauses excluding judicial review of citizenship status determinations except on narrow procedural grounds (fraud or clear jurisdictional error). Courts may not substitute their policy judgment for Parliament’s on questions of who may be admitted to the nation and on what terms. This is consistent with and protected by the broader JR restrictions in CS2 (Executive Decisions Act).
- d) Parliamentary sovereignty. The Act will include a statutory declaration that the Citizenship Act represents the settled will of Parliament on questions of citizenship, nationality, and the relationship between the British state and the British people; that no court, domestic or international, may set aside or disapply its provisions on the basis of incompatibility with the ECHR, customary international law, or any other international obligation not expressly incorporated by Parliament; and that the ordinary meaning of the text as enacted by Parliament shall prevail in all cases.

OPERATIONAL

Civil Service Code reform. The reformed Civil Service Management Code (CS6) will require that officials’ primary commitment is to British law as enacted by Parliament, not to international law, supranational obligations, or EDI ideology. Officials implementing the Citizenship Act are protected from professional sanction for carrying out lawful ministerial decisions, consistent with the professional regulatory immunity provisions in CS2.

Equality Act transition. A 12-month transition period allows public bodies to restructure their equality functions from the current group-based framework to the new Citizen Duty framework. The Equality and Human Rights Commission’s mandate will be amended to reflect the new statutory architecture.

Summary of Legislative Requirements

The PP1.1 framework is built on the Citizenship Act 2029, a single piece of primary legislation introduced in the first King’s Speech alongside the Immigration Sovereignty and Human Rights Reform Act (PP1.3), the Immigration Reform Act (PP1.2), and the supporting provisions of CS2 (Executive Decisions Act). The Equality Act reforms may be enacted as a schedule to the Citizenship Act or as a standalone Equality Act 2010 (Amendment) Act, depending on parliamentary timetabling.

Citizenship Act 2029 (provisions)

On the face of the Act:

Establishment of the five-tier citizenship framework (Indigenous British Citizen, Hereditary British Citizen, Inherited Conditional British Citizen, British Subject, Guest). Codification of jus sanguinis as the basis for British citizenship. Birth status determination tables mapping parental status to child’s citizenship tier. End of automatic jus soli for children of non-citizens. Restoration of the Indigenous/naturalised distinction. Three-generation pathway from British Subject to Indigenous British Citizen via ICBC status. Citizenship Test and British Subject Test as statutory requirements for specified tiers. Swiss-model local authority involvement in Subject status determinations. 10-year residence requirement for Subject status. 10-year re-registration requirement for ICBC and British Subject holders. Revocability provisions for conditional statuses (criminality, absence, fraud, welfare dependency). Statelessness provisions compliant with the 1961 Convention.

Establishment of the Citizenship Register as authoritative central database. Establishment of the Fit and Proper Persons Register for non-citizens. Mandatory status determination for all residents by Year 5. Integration with UKVI, Employer Checking Service, NHS Spine, DWP, DVLA, and electoral register systems.

Restriction of the parliamentary and local government franchise to Indigenous and Hereditary British Citizens. Restriction of postal voting to Armed Forces personnel and medically certified voters. Reservation of public office, House of Lords, Privy Council, senior judiciary, and security/defence/intelligence roles to British Citizens. Electoral Commission duties regarding bloc voting.

Abolition of the Public Sector Equality Duty (Section 149, Equality Act 2010). Replacement with Public Sector Citizen Duty. Abolition of positive action provisions (Sections 158–159). Narrowing of indirect discrimination doctrine in immigration/citizenship contexts. Statutory repudiation of the Macpherson “institutional racism” framework.

Ouster clauses excluding judicial review except on narrow procedural grounds. Parliamentary sovereignty declaration.

Repeal and replacement of relevant provisions of the British Nationality Act 1981 (Sections 1, 2, 6, 40 and associated schedules). Amendment of the Representation of the People Act 1983 (Schedule 1). Amendment of the Act of Settlement 1701.

Delivered operationally:

Presumption process for existing residents (pre-1983, 1983–2029, unproven parentage). Documentation support via GRO, witness statements, circumstantial evidence, DNA testing. Special provisions for vulnerable and elderly populations. Public information campaign (Years 3–5). Phased reclassification through existing administrative touchpoints (passport renewal, benefit claims, electoral registration, right-to-work checks, GP registration, school enrolment, driving licence renewal, council tax, pension claims). Local authority Citizenship Officers designated. Test development commissioned within 12 months. Local authority training and capacity building for Swiss-model assessment role. Electoral roll cleansing within 12 months. Postal vote transition. Equality Act transition (12 months). Civil Service Code amendment.

Timeline

#### PP1.2: The Immigration Reset

Governing Principle

Britain’s immigration system is broken by design. Over 25 distinct visa categories, each with different rules, fees, and pathways, create a labyrinth that confuses applicants, enables gaming, and imposes administrative costs on businesses, migrants, and the state. The system’s complexity is not accidental; it is the product of decades of incremental expansion by governments that lacked the political will to set clear limits and enforce them. Every loophole exists because a minister found it easier to create a new route than to close an existing one. Every abuse exists because the system was designed to process volume, not to protect the national interest.

The numbers are damning. In the year ending June 2025, approximately 1.2 million non-citizen visas were granted. Net migration reached 728,000 in 2024 – the highest figure ever recorded. Student visas alone accounted for over 430,000 grants, with 10% of holders transitioning to asylum claims and 20% dropout rates at suspect institutions. The Health and Care Worker visa, introduced to address genuine shortages, generated 389,600 dependants by 2024 while 39,000 sponsors lost licences due to abuse. The family route drives perpetual chain migration, particularly from South Asian communities where transnational marriage practices create self-sustaining inflows. Foreign nationals received £10.1 billion – 26% – of Universal Credit disbursements in 2024. The visa system has become an immigration industry, generating billions in fees for educational institutions, recruitment agencies, and immigration lawyers while socialising the costs onto British taxpayers.

The fundamental failure is incentive misalignment. Employers who import cheap labour do not bear its lifetime fiscal cost – estimated at £150,000–£465,000 per low-skilled migrant by the OBR and Migration Advisory Committee. Universities that recruit international students do not bear the cost of those who overstay, claim asylum, or enter the informal economy. Sponsors who bring in workers are not liable when those workers become public charges. The British taxpayer subsidises every stage of the process: the NHS treatment (via the inadequate Immigration Health Surcharge), the education of dependants, the housing pressure, the benefit claims, and ultimately the enforcement costs of removing those who should never have been admitted. This is not immigration policy. It is a subsidy to capital at the expense of labour, mediated by a bureaucracy too complex to be held accountable.

Progress will replace this system with one built on three principles. First, simplicity: 25+ visa categories reduced to 7, each with a clear purpose and no settlement pathway except through the citizenship framework established in PP1.1. Second, true cost internalisation: the Visa Insurance system will require sponsors to purchase commercial insurance covering the projected lifetime fiscal risks of every migrant they bring in, transferring the cost from taxpayers to those who benefit from imported labour. Third, democratic control: hard caps on every category, enforced by statute, with Parliament – not the Migration Advisory Committee, not the courts, not the employers’ lobby – determining how many people enter Britain each year.

The target is non-citizen immigration of approximately 110,000 per year – down from 1.2 million. This comprises: 50,000 students at elite institutions, 30,000 genuinely high-skilled workers earning £60,000+, 20,000 citizen spouses, 5,000 exceptional talent and investors, and 5,000 diplomatic and governmental. Combined with emigration targets (detailed in PP1.3 and PP1.4), this produces net migration of negative 350,000–450,000 annually, reducing the non-citizen population by 3.5–4.5 million over a decade and returning Britain to a population of 63–65 million by 2034.

This policy interacts with:

- PP1.1 (The Citizenship Act): Defines who may belong; PP1.2 controls who may enter and on what terms
- PP1.3 (Asylum, Removal, and Sovereignty): HRA amendments enabling enforcement; deportation and removal mechanisms
- PP1.5 (Enforcement and Internal Control): UK E-Verify and biometric infrastructure that operationalise visa conditions
- PP1.6 (The Economic Transition): Skills training and automation that replace the labour supply currently provided by immigration
- E2 (Prosperity Zones Act): Prosperity Zone Visa for high-skilled migration tied to zone HQs
- C3 (Malebranche / Public Integrity Act): Investigation of visa fraud, fake qualifications, and sponsor abuse
- CS2 (Executive Decisions Act): JR restrictions and ouster clauses protecting immigration legislation from judicial override

##### PP1.2.1: Visa System Simplification

The Problem

The current immigration system comprises over 25 distinct visa categories (see Appendix 1 for a full catalogue): Partner Visas, Family Visas, UK Residency & ILR, Short Stay Visit Visas, Student Visas, EU Settlement Scheme, BN(O) Visa, Private Life Visa, Returning Resident Visa, Skilled Worker Visa, Innovator Founder Visa, Graduate Visa, Health and Care Worker Visa, Minister of Religion, Post-Study Work / Graduate Visa, Scale-Up Visa, Senior or Specialist Worker Visa, Expansion Worker Visa, Graduate Trainee Visa, Secondment Worker Visa, Service Supplier Visa, Temporary Worker Visa, Creative Worker Visa, Seasonal Work Visa, High Potential Individual Visa, Government Authorised Exchange Visa, International Agreement Visa, Overseas Domestic Worker Visa, Youth Mobility Scheme, Artists & Entertainers Visa, Frontier Worker Permit, Global Talent Visa, International Sportsperson Visa, Service Providers from Switzerland Visa, Turkish Businessperson Visa, Transit Visa, Standard Visitor Visa, Marriage Visitor Visa, Permitted Paid Engagement Visa, Domestic Worker in a Private Household Visa, Representative of an Overseas Business Visa, UK Ancestry Visa, Start-up Visa (legacy), Investor Visa (legacy), Global Business Mobility Routes, Humanitarian Protection, Discretionary Leave, Stateless Person Visa, Refugee Status, Dependant Visas, and the Electronic Travel Authorisation.

This complexity creates confusion for legitimate applicants, enables gaming by those who exploit the gaps between categories, and imposes enormous administrative costs on the Home Office, employers, and the immigration tribunal system. Multiple categories serve overlapping purposes, creating arbitrage opportunities. The Graduate Visa, for example, provides two years of unsponsored work with no job offer required, functioning as a de facto open work permit that undermines the salary thresholds of the Skilled Worker route. The Health and Care Worker Visa offers a discounted fee (£284 vs £719+) and reduced salary threshold (£20,960 vs £38,700), creating a subsidised pathway into sectors where domestic training has been chronically neglected. Legacy routes and transitional provisions create permanent loopholes.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Immigration Reform Act will establish:

- a) Seven simplified visa categories replacing all existing routes:

This reduces complexity from 25+ categories to 7 with clear purposes, hard caps, and no ambiguity about pathways.

- b) Abolition of routes. The following are abolished without replacement:
- Graduate Visa / Post-Study Work: Students complete their studies and return home, unless they secure genuine skilled employment meeting the £60,000 salary threshold under the Skilled Worker route
- Health and Care Worker Visa: No special discount or reduced threshold; healthcare workers compete under the standard Skilled Worker route at £60,000+, phased over 5 years as domestic training capacity scales (see PP1.6)
- UK Ancestry Visa: Replaced by the Heritage Return route for those who qualify as Hereditary British Citizens under PP1.1
- Youth Mobility Scheme: Abolished
- All Global Business Mobility sub-routes: Senior Specialist, Expansion Worker, Graduate Trainee, Secondment Worker, Service Supplier – collapsed into the single Skilled Worker category
- Private Life Visa (20 years): Abolished; long residence does not create entitlement to remain
- Turkish Businessperson Visa: Legacy route closed
- Investor Visa: Remains closed to new applicants
- All dependant visa routes for non-citizen-spouse categories: Student and Skilled Worker visa holders may not bring dependants. Seasonal Workers may not bring dependants.
- c) Maximum visa duration. All temporary work visas (Skilled Worker, Seasonal Worker) carry a maximum duration of 7 years across all categories. No extensions beyond this limit. This ensures “temporary” means temporary – workers rotate out, preventing de facto settlement. The only route to permanent residence is through the citizenship framework in PP1.1 (British Subject status after 10 years, requiring the British Subject Test).
- d) Sponsor liability for departure. A new statutory duty requires employers to ensure workers they bring in are returned to the country of origin upon visa expiry. Failure to comply results in: loss of sponsor licence, financial penalties proportionate to the number of overstayers, and prohibition from future sponsorship.

OPERATIONAL

Transition period. Existing visa holders retain the remainder of their current permission. No retrospective cancellation of valid visas. Visas expiring after commencement are processed under the new rules. An 18–24 month notice period applies before non-renewal takes effect for existing holders. New applications are processed under the new categories from commencement.

Sponsor notification. All current sponsors notified of new obligations, caps, and Visa Insurance requirements within 60 days of Royal Assent. Transition period of 12 months for sponsors to achieve compliance with new requirements.

##### PP1.2.2: The Visa Insurance System

The Problem

The most important structural failure of the current immigration system is that the long-term costs of immigration are borne by British taxpayers rather than by those who benefit from importing labour. An employer who recruits a care worker from Nigeria at £20,960 per year captures the economic benefit of cheap labour while the lifetime fiscal cost – healthcare, potential welfare dependency, education of dependants, housing pressure, and eventual pension claims – falls on the state. The Immigration Health Surcharge (£1,035 per year for most adults) covers a fraction of true healthcare costs and nothing else. The Immigration Skills Charge (£1,000 per year) is trivial relative to the cost of the training deficit it is supposed to address.

The OBR estimates that low-wage migrants impose lifetime net fiscal costs of £150,000 or more. The Migration Advisory Committee’s 2025 analysis found net fiscal costs of £109,000 per person for family route migrants and £300,000–£430,000 for asylum and refugee route entrants. Dutch fiscal studies show costs of €263,000 (~£225,000) per “non-Western” family migrant and €433,000 (~£370,000) per “non-Western” asylum migrant. These costs are systematically hidden from the public and unaccounted for in immigration policy.

The Visa Insurance system solves this by internalising the true costs of immigration into the visa process. It is a systemic reform which aligns the incentives of the government, visa sponsors, and immigration policymakers with the interests of the British people. It will drive debates across a wide range of topics – for example, “why mandate vet-only SPS inspections when paraprofessionals would suffice?” – because every unnecessary visa becomes an insurable cost that someone must bear.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Immigration Reform Act will insert a new Section 3E into the Immigration Act 1971, modelled on the structure of Section 70A (Immigration Skills Charge) inserted by the Immigration Act 2016:

3E Visa Insurance Requirement

(1) A sponsor must secure and maintain migration risk insurance from a provider approved by the Migration Risk Authority each time it assigns a certificate of sponsorship to a worker or student.

(2) The Secretary of State must by regulations specify – (a) the minimum coverage requirements for migration risk insurance policies; (b) the tiered premium structure based on actuarial risk factors including origin country, occupation, age, and salary; (c) the criteria for approval of insurance providers by the Migration Risk Authority; (d) exemptions, which may include categories of sponsored workers or students, specified occupations, or specified circumstances.

(3) Any purported assignment of a certificate of sponsorship is invalid whilst the obligation to secure migration risk insurance under subsection (1) is outstanding.

(4) The Secretary of State may by regulations provide for – (a) the transfer of insurance policies between sponsors where a sponsored worker changes employer; (b) the circumstances in which premiums may be refunded; (c) claims procedures where a sponsored migrant draws upon public services or welfare in excess of defined thresholds; (d) the establishment and functions of the Migration Risk Authority.

(5) Regulations under this section – (a) are to be made by statutory instrument; (b) may make different provision for different cases; (c) may include transitional provision; (d) may not be made unless a draft has been laid before, and approved by resolution of, each House of Parliament.

(6) For the purposes of this section – (a) “migration risk insurance” means insurance covering projected lifetime fiscal risks to public services arising from sponsored migration, including healthcare costs, potential welfare claims, and other contingencies as specified in regulations; (b) “Migration Risk Authority” means the body established under regulations to approve insurance providers and oversee the visa insurance scheme; (c) “sponsor” has the meaning given by Immigration Rules.

Consequential Amendment: Schedule 2 (Administrative Provisions as to Control on Entry) is amended to insert after paragraph 30A:

30B An immigration officer may refuse entry clearance or leave to enter where the sponsor has not complied with the requirements of section 3E (visa insurance requirement).

Core insurance mechanism. Sponsors pay regular annual premiums to Migration Risk Authority (MRA)-approved insurers during the sponsorship period. Insurers underwrite the full projected lifetime fiscal risks using actuarial models based on OBR data and historical outcomes. Premiums are calibrated to cover potential net costs of £100,000–£400,000 in lifetime public service draws for higher-risk profiles.

- Premium structure: Annual premiums depend on tiered risk factors (see below). Premiums end upon visa expiry, employment change (with policy transfer to the new sponsor), settlement, or citizenship.
- Claims handling: If a migrant exceeds defined thresholds (e.g., net annual welfare draws >£5,000), the insurer covers the cost. Risk is pooled across migrants, with reinsurance for extreme events and a sovereign backstop funded by scheme surpluses.
- Deportation liability: Insurers are liable for the full cost of removal and deportation if the insured migrant: (a) overstays their visa; (b) commits a criminal offence resulting in deportation; (c) becomes a public charge beyond insured thresholds; or (d) is otherwise subject to removal action. Estimated deportation costs of £10,000–£20,000 per person are priced into premiums. This creates a powerful incentive for insurers to accurately price high-risk applicants, monitor compliance, and cooperate with enforcement.
- Migrant contributions: Migrants contribute 1–2% of salary toward the insurance, promoting shared responsibility. This replaces and integrates the current flat-rate Immigration Health Surcharge (£1,035 annually) with a dynamic, tier-adjusted surcharge.
- Sunset provisions: Liability fully transfers to the state upon citizenship.

Tiered insurance rates based on cultural similarity and meritocratic factors. Premiums are structured in explicit tiers reflecting cultural similarity to the United Kingdom, with CANZUK countries receiving priority placement due to shared language, legal traditions, values, and historical ties. Within each tier, rates are further adjusted meritocratically using empirical data on employment retention, net fiscal contribution, and integration outcomes.

OPERATIONAL

Migration Risk Authority. Established by statutory instrument within 6 months of Royal Assent. The MRA will: approve insurers and set minimum solvency and coverage requirements, publish standardised actuarial models incorporating nationality, age, qualifications, sector, and salary, audit insurer compliance, manage the sovereign backstop fund, and publish annual reports on scheme performance.

Piloting. The Visa Insurance system will be piloted in high-impact sectors (health and social care, hospitality) during the 12-month transition period before full rollout across all visa categories.

IHS abolition. The current flat-rate Immigration Health Surcharge is abolished upon full implementation of Visa Insurance. During the transition period, both systems may operate in parallel.

##### PP1.2.3: Fee Reform and the Training Investment Test

The Problem

Current visa fees fail to reflect the true fiscal and social costs of immigration, effectively subsidising employers who import labour rather than train locally. A Skilled Worker visa costs £719–£1,500. A Health and Care Worker visa costs just £284 – a discounted rate that actively incentivises importing cheap care workers rather than investing in domestic recruitment and training. A student visa costs £490, granting access to UK education, healthcare, and – via the Graduate route – two years of unsponsored work. These fees are trivial relative to the fiscal costs they generate.

The current system also fails to ask the right question. It asks whether employers can find local workers. It does not ask whether they could train them. This creates perverse incentives: employers underinvest in training, then claim “shortages” to justify importing labour. The Migration Advisory Committee assesses “shortage” without regard to whether roles could be automated or filled through domestic training. The result is a self-reinforcing cycle: cheap imported labour depresses wages, low wages deter domestic workers, the resulting “shortage” justifies more imported labour.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Immigration Reform Act will establish:

- a) Reformed fee structure. Visa fees will be substantially increased, scaled to incentivise higher-quality migration:

These fees are in addition to Visa Insurance premiums.

- b) Training Investment Test. All Skilled Worker visa sponsorship will require:
- Training threshold: Employers must demonstrate spending of at least 2% of payroll on training, apprenticeships, or skills development in the relevant occupational category over the preceding 3 years.
- Enhanced Skills Charge: Employers who have not met the training threshold must pay an enhanced Skills Charge of £10,000 per year per sponsored worker (up from £1,000), ring-fenced for domestic skills funding.
- Shortage occupation reform: The current Migration Advisory Committee “Shortage Occupation List” will be replaced with a distinction between genuinely scarce skills (roles requiring 5+ years’ specialist experience that cannot feasibly be trained domestically within 3 years, such as specialist surgeons or nuclear engineers) and trainable occupations (all other roles, subject to the full Training Investment Test).

This flips the incentive structure: instead of “we can’t find workers, give us visas,” employers must demonstrate “we’ve invested in training but still have genuine gaps.”

- c) Sponsor eligibility requirements. Only employers with a strong record of paying UK corporation tax may sponsor workers. Shell companies and tax-avoiding multinationals are excluded from the visa system. This prevents entities with no genuine commitment to the UK economy from accessing imported labour.
- d) Student visa reforms. The reduction from ~430,000 to 50,000 student visas will be allocated via Certificates of Sponsorship to each licensed institution based on quality metrics, with a reserved portion for STEM programmes and strategically important subjects. Eligibility requirements:
- B2 minimum English language proficiency
- Place at an institution meeting strict quality thresholds (primarily Russell Group; quality institutions outside the Russell Group allocated places based on educational merit)
- No work rights during study
- No dependants permitted
- No transition to the Graduate route (abolished)
- Transition to Skilled Worker route permitted only if employment secured at £60,000+ salary threshold

Institutions that cannot survive on domestic students and genuine international demand should close – they are not providing education but immigration services.

OPERATIONAL

Fee implementation. New fees take effect for all applications submitted after the commencement date. No retrospective application to existing visa holders.

Training Investment Test rollout. Employers given 12 months’ notice of the Training Investment Test requirement. The Migration Advisory Committee will publish guidance on qualifying training expenditure within 6 months of Royal Assent. HMRC will verify training expenditure claims through existing employer reporting mechanisms.

Student visa cap allocation. The Home Office will publish the institutional allocation methodology within 6 months. Institutions given 3 years to phase down international recruitment to cap levels, allowing orderly adjustment. The higher education transition is addressed in the Policy Interactions section (see PP1.2.6).

##### PP1.2.4: Family Route Reform

The Problem

The family visa route has become a significant driver of chain migration, particularly from South Asian communities where transnational marriage practices create perpetual inflows. Data from 2007–2024 shows births to foreign-born mothers rising from 25% to 34% in England and Wales, with non-UK-born women accounting for over half of births in London (56% in 2023). Sponsored relatives gain settlement, form families, sponsor further kin, and the cycle repeats. In 2025, 20,876 family reunion visas were granted, with 61,000 further grants under the broader family route – 17% of total immigration.

Cousin marriage compounds the problem. Consanguineous marriages produce significantly elevated rates of genetic disorders: British Pakistani communities account for approximately 3% of births but 30% of genetic birth defects in some NHS trusts. Transnational cousin marriages are also a primary mechanism for perpetual family route migration, often arranged without genuine consent.

The minimum sponsor income of £18,600 (set in 2012 and only recently increased to £38,700) was never adequate to ensure that family migrants would be self-sufficient. Chain migration – where initial migrants sponsor relatives, who sponsor further relatives – has no natural terminus under the current system.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Immigration Reform Act will establish:

- a) Cousin marriage ban. Marriage between first or second cousins will be prohibited in the United Kingdom. Cousin marriages conducted abroad will not be recognised for any legal purpose, including immigration, welfare, or inheritance. This addresses both public health (genetic disorders) and chain migration (transnational cousin marriages as a perpetual inflow mechanism). The prohibition applies to all marriages solemnised after commencement; existing marriages are not retrospectively invalidated but may not be used as the basis for immigration applications.
- b) Spousal visa restrictions. The Citizen Spouse visa will be available only to spouses of Indigenous or Hereditary British Citizens (not ICBC or British Subjects). Requirements:
- Genuine relationship: minimum 2 years prior to application, with evidence of cohabitation or regular contact
- English language proficiency: B1 minimum
- Financial independence: sponsor income £38,700+ or equivalent assets
- No immigration history involving deception, overstay, or illegal entry
- Annual cap: 20,000
- c) End of chain migration. Family visas are limited to spouse and minor children only. No automatic entitlement for parents, adult children, siblings, or extended family. Elderly dependent relative visas are abolished.
- d) Forced marriage enforcement. Strengthened enforcement of the Forced Marriage (Civil Protection) Act 2007 and Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014. The Act will require mandatory training for schools, GPs, and social workers on identifying forced marriage risk. Departure from the UK for suspected forced marriage abroad will trigger automatic passport cancellation. Cross-reference: C6 (Legal Equality Act) provides the broader enforcement framework for forced marriage, FGM, and honour-based abuse.

OPERATIONAL

Cousin marriage prohibition enforcement. The General Register Office will be directed to refuse registration of cousin marriages. Registrars will be required to verify the relationship between parties. For marriages conducted abroad, the Home Office will not recognise cousin marriages for any immigration purpose from the commencement date.

Income verification. HMRC real-time data will be used to verify sponsor income for Citizen Spouse applications, replacing self-declared income evidence.

##### PP1.2.5: Access to Public Services and Welfare

The Problem

In 2024, foreign nationals received one in every six pounds paid out from Universal Credit, at a cost of over £10 billion. The current system nominally restricts most visa holders from accessing public funds through the “No Recourse to Public Funds” (NRPF) condition, but this is widely circumvented: through fraudulent claims using false identities, through transition to asylum claims that trigger welfare access, through achieving ILR after five years (which unlocks full welfare access), and through the EU Settlement Scheme which grants welfare access to approximately 2.7 million settled status holders.

The fundamental principle is straightforward: British citizenship should be the threshold for full access to the welfare state. Those who have not earned citizenship should not draw from the common purse. The current system, where five years’ residence unlocks the same welfare rights as citizens whose families have contributed for generations, is unjust to British taxpayers and creates a powerful pull factor for low-skilled migration.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Immigration Reform Act will establish a statutory tiered access system:

- a) Citizenship as welfare threshold. Only British Citizens (Indigenous, Hereditary, or ICBC after a 5-year qualifying period) have access to non-contributory benefits. British Subjects may access contributory benefits (e.g., State Pension) based on their National Insurance record, but not means-tested benefits.
- b) Immigration Health Surcharge replaced by Visa Insurance. The current fixed IHS (£1,035/year) is abolished and replaced by mandatory Visa Insurance (PP1.2.2), priced by commercial insurers based on individual risk factors. Medical costs are fully covered by sponsor-provided Visa Insurance, eliminating the risk of uninsured migrants being denied care or the state absorbing emergency bills.
- c) Education surcharge for dependants. Visa holders bringing school-age dependants must pay an Education Surcharge of £8,000 per child per year, reflecting the approximate cost of state education. Paid upfront annually as a condition of visa grant/renewal. Non-refundable. Required in addition to Visa Insurance. Note: under the simplified visa system (PP1.2.1), only Citizen Spouse visa holders may bring dependants; this surcharge applies to that category.
- d) School attendance as visa condition. For visa holders with dependants, school attendance is a condition of the visa. Verified via Department for Education school census data. Persistent non-attendance (truancy) constitutes a visa breach and may result in: warning and remedial action requirement, visa curtailment if not remedied, or deportation of the family unit.
- e) Student loans restricted to citizens. Only British Citizens (Indigenous, Hereditary, or ICBC) are eligible for student loans. This prevents foreign nationals from accessing subsidised higher education and leaving without repaying.
- f) Legal aid excluded for immigration proceedings. Visa holders will not be eligible for legal aid in immigration proceedings. Those wishing to challenge immigration decisions must fund their own representation or rely on pro bono assistance.
- g) Social housing exclusion. Non-citizens are ineligible for social housing tenancies, including council housing, housing association properties, and any accommodation allocated via local authority housing registers. Local authorities are required to verify citizenship status before allocating social housing. Housing benefit claims from non-citizens are automatically rejected.

OPERATIONAL

DWP system integration. Within 12 months of Royal Assent, DWP systems will be integrated with the Citizenship Register (PP1.1.2) to automatically verify status for all benefit claims. Claims from individuals whose status does not qualify for the relevant benefit will be automatically rejected.

NHS entitlement verification. NHS Trusts will be required to verify patient status via the Citizenship Register before providing non-emergency treatment. Visa Insurance details will be checked at the point of registration. Emergency treatment remains available to all, with costs recovered from insurers or, for uninsured unlawful migrants, treated as enforcement costs.

##### PP1.2.6: Policy Interactions

Reducing Pull Factors via Foreign Policy

The Immigration Reform Act operates alongside foreign policy measures to reduce migration pressure at source:

Bilateral return agreements. Effective deportation requires cooperation from origin countries. Progress will negotiate agreements with major source countries (Albania, Pakistan, India, Nigeria, Vietnam) for acceptance of returnees. Visa allocations will be linked to cooperation on returns – countries refusing to accept deportees face reduced or suspended visa issuance. Aid and trade leverage will be used to secure cooperation.

Foreign aid reorientation. Foreign aid will serve British interests, including reducing migration pressure: funding refugee camps and processing in regions of origin to keep displacement local, supporting economic development that reduces emigration push factors, and conditioning aid on cooperation with returns and border control.

Diplomatic consequences. Countries that facilitate illegal migration or refuse cooperation will face visa restrictions for officials and elites, reduced diplomatic engagement, and trade and investment implications.

Higher Education Transition

The reduction from ~430,000 to 50,000 student visas will require adjustment in the higher education sector:

- Impact concentration: The reduction primarily affects “visa mill” institutions dependent on international students as an immigration business. A record 51% of international students already attend Russell Group universities; these 24 institutions would receive the majority of the 50,000 cap allocation.
- Non-Russell Group dependency: Since 2013, visas for students at lower-ranked universities have more than doubled, yet only one non-Russell Group institution ranks in the global top 100. Twenty-two institutions (collectively sponsoring ~49,000 students) would already fail proposed compliance thresholds.
- Quality institutions unaffected: Genuine polytechnic-style institutions and quality universities outside the Russell Group (Warwick, St Andrews, Bath, etc.) retain access within the cap based on educational merit.
- Transition period: 3-year phase-down to allow institutions to adjust. Institutions that cannot survive without visa mill income should use this period to wind down responsibly.
- No bailouts: The taxpayer will not subsidise universities built on unsustainable immigration arbitrage.

Detailed higher education funding reform is addressed in the Education policy paper.

Nationality-Based Entry Policy

UK Home Office data and Danish government statistics reveal significant variation in offending rates by nationality. The Citizenship Register and crime statistics infrastructure (PP1.1.2) will enable evidence-based entry policy:

This evidence-based approach replaces arbitrary country categorisations with defensible, data-driven criteria updated as statistics evolve. It is supported by the establishment of accurate crime statistics by nationality and visa status (PP1.1.2) and Malebranche investigative capacity (C3).

Fiscal Impact

Costs: Enhanced enforcement (additional Border Force, Immigration Enforcement, detention capacity). Skills transition investment (PP1.6). Voluntary repatriation payments (PP1.4).

Savings: Reduced welfare expenditure (foreign nationals currently receive £10.1bn of Universal Credit). Reduced public service pressure (each low-skilled migrant costs £150,000–£430,000 in lifetime fiscal terms). Reduced housing benefit (non-citizens excluded from social housing). NHS savings (Visa Insurance transfers healthcare costs to sponsors/insurers). Visa Insurance premium revenue.

Net fiscal impact: The lifetime fiscal cost of a low-skilled migrant (£150,000–£430,000) vastly exceeds the cost of any transitional measures. Every prevented arrival or facilitated departure is fiscally positive.

Summary of Legislative Requirements

The PP1.2 framework is built on the Immigration Reform Act, introduced in the first King’s Speech alongside the Citizenship Act 2029 (PP1.1) and the Immigration Sovereignty and Human Rights Reform Act (PP1.3). The Visa Insurance provisions amend the Immigration Act 1971.

Immigration Reform Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act:

Replacement of 25+ visa categories with 7 simplified categories (Heritage Return, Citizen Spouse, Student, Skilled Worker, Seasonal Worker, Exceptional Talent, Diplomatic). Hard statutory caps on each category. Abolition of the Graduate Visa, Health and Care Worker Visa (as separate route), UK Ancestry Visa, Youth Mobility Scheme, all Global Business Mobility sub-routes, Private Life Visa, Turkish Businessperson Visa, and all dependant visa routes except Citizen Spouse. Maximum 7-year duration for all temporary work visas. Sponsor statutory duty to ensure worker departure upon visa expiry. Sponsor liability for overstayers.

Visa Insurance system: insertion of Section 3E into the Immigration Act 1971. Establishment of the Migration Risk Authority. Tiered premium structure based on cultural similarity and meritocratic factors. Deportation liability for insurers. Migrant salary contribution (1–2%). Abolition and replacement of the Immigration Health Surcharge.

Reformed fee structure (£500–£5,000 depending on category). Training Investment Test (2% payroll threshold; £10,000 enhanced Skills Charge). Replacement of the Shortage Occupation List with genuinely scarce skills / trainable occupations distinction. Sponsor eligibility restricted to UK corporation tax payers.

Prohibition of first and second cousin marriage. Non-recognition of foreign cousin marriages for legal purposes. Citizen Spouse visa restrictions (Indigenous/Hereditary sponsors only; 2-year relationship; B1 English; £38,700 income; 20,000 cap). End of chain migration (spouse and minor children only). Strengthened forced marriage enforcement.

Statutory tiered access to public services and welfare. Citizenship as welfare threshold. Education Surcharge (£8,000/child/year). School attendance as visa condition. Student loans restricted to citizens. Legal aid excluded for immigration proceedings. Social housing exclusion for non-citizens.

Nationality-based entry policy (moratorium, enhanced vetting, standard processing tiers). Student visa cap allocation to institutions based on quality metrics. Higher education 3-year transition period.

Delivered operationally:

Transition period for existing visa holders (18–24 months’ notice). Sponsor notification within 60 days. Migration Risk Authority established within 6 months. Visa Insurance pilot in high-impact sectors during 12-month transition. IHS abolished upon full Visa Insurance implementation. Fee implementation from commencement date. Training Investment Test with 12 months’ employer notice. MAC guidance on qualifying training expenditure within 6 months. Student visa institutional allocation methodology published within 6 months; 3-year phase-down. Cousin marriage prohibition: GRO direction and registrar guidance. HMRC income verification for Citizen Spouse applications. DWP system integration with Citizenship Register within 12 months. NHS entitlement verification via Citizenship Register. Bilateral return agreement negotiations. Foreign aid reorientation.

Timeline

#### PP1.3: Asylum, Removal, and the Restoration of Sovereignty

Governing Principle

Pop-Pol cannot function if the state lacks the power to remove people who have no right to be here. Every cap, every threshold, every visa reform in PP1.2 is meaningless if failed asylum seekers cannot be deported, if foreign national offenders cannot be expelled, and if visa overstayers can melt into the informal economy with effective impunity. The immigration system’s credibility rests entirely on enforcement – and enforcement in Britain has been systematically disabled.

The numbers tell the story. In 2022, just 3,501 people were deported from the United Kingdom. In the same year, net migration was 764,000. There are an estimated 800,000–1.2 million unlawful migrants living and working in Britain. The failed asylum backlog stands at approximately 92,000 cases. There are 10,772 foreign national offenders in British prisons – 12.3% of the total prison population – with 25% of deportation cases delayed by ECHR appeals under Articles 3 and 8. The asylum system has become a de facto immigration route: 44,797 people arrived via irregular routes in 2023, of whom 90% claimed asylum. The 76% grant rate for small boat arrivals reflects not the merits of individual cases but the impossibility of returning people to countries where courts have determined a “real risk” of Article 3 treatment – a category that has expanded to encompass much of the developing world.

The obstacle is not administrative capacity. It is legal architecture. The Human Rights Act 1998, by incorporating the ECHR into domestic law, has enabled UK courts to apply expansive interpretations of Articles 3 (prohibition of torture or inhuman treatment) and 8 (right to private and family life) that routinely frustrate executive enforcement of border controls and removals. Critically, this is driven primarily by domestic courts rather than by Strasbourg itself – there have been only 13 adverse rulings against the UK in deportation/extradition cases since 1980, compared to the thousands of Article 3 and Article 8 invocations in domestic tribunals. The HRA’s Section 3 interpretive obligation forces courts to “read down” immigration statutes to achieve Convention compatibility. Section 6 renders it unlawful for the Home Office to act incompatibly with Convention rights. Section 7 provides standing for speculative claims and enables interim relief that suspends removals pending determination. The result is a judicial veto over immigration policy that Parliament never intended and the electorate has never endorsed.

Though comprehensive repeal of the HRA and withdrawal from the ECHR may be desirable long-term aims, they would entail potentially debilitating legislative complexity – likely requiring renegotiation of the Trade and Cooperation Agreement, the Windsor Framework, and the Northern Ireland Protocol, work that could saturate one or more parliamentary terms while leaving immigration uncontrolled. A faster and more efficacious approach lies in targeted statutory amendments that disapply key HRA mechanisms specifically in the context of migration, asserting parliamentary sovereignty through primary legislation impervious to judicial override. These measures achieve the substantive benefits sought from broader ECHR disengagement while minimising diplomatic and constitutional disruption.

Alongside the legal reforms, Pop-Pol requires operational mechanisms for managed departure: voluntary repatriation incentives for those who choose to leave with dignity and financial support, and accelerated removal for those who do not. The target is emigration of 500,000–650,000 per year, comprising visa non-renewals (300,000–400,000), voluntary repatriation (50,000–100,000), deportations (50,000–100,000), and natural emigration (100,000). Combined with non-citizen immigration of ~110,000 (PP1.2), this produces the net negative migration of 350,000–450,000 annually that Pop-Pol requires.

This policy interacts with:

- PP1.1 (The Citizenship Act): Defines the status framework; PP1.3 enforces it through removal of those with no right to remain
- PP1.2 (The Immigration Reset): Controls inflows; PP1.3 manages outflows and prevents stock accumulation
- PP1.5 (Enforcement and Internal Control): Biometric borders, UK E-Verify, and local authority powers that identify those subject to removal
- PP1.6 (The Economic Transition): Labour market transition that absorbs the economic impact of reduced immigration
- CS2 (Executive Decisions Act): Broader JR restrictions, statutory codification of JR grounds, and ouster clauses that complement the immigration-specific HRA amendments
- C3 (Malebranche / Public Integrity Act): Investigation of organised immigration crime, visa fraud, and smuggling networks

##### PP1.3.1: Restoring Parliamentary Sovereignty – Amendments to the Human Rights Act 1998

The Problem

The Human Rights Act 1998 has facilitated extensive judicial intervention in immigration and asylum decisions through three mechanisms:

Section 3 (interpretive obligation) requires that all legislation be read and given effect “so far as it is possible to do so” in a manner compatible with Convention rights. In immigration cases, this has permitted courts to adopt strained interpretations that prioritise ECHR obligations over explicit statutory intent. When Parliament legislates that a particular category of person should be removed, Section 3 enables courts to “read in” exceptions, qualifications, and procedural requirements that Parliament did not enact and did not intend.

Section 6 (acts of public authorities) renders it unlawful for any public authority – including the Home Office, Border Force, and immigration tribunals – to act in a way incompatible with Convention rights. This subjects every routine administrative decision to systemic ECHR scrutiny. A decision to refuse an asylum claim, to deport a foreign national offender, or to remove a visa overstayer must satisfy Convention compatibility at every stage. The effect is that officials making operational decisions must second-guess whether a court might subsequently find their action incompatible with an expansively interpreted Convention right.

Section 7 (proceedings) permits persons claiming to be victims of unlawful acts under Section 6 to bring proceedings and seek remedies, including damages and injunctive relief. In practice, this enables last-minute claims – often based on generalised country conditions rather than individualised risk – that suspend removal while the claim is determined. The combination of generous standing rules, no time limits calibrated to immigration enforcement, and the availability of interim relief creates a system in which removal can be indefinitely delayed through sequential legal challenges.

The interaction of these three sections with ECHR Articles 3 and 8 is particularly destructive. Article 3’s absolute prohibition on return to torture has been expanded by domestic courts far beyond its original scope – the Chahal and Saadi principles mean that even terrorists and serious criminals cannot be removed where there is a “real risk” of Article 3 treatment, regardless of the danger they pose to the UK. Article 8 has been weaponised to prevent the removal of individuals who have formed “private and family life” in the UK, even where that life was established unlawfully or during a period of temporary permission.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The proposed reforms will be consolidated within an Immigration Sovereignty and Human Rights Reform Act, introduced as priority legislation in the first parliamentary session. Each amendment preserves core civil liberties in non-migration domains while eliminating procedural avenues that currently enable protracted appeals and injunctions.

- a) Amendment to Section 3: Limitation on compatible interpretation in migration legislation.

Insert new subsection (3A):

“This section shall not apply to any provision of primary or subordinate legislation relating to immigration, asylum, deportation, removal, or nationality. In respect of such provisions, the ordinary meaning of the text as enacted by Parliament shall prevail, and no obligation arises to interpret the provision so as to achieve compatibility with Convention rights where this would conflict with the express or implied intention of Parliament.”

Effect: This prevents courts from “reading in” expansive ECHR protections that have historically impeded removals. Parliamentary intent in border enforcement legislation remains paramount. The disapplication is confined to immigration and nationality contexts; Section 3 continues to operate normally in all other areas of law.

- b) Qualified disapplication of Section 6: Acts of public authorities in migration decisions.

Substitute Section 6(1) with new provision (1A):

“A public authority shall not be obliged under this Act to act compatibly with Convention rights when exercising functions under legislation concerning immigration control, asylum determination, deportation, or nationality, except in respect of protections against arbitrary deprivation of life or liberty equivalent to Articles 2 (Right to Life) and 5 (Right to Liberty and Security) of the Convention in their original scope. In all other respects, such functions shall be exercised in accordance with the relevant statutory framework and Immigration Rules without regard to Convention compatibility.”

Effect: This eliminates the primary mechanism by which domestic courts impose ECHR-derived barriers to removal, particularly under Articles 3 and 8. By preserving only the most fundamental protections (right to life and liberty from arbitrary detention), it restores executive discretion in risk assessments and public interest balancing. The Home Office can make immigration decisions based on the law as Parliament enacted it, without the overlay of judicially-expanded Convention rights.

- c) Restriction of Section 7: Standing, remedies, and time limits for migration-related claims.

Amend Section 7 to include new subsections:

(1B) Proceedings under this section in respect of acts or decisions relating to immigration, asylum, deportation, or nationality may only be brought where the claimant establishes, on the balance of probabilities, a direct and substantiated personal risk distinct from general conditions in the country of proposed removal.

(1C) Any such proceedings must be instituted within 14 days of the relevant decision or act, with no power to extend time limits save in exceptional circumstances certified by the Secretary of State.

(1D) No damages shall be awarded in respect of such proceedings, and courts shall have no jurisdiction to grant interim relief suspending removal pending determination unless the threshold in subsection (1B) is prima facie satisfied.

Effect: These procedural constraints substantially reduce the volume of speculative judicial reviews and last-minute injunctions that currently delay or prevent removals. The 14-day time limit, the requirement for individualised (not generalised) risk, the bar on damages, and the restriction on interim relief together curtail abuse of process while maintaining access to justice for meritorious claims of grave individual peril.

- d) Supplementary measures. Concurrently with the above amendments, the Government will issue:
- Statutory guidance to the judiciary emphasising deference to executive expertise in foreign policy and country risk evaluations, and clarifying that “living instrument” expansions of Convention rights should not influence domestic migration adjudication
- A statutory instrument precluding reliance on customary international law (including non-refoulement obligations under the 1951 Refugee Convention) as grounds for challenging removal decisions absent express statutory incorporation. This reasserts the dualist principle already codified in CS2 (Executive Decisions Act): unincorporated international law is not enforceable in domestic courts.
- e) Ouster clauses. The Immigration Sovereignty Act will include ouster clauses protecting the HRA amendments from judicial challenge. Courts may not set aside or disapply the amendments on any ground, including incompatibility with the ECHR or customary international law. This is consistent with and reinforced by the broader JR restrictions in CS2.

OPERATIONAL

Judicial guidance. Within 7 days of Royal Assent, the Lord Chancellor will issue Practice Directions to the immigration tribunals and Administrative Court reflecting the new statutory framework. Immigration judges will be directed to apply the ordinary meaning of immigration legislation without the Section 3 interpretive overlay. Pre-drafted Practice Directions will be prepared during the legislative passage period so that issuance is immediate upon Royal Assent.

Home Office operational guidance. Within 14 days, the Home Office will issue updated guidance to caseworkers reflecting the removal of Section 6 constraints. Guidance will be drafted in parallel with the Bill’s passage through Parliament, ready for distribution upon Royal Assent. Risk assessments for removal decisions will be conducted under the statutory framework and Immigration Rules, not under ECHR compatibility tests. The legal advice obligation reforms in CS2 apply: government lawyers must provide constructive, implementation-focused advice rather than risk-averse counsel designed to frustrate ministerial direction.

##### PP1.3.2: Asylum Reform and Offshore Processing

The Problem

The asylum system has been repurposed as an immigration route. In 2023, 44,797 people arrived via irregular routes – predominantly Channel crossings – of whom 90% claimed asylum. The 76% grant rate for small boat arrivals reflects not the merits of individual claims but the effective impossibility of returning people once they reach UK soil. The failed asylum backlog stands at approximately 92,000 cases. Processing delays averaging 12–18 months provide a de facto right to remain, with claimants accommodated at public expense (£49.18 per week plus housing) while their cases are determined. Many abscond into the informal economy during this period. The total asylum population, including dependants, is approximately 200,000.

The 1951 Refugee Convention was designed for a world of approximately 200,000–300,000 refugees in the aftermath of the Second World War. The global refugee population now exceeds 30 million. The Convention’s core principle – non-refoulement (non-return to persecution) – has been expanded far beyond its original scope. Article 31, which protects refugees entering a state without documents, applies only to those who have come “directly” from a territory where their life or freedom was threatened. Individuals crossing the Channel from France – a safe, democratic country with a functioning asylum system – are not coming “directly” from persecution. Section 37 of the Nationality and Borders Act 2022 already addresses this, creating a rebuttable presumption against “coming directly” for those who transit through safe third countries. This provision remains in force.

The Refugee Convention’s Article 33(2) itself provides exceptions to non-refoulement: a refugee loses protection where they pose a danger to security or, having been convicted of a “particularly serious crime,” constitute a danger to the community. The Nationality and Borders Act 2022 (Section 38) defines “particularly serious crime” as any offence attracting a sentence of 12 months or more. But the absolute nature of ECHR Article 3, as interpreted by domestic courts via the HRA, overrides these Convention exceptions. Even where the Refugee Convention would permit return, the HRA prevents it.

This is why the HRA amendments in PP1.3.1 are essential precursors to asylum reform: without removing the Article 3 judicial override, no operational measure – including offshore processing – can function effectively.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Immigration Sovereignty and Human Rights Reform Act will establish:

- a) Offshore processing. All asylum claims made by persons arriving via irregular routes (Channel crossings, clandestine entry, visa overstay) will be processed offshore in British Overseas Territories pending determination and, for failed claimants, repatriation. This:
- Removes the pull factor: Arrival on the UK mainland no longer guarantees access to UK accommodation, services, or the ability to abscond during processing
- Reduces legal obstruction: British Overseas Territories, while under UK sovereignty, provide a more controlled environment with reduced scope for judicial intervention via domestic courts, reinforced by the HRA amendments in PP1.3.1
- Enables efficient processing: Concentrated facilities in a single location allow rapid determination without the dispersal, accommodation, and transport costs of mainland processing
- Facilitates removal: Failed claimants are already outside the UK mainland, simplifying logistics for return to country of origin or safe third country

Suitable locations include Ascension Island and British Indian Ocean Territory. Facilities will provide humane but basic accommodation during the processing period. This is not the Rwanda model (transfer to a third country under bilateral agreement); this is processing on British sovereign territory, under British law, avoiding the legal and diplomatic complications that plagued the Rwanda scheme.

- b) Capped humanitarian visa. Genuine refugees – a small minority given transit through multiple safe countries – will be resettled via a capped humanitarian visa route, not admitted directly to the UK from offshore processing. The cap will be set by Parliament annually, ensuring democratic control over the number of refugees resettled.
- c) Reinforcement of “first safe country” provisions. The Act will reaffirm and strengthen Section 37 of the Nationality and Borders Act 2022, making the rebuttable presumption against “coming directly” effectively irrebuttable for those who have transited through any country that is a signatory to the Refugee Convention or the ECHR.
