The burden of proof rests on the claimant to demonstrate that they could not reasonably have sought protection in any transit country.
- d) Expedited determination. Asylum claims processed offshore will be subject to a statutory 28-day determination period. Claims not determined within 28 days are deemed refused unless the Home Office certifies that exceptional complexity requires extension (maximum further 28 days). This replaces the current 12–18 month average processing time.

OPERATIONAL

Facility construction. Existing military and government infrastructure on designated British Overseas Territories will be requisitioned and adapted within 90 days of Royal Assent. The Royal Engineers and contracted modular construction firms will deploy prefabricated accommodation units (the same type used for forward operating bases, achievable in 8–12 weeks from order to habitable). Initial capacity of 5,000 places within 90 days, scaling to full 50,000-per-year throughput capacity within 6 months through modular expansion. MoD will lead the construction sprint under emergency procurement rules; FCDO will manage host territory liaison.

Transfer logistics. Border Force will establish the offshore transfer operation within 30 days of Royal Assent, using existing military transport aircraft supplemented by chartered flights. First transfers within 60 days of Royal Assent. Claimants transferred within 72 hours of arrival and initial screening.

Processing capacity. The Home Office will recruit and deploy dedicated asylum caseworkers to offshore facilities on an emergency basis. Recruitment begins during legislative passage; first cohort deployed alongside facility readiness. Target: 200 caseworkers for 50,000 annual throughput (approximately 5 determinations per caseworker per week). Surge capacity via secondment from other Home Office functions during the backlog clearance phase.

##### PP1.3.3: Accelerated Removal of Foreign National Offenders and Failed Asylum Seekers

The Problem

There are 10,772 foreign national offenders (FNOs) in British prisons as of June 2025, constituting 12.3% of the total prison population. Albanian nationals alone represent 12% of all FNOs despite Albanians comprising less than 0.1% of the UK population – a conviction rate 30 times that of British nationals. Approximately 60% of Albanian convictions relate to drug offences. Romanian and Polish nationals account for the second and third highest first prison receptions. Foreign nationals account for 26% of convictions for sexual assault.

The UK Borders Act 2007 provides for automatic deportation for sentences exceeding 12 months, yet 25% of deportation cases are delayed by ECHR appeals under Articles 3 and 8. The Early Removal Scheme (Criminal Justice Act 2003 amendments) permits removal up to 18 months before sentence completion, but uptake is limited by legal challenges and lack of destination country cooperation.

The failed asylum backlog of approximately 92,000 cases represents individuals who have been determined to have no right to remain but who have not been removed. Many have absconded. The estimated stock of 800,000–1.2 million visa overstayers represents a further population living and working unlawfully, with only 3,501 deportations achieved in 2022.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Immigration Sovereignty and Human Rights Reform Act will establish:

- a) Automatic deportation for any custodial sentence. The current threshold of 12 months under the UK Borders Act 2007 will be reduced to any custodial sentence. A foreign national who receives any prison sentence will be subject to automatic deportation proceedings. The HRA amendments in PP1.3.1 remove the Article 3 and Article 8 obstacles that currently prevent enforcement.
- b) No early release for FNOs pending deportation. FNOs will serve their full sentence and be transferred directly to removal at sentence completion. There will be no release into the community pending deportation arrangements. Where removal cannot be effected immediately (e.g., destination country delays), the FNO will be held in immigration detention.
- c) Prisoner transfer agreements. The Act will empower the Secretary of State to negotiate and conclude prisoner transfer agreements with origin countries, enabling FNOs to serve the remainder of their sentences in their country of nationality. Agreements will be prioritised with high-FNO-population countries: Albania, Romania, Poland, Ireland, Lithuania, Jamaica, Somalia, and Pakistan.
- d) Expanded denaturalisation. For dual nationals who have obtained British citizenship, the grounds for deprivation under Section 40 of the British Nationality Act 1981 will be expanded to include: serious criminality (any custodial sentence), prolonged welfare dependency without contribution, demonstrated failure of integration, and demonstrated primary loyalty to a foreign state. Deprivation appeals will be expedited via a specialist tribunal with a 28-day determination period.
- e) Failed asylum backlog clearance. The Act will create a statutory fast-track process for the 92,000-case backlog: cases not determined within 90 days of commencement are deemed refused; claimants have 14 days to submit fresh evidence; removal directions issued automatically upon refusal; the HRA amendments in PP1.3.1 prevent interim relief suspending removal.

OPERATIONAL

Deportation flights. The Home Office will establish chartered deportation flights within 14 days of Royal Assent using pre-negotiated charter contracts (prepared during legislative passage). Target: weekly flights to Albania, Nigeria, Pakistan, and India from Week 3. Flight schedules increase to twice-weekly for high-volume destinations by Month 3.

Detention capacity. Immediate requisition of surplus military estate (barracks, training facilities) under emergency powers, providing 5,000 additional detention places within 30 days. Further expansion to 10,000 places within 6 months through a combination of repurposed military/prison estate and contracted modular facilities. The current estate of approximately 2,300 places is wholly inadequate; the 30-day surge to 7,300 total places enables the initial enforcement push while permanent expansion is completed.

Overstayer enforcement. Immigration Enforcement will commence scaled-up operations against the overstayer population from Day 1, supported by the UK E-Verify system (PP1.5) which will make it impossible for overstayers to work, rent, bank, or access services. The combination of hostile environment (PP1.5) and voluntary repatriation incentives (PP1.3.4) is designed to make voluntary departure more attractive than remaining unlawfully. Intelligence-led operations targeting known overstayer concentrations will begin immediately; systematic enforcement via E-Verify follows as the system comes online (PP1.5 timeline).

##### PP1.3.4: Voluntary Repatriation

The Problem

Pop-Pol requires net emigration of 350,000–450,000 per year. Voluntary repatriation incentives alone cannot achieve these numbers – European experience demonstrates this starkly. Sweden’s scheme achieved only 4 grants from 68 applications in 2024, despite offering approximately £750 per adult (rising to £27,000 in 2026). The UK’s current £3,000 scheme achieved approximately 6,800 assisted returns in 2024. Even at 50,000 voluntary returns annually (7x current levels), this would represent only 10–15% of the required outflow.

Voluntary repatriation is therefore a useful supplement, not a primary mechanism. The heavy lifting comes from visa non-renewal (PP1.2), reduced new immigration (PP1.2), and accelerated removals (PP1.3.3). But voluntary incentives serve essential functions: they provide a humane option for those wishing to leave; they reduce enforcement costs and legal challenges; they signal government seriousness about Pop-Pol; and they establish infrastructure for larger-scale managed departures.

The fiscal case is compelling regardless. At £7,000–10,000 per adult, the scheme becomes net-positive immediately for virtually all target cohorts:

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Immigration Reform Act will establish:

- a) The Voluntary Repatriation Scheme. A statutory scheme offering financial incentives for non-citizens to leave the United Kingdom permanently:
- Base payment: £7,000 per adult – sufficient to be transformative in origin countries (representing 5–20 years’ average income in major source countries), clearly fiscally positive for the UK
- Enhanced payment: £10,000 for priority cohorts (failed asylum seekers, visa overstayers, those with removal orders)
- Child payment: £3,000 per dependent child
- Household cap: £25,000 maximum per household
- Review mechanism: Annual assessment of uptake rates; Secretary of State authorised to increase payments by up to 50% if uptake falls below targets
- b) Re-entry bans. Participants accepting voluntary return payments become subject to mandatory 10-year re-entry bans (increased from current 5-year bans). Self-funded departures without assistance attract shorter 12-month bans, incentivising take-up of the scheme over informal departure.
- c) Biometric registration. All participants undergo biometric enrolment (fingerprints, iris scan) shared with border systems and international partners to prevent re-entry under different identities.
- d) Phased payments (anti-gaming). Rather than lump-sum payments on departure:
- 40% paid on departure confirmation (travel completed, exit verified)
- 30% paid after 6-month verification of residence in origin country (via embassy/consular check or digital verification)
- 30% paid after 18-month verification
- e) No double-dipping. Individuals who previously received voluntary return assistance from UK or EU member states are ineligible. Database sharing with European partners prevents repeat claims.
- f) Destination country cooperation. Payments are contingent on receiving country confirmation of arrival and residence. Countries refusing cooperation face reduced visa allocations under the bilateral agreements framework (PP1.2.6).

OPERATIONAL

Repatriation Centres. Co-locate with existing Jobcentre Plus offices in areas with high non-citizen populations, using dedicated wings or floors. No new construction required for initial rollout. Staffed with multilingual caseworkers providing: practical assistance (travel booking, document preparation, destination country information), embassy coordination, phased payment verification, and post-departure support. Target: 20 centres operational within 30 days of Royal Assent (using existing DWP estate), scaling to 50 within 6 months as dedicated premises are secured where needed.

Government App/Website. A digital platform for: eligibility checking, application submission, payment tracking, destination country resources, and post-departure verification (geolocation opt-in for final payment tranches).

Gaming prevention. The following mitigations address known risks:

##### PP1.3.5: The Execution Plan – Composition and Sequencing of Population Reduction

The Problem

Pop-Pol targets a net non-citizen reduction of 3.5–4.5 million over a decade, returning Britain’s population from a projected ~71 million (under current trends) to 63–65 million by 2034. This requires achieving net emigration of 350,000–450,000 per year – a radical departure from current trends. The target must be achieved without mass forced deportations, humanitarian crisis, civil unrest, or international isolation. This demands careful sequencing across multiple mechanisms affecting distinct cohorts.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The statutory framework is established by the Citizenship Act 2029 (PP1.1), the Immigration Reform Act (PP1.2), and the Immigration Sovereignty and Human Rights Reform Act (this policy). No additional primary legislation is required for the execution plan itself. The plan is delivered operationally within the statutory framework.

OPERATIONAL

Composition of the annual net reduction:

Total gross non-citizen departures: ~530,000–750,000/year. Non-citizen immigration: ~110,000/year. Net non-citizen reduction: ~420,000–640,000/year.

Hereditary British Citizen returns (~200,000/year) are counted separately – these are British people coming home, not immigration.

Phased implementation:

Phase 1 – Notification and Registration (Months 1–3):

- Central Register: all non-citizens required to register with the Home Office within 90 days. Registration captures: current visa status, employment, residence, dependants, intended future plans. The registration system will be built on existing UKVI infrastructure – this is a data collection exercise, not a new IT build.
- Status Letters: issued on a rolling basis as registrations are processed. Those on time-limited visas are notified of the non-renewal policy and given 12 months’ notice (reduced from 18–24 months; visa holders have always known their visa has an expiry date – the notice period confirms non-renewal, not the existence of an end date).
- Employer Notification: sponsors notified of obligations under the Visa Insurance system within 14 days of Royal Assent, with 6-month transition period for compliance.

Phase 2 – Graduated Implementation (Months 4–36):

- Visa expirations: enforced on a rolling basis as existing visas expire. No retrospective cancellation of valid visas – holders have the remainder of their current permission, but are on notice that renewal will not be granted.
- Voluntary repatriation: incentive schemes operational from Month 1. Phased payment system ensures orderly departures.
- Removals: commence immediately upon Royal Assent. Failed asylum backlog fast-track begins Week 1. FNO deportation flights from Week 3. Overstayer enforcement scales alongside E-Verify rollout (PP1.5).

Phase 3 – Steady State (Year 3 onwards):

- Annual non-citizen visa grants at target levels (~110,000)
- Continuous enforcement of registration, right-to-work, and right-to-rent checks (PP1.5)
- Ongoing voluntary repatriation scheme for remaining eligible cohorts
- Three-generation pathway (PP1.1) operational for long-term residents

Preventing humanitarian crisis:

Pop-Pol is designed to avoid the scenarios that characterise forced mass displacement:

- No retrospective revocation of valid visas. All departures are either: (a) expiration of time-limited visas without renewal; (b) voluntary repatriation with financial support; or (c) removal of those with no legal right to remain.
- Notice periods. 12 months’ notice for non-renewal. Visa holders have always known their visa carries an expiry date – the notice confirms non-renewal, not the existence of an end date. 12 months is more than sufficient to arrange affairs and plan departure.
- Financial support. Voluntary repatriation payments (£7,000–£10,000/adult) provide meaningful resettlement assistance. Phased payments incentivise genuine departure.
- Destination country coordination. Bilateral agreements with major origin countries (India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Albania) ensure returnees are accepted and supported. Countries refusing cooperation face reduced visa allocations.
- Gradual pace. 350,000–450,000 net reduction annually is significant but manageable – equivalent to reversing 1–2 years of recent net migration per year.

Honest communication:

Government messaging will be transparent about Pop-Pol’s objectives and mechanisms. Some economic disruption during transition is inevitable and necessary. Wage rises in affected sectors are a feature, not a bug – representing a transfer from capital to labour and from taxpayers (who currently subsidise low wages via tax credits) to workers. This is consistent with Progress’ broader commitment to a high-wage, high-productivity economy. Pop-Pol is not punitive toward individuals; it is a correction of decades of policy that ignored the democratic will of the British people and imposed costs on those least able to bear them.

Summary of Legislative Requirements

The PP1.3 framework is built on the Immigration Sovereignty and Human Rights Reform Act, introduced in the first King’s Speech alongside the Citizenship Act 2029 (PP1.1) and the Immigration Reform Act (PP1.2). Voluntary repatriation provisions are enacted within the Immigration Reform Act.

Immigration Sovereignty and Human Rights Reform Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act:

Amendment to HRA Section 3: disapplication of interpretive obligation for immigration, asylum, deportation, removal, and nationality legislation. Amendment to HRA Section 6: qualified disapplication for public authority acts in migration decisions, preserving only Articles 2 and 5 protections. Amendment to HRA Section 7: 14-day time limit for migration claims; individualised risk requirement (balance of probabilities); bar on damages; restriction on interim relief. Statutory guidance mandating judicial deference to executive country risk assessments. Statutory instrument precluding reliance on customary international law as grounds for challenging removal. Ouster clauses protecting the Act from judicial challenge.

Offshore processing of irregular arrival asylum claims on British Overseas Territories. Capped humanitarian visa for genuine refugees. Reinforcement of “first safe country” provisions (effectively irrebuttable presumption). 28-day statutory determination period for offshore claims.

Automatic deportation for any custodial sentence (reduced from 12-month threshold). No early release for FNOs pending deportation. Prisoner transfer agreement powers. Expanded denaturalisation grounds for dual nationals. Failed asylum backlog fast-track (90-day determination, 14-day fresh evidence, automatic removal directions).

Immigration Reform Act – voluntary repatriation provisions:

Voluntary Repatriation Scheme (£7,000–£10,000 per adult; £3,000 per child; £25,000 household cap). 10-year re-entry bans. Biometric registration. Phased payment structure (40/30/30). No double-dipping provision. Destination country cooperation requirement.

Delivered operationally:

Judicial Practice Directions within 7 days. Home Office operational guidance within 14 days. Chartered deportation flights from Week 3. Offshore facility adaptation commenced immediately (Royal Engineers + prefab modules; initial 5,000 capacity within 90 days). First offshore transfers within 60 days. Border Force offshore transfer operation from Month 2. Asylum caseworker recruitment and deployment (200 target for 50,000 annual throughput). Immigration detention surge to 7,300 places within 30 days; 10,000 within 6 months. Repatriation Centres: 20 operational within 30 days (co-located with Jobcentres), 50 within 6 months. Digital repatriation platform live on Day 1. Non-citizen registration portal live on Day 1; 90-day registration deadline. Status letters issued on rolling basis. Employer notification within 14 days. Phased visa non-renewal enforcement. Failed asylum backlog fast-track commenced Week 1.

Timeline

#### PP1.4: The British Family

Governing Principle

Pop-Pol is not solely a migration policy. It is a population policy, and population is determined by two variables, not one. The obsessive focus of Britain’s political class on immigration numbers, however inadequate even on that front, has obscured a crisis equally existential: the British people have stopped having children.

The Total Fertility Rate collapsed to a record low of 1.44 in 2023 and is estimated to have fallen further to approximately 1.41 by 2024. The replacement rate (the level at which a population sustains itself without immigration) is 2.08. Britain has been below replacement since 1973 and the gap is widening. Natural population change (births minus deaths) is projected to turn negative by 2030. From that date, every person added to the British population will be an immigrant. The Office for National Statistics projects that, absent intervention, the indigenous British population will decline by approximately 5 million over the next 50 years, even as the total population rises through immigration. This is not a demographic transition. It is demographic replacement by a different mechanism to immigration: one driven not by border failure but by the economic, cultural, and institutional destruction of the British family.

The causes are well-documented. The average age of first-time mothers has risen from 23.7 in 1970 to 30.9 in 2023. The average age of first marriage has risen from 23 (women) and 25 (men) in 1970 to 32 and 34 respectively. The proportion of children born outside marriage has risen from 8% in 1970 to over 51% in 2023. Housing costs consume 30-40% of median household income in London and the South East. Childcare costs in the UK are the third highest in the OECD, averaging £14,000 per year for a full-time nursery place. The economic structure of modern Britain effectively requires dual incomes to maintain a household, compressing the window of fertility and making three or more children a financial impossibility for most families. Meanwhile, cultural signals uniformly discourage family formation: career prioritisation, consumption-oriented lifestyles, housing insecurity, and a pervasive institutional indifference (occasionally rising to open hostility) toward motherhood, fatherhood, and the intact family unit as a social ideal.

This is not inevitable. International evidence demonstrates that determined state action can arrest and partially reverse fertility decline. Hungary’s pro-natal programme, introduced from 2010, combined generous child subsidies, income tax exemptions for mothers of multiple children, subsidised housing loans, and cultural investment in the prestige of family life. Hungarian TFR rose from 1.23 in 2011 to approximately 1.59 by 2021, a 29% increase. Poland’s Family 500+ programme, providing 500 PLN per month per child (approximately £100), lifted TFR from 1.29 to 1.46 within three years of introduction. The Czech Republic’s three-year parental leave with partial wage replacement sustains a TFR of approximately 1.7. Israel, the only developed nation at or above replacement, maintains a TFR of 3.0 through a combination of generous child benefits, cultural reverence for family, and a national identity bound to demographic continuity. France’s long-standing politique familiale, encompassing direct transfers, subsidised childcare, and tax splitting (quotient familial), has sustained a TFR of approximately 1.8, the highest in Western Europe.

None of these programmes alone has restored replacement fertility. But the pattern is clear: generous financial support, cultural reinforcement, and structural economic reform in combination can deliver TFR increases of 0.3-0.6 points. Applied to Britain’s 1.41 baseline, a comprehensive programme modelled on the most successful elements of these international examples, combined with the broader economic reforms in Progress’ platform (E1 energy cost reduction, E2 Prosperity Zones, E6 Tax Reset), makes a target of 1.8-2.0 within ten years ambitious but credible.

Who we are incentivising matters as much as how many. Britain’s welfare system has, for decades, inadvertently concentrated family formation among households least equipped to sustain it. Generous per-child welfare entitlements, requiring neither marriage nor employment, have subsidised large families in workless or welfare-dependent households while offering nothing to the working, self-supporting families whose children are statistically most likely to become productive, tax-contributing citizens themselves. The result is a perverse inversion: the demographic segments with the highest educational attainment, the strongest employment records, and the greatest capacity to raise well-supported children are precisely those having the fewest, because for them the costs of parenthood are unsubsidised and the opportunity costs are enormous. Meanwhile, the segments with the weakest economic foundations have faced no financial disincentive to large families and, in many cases, a positive financial incentive.

Pop-Pol corrects this. The most generous instruments in this policy are structured to flow to married, self-supporting households: tax exemptions that reward earners, a Family Formation Loan conditional on marriage and employment, a Carefare Allowance built on a wage-replacement model. The progressive child allowance, the centrepiece of direct support, is conditional on marriage and household self-sufficiency. This is not punitive toward those on low incomes; it is a recognition that the state’s pro-natal investment should be directed where it will produce the strongest outcomes for children, for families, and for the nation. The welfare system provides a baseline; the pro-natal system provides transformative support to those building stable, self-sustaining family units. The two are distinct in purpose and design.

The philosophical case is inseparable from Pop-Pol’s broader framework. Burke’s conception of society as an intergenerational partnership (“between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born”) is meaningless if the last category dwindles to nothing. The Philosophy of Progress is explicit:

- #32 (Rights of Inheritance): The right of parents to pass on wealth, property, and cultural inheritance to their children is foundational. A society that taxes, burdens, or culturally devalues this transmission is one that has severed the intergenerational chain.
- #54 (Conservation): We are custodians, not owners, of what our forebears entrusted to us. The duty of conservation includes the conservation of the people themselves: not in any racial-essentialist sense, but in the sense that a continuous, self-sustaining population is the precondition for every other form of national continuity.
- #33 (Definition of “People”): A people defined by shared language, traditions, and territory requires biological as well as cultural reproduction. Immigration can supplement but cannot substitute for the renewal of the existing population.
- #38 (Philia): Aristotelian civic friendship, the high-trust social cohesion on which functional democracy depends, is built within families and transmitted between generations. The family is the first school of citizenship.

Progress’ Pop-Pol therefore operates on both sides of the demographic equation simultaneously: PP1.2 and PP1.3 address the immigration variable; PP1.4 addresses the fertility variable. Neither alone is sufficient. Without immigration reform, pro-natal investment is swamped by inflows that render demographic recovery irrelevant. Without pro-natal reform, immigration restriction produces a shrinking, ageing population incapable of sustaining its own institutions. The two are architecturally interdependent.

This policy interacts with:

- PP1.1 (The Citizenship Act): The five-tier citizenship framework determines whose children are born as Indigenous British Citizens; the pro-natal programme targets this population
- PP1.3 (Asylum, Removal, and Sovereignty): Voluntary repatriation and removal reduce the non-citizen population; pro-natal policy rebuilds the citizen population
- PP1.5 (Enforcement and Internal Control): E-Verify and the Citizenship Register provide the administrative infrastructure for targeting benefits to citizens
- PP1.6 (The Economic Transition): Labour market transition to high-wage, high-productivity economy makes family formation economically viable
- E1 (Cheapest Energy on Earth): Energy cost reduction as indirect fertility lift via reduced household expenditure
- E2 (Prosperity Zones): Regional economic regeneration restoring family-formation viability outside London
- E6 (Tax Reset): Tax reform creating fiscal space for pro-natal transfers and removing anti-family distortions
- C6 (Legal Equality Act): Family court reform, enforcement of parental obligations

##### PP1.4.1: Pro-Natal Financial Support

The Problem

Britain’s financial architecture is structured against family formation. A family with two children on median household income (approximately £34,500) faces childcare costs of £20,000–£28,000 per year for two full-time nursery places. The child benefit system (£25.60/week for the eldest child, £16.95 for subsequent children) is derisory by international standards, providing approximately £2,200/year for a two-child family against costs that dwarf this figure by an order of magnitude. The High Income Child Benefit Charge claws back payments from families where one earner exceeds £60,000, a threshold that in London and the South East represents a modest professional salary wholly inadequate for a single-income family with children. The two-child limit on Universal Credit, introduced in 2017, actively penalises larger families among the poorest households.

Meanwhile, the tax system treats parenthood as fiscally irrelevant. There is no meaningful tax differentiation between a single adult and a parent supporting three children. The marriage allowance (a transferable allowance of just £1,260) is so trivial as to be administratively pointless. France’s quotient familial splits household income by the number of family members for tax purposes, producing substantial savings for larger families; Britain has nothing comparable.

The result is a system in which having children is an unsubsidised private cost borne disproportionately by those who undertake it, while the benefits of a sustained population (tax revenues, economic dynamism, cultural continuity, social security funding) accrue to society at large. This is a textbook free-rider problem, and it is one of the principal drivers of fertility collapse. Worse, the only substantial per-child payments that do exist (UC child elements) carry no marriage or employment condition, meaning the financial incentive structure for large families is strongest for workless households and weakest for the self-supporting working families whose fertility decline is the primary driver of the demographic crisis.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The British Family Act will establish:

- a) Progressive child allowance. A new statutory child allowance replacing child benefit, structured to incentivise larger families among married, self-supporting households:

The progressive structure is deliberate: it is the third and fourth children, the births that move a family from below-replacement to replacement and above, that Pop-Pol most urgently needs to incentivise. Payments are made to the mother. There is no high-income taper; universality among eligible households eliminates administrative complexity and ensures the cultural signal is clear.

Eligibility conditions (all must be met):

- Citizenship: At least one parent must be an Indigenous British Citizen, Hereditary British Citizen, or Inherited Conditional British Citizen (PP1.1). British Subjects and Guests are ineligible.
- Marriage: Parents must be married or in a registered civil partnership. Cohabiting couples are eligible for the 1st-child rate only; the progressive escalation (2nd child and above) requires marriage. This is a deliberate incentive for formalised partnership as the foundation of stable family life.
- Household self-sufficiency: At least one parent must be in employment, self-employment, or receiving the Carefare Allowance (PP1.4.2) at the point of claim and on an ongoing basis. Households where both parents are in receipt of out-of-work benefits (excluding Carefare and statutory sick pay) are eligible for the standard UC child element but not the progressive child allowance. The pro-natal programme is designed to reward and enable families that are building self-sustaining lives; the welfare system provides the safety net.
- b) Multi-child income tax exemptions. Following the Hungarian model:
- Parents of 2 children: 33% reduction in personal income tax liability
- Parents of 3 children: 50% reduction in personal income tax liability
- Parents of 4+ children: lifetime personal income tax exemption for the mother

The lifetime exemption for mothers of four or more children is the single most powerful pro-natal incentive available, and the Hungarian experience confirms its effect. It signals unambiguously that the state regards large-family motherhood as a contribution to the nation equivalent to, and arguably exceeding, salaried economic activity. These exemptions are inherently targeted: they reward earners, and the value scales with income. A mother earning £50,000 with four children retains her entire salary. This is a direct, substantial incentive for productive, high-earning women to have large families rather than forgoing children for career progression.

- c) Abolition of the two-child limit. The Universal Credit two-child limit will be repealed immediately. Families of all sizes will receive UC child elements without restriction. This is a distinct instrument from the progressive child allowance: it removes a punitive cap on the welfare baseline while the child allowance builds the aspirational incentive structure above it.
- d) Family Formation Loan. A state-backed interest-free loan of up to £30,000 for married couples at the birth of their first child, with progressive debt forgiveness tied to subsequent children:
- 1st child: loan issued
- 2nd child: 33% of outstanding balance forgiven
- 3rd child: 66% of outstanding balance forgiven
- 4th child: 100% forgiven

This mirrors the Hungarian Baby Loan (Babaváró), which has achieved very high uptake and measurably accelerated family formation timelines. Eligibility: married couples where at least one partner is an Indigenous or Hereditary British Citizen, aged 21-40, with a minimum of two years’ continuous employment or self-employment history. The employment condition ensures the loan flows to households with demonstrated economic stability; the marriage condition ensures it flows to partnerships with the institutional commitment that correlates with family longevity.

OPERATIONAL

HMRC systems update. Child allowance payments will be administered through existing HMRC infrastructure (replacing the child benefit system). The progressive structure requires updated payment tables but no new delivery mechanism. Marriage and employment verification via RTI feeds and HMRC/DWP data matching. Target: new payment rates effective within 3 months of Royal Assent.

Tax exemption administration. Multi-child income tax exemptions administered via PAYE coding notices. Employers notified via RTI. Self-assessment adjustments for self-employed parents. Implementation within first full tax year following Royal Assent.

UC amendment. DWP will amend Universal Credit regulations via Statutory Instrument to remove the two-child limit. Effective within 28 days of Royal Assent.

Family Formation Loan. Administered by a dedicated unit within HMRC or a new arms-length body. Application via existing Government Gateway infrastructure. Eligibility verified against the Citizenship Register (PP1.1), GRO marriage records, and RTI employment history. Loan disbursement and forgiveness tracking integrated with birth registration system. Target: accepting applications within 6 months of Royal Assent.

##### PP1.4.2: Carefare: Supporting Mothers at Home

The Problem

The dominant policy consensus of the last three decades has treated maternal employment as an unqualified good and state-funded childcare as the primary mechanism for achieving it. The result has been a system that subsidises the separation of mothers from their infants while providing no support for mothers who choose to care for their own children, an arrangement so perverse that its persistence can only be explained by ideological commitment rather than empirical reasoning.

The evidence on infant development is unambiguous. Extensive longitudinal research, including the NICHD Study of Early Child Care (the largest and longest-running study of its kind), demonstrates that children under three who spend more than 30 hours per week in non-maternal care exhibit elevated cortisol levels, increased behavioural problems, and reduced attachment security compared to those cared for primarily by their mothers. The effect is most pronounced for children under 18 months. The quality of institutional care is largely irrelevant to this finding: it is the absence of the primary attachment figure, not the quality of the substitute, that drives the effect.

Yet British policy actively pushes mothers of very young children into employment. Universal Credit work conditionality applies when the youngest child turns 3 (reduced from 5 in 2023). Tax-Free Childcare subsidises nursery places but provides nothing for at-home care. The 30-hour “free” childcare entitlement (for working parents of 3-4 year olds) is explicitly conditional on both parents being in employment. A mother who stays home to care for her child receives nothing. The entire system is designed around the assumption that institutional childcare is preferable to maternal care, despite the developmental evidence to the contrary.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The British Family Act will establish:

- a) The Carefare Allowance. A statutory entitlement for mothers to receive partial wage replacement for up to three years following the birth of each child, conditional on the mother (or father, where the mother is the higher earner and both agree) remaining the child’s primary carer:
- Year 1: 70% of previous earnings (capped at £30,000/year)
- Year 2: 50% of previous earnings (capped at £22,000/year)
- Year 3: 40% of previous earnings (capped at £18,000/year)
- Minimum payment for those with limited employment history: £10,000/year

The allowance replaces statutory maternity pay (currently 90% for 6 weeks, then £184.03/week for 33 weeks) and extends support to three full years, the period during which developmental evidence most strongly favours maternal care.

Eligibility conditions:

- Citizenship: Mother (or designated primary carer) must be an Indigenous British Citizen, Hereditary British Citizen, or ICBC
- Marriage: Conditional on marriage or registered civil partnership
- Employment history: The earnings-linked tiers (70%/50%/40%) require a minimum of 12 months’ continuous employment or self-employment in the two years preceding the birth. Those without qualifying employment history receive the minimum flat-rate payment (£10,000/year). This structure ensures that the most generous provision flows to women who have established themselves in the workforce and are pausing careers to raise children, while still providing meaningful support to those entering motherhood from less established positions.

Carefare is counted as “employment” for the purposes of progressive child allowance eligibility (PP1.4.1). A mother on Carefare meets the household self-sufficiency condition. This is critical: a single-earner family where the father works and the mother is on Carefare qualifies for the full progressive child allowance, the full transferable tax allowance, and the multi-child tax exemptions. The system works as an integrated whole.

- b) Pre-school provision from age 3. Universal free pre-school provision (30 hours/week) for all children aged 3-4, regardless of parental employment status. The existing 30-hour entitlement’s employment conditionality will be abolished. This is the age at which socialisation and structured learning environments become developmentally beneficial, not before.
- c) Removal of UC work conditionality for primary carers. Mothers (or designated primary carer fathers) with children under 5 will be exempt from all Universal Credit work search and work availability requirements. The current regime, which applies conditionality from age 3, will be abolished.

OPERATIONAL

Carefare administration. Administered through HMRC using existing maternity pay infrastructure, extended to three years. Employers will continue to process Year 1 payments via payroll (as with current SMP), with HMRC reimbursement. Years 2 and 3 paid directly by HMRC. Transition from employer-administered to direct payment occurs automatically. Employment history verified against RTI records.

Childcare entitlement reform. The Department for Education will amend early years funding regulations via Statutory Instrument to remove employment conditionality from the 30-hour entitlement. Local authorities already administer the entitlement; the change is to eligibility criteria, not delivery infrastructure. Effective within 3 months of Royal Assent.

UC conditionality. DWP will amend UC regulations via Statutory Instrument to exempt primary carers of children under 5 from all work-related requirements. Effective within 28 days of Royal Assent.

##### PP1.4.3: Marriage and Divorce Reform

The Problem

Marriage rates in England and Wales have fallen to historic lows. In 2021, there were 158,000 marriages, down from 340,000 in 1970 and the lowest figure since records began in 1837. The marriage rate per 1,000 unmarried adults has halved since 1990. Cohabitation has risen correspondingly, but cohabiting couples are significantly more likely to separate than married couples: approximately 50% of cohabiting parents separate before their child’s fifth birthday, compared to approximately 15% of married parents.

The introduction of no-fault divorce in April 2022 (Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020) reduced the minimum period from filing to final order to six months. This was presented as a modernisation. In practice, it removed the last institutional friction discouraging marital dissolution and signalled that the state regards marriage as a contract of convenience terminable at will, rather than a binding commitment with obligations to third parties, principally children.

The family courts compound the problem. Despite the Children Act 1989’s presumption that the welfare of the child is paramount, and the Children and Families Act 2014’s presumption of parental involvement, in practice mothers receive primary residence in approximately 90% of contested cases. Enforcement of contact orders is negligible: the Family Court Statistics Quarterly shows that enforcement applications succeed in a minority of cases, and meaningful sanctions (committal, transfer of residence) are almost never imposed. Parental alienation, the systematic destruction of a child’s relationship with one parent by the other, is widespread but judicially unrecognised. The result is a system that incentivises divorce (the resident parent gains near-total control of the children plus financial maintenance), penalises marriage (the non-resident parent, overwhelmingly fathers, faces financial obligations with minimal enforceable rights), and traumatises children.

The tax system reinforces the problem. The marriage allowance is worth a maximum of £252 per year, a rounding error. Universal Credit imposes an effective marriage penalty: cohabiting couples receive less than two single individuals living apart, creating a direct financial disincentive to partnership formation. The combined effect of the tax and welfare system is to treat marriage as fiscally neutral at best and actively punitive at worst.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The British Family Act will establish:

- a) Full transferable tax allowance. The personal allowance (currently £12,570) will be fully transferable between married couples and civil partners, regardless of the earning split. A single-earner married couple will therefore have an effective personal allowance of £25,140, delivering a tax saving of up to £2,514 per year at the basic rate, and more where higher-rate relief applies. This replaces the current derisory £252 marriage allowance with a genuine financial incentive for marriage and for single-earner family arrangements (complementing the Carefare Allowance in PP1.4.2).
- b) Removal of Universal Credit marriage penalty. UC will be reformed so that the assessment for married and cohabiting couples produces no less than the combined entitlement of two single individuals. The means-tested taper and benefit cap will be recalculated to ensure that formalising a partnership never reduces net household income.
- c) Divorce reform. The Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020 will be repealed and replaced with provisions in the British Family Act establishing:
- Minimum separation period: Two years (increased from current 6 months) before a divorce petition may be filed, except where there is evidence of domestic abuse, criminality, or abandonment
- Mandatory mediation: Where children are involved, both parties must complete a minimum of six mediation sessions before the court will accept a petition. Legal aid will be restored for mediation in all cases involving children.
- Cooling-off period: A further 6-month period between acceptance of petition and grant of decree absolute, during which reconciliation services are available and either party may withdraw
- d) Family court reform. Amendments to the Children Act 1989 and Children and Families Act 2014:
- Statutory presumption of 50/50 shared custody as the default arrangement, rebuttable only on evidence of abuse, neglect, or genuine welfare risk. Not on the basis of “primary carer” status, geographic convenience, or status quo arguments.
- Enforcement of contact orders: Courts must impose escalating sanctions for non-compliance: fines, community service, variation of residence order, and ultimately committal. The current regime of unenforceable orders is abolished.
- Parental alienation: Statutory recognition of parental alienation as a form of child abuse. Where established, it constitutes grounds for transfer of residence to the alienated parent.
- Legal aid restoration: Legal aid will be restored for all private family law proceedings involving children

OPERATIONAL

Tax allowance implementation. HMRC will amend PAYE coding to enable full personal allowance transfer between married couples. Implementation via existing Marriage Allowance infrastructure, extended to full transferability. Target: first full tax year following Royal Assent.

UC reform. DWP will amend UC regulations via Statutory Instrument to remove the couple penalty. This requires recalibration of standard allowances and taper rates. Target: within 6 months of Royal Assent, ensuring alignment with the annual UC uprating cycle.

Mediation service expansion. The Ministry of Justice will commission expanded mediation capacity via existing Family Mediation Council-accredited providers. Legal aid for mediation reinstated via amendment to the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012 (Schedule 1). Target: capacity in place within 12 months.

Judicial training. The Judicial College will develop and deliver training on the new shared custody presumption, parental alienation recognition, and enforcement obligations. Rolled out to all family court judges within 6 months.

##### PP1.4.4: Abolition of Inheritance Tax

The Problem

Inheritance Tax is the taxation of intergenerational continuity. It is levied at 40% on estates above the nil-rate band (£325,000, frozen since 2009; plus a residence nil-rate band of £175,000 where a main residence is passed to direct descendants). In practice, the freezing of thresholds against rising property values has dragged hundreds of thousands of ordinary families into a tax originally designed for the very wealthy. HMRC receipts from IHT exceeded £7 billion in 2023-24 and are projected to rise to £9 billion by 2028.

The tax is indefensible on every level. Economically, it represents double or triple taxation: income that has already been taxed via PAYE, NICs, and VAT is taxed again at death. It distorts behaviour: families restructure assets, establish trusts, and make lifetime transfers to avoid a charge that falls most heavily on those without the advice or foresight to plan around it, principally middle-class families whose wealth is concentrated in a single family home. The ultra-wealthy, with access to agricultural relief, business relief, and sophisticated trust structures, pay proportionally far less. IHT is therefore regressive in practice despite being progressive in theory.

The deeper objection is philosophical. The Philosophy of Progress (#32) affirms the right of inheritance as foundational. The family is an intergenerational institution; the transmission of property, wealth, knowledge, and values from parents to children is the mechanism by which civilisation sustains itself across generations. A state that confiscates 40% of a family’s accumulated wealth at death is one that regards each generation as an isolated economic unit, severing the chain of obligation and aspiration that binds grandparents to grandchildren. This is incompatible with Burke’s conception of society, with the custodial ethic of the Philosophy of Progress, and with the demographic objectives of Pop-Pol, which require among other things that young families have access to inherited wealth for housing deposits, business formation, and the economic security that underpins family formation.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Finance Act (first Budget following formation of government) will provide:

- a) Complete abolition of Inheritance Tax. IHT is abolished in its entirety. No nil-rate band, no residence nil-rate band, no taper, no charge. The Inheritance Tax Act 1984 is repealed.
- b) Anti-avoidance simplification. The existing seven-year rule for potentially exempt transfers, the complex trust taxation regime, and the associated reporting obligations are abolished alongside the tax itself. The administrative savings, both for HMRC and for families currently spending thousands on estate planning, are substantial.
- c) Revenue offset. The £7-9 billion annual revenue from IHT will be offset through:
- Reduced public expenditure enabled by broader civil service reform (CS1-CS6), particularly the dramatic reduction in civil service headcount and managerial layer
- Increased tax receipts from economic growth driven by Prosperity Zones (E2) and the broader Tax Reset (E6)
- Elimination of IHT administration costs within HMRC (estimated £400-600 million including compliance staff, tribunals, and dispute resolution)
- The dynamic effects of released capital: inherited wealth deployed into housing, business formation, and consumption generates VAT, income tax, and corporation tax receipts that partially offset the static revenue loss

Pop-Pol’s fiscal impact is also relevant here: each avoided lifetime fiscal cost of a low-wage migrant (£150,000+) or asylum claimant (£300,000+) contributes to the fiscal space for IHT abolition.

OPERATIONAL

HMRC wind-down. HMRC’s IHT division will be wound down over 12 months following Royal Assent. Outstanding cases and assessments will be concluded. No new assessments will be raised for deaths occurring after the abolition date. Staff redeployed to other HMRC functions (including the Citizenship Register and Visa Insurance administration under PP1.1 and PP1.2).

Probate simplification. The Ministry of Justice will issue amended probate guidance reflecting the abolition of IHT reporting requirements. Estate administration timelines will shorten significantly without the need for HMRC clearance.

##### PP1.4.5: Expat Return and the Reversal of British Emigration

The Problem

In 2024, an estimated 257,000 British nationals emigrated from the United Kingdom, the highest figure since 1964. Across the diaspora, approximately 5.5 million British-born citizens live abroad. Many of these are highly skilled professionals in medicine, engineering, finance, technology, and academia: precisely the human capital that Britain most urgently needs to retain and recover. The brain drain is self-reinforcing: as public services deteriorate, crime rises, housing becomes unaffordable, and the tax burden increases, the most mobile and capable citizens leave, further degrading the conditions that drove their departure.

Current return flows stand at approximately 143,000 per year, a net loss of over 100,000 British nationals annually. Pop-Pol targets 200,000 returns per year, requiring both the elimination of push factors (which is the work of Progress’ broader platform) and the creation of active pull incentives.

This is not immigration. These are British people, Hereditary British Citizens under the PP1.1 framework, coming home. Their return strengthens the nation demographically, fiscally, and culturally. They bring skills acquired abroad, international networks, capital, and a renewed appreciation for the country they left and the reforms that made return viable.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The British Family Act and Immigration Reform Act (PP1.2) will jointly establish:

- a) Heritage Return Visa. Already provided for in PP1.2: a streamlined re-entry route for Hereditary British Citizens (second and third generation diaspora) who may not hold current British passports or documentation. The Heritage Return Visa provides immediate right to reside, work, and access public services upon verification of Hereditary British Citizen status against the Citizenship Register. No visa fees. No sponsorship requirement. No minimum income threshold.
- b) Return Incentive Package. A statutory package for British nationals returning after 3+ years of continuous residence abroad:
- Relocation grant: £5,000 per adult, £2,500 per child (household cap £15,000)
- Temporary tax relief: 50% reduction in income tax liability for the first two tax years following return, tapering to 25% in Year 3
- Professional recognition: Statutory fast-track for recognition of overseas professional qualifications (medicine, law, engineering, teaching, accountancy). 28-day determination by the relevant professional body, with a presumption of recognition for qualifications obtained in comparable jurisdictions (Five Eyes, EU, Switzerland, Japan, South Korea, Singapore).
- Priority housing: Returning British families with children given priority status in local authority housing allocation and eligibility for the Family Formation Loan (PP1.4.1)
- c) Pension portability. Statutory requirement for full recognition and transfer of overseas pension entitlements. Returning Britons must not face pension disadvantage for years spent contributing abroad.

OPERATIONAL

Outreach programme. A dedicated unit within the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office will run a “Come Home” programme targeting the British diaspora:

- Targeted digital advertising in high-diaspora locations (Australia, USA, Canada, UAE, Spain, France)
- British embassy and consulate outreach events: quarterly “Return to Britain” information sessions
- Dedicated web portal and caseworker support for returning families
- Alumni partnerships with British universities for diaspora contact

Professional recognition fast-track. Relevant professional regulators (GMC, SRA, Engineering Council, TRA, ICAEW) will be issued statutory guidance requiring 28-day determination of overseas qualification recognition. The relevant Secretary of State will have reserve powers to direct recognition where a regulator fails to meet the statutory deadline. Prepared and issued within 3 months of Royal Assent.

HMRC tax relief administration. Return tax relief administered via Self Assessment with PAYE adjustment for employed returnees. Eligibility verified against HMRC departure records and Citizenship Register. Operational within first full tax year following Royal Assent.

Summary of Legislative Requirements

The PP1.4 framework is built on the British Family Act, a single piece of primary legislation introduced in the first King’s Speech alongside the Citizenship Act 2029 (PP1.1), Immigration Reform Act (PP1.2), and Immigration Sovereignty and Human Rights Reform Act (PP1.3). Inheritance Tax abolition is enacted via the first Finance Act. Expat return provisions are shared between the British Family Act and the Immigration Reform Act (PP1.2).

British Family Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act:

Progressive child allowance (£200-£500/month per child, escalating by birth order). Eligibility conditions: citizenship (IBC, HBC, ICBC), marriage (required for escalation above 1st child), household self-sufficiency (at least one parent in employment, self-employment, or Carefare). Multi-child income tax exemptions (33%/50%/lifetime for 2/3/4+ children). Abolition of the UC two-child limit. Family Formation Loan (£30,000, progressive forgiveness by child number; conditional on marriage and 2-year employment history). Carefare Allowance (three-year partial wage replacement for primary carers; earnings-linked tiers conditional on 12-month employment history; marriage required). Removal of employment conditionality from 30-hour childcare entitlement. UC work conditionality exemption for primary carers of children under 5. Full transferable personal tax allowance for married couples. Removal of UC marriage penalty. Divorce reform: two-year separation minimum, mandatory mediation, six-month cooling-off. Family court reform: 50/50 shared custody presumption, contact order enforcement, parental alienation recognition. Legal aid restoration for private family law proceedings and mediation. Heritage Return visa eligibility criteria and rights. Return Incentive Package (relocation grant, tax relief, professional recognition fast-track, priority housing). Pension portability for returning nationals.

Finance Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act:

Repeal of the Inheritance Tax Act 1984. Abolition of IHT in its entirety. Consequential repeals of associated reporting, trust taxation, and compliance obligations.

Delivered operationally:

Child allowance payments via HMRC with marriage/employment verification (3 months from Royal Assent). Tax exemption administration via PAYE coding (first full tax year). UC two-child limit removal via SI (28 days). UC work conditionality exemption via SI (28 days). Family Formation Loan unit established with Citizenship Register and RTI integration (6 months). Carefare Allowance administered via extended SMP infrastructure with employment history verification. Childcare entitlement reform via SI (3 months). UC marriage penalty removal via SI (6 months). Mediation capacity expansion (12 months). Judicial training on shared custody and parental alienation (6 months). IHT division wind-down (12 months). Probate simplification guidance. FCDO “Come Home” programme launch (3 months). Professional recognition fast-track guidance (3 months). Return tax relief via HMRC (first full tax year).

Timeline

#### PP1.5: Enforcement and Internal Control

Governing Principle

A nation that cannot identify who is within its borders, cannot verify whether they have the right to be there, and cannot compel their departure when they do not, is not enforcing an immigration system. It is maintaining a fiction. Britain’s enforcement architecture (porous borders, manual document checks, an uncoordinated patchwork of databases, negligible penalties for employing or housing illegal migrants, and an Immigration Enforcement directorate that achieved 3,501 deportations against an estimated unlawful population of 800,000-1.2 million) does not represent a system that is struggling. It represents a system that does not functionally exist.

The UK is one of the only developed nations with no comprehensive entry-exit tracking system. The Home Office cannot say, with any precision, how many people are in the country, how many have overstayed their visas, or where they are. The International Passenger Survey, a voluntary questionnaire administered to a sample of travellers at selected ports, remained until recently the primary basis for migration statistics. The United States has operated the US-VISIT biometric entry system since 2004 and is transitioning to the Biometric Exit programme. Australia’s SmartGate system captures biometric data at both entry and departure. The UAE’s iris-scan border system in Abu Dhabi processes millions of crossings with near-perfect accuracy. Britain, by contrast, only introduced systematic exit checks in 2015, and these remain incomplete: ferry and private aviation routes have limited coverage, and the data feeds into a system with no single unified database and no automated mechanism for identifying overstayers in real time.

Internal enforcement is equally absent. The right-to-work check system requires employers to inspect physical documents (passports, visa cards, share codes) and form a subjective judgment about their validity. The right-to-rent scheme imposes a similar burden on landlords. Both systems are easily circumvented by competent forgery or identity fraud, create genuine discrimination risks (landlords and employers facing Equality Act liability for being too rigorous), and provide a built-in defence for non-compliance: “I checked the documents and they appeared genuine.” The result is a shadow economy estimated at 10-15% of GDP, sustained by a workforce whose immigration status is effectively unverifiable.

Pop-Pol’s entire enforcement architecture (visa non-renewals, voluntary repatriation, accelerated removal, and the broader population reduction targets) depends on solving this problem. You cannot enforce visa conditions you cannot track. You cannot remove overstayers you cannot find. You cannot deter illegal employment you cannot detect. PP1.5 provides the infrastructure without which PP1.1, PP1.2, PP1.3, and PP1.6 are policy documents rather than policy.

This sits within a broader enforcement philosophy: making it administratively impossible to live and work in the UK without lawful immigration status. The objective is not to create a police state or to subject citizens to surveillance. Citizens, once verified, move through the system frictionlessly. The objective is to make the informal economy unviable, to make overstaying unattractive, and to ensure that the state possesses the information it needs to enforce the laws that Parliament has enacted. Every serious immigration system in the world operates on this principle. Britain’s does not, and that is why it fails.

This policy interacts with:

- PP1.1 (The Citizenship Act): The Citizenship Register and Fit and Proper Persons Register are the authoritative databases against which all verification checks are performed
- PP1.2 (The Immigration Reset): Visa Insurance and sponsorship obligations are enforced through E-Verify and biometric borders
- PP1.3 (Asylum, Removal, and Sovereignty): Removal mechanisms depend on identification and location of enforcement targets
- PP1.4 (The British Family): Enforcement infrastructure ensures pro-natal benefits flow only to eligible citizens
- PP1.6 (The Economic Transition): Labour market transition requires that employers cannot access cheap illegal labour as a substitute for automation and domestic skills investment
- CS2 (Executive Decisions Act): Ouster clauses protecting enforcement decisions from judicial activism
- C3 (Malebranche / Public Integrity Act): Investigation of organised immigration crime, document fraud, and smuggling networks
- C6 (Legal Equality Act): Equality Act reform enabling enforcement without discrimination liability

##### PP1.5.1: Biometric Entry and Exit

The Problem

The UK does not have a functioning entry-exit tracking system. While entry data is captured through e-passport gates and manual border checks, departure data remains incomplete. The exit checks introduced in 2015 rely on Advance Passenger Information (API) submitted by carriers, supplemented by e-passport gate scans at selected departure points. Coverage gaps persist: not all ferry routes provide real-time API data; private aviation is largely unmonitored; the Eurostar departure process captures data but integration with Home Office systems is inconsistent; and land border crossings in Northern Ireland, governed by Common Travel Area arrangements, are entirely untracked.

The consequence is that the Home Office cannot generate, in real time, a list of individuals whose visas have expired and who have not departed. Overstayer identification relies on periodic data matching exercises, comparing entry records against departure records in batch processing that may lag by weeks or months. By the time an overstayer is identified, they have had ample opportunity to move, change identity, or establish themselves in the informal economy. The International Passenger Survey estimated net migration at 212,000 in 2012; the ONS later revised this to 504,000 on the basis of improved data, a correction of 138%, demonstrating that the UK government literally did not know how many people were entering and leaving the country within a margin of hundreds of thousands.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Immigration Reform Act (PP1.2) will establish:

- a) Mandatory biometric capture at all entry and exit points. Every person entering or leaving the United Kingdom, citizen and non-citizen alike, will be subject to biometric verification (facial recognition matched against passport chip data) at the point of crossing. This includes:
- All airports (e-passport gates upgraded to capture departure as well as arrival; manual lanes equipped with facial recognition terminals)
- Eurostar terminals (St Pancras, Ebbsfleet, Ashford; and reciprocal French/Belgian departure points under bilateral agreement)
- Ferry ports (Dover, Portsmouth, Holyhead, Liverpool, Hull, Harwich, Newcastle, all Scottish ports)
- Private aviation (FBO operators at all UK airfields required to submit biometric data for all passengers prior to departure)
- b) Carrier duties. Airlines, ferry operators, rail operators, and private aviation operators will be subject to statutory duties to:
- Verify travel documents against the Immigration Database prior to boarding/embarkation
- Transmit real-time biometric departure data to Border Force
- Refuse boarding to individuals flagged by the system (removal orders, travel bans, expired leave)
- Penalties for non-compliance: £10,000 per undocumented passenger carried; operating licence review for systematic failures
- c) Unified Immigration Database. A single authoritative database, integrating the Citizenship Register (PP1.1), visa records (UKVI), biometric entry/exit data (Border Force), and the Fit and Proper Persons Register (PP1.1), will serve as the single source of truth for immigration status across all government functions. The current fragmented architecture (ATLAS, CID, UKVI casework systems, PNC, Home Office Biometrics) will be consolidated.
- d) Automatic overstayer identification. The system will generate automated alerts when:
- A visa holder’s leave to remain expires without a recorded departure or extension application
- A 28-day grace period elapses without resolution (contact, extension, or departure)
- An individual subject to removal directions has not departed

Alerts trigger automatic referral to Immigration Enforcement for active case management. No manual intervention or batch processing required.

OPERATIONAL

e-Passport gate upgrade programme. Existing e-passport gates at major airports will be upgraded to capture departure biometrics (currently most gates are arrival-only or dual-function at limited capacity). Programme managed by Border Force with Home Office Digital, Data and Technology (DDaT). Target: all Tier 1 airports (Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester, Stansted, Luton, Birmingham, Edinburgh, Bristol) fully operational within 6 months. Tier 2 airports and all ferry/Eurostar terminals within 12 months.

Database consolidation. Home Office DDaT will lead the Unified Immigration Database programme, consolidating existing systems into a single platform. This is the highest-priority IT programme in the Home Office. Initial operating capability (entry-exit matching, automated overstayer alerts) within 6 months using existing data feeds. Full system integration within 18 months. Emergency procurement rules apply. Existing contractor relationships leveraged for speed; no multi-year procurement exercise.

Northern Ireland. The Common Travel Area with the Republic of Ireland presents a structural challenge. Pop-Pol’s approach: intelligence-led operations at key crossing points; mandatory carrier checks on air and sea routes between NI and GB; bilateral discussions with Ireland on data sharing for immigration enforcement purposes. The CTA is preserved but no longer treated as an excuse for enforcement passivity.

##### PP1.5.2: UK E-Verify (Mandatory Electronic Verification)

The Problem

The right-to-work and right-to-rent check systems are analogue relics in a digital age. An employer conducting a right-to-work check must: request original documents from the prospective employee; inspect them for signs of forgery; check that the photograph resembles the person; check the dates; record the document reference numbers; and repeat the process at expiry of time-limited leave. This is a manual, subjective, error-prone process that imposes real costs on employers, creates genuine discrimination risks (the Equality and Human Rights Commission has documented cases where landlords and employers rejected applicants with foreign-sounding names or appearances to avoid the complexity of document checks), and provides a ready-made defence for those who choose not to comply: “The documents looked genuine to me.”

The right-to-rent scheme, introduced by the Immigration Act 2014, imposes equivalent obligations on landlords. The hostile environment measures introduced alongside it were well-intentioned but poorly implemented: they relied on the same manual document checks, attracted widespread criticism for discrimination against lawful residents, and were partially rolled back following the Windrush scandal. The lesson of Windrush is not that enforcement is wrong. It is that enforcement based on subjective document inspection rather than authoritative database verification inevitably produces errors that fall disproportionately on those who look or sound “foreign” regardless of their actual status.

The solution is not less enforcement. It is better enforcement. The United States’ E-Verify system demonstrates the model: an employer enters an employee’s details into an online system; the system returns an instant yes/no determination against live government databases; the employer’s legal obligation is discharged by following the system’s determination. No document inspection. No subjective judgment. No discrimination risk. No “I didn’t know” defence. The binary nature of the check eliminates the very mechanism by which discrimination occurs: there is no room for a landlord to make a “judgment call” about whether a document looks genuine when the system provides a definitive answer. UK E-Verify is the backbone of Pop-Pol’s internal enforcement: every visa condition, every right-to-work restriction, every status determination in PP1.1 is only as enforceable as the system that verifies it in real time.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Immigration Reform Act (PP1.2) will establish:

- a) UK E-Verify system. A mandatory electronic verification system, querying the Unified Immigration Database (PP1.5.1) and Citizenship Register (PP1.1), providing instant binary (authorised/not authorised) determinations for:
- Right to work: All employers must verify every prospective employee through UK E-Verify before commencement of employment, and re-verify at intervals specified by the system for those with time-limited leave. Manual document checks are abolished as a compliance mechanism.
- Right to rent: All landlords and letting agents must verify prospective tenants. Physical document inspection is no longer a statutory excuse.
- Right to bank: All banks and building societies must verify account applicants. Existing accounts for individuals who fail verification will be flagged for review.
- Right to study: All universities and colleges must verify enrolled students against the system, with real-time notifications when a student’s leave expires or is curtailed.
- b) Fit and Proper Persons Register integration. Non-citizens are recorded on the Fit and Proper Persons Register (PP1.1.2), which feeds into the E-Verify system. The Register records: immigration status, visa conditions, employment restrictions, criminal record, compliance history (previous violations, sanctions, re-entry bans). Employers and landlords making E-Verify checks for non-citizens receive the binary authorisation plus any relevant conditions (e.g. restricted working hours for student visa holders).
- c) Statutory defence and strict liability. An employer, landlord, or institution that conducts a UK E-Verify check and acts in accordance with the result has a complete statutory defence against any civil or criminal liability relating to immigration compliance. Conversely, failure to conduct a check, or engagement of an individual despite a negative determination, constitutes a strict liability offence. The “I didn’t know” defence is extinguished.

OPERATIONAL

System development. UK E-Verify will be built on existing Home Office digital infrastructure (the Employer Checking Service and the Landlord Checking Service already provide rudimentary online checks). The critical enhancement is: full integration with the Unified Immigration Database and Citizenship Register; real-time status updates (not batch-processed); binary yes/no output with no ambiguity; and a mobile-accessible API enabling checks from any device. Development during legislative passage; beta launch to large employers within 3 months of Royal Assent; mandatory for all employers within 6 months; mandatory for landlords, banks, and universities within 12 months.

Transition support. Small businesses will receive dedicated support via a Business Immigration Compliance helpline and regional workshops. The transition from manual document checks to E-Verify is a simplification, not an additional burden: the system is faster, cheaper, and more legally certain than the existing process. HMRC will incorporate E-Verify compliance checks into existing PAYE registration and RTI processes.

##### PP1.5.3: Business Licence Consequences

The Problem

The current penalty regime for employing illegal workers is derisory. The maximum civil penalty is £45,000 per illegal worker (raised from £20,000 in 2024), but actual penalties imposed are typically far lower, often reduced on appeal or by demonstrating (however perfunctorily) that document checks were conducted. Criminal prosecution for knowingly employing illegal workers carries a maximum sentence of 5 years, but prosecutions are vanishingly rare: fewer than 20 employers per year are prosecuted, against an estimated hundreds of thousands of illegally employed workers. The expected cost of employing an illegal worker (probability of detection multiplied by likely penalty) is a rounding error compared to the savings from paying below-minimum-wage rates and avoiding employer NICs, pension contributions, and holiday pay. Pop-Pol requires that this calculus is inverted: the expected cost of non-compliance must vastly exceed any conceivable benefit.

Certain business sectors function as near-systematic vehicles for illegal employment. Car washes, nail bars, barber shops, vape shops, fast food outlets, and hand car valeting operations are disproportionately staffed by undocumented or illegally employed workers, often in conditions that amount to modern slavery. These businesses are frequently cash-only, making HMRC enforcement difficult; they are typically sole trader or micro-company structures, making director disqualification meaningless; and they are concentrated in sectors where local authority licensing provides the only meaningful regulatory touchpoint.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Immigration Reform Act (PP1.2) will establish:

- a) Escalating penalty framework. Penalties for employing individuals not authorised to work, as determined by UK E-Verify:

These are not theoretical maximums. The legislation will establish mandatory minimum penalties: courts and enforcement bodies will not have discretion to reduce below the statutory floor. The first-offence penalty of £100,000 per worker is calibrated to exceed any conceivable economic benefit from illegal employment, even for a single worker employed for a single day.

- b) High-risk sector enhanced licensing. Businesses in designated high-risk sectors (car washes, hand car valeting, nail bars, barber shops, vape shops, fast food outlets, and other sectors designated by the Secretary of State) will be subject to enhanced licensing conditions:
- Annual immigration compliance audit as a condition of the business licence
- Mandatory UK E-Verify records retained and available for inspection
- Cash-transaction limits (£1,000 per day) enforced via licensing conditions, forcing electronic payment trails
- Failure to comply with audit or record-keeping requirements is grounds for licence revocation without further offence
- c) Supply chain liability. Businesses that contract with suppliers or subcontractors who employ illegal workers will be liable for a civil penalty of £50,000 per worker where they have failed to require and verify E-Verify compliance through the supply chain. This addresses the common practice of using layers of subcontracting to insulate the principal employer from immigration enforcement.

OPERATIONAL

Enforcement capacity. Immigration Enforcement will establish dedicated Business Compliance Teams in each region, co-located with HMRC and local authority enforcement. Target: teams operational within 6 months. Intelligence-led targeting of high-risk sectors from Day 1, using existing HMRC, GLAA (Gangmasters and Labour Abuse Authority), and local authority intelligence.

High-risk sector licensing. Local authorities will incorporate immigration compliance audit requirements into existing licensing frameworks (premises licences, street trading licences, personal licences). Model licence conditions issued by the Home Office within 3 months. Local authorities with the highest concentrations of high-risk businesses will receive dedicated funding for enforcement capacity.

##### PP1.5.4: Local Authority Enforcement Powers

The Problem

Immigration Enforcement is a centralised Home Office function with approximately 5,000 staff covering the entire United Kingdom. This is wholly inadequate for systematic enforcement against an estimated illegal population of 800,000-1.2 million. Meanwhile, local authorities employ tens of thousands of environmental health officers, trading standards officers, licensing officers, housing inspectors, and other regulatory staff who routinely enter business premises, inspect conditions, and enforce compliance with a wide range of regulations. These officers regularly encounter indicators of illegal employment and housing (overcrowded HMOs, cash-only businesses with no employment records, workers unable to communicate in English, premises operating outside licensed hours) but have no legal power to act on immigration concerns and no obligation to report them. Pop-Pol cannot tolerate this gap. Local authority officers are the eyes and ears of regulatory enforcement at street level; excluding them from immigration enforcement is like building a burglar alarm with no sensors on the ground floor.

The disconnect is absurd. A trading standards officer inspecting a nail bar for product safety can observe ten workers with no employment contracts, no NI numbers, and no English, and has no authority to do anything about it. A housing inspector encountering 15 people living in a two-bedroom flat can enforce housing standards but cannot query whether any of the occupants have the right to be in the country.

Execution
