PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Immigration Reform Act (PP1.2) will establish:

- a) Local authority inspection and referral powers (all areas). Environmental health officers, trading standards officers, licensing officers, and housing inspectors will be granted statutory power to:
- Request proof of E-Verify compliance from any business during a routine inspection
- Conduct an E-Verify check on any individual encountered during a lawful inspection where there are reasonable grounds to suspect unlawful employment or residence
- Refer cases to Immigration Enforcement with a statutory duty on IE to respond within 14 days
- Issue an immediate compliance notice requiring a business to produce E-Verify records within 7 days; failure to comply constitutes grounds for licence review
- b) Embedded Immigration Enforcement officers (high-immigration areas). In local authority areas designated by the Secretary of State as “high-immigration areas” (based on non-citizen population density, overstayer intelligence, and enforcement referral rates), Immigration Enforcement officers will be embedded within local authority teams on a permanent basis. These officers will:
- Participate in joint inspections with local authority enforcement staff
- Exercise full IE powers (entry, search, arrest, detention) during joint operations
- Provide training and operational guidance to local authority officers
- Manage a shared intelligence database with the local authority
- c) Multi-agency operations. The Act will create a statutory framework for coordinated multi-agency enforcement operations combining:
- Immigration Enforcement + HMRC (tax evasion, NMW violations, cash economy)
- Immigration Enforcement + Police (organised immigration crime, trafficking, exploitation)
- Immigration Enforcement + GLAA (gangmaster licensing, labour abuse, modern slavery)
- Immigration Enforcement + Trading Standards/Environmental Health (business compliance, licensing)

Joint operations will be led by a designated lead agency with full powers of all participating bodies, avoiding the current situation where each agency can only act within its own silo during an operation.

OPERATIONAL

Local authority training. The Home Office will develop and deliver a training programme for local authority enforcement officers covering: indicators of illegal employment and housing; E-Verify check procedures; referral protocols; evidence gathering and preservation; and the legal framework for immigration-related enforcement. Rolled out to all local authorities within 6 months of Royal Assent. Priority training for authorities in designated high-immigration areas within 3 months.

Embedded officer deployment. IE officers will be deployed to designated high-immigration areas within 3 months. Initial deployment to the 30 local authority areas with the highest estimated non-citizen populations. Expansion based on referral rates and enforcement outcomes.

Multi-agency coordination. A national Multi-Agency Immigration Enforcement Board will be established within the Home Office, co-chaired by IE and HMRC, with standing membership from Police, GLAA, and the Local Government Association. Regional coordination hubs in each IE region. Quarterly joint operation cycles with pre-planned targeting based on shared intelligence.

##### PP1.5.5: The Victim Firewall

The Problem

Effective immigration enforcement must not come at the cost of public safety. If victims of crime who are themselves unlawfully present in the UK believe that reporting a crime will result in their deportation, they will not report. This is not a hypothetical concern: it is a documented reality across multiple jurisdictions, and it has specific and grave implications for the detection and prosecution of serious crimes including domestic violence, sexual offences, trafficking, and modern slavery, all of which disproportionately affect vulnerable migrant populations.

The perpetrators of these crimes rely on their victims’ fear of immigration enforcement to maintain control and evade justice. A trafficker who tells his victims that going to the police will result in their deportation is, under the current system, telling the truth. The absence of any formal separation between policing and immigration enforcement creates a structural incentive for victims to remain silent and for perpetrators to operate with impunity.

Progress’ position is clear: enforcement must be robust, comprehensive, and without exception for those who violate immigration law by their own choice. But a victim of rape, trafficking, or domestic abuse is not in the same moral category as a visa overstayer who has chosen to remain unlawfully. Pop-Pol is a population management programme, not a charter for impunity for criminals who prey on vulnerable migrants. The enforcement system must be capable of distinguishing between the two, and it must not sacrifice the prosecution of serious crime on the altar of immigration statistics.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Immigration Reform Act (PP1.2) will establish:

- a) Statutory Victim Firewall. Police forces, the Crown Prosecution Service, and victim support services will be subject to a statutory prohibition on sharing the immigration status or personal data of victims and witnesses of specified serious crimes with Immigration Enforcement during an active investigation and prosecution. The specified crimes are:
- Violence against the person (including domestic abuse)
- Sexual offences
- Trafficking and modern slavery
- Forced marriage and FGM (cross-ref C6)
- Child abuse and exploitation
- Kidnapping and false imprisonment
- b) Scope and limitations. The Firewall is carefully circumscribed:
- Duration: The Firewall applies during active investigation and prosecution only. Once proceedings are concluded (whether by conviction, acquittal, or discontinuation), the individual’s immigration status reverts to normal enforcement.
- Victims and witnesses only: The Firewall does not protect perpetrators. An individual who is the suspect or defendant in criminal proceedings receives no immigration protection.
- Good faith requirement: The Firewall does not protect fabricated or vexatious complaints. Where a complaint is determined to have been made in bad faith for the purpose of obtaining immigration protection, the Firewall is retrospectively disapplied and the complainant is referred to Immigration Enforcement.
- Serious crimes only: The Firewall applies to the specified serious offences listed above. It does not extend to minor offences, civil disputes, or immigration-related offences.
- c) Temporary leave to remain. Victims and witnesses protected by the Firewall will be granted temporary leave to remain for the duration of the investigation and prosecution, plus 90 days. This is not a pathway to settlement: it is a practical measure ensuring that victims are available to give evidence and that the criminal justice system can function. At the expiry of temporary leave, the individual’s immigration case is referred to the standard process.

OPERATIONAL

Police training. The College of Policing will develop and deliver training on the Victim Firewall to all forces within 6 months of Royal Assent. Frontline officers must understand: the scope and limitations of the Firewall; how to record and flag protected individuals; the prohibition on data sharing; and the consequences of breach.

CPS protocols. The CPS will issue updated guidance to prosecutors reflecting the Firewall provisions. Victim Liaison Officers will be trained to explain the Firewall to victims and witnesses, ensuring they understand that reporting a crime will not result in immediate immigration action.

Immigration Enforcement standing orders. IE will issue standing orders prohibiting enforcement action against individuals flagged as Firewall-protected in the Unified Immigration Database. The flag is applied automatically when a police force records a victim/witness under a qualifying offence. Removed automatically at prosecution conclusion plus 90 days.

##### PP1.5.6: Equality Act Reform (Enforcement Context)

The Problem

The Equality Act 2010 creates a paradox at the heart of immigration enforcement. Employers and landlords are legally required to verify immigration status (under the Immigration Act 2014 and Immigration Act 2016), but the Equality Act simultaneously exposes them to discrimination claims if their verification process has a disproportionate impact on individuals of particular racial or national origin. The result is that conscientious compliance with immigration law creates Equality Act liability, while negligent non-compliance provides an implicit defence (“I treated everyone the same by not checking anyone thoroughly”).

The Windrush scandal illustrated the problem in acute form. Individuals with a lawful right to remain were denied services because the manual document-check system produced false negatives, and those false negatives fell disproportionately on people of Caribbean origin. The political response was to weaken enforcement, rolling back elements of the hostile environment. The correct response was to replace the subjective, error-prone, discrimination-generating manual check system with an objective, authoritative, non-discriminatory electronic system. That is what UK E-Verify (PP1.5.2) achieves.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Citizenship Act 2029 (PP1.1) and the Immigration Reform Act (PP1.2) will jointly establish:

- a) Statutory safe harbour. Any person or organisation that conducts a UK E-Verify check and acts in accordance with the result is immune from any claim of direct or indirect discrimination under the Equality Act 2010 in respect of that action. This is a complete statutory defence. The binary nature of E-Verify (authorised/not authorised) eliminates discretion and therefore eliminates the mechanism by which discrimination occurs.
- b) Amendment to indirect discrimination doctrine. The Equality Act 2010 will be amended to provide that the application of immigration verification requirements mandated by statute does not constitute indirect discrimination on grounds of race, nationality, or ethnic origin, notwithstanding any disparate impact. This addresses the absurdity of a legal framework in which compliance with one statutory obligation (immigration checking) constitutes breach of another (equality law).
- c) Equality and Human Rights Commission mandate revision. The EHRC’s mandate will be amended to reflect the new framework. The Commission will not investigate, report on, or take enforcement action in respect of immigration verification conducted through UK E-Verify. The Commission’s resources will be redirected toward genuine discrimination (direct discrimination, harassment, victimisation) rather than the downstream statistical effects of lawful immigration enforcement.

The broader Equality Act reforms (abolition of the Public Sector Equality Duty, repudiation of the Macpherson framework, replacement with the Citizen Duty) are set out in PP1.1.5 and are not duplicated here.

OPERATIONAL

Employer and landlord guidance. The Home Office, in conjunction with HMRC and the Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities, will issue updated guidance to employers and landlords within 3 months of Royal Assent. The guidance will make clear: E-Verify compliance provides a complete statutory defence; manual document checks are no longer a lawful compliance mechanism; and no Equality Act claim can succeed where the employer or landlord has followed the E-Verify determination.

EHRC transition. The EHRC will issue revised Codes of Practice reflecting the amended mandate within 6 months. Existing guidance on right-to-work and right-to-rent checks will be withdrawn and replaced with E-Verify-specific guidance.

Summary of Legislative Requirements

The PP1.5 framework is built primarily on the Immigration Reform Act (PP1.2), with supporting provisions in the Citizenship Act 2029 (PP1.1). No additional standalone primary legislation is required; enforcement and internal control provisions are enacted as schedules and sections within the two parent Acts.

Immigration Reform Act (enforcement provisions)

On the face of the Act:

Mandatory biometric capture at all UK entry and exit points. Carrier duties: document verification, real-time departure data transmission, refusal of flagged individuals, penalties for non-compliance (£10,000 per undocumented passenger). Unified Immigration Database established as single source of truth. Automatic overstayer identification and referral system. UK E-Verify: mandatory electronic verification for employment, housing, banking, and education. Abolition of manual document checks as compliance mechanism. Strict liability for failure to verify; complete statutory defence for compliance. Fit and Proper Persons Register integration with E-Verify.

Escalating penalty framework for illegal employment (£100,000 first offence, licence revocation second offence, criminal prosecution for knowing/systematic). High-risk sector enhanced licensing with annual compliance audits and cash-transaction limits. Supply chain liability (£50,000 per worker for non-compliant subcontractors).

Local authority inspection and referral powers. Embedded IE officers in high-immigration areas. Multi-agency enforcement framework. National Multi-Agency Immigration Enforcement Board.

Statutory Victim Firewall: prohibition on police/CPS data sharing with IE for specified serious crimes. Temporary leave to remain for protected victims and witnesses. Scope limitations: active investigation/prosecution only; victims and witnesses only; good faith requirement.

Statutory safe harbour for E-Verify compliance. Indirect discrimination doctrine amendment. EHRC mandate revision.

Citizenship Act 2029 (enforcement-relevant provisions)

On the face of the Act:

Citizenship Register as authoritative database. Fit and Proper Persons Register for non-citizens. Equality Act reforms (PP1.1.5) providing the broader framework within which PP1.5.6 operates.

Delivered operationally:

e-Passport gate upgrade: Tier 1 airports within 6 months, full coverage within 12 months. Unified Immigration Database: initial operating capability within 6 months, full integration within 18 months. UK E-Verify: beta launch 3 months, mandatory for employers 6 months, mandatory for landlords/banks/universities 12 months. Business Compliance Teams deployed within 6 months. High-risk sector model licence conditions within 3 months. Local authority enforcement training: priority areas 3 months, all areas 6 months. Embedded IE officers to 30 highest-priority areas within 3 months. Multi-Agency Immigration Enforcement Board established within 3 months. College of Policing Victim Firewall training within 6 months. CPS Firewall protocols within 3 months. IE standing orders on Firewall within 14 days. Employer/landlord E-Verify guidance within 3 months. EHRC revised Codes of Practice within 6 months.

Timeline

#### PP1.6: The Economic Transition

Governing Principle

The central objection to Pop-Pol, repeated with varying degrees of sophistication by economists, business lobbies, and editorial boards, is that the British economy cannot function without mass immigration. The argument runs that immigrants fill jobs the British will not do, that sectors from agriculture to social care would collapse without foreign labour, that an ageing population requires an ever-growing base of young workers to fund pensions and healthcare, and that any reduction in immigration would produce catastrophic labour shortages, wage-price spirals, and economic contraction.

Every element of this argument is wrong, and its wrongness is not a matter of opinion but of readily observable fact.

The “jobs the British won’t do” claim is a euphemism for “jobs at the wages employers currently offer.” There is no role in the British economy so inherently undesirable that no domestic worker would perform it at any wage. There are only wages too low to attract domestic workers when those workers have access to a welfare system that provides a comparable standard of living without the requirement to work. The solution to this is not to import workers from countries where £8.50 an hour represents prosperity, thereby suppressing wages for the domestic working class while generating substantial fiscal costs through in-work benefits, housing support, healthcare, education, and pension accrual. The solution is twofold: raise wages to market-clearing levels (which immigration policy currently prevents), and reform the welfare system so that work always pays more than non-work (which is the remit of Progress’ broader economic platform). Britain had full employment and functioning agriculture, construction, hospitality, and care sectors before mass immigration. It will have them again.

The “ageing population” argument is the most intellectually dishonest of all. Immigrants age. An immigrant who arrives at 25 to work in social care will themselves require social care at 75. The policy of importing young workers to fund the care of the elderly is a demographic Ponzi scheme: it works only if immigration increases exponentially, each generation of imported workers requiring a still-larger generation behind them. The OBR’s own fiscal projections demonstrate that non-EU immigration is net-negative over a lifetime fiscal horizon for all but the highest-skilled cohorts. Importing 700,000 people per year to address an ageing population is not a solution; it is a deferral of the problem at the cost of transforming the nation beyond recognition. Pop-Pol addresses ageing honestly: through pro-natal investment (PP1.4), domestic skills training, care technology, and pension reform, not through the endless importation of young foreigners who will themselves grow old.

Some disruption during the transition is inevitable and necessary. Wages in affected sectors will rise, and this is a feature of the policy, not a defect: it represents a transfer from capital to labour and from taxpayers (who currently subsidise low wages via tax credits and housing benefit) to workers. Some businesses that are viable only because of access to artificially cheap foreign labour will either automate, restructure, raise prices, or close. This is the market functioning correctly. A business model predicated on the suppression of domestic wages through unlimited labour supply is not an enterprise worth preserving.

The transition is managed through four compensating mechanisms operating in parallel: skills investment to expand the domestic labour supply; automation and AI adoption to reduce the labour requirement; sector-by-sector transition planning calibrated to the pace of workforce adjustment; and, where genuinely necessary, tightly controlled residual immigration for roles that cannot be filled domestically within the transition period. These mechanisms, combined with the broader economic reforms in Progress’ platform (E1 energy cost reduction, E2 Prosperity Zones, E5 Skill Capital, E6 Tax Reset), create the conditions for a high-wage, high-productivity economy that does not depend on mass immigration to function.

The philosophical underpinning is straightforward. A national economy exists to serve the national interest: not the interests of employers seeking the cheapest possible labour, not the interests of foreign nationals seeking higher wages than their home countries provide, and not the interests of a Treasury fixated on headline GDP growth that accrues disproportionately to capital while real wages for domestic workers stagnate. GDP per capita, not aggregate GDP, is the measure that matters. Real wages, not employment statistics padded by low-productivity imported labour, are the metric of prosperity. Pop-Pol’s economic transition is designed to produce an economy in which British workers earn more, produce more, and live better, even if the aggregate economy contracts in the short term as it adjusts to a smaller but more productive workforce.

This policy interacts with:

- PP1.1 (The Citizenship Act): The five-tier framework determines who has the right to work; the economic transition ensures domestic citizens fill the roles vacated by non-citizen departures
- PP1.2 (The Immigration Reset): Visa Insurance, caps, and fee structures that end the cheap labour subsidy
- PP1.3 (Asylum, Removal, and Sovereignty): Removal mechanisms that prevent stock accumulation of unlawful workers in the informal economy
- PP1.4 (The British Family): Pro-natal policy that rebuilds the domestic working-age population over the medium to long term
- PP1.5 (Enforcement and Internal Control): E-Verify and biometric borders that make it impossible to work without lawful status
- E1 (Cheapest Energy on Earth): Energy cost reduction enabling automation and reducing business input costs
- E2 (Prosperity Zones): SEZs with tightly controlled Prosperity Zone Visas for world-class talent
- E5 (Skill Capital and Training): Growth and Skills Levy, apprenticeship reform, and rapid-training infrastructure
- E6 (Tax Reset): Full capital expensing for automation investment; broader tax reform creating a competitive business environment

##### PP1.6.1: Skills Training and Domestic Labour Supply

The Problem

Britain has approximately 9 million economically inactive working-age adults. Of these, roughly 5 million are outside the student and early-retiree categories: they are of working age, not in education, and not yet at retirement, but not working and not seeking work. The reasons include long-term sickness (2.8 million, a figure that has risen by 700,000 since 2019), caring responsibilities, discouragement, and the simple economic calculus that the welfare system provides an income not dramatically inferior to what low-skilled work would offer after tax, childcare, and transport costs.

Simultaneously, Britain imports over 700,000 workers per year, many into roles that require relatively modest training: care work, warehousing, food processing, driving, basic construction trades, hospitality. The juxtaposition is extraordinary. A nation with 5 million available working-age adults is importing hundreds of thousands of workers annually to fill roles that, in many cases, require 12–24 weeks of training.

The skills system itself is dysfunctional. The Apprenticeship Levy, introduced in 2017, has presided over a 40% decline in apprenticeship starts. Large employers divert levy funds into management training for existing staff rather than training new entrants. Small employers find the system bureaucratically impenetrable. The construction sector needs 60,000+ new skilled workers per year to meet demand; it is producing a fraction of that. Healthcare training places are rationed: medical school places have been capped for decades while the NHS imports 30,000+ international recruits per year. The entire structure is designed as though domestic labour supply is a fixed quantity and immigration is the balancing variable. Pop-Pol inverts this: immigration is the fixed quantity (capped at approximately 110,000 per year under PP1.2), and domestic labour supply is the variable to be maximised.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Growth and Skills Act (cross-referenced with E5 Skill Capital) will establish:

- a) Growth and Skills Levy. The Apprenticeship Levy will be replaced with a Growth and Skills Levy with expanded scope:
- Levy funds may be spent on: apprenticeships, modular vocational training (12–52 weeks), rapid-training bootcamps, industry certification programmes, and degree-level technical education
- Mandatory minimum spend: 75% of levy funds must be spent on new entrant training (workers in role for less than 12 months), preventing diversion into management training for existing staff
- Small employer incentive: businesses below the levy threshold receive a 110% tax credit on qualifying training expenditure
- Sector priorities: the Secretary of State will designate “national priority sectors” (initially construction, healthcare, social care, logistics, agriculture, energy) that receive enhanced levy funding rates and accelerated approval for training programmes
- b) Medical and healthcare training expansion. A statutory duty on the Secretary of State for Health to double medical school places within 5 years. Nursing, midwifery, and allied health training places expanded by 50% within 3 years. Training bursaries restored for nursing and allied health students (abolished in 2017, directly contributing to the recruitment crisis that is used to justify international recruitment).
- c) Rapid-training bootcamps. A statutory framework for accredited intensive training programmes (12–24 weeks) in designated shortage occupations. Bootcamps will be employer-co-designed, with guaranteed job interviews upon completion. Funding via the Growth and Skills Levy for employed trainees; via DWP for those transitioning from economic inactivity. Initial priority sectors: construction trades (bricklaying, plastering, electrical, plumbing), HGV driving, care work (with enhanced qualification pathway), warehouse operations, agricultural skills.
- d) Economic inactivity activation. Reform of the welfare-to-work system to make the transition from inactivity to employment financially unambiguous:
- Work always pays: Taper rates reformed so that every additional pound earned increases net income. No effective marginal tax rates above 60% for any household.
- Health-to-work pathway: For the 2.8 million long-term sick, a new Health and Work Service providing integrated occupational health, rehabilitation, and phased return-to-work support. Fit note reform: GPs will no longer issue open-ended fit notes; all fit notes will specify a return-to-work date or a mandatory reassessment date within 12 weeks.
- Conditionality reform: UC work search requirements genuinely enforced, with meaningful sanctions for non-compliance (currently undermined by the 75% sanction reduction rate on mandatory reconsideration). Sanctions will be proportionate but real.
- e) Construction target. A national target of 60,000 new skilled construction workers per year, supported by: dedicated construction bootcamps at 50 locations nationwide; a Construction Skills Bursary (£5,000 per trainee) for career-changers entering construction trades; fast-track CSCS certification for bootcamp graduates; and employer co-investment via the Growth and Skills Levy.

OPERATIONAL

Levy transition. HMRC will administer the levy transition within the first full tax year. Updated guidance to employers within 3 months of Royal Assent. Digital Apprenticeship Service reformed to accommodate expanded training categories.

Medical school expansion. The Office for Students and Health Education England (or successor body) will commission additional medical school places. Year 1: planning and infrastructure (conversion of existing university estate, partnership agreements). Year 2: first expanded cohort admitted. Year 5: doubled capacity fully operational. Interim measure: accelerated recognition of overseas-qualified British doctors returning under PP1.4.5.

Bootcamp accreditation. Ofqual and the Institute for Apprenticeships and Technical Education will establish a fast-track accreditation process for bootcamp programmes. Target: first accredited programmes operational within 6 months. Employer co-design panels convened within 3 months.

Health and Work Service. DWP and DHSC will jointly establish the Health and Work Service, initially co-located with Jobcentre Plus offices in areas of highest economic inactivity. Target: 50 locations operational within 6 months, national coverage within 18 months.

##### PP1.6.2: Automation and AI Adoption

The Problem

The United Kingdom has one of the lowest rates of industrial automation in the developed world. South Korea deploys 1,012 robots per 10,000 manufacturing employees. Japan deploys 399. Germany deploys 397. The UK deploys approximately 100. In warehousing and logistics, the gap is equally stark: Amazon’s US fulfilment centres deploy over 750,000 robots; British warehousing remains overwhelmingly manual. In agriculture, Dutch and Danish farms achieve yields per worker several multiples of British equivalents through precision agriculture, automated milking, and robotic harvesting.

The reason for this underinvestment is not technological incapacity. It is that cheap foreign labour has been a more convenient alternative. Why invest £500,000 in a robotic picking system when you can hire 20 seasonal workers from Romania at minimum wage? Why automate a car wash when you can staff it with undocumented migrants at £5 an hour? The availability of cheap, compliant, disposable foreign labour has functioned as a subsidy to low-productivity business models, suppressing both wages and capital investment. Pop-Pol removes this subsidy. The Visa Insurance system (PP1.2) forces employers to price the true fiscal cost of foreign labour. The immigration cap restricts supply. The economic transition requires that British industry responds as every other advanced economy has responded: by investing in capital, technology, and productivity rather than in the import of human beings.

The timing is propitious. We are at an inflection point in general-purpose AI capability. Large language models are already displacing administrative, analytical, and creative labour. Embodied AI, autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), and automated guided vehicles (AGVs) are moving rapidly from warehouse pilots to commercial deployment. Agricultural robotics, care robotics, and autonomous vehicles are within years of viability, not decades. The question is not whether automation will transform the British labour market but whether Britain will lead the transformation or be dragged into it after the competitive advantage has accrued elsewhere. This creates the conditions for Britain to lead: by removing the cheap-labour crutch that delays investment, by slashing energy costs (E1) that make automation uneconomic, and by providing the fiscal and regulatory incentives that accelerate adoption.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Finance Act and Growth and Skills Act will jointly establish:

- a) Full capital expensing for automation. Permanent 100% first-year capital allowances for investment in: industrial robots, AMRs/AGVs, automated production lines, AI/ML systems, agricultural automation (precision agriculture, robotic harvesting, automated milking), care technology (remote monitoring, automated medication management, mobility assistance), autonomous vehicles, and software systems that directly replace manual labour. This is not a temporary incentive; it is a permanent feature of the tax code, signalling that Britain is structurally committed to capital-intensive, high-productivity business models.
- b) Energy cost reduction. Cross-referenced with E1 (Cheapest Energy on Earth). Energy costs are the single largest variable input cost for automated systems. Britain’s industrial electricity prices are among the highest in the developed world (approximately 2–3x the US, 1.5–2x France). E1’s target of the developed world’s cheapest energy by 2034 (via nuclear investment, grid reform, and elimination of green levies) is an essential precondition for automation viability. The economic transition is architecturally dependent on E1 delivery.
- c) Regulatory reform for autonomous systems. The Growth and Skills Act will include provisions:
- Statutory framework for autonomous vehicle deployment on public roads (building on the Automated Vehicles Act 2024, with accelerated certification timelines)
- Regulatory sandbox for agricultural autonomous systems (robotic harvesters, autonomous tractors, drone crop management) with presumptive approval for systems certified in comparable jurisdictions (EU, USA, Japan, South Korea, Australia)
- Fast-track Health and Safety Executive approval pathway for industrial robotics in sectors designated as national priority
- AI deployment framework: statutory clarification that AI systems may perform functions currently restricted by regulation to human workers, subject to outcome-based standards rather than process-based requirements

OPERATIONAL

Automation Investment Service. A dedicated advisory service within the Department for Business and Trade, providing: sector-specific automation roadmaps for SMEs; supplier matching (connecting British businesses with robotics and AI providers); financing guidance (capital expensing, R&D tax credits, British Business Bank facilities); and implementation support. Target: operational within 6 months, with initial focus on Tier 1 sectors (hospitality, warehousing, agriculture).

Demonstration centres. The Government will fund 10 regional Automation Demonstration Centres, co-located with Prosperity Zones (E2) or existing Catapult centres, showcasing commercially available automation for priority sectors. Each centre will include working demonstrations of: warehouse robotics, agricultural automation, care technology, food processing automation, and construction technology. First 5 centres operational within 12 months.

Sector-specific automation targets. The Department for Business and Trade will publish sector automation targets aligned with the labour market transition tiers (PP1.6.3), establishing clear expectations for the pace of capital substitution. Targets are advisory, not mandatory; the combination of labour scarcity (immigration cap), cost pressure (Visa Insurance), and fiscal incentive (capital expensing) will drive adoption without compulsion.

##### PP1.6.3: Labour Market Transition by Industry

The Problem

The economic transition cannot be managed as a single national event. Different sectors have different levels of foreign-born workforce dependency, different automation potential, different training lead times, and different sensitivity to wage increases. A one-size-fits-all approach would produce simultaneous disruption across the entire economy. Pop-Pol therefore requires sector-by-sector transition planning, sequenced across three tiers according to the pace at which domestic substitution is feasible.

The current foreign-born workforce shares by sector illustrate the scale of the challenge:

These figures represent the workforce that must be progressively replaced by domestic workers, automation, or a combination of both. The transition is not optional: PP1.2’s immigration cap and PP1.3’s removal mechanisms will reduce the foreign-born workforce regardless. PP1.6.3 ensures the economy absorbs the transition rather than being overwhelmed by it.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

No additional primary legislation required beyond the Growth and Skills Act (PP1.6.1) and Finance Act (PP1.6.2). The sector transition is delivered operationally within the statutory framework established by those Acts and by PP1.2 (visa caps and non-renewal schedules).

OPERATIONAL

Tier 1: Immediate Transition (Years 1–3)

Hospitality/Catering, Warehousing/Logistics, Gig Economy

These sectors have the highest automation potential, the shortest training lead times, and the lowest barriers to domestic workforce substitution. Compensating policies:

- Energy cost reduction (E1) directly reduces operating costs, offsetting wage increases
- Full capital expensing for self-service kiosks, automated kitchens, warehouse robotics, autonomous delivery
- Rapid-training bootcamps (12-week hospitality skills, warehouse operations certification, driving qualifications)
- Welfare reform ensuring work always pays more than benefits (PP1.6.1d)
- Gig economy: UK E-Verify (PP1.5.2) eliminates undocumented gig workers; platform companies required to verify all contractors. Higher domestic wages in the gig economy will follow naturally from reduced supply.

Expected outcome: 80%+ domestic workforce substitution within 3 years. Remaining gaps filled by short-term seasonal visas under PP1.2 where demonstrable need exists.

Tier 2: Medium-Term Transition (Years 3–7)

Construction, Social Care, Agriculture

These sectors require longer training pipelines, more complex automation, and (in agriculture’s case) seasonal patterns that complicate domestic substitution. Compensating policies:

- Construction: 60,000 new skilled workers per year target (PP1.6.1e); planning liberalisation (cross-ref broader Progress platform) increasing demand and therefore wages; Construction Skills Bursary; modular and offsite construction (reducing on-site labour requirement by 30–50%)
- Social Care: domestic training expansion (care bootcamps, NVQ fast-track); significantly higher wages funded by combination of local authority reform (CS3), NHS management layer reduction, and explicit social care levy; care technology deployment (PP1.6.4); Carefare system (PP1.4.2) reducing demand by supporting family-based care for the elderly
- Agriculture: phased transition from manual seasonal labour to automated harvesting, precision agriculture, and vertical farming; seasonal visa allocation (PP1.2) maintained during transition but progressively reduced as automation capacity scales; horticultural automation R&D funded via the Growth and Skills Levy

Expected outcome: 60–80% domestic substitution within 7 years. Agriculture retains the highest residual dependency on controlled seasonal immigration.

Tier 3: Long-Term Transition (Years 5–10)

NHS/Healthcare, IT/Tech

These sectors require the longest training pipelines and, in IT/Tech’s case, compete in global labour markets where some degree of international mobility is inherent. Compensating policies:

- NHS/Healthcare: doubled medical school places (PP1.6.1b) producing first additional graduates from Year 7; nursing bursary restoration producing increased domestic supply from Year 4; return programme for British-trained healthcare professionals working abroad (PP1.4.5); higher wages funded by management layer elimination and procurement reform; GP training expansion
- IT/Tech: Prosperity Zone Visas (E2) for genuinely world-class talent; Growth and Skills Levy funding for advanced technical training; Unicorn Farm (E2) creating demand for domestic tech talent; domestic computer science and engineering training expansion. London’s 30% foreign-born tech workforce will partially self-correct as Prosperity Zones redistribute tech activity to other regions.

Expected outcome: NHS domestic staffing at 90%+ within 10 years. IT/Tech retains a controlled international component via Prosperity Zone Visas, but the majority of the workforce is domestically trained and supplied.

Sector transition monitoring. The Department for Business and Trade will publish quarterly Labour Market Transition Reports tracking: domestic workforce substitution rates by sector; wage movements; automation adoption; training pipeline volumes; and remaining foreign-born workforce shares. The Secretary of State will have power to adjust visa allocations (within the PP1.2 cap) between sectors based on transition progress, accelerating allocation reductions in sectors ahead of schedule and maintaining allocations in sectors experiencing genuine difficulty.

##### PP1.6.4: Supporting the Ageing Population

The Problem

Britain’s population is ageing. The old-age dependency ratio (the ratio of over-65s to working-age adults) is projected to rise from approximately 30% to 40–50% by 2050 under current trends. The dominant policy response has been to frame this as an argument for mass immigration: import young workers to care for the old, to fund their pensions, and to sustain the tax base. This is the demographic Ponzi scheme described in the Governing Principle. It fails on its own terms because the imported workers themselves age, and it fails on ours because it requires the permanent transformation of the nation’s population.

Pop-Pol’s approach is honest about the challenge and serious about the alternatives. The ageing population requires: more domestic healthcare and care workers (PP1.6.1); care technology that reduces the labour intensity of elderly care; family structures that distribute caring responsibilities more broadly than the current institutional model (PP1.4.2); and pension and retirement reform that extends productive working lives voluntarily and removes the perverse incentives that encourage premature exit from the labour market.

None of this is easy. All of it is preferable to the alternative, which is the indefinite importation of foreign populations at a scale that extinguishes the nation as a recognisable entity within a generation.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The British Family Act (PP1.4) and Growth and Skills Act (PP1.6.1) contain the primary legislative provisions. Additional provisions in the Pensions Act (new):

- a) Health and care workforce transition. Domestic training, retention, and return programmes as set out in PP1.6.1 and PP1.6.3 (Tier 3). The critical addition here is a statutory pay framework for social care workers, establishing a minimum hourly rate indexed to the median wage (initially set at 80% of median hourly earnings, approximately £13.50/hour at current levels). Social care has been chronically underpaid precisely because immigration has suppressed wages; the resulting labour scarcity will force wages up regardless, but the statutory framework ensures the increase is sustained and predictable, enabling long-term career planning and reducing turnover.
- b) Care technology adoption. Provisions within the Growth and Skills Act enabling:
- Full capital expensing for care technology (remote monitoring systems, automated medication management, smart home adaptations, mobility assistance devices, AI-assisted diagnostics and triage)
- NHS and local authority procurement reform: statutory requirement to assess automation and technology solutions before approving workforce expansion requests
- Telehealth and remote monitoring as default for chronic condition management, reducing the in-person care workforce requirement
- Care technology certification: fast-track MHRA/CQC approval for care devices and AI systems certified in comparable jurisdictions
- c) Family-based care support. The Carefare system (PP1.4.2) provides the foundation. Additional provisions:
- Carer’s allowance reform: the current Carer’s Allowance (£81.90/week, with a derisory earnings limit of £151/week) will be substantially increased and the earnings limit abolished. Carers of elderly family members will receive a minimum of £200/week with no cap on concurrent earnings, enabling family members to combine part-time work with caring responsibilities.
- Housing policy: planning guidance prioritising multi-generational housing designs (granny flats, annexes, extended family homes). Permitted development rights for single-storey annexes on residential properties.
- Tax relief: costs of adapting a property for an elderly family member (stairlifts, wet rooms, ground-floor conversions) treated as deductible expenses against income tax.
- d) Pension and retirement reform. Provisions in a new Pensions Act:
- Flexible retirement: statutory right to phase retirement between ages 60 and 70, reducing hours progressively while drawing partial pension. Employers of 50+ staff must offer flexible retirement options.
- Age discrimination reform: strengthen protections for workers aged 60+ who wish to continue working. Prohibit mandatory retirement ages except in roles with genuine safety requirements (pilots, surgeons, etc.).
- Pension incentives for extended working: additional State Pension accrual of 1% per year for each year worked beyond State Pension age, up to age 75.
- Remove perverse incentives: reform of pension tax relief and lifetime allowance rules that discourage continued working (partially addressed by lifetime allowance abolition in 2024, but further simplification needed).

OPERATIONAL

Social care pay framework. DHSC will implement the statutory pay framework via regulations within 6 months. Local authority funding settlements adjusted accordingly. The wage increase is funded by: management layer reduction across the care system; reduced agency staff costs (higher permanent wages reduce reliance on expensive temporary staff); and, over time, reduced immigration-related fiscal costs as the non-citizen population declines.

Care technology procurement. NHS England and local authorities will be required to publish annual care technology adoption plans. A dedicated Care Technology Fund (£500 million over 5 years) will be established within DHSC to co-fund adoption by care homes, domiciliary care providers, and GP practices. First allocations within 6 months of Royal Assent.

Carer’s Allowance reform. DWP will amend Carer’s Allowance regulations via Statutory Instrument within 3 months. Earnings limit abolition effective immediately. Payment increase phased: £150/week from Month 3, £200/week from Month 12.

Multi-generational housing. DLUHC will issue updated planning guidance within 6 months, with permitted development rights for annexes enacted via SI. Local Development Plans to incorporate multi-generational housing requirements at next review.

##### PP1.6.5: Evidence-Based Entry for Residual Immigration

The Problem

Pop-Pol does not propose zero immigration. The immigration cap under PP1.2 permits approximately 110,000 non-citizen entries per year, comprising Prosperity Zone Visas for world-class talent (E2), limited skilled worker visas, seasonal agricultural workers, and a capped humanitarian visa. Even within this tightly controlled residual, the composition of immigration matters as much as the quantity. Not all source nationalities present equivalent integration outcomes, equivalent fiscal contributions, or equivalent public safety profiles. Ignoring this reality in the name of procedural equality is not fair; it is negligent.

The data is unambiguous. Albanian nationals in the UK have a conviction rate of approximately 4,028 per 100,000, compared to 136 per 100,000 for British nationals: a ratio of roughly 30:1. Approximately 60% of Albanian convictions relate to drug offences. Albanian nationals constitute 12% of all foreign national offenders in British prisons despite comprising less than 0.1% of the UK population. Danish government statistics (the most comprehensive in Europe) show that non-Western immigrants committed 29.6% of violent crimes while comprising 10.6% of the population. Swedish data tells a comparable story: immigrants from certain regions are dramatically overrepresented in serious crime statistics, particularly sexual offences.

These are not cultural generalisations. They are statistical facts derived from national crime databases. To refuse to act on them, to pretend that an applicant from Albania and an applicant from Japan present equivalent risk profiles, is to prioritise ideological comfort over the safety of the British public. Progress’ position is that immigration policy must be evidence-based, which means nationality-specific risk assessments must inform entry decisions, just as they inform visa policy in Australia, the Gulf states, Japan, and every other country that takes border security seriously.

Execution

PRIMARY LEGISLATION

The Immigration Reform Act (PP1.2) will establish:

- a) Nationality-based tiered entry. The Secretary of State will maintain a classified Nationality Risk Assessment, updated annually, based on:
- Conviction rates of existing UK residents from each nationality (per 100,000, benchmarked against the British-national baseline)
- Offending data from comparable jurisdictions (Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Netherlands, Germany, Australia)
- Integration indicators: employment rates, welfare dependency rates, English language proficiency, cultural integration metrics
- Security intelligence: terrorism risk assessments, organised crime involvement, intelligence from Five Eyes and European partners

Based on this assessment, source nationalities will be categorised into three tiers:

This is not racial profiling. It is actuarial risk assessment of the kind that every insurance company, every bank, and every intelligence agency in the world conducts as a matter of routine. An Albanian with a clean record and an offer from a Prosperity Zone employer may still be admitted under the exceptional cases provision; the moratorium is on routine, unsupervised entry from nationalities with demonstrated risk profiles, not a ban on individuals who can demonstrate their suitability.

- b) Accurate crime statistics as precondition. The Act will impose a statutory duty on the Home Office and Ministry of Justice to publish annual crime statistics disaggregated by nationality, visa status, and citizenship tier (PP1.1). This data does not currently exist in a consistent, publicly available format. Without it, evidence-based entry policy is impossible. The existing practice of suppressing or failing to collect nationality-disaggregated crime data is incompatible with responsible immigration management and will end.
- c) Cross-reference with Prosperity Zone Visas (E2). The Prosperity Zone Visa route (E2) operates under a distinct framework: applicants are individually assessed against the Prosperity Zone’s sector-specific skills requirements, and the employer co-investment (Visa Insurance) provides financial accountability. Prosperity Zone Visa applicants from Moratorium-tier nationalities may still be considered under the enhanced vetting process if they meet the exceptional individual standard. The tiered system is primarily targeted at the general skilled worker, family, and student routes.

OPERATIONAL

Nationality Risk Assessment. The Home Office, in conjunction with the National Crime Agency, MOD, and the intelligence services, will compile the first Nationality Risk Assessment within 6 months of Royal Assent. Classification decisions are made by the Secretary of State and are not subject to judicial review (protected by ouster clause under CS2). The Assessment is classified; the resulting tier allocations are published.

Crime statistics publication. The Home Office and MOJ will publish the first nationality-disaggregated crime statistics report within 12 months. Data collection commences immediately upon Royal Assent via amendment to police recording standards (issued as a direction to all Chief Constables under the Police Act 1996). Court recording systems amended to capture nationality and visa status at conviction.

International data sharing. Bilateral agreements with Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Netherlands, and Australia for sharing nationality-disaggregated crime and integration data. Memoranda of understanding targeted within 12 months.

##### Summary of Legislative Requirements

The PP1.6 framework is distributed across multiple Acts: the Growth and Skills Act (new), provisions within the Finance Act, provisions within the Immigration Reform Act (PP1.2), the British Family Act (PP1.4), and a new Pensions Act. The sector transition plan and supporting measures are delivered operationally.

Growth and Skills Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act:

Growth and Skills Levy replacing the Apprenticeship Levy. 75% new entrant training minimum spend. Small employer 110% tax credit. National priority sector designation power. Statutory duty to double medical school places within 5 years. Nursing and allied health training expansion (50% within 3 years). Bursary restoration. Rapid-training bootcamp statutory framework. Construction Skills Bursary. Health and Work Service establishment. Fit note reform. Regulatory framework for autonomous systems (agricultural, industrial, vehicular). Care technology certification fast-track.

Finance Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act:

Permanent full capital expensing for automation investment (robots, AMRs/AGVs, AI systems, agricultural automation, care technology, autonomous vehicles). No sunset clause.

Pensions Act (provisions)

On the face of the Act:

Flexible retirement statutory right (ages 60–70). Enhanced age discrimination protections. Additional State Pension accrual for working beyond SPA. Pension simplification.

Immigration Reform Act (enforcement-relevant provisions)

On the face of the Act:

Nationality-based tiered entry (Moratorium, Enhanced Vetting, Standard). Nationality Risk Assessment power for Secretary of State. Ouster clause protecting classification decisions. Statutory duty to publish nationality-disaggregated crime statistics.

Delivered operationally:

Levy transition guidance (3 months). Growth and Skills Levy operational (first full tax year). Medical school expansion planning (Year 1), first cohort (Year 2), full capacity (Year 5). Bootcamp accreditation and first programmes (6 months). Employer co-design panels (3 months). Health and Work Service: 50 locations (6 months), national coverage (18 months). Construction bootcamps at 50 locations (12 months). Automation Investment Service (6 months). Automation Demonstration Centres: first 5 (12 months), all 10 (18 months). Sector Labour Market Transition Reports (quarterly from Month 6). Social care pay framework (6 months). Care Technology Fund: first allocations (6 months). Carer’s Allowance increase: £150/week (Month 3), £200/week (Month 12). Multi-generational housing guidance (6 months). Nationality Risk Assessment compiled (6 months). Crime statistics data collection commenced (Day 1), first publication (12 months).

#### Beyond the Big Four

#### Education (EDU)

##### EDU1. Non-Peer-Review Academic Culture

It has come into more pronounced focus in recent history that peer review, historically a device used to try to guarantee the integrity and value of research by submitting it to trial-by-evaluation prior to publication, has had a strangulating effect on the health of science in general, and a profoundly credentialising effect in respect of a global ecosystem of research at high-academic level.

Double-blind peer review is extremely seldom practiced from one academic sector to the next. Researchers are commonly allowed to block evaluations by those peers of theirs who do not favour their work and invite it from those who support it, either honestly or for purely tribalistic reasons. The fiefdoms establishable by skilful political use of peer review are precisely what has permitted such phenomena as the rise to prominence of such evil figures as Eliezer Masliah. Elevated on the back of research later found to be entirely fraudulent, Masliah headed the neuroscience division of the US' National Institute of Aging, controlled billions in funding, and ultimately held back the field's development by decades.

Not only does this cabalry allow social competitiveness to rise above quality of thought and investigation as the main drivers of career success in research, it drives natural talent away from the field.

Britain can:

- Steal a march in the global R&D race that could have generational impact, and culminate in the creation of new technologies worth £ trillions in net economic value
- Create a globally unique culture of scientific and academic enquiry that will attract a disproportionate share of the finest minds in the world to our shores
- Become a figurehead and moral authority in the leadership of a revolution in academic and state-level epistemics

…by becoming a place where peer review functionally does not exist.

We can do this by adopting a Brabenic approach across higher academic institutions. Donald Braben, British author and Honorary Professor at University College London, founded BP Venture Research Unit in the 1990s. It backed forty radically un-reviewed projects with £20 million and, of these forty, fourteen resulted in “breakthroughs”. Quasicrystals, blue LEDs, chaotic fluid mixing, and squeezed states of light were among the breakthrough products.

We will eliminate:

- Incentives to back projects whose outcomes can be forecast ex-ante, a key impediment to both novelty and to our ability to harness the fullest available extent of a larger student body
- Committee scoring systems, which systematically reward research that looks similar to existing research and just-as-systematically strangles research that is too novel by evident comparison
- The need for continuous justification of funding against metrics – such as impact on social inequality, or on climate change – which, in many cases, require fundamental perversions of otherwise pure research intent to satisfy
- Cross-subsidy, whereby projects are funded from multiple sources, creating a “stop-start” tempo to research, preventing the development of critical mass in infrastructure and expertise while disincentivising interdisciplinary collaboration

Therefore, on top of applications of Brabenic principles, we must adequately replace the present system with the following provisions:

- The training of a specific managerial class subset that will lead by the kind of patient, deep, cross-domain thinking that has historically produced scientific leaders
- The ‘Leadership Crucible’ approach, whereby the persons above are rotated through industry, policy and lab management contexts to foment the kind of interdisciplinary skill a Brabenic approach thrives on, becoming Crucibilists
- Lowering the average age at which researchers can expect to begin their first research, as part of Progress' general philosophy of allowing people to build career momentum at an earlier stage in their lives
- Ring-fenced funding for decades of deep science work, with provident channels set up by institutional backers as well as the public sector

By according to the following processional disciplines:

- Scale-up funding approaches, where preliminary trivial sums for the equivalent of proofs-of-concept are used to determine the researcher's personal reliability and the viability of their idea, which small amounts are then scaled up into regularly disbursed larger amounts
- A PARC-type approach to giving each researcher the chance to discuss their work in one within-discipline group context and one interdisciplinary group context, without weighting or scoring
- Freedom from deliverables and reporting that begins with what is reasonably necessary and can become progressively greater the stronger intermittent outcomes are; the better the work you produce, the more hassle you are spared. A true high-trust research dynamic

…we will find that there is no researcher of calibre anywhere in the world that would not relish the prospect of working under a system like this. If we can establish it, we will find them flocking to our shores.

##### EDU2. Affordable Academic Materials

By Alex Simmons

Researchers are paying exorbitant fees to both publish in and read scientific journals, due to the monopolistic behaviour of key firms. Owing to a collective action problem, not enough researchers or institutions are willing to break away from the monopolists and establish fairly priced journal access. Progress will legislate to force all institutions to move to fairly priced access models, making the vast majority of their research free to read by the public, massively reducing costs of publication and assuring Britain's leading role in scientific research for another generation.

#### Is Progress a Left Wing or Right Wing Party?

This is the wrong question.

The political class and the media are addicted to the spectrum. Every policy is instantly sorted into “left” or “right”, and every party is expected to occupy a coherent position along the line. This makes politics legible to commentators, but it makes politics useless to voters.

Here is the reality they refuse to confront: the median British voter holds some views to the right of the Conservative Party, and some views to the left of the Labour Party, simultaneously. They want lower immigration and cheaper energy and tougher sentencing. They also want a properly funded NHS, genuine worker protections, fair pay, and affordable childcare. No existing party serves this voter, because no existing party is designed to. Each party serves a coalition defined by ideology, not by need.

Progress is designed differently. We do not begin with a position on the spectrum and derive policies from it. We begin with problems and design solutions using what we call incentive engineering: the disciplined alignment of economic, legal, and social incentives so that the right outcomes emerge structurally, rather than being imposed by ideology or hoped into existence by goodwill.

The result is a policy platform that defies categorisation. Not because it is incoherent, but because reality is not ideological.

###### Economy

Our Prosperity Zones policy (E2) establishes special economic zones with 10% corporation tax, autonomous planning authorities, and minimal regulation. It is more radically free-market than anything the Conservatives or Reform have proposed. But our Hallmark policy (E5) guarantees every working person one nationally certified, portable skill qualification per year for fifteen years, backed by fifty new training colleges. That is a commitment to worker empowerment more ambitious than anything Labour have offered in their history. Both policies reflect the same principle: that people flourish when structural incentives reward productivity, investment, and ambition, whether those people are entrepreneurs or employees.

Our Tax Reset (E6) abolishes student loan interest, restores the personal allowance, and abolishes business rates for small premises, touching every household in the country. Our return of paid overtime (E11) legislates statutory overtime pay at 125%, mandates profit-sharing for large companies, and targets 10,000 employee-owned businesses. Our Dual-Mandate Unions (E12) restore sectoral bargaining and put worker directors on boards, while requiring unions to accept productivity obligations in return. This is not left or right. It is a structural bargain that serves both labour and enterprise, because the incentives are designed to make cooperation more profitable than conflict.

Our Great Planning Liberation (E4) inverts the planning system’s default to “yes” and strips away decades of regulatory accretion. It is more deregulatory than any party has dared propose. Meanwhile, our Procurement Revolution (E10) strategically directs state purchasing power to build British SMEs and industrial capacity. Free markets where freedom creates value; strategic direction where coordination is required. No ideology. Just engineering.

###### Crime

Our crime programme (C2) will double the police force, build 100,000 new prison places, impose compound sentencing on repeat offenders, and end early release. We will introduce mandatory minimum sentences for knife crime (C10) and declare war on the drug trade with maximum-severity enforcement against traffickers (C11). This is further to the right on street crime than the Conservatives have dared to go in forty years.

But we also create the Malebranche (C3), a 500-person anti-corruption unit with a £150 million budget to prosecute white-collar crime, procurement fraud, and institutional corruption, with whistleblower rewards of up to 10% of recovered funds. We impose unlimited criminal liability on public officials who concealed child sexual exploitation (C4), with no time limit, and create an uncapped compensation fund for every identified victim. Our victims’ rights reforms (C8) replace the broken Criminal Injuries Compensation Scheme with a harm-based system with no cap and no deadline. We put more priority on the protection of women and children than Labour have in the same period, and we back it with enforcement mechanisms, not with rhetoric.

Our championing of open justice (C1), including free court transcripts, public body-camera footage, and mandatory publication of disaggregated crime statistics, serves everyone who is not themselves pro-crime. Transparency is neither left nor right. It is the foundation of a system that works.

###### Civil Service Reform and the NHS

We will abolish the Cabinet Office (CS3), merge twenty-four departments down to ten (CS9), give ministers direct hire-and-fire power over senior officials (CS1), and build a British Grand École to train a new generation of public servants (CS10). This is a more radical programme of state reform than Thatcher ever attempted. But we pair it with the most vigorous defence of the NHS as a free public service that any party has offered: statutory safe staffing ratios enforceable by law (NHS2), 120,000 hospital beds (NHS1), a National Food Service and Community Kitchens programme (NHS5), and integrated social care with a guaranteed community care entitlement (NHS7). We are not cutting the state for its own sake. We are rebuilding it so that it actually works for the people it is supposed to serve.

The cheapest energy on Earth (E1), with 24 GW of new nuclear capacity, resumed North Sea licensing, and guaranteed industrial energy prices, is more pro-growth than any Conservative energy policy in decades. Driving down the cost of living (E8), with fuel duty cuts, abolished motor insurance tax, rail fare caps, and forty hours of funded childcare, delivers more material relief to working families than Labour have ever legislated. Same government. Same budget. Different incentives.

###### Immigration and the British Family

Our immigration programme (PP1.1 to PP1.6) is both more robust, and more European (taking after that bastion and light of international democracy, Switzerland), than anything ever seen in mainstream British politics: five-tier citizenship, hard visa caps at 110,000 entries per year, offshore asylum processing, biometric entry-exit tracking, and a managed reduction in the UK population to 63 to 65 million. But our British Family policy (PP1.4) is the most generous pro-natal programme ever proposed by a British party: progressive child allowances of up to £500 per month, lifetime personal income tax exemption for mothers of four or more children, a £30,000 Family Formation Loan with debt forgiveness per child, and abolition of Inheritance Tax. We reduce immigration and invest in British families, because the two are structurally linked, and because incentive engineering demands that you do not simply close one door without opening another.

###### The Thesis

Every example above follows the same logic. We do not pick a side and then rationalise the consequences. We identify what voters actually need, design incentives that produce those outcomes, and let the results fall where they may on a spectrum we did not build and do not recognise.

The old politics asks: are you left or right?

The new politics asks: does it work?

In Britain, Progress, alone, goes beyond Left and Right.
